sacctmgr is used to view or modify Slurm account information.
The account information is maintained within a database with the interface
being provided by slurmdbd (Slurm Database daemon).
This database can serve as a central storehouse of user and
computer information for multiple computers at a single site.
Slurm account information is recorded based upon four parameters
that form what is referred to as an association .

cluster is the name of a Slurm managed cluster as specified by
the ClusterName parameter in the slurm.conf configuration file.

## SPECIFICATIONS FOR USERS[#SECTION_SPECIFICATIONS-FOR-USERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Users can be created, modified, and deleted with sacctmgr. These
options allow you to set the corresponding attributes or filter on them
when querying for Users.
It is important to recognize the difference between a User and an Association.
There is a User entity that exists for each unique username. However, there
can be multiple User Associations for the same User. The combination of a
Cluster, Account, User, and optionally a Partition constitute a User
Association. When adding an existing User to another Account, you are creating
an additional User Association rather than modifying an existing User.
Account =< account >[#OPT_Account_3](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) Account name to add this user to.

With the SlurmDBD, we are able to collect data from multiple
clusters in a single location.
This does impose some constraints on the user naming and IDs.
Accounting is maintained by user name (not user ID), but a
given user name should refer to the same person across all
of the computers.
Authentication relies upon user ID numbers, so those must
be uniform across all computers communicating with each
SlurmDBD, at least for users requiring authentication.
In particular, the configured SlurmUser must have the
same name and ID across all clusters.
If you plan to have administrators of user accounts, limits,
etc. they must also have consistent names and IDs across all
clusters.
If you plan to restrict access to accounting records (e.g.
only permit a user to view records of his jobs), then all

options allow you to set the corresponding attributes or filter on them

It is important to recognize the difference between a User and an Association.
There is a User entity that exists for each unique username. However, there
can be multiple User Associations for the same User. The combination of a
Cluster, Account, User, and optionally a Partition constitute a User
Association. When adding an existing User to another Account, you are creating
an additional User Association rather than modifying an existing User.

## SPECIFICATIONS FOR USERS[#SECTION_SPECIFICATIONS-FOR-USERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Users can be created, modified, and deleted with sacctmgr. These
options allow you to set the corresponding attributes or filter on them
when querying for Users.
It is important to recognize the difference between a User and an Association.
There is a User entity that exists for each unique username. However, there
can be multiple User Associations for the same User. The combination of a
Cluster, Account, User, and optionally a Partition constitute a User
Association. When adding an existing User to another Account, you are creating
an additional User Association rather than modifying an existing User.

- Job 5001 (cuda_training) — State=FAILED, ExitCode=134:0, Elapsed=00:02:15, NCPUs=16, ReqMem=64G
- stderr excerpt: "CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered"

What that means
- ExitCode 134 = process aborted (SIGABRT). The job aborted after a CUDA runtime error.
- "illegal memory access" is a GPU-side memory access violation (device kernel tried to read/write an invalid address). Common causes:
  - out-of-bounds indexing or use-after-free in a CUDA kernel or kernel launched by a library (e.g., custom CUDA/C++ code or a fused kernel).
  - corrupted GPU memory due to race conditions or mismatched tensor shapes (e.g., indexing errors in PyTorch/CUDA kernels).
  - mismatched CUDA/driver/library versions or ABI incompatibility causing incorrect behavior.
  - hardware/GPU fault or driver issue (less common).
  - in multi-GPU / distributed jobs, an earlier GPU error on one rank can trigger abort across ranks.

Recommended next debugging steps (ordered)
1. Inspect the full stderr and the job’s StdErr/StdOut files (they often contain fuller stack traces). I can fetch the job details/path if you want.
2. Reproduce locally or on a single GPU with a small input to narrow the code region.
3. Run with CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 (export CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1) to force synchronous kernel launches; this usually produces a meaningful stacktrace pointing to the failing host call.
4. Run cuda-memcheck / compute-sanitizer (for native CUDA) to detect invalid device memory accesses.
5. If using PyTorch:
   - ensure tensors/indices sizes are correct; insert torch.cuda.synchronize() around suspect ops;
   - try a debug build or smaller batch size;
   - check for known NCCL/PyTorch issues and version mismatches (driver vs CUDA vs PyTorch).
6. Check node-level diagnostics:
   - run nvidia-smi, check dmesg/syslog for GPU/driver errors, and look for ECC or hardware fault messages.
7. If this is distributed training, confirm NCCL/env setup and network (IB) health; examine other ranks’ logs for earlier failures.

results.agent_response:
Summary (facts)
- Job 2001 (train_large_model) — State: FAILED, ExitCode=1:0, RunTime=00:05:32.
- sacct shows the job failed (historical record).
- scontrol show job 2001 reports Reason=OOM killer and MinMemoryNode=128G, Partition=gpu, NumNodes=4, NumCPUs=32.

Diagnosis (what went wrong)
- The job was terminated by the Linux OOM killer while running. That means a process on one of the allocated nodes consumed more memory than the kernel (or the cgroup limit) allowed, and the kernel killed the process to free memory.
- Given MinMemoryNode=128G, the job requested 128 GB per node. Either:
  - The job actually needed more than 128 GB on at least one node (under-requested memory), or
  - Memory accounting/cgroup limits were stricter than expected and the job hit an enforced limit, or
  - The application had an unexpected memory leak or spike that exceeded the requested limit.

What to check next (actionable, read-only checks you can run)
- Inspect the job’s stderr/stdout logs for lines like "Killed process" or out-of-memory traces (the job script’s output filename, often contains %j).
- Ask the node admin or check node kernel logs for OOM messages (dmesg/journalctl) on the node(s) that ran the job — these show which process was killed and why.
- Gather memory usage stats from accounting (if enabled):
  - sacct -j 2001 -o JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,MaxRSS,MaxVMSize,ExitCode
  - If MaxRSS is missing, check node logs or re-run with monitoring enabled.
- If you need per-process runtime stats for future runs, enable/peruse sstat while running or instrument the job to record peak RSS.

Remediation suggestions
- If the job legitimately needs more memory: increase the request (e.g., --mem= or --mem-per-cpu, or raise MinMemoryNode) and re-submit.
- If the job should fit in 128G: investigate and fix memory leaks / reduce batch sizes, use more efficient data loaders, or stream data instead of loading it all.
- If cgroups or cluster memory enforcement is unexpectedly strict: ask cluster admin to confirm cgroup memory settings and whether any system limits or node-level memory reservations are in place.
- To avoid silent kills, consider adding memory logging to the job (periodic free/top/ps outputs) and/or request a buffer above observed peak usage.

If you want, I can:
- Show the job’s sacct MaxRSS/MaxVMSize (run sacct command shown above), or
- Inspect the job’s stderr/stdout files if you give their paths, or

What the signals/exit code mean
- ExitCode 134 is consistent with an abort triggered by the runtime (commonly SIGABRT), which is what the CUDA runtime does when it detects an unrecoverable illegal memory access. scontrol's Reason=NonZeroExitCode confirms the job exited non‑normally.

What likely went wrong (most likely causes)
- A GPU kernel performed an out‑of‑bounds read/write or used an invalid pointer (illegal device memory access).
- A race/host-device synchronization bug (e.g., launching kernels asynchronously without checking errors).
- Mismatched CUDA driver vs. runtime or incompatible library (less likely but possible).
- In multi‑node/multi‑GPU training, corrupted buffers or a NCCL/messaging bug could have caused a GPU memory error.
- Less likely: hardware/GPU fault, but that should be verified if errors repeat on the same node.

1. Inspect the job stderr/stdout files produced by the batch (the cluster’s job output path). The sacct row already contained the CUDA error text — capture the full stderr file for stack traces.

5. Try a reduced configuration (single GPU, smaller batch) to see if it is deterministic.
6. Check for core dumps or kernel logs on the nodes used (dmesg / var/log/messages) for hardware errors.

results.agent_response:
Summary (facts)
- Job 5001 (cuda_training, user=alice) finished in state FAILED according to sacct.
- ExitCode=134:0, Elapsed=00:02:15.
- sacct captured this stderr snippet: "CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered".

What that means
- The job’s process aborted (ExitCode 134 = 128 + 6 → killed by signal SIGABRT) after a CUDA runtime error: an illegal memory access on the GPU.
- "illegal memory access" is a GPU-side memory violation (out-of-bounds write/read, use-after-free, or other memory-corruption inside a CUDA kernel). It usually causes the CUDA runtime to abort the process when the error is detected.

Most likely root causes (ordered by likelihood)
1. A bug in the GPU code (custom kernel or model code) causing out-of-bounds accesses or invalid pointer use.
2. A race condition / incorrect indexing in a kernel or in a multi-threaded GPU library (e.g., incorrect launch config).
3. Mismatched or incompatible versions (CUDA toolkit vs driver vs PyTorch/CUDA binary) causing runtime failures.
4. Bad input (very large batch size or tensors leading to invalid indexing or memory corruption).
5. Rare: hardware/GPU fault or driver bug (less likely but possible).

Suggested immediate checks and debugging steps
1. Inspect full stderr/stdout logs for job 5001 (the sacct snippet shows the CUDA error but full logs can have stack traces or host-side messages).
   - If you want, I can fetch scontrol_show for this job to find the StdErr/StdOut paths.
2. Reproduce locally or with a short run:
   - Run the job interactively or a reduced-version of it (smaller batch, fewer GPUs) to see if it fails quickly.
3. Enable synchronous error reporting to get a clearer backtrace:
   - Set CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 in the environment before running; this forces launches to be synchronous and often yields a more usable Python/C++ stack trace.
4. Run CUDA memory checks:
   - Use cuda-memcheck (or nsight tools) on the job binary or a minimal repro to catch the kernel and memory error locations.
5. Check software environment:
   - Confirm CUDA driver version matches the CUDA runtime/PyTorch CUDA build (nvidia-smi and python -c "import torch; print(torch.version.cuda)").
6. Check node/GPU health and system logs:
   - Inspect dmesg / kernel logs and nvidia-smi for ECC errors or GPU resets on the node that ran the job (if you have access to the node logs).
7. If using distributed kernels or NCCL, check for related errors (but the specific message here is a CUDA illegal memory access, not NCCL).

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, well-structured Slurm batch script makes jobs easier to run, debug, and reproduce. Below are best practices, common pitfalls, a short checklist, and a few concise example scripts (CPU, GPU, MPI, and array).

Key principles
- Be explicit about resources (time, CPUs, memory, GPUs). Under-requesting causes failures; over-requesting wastes cluster time.  
- Keep the runtime environment reproducible: modules/conda, container, git commit, and record the environment.  
- Use srun to launch your work inside the allocation (MPI or single-task processes). Avoid launching background processes without srun unless you know what you’re doing.  
- Test quickly with a short/cheap job before full-scale runs. Use small test inputs and short time limits.  
- Capture useful metadata in logs: SLURM job ID, node list, task/CPU/GPU counts, and job exit status.

Basic SBATCH directives to know
- #!/bin/bash — shebang.  
- #SBATCH --job-name=NAME  
- #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out (use %j → jobid)  
- #SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err (can be same as --output)  
- #SBATCH --partition=cpu|gpu|...  
- #SBATCH --nodes=N (for multi-node)  
- #SBATCH --ntasks=NTASKS (total MPI ranks; or 1 for single-process jobs)  
- #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=... or --cpus-per-task=... (for threads)  
- #SBATCH --mem=16G or --mem-per-cpu=4G  
- #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1 (or gpu:tesla:2) for GPUs  
- #SBATCH --time=HH:MM:SS or D-HH:MM:SS  
- #SBATCH --array=1-100%10 (array jobs)  
- #SBATCH --mail-user=you@domain --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL  
- #SBATCH --account=project (if accounting is required)  
- #SBATCH --qos=name (if needed)

Environment & runtime best practices
- Start in the submit directory: cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR" (Slurm sets this by default).  
- Load modules early (module load python/3.10 cuda/12.0) or activate conda env (source ~/miniconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh; conda activate env).  
- Print job metadata for debug:
  echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
  echo "NTASKS=$SLURM_NTASKS, CPUS_ON_NODE=$SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE"
- Use local scratch when I/O heavy: mkdir -p /scratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID; copy inputs there, run, rsync results back.  
- Use set -e and trap to catch signals and attempt graceful checkpointing:
  trap 'echo "SIGTERM received"; your_checkpoint_command' TERM INT
- Prefer srun to start processes (srun respects the allocation and Slurm task binding). For MPI builds, srun -n $SLURM_NTASKS ./a.out is standard. Some MPI implementations allow mpirun, but srun is generally recommended.
- Record reproducibility info: git rev-parse HEAD, pip freeze / conda env export, software module list.

Common pitfalls
- Not requesting enough memory → OOM kills. Use sacct output or past runs to size memory.  
- Launching processes without srun (they may run only on the submit node or be unmanaged).  
- Assuming GPUs are available — request with --gres and check partition/GPU type.  
- Using huge time limits for tests — wastes scheduler capacity.  
- Not copying large input files to node-local scratch — network/shared FS bottlenecks can slow runs.

Monitoring / debugging commands
- Submit: sbatch myjob.sh  
- Queue: squeue -u $USER or squeue -j <jobid>  
- Job details: scontrol show job <jobid> (detailed), sstat -j <jobid> (running job resource usage)  
- Accounting/history: sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS  
- Cancel: scancel <jobid>

Quick checklist before full run
- [ ] Small test completes within a short walltime.  
- [ ] Logs contain job ID, node list, and environment info.  
- [ ] Data staging (input copy and result sync) works.  
- [ ] Resource requests (cpus, mem, gpus) match the program.  
- [ ] Checkpoints or graceful exit handling configured for long jobs.

Example: simple CPU job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=test-cpu
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G

set -e
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
module load python/3.10
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
srun --cpu_bind=cores python train.py --epochs 2

Example: GPU job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=train-gpu
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G

set -e
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
module load cuda/12.0 python/3.10
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST (GPUS=$CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES)"
srun python train_gpu.py

Example: MPI / multi-node
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mpi-job
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=32
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00

cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
module load mpi/openmpi
echo "Starting MPI on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
srun -n $SLURM_NTASKS ./my_mpi_binary

Example: array job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array
#SBATCH --output=array-%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G

task_id=$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
echo "Array task $task_id for job $SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID"
srun ./process_chunk.sh $task_id

Wrap-up
- Keep scripts small, explicit, and versioned (store them in git).  
- Test locally or with tiny Slurm runs.  
- Use srun for launching tasks inside the allocation.  
- Record environment and job metadata to help debugging later.

If you want, tell me what kind of workload you run (GPU training, multi-node MPI, many short tasks, etc.) and I’ll draft a tailored example script and resource recommendations.

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise practical guide to submitting Slurm batch jobs (sbatch), with examples and useful tips.

1) Basic idea
- Create a batch script (a plain shell script) with Slurm directives in header lines starting with #SBATCH.
- Submit it with: sbatch my_script.sh
- sbatch prints a job ID on success. Check status with squeue -u youruser or squeue -j <jobid>.

2) Minimal batch script (CPU job)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_cpu_job
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job.%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00

# load modules, prepare env
module load python
srun python train.py   # or run your commands directly

3) GPU job example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_gpu_job
#SBATCH --output=gpu_job.%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1          # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00

module load cuda/11
srun python train_gpu.py

4) Common sbatch command-line options (can be in header or passed to sbatch)
- --partition=PARTITION
- --nodes=N
- --ntasks=N
- --cpus-per-task=N
- --mem=SIZE (e.g., 16G)
- --gres=gpu:N (GPU request)
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --job-name=NAME
- --output=FILE, --error=FILE
- --mail-user=you@domain, --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
- --array=1-100 or --array=1-100%10 (job arrays)
- --dependency=afterok:<jobid> (run after another job completes successfully)

Example one-line submit:
sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=32G --time=04:00:00 --job-name=train --output=out.%j.log run.sh

5) Interactive / allocation-based runs
- For an interactive allocation use salloc (or srun -p partition --pty bash) then run commands inside the allocation. Example:
salloc --partition=debug --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
srun --pty bash

6) Job arrays
- Use --array to submit many similar tasks:
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
Inside script, use the index via $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID.

7) Useful environment variables inside the job
- $SLURM_JOB_ID, $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, $SLURM_NTASKS, $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

8) Check status / logs / cancel
- squeue -u youruser  (view queue)
- squeue -j <jobid>    (single job)
- scancel <jobid>      (cancel)
- Output and error go to the files you set with --output/--error (or sbatch default job.%j.out)

9) Before submitting
- Check available partitions and node types: sinfo
- If requesting GPUs and you want them "available" first, inspect sinfo and only proceed if idle GPU nodes exist (admins may have site policies).
- Load required modules in the script (module load ...), do not rely on interactive environment.

10) Tips
- Keep the script self-contained (load modules, set paths).
- Test workflow interactively with smaller resources/time before full submit.
- Use --time conservatively: short jobs get scheduled faster.
- Use job arrays to avoid lots of small submissions.
- Use --dependency to chain jobs instead of polling.

If you want, tell me:
- the command you want to run, required resources (GPUs, CPUs, mem, time), partition, and whether it should be an array or interactive — I can draft a ready-to-submit sbatch script for you.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial covering the most common tasks, commands, and best practices you’ll need to run jobs on an HPC cluster.

1) Core concepts
- Controller (slurmctld) schedules jobs; compute nodes run jobs.
- Job = an allocation of resources (nodes/CPUs/GPUs/memory) for some time.
- Batch job = script submitted with sbatch. Interactive allocation = salloc / srun.
- Partitions are schedulable groups of nodes (like queues).
- TRES = tracked resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs, licenses, etc).

2) Submitting batch jobs (sbatch)
- Basic workflow: write a shell script with SBATCH directives, then run sbatch script.sh.
- Minimal example:
  #!/bin/sh
  #SBATCH --job-name=myjob
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=4
  #SBATCH --mem=16G
  #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out

  srun my_program arg1 arg2
- Important SBATCH options:
  --time=HH:MM:SS (or D-HH:MM:SS)
  --nodes=N
  --ntasks / --ntasks-per-node
  --cpus-per-task (for multithreaded tasks)
  --mem (total for job) vs --mem-per-cpu
  --partition=name
  --account=acct
  --qos=name
  --gres=gpu:1 (request GPUs)
  --output, --error (filename patterns support %j (jobid), %a (array index))
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345:12346 to run after jobs succeed.

3) Interactive & allocations (salloc, srun)
- salloc requests an allocation and gives you an interactive shell on the allocation:
  salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=01:00:00 --gres=gpu:1
- Use srun to launch tasks inside an allocation or to run tasks from a batch script:
  srun --ntasks=4 ./mpi_program
- For quick test shells you can also use srun --pty bash

4) Job arrays
- Useful for parameter sweeps; a single submission creates many jobs:
  #SBATCH --array=1-100%10    (100 tasks, at most 10 running concurrently)
- Inside the script use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (or %a in file names) to pick parameters or ranges.

5) Requesting GPUs and conditional considerations
- Request with --gres=gpu:count (or --gres=gpu:V100:1 if specific type allowed).
- When aiming to submit only if idle GPUs exist, check sinfo for idle GPU node counts first (idle nodes count must be >0).

6) Inspecting jobs and cluster state
- squeue shows current queued/running jobs. Useful options:
  squeue -u $USER
  squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.9l %.6D %R"  (custom format)
- sinfo shows partitions and node availability (allocated/idle/down counts):
  sinfo
  sinfo -N -l   (node-level)
- scontrol show job <jobid> prints detailed job fields (reasons, TRES, resources, dependencies).
- sstat -j <jobid> shows runtime resource usage for running jobs.
- sacct for historical/completed jobs and accounting (start/end/exitcode).

7) Cancelling, holding, requeuing (admin/user)
- Cancel: scancel <jobid> (or scancel -u username, scancel -p partition)
- Hold/release: scontrol hold <jobid>; scontrol release <jobid>
- Requeue: scontrol requeue <jobid> or scancel --signal? (admins normally use scontrol_requeue)

8) Common troubleshooting steps
- Job is PENDING: check REASON column in squeue. Common reasons: Resources, Priority, PartitionDown, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSMaxWalltime, User/QOS limits.
- If squeue doesn’t show a reason or you need more detail, run:
  scontrol show job <jobid>
- If job disappears from squeue and you expect history, check sacct to see completion/exit codes and runtime.
- For preemption/priority issues, sprio and sdiag can help diagnose scheduling behavior.

9) Useful environment variables available inside jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_NNODES, SLURM_NODELIST, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE

10) Monitoring & accounting
- sacct for completed jobs (filters by user; by default do not add extra state filters unless requested).
- sreport for usage reports (CPU-hours/GPU-hours) by user/account/partition.
- scontrol show config and scontrol ping for controller health (admins).

11) Best practices
- Always request realistic walltime; overestimating wastes queue priority, underestimating can kill jobs.
- Request memory explicitly (--mem or --mem-per-cpu); avoid relying on defaults.
- Test new code interactively (salloc/srun) on small inputs before a large sbatch run.
- Use job arrays for many similar/independent tasks instead of many separate sbatch calls.
- Redirect stdout/stderr to files; include %j or %a to avoid collisions.
- Check node/partition status (sinfo) before heavy submissions.
- For repeatable workflows, checkpoint and make jobs restartable.
- Be mindful of site-specific policies (accounts, QOS, node constraints).

12) Quick command summary
- Submit batch: sbatch script.sh
- Interactive allocation: salloc [options]
- Run in allocation or step: srun [options] command
- Show queue: squeue (squeue -u $USER)
- Show nodes/partitions: sinfo
- Job details: scontrol show job <id>
- Resource usage (running): sstat -j <id>
- Historic accounting: sacct
- Cancel job: scancel <id>
- Job arrays: sbatch --array=1-100 script.sh
- Request GPU: --gres=gpu:1

13) Where to read more
- The official Slurm docs are the canonical reference (sbatch, srun, salloc, squeue, sinfo, sacct pages).
- Your cluster’s local documentation / help pages for site-specific partitions, accounts, and GPU types.

If you tell me what you want to do (e.g., run a specific MPI job, use GPUs, create an array, or debug a pending job ID), I can give a ready-to-submit sbatch script or step-by-step commands for that scenario.
results.judge_reason: Used correct tool and provided comprehensive tutorial.

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, robust Slurm batch script makes jobs predictable, debuggable, and fair to other users. Below are practical guidelines, common pitfalls, and compact templates you can adapt.

1) Basic structure and essentials
- Use SBATCH directives at the top of the script:
  - job name (--job-name)
  - stdout/err paths (--output, --error)
  - partition/queue (--partition)
  - nodes/ntasks/CPUs-per-task (--nodes, --ntasks, --cpus-per-task)
  - memory (--mem or --mem-per-cpu)
  - walltime (--time)
  - GPUs (--gres=gpu:count) for GPU jobs
  - account/QOS if your cluster requires them (--account, --qos)
- Example minimal headers:
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=myjob
  #SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out
  #SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err
  #SBATCH --partition=gpu
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
  #SBATCH --mem=32G
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

2) Use srun to launch tasks (not plain mpirun) unless your site recommends otherwise
- Use srun for single-node multi-threaded jobs and for MPI, e.g. srun my_program or srun -n $SLURM_NTASKS mpiexec ...
- srun enforces the allocations and sets environment variables correctly.

3) Make the script reproducible and robust
- set -euo pipefail
- Optionally set ulimit -s unlimited for deep recursion or MPI
- cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR at start if you expect to run from submit directory
- Load modules or activate conda/venv explicitly (module load …; source activate …)
- Export thread/process environment variables (OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS)
- Checkpointing and requeue: trap signals (SIGTERM) and write progress files if long-running

4) Resource request tips
- Request only what you need (over-requesting wastes cluster resources and may delay scheduling).
- For hybrid MPI+OpenMP: set --ntasks for MPI ranks and --cpus-per-task for OpenMP threads; set OMP_NUM_THREADS accordingly.
- For memory-intensive jobs prefer --mem or --mem-per-cpu depending on allocation policy.
- For GPUs use --gres=gpu:N and prefer making your code respect CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (srun usually sets this).

5) Job arrays
- Use --array=1-100%20 for many similar tasks; use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in script to pick input files or indices.
- Limit concurrency with the %N to avoid overloading shared I/O or licensing.

6) Dependencies and workflows
- Use --dependency=afterok:JOBID,afterany,aftercorr:...
- For staged pipelines, consider job arrays + dependencies or a workflow manager (Snakemake, Nextflow).

7) Logging and outputs
- Use meaningful output filenames (include %x and %j for job name and id).
- Keep logs small and rotate/trim them for repeated array jobs.
- Save stdout/stderr and any important checkpoints to persistent storage (not local node tmp) unless temporary caching is intentional.

8) Common pitfalls
- Forgetting to set --time short enough → long queue placement; or too short → job killed.
- Forgetting to request enough CPUs for multi-threaded libraries → oversubscription and poor performance.
- Relying on interactive environment (PATH, modules) that aren’t loaded in the script.
- Writing large scratch files to the home filesystem — prefer node-local /tmp for short-lived large I/O.

9) Security, portability, and debugging
- Avoid hard-coding node hostnames unless absolutely required.
- Test interactively with a small allocation (salloc or an interactive partition) before a large sbatch.
- Add a small “smoke test” run in the script (or an option to run with smaller inputs) so you can iterate.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Sure — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial that covers the common concepts, commands, examples, and troubleshooting tips you’ll need to run jobs on an HPC cluster.

1) Quick architecture & concepts
- slurmctld: cluster controller / scheduler.
- slurmd: node daemon that runs tasks.
- slurmdbd: optional accounting DB service.
- Nodes: physical/virtual machines that run jobs.
- Partitions: named sets of nodes (like queues).
- Job: a submitted workload (batch or interactive).
- Job step: one parallel piece inside a job (srun creates steps).
- Allocation vs. job vs. step: sbatch/salloc allocate resources and create jobs; srun runs tasks/steps inside an allocation.

2) Key commands
- sbatch script.sh — submit a batch job (non-interactive).
- srun … — run a job step (interactive or inside an allocation).
- salloc … — request an interactive allocation (gives a shell with resources).
- squeue — view queued/running jobs.
- sinfo — view partitions and node status.
- sacct — historical accounting for completed jobs.
- scontrol show job <id> — detailed job information.
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.

3) Basic sbatch script (typical)
Example (replace with cluster-appropriate values):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1         # request 1 GPU (if available)

module load python/3.9
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- #SBATCH lines are directives interpreted by sbatch.
- --nodes, --ntasks, --cpus-per-task, and --mem define resources. ntasks often maps to MPI ranks; cpus-per-task to threads (OpenMP).
- --gres=gpu:N requests GPUs (cluster-specific GPU names may vary).
- %j in --output expands to job ID.

4) sbatch vs srun vs salloc (short)
- sbatch: submit a batch script, job runs later under scheduler.
- srun: within an allocation it launches tasks; srun can also launch immediate parallel jobs (but most batch scripts use sbatch + srun).
- salloc: get an interactive allocation (then use srun or run commands directly).

5) Useful sbatch options / features
- Job arrays: --array=1-100 to run many similar tasks (use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID).
- Dependencies: --dependency=afterok:12345 to start after job 12345 finishes successfully.
- QOS/account: --qos=..., --account=... (cluster policy controlled).
- Email notifications: --mail-user=you@org --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
- Time format: HH:MM:SS or D-HH:MM:SS (cluster may accept different formats).

6) Environment variables available in jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (when arrays), SLURM_JOB_NAME.
Use these in scripts to adapt behavior per job/array index.

7) MPI and multi-node jobs
- Request nodes and tasks: e.g., --nodes=4 --ntasks-per-node=8 (or --ntasks=32).
- Launch MPI with srun mpirun-wrapper: srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_app or srun ./my_mpi_app (cluster MPI config-dependent).
- Avoid mixing mpirun and srun unless your cluster docs recommend it.

8) GPUs and containers
- GPUs: request with --gres=gpu:N or cluster-specific gres keys. Check sinfo for GPU partitions/nodes.
- Containers: Singularity / Apptainer often used. Example: singularity exec image.sif python train.py inside job script.

9) Monitoring & debugging
- squeue -u $USER to see your jobs.
- scontrol show job <id> for detailed config and reason for pending state.
- sstat -j <jobid> for realtime resource usage (running jobs).
- sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed for accounting of finished jobs.
- Examine job-<id>.out / job-<id>.err files written by --output/--error.
- Pending reasons (from squeue REASON column): Resources, Priority, Dependency, QOS, PartitionTimeLimit, etc. Use scontrol show job <id> for extra detail if needed.

10) Common pitfalls & best practices
- Over-requesting memory or GPUs reduces scheduler fit; request realistic resources.
- For multi-threaded codes, match cpus-per-task to number of threads (export OMP_NUM_THREADS accordingly).
- Prefer specifying --mem-per-cpu when you want memory scaled by CPU.
- Use job arrays for many similar short tasks (more efficient than many single-job submissions).
- Keep runtime estimates realistic; long requests can push you to the back of the queue.
- Save checkpoints frequently for long runs; enable restart logic.

11) Troubleshooting quick checklist
- Job stuck PENDING: check REASON in squeue; if “Resources” you may need to wait or request fewer resources/another partition; if “Dependency” or “QOS” check job options.
- Job fails quickly with ExitCode != 0: check stderr file and node/step info with scontrol show job.
- No GPUs available: use sinfo to inspect GPU node states and partitions.
- Account/QOS limits: contact admins or use sacctmgr_list (admins) to inspect limits.

12) Where to go next (advanced topics)
- Fairshare and priorities: sprio, sshare.
- Reservations: scontrol show reservation / scontrol create reservation (admin).
- Scheduler tuning & diagnostics: sdiag, sprio_weights, slurmctld logs (admin).
- Accounting reports: sreport for CPU/GPU-hour reports.

If you want:

- a ready-to-submit example for MPI or GPU training (I can generate one),

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a “good” Slurm batch script is clear, reproducible, portable, and requests only the resources you actually need. Below is a concise checklist, common pitfalls, and several short example scripts you can adapt.

Quick checklist (what to include)
- Shebang and strict shell settings: e.g., #!/bin/bash and set -euo pipefail.
- SBATCH directives (one per logical requirement) before any executable commands:
  - Job name (--job-name)
  - Partition/queue (--partition)
  - Time limit (--time)
  - Nodes / tasks / CPUs / memory (--nodes, --ntasks, --cpus-per-task, --mem or --mem-per-cpu)
  - GPUs if needed (--gres=gpu:COUNT)
  - Account/QOS if required (--account, --qos)
  - Output and error paths (--output, --error) (include jobid and jobname in filenames)
  - Email notifications (--mail-type, --mail-user) if you need them
- Use srun to launch tasks inside the allocation (srun integrates with Slurm’s scheduler and resource accounting).
- Load modules or activate environments near the top, after SBATCH directives.
- Staging: copy input data to local (node) scratch at start; copy results back and rm scratch at end.
- Logging: redirect stdout/stderr to files and include timestamps in logs if helpful.
- Resource-conscious requests: request only what you need (over-requesting hurts throughput and delays your jobs).
- Exit/cleanup: trap signals and clean up temporary files (trap '...' EXIT).
- Use job arrays for many similar small jobs (--array).
- Add comments describing purpose, expected runtime, resource needs, and how to reproduce.

Common pitfalls
- Forgetting SBATCH directives must be at top of script (before executable commands).
- Using mpirun instead of srun on clusters that require srun (prefer srun unless documentation says otherwise).
- Not setting --cpus-per-task for multi-threaded code (leads to oversubscription).
- Not staging I/O to local fast storage (causes heavy shared filesystem load).
- Ignoring time/memory limits (causes job to be killed and lose work).
- Not testing interactively in a small debug partition before large runs.

Useful environment variables available inside the job
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NAME, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_NODELIST, SLURM_NNODES, etc. Use them for logging or conditional behavior.

Testing and debugging tips
- Test interactively on a debug partition or with a small allocation: srun --pty -p debug --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 bash
- sbatch --test-only <script> to check parsing without submitting (if available on your cluster)
- Use sacct, squeue, scontrol show job, and seff (if available) to inspect job state and efficiency after runs.

Examples

1) Simple single-node CPU job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err

set -euo pipefail
module load python/3.10
echo "Started $SLURM_JOB_NAME ($SLURM_JOB_ID) on $(hostname) at $(date)"
srun python train.py --threads $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

2) GPU job (single GPU)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-train
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=6
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out

set -euo pipefail
module load cuda/12.0
module load anaconda
source activate myenv
echo "CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=$CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"
srun --gpu-bind=none python train_gpu.py

3) MPI / multi-node (use srun to launch MPI)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mpi-job
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=32
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out

set -euo pipefail
module load openmpi
srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_program   # srun will launch across nodes

4) Job array (many similar short tasks)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array-job
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%A_%a.out

set -euo pipefail
TASK_ID=$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
srun python run_task.py --task $TASK_ID

Advanced tips
- Use --exclusive if you need a node entirely to avoid noisy neighbors (but this reduces throughput).
- For multi-GPU jobs, ensure your program sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES per rank, or use srun --gpus-per-task.
- Use cgroups and job constraints if your cluster requires them; consult local docs.
- For long-running work, checkpoint periodically and use --requeue if supported.
- For reproducibility, record the module list (module list > modules.txt) and job environment (env > env.txt).
- Consider wrapping complicated workflows with workflow managers (Snakemake, Nextflow, etc.) that can submit many dependent jobs and manage retries.

If you want, paste your current script and tell me:
- target partition (cpu/gpu),

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Short answer: write a job script with SBATCH directives (or pass sbatch flags), then run sbatch <script>. Below are the common fields, a minimal example, and the useful commands to monitor and control jobs.

What you need to specify
- Job name: --job-name=NAME or #SBATCH --job-name=NAME
- Walltime: --time=HH:MM:SS
- CPUs: --cpus-per-task=N
- Memory: --mem=SIZE or --mem-per-cpu=SIZE (e.g., 32G)
- GPUs: --gres=gpu:N (e.g., --gres=gpu:2)
- Partition/queue: --partition=PARTITION
- Account/QoS: --account=ACCOUNT, --qos=QOS (if your site requires)
- Output files: --output=slurm-%j.out ( %j = jobid )
- Email (optional): --mail-user=you@domain --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL

Minimal sbatch script example
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out

# Load modules / activate env
module load cuda/12.0 python/3.10
source ~/venv/bin/activate

# Run your command (use srun for parallel MPI/launch within the allocation)
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes and best practices
- sbatch submits a batch script and exits. Use srun inside the script to launch tasks within the allocation. Use srun or salloc for interactive runs.
- You can also pass resources on the sbatch command line: sbatch --time=01:00:00 --gres=gpu:1 job.sh
- Job arrays: use --array=1-100 and $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to run many similar tasks.
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 to start after another job finishes successfully.
- Environment: SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_NODELIST are set in the job environment.
- GPU conditional submissions: if you need to submit only when idle GPU nodes exist, check sinfo first to confirm idle GPU nodes are available (your cluster may treat allocated/drained/down nodes as unavailable).
- Common failure causes: requesting more resources than allowed by the partition/account, wrong partition name, exceeding time or memory limits, missing account or QOS.

Useful commands to monitor and manage jobs
- squeue -u $USER (view active PENDING/RUNNING jobs)
- squeue -j <jobid> (view a specific active job)
- scontrol show job <jobid> (detailed job info)
- sacct -j <jobid> (historical/completed job accounting)
- scancel <jobid> (cancel a job)
- sstat -j <jobid> (live resource usage for running job)
- sinfo (view partition/node availability)

- whether you want an example tuned to GPUs, MPI, or arrays, or
- provide a script or the command you intend to run and I can help construct the sbatch script.

(If you'd like me to actually submit a script for you, tell me the script path or paste it — note: I must hand the submit action to the cluster operator to execute.)

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Sure — here’s a compact Slurm tutorial covering the common commands, a sample batch script, how to run interactively, monitoring & debugging, job arrays/dependencies, GPU requests, and some best practices.

Quick overview of core commands
- sbatch: submit a batch script (non-interactive).
- srun: launch tasks (used inside jobs or to create job steps / interactive runs).
- salloc: allocate resources interactively (gives you a shell/allocation).
- squeue: view current queue and job states.
- sinfo: view partitions and node states/capacity.
- sacct: query historical/accounting information for completed jobs.
- scontrol: view/change detailed Slurm entity state (jobs, nodes, partitions).
- scancel: cancel jobs.

Minimal batch script example (save as job.sh and run sbatch job.sh)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my-job
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1               # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00            # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job.%j.err

module load python/3.10
# run with srun so Slurm tracks task(s)
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- sbatch returns immediately with a job ID; the job may wait in queue until resources are available.
- Use --mem (total per node) or --mem-per-cpu; use --cpus-per-task for multi-threaded tasks (OpenMP etc).
- For multi-node MPI jobs request --ntasks and use srun -n $SLURM_NTASKS mpirun/your-mpi-app.

Interactive usage
- Get an interactive allocation (then run commands inside it):
  salloc --partition=interactive --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=01:00:00
  srun --pty bash -i
- Or single-command interactive:
  srun --partition=interactive --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash

Checking queue & nodes
- squeue -u $USER         # your jobs
- squeue -j JOBID         # info for a job
- squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R"  # custom columns (example)
- sinfo                   # partition/node counts and states (alloc/idle/down)
- sinfo -N -l             # per-node details

Diagnose pending jobs
- squeue shows reason column (REASON or RE) for pending jobs (PD state).
- For more detail: scontrol show job JOBID — shows constraints/feasible nodes and reason text.

Historical/accounting queries
- sacct -j JOBID                     # post-run accounting for that job
- sacct -u username --starttime=2024-01-01  # user history from date
- sacct output can be formatted (--format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,ExitCode,...)

Live job stats & debugging
- sstat -j JOBID                      # live resource usage for running jobs (CPU%, RSS, I/O)
- Check output/error files (--output/--error) for job logs.
- scontrol show job JOBID             # full job config + allocation info
- scontrol show node nodename         # node-level state and reason (if down/drained)
- If a job fails quickly, use sacct -j JOBID --format=Elapsed,ExitCode,State to inspect exit code.

Job arrays & dependencies
- Arrays: in SBATCH header or sbatch: #SBATCH --array=1-100%10
  Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in script to index work.
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 script.sh
  Common types: afterok, afterany, aftercorr, singleton, after.

GPU requests
- Request GPUs with --gres=gpu:N (example: --gres=gpu:2).
- To make conditional submit decisions (e.g., "only submit if GPU nodes idle"), you must check sinfo first to ensure idle GPU nodes exist. (For cluster ops: use sinfo to verify idle GPU nodes before submission.)

Common states you’ll see in squeue
- R: running
- PD: pending (waiting); REASON column explains why
- CG: completing
- S: suspended
- F: failed

Cancel/hold/requeue
- Cancel a job: scancel JOBID
- Hold a job: scontrol hold JOBID
- Release hold: scontrol release JOBID
(These are cluster-changing actions — use your admin tools or ask your operator if you need help.)

Best practices / tips
- Request realistic time limits: overestimating wastes scheduling; underestimating leads to timeouts.
- Test on small jobs first (short walltime, small data) before scaling up.
- Pin CPUs and set OMP_NUM_THREADS consistent with --cpus-per-task for threaded apps.
- Use job arrays for embarrassingly parallel tasks rather than many independent sbatch submissions.
- Capture both stdout/stderr to files (--output, --error) and include job ID in filenames e.g., job.%j.out.
- Check sinfo before large submissions to see partition/node availability.
- Use salloc/srun for interactive debugging and quick experiments.
- For reproducibility, log the environment (module list, git commit, python env list) from the job script.

Quick cheat-sheet (examples)
- Submit: sbatch job.sh
- Check your queue: squeue -u $USER
- Show detailed job: scontrol show job JOBID
- Cancel: scancel JOBID
- Interactive allocate: salloc --time=01:00:00
- Interactive run: srun --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash
- List partitions/nodes: sinfo -s
- Historical job info: sacct -j JOBID --format=JobID,JobName,User,State,ExitCode,Elapsed

If you want, I can:
- Walk through converting a specific script you have into an sbatch script.
- Show an example for MPI multi-node sbatch.
- Give a short checklist for debugging a job that’s stuck pending (I can query your live cluster with sinfo/squeue if you want that). Which would you like?

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Short answer: write clear, minimal SBATCH directives that exactly request the resources you need, prepare the environment (modules, conda, etc.), run your job with srun (or the launcher your site prefers), capture useful environment/logging information, and make the script reproducible and testable. Below are a checklist, explanations of common options, a few short templates, and practical tips.

Checklist (what every batch script should do)
- Start with a shebang (#!/bin/bash) and safe shell options (e.g., set -euo pipefail).
- Set SBATCH directives for job-name, output, error, partition, time, nodes/ntasks/cpus-per-task, memory and GPUs (gres) as appropriate.
- Load modules / activate environments explicitly.
- cd to the intended working directory or use absolute paths.
- Stage input data and outputs (or reference shared filesystem paths).
- Use srun for the actual program (srun integrates with Slurm and sets task ranks).
- Print minimal runtime diagnostics (date, hostname, env, nproc, free -h, nvidia-smi for GPUs).
- Log stdout/stderr to files with useful names (include %j jobid or %x job name).
- Keep walltime reasonable and add safety margins; use checkpointing if long runs.
- Include cleanup/exit handling where needed (trap on TERM).

Common SBATCH options and what they mean
- --job-name=NAME : human-readable job name.
- --output=FILE, --error=FILE : files for stdout/stderr; use %j (jobid) or %x (jobname).
- --partition=PART : which partition/queue.
- --time=HH:MM:SS : walltime limit (always set).
- --nodes=N : number of nodes.
- --ntasks=NT : number of tasks total (MPI ranks).
- --cpus-per-task=M : threads per task (for OpenMP).
- --mem=MEM or --mem-per-cpu= : RAM reservation.
- --gres=gpu:K or gpu:V100:K : request GPUs.
- --exclusive : node exclusive allocation.
- --account=NAME / --qos= : accounting/QoS tags if your cluster requires them.
- --array=0-99%10 : job arrays; %10 caps concurrent tasks to 10.
- --dependency=afterok:12345 : run after another job finishes successfully.
- --mail-type=FAIL,END,BEGIN --mail-user=you@org : email notifications.

Basic single-node CPU template
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x_%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G

set -euo pipefail
date
echo "Job: $SLURM_JOB_ID $SLURM_JOB_NAME"
module purge
module load python/3.10
cd /home/$USER/myproject
echo "Loaded modules:"; module list

srun python train.py --epochs 10 --data /scratch/$USER/data

GPU single-node template
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu_train
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%j.out
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=6
#SBATCH --mem=32G

set -euo pipefail
date; hostname
module purge
module load cuda/12.0 cudnn
source ~/envs/myenv/bin/activate
nvidia-smi
srun --cpu_bind=cores python train_gpu.py --batch 64

Job array example (many similar short tasks)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array_job
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x_%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --array=0-99%20
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G

set -euo pipefail
TASK_ID=$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
echo "Running array task $TASK_ID"
srun python process_chunk.py --chunk $TASK_ID

Good practices and tips
- Test small first: run with --time=00:05:00 and small inputs, and check logs.
- Prefer srun for MPI and parallel programs; many sites require srun rather than mpirun for correct Slurm integration.
- Distinguish ntasks vs cpus-per-task: ntasks is number of MPI ranks; cpus-per-task is threads each rank uses.
- Use --mem-per-cpu when you want memory tied to CPU count; use --mem when you want node-level memory.
- Include module list and environment information in logs for reproducibility.
- Use %j and %x in filenames so a single directory can hold many job outputs without collision.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Sure — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use whether you’re a user submitting jobs or learning the basics. If you want a deep dive into any section (batch scripts, GPUs, debugging, admin topics), tell me which and I’ll expand.

1) What Slurm is (very short)
- Slurm is a workload manager for scheduling batch and interactive jobs on HPC clusters. Key components: slurmctld (controller/scheduler), slurmd (node daemons), and optionally slurmdbd (accounting).

2) Common Slurm concepts
- Partition: a named group of nodes (like a queue).
- Job: a submitted workload (batch or interactive).
- Job states: PENDING (PD), RUNNING (R), COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.
- Resources: nodes, CPUs, memory, GPUs, licenses, QOS, accounts.
- Job array: many similar jobs with a single submission (indexed tasks).

3) Important commands (quick reference)
- sbatch <script.sh> — submit a batch job
- srun [options] — run a command under Slurm (interactive or within scripts)
- salloc [options] — allocate an interactive allocation
- scancel <jobid> — cancel job(s)
- squeue [filters] — view queued/running jobs (squeue -u $USER)
- sinfo — see partition/node availability
- sacct -j <jobid> — view historical accounting for completed jobs
- scontrol show job <jobid> — show detailed job info
- sstat -j <jobid> — runtime stats for running jobs

4) Minimal sbatch script (example)
- Example header lines you put at top of script (each is a separate line):
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=myjob
  #SBATCH --partition=gpu
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
  #SBATCH --mem=32G
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
  #SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
- Then your commands:
  module load python/3.10
  srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- --gres=gpu:1 requests one GPU. Different clusters may use different gres names (gpu, gpu:V100, etc.).
- Use %j in output filenames to include the job ID.

5) Interactive jobs
- salloc --partition=gpu --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
- srun --pty bash   (or srun --mpi=pmix --pty bash)
- Or srun --x11 to forward display

6) Job arrays
- #SBATCH --array=1-100%10 runs 100 tasks but only 10 concurrently.
- Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the job to index input files.

7) Dependencies and chaining
- sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> second_job.sh
- Dependency types: after, afterok, afternotok, singleton, etc.

8) Monitoring & debugging
- squeue -j <jobid> or squeue -u $USER
- If a job is PENDING, squeue often shows a reason column: e.g., Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, PartitionDown, Dependency.
- For more details: scontrol show job <jobid> (includes reason in more detail).
- Check slurm-%j.out and .err for your program output.
- For runtime metrics while running: sstat -j <jobid>

9) Best practices
- Submit a small quick test job first (30s–1m) to ensure the environment modules, paths, and data are correct.
- Request conservative resources, then scale up. Over-requesting harms scheduling and may increase wait time.
- Specify a realistic walltime; shorter requests often start sooner.
- Put module loads and environment setup in the script (do not rely on interactive env).
- Use checkpoints or save intermediate outputs to shared storage to avoid losing long runs.
- Use job arrays for parallel parameter sweeps rather than many small independent sbatch files.

10) GPU-specific tips
- Use --gres=gpu:N to request GPUs.
- Use nvidia-smi or gpustat inside a running job to verify GPU assignment.
- For conditional GPU submissions (if you asked to submit only when idle GPUs exist), admins/operators should check sinfo to verify idle GPU nodes first.

11) Accounting & history
- sacct -u $USER --starttime=2024-01-01 shows past usage (CPU/GPU hours, exit codes).
- sreport can generate summaries (CPU-hours/GPU-hours) across accounts/time windows.

12) Common trouble reasons
- "Resources" — requested resources not available right now.
- "ReqNodeNotAvail" — specific node constraints unmet.
- "Priority" — higher-priority jobs scheduled first.
- "Dependency" — job is waiting for another job to finish.
- "PartitionDown/Drained" — partition or nodes unavailable.

13) Where to learn more
- Ask me for examples tailored to: GPU job, MPI job across nodes, Slurm arrays, dependency chains, or an sbatch script for your exact command.
- Official docs: slurm.schedmd.com (for command syntax and admin topics).

If you want, tell me:
- the command or program you want to run, plus requested CPUs, memory, GPUs, partition, and walltime, and I’ll generate a ready-to-submit sbatch script for you.

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, robust Slurm batch script makes jobs easier to run, debug, and reproduce. Below is a compact checklist of best practices, followed by small example scripts (CPU, GPU, and job-array) and a short troubleshooting/debug checklist.

Key principles
- Be explicit about resources: request only what you need (time, CPUs, memory, GPUs). Use --mem-per-cpu when memory scales with CPU threads.
- Specify output/error files with job and task identifiers so logs don’t collide (use %j, %A, %a).
- Use modules or a container to make the runtime environment reproducible; record module list / git commit / env for traceability.
- Use srun to launch parallel tasks (MPI or multi-process) unless your MPI implementation requires mpirun; for single-process scripts srun still handles Slurm allocation properly.
- Stage I/O to fast node-local or scratch storage when possible; avoid heavy I/O to shared home.
- Fail fast and log context: set -euo pipefail, trap errors, and log SLURM env vars (SLURM_JOB_ID, NODELIST, NTASKS, CPUS_PER_TASK, ARRAY_TASK_ID).
- For arrays and many small jobs, throttle concurrency with --array=1-100%N to avoid overload.
- Keep walltime conservative but realistic; jobs killed for exceeding time are lost work — use checkpoints if long-running.
- Test interactively or in a short debug partition before large runs.

Common sbatch directives (most useful)
- --job-name=NAME
- --output=logs/%x_%A_%a.out (use %x jobname, %A array master jobid, %a array index, %j jobid)
- --error=logs/%x_%A_%a.err or combined --output=... (stderr merged to stdout)
- --time=DD-HH:MM:SS or HH:MM:SS
- --partition=NAME
- --ntasks=N          (total MPI ranks / processes)
- --cpus-per-task=N   (threads per task; use for OpenMP / data loaders)
- --mem=4G or --mem-per-cpu=2G
- --gres=gpu:N        (for GPU requests) and optionally --constraint
- --array=1-100%20    (job arrays with concurrency cap)
- --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL --mail-user=you@example.com
- --account=ACCOUNT --qos=QOS (site-specific)
- --export=ALL or --export=NONE and then export only needed envvars
- --chdir=DIR         (run from a specific dir)

Useful environment variables inside the script
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NAME
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID
- SLURM_JOB_NODELIST (nodes allocated)
- SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise guide to submitting jobs with Slurm.

Basic concepts
- Batch jobs: submit a shell script with sbatch. The script contains resource requests and the commands to run.
- Interactive jobs: use salloc or srun --pty for an interactive allocation.
- Monitor: squeue (running/pending), sacct (historical/accounting), scancel (cancel).

Minimal batch script (example)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00

module load python
srun python my_script.py

Notes:
- #!/bin/bash must be first line.
- #SBATCH lines set job options inside the script.
- slurm-%j.out will contain stdout/stderr; %j expands to the job ID.
- srun is used inside the job to launch tasks; for single-process jobs srun is optional but recommended.

Common sbatch options (cli or #SBATCH)
- --partition=PARTITION (or #SBATCH --partition=...)
- --gres=gpu:1 (for GPUs)
- --cpus-per-task=N
- --mem=8G (per node, unless your cluster interprets otherwise)
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --job-name=NAME
- --output=FILE, --error=FILE (or --output=FILE to capture both)
- --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@example.com
- --array=1-100 or --array=1-100%10 (job arrays; use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside script)
- --dependency=afterok:12345 (run after job 12345 completes successfully)

Example submit command (from shell)
sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=32G --time=04:00:00 --job-name=train --output=train.%j.log train.sh

Quick one-liner submission
sbatch --wrap="python train.py --epochs 10" --time=00:30:00 --cpus-per-task=2

Interactive session
- Request an interactive allocation: salloc --partition=interactive --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
- Then run srun --pty bash or run commands in that allocation.

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -u $USER to see your queued/running jobs
- squeue -j <jobid> or scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed state/pending reason
- sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed for historical results
- scancel <jobid> to cancel

GPU-submission caveat
- If you asked for an interactive conditional GPU submission, only nodes shown as idle in sinfo are eligible. (This is cluster policy detail; check sinfo if needed.)

Best practices / tips
- Explicitly set --time; jobs that exceed time are killed.
- Request only the resources you need to improve scheduling.
- Use job arrays for parameter sweeps instead of many separate jobs.
- Capture stderr/stdout to files for post-mortem.
- Load modules / activate conda inside the script; the script runs in the submit directory by default.
- Check cluster docs or admins for account/QOS limits, partition names, and GPU accounting.

If you want, tell me:
- whether you need a CPU or GPU job,
- how many CPUs/GPU/memory and expected runtime,
and I can draft a ready-to-submit sbatch script for you.

Great — here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference and starter guide. It covers the usual commands, a sample batch script, interactive use, job arrays & dependencies, checking/debugging jobs, and some best practices.

1) Key commands (what they do)
- sbatch: submit a batch script (non-interactive).
- srun: launch tasks/steps (can be used inside a batch job or from an allocation).
- salloc: get an allocation for interactive work (then use srun or a shell).
- squeue: view current queue (running/pending jobs).
- sacct: view historical/accounting records for completed/failed jobs.
- scontrol show job <id>: show detailed job info.
- scancel <id>: cancel a job.

2) Basic sbatch batch script (example)
- Save as job.sh and submit with: sbatch job.sh
Example contents (put these lines near top of your script):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out        # %j expands to jobid
#SBATCH --error=job-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1               # request 1 GPU
# any module loads or env setup
module load python
# run your program; prefer srun for parallel/mpi-aware launch
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- #SBATCH directives are parsed by sbatch; you can also pass these options on sbatch command line (e.g., sbatch --time=01:00:00 job.sh).
- Use meaningful --job-name and set --output/--error so logs are captured.

3) Interactive allocation and running
- Request an interactive allocation:
  salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00 --cpus-per-task=4
- Inside the allocation, start an interactive shell or processes:
  srun --pty bash   (starts a shell on allocated nodes)
  srun -n4 ./mpi_program   (runs 4 MPI tasks)

4) Job arrays (parameter sweeps)
- Use --array to submit many similar tasks with one job:
#SBATCH --array=1-100%20    # run indices 1..100, max 20 concurrently
Access index with $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script:
python run_case.py --case $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID

5) Job dependencies
- Submit job B after job A succeeds:
  jid=$(sbatch jobA.sh | awk '{print $4}')    # capture job id from sbatch output
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:$jid jobB.sh
- Common dependency types: afterok, afterany, aftercorr, after, singleton, expand.

6) Common resource request options
- --nodes=N            number of nodes
- --ntasks=T           total tasks (MPI ranks)
- --cpus-per-task=C    CPUs/threads per task (for multithreaded tasks)
- --mem=16G or --mem-per-cpu=4G
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --partition=name
- --qos=name
- --account=name
- --gres=gpu:1         GPUs (or gpu:V100:2 to request type)
- --job-name, --output, --error, --mail-type, --mail-user

7) Checking and debugging jobs
- squeue -u $USER shows your queued and running jobs (REASON column for pending).
- scontrol show job <jobid> gives detailed fields, including dependency and resources.
- sacct -j <jobid> -o JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed shows historical outcome.
- sstat -j <jobid> can show runtime resource usage for running jobs (cpu%, rss).
- If a job is pending, first check squeue’s REASON. For detailed reasons, scontrol show job <id> may show required resources or node constraints.
- Common pending reasons: Resources, ReqNodeNotAvail, Priority, QOSDenied, Dependency.

8) Good practices / tips
- Test at small scale first (short time, 1 CPU) before large runs.
- Request realistic CPU/GPU/memory — over-requesting wastes queue slots and increases wait time.
- Always capture stdout/stderr with --output/--error (use %j for job id).
- Use modules or environment setup in the script (module load ...).
- Prefer srun for launching parallel tasks inside Slurm jobs (it sets up ranks and allocates tasks).
- For GPUs, prefer frameworks that detect CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES; Slurm sets this when you request --gres=gpu.
- Use job arrays for embarrassingly parallel parameter sweeps (easier than many sbatch calls).
- Use checkpoints or periodic saves for long jobs; consider shorter walltime and automatic requeue if supported.
- For MPI, match mpirun/mpiexec usage to your cluster’s recommended launcher; many sites recommend srun to launch MPI.

9) Resource accounting and history
- sacct for historical usage (states, exit codes, elapsed, consumed resources).
- sreport for aggregate usage reports (CPU/GPU-hours by user/account/partition).
- scontrol_license to inspect tracked licenses.

10) Where to learn more
- Official Slurm docs: https://slurm.schedmd.com/ (sbatch, srun, salloc pages are very helpful).
- Your cluster’s user guide — it often contains site-specific partitions, nodes, and best practices.

If you want, I can:

- Explain a specific option in detail (e.g., heterogeneous jobs, --ntasks vs --cpus-per-task).
- Walk through interpreting a pending job (if you give me a job ID; I’ll run squeue and explain).

Which of those would you like next?

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?

Good question — a “good” Slurm batch script is clear, reproducible, requests just the resources you actually need, and launches your job in a way the scheduler expects (usually via srun). Below are concise guidelines, a compact template, several common examples, and a checklist to help you write robust, portable scripts.

Short guidelines
- Put scheduler directives in #SBATCH header lines (or pass equivalent flags to sbatch).
- Request accurate resources: nodes, ntasks, cpus-per-task, mem, time, gres (gpus), QOS/account/account.
- Use srun to launch work (preferred over plain mpirun unless your MPI vendor requires mpirun).
- Set environment (modules/conda/singularity) explicitly so the run is reproducible.
- Redirect stdout/stderr to job-specific files (use %j / %x for jobid/jobname).
- Use set -e and traps for safer failure handling and to enable cleanup.
- For arrays use --array and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID; throttle massive arrays with %limit.
- Keep the walltime conservative but not excessive — underestimating causes kill; overestimating wastes queue time.

Minimal template (fill values)
# SBATCH lines:
#SBATCH --job-name=job-name
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out       # %x=jobname %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu               # or cpu/short/long etc.
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                  # if GPU needed
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# Shell setup and safety
set -euo pipefail
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST started at $(date)"

# Load modules / activate env
module purge
module load gcc/10 python/3.10 cuda/12.1
source /path/to/conda.sh && conda activate myenv

# Export threading settings when using OpenMP or BLAS
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=${OMP_NUM_THREADS}

# Run the workload with srun
srun --mpi=pmix_v3 my_program --arg value

# Optional cleanup
echo "Job finished at $(date)"

Example 1 — single-node multi-threaded job
#SBATCH --job-name=py-train
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=16
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00

set -e
module load python/3.10
source activate myenv
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
srun python train.py --batch 128

Example 2 — MPI multi-node job (use srun)
#SBATCH --job-name=mpi-job
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=8
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00

module load mpi/openmpi
srun --mpi=pmix_v3 ./my_mpi_executable -arg

Notes: ntasks = total ranks. ntasks-per-node × nodes = total ntasks. Use cpus-per-task for per-rank threads.

Example 3 — GPU training (single node, 4 GPUs)
#SBATCH --job-name=gpu-train
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=64G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:4
#SBATCH --time=12:00:00

module load cuda/12.1 cudnn
source activate pytorch
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
srun python train_gpu.py --gpus 4

Example 4 — job array (parameter sweep)
#SBATCH --job-name=array
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%A_%a.out
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G

param_file=params.txt
PARAM=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" $param_file)
srun python run_param.py --param "$PARAM"

Best-practice checklist
- Request actual resources: measure small runs first, then scale your requests.
- Prefer srun for execution; it integrates with the job allocation.
- Use #SBATCH --output and --error with %j/%x for unique logs.
- Set environment variables controlling thread counts (OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS).
- Use --cpus-per-task for threaded codes and --ntasks for MPI ranks.
- For GPUs, request --gres=gpu:N and ensure your framework sees the GPUs (check CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES).
- Use --time realistically (underestimate => kill; too long => long queue wait).
- Use modules or container images for reproducibility (Singularity/Apptainer).
- Add --mem or --mem-per-cpu to avoid node OOM kills. Be explicit — default may be low.
- Add small checkpoints/logging so you can resume or diagnose failures.
- For long workflows, consider --dependency options to chain jobs or --array with % limit.

Robustness and failure handling
- set -euo pipefail to stop on errors.
- trap '... cleanup ...' EXIT to copy logs or free temporary storage.
- Consider --requeue if you want the scheduler to requeue on preemption (cluster must allow).
- For very long work, use application-level checkpointing.

Debugging tips
- Test interactively first: salloc --nodes=1 --time=00:30:00 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1
- Use small test scripts and sbatch --test-only to check directive parsing (sbatch --test-only script.sh).
- Inspect queue with squeue -j <jobid> or squeue -u $USER.
- If pending, check reason: squeue -o "%i %t %r %P %j %u %M %D" or scontrol show job <jobid>.
- For crashed or finished jobs, use sacct -j <jobid> -o JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS.
- Capture standard output/error for failure traces.

Common pitfalls
- Mixing ntasks/cpus-per-task wrong — causes oversubscription or idle CPUs.
- Not setting OMP_NUM_THREADS when cpus-per-task > 1 (leads to oversubscribe).
- Using mpirun without srun on some clusters — can cause allocation mismatch; prefer srun.
- Forgetting --gres=gpu:X for GPU jobs; scheduler won’t allocate GPU otherwise.
- Not directing logs to unique files (overwriting previous runs).
- Requesting insufficient memory leads to OOM kill with ExitCode=137.

Quick reference commands
- Submit: sbatch myscript.sh
- Interactive allocation: salloc ...
- Watch queue: squeue -u $USER
- Show job: scontrol show job <jobid>
- Job accounting: sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed

results.prompt: How do I submit a job?
results.agent_response:
Good question — here’s a concise guide to submitting a Slurm batch job and the common options you’ll need.

1) Write a batch script
- Start with a bash shebang and SBATCH directives (one per-line). That file contains resource requests and the commands to run.
- Minimal example (save as myjob.sh):
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=myjob
  #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
  #SBATCH --time=01:00:00         # HH:MM:SS
  #SBATCH --partition=short
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  #SBATCH --mem=8G
  module load python
  python train.py --epochs 10

- GPU example (request 1 GPU):
  #SBATCH --partition=gpu
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

- Array job example:
  #SBATCH --array=1-10
  # use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script

2) Submit the script
- sbatch myjob.sh
- sbatch prints the job ID on success (e.g., Submitted batch job 12345).

3) Monitor and inspect jobs
- squeue -u $USER (show your queued/running jobs)
- squeue -j 12345 or scontrol show job 12345 for detailed info
- sstat -j 12345 for runtime resource usage (running jobs)
- sacct -j 12345 for historical/accounting info after completion

4) Cancel or manage jobs
- scancel 12345 (cancel)
- You can set dependencies with --dependency=afterok:<jobid> when submitting new jobs.

5) Output, logs, and environment
- Stdout/stderr go to files set by --output and --error (default slurm-%j.out).
- Useful env vars: $SLURM_JOB_ID, $SLURM_NTASKS, $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, $SLURM_NODELIST, $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID.

6) Common SBATCH options (quick reference)
- --job-name=NAME
- --output=FILE, --error=FILE
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --partition=PART
- --nodes=N, --ntasks=N, --cpus-per-task=N
- --mem=SIZE or --mem-per-cpu=SIZE
- --gres=gpu:N
- --array=RANGE
- --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL --mail-user=you@domain

7) Interactive runs (if you need an interactive allocation)
- salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
  then srun --pty /bin/bash   (or srun python -u script.py)
- Or srun --pty --partition=short --time=00:30:00 bash

Troubleshooting tips:
- If sbatch fails, check the partition name, resource requests, and time format.
- If job stays PENDING, run squeue -j <jobid> and look at the REASON field (insufficient resources, priority, or partition limits).
- For email/notification issues, ensure your mail address is correct and cluster mails are allowed.
