results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial covering the common workflows, commands, examples, and quick diagnostics you’ll use day-to-day.

Basic concepts
- Controller (slurmctld) schedules jobs; compute nodes run them.
- Jobs are either batch (sbatch), interactive (salloc + srun), or run tasks inside allocations (srun).
- Key resources: partition (queue), nodes, CPUs, memory, GPUs (gres), time limit, accounts/QOS.
- Job metadata/env: SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_NODELIST, etc.

Common commands
- sbatch script.sh — submit a batch job.
- srun [opts] --pty bash — run a job step or start interactive shell inside an allocation.
- salloc [opts] — allocate resources for interactive use (then use srun inside).
- squeue — show active queue (RUNNING, PENDING), use -u user, -p partition, -j jobid filters.
- sinfo — show partition/node availability and states.
- scancel JOBID — cancel a job (or scancel --user=username).
- sacct — query historical/completed job accounting.
- scontrol show job JOBID — detailed job info; scontrol show config for controller settings.
- sstat JOBID — runtime resource stats for a running job.
- sreport / sshare — accounting and fairshare reports.
- scontrol_reservation_show / squeue --reservation=name — reservation info.

Minimal batch script example
(put in script.sh)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err

module load python
srun python myscript.py

Submit:
$ sbatch script.sh
Capture job id:
$ jid=$(sbatch --parsable script.sh)

GPU example
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00

Interactive GPU session
$ salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00
then inside allocation:
$ srun --pty bash

Job arrays (many similar tasks)
#SBATCH --array=1-100%20
Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside your script to index work. %20 limits concurrent tasks to 20.

Dependencies
- Run job B after job A succeeds:
$ sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 jobB.sh

Checking queue & details
- Show your jobs:
$ squeue -u $USER
- Show one job (brief):
$ squeue -j 12345 -o "%.18i %.9P %.30j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R"
- If more detail needed:
$ scontrol show job 12345
- If squeue doesn’t show a finished job, query history:
$ sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed

Diagnosing pending jobs
1) squeue -l or include REASON column to see why it’s pending.
2) For a detailed reason: scontrol show job JOBID
3) Common reasons: Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSLimit, Dependency.

Resource/partition status
$ sinfo
Shows partitions and NODES(A/I/D) counts. Use sinfo -o or sinfo -l for more detail.

Runtime stats for running jobs
$ sstat -j JOBID
(useful for CPU%, memory, I/O while job runs)

Cancel and hold
- Cancel a job: scancel 12345
- Hold a job: scontrol hold 12345
- Release: scontrol release 12345

Accounting and history
- sacct --user=username --starttime=YYYY-MM-DD — historical jobs with ExitCode, time, memory.
- sreport — GPU/CPU-hour usage reports by account/user/partition.

Best practices
- Test at small scale first (short time, small resources).
- Request realistic time limits; over-requesting wastes queue fairness and may delay start.
- Prefer --mem-per-cpu when memory scales with CPU; use --mem for whole-node requests.
- Use job arrays for many similar independent tasks to avoid many small sbatch submissions.
- Collect stdout/stderr to files with --output/--error (include %j jobid).
- Use modules or container runtimes (Singularity/Apptainer) to fix environments.
- Check sinfo before submitting to pick appropriate partition and verify idle nodes.
- Use --parsable to get machine-readable job id for scripting.
- Add checkpointing or periodic saves for long jobs.
- Respect QOS/account and account association (--account=...). If preemption is possible, use --no-requeue or checkpoint.

Examples of useful flags
- --partition, -p
- --time, -t (format D-HH:MM:SS or minutes)
- --nodes, -N
- --ntasks, -n
- --cpus-per-task, -c
- --mem (or --mem-per-cpu)
- --gres=gpu:1
- --job-name, -J
- --output, -o and --error, -e
- --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@domain
- --dependency=afterok:ID,afterany:ID
- --array=1-100%10
- --account=acctname
- --qos=name

Quick troubleshooting checklist
- Job pending long? Check squeue REASON → scontrol show job for details.
- Job failed quickly? Inspect slurm-%j.err and stdout, and sacct for ExitCode.
- Job not found in squeue? Use sacct to find past jobs.
- Nodes down/drained? sinfo and sinfo -R (reasons) show node problems.
- Low priority? Use sprio to view priority factors and sshare to see fairshare.

Where to read more
- slurm.schedmd.com documentation (sbatch, srun, salloc, squeue, sinfo, sacct pages).
- Local cluster user guide / policies (accounts, partitions, QOS, storage quotas).

If you want, I can:
- Create a starter sbatch script tailored to your code (tell me #CPUs, memory, GPUs, partition, time).
- Walk through interpreting a specific squeue or scontrol show job output if you paste it.
- Show how to set up job arrays or dependency chains for a workflow.

  # example: kill background children if any

- Trap + cleanup: ensures background children and temp files are handled when the job is terminated or on exit.
- Logging: write timestamps, job ID, node list, and SLURM env vars to output to make postmortem debugging easier.
- Use srun to launch tasks (MPI/parallel) rather than plain mpirun where possible — srun is Slurm-aware.
- Temporary files: use per-job TMPDIR to avoid collisions and ensure cleanup.
- Arrays: use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index work safely.
- Resource requests: be explicit (cpus-per-task, mem, gres). Don’t assume defaults.

Optional extras
- Redirect combined stdout/stderr to a single file with exec > >(tee -a "$LOG") 2>&1 if you want live/local copy plus persistent log.
- Checkpointing hooks (trap and save state) for long-running jobs.
- Validate inputs early and fail with clear messages rather than letting long runs continue.

results.prompt: Explain basic Slurm submission steps
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise, practical guide to the basic Slurm job-submission workflow and the common commands and options you’ll use.

1) Prepare a batch script
- Create a shell script (e.g., job.sh) that sets SBATCH directives at the top and runs your commands. SBATCH lines tell Slurm what resources and policies to use.

Minimal example (job.sh):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob           # job name
#SBATCH --partition=gpu            # partition/queue
#SBATCH --nodes=1                  # nodes
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                 # tasks (MPI processes)
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4          # threads per task (OpenMP)
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00            # walltime (HH:MM:SS)
#SBATCH --mem=16G                  # memory for the job
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1               # request 1 GPU (if available)
#SBATCH --output=%x.%j.out         # stdout file (%x=jobname, %j=jobid)
#SBATCH --error=%x.%j.err          # stderr file

module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- Use #SBATCH lines or sbatch CLI flags. Both are equivalent; in-script directives are most common.
- --gres=gpu:N requests GPUs. --mem vs --mem-per-cpu: pick the one matching your cluster policy.
- %j in output names expands to job ID.

2) Submit the job
- sbatch job.sh
- sbatch prints a job ID (e.g., Submitted batch job 12345).

3) Monitor the job
- squeue -u yourusername  (or squeue -j 12345)
- Useful columns: JOBID, NAME, USER, ST (state), TIME, NODELIST(REASON)
- If a job is pending, the REASON column tells why (resources, QOS, dependencies, etc).

4) Inspect job details
- scontrol show job 12345  — detailed job configuration and allocated resources
- sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed — accounting info after job finishes
- sstat -j 12345  — runtime stats for running jobs (if supported)

5) Cancel or change
- scancel 12345  — cancel a job
- For hold/release/requeue/time-limit changes you’d use scontrol commands (admins may restrict some ops).

6) Interactive and allocation-based runs
- srun --pty --partition=debug --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 bash  — get an interactive shell on an allocation.
- salloc ...  — allocate resources interactively then run commands inside that allocation.

7) Arrays and dependencies
- Array jobs: #SBATCH --array=1-100  (or sbatch --array=1-100 job.sh). Use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script.
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 next_job.sh  — submit a job that waits for another to finish successfully.

8) Common sbatch flags (quick reference)
- -p / --partition, -N / --nodes, -n / --ntasks, -c / --cpus-per-task
- --mem, --time (-t), -J / --job-name, -o / -e (output/error), --gres
- --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@domain
- --wrap="command"  — submit a short command without a script
- --export=ALL,VAR=value  — control environment variables passed to the job

9) Best practices
- Test interactively with a small allocation before large batch runs.
- Request realistic resources and conservative walltime (over-requests can delay scheduling).
- Redirect output to files for debugging; include identifiable job name or jobid.
- Use job arrays for many similar tasks to reduce scheduler load.
- Check pending reasons with squeue and scontrol show to diagnose scheduling delays.
- Clean up temporary files and avoid assuming a global working directory.

10) Troubleshooting pointers
- If pending due to resources, check sinfo (partition/node availability) and node state.
- Use scontrol show job <id> for more detail if squeue lacks information.
- Use sacct after jobs finish to see exit codes and runtime.

If you want, I can:
- Show a tailored example sbatch script for your application (CPU vs GPU, MPI vs single-process).
- Explain how to write array jobs or dependency chains.
- Walk through common pending reasons and how to resolve them.
results.judge_reason: Provided comprehensive, accurate guide with no unnecessary tool calls.

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a “good” Slurm batch script is clear about resource requests, reproducible, robust to failures/signals, and easy to test/debug. Below are concise guidelines, an annotated example template you can adapt, and a short checklist of best practices.

High-level rules
- Request only the resources you actually need: partition, nodes, ntasks, cpus-per-task, gres (GPUs), time, memory. Over-requesting wastes cluster capacity; under-requesting causes failures.
- Make intent explicit with #SBATCH headers (or equivalent sbatch cmdline flags). Prefer in-script directives so the job is self-contained.
- Set up a reproducible runtime environment (modules, conda/env activation, container) and record versions (git commit, pip freeze).
- Use srun for parallel/accelerated work when possible (srun knows Slurm’s allocation and topology). Use mpirun only if your MPI implementation requires it — prefer srun for MPI on modern clusters.
- Add simple failure handling and debugging aids (set -euo pipefail, traps to handle TERM signals).
- Test locally / with a tiny allocation before large runs. Use job arrays for parameter sweeps.

Annotated example template
(Adapt fields like partition, time, gres, mem, nodes for your cluster.)

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my_analysis             # job name
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out                 # %x = job name, %j = job id
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err                  # separate stderr file (optional)
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                    # partition/queue
#SBATCH --nodes=1                          # number of nodes
#SBATCH --ntasks=1                         # number of MPI ranks/tasks
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8                  # threads per task (OpenMP / threads)
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                       # GPUs per node (use cluster convention)
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00                    # walltime (HH:MM:SS)
#SBATCH --mem=32G                          # memory (or use --mem-per-cpu)
#SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL,END               # optional notifications
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# Fail fast and make debugging easier
set -euo pipefail
trap 'echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID received SIGTERM or ended"; exit 1' TERM

# Optional: log some Slurm environment variables for debugging
echo "Job: $SLURM_JOB_ID, Name: $SLURM_JOB_NAME"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_NODELIST, NTASKS: $SLURM_NTASKS, CPUS_PER_TASK: $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"

# Switch to working directory (or use --workdir)
cd $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR

# Load modules or activate environments
module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/11.8
source /path/to/venv/bin/activate

# Export thread controls for hybrid codes
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=$OMP_NUM_THREADS

# Use SLURM_TMPDIR for temporary scratch if available
mkdir -p $SLURM_TMPDIR/myjob && cd $SLURM_TMPDIR/myjob

# Run the work — prefer srun
srun --mpi=pmix bash -c 'python train.py --config configs/foo.yaml'

# Optional: copy outputs back to $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR
cp -r $SLURM_TMPDIR/myjob/* $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR/

Key explanations and tips
- Job naming and outputs: use --output with %x/%j so logs are easy to find and unique. Consider --open-mode=append if you rerun.
- Time limits: request slightly more than expected runtime. If you don’t know, run a short debug job and profile. Large overestimates can hurt scheduling fairness.
- CPUs vs tasks:
  - Pure MPI: set --ntasks=N and --cpus-per-task=1 (or >1 for multi-threaded MPI).
  - Threaded/OpenMP: set --ntasks=1 and --cpus-per-task=threads.
  - Hybrid: set both accordingly (ntasks = MPI ranks per node * nodes).
- GPUs: use the cluster’s convention (usually --gres=gpu:COUNT). Avoid assuming driver visibility; use nvidia-smi to check.
- Memory: prefer --mem-per-cpu when memory scales with threads, or --mem for whole-job memory.
- Containers: use Singularity/Apptainer for reproducibility. For GPU containers use the runtime flag (e.g., singularity exec --nv).
- Job arrays: use #SBATCH --array=1-100 to sweep many parameter sets. Inside the script, use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index parameters/files.
- Dependencies: chain jobs with --dependency=afterok:<jobid> for workflows.
- Resource accounting: request QoS/account if your cluster requires it.
- Testing/debugging: use small resources and small datasets first. For interactive debugging, use salloc/srun --pty or the cluster’s interactive partition.
- Cleanup and exit codes: ensure non-zero exit codes are propagated. Use set -e and check return codes when using conditional sequences.
- Signal handling: trap TERM to checkpoint or clean temporary files when possible. Slurm sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL.

Useful commands to monitor and diagnose jobs
- squeue -j $JOBID or squeue -u $USER to view active jobs and reasons.
- sacct -j $JOBID --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS,TotalCPU to see final usage.
- scontrol show job $JOBID for detailed job config and reason for pending state.
- sinfo to inspect partitions and node states.

Small checklist before submitting
- [ ] Does the #SBATCH header accurately reflect resources?
- [ ] Are modules/containers pinned to versions or a recorded environment snapshot included?
- [ ] Is output/error redirected to sensible files (with jobid)?
- [ ] Are thread/MPI env vars set (OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS)?
- [ ] Is there a small test submission that runs and produces expected results?
- [ ] Are temporary files placed on $SLURM_TMPDIR and cleaned/copied back?

If you want, I can:
- Provide a more specific template tuned to MPI, GPU deep learning, or a Python data pipeline.
- Review a draft of your script and suggest improvements (paste it here).

Useful options you’ll commonly use (can go in the script as #SBATCH lines or on the sbatch command line):

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Here’s a compact, practical Slurm tutorial you can use to get started, submit jobs, and debug common problems. I’ll cover core concepts, common commands, example job scripts (batch and interactive), job arrays & dependencies, resource/GPU guidance, and quick troubleshooting tips.

Core concepts
- slurmctld: the controller (scheduler) that accepts and runs jobs.
- Node / partition: nodes are compute machines; partitions are named queues (groups of nodes) you submit to.
- Job: a unit of work you submit (sbatch) or run interactively (srun/salloc).
- TRES/gres: trackable resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs). GPUs are requested via gres (e.g., --gres=gpu:1).
- QOS, accounts, fairshare: policies that control priority and limits.
- Job states: PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.

Quick commands (most useful)
- sbatch <script.sh> — submit a batch job.
- srun ... — run a command inside an allocation (interactive or inside job).
- salloc ... — allocate resources interactively (gives a shell).
- squeue [-u user] [-p partition] — view queued/running jobs.
- sinfo — view partitions and node states.
- sacct — query finished job accounting/history.
- scontrol show job <id> — show detailed job info.
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.
- sstat -j <jobid> — (running jobs) live stats (CPU, memory).
- scontrol show node <nodename> — node details.

Simple sbatch script (example)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=job-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
# If you need GPUs:
# #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Notes:
- %j expands to the job ID in output filenames.
- Use module load (or your site’s environment management) to set environment.
- Put srun before the main command in scripts to ensure correct allocation/smp behavior.

Interactive / debug sessions
- Quick interactive shell on a partition:
  srun --partition=debug --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 --time=00:30:00 --pty bash
- Or request an allocation and then run commands:
  salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=8 --time=01:00:00
  Then run srun or the commands you need in the allocation shell.

Job arrays
- For many similar tasks (e.g., parameter sweeps):
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10
# inside script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- %10 limits concurrent tasks to 10.

Job dependencies
- Submit job B after A completes successfully:
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobidA> jobB.sh
- other options: afterany, aftercorr, singleton, etc.

Checking job status & reasons
- squeue -j <jobid> or squeue -u $USER shows pending reasons (if reported).
- If squeue doesn’t show a reason or you need more detail: scontrol show job <jobid>.
- Common pending reasons: Resources, Priority, PartitionTimeLimit, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSMaxJobsPerUser.

GPU-specific tips
- Request GPUs explicitly: --gres=gpu:1 (or gpu:tesla:2 if your cluster uses types).
- Use sinfo to find GPU partitions: sinfo -o "%P %G %D %C" or ask your admin for partition names.
- When checking availability for conditional submissions, only count nodes listed as idle for GPU allocation (allocated/mixed/down/drained are not available).
- Inside job, GPU devices are typically visible via nvidia-smi; environment variables like CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES may be set.

Accounting & historical data
- sacct -j <jobid> or sacct -u <user> to view completed jobs (exit codes, elapsed, resource usage).
- sreport and sshare for usage/fairshare summaries (admin-level).

Common troubleshooting checklist
- Job stuck PENDING:
  - Run squeue to see the reason. If not present, scontrol show job <id>.
  - Check partition limits, QOS, account charges/limits.
  - Check node states with sinfo; if nodes are drained/down they reduce capacity.
- Job fails quickly with non-zero exit:
  - Inspect job-%j.err and job-%j.out.
  - Verify modules, paths, environment variables in the batch script.
  - Use small test jobs with shorter time and less memory to reproduce.
- Job out-of-memory:
  - Increase --mem or request more CPUs-per-task if memory is per-core.
  - Use ulimit or check container limits if running inside one.
- Node-specific hardware failures:
  - scontrol show node <name> and sinfo -R to see reasons/drain messages.
- No GPU seen inside job:
  - Confirm --gres is requested in sbatch/srun.
  - Check nvidia-smi; confirm module/drivers loaded.

Best practices
- Start small: request minimal resources and short walltime for testing.
- Make output and error files explicit so logs are preserved.
- Use job arrays for parameter sweeps rather than many individual sbatch calls.
- Use dependencies to serialize multi-stage workflows.
- Keep reproducible environment: modules, container images (Singularity/Apptainer).
- Ask your cluster admins for site-specific queues, limits, and recommended partitions.

Useful environment variables inside jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NAME, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE, SLURM_NODELIST

Where to learn more
- Your cluster’s user guide / FAQ (site-specific policies and partitions).
- Official Slurm docs (scheduling, sbatch, srun, scontrol): see slurm.schedmd.com
- For command syntax and reason codes: use lookup_slurm_docs or man pages (man sbatch, man squeue).

If you’d like, I can:
- Create a job script tailored to your application (give partition, CPUs, memory, GPUs, time).
- Walk through diagnosing a specific stuck or failed job (give job ID).
- Show example sbatch + sbatch dependency + array combined script.

Which of the above would you like next?

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It shows defensive shell settings, clean setup/teardown, recommended SBATCH directives, sensible environment handling (threading, modules, venv), and how to launch your workload with srun. Comments explain why each block is useful.

Example safe sbatch script pattern
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=example_job             # short name
#SBATCH --output=%x-%j.out                 # %x=name, %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                    # change to your partition
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                       # request GPUs if needed
#SBATCH --account=your_account             # optional
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL               # optional notifications
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

# ----------------- defensive shell setup -----------------
set -euo pipefail        # fail fast on errors / undefined variables / pipeline failures
IFS=$'\n\t'              # safer word-splitting

# Helpful env shorthands provided by Slurm:
# $SLURM_JOB_ID, $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, $SLURM_NTASKS, $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR, ...
echo "Starting job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $(hostname) at $(date)"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST  Tasks: $SLURM_NTASKS  CPUs/task: $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK"

# ----------------- temporary workspace & cleanup -----------------
TMPDIR=${TMPDIR:-/scratch/${USER}/${SLURM_JOB_ID}}
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"
chmod 700 "$TMPDIR"

cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Cleanup: return code $rc"
  # copy back artifacts if running on remote scratch (safe example)
  # rsync -av "$TMPDIR"/results/ "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"/results/ || true
  rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
}
trap cleanup EXIT

# ----------------- environment / modules / venv -----------------
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"    # run where user submitted
module purge
module load python/3.10   # example; use your site's modules

# Set threaded-library affinities to match allocated CPUs
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}
export MKL_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}
export NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-1}

# Activate virtualenv / conda if needed
# source /path/to/venv/bin/activate

# ----------------- optional GPU check -----------------
if command -v nvidia-smi &>/dev/null; then
  echo "GPUs visible on node:"
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.total --format=csv,noheader
fi

# ----------------- run your job (use srun for Slurm-managed launch) -----------------
# - Prefer srun for launching parallel work so Slurm can track processes.
# - Use --cpu-bind or --distribution if needed for affinity.
srun --cpu-bind=cores my_program --arg1 val1

# For MPI-style jobs, use: srun --mpi=pmix ./a.out
# For single-process jobs that internally multi-thread, just run the command (srun is still fine).

# ----------------- finish -----------------
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID finished at $(date)"

Best-practice notes (short)
- Put all SBATCH directives at the top (before any non-comment line); sbatch stops parsing after the first non-comment.
- Use set -euo pipefail and trap cleanup to avoid leaving junk and to capture failures.
- Prefer srun (not mpirun) unless you have a special MPI runtime requirement; srun integrates with Slurm for accounting and node-local launch.
- Set OMP_NUM_THREADS / MKL_NUM_THREADS to SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK to avoid oversubscription.
- Don’t hard-code absolute paths to cluster-specific commands; use module system or documented environment modules.
- Be cautious with credentials and environment variables (don’t write secrets to shared TMPDIR).
- For array jobs include #SBATCH --array=1-100%10 and use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to isolate per-task work directories.
- For GPU conditional logic: if you need to submit only when idle GPUs exist, query sinfo first (operator-side requirement for conditional submits).

If you want, I can produce:
- a version tailored for multi-node MPI (showing srun --mpi and NMPI layout),
- a GPU-training template that includes torch/cuda checks and checkpoint safe-save/restore,
- or an array-job template that safely creates per-task tempdirs and collects results. Which one would you like?

results.prompt: Explain basic Slurm submission steps
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise, practical guide to the basic Slurm batch-submission workflow and the most-used options.

1) Prepare a batch script
- Create a shell script (e.g., myjob.sh) starting with a shebang (#!/bin/bash).
- Add SBATCH directives (lines beginning with #SBATCH) to request resources and set job metadata. Common directives:
  - --job-name=NAME
  - --partition=PARTITION
  - --nodes=N
  - --ntasks=NTASKS
  - --cpus-per-task=CPUS
  - --mem=16G (or --mem-per-cpu=4G)
  - --time=HH:MM:SS
  - --output=slurm-%j.out / --error=err-%j.out
  - --account=ACCOUNT, --qos=QOS
  - --gres=gpu:1  (or cluster may support --gpus=)
  - --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@site.edu
- After the SBATCH lines, put the commands to run (module loads, srun, mpirun, python, etc.). Use srun for launching MPI/parallel tasks where possible.

Example minimal script:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=hello
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --output=job-%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py

2) Submit the job
- sbatch myjob.sh
- sbatch prints the assigned job ID and exits; the job may remain pending until resources free up.
- Command-line options override scripts: sbatch --time=02:00:00 myjob.sh

3) Monitor the job
- squeue -u $USER (shows PENDING / RUNNING jobs)
- squeue -j <jobid> or scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed info (allocations, reason for pending)
- sstat -j <jobid> for live stats of running jobs (if supported)
- sacct -j <jobid> for accounting info after completion

4) Common job operations
- Cancel: scancel <jobid>
- Hold / release / requeue: scontrol hold/release/requeue <jobid> (admin actions)
- Job arrays: #SBATCH --array=1-100 and access index via $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- Dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> myjob.sh

5) Interactive testing and debugging
- salloc --partition=short --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --time=00:30:00   (gives an interactive allocation)
- sbatch small test scripts before scaling to many nodes
- Use small time limits and check slurm-<jobid>.out to iterate quickly

6) Useful tips / gotchas
- Always request a realistic time limit; short limits help scheduling and faster turnaround.
- Time format is HH:MM:SS (some clusters accept days).
- Output file defaults to slurm-<jobid>.out unless overridden.
- Prefer srun to launch tasks inside batch scripts (it integrates with Slurm’s job step management).
- GPU and other resource flags can be cluster-dependent (gres or --gpus). Check local cluster docs.
- If a job is pending, check the REASON column in squeue; scontrol show job <id> gives more detail.
- Use sacct for historical accounting (finished jobs), squeue for current queue.

If you want, I can:
- Provide a tailored example script for your application (MPI, GPU PyTorch, multi-task), or
- Show common sbatch examples for arrays, dependencies, or GPU requests. Which would you like?

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, well‑written batch script makes jobs more reliable, reproducible, and debuggable. Below are practical guidelines, common pitfalls, and a few compact example scripts you can adapt.

Core principles
- Request only what you need and be explicit. Accurate time/memory/CPU/GPU requests reduce queue wait time and scheduling inefficiency.
- Keep environment setup inside the script (module loads, conda/singularity setup) so the job is reproducible.
- Use srun to launch workload processes so Slurm controls placement and accounting (especially for MPI/parallel jobs).
- Make output/logging predictable (use SLURM variables) and capture both stdout and stderr.
- Fail fast and surface useful diagnostic info (set -euo pipefail, print Slurm env vars, trap signals for cleanup/checkpoint).
- Test interactively or with a very short test job before running large/long requests.

Useful #SBATCH options (common and recommended)
- --job-name=NAME             (human‑readable name)
- --partition=PART            (or -p)
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --nodes=N
- --ntasks=NT                 (total MPI ranks / processes)
- --ntasks-per-node=TPN
- --cpus-per-task=CPT         (threads per task, for OpenMP)
- --mem=MEM or --mem-per-cpu=MEM
- --gres=gpu:COUNT            (GPU requests)
- --output=path/%x-%j.out     (%x job name, %j jobid)
- --error=path/%x-%j.err
- --mail-type=END,FAIL,BEGIN   and --mail-user=you@domain
- --array=0-N%M               (job arrays)
- --constraint=...            (node feature constraints)
- --exclusive                 (reserve whole node)
- --requeue/--no-requeue      (control requeue behavior)
Tip: put commonly changed values at top as variables so it's easy to modify.

Slurm environment variables your script should reference
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NAME
- SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR
- SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (for arrays)

Good scripting practices
- Start robustly:
  - set -euo pipefail
  - IFS=$'\n\t'
- Clean module state: module purge; module load <needed modules>
- Create and use per‑job scratch directory: TMPDIR=$SCRATCH/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID; mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"
- Use srun for every parallel/mpi process: srun --mpi=pmix ./my_mpi_app
- Redirect logs: --output=logs/%x-%j.out and capture stderr
- Use %j and %x in filenames to avoid collisions
- Trap termination to checkpoint or copy data back:
  - trap 'echo "SIGTERM received"; do_cleanup' TERM
- Use --test-only (sbatch --test-only) or short test jobs to validate
- Avoid backgrounding processes unless you manage them; Slurm expects the job script to manage lifecycle
- Prefer --mem-per-cpu for CPU-heavy apps, --mem for node-level reservations
- For GPUs: request --gres=gpu:N and ensure your container/runtime will see them (nvidia/cuda drivers on nodes)
- For MPI: prefer srun to mpirun unless your MPI is launched explicitly via mpirun configured for Slurm; ensure ranks match NTASKS

Debugging tips
- Print SLURM variables at start (echo "Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST ...")
- Run small scale locally or via an interactive allocation (salloc/srun --pty)
- Use sacct --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed to inspect completed jobs
- Use --mail-type=FAIL to notify on failures
- Reproduce environment locally with module list and container images

Examples

Minimal serial job
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=hello
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=1G
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
set -euo pipefail
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
./my_program --input data.in

GPU job (single node, 1 GPU)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=train
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
set -euo pipefail
module purge
module load cuda/11.8 python/3.10
source /path/to/env/bin/activate
srun python train.py --epochs 50

Job array example (parameter sweep)
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=array-job
#SBATCH --partition=short
#SBATCH --array=0-9%4
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --mem=4G
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%A_%a.out
set -euo pipefail
PARAMS=(alpha beta gamma delta epsilon zeta eta theta iota kappa)
MY_PARAM=${PARAMS[$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID]}
srun ./run_experiment --param "$MY_PARAM"

Advanced tips (short)
- Use cpu binding and topology hints: srun --cpu_bind=cores --hint=nomultithread
- Use --gres-flags=enforce if you must strictly enforce GPU allocation (if supported)
- Use containers (singularity) for reproducible environments: singularity exec image.sif python ...
- For long jobs add checkpointing and requeue support
- Use job dependencies: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> next_job.sh
- Monitor resource usage with sstat for running jobs and sacct/sreport for historical usage

Common mistakes to avoid
- Underestimating time and getting killed (ask for a realistic time)
- Not loading modules or relying on interactive shell state
- Writing output to a shared filesystem without staging (can be slow)
- Launching MPI processes without srun or mismatched NTASKS
- Over-requesting resources (wastes queue capacity) or under-requesting (causes job failure)

If you want, tell me:
- whether your workload is serial, multi‑threaded, MPI, or GPU;
- typical runtime and resource needs;
and I can produce a tailored script for your cluster and use case.

Minimal steps

2. Submit it with: sbatch my_job.sh
3. Check status with: squeue -u your_username (or sacct for finished jobs)

#SBATCH --mem=8G

python train.py --epochs 10

GPU example

#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1          # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --output=gpu-%j.out

module load cuda/11.8
python train_gpu.py

Common useful sbatch options
- --partition or -p: partition/queue
- --time or -t: runtime limit (HH:MM:SS or D-HH:MM:SS)
- --ntasks, --cpus-per-task: MPI vs thread cores
- --nodes: number of nodes
- --gres=gpu:N: request GPUs
- --mem or --mem-per-cpu: memory
- --job-name or -J, --output, --error
- --mail-type/--mail-user: email notifications
- --qos: quality of service
- --array=1-100: job arrays
- --dependency=afterok:<jobid>: chain jobs
- --export=ALL or --export=VAR=val: environment variables

Interactive / debug
- salloc to allocate an interactive allocation, then srun / bash inside it.
- srun --pty bash -i for a direct interactive shell (if allowed).

Tips / best practices
- Request only what you need (time, CPUs, mem, GPUs) to avoid long waits.
- Put module loads/conda activate and setup in the script so runs are reproducible.
- Use --output with %j or --job-name for easier logs.
- For MPI/ multi-node, use srun within the script to launch tasks across nodes.
- For GPU jobs, ensure your code respects CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES or uses local rank when launched with srun.

- resources you need (CPUs, GPUs, mem, time, partition),
and I can draft a ready-to-submit sbatch script for you.

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Sure — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial that covers the common workflows, commands, examples, and troubleshooting tips you’ll need to run jobs on an HPC cluster.

What Slurm is (quick)
- Slurm is a job scheduler: it allocates nodes/CPUs/GPUs, queues jobs, and enforces limits (time, mem, QOS, accounts).
- Key components: slurmctld (controller), slurmd (node daemon), scheduler, and accounting DB.

Common CLI tools
- sbatch: submit a batch script (non-interactive jobs).
- srun: run a job step (can be used inside a batch or for interactive tasks).
- salloc: allocate resources interactively (gives you an allocation to run commands with srun).
- squeue: view the queue and job states.
- scancel: cancel jobs.
- sinfo: view partitions and node states.
- scontrol show job <JOBID>: detailed job info and pending reason.
- sacct: historical/accounting info about completed jobs.
- sstat: runtime resource stats for running jobs.

Basic batch job script (example)
- Save as train.sh and submit with: sbatch train.sh

Example train.sh:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=train-demo
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1              # request 1 GPU (if cluster supports GPUs)
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com

module load cuda/11.8
srun python train.py --epochs 10

Key sbatch/srun options (common)
- --partition (or -p): partition/queue name
- --nodes, --ntasks, --ntasks-per-node
- --cpus-per-task (or -c): threads per task
- --gres=gpu:<count> : GPUs
- --mem or --mem-per-cpu
- --time: wallclock limit (HH:MM:SS)
- --output / --error: paths for stdout/stderr
- --job-name
- --array=1-100[%20]: job arrays, with concurrency limit
- --dependency=afterok:<jobid> : dependencies between jobs

Interactive work
- Get an interactive allocation:
  salloc --partition=interactive --nodes=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --time=01:00:00
  Then run: srun --pty bash   (or srun --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash)
- Or launch a single interactive command:
  srun --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=00:30:00 python -i script.py

Job arrays
- Submit many similar jobs: #SBATCH --array=1-100
- Use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside your script to pick input/seed.
- Useful for parameter sweeps or many small independent tasks.

Dependencies and pipelines
- Chain jobs:
  j1=$(sbatch job1.sh)   # returns job submission line with ID
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid> job2.sh
- Dependencies: afterok, afterany, aftercorr, singleton, expand.

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -u $USER         : list your active jobs
- squeue -j <JOBID>       : check a specific job
- scontrol show job <JOBID> or scontrol show jobid <JOBID> : full details (look for Reason)
- sacct -j <JOBID> -o JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed : historical/completed info
- tail -n 200 slurm-<jobid>.out : check your job’s stdout/stderr
- sstat -j <jobid>        : real-time stats for a running job (CPU, memory, I/O)

Common pending reasons & fixes
- Resources: waiting for nodes/GPUs — reduce resource request, change partition, or wait.
- Priority: low priority — use fairshare/QOS adjustments or request maintenance window.
- PartitionDown or NodeDown: admins must fix nodes; choose another partition if available.
- Dependency: job waiting for dependency to finish — ensure dependent job completed successfully.
- QOS or account limit: check quotas or ask admin to increase.

Good practices
- Ask only for what you need: over-requesting time/CPUs/GPUs delays scheduling.
- Test with short, small jobs first.
- Set a realistic --time; jobs killed at time limit are often lost work.
- Use job arrays for many similar small tasks instead of many separate submissions.
- Redirect logs (use --output and --error) and check them for failures.
- Use modules/environment setup at script start so runs are reproducible.
- Use checkpoints or periodic saves for long jobs.
- Include --mail-type or add explicit monitoring if results are critical.

Advanced: GPUs, multi-node MPI, and topology
- GPUs: request with --gres=gpu:<N>. If you need specific models or binding, consult cluster docs.
- MPI: typically use srun to launch MPI tasks across nodes (srun launches processes and binds them correctly).
- Affinity: use --cpus-per-task and environment variables (OMP_NUM_THREADS) to control thread binding.

Troubleshooting checklist (if job doesn’t start or fails quickly)
1. squeue -j <JOBID> and scontrol show job <JOBID> — look at State and Reason.
2. sinfo -N -l or sinfo --partition=<name> — check node and partition health.
3. Check account/QOS limits (contact admin if you hit limits).
4. Inspect job stdout/err files and module/environment loads.
5. Run a tiny job that just prints hostname and env to ensure your script works.

Where to learn more
- Cluster-specific documentation (policies, partitions, module lists).
- Slurm official docs (sacct, sbatch, srun, scontrol man pages).
- Ask cluster admins for best practices and available partitions/QOS.

If you want, I can:
- Give a minimal one-line test job to verify your environment.
- Review a job script you’re planning to submit.
- Show commands to investigate why a specific job (give job ID) is pending or failed.

Which would you like next?

results.prompt: Show me a safe sbatch script pattern
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, safe sbatch script pattern you can copy and adapt. It includes defensive shell settings, common SBATCH directives, signal trapping/cleanup, environment capture, and recommended runtime practices (use srun for commands, stage I/O to fast local scratch, etc.). Put ALL #SBATCH lines before the first non-comment line in the script.

Example safe sbatch script pattern (edit values to your site/needs):

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob                 # short name
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out            # %j = jobid
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                  # partition name
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                     # request 1 GPU (if needed)
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00                  # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL              # optional
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com       # optional
#SBATCH --export=ALL                      # or NONE and explicitly set env

# ---- defensive shell options ----
set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

# ---- useful env / bookkeeping ----
echo "Job: ${SLURM_JOB_ID} on ${SLURM_JOB_NODELIST}"
echo "Started at: $(date)"
echo "Command line: $0 $*"

# ---- setup local scratch and cleanup ----
SCRATCH_DIR="${TMPDIR:-/scratch}/${USER}/job_${SLURM_JOB_ID}"
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH_DIR"
echo "Using scratch: $SCRATCH_DIR"

cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Cleaning up. Exit code=$rc"
  # Example: copy results back, remove large temp files
  # rsync -av --remove-source-files "$SCRATCH_DIR"/ /home/${USER}/results/job_${SLURM_JOB_ID}/
  rm -rf "$SCRATCH_DIR"
  echo "Cleanup done at: $(date)"
}
trap 'cleanup' EXIT INT TERM

# ---- load modules / conda / env ----
module purge
module load cuda/12.1   # example; use your site modules
# source /path/to/conda.sh
# conda activate myenv

# ---- resource-affinity hints (optional) ----
# export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-8}
# export MKL_NUM_THREADS=${OMP_NUM_THREADS}

# ---- run work using srun (not plain mpirun unless site requires) ----
# srun will respect the allocation and integrate with Slurm accounting
srun --cpu_bind=cores my_program --input data.in --output "$SCRATCH_DIR"/out.bin

# ---- final status ----
echo "Finished at: $(date)"

Short notes / best practices
- Always keep #SBATCH directives at top (before any non-comment). Slurm stops reading #SBATCH after first non-comment line.
- Use set -euo pipefail and a trap handler to ensure cleanup runs on failure/kill.
- Use srun for commands inside the job so Slurm applies the allocation and task pinning.
- Stage large I/O to node-local fast scratch ($TMPDIR or /tmp) and copy back on exit; avoid NFS hot-spotting.
- Set OMP_NUM_THREADS / MKL_NUM_THREADS to match cpus-per-task to avoid oversubscription.
- Use --output/--error with %j for traceable logs; consider --open-mode=append if reruns should append.
- Prefer --export=NONE and explicitly pass only needed env vars to avoid leaking secrets.
- For GPU work, request gres and ensure CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is handled by your site or set via srun.
- Keep runtime limits slightly higher than expected to avoid premature timeout; monitor and tune.

If you want, tell me:
- the job type (GPU/CPU, MPI, multi-task), and I’ll produce a tuned template (MPI, multi-node, or GPU-training) for your cluster conventions.

results.prompt: Explain basic Slurm submission steps
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise, practical overview of the basic Slurm batch-submission workflow and the common options you’ll use.

1) Create a batch script
- Start with a shell shebang: #!/bin/bash
- Put all Slurm options as #SBATCH directives at the top (before the first non-comment line) or pass them on the sbatch command line.
- Typical directives to include:
  - Partition: #SBATCH -p gpu
  - Job name: #SBATCH -J myjob
  - Time limit: #SBATCH -t 02:00:00  (HH:MM:SS)
  - Nodes/tasks/CPUs:
    - #SBATCH -N 1            (nodes)
    - #SBATCH --ntasks=1     (tasks, MPI ranks)
    - #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  - Memory: #SBATCH --mem=16G  or per-cpu #SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G
  - GPUs: #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1  (or #SBATCH --gpus=1 on newer Slurm)
  - Output files: #SBATCH -o myjob.%j.out  #SBATCH -e myjob.%j.err
  - Account/QOS: #SBATCH -A myacct  #SBATCH --qos=high
  - Job arrays: #SBATCH --array=1-10%2
  - Dependencies (when submitting): sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 script.sh
- After directives, load modules, set up env, copy data if necessary, then launch your app (prefer srun for process launch under Slurm).
Example minimal script:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH -J myjob
#SBATCH -p gpu
#SBATCH -N 1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH -t 02:00:00
#SBATCH -o myjob.%j.out

module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --epochs 10

2) Submit the job
- Submit: sbatch myscript.sh
- sbatch will print: Submitted batch job <JOBID>

3) Monitor job state
- squeue -u $USER (shows RUNNING/PENDING etc.)
- squeue -j <JOBID> or scontrol show job <JOBID> (detailed)
- sstat -j <jobid> (live resource usage for running jobs)
- sacct -j <JOBID> (after completion for accounting/exit codes)

4) Inspect reasons for pending jobs
- squeue shows a PENDING reason column; for a specific job you can also run scontrol show job <JOBID> to see detailed pending reason.

5) Cancel / modify
- Cancel: scancel <JOBID>
- Some job attributes (like time limit or account) can be changed by admins with scontrol update; normal users can’t arbitrarily change most attributes after submission.

6) Job arrays & environment variables
- Use #SBATCH --array=1-100 and inside the script reference $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- Useful env vars: $SLURM_JOB_ID, $SLURM_NTASKS, $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK

7) Debugging & good practices
- Test interactively on a small interactive allocation (salloc or srun --pty) or run a very short job first.
- Request realistic time and memory; under-requesting causes OOM/timeouts, over-requesting increases wait time and wastes quota.
- Capture stdout/stderr to files with jobid substitution (%j) for debugging.
- Use srun to launch MPI or parallel tasks so Slurm manages placement.
- For reproducibility, record module list and environment in the output.
- Stage large data to node-local or parallel filesystem before running if I/O is heavy; clean up temporary files.
- Use job arrays to run many similar tasks efficiently (and throttle with %N).

8) Useful commands quick cheat-sheet
- Submit: sbatch script.sh
- Show queue: squeue -u $USER
- Show job: scontrol show job <JOBID>
- Live stats: sstat -j <JOBID>
- Accounting/historical: sacct -j <JOBID>
- Cancel: scancel <JOBID>

If you want, I can:
- Show an example script tailored to your application (MPI / GPU / multi-threaded).
- Explain differences between ntasks, cpus-per-task, and tasks-per-node.
- Walk through creating and submitting a job array or a GPU-conditional submit. Which would you like?

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, well‑written sbatch script makes jobs reliable, debuggable, and efficient. Below is a compact checklist, followed by a small reusable script template and explanations of the most important directives and best practices.

Checklist (what every good script includes)
- Shebang and fail-fast shell settings (set -euo pipefail).
- Explicit SBATCH directives: job-name, output/error, time, partition, account/QOS, nodes/ntasks/cpus-per-task, memory or mem-per-cpu, gres for GPUs.
- Use srun to launch the actual workload (not plain executable calls) so Slurm tracks tasks correctly.
- Load modules / activate environments before srun.
- Use absolute paths for input/output and stage large data to the compute filesystem.
- Log useful environment variables (SLURM_JOB_ID, NODELIST, etc.) and the job script itself for reproducibility.
- Use traps (SIGTERM) for graceful shutdown or checkpointing when possible.
- Give conservative (not minimal) time limits; test interactively first.
- For arrays, use --array and $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID; throttle large arrays with %limit.

Minimal sbatch template
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob_name
#SBATCH --output=/path/to/logs/%x_%A_%a.out   # %x job-name, %A master jobid, %a array id
#SBATCH --error=/path/to/logs/%x_%A_%a.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --account=proj123
#SBATCH --qos=normal
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
#SBATCH --mem=32G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                # request 1 GPU (if needed)
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10            # optional: job array of 100 with max 10 concurrent

set -euo pipefail
umask 022

echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_NAME ($SLURM_JOB_ID) started on $(date)"
echo "Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
echo "Array task: ${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID:-NA}"

module purge
module load python/3.10 cuda/12.0        # load required modules
source /path/to/venv/bin/activate        # or container runtime (singularity/podman/docker)

# change to the directory where data/script reside
cd /path/to/working/dir

# if array job: compute input based on SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
INPUT_FILE=$(printf "inputs/input_%03d.txt" "$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID")

# run with srun so Slurm applies allocation & tracking
srun --mpi=none python train.py --input "$INPUT_FILE" --epochs 10

echo "Job finished at $(date)"

Key directive explanations
- --time: set slightly higher than expected runtime. If a job is killed due to timeout you lose work; for long jobs consider checkpointing.
- --nodes, --ntasks, --cpus-per-task: map to your parallelism model. For MPI use ntasks (one per rank) and srun --mpi; for multi-threaded codes use cpus-per-task.
- --mem vs --mem-per-cpu: use --mem for per-node memory allotment, --mem-per-cpu for per-core.
- --gres=gpu:N: request GPUs; Slurm usually sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES automatically; don’t hardcode GPU indexes.
- --output/--error: include %A and %a in names for arrays to avoid collisions.
- --array: throttle with %limit so scheduler/DB isn’t overwhelmed.
- --mail-type/mail-user: helpful for long jobs but may spam for frequent failures.

Good practices and tips
- Test interactively first: srun --pty --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 bash to iterate quickly.
- Start small: run a short, small test to validate I/O, modules, environment, and dependencies before large runs.
- Use containers (Singularity/Apptainer) or pinned environments for reproducibility.
- Stage input data to fast shared storage (or node-local when appropriate) and write outputs to stable storage.
- Be explicit about working directories (cd at top of script) to avoid confusing relative-path writes.
- Record the exact job script in logs (cp $0 "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR/job-${SLURM_JOB_ID}.sh") so you can reproduce.
- Make output idempotent: avoid writing to the same file from different tasks without coordination.
- Handle signals: trap SIGTERM to checkpoint if your workload supports graceful shutdown.
- Resource matching: request only what you need (don't over-request CPUs/GPU) — it helps scheduling fairness.
- Use --hint=nomultithread if hyperthreading hurts your workload, or --cpu-bind to control binding.
- For MPI, prefer srun --mpi=pmi2 or pmi2/spawn appropriate to your MPI build; don’t use mpirun without checking integration.
- Avoid heavy per-job metadata logging to the scheduler; aggregate logs off-node for analysis.

Monitoring and debugging
- While running: use squeue -j <jobid> and sstat -j <jobid> for live stats (sstat works for running jobs).
- After completion: sacct -j <jobid> to inspect exit codes and runtime.
- Capture stderr/stdout separately for easier failure triage.
- If jobs are pending, squeue shows pending reason. Use that to tune resource requests or QOS.

Common pitfalls
- Using relative paths or writing large scratch files to a non-local filesystem that’s slow.
- Forgetting to load modules / activate env in the batch script (works in interactive shell but not in batch).
- Requesting fewer cpus than threads spawned (causes oversubscription).
- Not providing enough time and getting killed at the last minute.
- Overloading login/submit nodes by launching heavy pre/post-processing in the submit host rather than inside the allocated job.

If you want, tell me:
- what kind of workload (MPI, multi-thread, GPU, single-task, array) and I’ll generate a tuned example script for that case, or
- paste your current batch script and I’ll review and suggest improvements.

#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=myjob.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=myjob.%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=standard
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00         # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G

module load python

- --nodes=N
- --ntasks-per-node=M
- --cpus-per-task=K

- --output=FILE, --error=FILE
- --account=ACCOUNT (or --acct=)
- --qos=QOS
- --dependency=afterok:<jobid> (job dependencies)
- --array=1-100 (job arrays)

You can also pass options on the sbatch command line:
sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=04:00:00 my_gpu_job.sh
or submit a one-liner:
sbatch --wrap="python quick_task.py" --time=00:10:00 --partition=short

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference — concepts, common commands, job script examples, troubleshooting tips, and best practices.

1) What Slurm is (brief)
- Slurm is a workload manager/scheduler for clusters. It allocates resources (nodes/CPUs/GPUs/memory), runs jobs, and enforces limits (time, QOS, partitions, accounts).

2) Key concepts & terminology
- Job: a batch or interactive workload submitted to Slurm.
- Node: a compute server.
- Partition: a named set of nodes (like a queue).
- QOS / account: policies and limits for users/groups.
- Allocation types: batch (sbatch), interactive allocation (salloc), and immediate runs (srun).
- Job array: many similar jobs managed as a single submission.
- Scheduler states: PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, NODE_FAIL, etc.

3) Common read-only commands (view cluster state)
- sinfo — view partition/node status (allocated/idle/down counts).
- squeue — view queued/running jobs (jobid, user, state, time, nodes).
- sacct — historical accounting (completed/failed jobs).
- scontrol show job <jobid> — detailed job info.
- scontrol show node <nodename> — detailed node info.
- sdiag / sprio / sshare — scheduler diagnostics, priority/fairshare.

4) Common mutating commands (submit/control jobs)
- sbatch <script.sh> — submit a batch script.
- srun [options] <command> — run a command in an allocation (or submit an interactive job if used inside salloc).
- salloc — get an interactive allocation, then use srun inside it.
- scancel <jobid> — cancel a job.
- scontrol hold/release/requeue — control job state (admins).

5) Typical sbatch header example
Use directives at top of script (they map to sbatch options):

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out        # %j = jobid
#SBATCH --error=slurm-%j.err
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00              # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                 # request 1 GPU
#SBATCH --array=1-100%10             # job array, max 10 concurrent

# load modules, run
module load python/3.10
srun python train.py --config cfg${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}.yaml

6) Important sbatch/srun options (common)
- --partition=NAME
- --time=HH:MM:SS
- --nodes=N and --ntasks / --ntasks-per-node
- --cpus-per-task (for multi-threaded tasks)
- --mem or --mem-per-cpu
- --gres=gpu:N (request GPUs)
- --job-name, --output, --error
- --array=IDX or START-END%MAXCONC (job arrays)
- --dependency=afterok:<jobid> (chain jobs)

7) Job arrays
- Submit once with --array=1-100; inside script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID.
- Useful for parameter sweeps; reduces scheduler overhead.

8) Dependencies
- --dependency=afterok:12345 (run only if job 12345 succeeds)
- Other types: afterany, aftercorr, after, singleton

9) Interactive work
- salloc --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00
- srun --pty bash  (or srun --x11 for GUI, or use srun to launch commands inside allocation)

10) Checking why a job is pending or stuck
- squeue -j <jobid> (see PENDING reason column)
- If squeue lacks detail, use scontrol show job <jobid> for full pending reason and constraints
- Common PENDING reasons: Resources, Priority, Dependency, Partition/QOS limits, ReqNodeNotAvail

11) Inspecting completed/failed jobs
- sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,ElapsedRaw
- Check slurm-%j.out and slurm-%j.err for stdout/stderr paths from your job script.

12) Resource accounting & limits
- sshare — view fairshare and usage.
- sacctmgr show user/account — account limits and associations (admin-only).
- QOS can impose max runtime, max jobs, preemption behavior.

13) Node/partition health
- sinfo — quick view of partitions and node counts (allocated/idle/down).
- sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons — list nodes in drain/down with reasons.
- scontrol show node <node> — detailed node condition (e.g., real memory, CPUs, features, reason).

14) Troubleshooting checklist
- For pending jobs: squeue (reason) → scontrol show job (details) → sinfo (are nodes free?) → check QOS/account limits.
- For failed jobs: sacct to see ExitCode → check stdout/stderr and job script for resource insufficiency or module errors.
- For running job issues: sstat <jobid> for live job resource usage (if supported).
- For scheduler problems: sdiag and sprio to inspect backfill and priorities (admin).

15) Best practices
- Do small test runs locally or with tiny resources before large runs.
- Request resources accurately (under-requesting causes failures; over-requesting wastes scheduling capacity).
- Use checkpoints and write intermediate output to persistent storage.
- Use job arrays for many similar runs.
- Use modules or containers (Singularity/Apptainer) for consistent environments.
- Capture stdout/stderr with descriptive file names (include %j).
- Don’t run large interactive workloads on login nodes — use salloc.
- Monitor quotas and fairshare; discuss change requests with admins.

16) Performance & scaling tips
- Use --cpus-per-task for multi-threaded programs (OpenMP).
- Use mpirun or srun for MPI jobs (prefer srun or MPI compiled with Slurm).
- Pack tasks per node intentionally: use --ntasks-per-node and task binding options (--cpu-bind).
- For GPU jobs, match CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES/OMP_NUM_THREADS to requested resources.

17) Where to learn more (official docs)
- Slurm official docs and man pages (man sbatch, srun, squeue, sinfo, sacct, scontrol).
- slurm.schedmd.com — reference and admin guides.
- Your cluster’s user guide / wiki for local policies (partitions, QOS, scratch, reservation rules).

If you want, I can:
- Walk through building a job script for a specific workflow (MPI, GPU, or multi-threaded).
- Explain a specific command or output (e.g., interpret your squeue line).
- Provide a checklist for debugging a particular job ID (if you give the job ID).

#!/bin/bash
#
# Safe, minimal sbatch job script pattern — edit the SBATCH values and the run steps below.
#
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob                 # short name
#SBATCH --output=%x.%j.out               # %x=jobname, %j=jobid
#SBATCH --error=%x.%j.err
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00                  # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --partition=gpu                  # or cpu partition name
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G                        # or --mem-per-cpu=4G
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1                     # only if you need GPUs
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL             # optional
#SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com      # optional
#SBATCH --export=ALL                     # export environment (or list vars)

set -euo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

# ---- Prepare job-local tmpdir and cleanup ----
# Use a unique tmpdir (local fast storage if available)
TMPDIR=${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/${USER}_${SLURM_JOB_ID}
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"
cleanup() {
  rc=$?
  echo "Job exiting with status $rc at $(date)"
  # copy logs/artifacts back to $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR or $SCRATCH here if needed
  # tar -czf "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR/${SLURM_JOB_NAME}_${SLURM_JOB_ID}.tgz" "$TMPDIR" || true
  rm -rf "$TMPDIR"
}
trap 'cleanup' EXIT
trap 'echo "Received SIGTERM, attempting graceful shutdown"; kill -- -$$' TERM INT

# ---- Diagnostics: useful info for debugging ----
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) started on $(hostname) at $(date)"
echo "Partition: $SLURM_JOB_PARTITION; Nodes: $SLURM_JOB_NODELIST"
echo "Working directory: $SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
echo "TMPDIR: $TMPDIR"
echo "Environment:"
env | sort

# ---- Environment tuning ----
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=${SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK:-4}   # thread libraries respect this
ulimit -c 0                                        # disable core dumps (optional)

# Load modules / activate envs
module purge
module load cuda/12.0 python/3.10   # example; use your site's modules
source ~/venvs/myenv/bin/activate

# Move to submission directory (good practice)
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"

# ---- Run the actual work with srun (preferred for proper Slurm accounting) ----
# Use srun so Slurm can track tasks and propagate signals correctly.
srun --cpu-bind=cores my_executable --threads "$OMP_NUM_THREADS" \
     --input data/input.dat --output results/out.${SLURM_JOB_ID}.dat

# Optionally run postprocessing (also via srun if it needs allocation)
# srun python postprocess.py results/out.${SLURM_JOB_ID}.dat

echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID finished at $(date)"

Notes / best practices:
- Put all #SBATCH directives at the top of the file before any executable lines; sbatch stops parsing directives at the first non-comment, non-whitespace line.
- Use set -euo pipefail and traps to ensure cleanup runs and failures are noticed.
- Use a job-local TMPDIR (fast local disk) and remove it in cleanup; copy outputs back to persistent storage before removing.
- Prefer srun to launch processes inside the allocation so Slurm can manage/kill them properly and account for resources.
- Set OMP_NUM_THREADS from SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK and tune thread affinity (e.g., --cpu-bind) for hybrid MPI/OpenMP jobs.
- Use explicit memory (--mem or --mem-per-cpu) and cpus (--cpus-per-task, --ntasks) requests to avoid OOM kills and scheduling surprises.
- Handle SIGTERM in your job so long-running programs can checkpoint or exit cleanly; trap kills process group to avoid stray children.
- Keep modules and virtualenv activation inside the script to ensure reproducible environments.
- For GPU jobs, request --gres=gpu:N and ensure your code targets the allocated devices (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set by Slurm on many systems).
- Log useful job metadata (hostname, node list, env, job id) at start for debugging.

If you want, I can adapt this template for: MPI jobs, multi-node GPU training (distributed), or for a specific cluster's module names and scratch paths. Which type would you like?

results.prompt: Explain basic Slurm submission steps
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise guide to the basic Slurm job submission workflow and the common options you’ll use.

1) Create a job script
- A job script is a shell script that contains SBATCH directives (job metadata) and the commands to run.
- Place SBATCH lines near the top, each beginning with #SBATCH.
- You do not need to make the file executable for sbatch to run it.

Example minimal script (save as job.sh):
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00        # HH:MM:SS
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --output=job.%j.out

module load python
srun python train.py     # or your command(s) here

2) Submit the job
- Use sbatch:
  sbatch job.sh
- sbatch prints a job ID on success (use that ID to monitor or cancel).

3) Monitor job state
- squeue to see queued/running jobs:
  squeue -u <username>
  squeue -j <jobid>
- For step-level details or to diagnose pending reasons you can use:
  scontrol show job <jobid>

4) View job output and accounting
- Stdout/stderr written to files you set with --output / --error (or combined with --output).
- For completed jobs and historical info, use sacct:
  sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,ExitCode

5) Cancel or manage jobs
- Cancel:
  scancel <jobid>
- Hold / release / requeue — cluster admin tools (scontrol variants) may be required.

6) Interactive jobs and allocations
- Short interactive shell allocation:
  srun --partition=interactive --pty bash
  (or)
  salloc --time=01:00:00 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4
- Use srun inside an allocation to launch tasks.

7) Common resource options
- Partition: --partition=NAME
- Nodes: --nodes=N
- Tasks: --ntasks=N
- CPUs per task: --cpus-per-task=N
- Memory: --mem=8G or --mem-per-cpu=2G
- GPUs: --gres=gpu:1 (or gpu:V100:2)
- Walltime: --time=HH:MM:SS
- Account/QoS: --account=acct --qos=long
- Job name, output: --job-name, --output

8) Useful features
- Job arrays: --array=1-100 to submit many similar jobs with $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID
- Dependencies: --dependency=afterok:<jobid> (run only after another succeeds)
- Email notifications: --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@domain
- Environment: load modules in the script; copy needed files to $TMPDIR if local scratch used.

9) Pre-submit checks and tips
- Check available partitions and node counts with sinfo
- Ensure requested resources (GPU type, partition, account) exist on your cluster
- Keep time/memory conservative for short/development runs to improve scheduling
- Test interactively or with small jobs before large submissions

10) Troubleshooting
- If job stays PENDING, run squeue -j <jobid> and inspect the REASON column. For detailed reason text use scontrol show job <jobid>.
- For failures, inspect the job.%j.out (and .err) files; use sacct for exit codes.

If you want, I can:
- Show a tailored example sbatch script for your workload (give CPU/GPU/time/memory).
- Explain how to submit a job array or set up dependencies.
- Or check current partitions/nodes (I’ll need to run sinfo).

results.prompt: How do I write a good Slurm batch script?
results.agent_response:
Good question — a clear, well-written batch script makes jobs easier to run, debug, and reproduce. Below are practical rules, common options, useful environment tricks, debugging tips, and two compact example scripts (simple and advanced).

Key principles
- Be explicit: request the resources you actually need (CPUs, memory, GPUs, time, partition, account/QOS).
- Fail fast and log: set bash safety flags, capture stdout/stderr, record timestamps and host info.
- Reproducible environment: load modules or activate conda/venv, capture versions/commit IDs.
- Use srun for parallel work inside the allocation; sbatch only submits the script.
- Avoid heavy I/O on shared storage — stage to node-local scratch when possible.

Header / syntax
- Put sbatch options as comments starting with #SBATCH (or pass them to sbatch on the command line).
- Example options you’ll use often:
  - --job-name=NAME
  - --partition=PART
  - --nodes=N
  - --ntasks=N (MPI tasks)
  - --cpus-per-task=M (for multithreaded tasks / OpenMP)
  - --mem=Xm or --mem-per-cpu=Ym
  - --gres=gpu:V (e.g., gpu:1)
  - --time=HH:MM:SS
  - --output=path/to/%x-%j.out and --error=...
  - --mail-type=END,FAIL --mail-user=you@example.com
  - --array=1-100%10 (job arrays with concurrency limit)
  - --account=project --qos=name
- Difference notes:
  - --mem is per node, --mem-per-cpu is per CPU.
  - Respect node layout: request CPUs/GPU counts that match node topology.

Bash best-practices inside the script
- Use strict bash options:
  - set -euo pipefail
- Add logging:
  - echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID ($SLURM_JOB_NAME) starting on $(hostname) at $(date)"
- Trap SIGTERM for graceful cleanup:
  - trap 'echo "SIGTERM received; cleaning up"; cleanup_cmds' TERM
- Export/define thread settings:
  - export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
  - export MKL_NUM_THREADS=$OMP_NUM_THREADS
- Use SLURM env vars: SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_NODELIST

Environment setup and reproducibility
- Load modules: module purge; module load python/3.10 cuda/12.0
- Activate environments: source /path/to/venv/bin/activate or conda activate env
- Record versions: python -c "import sys; print(sys.version)"; module list
- Optionally capture git commit: git rev-parse HEAD > commit.txt
- Keep scripts in version control and include the script in job output for traceability.

I/O and data handling
- Avoid writing many small files to shared filesystem; use node-local scratch ($TMPDIR, /dev/shm) for heavy I/O and stage out results at job end.
- Use rsync or cp for staged transfer; ensure cleanup on exit.
- Prefer streaming and chunked writes; compress logs if large.

Parallelism and GPUs
- For MPI: use srun --mpi=pmix -n $SLURM_NTASKS your_mpi_executable
- For hybrid (MPI+OpenMP): request cpus-per-task and set OMP_NUM_THREADS accordingly
- For GPU jobs: --gres=gpu:N and inside the job you can rely on CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set by the scheduler (or set it yourself if needed)
- Use device affinity tools (numactl, taskset) for performance-critical jobs

Job arrays and dependencies
- Use --array=START-END[%CONCURRENCY] and refer to SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside the script
- Chain jobs with --dependency=afterok:<jobid> or afterany

Security and secrets
- Don’t hardcode credentials. Read them from files with restricted permissions or environment variables injected at runtime.

Common pitfalls to avoid
- Over-requesting resources (wastes quota & delays scheduling)
- Forgetting to set cpus-per-task for multithreaded code (leads to oversubscription)

#SBATCH --job-name=myjob
#SBATCH --partition=compute
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1

#SBATCH --mem=8G

results.prompt: Slurm tutorial
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise, practical Slurm tutorial you can use as a quick reference: basic commands, typical sbatch examples (CPU, GPU, MPI, arrays), interactive usage, monitoring / debugging tips, and best practices.

Quick command reference
- sinfo — show partitions and node states (allocated/idle/down).
- squeue — show queued and running jobs (use -u $USER to filter).
- sbatch myjob.sh — submit a batch job script (non-interactive).
- srun — run a command inside an allocation or start tasks inside a batch job.
- salloc — request an interactive allocation (then use srun or run shell).
- scancel JOBID — cancel a job.
- scontrol show job JOBID — show detailed job configuration and reason for pending.
- sacct -j JOBID — accounting info for completed jobs.
- sstat -j JOBID — runtime stats for a running job (live resource usage).
- sinfo -R — list nodes in DRAIN/DOWN with reasons.

Minimal sbatch batch script (CPU job)
- Example file: myjob.sh
  #!/bin/bash
  #SBATCH --job-name=test
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
  #SBATCH --mem=8G
  #SBATCH --time=01:00:00
  #SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out
  module load python
  python train.py

- Submit: sbatch myjob.sh
- Output file: slurm-<JOBID>.out

Requesting GPUs
- Single-node GPU example:
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --ntasks=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1         # request 1 GPU (driver depends on cluster)
  #SBATCH --mem=32G
  #SBATCH --time=04:00:00

MPI / multi-node parallel job
- Use mpirun / srun inside the batch script:
  #SBATCH --nodes=2
  #SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=32
  #SBATCH --time=02:00:00
  module load mpi
  srun my_mpi_program   # srun launches the MPI tasks across allocation

Interactive usage
- Quick interactive allocation:
  salloc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00
  srun --pty bash -i      # get an interactive shell
- Or run a single interactive command:
  srun --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=01:00:00 python -i

Job arrays (many similar tasks)
- Example (100 tasks, at most 10 concurrently):
  #SBATCH --array=1-100%10
- Inside the script use $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to pick input per-task.

Dependencies and chaining jobs
- Submit job B to run after job A completes successfully:
  sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid_A> jobB.sh

Monitoring and debugging
- squeue -u $USER — show your queued/running jobs
- squeue -j <JOBID> — get state and (usually) pending reason
- If squeue does not show a useful reason, run:
  scontrol show job <JOBID>   — detailed pending reason or required resources
- For running jobs:
  sstat -j <JOBID>   — live CPU/memory usage (if enabled)
  sacct -j <JOBID>   — accounting info after job finishes (exit code, elapsed)
- Common pending reasons: Resources, Priority, PartitionDown, QOS, License. Use scontrol show job to get the detailed reason string.

Common #SBATCH options (most used)
- --job-name=NAME
- --nodes=N, --ntasks=N, --ntasks-per-node=N
- --cpus-per-task=N
- --mem=SIZE or --mem-per-cpu=SIZE
- --time=DD-HH:MM:SS or HH:MM:SS
- --gres=gpu:N
- --partition=NAME
- --output=FILE and --error=FILE (or combined with --output=slurm-%j.out)
- --mail-user=you@site --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL

Environment variables available in jobs
- SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, SLURM_NTASKS, SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, etc. Use them in scripts to adapt behavior.

Best practices
- Always test with a small, short job first (1 node, short time) to verify script and modules.
- Request realistic resources: over-requesting time or memory reduces scheduler throughput and can delay your job.
- Set --time to a sensible upper bound — shorter limits often help the job start sooner.
- Use output files named with %j (job ID) so logs don’t collide across runs.
- Capture exit codes in scripts and fail fast (set -e).
- If pending, check squeue and scontrol for the reason before contacting admins.
- For GPU jobs, confirm cluster uses gres=gpu and what GPU types are available (sinfo shows node resources).
- Keep software environment reproducible (modules, virtualenv/conda, container images if supported).

Troubleshooting tips
- Job never starts: check squeue for pending reason; check sinfo for partition/node availability.
- Job fails quickly: inspect slurm-<JOBID>.out and check the batch script for missing modules or wrong paths.
- Out-of-memory: increase --mem or detect memory leak; use sacct to see ExitCode and signal (e.g., OOM killed).
- Unexpected task placement: check --ntasks, --cpus-per-task and use srun with --cpu-bind options if needed.

Where to learn more
- The official Slurm documentation is authoritative (sacct, srun, sbatch, scontrol pages). If you want, I can fetch specific doc pages or give cluster-specific templates.

Would you like:
- a ready-to-use template for CPU, GPU, or MPI jobs tailored to your cluster defaults?
- help debugging a specific job script or a pending job ID? (If so, tell me the job ID or which template you want.)
