results.prompt: Use official Slurm docs to explain the pending reason Priority
results.agent_response:
Summary (what the pending reason "Priority" means)
- When squeue shows a pending reason of "Priority" it means the scheduler attempted to place the job but found one or more other jobs with higher scheduling priority that are being favored for the same partition/resources. In short: the job is waiting because other job(s) have higher computed job_priority and are ahead in the scheduler's ordering.

Why that happens (how priority is computed)
- Slurm's default multifactor priority plugin computes a job priority as a weighted sum of several factors. The canonical formula (from the Slurm docs) is:
  Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge*age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc*assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare*fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize*job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition*partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS*QOS_factor + SUM(TRES_weight_* * TRES_factor_ ) - nice_factor
- Factors include (not exhaustive): age (how long job has waited), association/account priority, fairshare, job size, partition priority, QOS, TRES (resource) factors, site factors, and a "nice" adjustment. Each factor is normalized (0.0–1.0) and weightings in slurm.conf determine their influence. The final job_priority is an integer (0 .. 4294967295); larger = higher scheduling precedence.
- Because of these factors, a job may be pending for "Priority" even if resources are free for it now — the scheduler prefers to run higher-priority jobs first.

How to investigate (commands to run)
- See the pending reason in the queue: squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %T %R" (shows reason column).
- See job priority values and components: sprio (gives priorities/factors for pending jobs).
- Inspect a job's detailed priority and reason: scontrol show job <jobid> (shows JobPriority and detailed fields).
- List jobs ordered by priority to find which ones are in front: squeue --sort=-p (or use sprio combined with squeue).

Remedies / next steps
- Wait: age_factor increases over time, so the job's priority can grow and eventually run.
- If you need higher precedence, options include:
  - Submit under a higher QOS (if allowed).
  - Ask an admin to adjust association/account priority or partition priority.
  - Use sbatch --nice (or set a lower nice value) if your site permits (note: changing nice often requires privilege or configured QOS).
  - Reduce the job's requested resources or walltime so it fits available slots earlier.
  - Administrators can change priority weights in slurm.conf (PriorityWeight*) or adjust fairshare/account settings via sacctmgr — these are cluster-admin actions.
- Note: many priority changes require admin privileges (sacctmgr/scontrol/slurm.conf edits).

References (official Slurm docs)
- Job reason codes (explains "Priority" as a pending reason): https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html
- Multifactor priority plugin (factors, formula, configuration): https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html

If you want, I can:
- Show which jobs are currently ahead of a specific pending job (I can run sprio and squeue) — tell me the job ID to inspect.
- Or, if you want to change a job's priority or submit with a different QOS/nice, tell me what change you want and I will transfer to the operator (admin) to perform it.

results.prompt: Use Slurm documentation to explain sbatch dependency afterok
results.agent_response:
Summary (from the official Slurm sbatch/job-array docs)

What afterok means
- --dependency=afterok:<jobid> makes the submitted job wait until the specified job(s) complete successfully (exit code 0).
- The dependent job will remain pending with reason "Dependency" until all listed afterok conditions are satisfied.
- If any specified job finishes with a non‑zero exit (FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT, etc.), that particular afterok dependency is not satisfied and the dependent job will not run because of that dependency (use afterany to proceed regardless of success).

Syntax and common forms
- Single job: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 myscript.sh
- Multiple jobs (example form shown in docs): sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345:12346 myscript.sh
  - (The job-list is given after the dependency type in the documented examples.)
- Job-array element dependency: sbatch --dependency=afterok:1000_4 myscript.sh
- You can chain dependencies: submit job A, then submit job B with --dependency=afterok:<A>, then C with --dependency=afterok:<B>, etc.

Job-array semantics
- If you depend on an entire array job (ArrayJobID), afterok is satisfied only after all tasks in that array complete successfully (the highest exit code among tasks is used to interpret success/failure for afterok/afternotok).

Behavior when the dependency job already finished
- If the referenced job(s) already completed successfully at submission time, the afterok dependency is immediately satisfied for that job.
- If the referenced job(s) already completed with failure/non-zero exit, that afterok dependency will not be satisfied.

Practical notes
- sbatch prints the new job ID on submission; use that ID in later --dependency arguments to chain jobs.
- If your downstream job must run regardless of upstream success, use --dependency=afterany:<jobid>.
- Pending jobs waiting on dependencies show reason "Dependency" in squeue.

References
- Slurm sbatch and Job Array Support documentation (sbatch --depend and Job Dependencies) — see the official Slurm docs for exact option formatting and more examples.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Use local Slurm docs to explain when to use sacct versus squeue
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Use squeue for live, real‑time queue state (running, pending, recently submitted jobs) and for immediate troubleshooting (why a job is pending, current walltime/elapsed).
- Use sacct for historical/accounting information about jobs that have finished or for job exit codes, detailed accounting fields, and aggregated usage stored in the Slurm DB or accounting log.

Why (concise)
- Data source
  - squeue reads the scheduler’s current queue data (slurmctld) and shows active RUNNING/PENDING jobs and steps.
  - sacct reads the accounting records (slurmdbd / job accounting log) and returns stored records for jobs and job steps (including COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMEOUT etc.).
- Freshness & scope
  - squeue = live, instantaneous view. Good for “what’s running now?” or “what’s blocking my pending job?”
  - sacct = persisted history. Good for “what did my job exit with?” or “show me all of my jobs last month.”
- Fields and detail
  - squeue shows queue/state, node allocation, time used/left, and pending reason (useful for scheduling troubleshooting).
  - sacct can report exit codes, elapsed time, resource usage aggregated in accounting fields, and produces per-job and per-step records; format can be customized with --format.
- Operational considerations
  - sacct makes RPC calls to slurmdbd; excessive/looped sacct calls can impact slurmdbd performance (don’t poll sacct in tight loops).
  - sacct output may include multiple records per job (job + steps), and often requires specifying a starttime or other filters to narrow results.
- Practical troubleshooting flow (recommended)
  1) If the job is active or pending now: run squeue -j <jobid> (or squeue -u <user>) to see state and pending reason.
  2) If squeue shows no such job (not in queue): use sacct -j <jobid> to find historical records and exit codes.
  3) For more detailed pending/launch reasons for an active pending job you can run scontrol show job <jobid> after squeue if the reason column isn’t sufficient.

Example commands (typical)
- squeue -j 12345
- squeue -u alice
- sacct -j 12345 --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,ReqMem
- sacct --starttime=2024-04-01 -u alice

References
- squeue: live queue/scheduling display (see squeue docs)
- sacct: accounting/history display; consult sacct docs (note performance warning about slurmdbd RPCs)

If you want, I can list the exact minimal fields to request with sacct or show example squeue/scontrol commands for a specific pending reason.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of

either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## NSS Configuration [#NSS_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## Slurm Configuration [#SLURM_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/pam_slurm_adopt.html)
PrologFlags=contain must be set in the slurm.conf. This sets up the
"extern" step into which ssh-launched processes will be adopted. You must also
enable the task/cgroup plugin in slurm.conf. See the
[Slurm cgroups guide.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroups.html)
CAUTION This option must be in place before using this module.
The module bases its checks on local steps that have already been launched. Jobs
launched without this option do not have an extern step, so pam_slurm_adopt will
not have access to those jobs.
LaunchParameters=ulimit_pam_adopt will set RLIMIT_RSS in processes
adopted by the external step, similar to tasks running in regular steps.
The UsePAM option in slurm.conf is not related to pam_slurm_adopt.

Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One

calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.

- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine

used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated

The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

in the slurm.conf configuration file.

SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin

When a GRES has a type associated with it and a limit is applied
over this specific type (e.g. MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 ) if a
user requests a generic gres, the type's limit will not be enforced. In this
situation an additional lua job submit plugin to check the user request may
become useful. For example, if one requests --gres=gpu:2 having a

results.agent_response:
I checked the Slurm job state documentation (job_state_codes). Short definitions, common causes, and what to check for each state:

RUNNING
- What it means: The job has been allocated resources and its tasks are currently executing on node(s).
- Common causes why you see it: Normal execution; may also be in RUNNING while launch/cleanup flags (e.g., CONFIGURING, COMPLETING) are set briefly.
- What to check: squeue (shows elapsed time), sstat (live resource usage for a running job), stdout/stderr files, and node health. Use scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed allocation info.

PENDING
- What it means: The job is queued and waiting to start; Slurm will report a reason why it hasn’t begun.
- Common causes: waiting for free CPUs/GPUs/nodes, higher-priority jobs, unmet dependency or BeginTime, association/account/QOS limits, licenses, or partition/node state (down/drained).
- What to check: squeue (the REASON column), scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed reason, sprio or sdiag for priority/backfill info, and sinfo to inspect partition/node availability.

FAILED
- What it means: The job terminated unsuccessfully — typically finished with a non‑zero exit code or encountered a failure (launch failure, prolog/epilog error, node failure, etc.).
- Common causes: application crash, segmentation fault, failures in job prolog/launch, node problems, or resource exhaustion not captured by a dedicated state (e.g., generic failure).
- What to check: sacct -j <jobid> to see ExitCode and state history, stderr/stdout logs, scontrol show job <jobid> for any reported failure details, and node logs if a node issue is suspected.

TIMEOUT
- What it means: The job was terminated because it exceeded its configured TimeLimit.
- Common causes: actual runtime exceeded --time, unexpected hang/infinite loop, or an underestimated runtime.
- What to check: sacct/squeue to confirm TIMEOUT, your job’s requested TimeLimit (--time in sbatch/salloc/srun), job logs to see where it stopped, and consider increasing --time, adding checkpointing, or splitting the work.

If you want concrete troubleshooting for a specific job (job ID), tell me the job ID and whether you want me to inspect the queue or accounting output; I can show the exact squeue/sacct fields you should look at.

results.prompt: Use local Slurm docs to explain how reservations work
results.agent_response:
I looked up the local Slurm documentation on reservations and summarized the key points below (source: Slurm Advanced Resource Reservation Guide).

What a reservation is
- A reservation reserves specified resources (nodes, CPU cores, licenses, burst buffers) for a defined time window so selected users/accounts/QOS can run jobs there.
- A reservation identifies resources and a time period when those resources are available.

Scope and resource model
- Reservations that include nodes/cores are associated with a single partition and by default cannot span multiple partitions. The exception is when you explicitly specify node names — then a reservation may include nodes from different partitions.
- You can reserve full nodes or a set number of cores. Reserved burst buffers and licenses are treated slightly differently than nodes/cores.

Access control and who can use a reservation
- Reservations can be limited to particular users, accounts, or QOS values. Only jobs meeting the access controls may run in that reservation.
- By default, jobs must explicitly request the reservation (for example sbatch --reservation=<name>) to run there.

Timing and node selection
- A reservation has a start time and duration (or start and end times).
- If you don’t specify explicit nodes, Slurm will automatically select nodes to satisfy the reservation while avoiding overlaps with other reservations (unless flags change that behavior).

Important reservation flags and behaviors
- OVERLAP: allows reservations to overlap in time on the same nodes (useful for nested/reserved slices).
- MAGNETIC: makes a reservation “attract” eligible jobs even if they don’t request the reservation name. Magnetic reservations will only attract homogeneous jobs; heterogeneous jobs must explicitly request the reservation.
- MAINT (maintenance): a special overlapping reservation type for maintenance windows. Nodes in a MAINT reservation show up in maint state, won’t be used as replacements for other reservations, and time is reported as PlannedDown in usage.
- REPLACE / REPLACE_DOWN: controls whether nodes that are DOWN/DRAINED or even currently allocated to jobs should be replaced so the reservation retains a constant resource pool. REPLACE can move a reservation to new idle nodes if necessary (with caveats for reservations specified as cores across nodes).
- Default: nodes that are DOWN or DRAINED will be replaced for a reservation, but allocated nodes are not replaced unless REPLACE is used.

Limitations and notes
- Reservations are not compatible with Slurm’s gang scheduler plugin (because reservation termination times may make gang scheduling infeasible).
- Magnetic reservations will not attract heterogeneous jobs unless the job explicitly requests the reservation.
- Maintenance reservations differ from generic overlapping reservations in how they present node state and how accounting reports treat the time.

Typical commands (from the docs)
- Create: scontrol create reservation starttime=<time> duration=<mins|time> users=<userlist> nodes=<nodelist|nodecnt> flags=<flags>
  - Example (illustrative): scontrol create reservation starttime=now duration=60 users=alice nodes=node05 flags=magnetic
- View: scontrol show reservation (or scontrol show res) to inspect reservation details.
- Jobs can request a reservation when submitting: e.g., sbatch --reservation=<reservation_name> <script>
- You can view queue entries tied to a reservation with squeue --reservation=<name>.

If you want, I can:
- Show the exact scontrol examples from the local doc,
- Or explain how to create a reservation for a given user/partition/time and which flags you should pick for your use case. Which would you like?

results.prompt: Use Slurm documentation to explain how GRES is configured in slurm.conf
results.agent_response:
Summary (from the official Slurm docs)
- Slurm manages “Generic RESources” (GRES) such as GPUs through two places:
  - slurm.conf: declares which GRES types the controller manages and how many of each are expected on each node.
  - gres.conf (one per node or on controller + cloud nodes): gives per-node device details (device files, core affinities, counts, AutoDetect etc.). If slurm.conf fully describes a GRES type (no File/Cores/Links needed), a per-node gres.conf may be omitted.

Key slurm.conf parameters
- GresTypes
  - A global comma-separated list of GRES type names that slurmctld will manage (for example: GresTypes=gpu,mps).
  - If you do not list a type here, Slurm will not treat it as a managed GRES.
- NodeName ... Gres=...
  - Each NodeName line may include a Gres= specification that tells slurmctld how many of a type to expect on that node.
  - Syntax examples:
    - NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2
    - NodeName=node01 Gres=gpu:4,mps:1
  - The Gres specification follows the same per-node resource model as other resources. If a node reports fewer resources than configured, Slurm will place the node into DRAIN.
  - For Slurm to recognize MIG partitions as separate GRES you still list them via Gres= (e.g., Gres=gpu:2) and can use an optional GRES type substring to distinguish MIG sizes (see MIG docs).

Role of gres.conf (per-node file)
- Location: same directory as slurm.conf on the node (and controller for cloud setups).
- Purpose: give detailed device mapping and metadata that slurm.conf cannot express, e.g.:
  - Name=<gres-name> (e.g. Name=gpu)
  - Type=<optional type string>
  - File=/dev/... or device list
  - Count=NN (for resources without explicit device files)
  - COREs=cpu-list (CPU affinity(s))
  - AutoDetect=<backend> (nvml, rsmi, nvidia, oneapi, nrt) — see below
- If slurm.conf already completely describes a GRES (no File/Cores/Links needed or it’s autodetected), you may omit per-node gres.conf.

AutoDetect and GPU specifics
- AutoDetect in gres.conf (e.g. AutoDetect=nvml) lets Slurm query the node’s GPU library to fill device details automatically.
- AutoDetect=nvml (or rsmi for AMD) also enables some accounting metrics; nvml/rsmi must be available on the node.
- Newer options: AutoDetect=nvidia (detects NVIDIA GPUs without nvml but won’t detect MIG or NVLink), AutoDetect=oneapi, etc.
- For NVIDIA MIGs: use AutoDetect=nvml on nodes with MIG, keep Gres= in slurm.conf to state expected counts, and optionally specify a GRES type that is a substring of the MIG profile string so Slurm can distinguish different MIG partitions.

Accounting / TRES interaction
- If you enable AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu (and proper AutoDetect), Slurm will collect gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil as TRES metrics for accounting (gpuutil/gpumem only available when supported by the AutoDetect backend; MIGs have limitations).

Common pitfalls & notes
- You must list types in GresTypes and specify Gres= on NodeName lines. Omitting either will cause Slurm not to manage the devices or mark nodes DRAIN if counts don’t match.
- Mismatch between slurm.conf and actual node devices -> node is placed in DRAIN.
- Place gres.conf on each compute node (or use AutoDetect + a controller copy for cloud nodes) and ensure the slurmd can read the device files.
- Users request GRES in jobs with --gres (e.g. sbatch --gres=gpu:1), but that is a runtime usage topic—slurm.conf/gres.conf must first be configured for the scheduler to offer them.

Minimal step-by-step to enable GPUs (example)
1. In slurm.conf:
   - Add the GRES types: GresTypes=gpu
   - Add Gres= counts on NodeName lines: NodeName=node01 Gres=gpu:4
2. On each node (or use AutoDetect):
   - Create /etc/slurm/gres.conf with entries like:
     AutoDetect=nvml
     Name=gpu Type=tesla File=/dev/nvidia[0-3] COREs=0,1,2,3
   - or let AutoDetect populate details if supported.
3. Restart or reconfigure Slurm services (slurmctld/slurmd) so the controller and daemons pick up the changes (slurmctl reconfigure / service restarts as your site policy).
4. Test with scontrol show node and scontrol show config or by submitting a job that requests --gres=gpu:1.

Where to read more (official pages used)
- slurm.conf man page (GresTypes and Gres parameters)
- gres.conf man page (per-node device syntax and AutoDetect)
- GRES scheduling doc (overview, MIG guidance, accounting/TRES notes)

If you want, I can paste exact example snippets from the Slurm docs (gres.conf examples and slurm.conf examples) or walk through a specific slurm.conf/gres.conf you have and mark needed edits. Which would you prefer?

By default, no GRES are enabled in the cluster's configuration.
You must explicitly specify which GRES are to be managed in the
slurm.conf configuration file. The configuration parameters of
interest are GresTypes and Gres .

as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources
than configured will be placed in a DRAIN state.

## MIG Management [#MIG_Management](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Beginning in version 21.08, Slurm now supports NVIDIA
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) devices. This feature allows some newer NVIDIA
GPUs (like the A100) to split up a GPU into up to seven separate, isolated GPU
instances. Slurm can treat these MIG instances as individual GPUs, complete with
cgroup isolation and task binding.
To configure MIGs in Slurm, specify
`AutoDetect=nvml` in gres.conf for the
nodes with MIGs, and specify `Gres`
in slurm.conf as if the MIGs were regular GPUs, like this:
`NodeName=tux[1-16] gres=gpu:2`. An optional
GRES type can be specified to distinguish MIGs of different sizes from each
other, as well as from other GPUs in the cluster. This type must be a substring
of the "MIG Profile" string as reported by the node in its slurmd log under the

## Accounting [#Accounting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
GPU memory and GPU utilization can be tracked as
[TRES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/tres.html) for tasks using GPU
resources. If `AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu` is configured,
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil will automatically be configured and gathered from
GPU jobs. gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil can also be set individually when
gres/gpu is not set.
gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil are only available for NVIDIA GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=nvml`, and AMD GPUs when using
`AutoDetect=rsmi`.
NVML does not support utilization metrics for MIGs, so Slurm does not
provide gpumem or gpuutil accounting for MIG devices. See
[NVIDIA's MIG User Guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/mig-user-guide/).
Here is an example node with two NVIDIA A100 GPUs:
```text
$ nvidia-smi -L GPU 0: NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB (UUID: GPU-...) GPU 1: NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB (UUID: GPU-...)

## MIG Management [#MIG_Management](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Beginning in version 21.08, Slurm now supports NVIDIA
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) devices. This feature allows some newer NVIDIA
GPUs (like the A100) to split up a GPU into up to seven separate, isolated GPU
instances. Slurm can treat these MIG instances as individual GPUs, complete with
cgroup isolation and task binding.
To configure MIGs in Slurm, specify
`AutoDetect=nvml` in gres.conf for the
nodes with MIGs, and specify `Gres`
in slurm.conf as if the MIGs were regular GPUs, like this:
`NodeName=tux[1-16] gres=gpu:2`. An optional
GRES type can be specified to distinguish MIGs of different sizes from each
other, as well as from other GPUs in the cluster. This type must be a substring
of the "MIG Profile" string as reported by the node in its slurmd log under the
`debug2` log level. Here is an example slurm.conf
for a system with 2 gpus, one of which is partitioned i...

## AutoDetect [#AutoDetect](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,
configuration details will automatically be filled in for any system-detected
GPU. This removes the need to explicitly configure GPUs in gres.conf, though the
Gres= line in slurm.conf is still required in order to tell slurmctld how
many GRES to expect.
Note that AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
and AutoDetect=oneapi need their corresponding GPU management libraries
installed on the node and found during Slurm configuration in order to work.
Both AutoDetect=nvml and AutoDetect=nvidia detect NVIDIA GPUs.
AutoDetect=nvidia (added in Slurm 24.11) doesn't require the
nvml library to be installed, but doesn't detect MIGs or NVlinks.
When AutoDetect needs to load a GPU management library as stated above it
will usually unload this library immediately after t...

slurm.conf configuration file. The configuration parameters of

as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources

What the sshare fields mean (brief)
- Norm Shares: your normalized share target (what fraction of resources you “should” get).
- Effectv Usage: your recent usage normalized to your parent (this decays over time).
- Fair-share factor (Level FS) = NormShares / EffectvUsage. If Level FS > 1 the association is under‑served (gets higher priority); if Level FS is between 0 and 1 it is over‑served (gets lower priority).

- root: 1.000 / 0.000 => effectively very large (root is strongly under‑served; gets very high priority)

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sshare.html)
Executing sshare sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sshare or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sshare or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sshare to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Use official Slurm docs to explain the pending reason Priority
results.agent_response:
Short answer (from the official Slurm docs)

- "Priority" is a job pending reason that means the scheduler attempted to place the job but found one or more jobs with higher scheduling priority for the same partition/nodes. The scheduler therefore left this job pending because other jobs outrank it in the priority ordering. (See Job Reason Codes: "Priority".)

What Slurm uses to compute that priority (from the Multifactor Priority plugin)
- By default Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin. A job's priority is a weighted sum of enabled factors, for example:
  site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * QOS_factor + SUM(TRES_weights * TRES_factors) - nice_factor
- Each factor is normalized (0.0–1.0) and the final job priority is an integer (0 .. 4294967295). Higher numbers = higher scheduling precedence. (See priority_multifactor.)

Why you see "Priority" instead of some other reason
- The scheduler reports the first reason it encounters for why the job cannot start. If the scheduling attempt finds higher-priority jobs blocking allocation, it reports "Priority" even if other constraints also apply. (See Job Reason Codes.)

How to inspect and influence this
- Inspect actual per-job priority values and factors with the sprio utility (and sprio --weights to see configured weights).
- Check slurm.conf for PriorityType and the PriorityWeight* settings to see which factors and weights are active.
- Common ways to raise a job's priority: let the job age (age factor), change its QOS or association priority, change nice value, request a partition with higher partition_factor, or adjust fairshare/association/QOS limits (requires admin/config changes).

References (official Slurm docs)
- Job Reason Codes — "Priority" entry: https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html
- Multifactor Priority plugin (priority factors and formula): https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html
- sprio / priority tools documentation is linked from the priority page.

If you want, I can show you current priority values for jobs in the queue (sprio) or explain how a specific job's priority is being computed — tell me which job ID to inspect.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.
Since each array element can have a different exit code, the interpretation of
the afterok and afternotok clauses will be based upon the highest

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.

Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:

```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text

A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Use local Slurm docs to explain when to use sacct versus squeue
results.agent_response:
Good question — both show job information but have different scopes and backends. Use this quick guide:

When to use squeue (real-time queue view)
- Immediate, live state of active jobs (RUNNING, PENDING, SUSPENDED).  
- See where a job is waiting or what nodes it’s allocated to, plus the pending REASON.  
- First tool to debug “why isn’t my job starting?” or to confirm a job is currently running.  
- Lightweight query of slurmctld (does not require slurmdbd).  
- Useful options: show partition/node, format columns, view by user or jobid.

When to use sacct (accounting / historical records)
- Historical and accounting data: completed, failed, cancelled, timed-out jobs and their ExitCode, elapsed, requested/used resources.  
- Produce reports and postmortem resource-usage queries (CPU-hours, memory, exit codes).  
- Queries slurmdbd / accounting storage (may be empty if accounting isn’t configured for your cluster).  
- Can be heavier on slurmdbd — avoid tight loops or excessive calls.

Practical rules of thumb
- To check an active job: run squeue <jobid> (if squeue shows nothing for that ID, then use sacct to find completed/failed records).  
- To investigate why a pending job isn’t starting: squeue (pending reason); if you need historical runs or exit codes, use sacct.  
- To get live resource usage for a running job (CPU%, memory): use sstat (not sacct).  
- For detailed job configuration or step-level info: use scontrol show job <id>.

Performance/behavior notes
- sacct requires accounting configured and contacts slurmdbd; it can be slower and should not be polled in tight loops.  
- squeue is the authoritative live view of the scheduler state; it does not show completed jobs.

If you want, I can give short example commands for the common checks you run (show pending reason, fetch exit code for a finished job, generate a 7‑day usage report). Which examples would help?

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Executing sacct sends a remote procedure call to slurmdbd . If
enough calls from sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmdbd daemon come in at once, it can result in a
degradation of performance of the slurmdbd daemon, possibly resulting in a
denial of service.
Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmdbd from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sacct to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Use official Slurm docs to explain QOS limits such as MaxJobs and MaxCPUs
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise, doc‑based explanation of common QOS limits (with behavior notes and examples). Sources: Slurm QOS and Resource Limits pages (https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html, https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html).

What a QOS limit is
- A QOS limit caps a resource or submission metric for jobs that request that QOS. QOS limits mirror limits that can also be set on user/account/partition/cluster associations; when a QOS defines a limit it overrides association limits (see precedence below).

Key limits (definitions)
- MaxJobs
  - Maximum number of jobs that may be concurrently active (RUNNING or PENDING as enforced) that are associated with that QOS (or that count point in the hierarchy).
  - If a submission would cause the limit to be exceeded the job will pend unless the QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit (see DenyOnLimit).
- MaxCPUs
  - Maximum number of CPUs (cores) that may be concurrently allocated to jobs using that QOS. This is enforced against the sum of CPU allocations for matching jobs.
  - CPUs are counted as integer core units (not time-weighted).
- MaxNodes / MinNodes / Max[Time|Wall]
  - Limits on node counts or job wall time. (Note: some of these limits have special precedence rules; see hierarchy note.)
- MaxSubmitJobs, MaxSubmitJobsPerUser
  - Limits on the number of jobs that may be submitted within some context (global, per-user, etc.). These control submission rate/quantity rather than resource allocation.
- MaxTRES / GrpTRES / MaxTRESPerNode
  - TRES = Trackable RESources (e.g., cpu, mem, gres/gpu). MaxTRES can set absolute limits on TRES usage (for example cpu=2000,gpu=10,mem=100000).
  - GrpTRES limits group (aggregate) usage across the QOS.
  - MaxTRESPerNode or Max[Something]PerNode is applied per node.
- MaxGRES / GRES-related limits
  - Limits specifically for GRES (Generic RESources) such as GPUs; used when you want to constrain GPU counts.
- Flags=Relative
  - When set, numeric limits are treated as percentages of total cluster resources (e.g., cpu=50 means 50% of all CPUs). Memory limits should be set without units when using Relative (1MB = 1%).

Behavioral rules and enforcement
- Hierarchy / precedence
  - Limits are enforced according to a fixed hierarchy (partition QOS, job QOS, user association, account association(s) ascending, root/cluster association, partition limit, none). The first place a limit is defined in this list is used. You can change partition-vs-job QOS precedence with Flags=OverPartQOS.
- What happens when a limit would be exceeded
  - Default: a job that would violate a Max* limit will pend until resources are available.
  - If Flags=DenyOnLimit is set on the QOS, jobs that would violate the QOS “Max” limits will be denied at submission time (rejected), rather than pended.
  - Group (Grp) limits are treated as Max limits when DenyOnLimit is applied.
- Interaction with partitions and associations
  - A Partition QOS (a QOS attached to a partition) carries the QOS limits into the partition view and (by default) is applied before a job’s requested QOS. OverPartQOS reverses that order.
- Relative QOS nuance
  - With Flags=Relative, limits are percentages and may be computed either cluster-wide or relative to a partition when used as a partition QOS; slurmctld must be reconfigured/restarted to pick up some flag changes.
- Units and types
  - CPU limits are counts. Memory limits are normally specified with units (MB/GB) but when using Relative you should set memory with no units so it’s treated as a percentage.

Examples (from docs)
- If a partition QOS sets MaxJobs=20 and a user-association sets MaxJobs=4, the partition QOS value (20) takes effect because of the hierarchy—unless OverPartQOS is used to reverse precedence.
- If a QOS has cpu=50 and Flags=Relative, that means jobs using the QOS can consume up to 50% of total cluster CPUs (values above 100 are treated as 100).

Practical notes for admins and users
- Use MaxTRES (or specific MaxCPUs/MaxGRES) when you need precise control over specific resource types (CPUs vs GPUs vs memory).
- Use DenyOnLimit when you prefer immediate rejection at submission instead of a job silently queueing/pend-ing.
- Remember the hierarchy: setting limits at the right level (partition vs QOS vs association) matters.
- When changing QOS flags or limits, reconfiguration may be required for some flags (e.g., Relative) to take effect.

Where to read more
- QOS reference and options: https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html
- Resource limits and hierarchy: https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html

If you want, I can:
- extract the exact sacctmgr commands to set common limits (e.g., set MaxCPUs for QOS foo) and give examples, or
- show how a submission would be evaluated under a specific set of QOS/partition/association limits you provide. Which would you like?

Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as

results.agent_response:
I looked up the official Slurm job-state docs and summarized the four states you asked about. Short definitions, common causes, and how to inspect/act:

- RUNNING
  - What it is: The job has been allocated resources and its tasks are actively executing.
  - Notes: Jobs may also carry flags (e.g., CONFIGURING, COMPLETING) while in/around RUNNING. Resource usage for a running job can be inspected.
  - How to inspect: squeue (shows job ID, name, state); sstat -j <jobid> for live CPU/memory/I/O details.
  - User action: If you need to debug performance, check logs on the allocated nodes and use sstat; to terminate, cancel the job.

- PENDING
  - What it is: The job is queued and waiting to start. Slurm will usually show a reason code explaining why it hasn’t started (e.g., Resources, Priority, Dependency, PartitionTimeLimit, QOS limit).
  - Common reasons: no free resources, partition or account limits, job dependencies, node maintenance/drain, or scheduling priority.
  - How to inspect: squeue -j <jobid> (shows reason in the REASON column if available) or scontrol show job <jobid> for a detailed pending reason.
  - User action: Review the REASON, adjust resource/time/QOS/account requests, remove or satisfy dependencies, or contact admin if nodes are drained.

- FAILED
  - What it is: The job finished but unsuccessfully — Slurm considers it failed (non-zero exit code or other failure condition).
  - Common causes: application exit with error status, prolog/epilog failures, launch failures (LAUNCH_FAILED), node failure, or out-of-memory.
  - How to inspect: sacct -j <jobid> (shows ExitCode and final state), and scontrol show job <jobid> for extra diagnostics; check stdout/stderr files and node logs.
  - User action: Inspect exit code and logs, reproduce locally if possible, adjust job script/environment, or request node checks if hardware failure suspected.

- TIMEOUT
  - What it is: The job was terminated because it exceeded its requested TimeLimit. TIMEOUT is a terminal (failed) state caused by walltime overrun.
  - Notes: TIMEOUT differs from FAILED in that the termination reason is exceeding TimeLimit. Depending on configuration, jobs may be requeued automatically if requeue options are set.
  - How to inspect: sacct -j <jobid> (shows State=TIMEOUT and the recorded elapsed time); scontrol show job <jobid> can also show time-limit and elapsed.
  - User action: Increase the job TimeLimit for future submissions, optimize the job to finish sooner, or enable/review requeue behavior if appropriate.

Extra notes
- Slurm reports a single state string but jobs have base states + optional flags (see Slurm docs for state flags).
- Commands useful for investigating:
  - squeue -j <jobid>
  - scontrol show job <jobid>
  - sacct -j <jobid> -o JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS
  - sstat -j <jobid> (for running jobs)

If you want, tell me a job ID and which state you’re seeing and I can run the appropriate Slurm queries (squeue/scontrol/sacct) and explain the specific reason and next steps.

results.prompt: Use local Slurm docs to explain how reservations work
results.agent_response:
Summary — what a Slurm reservation is
- A reservation is a named, time-limited hold on specific resources (nodes, cores, memory, partition) that guarantees those resources for the specified users/accounts/QoS during StartTime..EndTime. Use the word "reservation" to refer to it.

Key behaviors
- Reservations are created (typically) with scontrol create reservation and shown with scontrol show reservation (or scontrol_reservation_show).
- Jobs may be required to explicitly request the reservation (sbatch --reservation=<name>) unless the reservation was created with the MAGNETIC flag.
- A job using a reservation must be entirely contained within that reservation’s resources and will be cancelled when the reservation reaches its EndTime (unless ResvOverRun is configured in slurm.conf to allow overrun).
- Reservations are considered for scheduling before non-reserved jobs that would use the same resources — they don’t change a job’s base priority, but they act as a scheduling enhancement for eligible jobs.
- By default Slurm will not reserve resources that are expected to be occupied by running jobs at the StartTime; use the ignore_jobs flag at creation if you want to force a reservation that may require cancelling running jobs beforehand.
- MAGNETIC reservations “attract” eligible jobs without those jobs specifying the reservation name; magnetic reservations will not attract heterogeneous jobs unless those jobs explicitly request the reservation.
- REPLACE / REPLACE_DOWN flags control whether Slurm will replace nodes that are down/drained (REPLACE_DOWN) or even nodes currently allocated to jobs (REPLACE). REPLACE of allocated nodes has limitations (e.g., not supported for reservations that request cores spanning multiple nodes).

Access control and filters
- Reservations can be limited by user, account, partition, QOS. You can also explicitly exclude users by prefixing with a minus (e.g., user=-alice).
- You can create reservations for full nodes (Nodes=...) or for counts of cores (CoreCnt=...), or by NodeCnt, etc., depending on how fine-grained you need the reservation to be.

Common flags and their meaning
- MAGNETIC — jobs that meet access constraints may run without specifying the reservation name.
- REPLACE, REPLACE_DOWN — controls replacing nodes that are allocated/down.
- IGNORE_JOBS — allow creation even if currently running jobs prevent reservation (you may need to cancel those jobs manually).
- MAINT — mark reservation as maintenance for accounting purposes.

Typical commands / examples
- Create a simple reservation:
  scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 NodeCnt=1 CoreCnt=2 User=alan
  (Slurm prints the generated ReservationName.)
- Create a magnetic reservation on a single node:
  scontrol create reservation user=user1 nodes=node05 starttime=now duration=10 flags=magnetic
- Use a reservation when submitting:
  sbatch --reservation=alan_6 -N4 my.script
- Inspect reservations:
  scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name>
  or the equivalent reservation show tool (scontrol_reservation_show)
- See jobs tied to a reservation:
  squeue --reservation=<name>

Notes, limits, and admin controls
- Reservation names are auto-generated (first user/account plus numeric suffix) unless you explicitly name them.
- Jobs started in the reservation are cancelled at EndTime unless ResvOverRun permits continuation.
- Magnetic reservations cannot “attract” heterogeneous jobs unless the job explicitly requests the reservation.
- Some behaviors (overrun policy, reservation replacement behavior) can be controlled by slurm.conf settings (e.g., ResvOverRun) and flags passed at creation.

Where to read more
- The official Slurm "Advanced Resource Reservation" guide (reservations) documents creation options, flags, access control, magnetic reservations, REPLACE behavior, and examples — see the Slurm docs reservations page for full details.

If you want, I can:
- show current reservations on this cluster (scontrol_reservation_show), or
- create a reservation for you (tell me StartTime, Duration/EndTime, resources, users/accounts/QoS and any flags); note: creating/modifying reservations is a cluster mutation, so I’ll transfer this request to the operator when you confirm.

results.prompt: Use Slurm documentation to explain how GRES is configured in slurm.conf
results.agent_response:
Summary — how GRES is configured (from the Slurm docs)
- GRES (Generic RESources) describe resources like GPUs, MPS instances, FPGAs, licenses, etc. Two places hold GRES configuration:
  1. slurm.conf — cluster-wide declarations (GresTypes and per-NodeName Gres= entries)
  2. gres.conf — per-node, detailed device mapping (Name, Type, File, Count, COREs, Links, AutoDetect)
- Slurm uses those configs to advertise GRES to the scheduler and to enforce --gres requests from users (srun/sbatch --gres).

Key slurm.conf items
- GresTypes
  - Declares the names of GRES types that may be used cluster-wide.
  - Example: GresTypes=gpu,mps
- NodeName ... Gres=
  - Each NodeName entry may include a Gres= list to declare how many of each GRES that node provides.
  - Format: Gres=<name>:<count>[,<name>:<count>...]
  - Example:
    - NodeName=compute[01-04] CPUs=64 RealMemory=250000 Gres=gpu:4
- Placement/availability
  - If slurm.conf fully describes the resources (and no per-device mapping like File/COREs/Links is required), you can omit a node gres.conf; otherwise place a gres.conf on each node (or on all cloud nodes + controller for cloud).
- Applying changes
  - Changes take effect on restart of slurm daemons, on receipt of SIGHUP, or by running scontrol reconfigure (docs: slurm.conf).

Key gres.conf items (per-node detailed mapping)
- File location: same directory as slurm.conf (typically /etc/slurm/)
- Entries describe each device instance for that node. Common fields:
  - Name= (required) — resource name used by Slurm and by --gres (e.g., Name=gpu)
  - Type= (optional) — vendor/model/type string (e.g., Type=tesla)
  - File= — device file(s) (e.g., File=/dev/nvidia0 or File=/dev/nvidia[0-3])
  - Count= — logical count when you want to expose e.g. many MPS instances
  - COREs= — CPU core affinity mapping
  - Links= — symbolic link info
  - AutoDetect=nvml (or other) — let Slurm/driver autodetect GPU devices via NVML
- Example snippets (from the docs):
  - AutoDetect=nvml
    Name=gpu Type=gtx560 File=/dev/nvidia0 COREs=0,1
    Name=gpu Type=tesla File=/dev/nvidia1 COREs=2,3
  - Or explicit:
    Name=gpu Type=tesla File=/dev/nvidia[0-3] COREs=0-31

How users request GRES
- sbatch/srun/salloc: --gres=<name>:<count> (or --gres=gpu:1)
  - Example in batch script:
    #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

Visibility and verification (commands referenced in docs)
- sinfo / scontrol / squeue show GRES info:
  - sinfo and sinfo --Node show partition/node GRES presence (sinfo displays GRES column in some formats).
  - scontrol show node <node> shows Gres and detailed node fields.
  - After jobs start, squeue shows GRES allocations for running jobs.
- Use the gres.conf and slurm.conf docs to confirm syntax and examples.

Practical checklist to add GPUs (typical flow)
1. In slurm.conf: add GresTypes=gpu (and on each NodeName add Gres=gpu:<N>).
2. On each node (or controller+cloud nodes): create /etc/slurm/gres.conf describing devices (Name=gpu File=... or AutoDetect=nvml).
3. Restart or reconfigure slurmd and slurmctld (or use scontrol reconfigure / send SIGHUP) so slurm picks up the new GRES.
4. Test: sinfo / scontrol show node / srun --gres=gpu:1 hostname.

Notes & tips from docs
- If slurm.conf fully describes a GRES type (no per-device File/COREs/Links needed), the node-level gres.conf may be omitted.
- AutoDetect=nvml is useful for NVIDIA GPUs so you don’t have to list every /dev/nvidia device.
- Use distinct names (Name=) if you want multiple GRES types (e.g., Name=gpu and Name=mps).
- Proper cgroup and device plugin configuration may also be needed to enforce device isolation (see cgroup.conf docs if you run into allocation / permissions problems).

## RELOCATING CONTROLLERS[#SECTION_RELOCATING-CONTROLLERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
If the cluster's computers used for the primary or backup controller
will be out of service for an extended period of time, it may be
desirable to relocate them.
In order to do so, follow this procedure:
1. Stop the Slurm daemons on the old controller and nodes.
2. Modify the slurm.conf file appropriately.
3. Copy the files from the StateSaveLocation to the new controller or ensure
that they are accessible to the new controller via a shared drive.
4. Distribute the updated slurm.conf file to all nodes.
5. Restart the Slurm daemons on the new controller and nodes.
There should be no loss of any pending jobs. Any running jobs will get the
updated host info and finish normally.
Ensure that any nodes added to the cluster have the current
slurm.conf file installed.

configuration information, the nodes to be managed, information about

results.prompt: Use official Slurm docs to explain the pending reason Priority
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- The pending reason "Priority" means the scheduler found one or more jobs with higher priority that must be scheduled before this job. In other words, your job is waiting because other jobs score higher under Slurm’s priority algorithm for the partition/resources you requested.

Why this happens (from the official docs)
- Job reason codes doc: “Priority — One or more higher priority jobs exist for the partition associated with the job or for resources requested.” (job_reason_codes)
- Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin by default; job priority is a weighted sum of factors such as age, fairshare, association, job size, partition, QOS, TRES factors, site factor and nice. The plugin configuration (PriorityType and the PriorityWeight* settings) determines how those factors combine into a job priority value. (priority_multifactor)

How to diagnose (commands)
- See the pending reason in the queue:
  - squeue (show the REASON column or use -o to include %R)
- Inspect the job’s priority and details:
  - scontrol show job <jobid>  (shows JobPriority and related fields)
- See per-job priority breakdown and ranking:
  - sprio -l   (or sprio for a summary) — shows priority values and factors
- Verify scheduler priority configuration:
  - scontrol show config | grep -i Priority

What you can do about it
- Wait: higher-priority jobs will run and free resources.

results.agent_response:
Summary (from the official Slurm sbatch docs)

- What afterok does
  - afterok is a submission-time dependency type. A job submitted with --dependency=afterok:jobid[,jobid...] will not become eligible to run until the listed job(s) have completed successfully (i.e., exited with code 0). Only when all specified predecessor jobs finish with exit code 0 is the dependency considered satisfied.

- Syntax
  - Command-line:
    --dependency=afterok:12345
    --dependency=afterok:12345,12346
  - In a script:
    #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:12345
  - Multiple dependency specifications may be combined (comma-separated), e.g. --dependency=afterok:12345,afterany:12346

- Job arrays and task IDs
  - You may reference array tasks using the usual job array notation (e.g. afterok:1234_5). You can also reference the array master id depending on what you need.

- Typical usage patterns
  - Serial chaining:
      jid1=$(sbatch job1.sh | awk '{print $NF}')
      sbatch --dependency=afterok:$jid1 job2.sh
  - Multiple predecessors: the dependent job waits until every listed predecessor completes successfully.

- Behavior on predecessor failure
  - If any listed predecessor exits with a non‑zero status, the afterok dependency is not satisfied for that predecessor. The dependent job will remain pending on its dependency (it will not run). If you want the dependent job to run regardless of predecessor exit status, use afterany; if you want it to run only when predecessors fail, use afternotok.

- Notes / reminders from the sbatch manual
  - Dependencies are recorded at submission time by job ID(s). If you submit jobs programmatically, capture the numeric job IDs returned by sbatch and use them in the dependent sbatch call.
  - Dependency types and full --dependency syntax (multiple types, commas, etc.) are described in the sbatch man page.

If you want, I can show a concrete chained-submission example (shell one-liners) or list the related dependency types (afterany, afternotok, after, singleton, serial, etc.) with short explanations.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote

in a denial of service.

procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Use local Slurm docs to explain when to use sacct versus squeue
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Use squeue for current, real‑time queue state (running & pending jobs) and for immediate scheduling/pending reasons.
- Use sacct for historical/accounting data (completed/failed/cancelled jobs, exit codes, billed CPU/GPU/time, job step records).

When to pick each (details)
- squeue
  - Shows live queue: RUNNING, PENDING, etc., and the pending reason column.
  - Use it to check whether a job is active now, to inspect why a job is waiting, or to view current cluster load.
  - Lightweight (talks to slurmctld), best for frequent/interactive checks.
  - For per‑step or runtime questions about a running job pair squeue with sstat or scontrol show step.

- sacct
  - Reads the job accounting DB/log (slurmdbd or accounting log). Shows completed, failed, cancelled, timed‑out jobs, exit codes, elapsed time, resources used, and job steps.
  - Use it for post‑mortem analysis, usage/accounting reports, checking exit codes or historical resource consumption, or aggregated reports over a time window.
  - Can be slower and imposes load on slurmdbd — avoid calling it in tight loops and use date filters (e.g., --starttime) to limit queries.
  - If accounting is not enabled on the cluster, sacct may not return records for older jobs.

Common workflow tips
- To diagnose a pending job: run squeue (single call). If squeue shows nothing for the job (missing from active queue), check sacct -j <jobid> to see if it already finished/failed.
- To get live resource usage for a running job: squeue (to confirm RUNNING) + sstat (for CPU/memory I/O).
- For user/account usage or historical reports: sacct (or sreport for aggregated CPU/GPU hour reports).

Permission/behavior notes
- sacct queries slurmdbd and may return more info for privileged users; squeue is typically available to normal users for jobs they can see.
- The availability and content of sacct depend on the cluster’s AccountingStorageType and retention policies.

If you want, I can show example squeue and sacct commands for common checks (pending reason, exit code, resource usage).

Accounting information for jobs invoked with Slurm are either logged
in the job accounting log file or saved to the Slurm database, as

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Executing sacct sends a remote procedure call to slurmdbd . If
enough calls from sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmdbd daemon come in at once, it can result in a
degradation of performance of the slurmdbd daemon, possibly resulting in a
denial of service.
Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmdbd from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sacct to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

When a GRES has a type associated with it and a limit is applied
over this specific type (e.g. MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 ) if a
user requests a generic gres, the type's limit will not be enforced. In this
situation an additional lua job submit plugin to check the user request may
become useful. For example, if one requests --gres=gpu:2 having a
limit set of MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 , the limit won't be
enforced so it will still be possible to get two teslas.
This is due to a design limitation. The only way to enforce such a limit

## Tools[#tools](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.
See man sacctmgr for details on this tools and examples of
its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.
Note: The precedence order specified above is respected except for the
following limits: Max[Time|Wall], [Min|Max]Nodes. For these limits, even

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of

either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every

to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text

### Example 14: Consumable resources with task affinity and customized allocation and distribution [#Example14](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cpu_management.html)
A job requires 18 CPUs (18 tasks with no overcommitment). Run the job in the
default partition. Allocate 6 CPUs on each node using block allocation within
nodes. Use cyclic distribution of tasks to nodes and block distribution of
tasks for CPU binding.
slurm.conf options:
```text
SelectType=select/cons_tres SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core,CR_CORE_DEFAULT_DIST_BLOCK TaskPlugin=task/affinity
```
Command line:
```text
srun --nodes=3-3 --ntasks=18 --ntasks-per-node=6 --distribution=cyclic:block --cpu-bind=cores ...
```
Comments:

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.

For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.
