config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV

Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be

results.prompt: Look up Slurm job state codes and explain RUNNING PENDING FAILED and TIMEOUT
results.agent_response:
Per the Slurm documentation (job_state_codes), here are concise meanings and what to check for each state:

- RUNNING
  - Meaning: The job has been allocated resources and is executing on the nodes.
  - Common signs/flags: may show flags like COMPLETING, LAUNCH_FAILED, CONFIGURING (when just starting).
  - How to inspect: squeue -j <jobid> to see allocation/state; sstat -j <jobid> for per-step runtime/CPU/memory; scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed allocation fields.

- PENDING
  - Meaning: The job is queued and waiting to be started. It has not begun execution.
  - Typical reasons: waiting for resources (no free nodes/GPUs), higher-priority jobs, partition limits/QOS, job dependencies, node/partition maintenance, or association/account limits.
  - How to inspect: squeue (shows a REASON column); for more detail use scontrol show job <jobid> which prints the pending reason and dependency info.

- FAILED
  - Meaning: The job completed unsuccessfully (Slurm considers it failed). Usually corresponds to a non‑zero exit code or an internal failure.
  - Common causes: application crash, nonzero exit from script, prolog/epilog failure, node failure, launch failure, out-of-memory, etc.
  - How to inspect: sacct -j <jobid> -o JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed to see ExitCode and state; check job stderr/stdout files and scontrol show job <jobid> for additional failure comments.

- TIMEOUT
  - Meaning: The job was terminated because it exceeded its requested TimeLimit.
  - Behavior: Slurm marks the job TIMEOUT (a terminal state). The elapsed time will typically equal or exceed the requested timelimit.
  - How to avoid/handle: request a longer --time, enable checkpointing, or use --signal to get a termination signal before the hard limit; inspect with sacct -j <jobid> and check the requested Timelimit vs Elapsed.

results.prompt: Use local Slurm docs to explain how reservations work
results.agent_response:
I looked up the local Slurm documentation on reservations and summarized the key points and common commands below.

What a reservation is
- A reservation reserves specific resources (nodes, cores, licenses, burst buffers) for a defined time window so only allowed users/accounts/QOS/partitions may use them.
- A reservation is tied to a time period (StartTime + Duration/EndTime).
- By default reservations are associated with a single partition (they cannot span partitions) unless the reservation is created with explicit node names.

Common uses
- Reserve an entire machine for maintenance.
- Reserve nodes/cores for a particular user, account, or QOS for a workshop or debugging session.
- Reserve licenses or burst buffers (these are handled slightly differently than cores/nodes).

Create a reservation (examples)
- Basic: scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 NodeCnt=1 CoreCnt=2 User=alan
- Specific nodes: scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 Nodes=tux8,tux9 CoreCnt=2,4 User=brenda
- Restrict/deny users: you can specify users/accounts/QOS that are allowed, or explicitly prevent specific users (e.g., user=-alan).
- Flags you’ll commonly see:
  - maint — identify the reservation as maintenance for accounting.
  - ignore_jobs — allow creating the reservation even if running jobs occupy the resources (you may cancel those jobs).
  - NO_HOLD_JOBS_AFTER_END — let jobs continue running after reservation end instead of putting them on HOLD.

Inspect a reservation
- scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name>
- The create command returns the generated reservation name if you don’t supply one (Slurm generates a name based on the first user/account plus a suffix).

Using a reservation
- Jobs must explicitly request the reservation when submitted: sbatch --reservation=<ReservationName> ...
- The job must fit entirely within the reservation time window and resource allocation.
- Jobs in the reservation are considered for scheduling before non-reserved jobs (reservation gives scheduling preference but does not change job priority).

End of reservation and overrun
- Jobs are normally cancelled when the reservation EndTime is reached unless ResvOverRun (in slurm.conf) lets jobs continue for a configured overrun period.
- Default behavior when a reservation ends: jobs submitted to that reservation are removed from the reservation and put on HOLD (unless NO_HOLD_JOBS_AFTER_END was set).

Delete a reservation
- Reservations are automatically removed after EndTime.
- You can manually delete: scontrol delete ReservationName=<name>
- A reservation cannot be deleted while jobs are running inside it.

Limitations / notes
- Reservations cannot span multiple partitions unless you list explicit node names.
- Reservations may not be compatible with certain scheduler plugins (e.g., Slurm’s gang scheduler) because job termination timing can be affected.
- By default only resources not expected to have a running job at the reservation start can be reserved; use ignore_jobs to override.

Useful commands (quick reference)
- Create: scontrol create reservation StartTime=... Duration=... Nodes=... NodeCnt=... CoreCnt=... User=... Account=... Partition=...
- Show: scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name>
- Delete: scontrol delete ReservationName=<name>
- Submit a job into a reservation: sbatch --reservation=<name> myscript.sh

If you want, I can:
- show current reservations from the cluster (scontrol_reservation_show), or
- help craft an scontrol create reservation command for a specific time/resources/users you have in mind.

results.prompt: Use Slurm documentation to explain how GRES is configured in slurm.conf
results.agent_response:
Summary (from Slurm docs):
- Slurm manages Generic RESources (GRES) such as GPUs, MPS instances, NVLinks, MIG slices, etc. Two config locations are involved: slurm.conf (cluster-wide) and gres.conf (per-node detailed descriptions). See the Slurm docs: the "Generic Resource (GRES) Scheduling" page and the gres.conf manpage.

Key slurm.conf settings
- GresTypes
  - Lists the GRES types that slurmctld will manage (comma-separated). Example:
    GresTypes=gpu,mps
  - If a type is not listed here, Slurm will not manage it.
- Gres (on NodeName lines)
  - Describes how many of a given GRES each node is expected to have. It is placed on NodeName (or NodeName/Partition entries) and uses type:count pairs.
  - Example:
    NodeName=node[01-04] Gres=gpu:4,mps:100
  - The Gres= value tells slurmctld how many of each resource to expect per node. If a node reports fewer resources than configured, Slurm will place that node into DRAIN so the mismatch can be fixed.

gres.conf (per-node details)
- Purpose: provide per-node device-level info when slurm.conf's Gres= line is not sufficient (for example you need File, COREs, Links, Count or custom Type strings). gres.conf resides in the same directory as slurm.conf (and is usually present on each compute node).
- Typical fields and examples:
  - AutoDetect=nvml (or nvml/nvidia/rsmi/oneapi/nrt) — let Slurm autodetect GPU devices and fill device details.
  - Name= (the GRES name, e.g., gpu)
  - Type= (optional subtype, e.g., tesla, or MIG profile substring)
  - File= (device filename, e.g., /dev/nvidia0 or /dev/nvidia[0-3])
  - COREs= (CPU core bindings for the device)
  - Count= (when you want to expose a logical count)
  Example entries:
    AutoDetect=nvml
    Name=gpu Type=tesla File=/dev/nvidia[0-3] COREs=0,1
    Name=mps Count=100 File=/dev/nvidia0 COREs=0,1

Notes and important behaviors
- You must set both: list the types in GresTypes and declare Gres= on nodes. AutoDetect in gres.conf can populate device details, but slurm.conf's Gres= is still required so slurmctld knows how many to expect.
- Requesting GRES in jobs: users request them with --gres, e.g. sbatch --gres=gpu:1 (or inside a job script: #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1).
- MIG support: for NVIDIA MIG-capable GPUs you can use AutoDetect=nvml in gres.conf and then set Gres in slurm.conf as if MIG instances were regular GPUs (e.g., NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2). You may also use a Type string that is a substring of the MIG profile to distinguish sizes.
- Mismatch handling: nodes that report fewer GRES than the configured Gres= will be drained until corrected.
- Placement/Accounting: GRES are accounted and scheduled like other consumable resources; sbatch/srun will allocate them and Slurm enforces exclusivity/quantity as requested.

Minimal example (slurm.conf + per-node gres.conf style)
- slurm.conf:
  GresTypes=gpu,mps
  NodeName=node[01-04] RealMemory=196608 Sockets=2 CoresPerSocket=20 ThreadsPerCore=2 Gres=gpu:4,mps:100
  PartitionName=gpu Nodes=node[01-04] Default=NO MaxTime=INFINITE State=UP

- gres.conf (on each node, or with AutoDetect=nvml on nodes with NVML):
  AutoDetect=nvml
  # or explicit devices:
  Name=gpu Type=tesla File=/dev/nvidia[0-3] COREs=0,1

References consulted (Slurm docs):
- gres (Generic Resource scheduling) page — explains GresTypes and Gres usage, AutoDetect, MIG notes.
- gres.conf manpage — file-level syntax and examples for Name, Type, File, Count, COREs, AutoDetect.

If you want, I can:
- show more concrete examples for MIG or multi-type GPU fleets,
- extract the exact slurm.conf manpage snippets for GresTypes/Gres parameters,
- or validate how your current slurm.conf + node gres.conf should be written if you paste them here.

## Configuration [#Configuration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
By default, no GRES are enabled in the cluster's configuration.
You must explicitly specify which GRES are to be managed in the
slurm.conf configuration file. The configuration parameters of
interest are GresTypes and Gres .
For more details, see [GresTypes](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) and [Gres](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) in the slurm.conf man page.
Note that the GRES specification for each node works in the same fashion
as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources
than configured will be placed in a DRAIN state.

## MIG Management [#MIG_Management](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Beginning in version 21.08, Slurm now supports NVIDIA
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) devices. This feature allows some newer NVIDIA
GPUs (like the A100) to split up a GPU into up to seven separate, isolated GPU
instances. Slurm can treat these MIG instances as individual GPUs, complete with
cgroup isolation and task binding.
To configure MIGs in Slurm, specify
`AutoDetect=nvml` in gres.conf for the
nodes with MIGs, and specify `Gres`
in slurm.conf as if the MIGs were regular GPUs, like this:
`NodeName=tux[1-16] gres=gpu:2`. An optional
GRES type can be specified to distinguish MIGs of different sizes from each
other, as well as from other GPUs in the cluster. This type must be a substring
of the "MIG Profile" string as reported by the node in its slurmd log under the
`debug2` log level. Here is an example slurm.conf

## AutoDetect [#AutoDetect](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,
configuration details will automatically be filled in for any system-detected
GPU. This removes the need to explicitly configure GPUs in gres.conf, though the
Gres= line in slurm.conf is still required in order to tell slurmctld how
many GRES to expect.
Note that AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
and AutoDetect=oneapi need their corresponding GPU management libraries
installed on the node and found during Slurm configuration in order to work.
Both AutoDetect=nvml and AutoDetect=nvidia detect NVIDIA GPUs.
AutoDetect=nvidia (added in Slurm 24.11) doesn't require the
nvml library to be installed, but doesn't detect MIGs or NVlinks.

will usually unload this library immediately after t...

## Configuration [#Configuration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
By default, no GRES are enabled in the cluster's configuration.
You must explicitly specify which GRES are to be managed in the
slurm.conf configuration file. The configuration parameters of
interest are GresTypes and Gres .
For more details, see [GresTypes](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) and [Gres](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) in the slurm.conf man page.
Note that the GRES specification for each node works in the same fashion
as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources
than configured will be placed in a DRAIN state.

Beginning in version 21.08, Slurm now supports NVIDIA
Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) devices. This feature allows some newer NVIDIA

cgroup isolation and task binding.

## AutoDetect [#AutoDetect](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,
configuration details will automatically be filled in for any system-detected
GPU. This removes the need to explicitly configure GPUs in gres.conf, though the
Gres= line in slurm.conf is still required in order to tell slurmctld how
many GRES to expect.
Note that AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
and AutoDetect=oneapi need their corresponding GPU management libraries
installed on the node and found during Slurm configuration in order to work.
Both AutoDetect=nvml and AutoDetect=nvidia detect NVIDIA GPUs.
AutoDetect=nvidia (added in Slurm 24.11) doesn't require the

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain job array IDs, task IDs, and %A/%a output placeholders
results.agent_response:
Summary from the Slurm docs — concise definitions, placeholders, and examples.

Key terms
- JobID (SLURM_JOB_ID / %j): the unique Slurm job identifier for a job record/step.
- ArrayJobID (SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID / %A): the master job allocation number for a job array — the single job id Slurm prints when you submit the array (e.g., "Submitted batch job 12345"). Use %A in filename patterns to get that master id.
- ArrayTaskID (SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID / %a): the array index value for the current array element (the number from your --array specification). Use %a in filename patterns to get the element’s index.

Environment variables (set for array jobs)
- SLURM_JOB_ID — job id for the current job record/step.
- SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — job array’s master job allocation number (the first job id of the array).
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — this task’s array index.
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX — count and bounds for the array indices.

Filename replacement symbols (sbatch --output/--error pattern)
- %A — Job array's master job allocation number (ArrayJobID).
- %a — Job array index number (ArrayTaskID).
- %j — jobid (SLURM_JOB_ID).
- %J — jobid.stepid (e.g., "128.0").
- %% — literal percent sign; %b is array index modulo 10 (less commonly used).
Example:
- sbatch --array=1-10 --output=slurm-%A_%a.out myjob.sh
  - For array master id 12345 and element index 3 this expands to slurm-12345_3.out.

Addressing and operating on array elements
- scontrol and scancel accept the ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID notation to identify one element:
  - scancel 20_4  (cancels element index 4 of array job 20)
  - scancel 20    (cancels the whole array)
- Dependencies can target single elements or whole arrays:
  - sbatch --depend=after:123_4 my.job  (depend on element 4 of job array 123)
  - sbatch --depend=afterany:123 my.job (depend on entire array)

Behavior notes / gotchas from the docs
- The --array option defines the list of indices (e.g., --array=0-31, --array=1,3,5).
- The smallest index allowed may be 0 (cluster MaxArraySize applies).
- Slurm creates a single job record for the array and creates per-element records as needed; the first task is often a placeholder and may run last — this can make the mapping between SLURM_JOB_ID and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID non-monotonic (see docs: “the task with the lowest SLURM_JOB_ID will have the highest SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID”).
- To guarantee unique per-task output files, include both %A and %a (or %j) in the pattern.

If you want, I can paste exact sbatch / job_array doc snippets or show a few concrete examples you can copy into your job script.

job array support.
The JobID is a unique identifier for the job.
The ArrayJobID is the JobID of the first element of the job
array.
The ArrayTaskID is the array index of this particular entry, either a
single number of an expression identifying the entries represented by this

The optional job ID specified with the scontrol show job or
scontrol show step commands can identify job array elements by
specifying ArrayJobId and ArrayTaskId with an underscore between
them (e.g. <ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskId>).

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .
```text
$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...

Snippet:
## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## NSS Configuration [#NSS_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

The srun command is used to launch applications.
By default, the application is launched only on the first component of a
heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
srun's "--het-group" option defines which hetjob component(s) are to have
applications launched for them. The --het-group option takes an expression
defining which component(s) are to launch an application for an individual
execution of the srun command. The expression can contain one or more component

in a hyphen separated list. By default, an application is launched only on

## Submitting Jobs [#submitting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The salloc , sbatch and srun commands can all be used
to submit heterogeneous jobs.
Resource specifications for each component of the heterogeneous job should be
separated with ":" character.
For example:
```text
$ sbatch --cpus-per-task=4 --mem-per-cpu=1 --ntasks=128 : \ --cpus-per-task=1 --mem-per-cpu=16 --ntasks=1 my.bash
```
Options specified for one component of a heterogeneous job (or job step) will
be used for subsequent components to the extent which is expected to be helpful.
Propagated options can be reset as desired for each component (e.g. a different
account name could be specified for each hetjob component.
For example, --immediate and --job-name are propagated, while
--ntasks and --mem-per-cpu are reset to default values for each
component.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Submitting Jobs [#submitting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The salloc , sbatch and srun commands can all be used
to submit heterogeneous jobs.
Resource specifications for each component of the heterogeneous job should be
separated with ":" character.
For example:
```text
$ sbatch --cpus-per-task=4 --mem-per-cpu=1 --ntasks=128 : \ --cpus-per-task=1 --mem-per-cpu=16 --ntasks=1 my.bash
```
Options specified for one component of a heterogeneous job (or job step) will
be used for subsequent components to the extent which is expected to be helpful.
Propagated options can be reset as desired for each component (e.g. a different
account name could be specified for each hetjob component.
For example, --immediate and --job-name are propagated, while
--ntasks and --mem-per-cpu are reset to default values for each
component.

## Launching Applications (Job Steps) [#job_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The srun command is used to launch applications.
By default, the application is launched only on the first component of a
heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
srun's "--het-group" option defines which hetjob component(s) are to have

## Job Allocation [#job_allocation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_launch.html)
The first step of the process is to create a job allocation, which is
a claim on compute resources. A job allocation can be created using the
salloc , sbatch or srun command. The salloc and
sbatch commands create resource allocations while the srun
command will create a resource allocation (if not already running within one)
plus launch tasks. Each of these commands will fill in a data structure

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Snippet:
## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor) to compute a single numeric job priority as a weighted sum of independent factors. Three of the most important pieces that control queue ordering are: the fairshare factor (how much a user/account has recently consumed), the Fair Tree algorithm (how fairshare is computed across accounts/users), and the configured PriorityWeight* values (how strongly each factor influences ordering).

How job priority is computed (conceptual)
- Job_priority = site_factor
  + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor
  + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
  + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
  + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
  + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
  + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
  + SUM(TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X)
  - nice_factor
- Each factor is a floating value (roughly 0.0–1.0). The PriorityWeight* entries are unsigned integers; together they scale each factor’s contribution before the total is converted to the final integer priority (0 .. 4294967295).

Fairshare factor — what it means and how it behaves
- Fairshare reduces priority for users/accounts that have used more of the cluster recently; it raises priority for users/accounts that have used less.
- Fairshare values are derived from historical usage per association/account/user and are normalized into a factor used in the multifactor formula.
- Two key configuration knobs:
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: controls how quickly past usage “decays” (short half-life forgets history quickly; long half-life keeps historical usage influential). A value of 0 disables decay (must then use PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod: optionally reset usage counters on a schedule (useful for enforcing quotas or fixed-period fairness).
- Tools to inspect fairshare: sshare (shows effective shares and usage) and sprio (shows factor contributions for pending jobs).

Fair Tree (the modern fairshare algorithm)
- Since Slurm 19.05 the Fair Tree algorithm is the default method used to convert historical usage into fairshare factors.
- Fair Tree is hierarchical: if two sibling accounts A and B are ordered by fairshare, then all children of A rank above all children of B. This preserves account-level ordering and avoids precision/tie problems seen in the older Classic algorithm.
- Benefits: stable ordering across account hierarchies, predictable behavior when account coordinators adjust shares, and reduced numerical tie/precision issues.
- If you need the older "classic" behavior you can still configure that explicitly, but Fair Tree is typically preferred.

Priority weights — how to make a factor matter (or not)
- PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, and per-TRES weights determine how strongly each factor affects final priority.
- If a weight is set to zero the corresponding factor contributes nothing.
- Typical default pattern: make PriorityWeightFairshare large relative to others so fairshare has strong influence (examples in docs use PriorityWeightFairshare=10000, others 1000).
- Example effects:
  - If PriorityWeightFairshare >> PriorityWeightAge, then users’ historical usage dominates scheduling (new jobs from under-used users jump ahead of old heavy users).
  - If PriorityWeightAge is high, long-waiting jobs will eventually win even if a user has been heavy.
- TRES weights allow bias by resource type (e.g., make GPU usage count differently than CPU usage in the fairshare calculations).

Practical tuning and debugging tips
- Decide policy first: do you want strict account-level fairness, or to allow aging to override recent usage?
- Typical levers:
  - Increase PriorityWeightFairshare to favor historical fairness.
  - Decrease PriorityDecayHalfLife to forget older usage sooner (helps new users recover).
  - Use PriorityUsageResetPeriod for hard periodic resets (monthly allocations, semester quotas).
  - Tune TRES weights to reflect relative cost/importance of GPUs vs CPUs.
- Inspect what Slurm is doing:
  - sshare — view current fairshare/usage for accounts and users.
  - sprio [--all] — show the numeric priority and per-factor contributions for pending jobs.
  - scontrol show config — see configured PriorityWeight* and decay/reset settings.
- When debugging why a particular job is low in the queue, run sprio (or scontrol show job) to see the fairshare_factor and all other factor contributions.

Short examples
- Two accounts A and B, equal job size mix, but A has consumed 4× more resources in the past week:
  - With PriorityWeightFairshare high, jobs from B will be scheduled ahead of A until usage evens out.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is short (e.g., 1 day), A’s advantage/penalty fades quickly and A’s jobs recover sooner.
- If PriorityWeightAge is large, even a user with poor fairshare will eventually have jobs win after waiting long enough.

Bottom line
- Fairshare (via Fair Tree) determines how recent historical consumption penalizes or boosts users/accounts.
- Priority weights control how much that fairshare (and other factors like age, job size, QOS, TRES) influence final queue ordering.
- Use sshare and sprio to inspect current effective shares and factor contributions; tune PriorityWeight* and PriorityDecayHalfLife/PriorityUsageResetPeriod to match your site’s fairness vs responsiveness goals.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current configured PriorityWeight* and fairshare settings from your cluster (scontrol show config and sshare/sprio).

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain burst buffer directives and stage-in or stage-out behavior
results.agent_response:
Summary from the official Slurm "Burst Buffer Guide" (key points and examples of behavior / directives):

What a "burst buffer" request is
- Slurm supports burst buffers via a plugin (e.g., datawarp or the generic lua plugin). The plugin is enabled with BurstBufferType in slurm.conf and governs available directive names, semantics, pools, timeouts and validation.
- Jobs request either job-specific burst buffers or (for DataWarp) create/destroy persistent burst buffers.

Where to put burst-buffer directives
- Put burst-buffer directives as commented lines in the batch script (they begin with the plugin directive string, e.g. #DW, #BB, or #BB_LUA). They may appear before, after, or mixed with #SBATCH lines.
- The directive string used for a plugin can be configured (the lua plugin uses #BB_LUA by default; DataWarp uses #DW and Slurm also supports a #BB form for persistent operations).

Command-line alternatives
- salloc, sbatch and srun accept --bb (inline directives) and --bbf (filename with burst-buffer operations). Note: --bb cannot create or destroy persistent burst buffers; behavior of --bb depends on the plugin.

Common directive fields and plugin differences
- DataWarp (plugin) commonly uses directives like #DW (job-specific) and Slurm also supports #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent for persistent buffers. For DataWarp, a job-specific request must include a capacity; if capacity is omitted the job is rejected.
- Fields you will see in docs/examples: capacity (size requested), pool (which pool to allocate from), access (access mode), name (for persistent buffers), hurry (option when destroying).
- The lua plugin is flexible; many lua-based deployments require only the presence of the directive (the plugin then runs the configured stages). Exact parameter names and semantics can vary by plugin/config.

Stage-in / stage-out behavior and lifecycle
- Burst-buffer work is performed in distinct stages that run at specific points in the job lifecycle:
  - staging-in / staged-in / pre-run — data is staged into the buffer before the job's main workload begins
  - running — job runs while buffer is available
  - post-run / staging-out / teardown — data is staged out and buffer is torn down after job completion
  - There are other internal states (pending, allocating, allocated, deleting, deleted, alloc-revoke, suspended, teardown-fail, complete).
- Slurm tracks a job's burst-buffer state in the job's BurstBufferState field (scontrol show job will display it).
- Stage-in must complete before the job enters the running state. Stage-out is performed after the job ends; some job dependencies respect stage-out timing (see dependencies below).

Timeouts, validation and diagnostics
- The burst-buffer plugin configuration exposes timeouts (e.g., StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout, ValidateTimeout) and other plugin-specific parameters. You can inspect plugin/pool status with scontrol show burst (example output includes pool sizes, allocated buffers, StageInTimeout/StageOutTimeout values).
- DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf enables verbose plugin logging for troubleshooting.

Job dependencies and stage-out
- Normal job dependencies (e.g., --dependency=afterok:JOB) wait for the dependent job to finish, but they do not necessarily wait for the first job's burst-buffer stage-out to finish.
- If you need a later job to wait until a previous job's stage-out completes, use the afterburstbuffer dependency (e.g., --dependency=afterburstbuffer:12345). This ensures the second job does not begin until the first job's stage-out is complete.

Heterogeneous jobs
- For heterogeneous jobs with multiple components, burst-buffer hooks run once per component that contains burst-buffer directives. Components without directives do not trigger burst-buffer stages.

Persistent burst buffers (DataWarp)
- With DataWarp you can create and destroy persistent burst buffers from Slurm using directives such as:
  - #BB create_persistent name=<name> capacity=<size> [access=...] [pool=...] ...
  - #BB destroy_persistent name=<name> [hurry]
- Persistent buffer lifecycle (allocating/allocated/deleting/deleted) differs from job-specific buffers.

How Slurm executes the directives
- Slurm parses the commented directive lines and hands actual stage operations to the configured plugin. The --bb option causes Slurm to create a temporary burst-buffer script internally which the plugin uses; --bbf reads a file of operations.

Useful commands for users and admins
- Inspect job burst-buffer state: scontrol show job <jobid> (look for BurstBufferState)
- Inspect configured burst buffers and pools: scontrol show burst
- Use scontrol show config / slurm.conf to see BurstBufferType and plugin config
- For debugging: enable DebugFlags=BurstBuffer and check plugin-specific logs

Practical notes / best practices
- Always check which plugin your site uses (DataWarp vs lua) because required parameters and directive names differ.
- For DataWarp jobs, always specify capacity and, if needed, pool and access to avoid job rejection.
- If downstream jobs depend on the staged-out data, use afterburstbuffer dependency so you wait for stage-out completion.
- Keep burst-buffer directives near the top of the script; placing them as comments avoids shell interpretation and ensures Slurm parses them.

If you want, I can:
- Show the exact directive syntax examples for the plugin your cluster uses (DataWarp or lua) — tell me which plugin or paste a sample burst_buffer.conf or one of your site's example job headers, and I’ll extract the exact directive lines from the docs for that plugin.
- Or fetch and paste the relevant sections from the Slurm guide (e.g., DataWarp or Lua examples).

In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include
burst buffer directives. These command-line options are available for salloc,
sbatch, and srun. Note that the `--bb` option cannot create or
destroy persistent burst buffers.
The `--bbf` option takes as an argument a filename and that file
should contain a collection of burst buffer operations identical to those used
for batch jobs.

buffer directives as the option argument. The behavior of this option depends
on which burst buffer plugin is used. When the `--bb` option is
used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

## Command-line Job Options [#command-line](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include
burst buffer directives. These command-line options are available for salloc,
sbatch, and srun. Note that the `--bb` option cannot create or
destroy persistent burst buffers.
The `--bbf` option takes as an argument a filename and that file
should contain a collection of burst buffer operations identical to those used
for batch jobs.
Alternatively, the `--bb` option may be used to specify burst
buffer directives as the option argument. The behavior of this option depends
on which burst buffer plugin is used. When the `--bb` option is
used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file
that is used internally by the burst buffer plugins.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain pending reasons Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, and QOS limits
results.agent_response:
Below are concise, doc-backed explanations (what the reason means, common causes, quick checks, and typical fixes) for the pending reasons you asked about. References: Slurm Job Reason Codes, Resource Limits, Priority (multifactor) and QOS docs.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - The scheduler could not find sufficient free resources to place the job (CPUs, memory, GPUs, nodes, sockets, or matching TRES/GRES).
- Common causes
  - No nodes with the requested TRES (e.g., --gres=gpu:...), not enough CPUs or memory on any single node, fragmentation across nodes, or all suitable nodes are already allocated.
  - Constraints like node features (-C / --constraint) or topology/heterogeneous requests that can't be satisfied.
- What to check
  - sinfo to see partition/node idle counts and TRES/GRES availability.
  - squeue to see what is currently running/allocating.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> for the job’s requested resources.
- Typical fixes
  - Relax resources/constraints (fewer GPUs, less memory, fewer specific features).
  - Submit with a different partition or different GRES type.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or enable preemption if policy allows.

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The job is eligible but lower-priority jobs are ahead; higher-priority workload(s) currently prevent this job from being scheduled.
- Common causes
  - Other queued jobs have higher multifactor priority (age, fairshare, QOS priority, job size, partition weight, etc.).
  - QOS/association priority settings or recent account usage (fairshare) favor other jobs.
- What to check
  - sprio (shows priority components for queued jobs) and sprio --weights (configured weights).
  - squeue to identify higher-priority jobs on the partition.
  - sshare to inspect fairshare usage.
- Typical fixes
  - Request a higher QOS (if allowed).
  - Ask an admin to adjust QOS/priority weights or run under a QOS that allows preemption.
  - Wait — priority factors (age/fairshare) may escalate the job over time.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The job requested specific node(s) or node characteristics that are currently not available or usable, so the scheduler cannot allocate them.
- Common causes
  - The job used explicit node requests (e.g., --nodelist, -w, heterogeneous node lists) and those nodes are down/drained/allocated or reserved.
  - A reservation prevents taking those nodes, or the nodes have been placed into maintenance/power-off states.
  - Node feature/constraint mismatch where nodes matching constraints are unavailable.
- What to check
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the exact node request.
  - sinfo (and sinfo -R / sinfo_reasons) or sinfo --Node to inspect node states (down/drain/reserved).
  - squeue --reservation=<name> if a reservation might be blocking nodes.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node list or relax constraints.
  - Wait for the nodes to come back (or ask admins to bring nodes up or clear the reservation).
  - If a reservation blocks the nodes, either use a different partition/QOS or coordinate with the reservation owner/admin.

4) QOS limits (pending reasons that indicate limit enforcement)
- What it means
  - The job would exceed a configured resource or count limit on a QOS, account, user association or partition; the scheduler set a limit-related pending reason (e.g., Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp*, MaxTRESPerUser).
- Common causes
  - Per-QOS or partition limits like MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, MaxTRESPerUser (GPU/CPU hours or counts), MaxNodes, MaxWall, etc. A job can pend when it would breach a limit unless DenyOnLimit is set (then it would be denied at submission).
  - Hierarchical enforcement: Partition QOS limits are evaluated first by default; job QOS and association limits follow (OverPartQOS can change precedence).
- What to check
  - sacctmgr (sacctmgr list associations / sacctmgr show qos) to inspect QOS and association limits.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see the job's QOS/association.
  - Resource Limits documentation to map the pending reason to the exact configured limit name.
- Typical fixes
  - Use a different QOS or partition with sufficient limits.
  - Request limit increases from admins (via sacctmgr).
  - Change the job request (smaller resource request, fewer concurrent jobs) to fit within limits.
  - If DenyOnLimit is set and you keep hitting rejects at submit, adjust the job/QOS or ask admins to change DenyOnLimit.

Short diagnostic checklist you can run (commands)
- scontrol show job <jobid>        # job’s requested resources, QOS, node list
- squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %D %R"  # queue row + reason
- sinfo -l / sinfo --Node          # partition and node availability, TRES/GRES
- sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons        # nodes in drain/down and the reasons
- sprio                             # priority breakdown for pending jobs
- sshare                            # fairshare / effective shares
- sacctmgr list qos / sacctmgr show qos  # QOS limits and flags

If you want, tell me one example JOBID and I can show the exact squeue / scontrol fields and the scheduler-assigned pending reason and give a targeted remediation.

Snippet:
# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

Snippet:
### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain job array IDs, task IDs, and %A/%a output placeholders
results.agent_response:
Short reference from the Slurm docs (job_array and sbatch pages) that explains the meanings and how to use the IDs, task index, and the %A / %a filename placeholders.

1) Basic terms
- Array job: a single sbatch submission that represents many similar tasks (submitted with --array).
- Array master job ID / ArrayJobID: the JobID associated with the array as a whole (the "first" job record for the array).
- Array task / ArrayTaskID (task index): the index value you specified in --array (e.g. 1,2,3 or 0-255:2). Each array element is one task.

2) Environment variables (available inside each batch script)
- SLURM_JOB_ID — the actual JobID for the running job element (each element may have its own job id).
- SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the array’s master job id (set to the first job id of the array).
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the index value for the current array element (the thing you usually use to pick input files, etc).
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX — count/min/max for the array indices.

Use these in your script, e.g.:
  input=data_${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}.txt

3) Job ID formatting and addressing
- Individual array elements are commonly represented as ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (e.g. 12345_3).
- squeue by default shows the array compactly (e.g. 1080_[5-1024]); squeue --array (or -r) can show each element on its own line.
- scontrol accepts either the array master job id (affects whole array) or the element form (affects only that element). Example:
  scontrol show job 101        # describes the array job record
  scontrol show job 101_3      # describes element task index 3

4) %A and %a filename placeholders (sbatch filename pattern)
- %A — expands to the array master job allocation number (the ArrayJobID).
- %a — expands to the array element index (the ArrayTaskID).
These are used in sbatch filename patterns such as --output and --error:
  sbatch --array=1-3 --output=slurm-%A_%a.out myjob.sh
If sbatch replies "Submitted batch job 36" for the array, element outputs will be:
  slurm-36_1.out, slurm-36_2.out, slurm-36_3.out

Notes and gotchas
- %A and %a are meaningful for array jobs; they are used to produce per-element filenames. The array element addressing format (ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID) is how Slurm and scontrol/scancel identify elements.
- Because of internal placeholder tasks, the mapping of element index ↔ SLURM_JOB_ID ordering can be non-obvious (the first task can be a placeholder). Use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index into inputs rather than relying on SLURM_JOB_ID ordering.
- You can cancel/operate on all elements with scancel <ArrayJobID> or on particular elements with scancel <ArrayJobID>_<TaskID> (e.g. scancel 20_4).

If you want, I can show short concrete examples (sbatch command + resulting filenames + sample script lines) tailored to your typical --array range.

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .
```text

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to compare afterok, afterany, afternotok, and singleton dependencies
results.agent_response:
I looked up the official Slurm sbatch/manual docs and summarized the four dependency types you asked about. Short definitions, when they trigger, examples and typical uses:

1) after
- What it means: make the job eligible to start after the specified job(s) have started (i.e., after the referenced job(s) begin execution).
- Triggers: when the referenced job(s) have started running (does not wait for completion).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=after:12345 myjob.sh
- Use case: start something that can run concurrently once a producer has begun (e.g., start a consumer once producer is running), or coordinate start ordering without waiting for completion.

2) afterok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have completed successfully (exit code 0).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have terminated with success (zero exit code).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 next-step.sh
- Use case: multi-step workflows where later steps must run only if earlier steps succeed (build → test → deploy).

3) afterany
- What it means: start after the specified job(s) have terminated, regardless of their exit code (success or failure).
- Triggers: when all referenced jobs have finished in any terminal state.
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afterany:12345 postprocess.sh
- Use case: always-run follow-up tasks (e.g., archive logs or collect metrics) whether the upstream job succeeded or failed.

4) afternotok
- What it means: start only after the specified job(s) have terminated with a non‑zero (failing) exit code.
- Triggers: when any/all referenced jobs have finished and returned a non‑zero exit (i.e., failed).
- Example: sbatch --dependency=afternotok:12345 failure_handler.sh
- Use case: run remediation/alerting/cleanup only when an upstream job fails.

5) singleton (special)
- What it means: no job ID is passed; the job is held until all previously submitted jobs with the same user and job name have finished. Ensures only one job with that name/user runs at a time.
- Triggers: the new job becomes eligible after earlier jobs with the same name and user have terminated.
- Example: sbatch --job-name=data_proc --dependency=singleton data_proc.sh
- Use case: serialize repeated submissions of the same job (avoid parallel runs of the same job-name by the same user).

Notes and tips
- Syntax: --dependency=type:jobid[:jobid...] (singleton has no jobid).
- Combine dependencies: you can specify multiple dependencies (comma-separated) to express complex conditions.
- Choose afterok for success-only chaining, afterany when you must always continue, afternotok for failure-only handlers, after when you only need start ordering, and singleton to serialize same-name jobs.
- These definitions come from the sbatch man page / Slurm documentation.

If you want, I can show exact sbatch examples for a concrete workflow (e.g., build→test→deploy with success/failure handlers) or look up how dependencies interact with job arrays. Which would you like?

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run

slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Snippet:
## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Summary — how Slurm orders the queue
- Slurm’s default is the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor). A job’s priority is a weighted sum of multiple factors (age, fairshare, job size, partition, QOS, TRES, site, nice, …). The larger the resulting integer, the higher the job is ordered in the queue and the sooner it is eligible to run.

High-level formula (concept)
- Job_priority = site_factor
  + PriorityWeightAge  * age_factor
  + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
  + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
  + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
  + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
  + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
  + SUM( TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X )
  - nice_factor
- Each factor produces a floating value roughly in [0.0, 1.0] (implementation-dependent). The configured PriorityWeight* values scale each factor’s contribution; weights are integers and the final priority is an integer (0 .. 2^32-1).

Fairshare (what it does)
- Purpose: prevent users/accounts that consumed many resources recently from always winning the scheduler. Fairshare reduces priority for heavy recent users and increases it for under-used users.
- It is driven by historical usage tracked per association (user/account), decayed over time by PriorityDecayHalfLife so older usage matters less.
- Key config knobs:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare: how strongly fairshare influences final priority (higher = more influence).
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: how quickly historical usage decays (e.g., 7-0 is 7 days). Smaller half-life → recent use matters more.
  - PriorityUsageResetPeriod: optional periodic reset of usage counters (useful if you want hard resets).
- You can inspect fairshare-related usage with sshare (reports effective shares/usage).

Fair Tree (Fair-share algorithm starting ~19.05)
- Fair Tree is the modern fairshare algorithm used by the multifactor plugin by default.
- Behavior:
  - Hierarchical: it respects account/user/account-group hierarchies so that if parent account A ranks ahead of sibling B, then all children of A rank ahead of all children of B. That prevents accidental local re-ordering inside an account that would hurt cross-account fairness.
  - Produces stable, rank-based fairshare factors and avoids precision issues and undesirable inversions that could occur in the older Classic algorithm.
  - Tie-handling is explicit and deterministic (but ties are permitted).
- Use when you have hierarchical accounting (accounts with subaccounts) and want consistent inter-account ordering.

Configured priority weights (how they change behavior)
- Weights are the administrator’s control knobs; they scale each factor’s effect on final priority:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare (commonly big, e.g., 10000): strong influence of fairshare.
  - PriorityWeightAge (e.g., 1000): lets jobs that waited a long time climb the queue (prevents starvation).
  - PriorityWeightJobSize (e.g., 1000): can favor smaller or larger jobs depending on how job_size_factor is defined.
  - PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS etc.: let you prefer jobs in particular partitions or QOS classes.
  - TRES weights (TRESWeight) let CPU, GPU, memory costs change priority (e.g., deprioritize GPU-heavy jobs).
- Example numeric intuition:
  - If PriorityWeightFairshare = 10000 and fairshare_factor for alice = 0.8, that contributes ≈ 8000 points.
  - If PriorityWeightAge = 1000 and age_factor = 0.5, that contributes ≈ 500 points.
  - Final priority is the sum of all such contributions (site + assoc + fairshare + …) minus nice_factor.
- Practical tuning guidance:
  - If fairness matters most, make PriorityWeightFairshare large relative to other weights.
  - If you want long-waiting jobs to eventually run despite fairshare, increase PriorityWeightAge.
  - If small jobs should be favored to improve throughput, tune PriorityWeightJobSize or PriorityFavorSmall.
  - Use PriorityDecayHalfLife to define how much history you want (short half-life = recent use matters; long half-life = long-term quotas).
  - Avoid making all weights zero or heavily skewing one factor unless intentional.

Diagnostics and inspection
- sprio: shows per-job priority and breakdown by factor (useful to see which factors contribute most).
- sshare: shows usage and effective shares for accounts/users (helps understand fairshare state).
- scontrol show config: view the Priority* settings in slurm.conf.
- sdiag and scheduler logs: for deeper scheduler behavior and backfill diagnostics.

Common interactions and gotchas
- Fairshare vs Age: a very large fairshare weight can cause a new or low-usage user’s job to jump ahead of long-waiting jobs unless you also raise PriorityWeightAge.
- TRES weights: assigning large positive weights to a TRES increases priority for jobs consuming that TRES (or the inverse, depending on factor setup); be careful when combining TRES weights with fairshare.
- QOS and partition factors can override account-level fairness for special classes (e.g., interactive or emergency QOS).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife = 0 disables decay (usage never decays) so the usage counters must be reset periodically with PriorityUsageResetPeriod or manually.
- Priority calculations use integers and limited precision; extremely large or tiny weights can lead to unintuitive ordering—test changes in a staging environment.

If you want, I can:
- show example slurm.conf snippets with recommended starting weights, or
- explain how to interpret sprio output for one or more real jobs, or
- suggest a tuning recipe for a cluster profile (research, bursty GPU, or throughput-focused). Which would you like?

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain burst buffer directives and stage-in or stage-out behavior
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, doc-based summary of Slurm burst-buffer directives and how stage‑in / stage‑out behave. I used the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) as the source.

What burst‑buffer directives are and where to put them
- Burst‑buffer directives are comment lines placed in batch scripts (they begin with #) that tell Slurm’s burst‑buffer plugin what storage to allocate and what data movement to run for the job.
- Directives may appear before, after, or interspersed with #SBATCH lines.
- The same directives can be supplied on the command line: sbatch/srun/salloc accept --bb (inline directives) and --bbf (a file of burst‑buffer operations). Note: --bb cannot create/destroy persistent buffers; --bbf points to a file formatted like the script directives.

Plugin differences (affects directive names and exact fields)
- DataWarp plugin: common directive names are #DW (job‑specific burst buffer directives) and #BB (used for persistent‑buffer create/destroy with DataWarp). DataWarp has extra, vendor-specific options; consult DataWarp docs for details.
- Lua plugin: default directive is #BB_LUA (configurable via burst_buffer.conf). The lua plugin is generic and relies on a site-provided burst_buffer.lua implementation for exact behavior.
- Exact token names and the allowed fields (stage_in, stage_out, capacity, pool, access, type, etc.) depend on the plugin; the guide documents the general fields but plugin docs (or your cluster’s burst_buffer.lua) define the precise syntax.

Job vs persistent burst buffers
- Job‑specific burst buffers: allocated for a job and released afterwards. Many plugins require a capacity; if a job requests a job‑specific buffer without specifying capacity the job may be rejected.
- Persistent burst buffers: (DataWarp only) may be created/destroyed with #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent and survive beyond a single job.

Stage‑in / stage‑out behavior and lifecycle
- Staging occurs at defined points in the job lifecycle. Slurm tracks burst buffer states such as: pending, allocating, allocated, staging‑in, staged‑in, pre‑run, running, staging‑out, post‑run, teardown, complete (these appear in the BurstBufferState shown by scontrol show job).
- Stage‑in: data movement from the backing filesystem into the allocated burst buffer is run before the job enters the running state (the job will wait for stage‑in to finish). After successful stage‑in the job proceeds to pre‑run / run.
- Stage‑out: after the job finishes running, post‑run hooks run to move data from the burst buffer back to the target filesystem (stage‑out). Stage‑out runs during the job’s post‑run / teardown phases (the job’s completion may be delayed until stage‑out finishes).
- Timeouts: plugins expose timeout controls (e.g., StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout in the burst‑buffer configuration/status). If staging times out or fails, the burst‑buffer plugin’s behavior depends on plugin/config (failure can lead to teardown or teardown‑fail states).
- Heterogeneous jobs: burst‑buffer hooks are run per job component that has directives — components without directives do not get burst‑buffer stages.

Typical directive components (conceptual, plugin-specific syntax varies)
- capacity=<size> (required for many job‑specific buffers)
- pool=<pool-name> (which pool to allocate from)
- stage_in=<source>:<bb-path> (request staging of source data into the buffer)
- stage_out=<bb-path>:<destination> (request staging of results out of the buffer)
- access=, type=, link/move/copy semantics — some plugins support copy vs link vs move semantics; exact names/options are plugin dependent

How to check status / diagnostics
- scontrol show job <jobid> includes a BurstBufferState field for jobs that requested burst buffers.
- scontrol show burst (or sview Burst Buffer tab) shows configured burst pools, allocated buffers, per‑job allocations, and plugin timeouts (StageInTimeout / StageOutTimeout).
- DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf increases burst‑buffer logging for debugging.

Practical notes and best practices
- Because stage‑in must finish before the job runs, large stage‑in operations can delay job start — account for that in scheduling and timeouts.
- Stage‑out can extend job completion time (post‑run); set StageOutTimeout appropriately and avoid leaving long, unneeded data in buffers.
- Request only the capacity you need; burst‑buffer size may affect scheduling.
- For cluster‑specific behavior and exact directive syntax/examples, consult your cluster’s burst_buffer.conf, burst_buffer.lua (if used), and the DataWarp/Lua plugin documentation in the Slurm Burst Buffer Guide.

Where to read the exact syntax
- See the official Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) for:
  - job submission directives and command‑line options (--bb / --bbf),
  - DataWarp and Lua plugin sections,
  - persistent buffer create/destroy (#BB create_persistent ...),
  - the list of burst buffer states and example scontrol output.

If you want, I can:
- paste the exact directive examples from the guide for the plugin your site uses (DataWarp or Lua), or
- check your cluster’s burst_buffer.conf and burst_buffer.lua (if you give me the file paths) to show the exact directive name and supported fields your cluster expects. Which would you prefer?

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

## Command-line Job Options [#command-line](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include
burst buffer directives. These command-line options are available for salloc,
sbatch, and srun. Note that the `--bb` option cannot create or
destroy persistent burst buffers.
The `--bbf` option takes as an argument a filename and that file
should contain a collection of burst buffer operations identical to those used
for batch jobs.
Alternatively, the `--bb` option may be used to specify burst
buffer directives as the option argument. The behavior of this option depends
on which burst buffer plugin is used. When the `--bb` option is
used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file
that is used internally by the burst buffer plugins.

These are the different possible burst buffer states:
- pending
- allocating
- allocated
- deleting
- deleted
- staging-in
- staged-in
- pre-run
- alloc-revoke
- running
- suspended
- post-run
- staging-out
- teardown
- teardown-fail
- complete

`scontrol show job`. This field only appears for jobs that requested
a burst buffer. The states `allocating`, `allocated`,

state `alloc-revoke` happens if a failure in Slurm's select plugin
