results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain pending reasons Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, and QOS limits
results.agent_response:
Below are concise, doc‑based explanations of the four common pending reasons you asked about, what they mean, how to diagnose them, and common ways to resolve them.

1) Resources
- What it means
  - Slurm could not find sufficient free resources that match the job request (CPUs, memory, GPUs, TRES, nodes, or node features/constraints). This includes cases where no single node satisfies a per‑node request (e.g., --mem-per-cpu, --ntasks-per-node) or where the requested combination of resources is not available.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (look at ReqTRES, NumNodes, MinNodes, NodeList/Constraints).
  - See cluster/node availability: sinfo -Nel (per-node free/alloc counts), sinfo (partition summary).
  - Check queue rows: squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %t %R %C %m" (reason column, requested resources).
- Typical fixes
  - Reduce resources requested (fewer CPUs, less memory, fewer GPUs, smaller node count).
  - Remove or relax constraints/--constraint/--nodelist/--exclude that force specific nodes.
  - Use a different partition with suitable nodes.
  - Wait for currently running jobs to finish or ask users/admins to free nodes.
  - For per‑node packing problems, change job layout (--ntasks-per-node, --nodes).

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The scheduler found one or more higher‑priority jobs which must run before this job. Slurm reports the first encountered blocking reason as "Priority".
- How to diagnose
  - Show job priority values: scontrol show job <jobid> (Priority field).
  - Inspect priority factors and queue ordering: sprio (or sprio -l / sprio -u <user>), sshare (fairshare usage).
  - Look for many older/higher‑QOS jobs in the same partition: squeue -p <partition> --sort=-p (or sort by priority/age).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit with a higher QOS (if permitted) or ask admin to adjust QOS/priority.
  - Reduce job size/time so it is scheduled sooner by the policy.
  - Wait—priority often resolves as higher priority jobs finish or as the job ages/fairshare changes.
  - Admin actions: change priority weights, adjust fairshare or QOS priorities.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means
  - The specific nodes requested by the job (via --nodelist, --exclude, or a constraint that pins nodes) are not available for allocation (they may be DOWN, DRAINED, allocated to other jobs, in a reservation, or otherwise unavailable).
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job: scontrol show job <jobid> (NodeList, Exclude, Constraint).
  - Check node states: sinfo -Nel or sinfo --Node (or sinfo_reasons to list down/drain nodes and reasons).
  - For a named node: scontrol show node <nodename> to see state/reason.
- Typical fixes
  - Remove explicit node requests or exclusions so the scheduler can choose available nodes.
  - Choose a different partition without the unavailable nodes.
  - Wait for the named nodes to come back online or be released from other jobs.
  - If nodes are down/drained, contact the cluster admin to repair/bring them back.

4) QOS limits (jobs blocked by QOS/account limits)
- What it means
  - The job is blocked because it would violate a QOS or association/account limit. Slurm reason codes related to QOS/limits include Max*PerAccount, AssocGrp, AssocMax and similar. Limits can be per‑QOS, per‑user, per‑account, or TRES (CPU/GPU/time) caps.
- How to diagnose
  - Inspect the job fields: scontrol show job <jobid> (QOS, Account, ReqTRES).
  - Check accounting/association limits: sacctmgr show assoc / sacctmgr list associations (or ask admin to run those).
  - See fairshare/usage: sshare and sprio may help show why QOS choice affects priority.
  - The squeue reason text will often indicate the specific limit name (e.g., MaxJobsPerUser).
- Typical fixes
  - Submit under a different QOS or account with higher limits (if you have access).
  - Reduce requested resources/time to stay within the QOS limits.
  - Wait until other jobs reduce your account's current usage (free up slots).
  - Request admin changes to the QOS/account limits (this is an administrative change).

Notes and troubleshooting tips
- Only one pending reason is shown (the reason encountered during scheduling); there can be multiple underlying causes. If you need the exact, low‑level scheduler decision you can combine scontrol show job <id>, sprio, sshare, and sinfo.
- Useful quick commands: squeue -j <id> -o "%i %P %u %t %R %l %M" ; scontrol show job <id> ; sinfo -Nel ; sprio ; sshare ; sacctmgr show assoc.
- If you want, tell me a job ID and I can walk through the exact squeue/scontrol outputs you should check and what they likely mean.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain job array IDs, task IDs, and %A/%a output placeholders
results.agent_response:
Summary from the Slurm docs (sbatch and job_array pages) — what job-array IDs, task IDs, and the %A / %a filename placeholders mean and how to use them.

Key concepts
- Job array: a collection of similar batch jobs submitted together via sbatch --array (or -a). Slurm treats the array as a single submission but creates per-task records as tasks start.
- Array (master) job ID: the job ID that sbatch prints when you submit the array (e.g., "Submitted batch job 36"). Slurm documentation calls this the array’s master job allocation number.
- Task (array index): the index value you request for each element of the array (for example the numbers in --array=1-100). Each element is frequently referenced as JobID_index notation (e.g., 36_1 for job 36 element 1).

Environment variables the scheduler sets (relevant ones)
- SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the array’s master job ID (the number sbatch printed for the array).
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the array index for this task (the value from --array).
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT — number of tasks in the array.
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX / SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN — highest / lowest index in the array.

Filename / output placeholders (percent escapes supported by sbatch)
- %A — the job array’s master job allocation number (the array job ID). Use this when you want a single identifier for the whole array.
- %a — the job array index (the task’s index value). Use this to make per-task files.
- %b — the job array index modulo 10 (rarely used; useful for simple hashing/sharding).
- %j — the jobid of the running job (generic job id expansion).
- %J — jobid.stepid (e.g., "128.0").

Examples
- sbatch --array=1-3 --output=out_%A_%a.txt my.job
  - If sbatch responded "Submitted batch job 36", the files created will be:
    out_36_1.txt, out_36_2.txt, out_36_3.txt
  - %A = 36 (array master id), %a = 1,2,3 (task indices)

A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.
The slurmd on startup will reach out to a slurmctld that you specify and the
config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV
records defined within the cluster itself.

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner
than expected.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

## FILENAME PATTERN[#SECTION_FILENAME-PATTERN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch allows for a filename pattern to contain one or more replacement
symbols, which are a percent sign "%" followed by a letter (e.g. %j).
\\ [#OPT_\\](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) Do not process any of the replacement symbols.
%% [#OPT_%%](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) The character "%".
%A [#OPT_%A](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) Job array's master job allocation number.
%a [#OPT_%a](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) Job array ID (index) number.
%b [#OPT_%b](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html) Job array ID (index) number modulo 10.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

A cluster consists of many different types of nodes that contribute to

slurm.conf is an ASCII file which describes general Slurm
configuration information, the nodes to be managed, information about
how those nodes are grouped into partitions, and various scheduling
parameters associated with those partitions. This file should be
consistent across all nodes in the cluster.

The partition configuration permits you to establish different job
limits or access controls for various groups (or partitions) of nodes.
Nodes may be in more than one partition, making partitions serve
as general purpose queues.
For example one may put the same set of nodes into two different
partitions, each with different constraints (time limit, job sizes,
groups allowed to use the partition, etc.).
Jobs are allocated resources within a single partition.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.

by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

Slurm controller and assigned a Slurm job ID. The batch script is not

## Manual Power Saving[#manual](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:
POWER_DOWN [#POWER_DOWN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.
POWER_DOWN_ASAP [#POWER_DOWN_ASAP](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs
will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the
node.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

Snippet:
## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Summary first
- Slurm’s queue ordering (when PriorityType=priority/multifactor) is a weighted sum of independent priority “factors” (age, fair‑share, job size, QOS, partition, TRES, site, nice, etc.). Each factor is normalized (roughly 0.0–1.0) and multiplied by a configured integer weight in slurm.conf; those products are summed to produce the final job priority score. Larger score → higher queue position.
- Fairshare is the factor that biases scheduling to favor accounts/users that are under‑served historically. The Fair Tree algorithm is the modern fairshare computation that uses the account hierarchy to produce consistent, hierarchical priorities.
- You tune behavior by changing the PriorityWeight* settings and fairshare parameters (PriorityDecayHalfLife, PriorityUsageResetPeriod, PriorityCalcPeriod) and by choosing/keeping Fair Tree.

How the multifactor priority formula works
- Concept: Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * QOS_factor + SUM(TRES_weight_x * TRES_factor_x) - nice_factor
- Each factor is a floating point value (0.0–1.0). Each PriorityWeight* and TRES_weight_* is an unsigned integer set in slurm.conf. The final job priority is an integer (0 … 4294967295).
- Changing a weight changes the relative importance of that factor compared with the others. E.g., increasing PriorityWeightFairshare will make historical usage (fairshare) more dominant when ordering jobs.

Fairshare — the idea and behavior
- Purpose: prevent a few users/accounts from monopolizing resources by lowering priority for accounts that have already consumed more than their fair share, while boosting priority for under‑served accounts.
- It does not impose hard caps; it only changes ordering. Over‑consuming accounts can still run if nothing else is eligible.
- Fairshare requires the Slurm accounting DB to compute historical usage.
- The fairshare factor is computed from account/user “composite usage” vs. their configured shares/weights; a larger fairshare factor means the account/user is more under‑served (so its jobs get higher priority).
- Historical usage is decayed over time according to PriorityDecayHalfLife (so old usage matters less). PriorityUsageResetPeriod can periodically reset tracked usage if desired.

Fair Tree (the modern fairshare algorithm)
- Introduced in Slurm 19.05 and the default fairshare algorithm.
- Works over the account hierarchy (tree): if account A and account B are siblings and A ranks higher than B, then all children of A will rank higher than all children of B. This preserves hierarchical ordering and prevents strange inversions.
- Benefits:
  - Hierarchical consistency: parent/child relations behave intuitively.
  - Stable ordering: reduces precision errors and odd tie behaviors that could happen with the older “classic” algorithm.
  - Account coordinators can’t accidentally make some users in their account get lower effective priority relative to other accounts’ users by reassigning weights inside the account tree.
- You can still choose the older Classic algorithm if desired, but Fair Tree is generally recommended.

TRES/TRES weights and other factors
- TRES (Trackable RESources) weights let you give extra priority to jobs requesting particular resources (CPU, energy, GRES/GPU, etc.). Example: set TRES_weight_gpu higher to give GPU jobs relatively more priority.
- QOS and partition factors: PriorityWeightQOS and PriorityWeightPartition let QOS and partition membership influence priority.
- Age factor: PriorityWeightAge increases scheduling priority over time so long‑waiting jobs eventually win.

Practical tuning recommendations
- Inspect current behavior with:
  - sprio -l (shows per‑job factor contributions) — useful to see which factors dominate.
  - sshare (shows account shares/consumption).
  - scontrol show config (to view the PriorityWeight* settings and decay parameters).
- Start with moderate weights; don’t make one weight orders of magnitude larger than the others unless you want it to dominate completely.
- If fairness feels “stuck” on old usage, reduce PriorityDecayHalfLife to make recent usage matter more, or reset usage with PriorityUsageResetPeriod.
- Use TRES weights to reflect site policy: e.g., if GPU time is scarce and should be rationed differently, bump TRES_weight_gpu.
- Combine fairshare with Age weight so the system balances fairness with waiting time (avoids starvation of small/over‑used accounts).
- Monitor results (sprio, sdiag) and iterate.

Quick numeric example (illustrative)
- Suppose: PriorityWeightFairshare=1000, PriorityWeightAge=100, fairshare_factor=0.8 (under‑served), age_factor=0.2 (short wait).
  - Contribution from fairshare = 1000 * 0.8 = 800
  - Contribution from age = 100 * 0.2 = 20
  - Total (plus any other factors) → fairshare dominates ordering here.
- If you reduce PriorityWeightFairshare to 100, then age and other factors can more easily change ordering.

Useful Slurm commands for inspection
- sprio -l — show factor values and weighted contributions per queued job.
- sshare — show account share usage and entitlement.
- scontrol show config — view PriorityWeight* and PriorityDecayHalfLife settings.
- lookup docs: priority_multifactor(see Slurm docs) and fair_tree pages (for algorithm details).

If you want, I can:
- Show how your cluster’s priority factors are currently configured (scontrol show config) and show sprio -l for specific queued jobs to explain exactly why those jobs are ordered as they are. (This is a read-only request; tell me which job IDs or if you want the global view.)

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain burst buffer directives and stage-in or stage-out behavior
results.agent_response:
Summary from the official Slurm "Burst Buffer Guide" (slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html):

What "burst buffer directives" are and where to put them
- Burst buffer requests are supplied as commented directive lines in a job script (they begin with # so they are ignored by the shell). Directives may appear before, after, or interspersed with #SBATCH lines.
- Which directive name and exact fields you use depends on the burst-buffer plugin configured on your system (examples below). You can also pass burst-buffer directives on the command line with sbatch/salloc/srun using --bb or with a file using --bbf.
- When Slurm parses a --bb argument it creates a temporary burst-buffer script for the plugin to run. Note: --bb cannot create or destroy persistent buffers; --bbf can pass a file of operations.

Plugin differences (common ones)
- datawarp (burst_buffer/datawarp)
  - Uses directives like #DW and also the generic #BB for persistent-buf create/destroy operations.
  - For job-specific buffers DataWarp normally requires a capacity be specified (a job without capacity will be rejected).
  - Persistent buffers may be created/destroyed with #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent (create_persistent name= capacity= [access=] [pool=] ...).
  - DataWarp-specific details (exact argument names & semantics) are documented in the DataWarp section and in vendor docs.
- lua (burst_buffer/lua)
  - Default directive is #BB_LUA (the literal string after the # can be changed via burst_buffer.conf Directive=).
  - The lua plugin is flexible; for many setups simply giving the directive is sufficient for Slurm to run all burst-buffer stages for the job.

Stage-in / stage-out behavior and lifecycle
- Staging is integrated into the job lifecycle. Typical transitions (as tracked by Slurm) include: pending -> allocating/allocated (persistent-only) -> staging-in -> staged-in -> pre-run -> running -> post-run -> staging-out -> teardown -> complete.
- Stage-in happens before the job's run starts (so input data can be copied to the burst buffer and exposed to the job). Stage-out happens after the job finishes (so output can be flushed from the burst buffer to durable storage).
- These stages are explicit states that appear in scontrol show job output in the BurstBufferState field for jobs that requested burst buffers.
- The burst-buffer plugin may enforce timeouts (example fields visible from scontrol show burst: StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout, ValidateTimeout, OtherTimeout). If a stage times out the job or burst-buffer allocation may fail depending on plugin/config.

What Slurm runs for each stage
- The burst-buffer plugin (and any helper scripts it calls) performs the requested actions:
  - allocate/associate a buffer (for job-specific or persistent buffers),
  - stage-in: copy or expose input data into the buffer for the job,
  - pre-run validation (some plugins validate the staged data),
  - post-run/stage-out: copy data out to final storage or persistent buffer,
  - teardown/destroy (if requested).
- For heterogeneous jobs, burst-buffer hooks run once per job component that has directives. If a component lacks directives, no hook runs for it.

Persistent vs job-specific buffers
- Persistent buffers exist beyond a single job and can be created/destroyed with #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent (DataWarp).
- Job-specific buffers exist only for the job lifecycle and follow the staging/teardown sequence.

How to request / pass directives
- In a batch script: include the plugin-specific directive comment(s) near the top of the script (the guide shows the exact directive formats per plugin).
- On the command line:
  - --bb "..." to pass inline burst buffer directives (Slurm turns this into a temporary internal script).
  - --bbf filename to pass a file containing burst-buffer operations.
- The exact keys (stage_in, stage_out, capacity, pool, access, paths, etc.) are plugin-dependent; consult the plugin section (DataWarp, Lua) for the exact syntax and examples.

Monitoring & status
- Use scontrol show burst to see burst buffer resources, pools, timeouts, and allocated buffers.
- Use scontrol show job to see a job's BurstBufferState (staging-in, staged-in, staging-out, etc.).
- Slurm and the plugin also log burst-buffer activity; enable DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf for verbose plugin logs (admin-only).

Accounting & limits
- Burst buffers can be tracked as TRES (e.g., bb/datawarp or bb/lua) so usage can be limited by association/QoS and appear in accounting if configured.

Where to find exact directive syntax and examples
- The guide's Job Submission Commands and the plugin sections (DataWarp, Lua) contain exact directive formats and examples. Because syntax differs by plugin, consult:
  - Slurm Burst Buffer Guide — Job Submission Commands
  - Slurm Burst Buffer Guide — DataWarp (for #DW/#BB create_persistent/destroy_persistent)
  - Slurm Burst Buffer Guide — Lua (for #BB_LUA usage and examples)

If you want, I can:
- fetch exact example directives for a specific plugin (DataWarp or Lua) and show example sbatch lines and a minimal script, or
- extract the relevant syntax snippet from the Slurm docs page for the plugin your cluster uses. Which plugin does your cluster use (datawarp or lua), or would you like me to pull examples for both?

Directive=BB_EXAMPLE

the default directive for this plugin (`#BB_LUA`) will be used.

requires the directive to be given. If the directive is given, Slurm will run

## Command-line Job Options [#command-line](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include
burst buffer directives. These command-line options are available for salloc,
sbatch, and srun. Note that the `--bb` option cannot create or
destroy persistent burst buffers.
The `--bbf` option takes as an argument a filename and that file
should contain a collection of burst buffer operations identical to those used
for batch jobs.
Alternatively, the `--bb` option may be used to specify burst
buffer directives as the option argument. The behavior of this option depends
on which burst buffer plugin is used. When the `--bb` option is
used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file
that is used internally by the burst buffer plugins.

The datawarp plugin calls two scripts:

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

Burst buffer resources can be placed in an advanced reservation using the
BurstBuffer option.
The argument consists of four elements:

- units has the same format as the suffix of capacity in the [Job Submission Commands](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html) section.

resources, but may use these reserved resources plus any which are generally
available. Some examples follow.

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

The normal mode of operation is for batch jobs to specify burst buffer
requirements within the batch script. Commented batch script lines containing a
specific directive (depending on which plugin is being used) will inform Slurm
that it should run the burst buffer stages for that job. These lines will also
describe the burst buffer requirements for the job.

### Lua [#submit_lua](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
The default directive for this plugin is `#BB_LUA`. The directive
used by this plugin may be changed by setting the Directive option in
burst_buffer.conf. Since the directive must always begin with a `#`
sign (which starts a comment in a shell script) this option should specify only
the string following the `#` sign. For example, if burst_buffer.conf
contains the following:
```text
Directive=BB_EXAMPLE
```
then the burst buffer directive will be `#BB_EXAMPLE`.
If the Directive option is not specified in burst_buffer.conf, then
the default directive for this plugin (`#BB_LUA`) will be used.
Since this plugin was designed to be generic and flexible, this plugin only
requires the directive to be given. If the directive is given, Slurm will run
all burst buffer stages for the job.

## Burst Buffer States and Job States [#states](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
These are the different possible burst buffer states:
- pending
- allocating
- allocated
- deleting
- deleted
- staging-in
- staged-in
- pre-run
- alloc-revoke
- running
- suspended
- post-run
- staging-out
- teardown
- teardown-fail
- complete
These states appear in the "BurstBufferState" field in the output of
`scontrol show job`. This field only appears for jobs that requested
a burst buffer. The states `allocating`, `allocated`,
`deleting` and `deleted` are used
for persistent burst buffers only (not for job-specific burst buffers). The
state `alloc-revoke` happens if a failure in Slurm's select plugin
occurs in between Slurm allocating resources for a job and actually starting
the job. This should never happen.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain pending reasons Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, and QOS limits
results.agent_response:
Below are concise, doc-backed explanations (what the scheduler means, common causes, and what to check/fix) for the pending reasons you asked about. All behavior below is from the Slurm documentation (job reason codes, QOS and resource-limits pages).

1) Resources
- What it means:
  - The scheduler could not find sufficient free resources to start the job given its request (CPUs, memory, GPU/GRES, TRES, sockets, cores, exclusive nodes, etc.). This is the generic “no suitable resources available now” reason.
- Common causes:
  - Not enough idle CPUs, memory, or GPUs in the partition; per-node resources are insufficient for the job’s per-node request.  
  - Nodes with the required features/constraints are busy, down, drained, or reserved.  
  - TRES/GRES (e.g., gpus) are already allocated to other jobs or are limited by association/QOS limits.
- What to check:
  - sinfo to view partition/node free vs allocated counts and node features.  
  - squeue to see currently running jobs consuming resources.  
  - scontrol show job <jobid> for the job’s requested TRES/features and the scheduler’s allocation attempt details.
- How to resolve:
  - Wait for resources to free, reduce resource request (fewer CPUs/GPU or less memory), remove/relax constraints, or request different partition. Admins can add capacity, change reservations, or adjust preemption/QOS settings.

2) Priority
- What it means:
  - The job is pending because one or more jobs with higher scheduling priority are eligible to run first. Slurm’s multifactor priority calculation (age, fairshare, QOS priority, job size, etc.) determines which jobs the scheduler prefers.
- Common causes:
  - Other jobs have higher QOS or higher multifactor priority (older jobs, favorable fairshare, higher QOS priority).  
  - Backfill/packing rules allow higher priority jobs to take the next available window.
- What to check:
  - sprio (or sprio --weights) to inspect job priorities and which factors dominate.  
  - squeue sorted by priority to see which jobs are scheduled ahead.  
  - sshare to inspect fairshare usage if that may be lowering your priority.
- How to resolve:
  - Request a higher QOS (if allowed), change job size/time to fit backfill windows, or wait. Admins can tune priority weights or QOS priorities.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means:
  - The job requested specific node(s) or node constraints (via --nodelist, --exclude, --constraint, features, or a node-count requirement) and no currently usable node satisfies that request. Unlike the generic Resources reason, this explicitly indicates the requested node(s) or constrained set are unavailable.
- Common causes:
  - You requested explicit node names that are down/drained/allocated or excluded.  
  - The constraint string or feature request matches no idle nodes.  
  - A node is reserved or otherwise not offered (maintenance/reservation).
- What to check:
  - scontrol show job <jobid> to see NodeList/ReqNodes/Constraints in the job request.  
  - sinfo (or sinfo_reasons / sinfo_node) to see node states, drains, and reasons.  
  - scontrol show node <nodename> for node details and reason fields.
- How to resolve:
  - Remove or relax the node list/constraint, correct the requested node names, or wait / ask admins to clear reservations or bring nodes back (if appropriate).

4) QOS limits (how they cause pending/rejection)
- What it means:
  - The job is being held back by configured QOS/association/account limits (MaxTRES, MaxJobs, MaxWall, GrpTRES, usage thresholds, etc.). Limits can apply per user, account, or QOS and may cause a job to pend until the cluster/association usage is under the limit.
- Important doc behaviors to know:
  - By default, if a job would breach a QOS limit when considered together with currently running jobs, the job will pend until resources or quota free up.  
  - If the QOS has Flags=“DenyOnLimit”, then jobs that violate the QOS Max limits as stand‑alone requests are rejected at submission time instead of pending. (Group limits are treated similarly when DenyOnLimit applies.)  
  - Partition-level QOS limits are applied before the job’s requested QOS unless OverPartQOS changes that behavior.  
  - There are also relative QOS modes (Flags=Relative) where limits are percentages of total cluster resources.
- What to check:
  - sacctmgr show qos (or sacctmgr show assoc) to inspect QOS limits and flags (MaxJobs, MaxTRESPerUser/PerAccount, DenyOnLimit, UsageThreshold, etc.).  
  - squeue/sacct to see current running usage and whether an account/association has hit a limit.  
  - scontrol show config for OverPartQOS / priority weight settings if behavior seems unexpected.
- How to resolve:
  - Request a different QOS without those limits, reduce job resource usage, wait for usage to drop, or ask admins to raise limits or change DenyOnLimit/OverPartQOS behavior.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain job array IDs, task IDs, and %A/%a output placeholders
results.agent_response:
Short answer first
- Job arrays are a single sbatch submission that creates many similar jobs (elements). The array has a single array-job ID (the "master" job allocation number) and each element has an index (task ID) and its own per-element job id.
- %A and %a are sbatch filename-replacement symbols: %A expands to the array's master job allocation number; %a expands to the element (array index) value. Use %A_%a (or SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID/SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID) to build unique filenames per element.

Key terms and mappings (from Slurm docs)
- Array submission: sbatch --array=1-100 myscript
  - The sbatch command returns a single array-job id (the array "master" id). Example: "Submitted batch job 36".
- Array element notation: <ArrayJobID>_<Index>
  - Example element reference: 36_4 (array 36, element index 4).
  - Referring to the whole array uses just the array id (36).
- Environment variables set for array jobs:
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the job id for the array (the array's master job allocation number).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the array element index (the task id for this element).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN — summary counts/min/max for the array.
  (These are set inside the batch script environment for each element.)
- Per-element SLURM_JOB_ID:
  - Each array element behaves like a regular job and has its own SLURM_JOB_ID visible inside the element. SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID groups the elements; SLURM_JOB_ID is the element’s job id.

Filename replacement symbols (sbatch --output / FILENAME PATTERN)
- %A — Job array's master job allocation number (the array id).
- %a — Job array ID (index) number (the element index).
- %b — Job array ID modulo 10 (useful for sharding by last digit).
- %j — jobid of the running job (useful for non-array jobs or per-element SLURM_JOB_ID).
- %% — literal percent sign.
Use these in --output/--error/--open-mode filename patterns. Example:
- sbatch --array=1-3 --output=slurm-%A_%a.out myscript
  - If sbatch returned "Submitted batch job 36", element 1 will write slurm-36_1.out, element 2 slurm-36_2.out, etc.

Examples showing how they relate
- Inside the script for array element index 4:
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID might be 36
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID will be 4
  - SLURM_JOB_ID will be the unique job id for that element (e.g., 1024)
- Referencing elements from commands:
  - scancel 36_4 cancels element 4 of array 36
  - scancel 36 cancels all elements of array 36
  - --depend=after:123_4 (depend on element 4 of array 123), or --depend=after:123 (depend on entire array)

Notes and gotchas
- The array index values come from the --array specification and may be non-contiguous (e.g., --array=1,3,5) or have steps (--array=1-10:2).
- You can limit concurrency with --array=0-31%4 (max 4 concurrent elements).
- %A is suitable for filenames to identify the array; %a is required to distinguish elements within that array. If you use %j (per-element jobid) it may be different from the array master id.
- Use the SLURM environment variables inside the script when you need programmatic control (filename creation, logging, scancel logic, dependencies).

If you want, I can show concrete examples (sbatch lines and expected filenames) for a particular array range / output pattern you plan to use.

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .
```text
$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Scontrol Command Use [#scontrol](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Use of the scontrol show job option shows two new fields related to
job array support.
The JobID is a unique identifier for the job.
The ArrayJobID is the JobID of the first element of the job
array.
The ArrayTaskID is the array index of this particular entry, either a
single number of an expression identifying the entries represented by this
job record (e.g. "5-1024").
Neither field is displayed if the job is not part of a job array.
The optional job ID specified with the scontrol show job or
scontrol show step commands can identify job array elements by
specifying ArrayJobId and ArrayTaskId with an underscore between
them (e.g. <ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskId>).
The scontrol command will operate on all elements of a job array if the
job ID specified is ArrayJobID .

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Snippet:
## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

below.

## Launching Applications (Job Steps) [#job_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The srun command is used to launch applications.
By default, the application is launched only on the first component of a
heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
srun's "--het-group" option defines which hetjob component(s) are to have
applications launched for them. The --het-group option takes an expression
defining which component(s) are to launch an application for an individual
execution of the srun command. The expression can contain one or more component
index values in a comma separated list. Ranges of index values can be specified
in a hyphen separated list. By default, an application is launched only on
component number zero. Some examples follow:

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

below.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Summary first
- Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin (PriorityType=priority/multifactor). A job’s composite priority is a weighted sum of several normalized “factors” (age, fair‑share, QOS, partition, job size, TRES, assoc, site, …). Each factor value is a floating-point 0.0–1.0 and each factor has an integer weight configured in slurm.conf. The scheduler sums weight * factor for enabled factors to produce the queue priority integer.
- In practice the three levers you asked about work together: configured priority weights determine how much each factor moves a job’s composite priority; fairshare (the FairTree algorithm for hierarchical shares) produces the fairshare factor that rewards under‑served accounts/users; and the age factor prevents starvation by increasing priority as a job waits.

How priorities are computed (formula)
- Conceptual formula (from the multifactor plugin):
  Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor
               + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
               + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
               + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
               + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
               + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor
               + SUM(TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X) - nice_factor
- Factors are 0.0–1.0; weights are unsigned integers in slurm.conf. The larger the final numeric priority, the earlier the job will be considered by the scheduler.

Fairshare and FairTree (what they do)
- Fairshare uses accounting data (SlurmDB) to compute how much of the cluster each association/account/user has consumed and compares that to configured shares/entitlements.
- FairTree is the hierarchy algorithm Slurm uses to apply shares in a tree of associations/accounts/projects. Parent nodes have shares that are split among children; FairTree computes each leaf’s effective entitlement from that hierarchy.
- The fairshare_factor is higher (closer to 1.0) for accounts/users that are under‑served relative to their entitlement, and lower (closer to 0.0) for over‑served accounts. The PriorityWeightFairshare multiplies that factor, so a high weight gives strong preference to under‑served users.
- Important config knobs: PriorityDecayHalfLife (how fast historical usage decays), PriorityCalcPeriod (recalc frequency), PriorityUsageResetPeriod (when to zero usage). Short half‑lives make fairshare respond quickly; long half‑lives enforce long‑term fairness.

Age factor (anti‑starvation)
- Age factor grows for a job as it sits in the queue. With a nonzero PriorityWeightAge this increases priority over time so small/low‑priority jobs eventually run.
- Tuning age weight trades fairness for job latency: raising PriorityWeightAge reduces starvation risk but can let users circumvent fairshare by waiting.

Configured priority weights (how to use them)
- Weights determine relative importance of factors. Typical effects:
  - PriorityWeightFairshare high → enforces entitlement-based fairness; under‑served users get scheduled sooner.
  - PriorityWeightAge high → reduces wait times for long‑waiting jobs, preventing starvation.
  - PriorityWeightQOS / PriorityWeightPartition → let QOS or partition selection strongly influence ordering.
  - TRES weights (e.g., TRESWeightGPU) let the scheduler prioritize or deprioritize jobs requesting costly resources.
- There is no fixed “correct” absolute number—only relative values matter. The plugin multiplies weight * factor, so doubling a weight doubles that factor’s contribution.
- Practical tuning advice:
  - Start with a sensible baseline (examine your cluster’s defaults with sprio -w or scontrol show config).
  - If you observe persistent unfair usage, raise PriorityWeightFairshare or increase PriorityDecayHalfLife for longer memory.
  - If jobs are starving, increase PriorityWeightAge.
  - If you want to bias against heavy GPU consumers, add TRES weights for GPU and tune them upward.
  - Make one change at a time and observe (sprio, sshare, squeue, sacct) for a few PriorityCalcPeriod cycles.

How to inspect what’s happening (commands)
- sprio -w — show currently configured weights and the per‑job priority breakdown (very useful).
- sprio — show per-job factor contributions.
- sshare — show configured shares and current usage/entitlements for accounts/users.
- scontrol show config — to read PriorityWeight* and decay/reset settings from slurm.conf.
- sacct / sreport — inspect historical usage to see who has consumed resources.
- Use these to diagnose whether fairshare or age is dominating and to justify weight changes.

Short numeric example
- If PriorityWeightFairshare = 1000 and a user’s fairshare_factor = 0.8 → fairshare contribution = 800.
- If PriorityWeightAge = 100 and the job’s age_factor = 0.3 → age contribution = 30.
- Composite priority adds those (plus other factors). In this example fairshare dominates.

Interactions and gotchas
- Fairshare only works if Slurm accounting is enabled and kept up to date.
- Very large fairshare weight can starve users who are over‑served for long periods unless you also tune decay/reset.
- Age and fairshare can conflict: a job from an over‑served account can eventually win if age weight is large enough.
- TRES weights allow resource‑type-specific bias (useful for GPUs, large-memory nodes).

If you want, I can:
- Show the current configured weights and settings (sprio -w / scontrol show config) for your cluster and a sprio breakdown for current queued jobs. (This is a read-only request; tell me which partition or user to focus on if any.)

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain burst buffer directives and stage-in or stage-out behavior
results.agent_response:
Summary — what burst‑buffer directives do
- Burst buffers are temporary fast storage that Slurm can allocate for a job and for which the burst‑buffer plugin will run configured “stages” to move data into and out of that storage.
- You declare burst‑buffer requirements and stage operations in your batch script (as commented directives) or on the command line (--bb / --bbf). The exact directive names and keywords depend on the burst‑buffer plugin in use (DataWarp, lua, etc.). See the Slurm “Burst Buffer Guide” for plugin‑specific syntax.

Where to put directives
- Put burst‑buffer directives as commented lines in the batch script (they may appear before/after/interspersed with #SBATCH lines).
- Or use salloc/srun/sbatch options: --bb (inline directives) or --bbf <file> (file containing operations). Note: --bb cannot create/destroy persistent burst buffers; --bbf reads a file of operations.

Lifecycle / stages (how stage‑in and stage‑out behave)
- Stages are run at specific points in a job’s lifecycle. Common stage states reported in scontrol show job (BurstBufferState) include: pending → allocating → allocated → staging‑in → staged‑in → pre‑run → running → post‑run → staging‑out → staged‑out → teardown → complete (plus failure variants such as teardown‑fail or alloc‑revoke).
- Stage‑in (staging‑in):
  - Occurs after resources and the burst buffer are allocated but before the job’s prologue/pre‑run and before the user job script begins execution.
  - Typical purpose: copy application input data from a backing store (global filesystem, persistent BB, etc.) into the job’s burst buffer so the job can read from fast local storage.
- Stage‑out (staging‑out):
  - Runs after the job finishes (after job run / post‑run hooks) but before the burst buffer teardown and final release of resources.
  - Typical purpose: copy output results from the job’s burst buffer back to a persistent location (project filesystem, persistent BB, etc.).
- The burst‑buffer plugin implements the actual copy actions and ordering (e.g., per‑component for heterogeneous jobs). For heterogeneous jobs, the hooks run once for each component that requested burst buffers.

What you specify in directives
- The directives describe:
  - whether the BB is job‑specific or persistent (some plugins support creation/destruction of persistent BBs),
  - capacity (size) and pool (which BB resource pool to use),
  - access mode or striping options (plugin dependent),
  - explicit stage operations: what source to stage in from and what destination to stage out to.
- Common fields mentioned by the docs: name, capacity, pool, access (plugin names/fields vary). Persistent BB creation/deletion uses specific create_persistent / destroy_persistent directives (DataWarp uses #BB for persistent ops).

Plugin differences (DataWarp vs generic lua)
- DataWarp (burst_buffer/datawarp):
  - Uses directive labels such as #DW for job operations and #BB for persistent create/destroy; capacity is required for job‑specific buffers.
  - Has plugin‑specific options — consult the DataWarp docs and the Slurm burst‑buffer page for exact keywords.
- Lua (generic) plugin:
  - Default directive is #BB_LUA (configurable). If the directive is present, the lua plugin will run all configured stages; exact behavior depends on the plugin’s Lua hooks.

Command‑line and file options
- --bb allows inline BB directives for salloc/sbatch/srun (Slurm will generate a temporary script file for the plugin); it cannot create/destroy persistent buffers.
- --bbf <file> reads a file of BB operations (same format used in scripts).
- For persistent BB creation/destruction, only some plugins (e.g., DataWarp) support it and may require different directive forms.

Failure/diagnostics
- Burst buffer stages appear in scontrol show job output under BurstBufferState; failures during staging or teardown produce corresponding failure states (staging‑out fail, teardown‑fail).
- Enable DebugFlags=BurstBuffer in slurm.conf or check the burst buffer plugin logs for troubleshooting.

Accounting and scheduling effects
- Burst buffer size can be used by the scheduler as a placement factor; BB resources can be tracked as TRES (e.g., bb/datawarp or bb/lua) in AccountingStorageTres.
- If a job requests a burst buffer and none are available, the job will wait pending until resources are free (the scheduler uses the BB request during allocation).

A minimal conceptual example (plugin names/keywords vary — check your plugin docs)
- In-script (conceptual):
  - #DW job capacity=100GB pool=fast
  - #DW stage_in source=/project/data/myinput dest=$DW_JOB_STRIPED
  - #DW stage_out source=$DW_JOB_STRIPED dest=/project/results/myjob
- Command line:
  - sbatch --bb="job capacity=100GB pool=fast; stage_in source=...; stage_out dest=..." job.sh
Note: the exact tokens (job, stage_in, source, dest, environment variables like $DW_JOB_STRIPED) are plugin dependent — consult the plugin section below.

Where to find exact syntax
- Refer to the Slurm Burst Buffer Guide (burst_buffer.html) for:
  - directive names per plugin (DataWarp, lua, etc.),
  - exact keywords for stage_in / stage_out operations,
  - persistent BB creation/destruction syntax,
  - examples and plugin‑specific notes.

If you tell me which burst‑buffer plugin your cluster uses (DataWarp, lua, or other) and share a short example of what you want to stage in/out (paths, sizes, persistent vs job‑local), I can give a concrete sbatch script snippet using the correct directive names and fields.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain pending reasons Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, and QOS limits
results.agent_response:
Below are concise, doc‑based explanations of the four Slurm pending reasons you asked about, what they mean, common causes, and how to diagnose or remediate them. Sources: Slurm job reason codes, QOS, and resource limits docs (job_reason_codes.html, qos.html, resource_limits.html).

1) Resources
- What it means
  - The job is pending because Slurm cannot currently find the compute resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs, TRES, nodes, sockets) required by the job request.
- Common causes
  - No nodes have enough free CPUs or memory to satisfy the per‑node or per‑job resource request.
  - Requested GRES (GPU type/count) are not idle on any node.
  - Exclusive/node‑level requests (e.g., --exclusive, --nodes=N with per‑node resource counts) cannot be satisfied by the available nodes.
  - Partition limits or reservations are holding the needed nodes.
- How to diagnose
  - squeue shows the pending reason (“Resources”).
  - Use sinfo (partition/node availability) and sinfo --Node or sinfo --long to see per‑node free resources.
  - Use scontrol show job <jobid> for the job’s requested TRES and details.
- Remediations
  - Reduce CPUs/memory/GPU count or change node/feature constraints.
  - Wait for running jobs to finish or request a different partition.
  - If resources are reserved/drained, consult the admin or check reservations (scontrol show reservation).

2) Priority
- What it means
  - The job is pending because other job(s) with higher scheduling priority are eligible to run before this job.
- Key notes from docs
  - Slurm computes job priority using a multi‑factor plugin (age, fairshare, QOS, job size, etc.). QOS contributes to priority if configured (PriorityWeightQOS > 0).
- Common causes
  - Newer jobs with a higher combined priority score (age, fairshare, QOS priority, etc.).
  - Your job’s account/user has lower fairshare or lower QOS priority.
- How to diagnose
  - squeue will list “Priority” as the reason and you can run sprio (or sprio --weights) to see priority factors for pending jobs.
  - sshare shows fairshare usage and effective shares.
- Remediations
  - Request a higher‑priority QOS (if permitted) or ask admins to adjust QOS/priority weights.
  - Reduce job size so it can fit into earlier backfill opportunities.
  - Wait — aging increases priority over time.

3) ReqNodeNotAvail (Requested Node Not Available)
- What it means
  - The job requested specific node(s) or node features that are not currently available (the requested node is down/drained/allocated, or feature constraints cannot be matched).
- Common causes
  - The job used node list/name constraints (e.g., --nodelist=) and that node is in use, drained, or down.
  - Feature (node feature/constraint) or partition membership mismatch (e.g., --constraint=featureX but no nodes with that feature are idle).
  - Reservation is on the node but your job isn’t matched to that reservation.
- How to diagnose
  - squeue shows the reason; use scontrol show job <jobid> to view nodelist/constraints.
  - Use sinfo and sinfo_reasons to see node states (DOWN, DRAIN) and reasons, and sinfo --Node to inspect node features and partition membership.
- Remediations
  - Remove or relax explicit node/nodelist constraints.
  - Choose a partition or constraint matching available nodes.
  - If the node is down/drained, contact admins or wait until it’s returned to service.

4) QOS limits (pending because of QOS/resource limits)
- What it means
  - The job is pending because the job’s requested resources or the job’s account/QOS would exceed configured limits (per‑QOS, per‑account, per‑partition limits). Depending on configuration, jobs that exceed limits either pend or are denied at submission.
- Key doc points
  - QOS and partition QOS can impose GrpTRES, MaxTRES, MaxJobs, MaxNodes, etc. Limits may be applied in a defined precedence (partition QOS may override job QOS unless Flags=OverPartQOS).
  - If a job request would breach a limit, by default the job will pend; if the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, the job may be denied on submission.
- Common causes
  - Your account or QOS has exceeded its allowed aggregate CPUs/GPU hours, concurrent jobs, or a per‑job/per‑node limit.
  - Partition QOS limits prevent the job from starting even if the job requests a different QOS.
- How to diagnose
  - squeue or scontrol show job <jobid> will show the pending reason (e.g., “AssocGrp”, “Max*PerAccount”, or a QOS‑related reason).
  - Use sacctmgr show qos and sacctmgr show association to inspect QOS and account limits.
  - Check resource_limits documentation for semantics of Max/Grp/PerJob/PerNode limits.
- Remediations
  - Request a different QOS or lower resource request.
  - Have an admin increase the QOS/account limits or change DenyOnLimit/OverPartQOS flags.
  - Redistribute jobs to other accounts/QOS if policy allows.

Quick troubleshooting checklist (commands to run)
- squeue -j <jobid> (confirm pending reason)
- scontrol show job <jobid> (detailed request, constraints, QOS)
- sinfo --long or sinfo --Node (node/partition availability and features)
- sprio / sprio --weights and sshare (priority/fairshare diagnostics)
- sacctmgr show qos / sacctmgr show association (QOS & limit settings)
- sinfo_reasons (if nodes are down/drained)

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can show the exact pending reason text and recommend the most targeted remediation steps.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain job array IDs, task IDs, and %A/%a output placeholders
results.agent_response:
Short answer (from the Slurm docs):

- Job array vs. array task
  - ArrayJobID (the job-array “master” ID): the JobID printed by sbatch when you submit an array. It identifies the whole array as a group. Slurm exposes this as SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID in the batch-script environment and as the ArrayJobID field in scontrol/squeue output.
  - ArrayTaskID (the array index / task ID): the index value from your --array specification (for example 1,2,3 or 0..N). Slurm exposes this as SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in the batch-script environment and as the ArrayTaskId field in scontrol/squeue output.
  - SLURM_JOB_ID (JobID): each running array element behaves like a normal job and has a job record / JobID when it starts. The ArrayJobID is the “master” group id; individual elements may have distinct JobIDs when they get created.

- %A and %a (sbatch filename-pattern replacements)
  - %A expands to the job array’s master job allocation number (ArrayJobID).
  - %a expands to the job array index (ArrayTaskID).
  - These percent-replacements are supported in sbatch filename patterns (e.g., -o/-e and other filename places). Example:
      #SBATCH -o slurm-%A_%a.out
    If sbatch printed “Submitted batch job 36” for an array and you have array element 1, the output file becomes slurm-36_1.out.
  - Related replacements: %j is the jobid of the running job, %J is jobid.stepid, %b is the array index modulo 10, etc. (See sbatch filename-pattern docs for the full list.)

- Useful practical notes from the docs
  - Environment variables available inside array tasks: SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN (plus the normal SLURM_JOB_ID, etc.).
  - squeue displays arrays compactly (e.g. 1080_[5-1024]) by default; use squeue --array (or -r) to show one element per line.
  - Some commands accept the ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID notation to refer to an element (for example scancel 20_4 cancels array job 20 element 4; scontrol show job 101_1 shows element 1).
  - Under normal scheduling behavior the first task submitted may be a placeholder; this can make the ordering of SLURM_JOB_ID vs. SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID non-intuitive (see job_array docs).

References: Slurm “Job Array Support” (job_array) and the sbatch man page (filename-pattern / output-environment variables).

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .
```text
$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.
