## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

```

## Submitting Jobs [#submitting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The salloc , sbatch and srun commands can all be used
to submit heterogeneous jobs.
Resource specifications for each component of the heterogeneous job should be
separated with ":" character.
For example:
```text
$ sbatch --cpus-per-task=4 --mem-per-cpu=1 --ntasks=128 : \ --cpus-per-task=1 --mem-per-cpu=16 --ntasks=1 my.bash
```
Options specified for one component of a heterogeneous job (or job step) will
be used for subsequent components to the extent which is expected to be helpful.
Propagated options can be reset as desired for each component (e.g. a different
account name could be specified for each hetjob component.
For example, --immediate and --job-name are propagated, while
--ntasks and --mem-per-cpu are reset to default values for each
component.

## Launching Applications (Job Steps) [#job_steps](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The srun command is used to launch applications.
By default, the application is launched only on the first component of a
heterogeneous job, but options are available to support different behaviors.
srun's "--het-group" option defines which hetjob component(s) are to have
applications launched for them. The --het-group option takes an expression
defining which component(s) are to launch an application for an individual
execution of the srun command. The expression can contain one or more component
index values in a comma separated list. Ranges of index values can be specified
in a hyphen separated list. By default, an application is launched only on
component number zero. Some examples follow:
- --het-group=2
- --het-group=0,4
- --het-group=1,3-5

When a job array is submitted to Slurm, only one job record is created.
Additional job records will only be created when the state of a task in the
job array changes, typically when a task is allocated resources or its state

Use of the scontrol show job option shows two new fields related to
job array support.
The JobID is a unique identifier for the job.
The ArrayJobID is the JobID of the first element of the job
array.
The ArrayTaskID is the array index of this particular entry, either a
single number of an expression identifying the entries represented by this
job record (e.g. "5-1024").

specifying ArrayJobId and ArrayTaskId with an underscore between

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## LOGGING[#SECTION_LOGGING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
Note that while Slurm daemons create log files and other files as needed,
it treats the lack of parent directories as a fatal error.
This prevents the daemons from running if critical file systems are
not mounted and will minimize the risk of cold-starting (starting
without preserving jobs).
Log files and job accounting files
may need to be created/owned by the "SlurmUser" uid to be successfully
accessed. Use the "chown" and "chmod" commands to set the ownership
and permissions appropriately.
See the section FILE AND DIRECTORY PERMISSIONS for information
about the various files and directories used by Slurm.
It is recommended that the logrotate utility be used to ensure that
various log files do not become too large.

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of

either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,

directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Explain queue priority using fairshare, Fair Tree usage, and configured priority weights
results.agent_response:
Summary — how Slurm combines fairshare, the Fair Tree algorithm, and configured priority weights

High level
- Slurm’s default priority scheme (PriorityType=priority/multifactor) computes a single job priority as a weighted sum of several normalized “factors” (each ranges 0.0–1.0). The scheduler ranks jobs by that composite priority (larger = higher rank).
- The formula (conceptually) looks like:
  Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor + SUM(TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X) - nice_factor
  (All factors are 0..1; weights are integers in slurm.conf. The final priority is an integer 0..4294967295.)
- In other words: each factor is computed independently, each weight scales how much that factor contributes, and the weighted results are summed to produce the final job priority.

Fair-share (what it does)
- Purpose: bias scheduling so users/accounts that have received less recent cluster service get higher priority; accounts/users that have consumed more resources are deprioritized until balance returns.
- Requires the Slurm Accounting DB (to know historical usage). It does not enforce a hard quota — it only affects ordering of queued jobs.
- Fair-share factor is a normalized score per account/user and is multiplied by PriorityWeightFairshare.
- Historical usage is decayed over time (see PriorityDecayHalfLife) so old usage matters less; the decay and reset parameters control how quickly “credit” is regained.

Fair Tree (the default fair-share algorithm)
- Fair Tree (available since Slurm 19.05) is a hierarchical algorithm that computes fair-share up the account tree:
  - If accounts A and B are siblings, and A has a higher fair-share factor than B, then all children (users/accounts) of A will also rank above children of B. This preserves ordering across the hierarchy.
  - Benefits: avoids precision/tiebreak errors, makes account coordinators less likely to accidentally harm user priorities across accounts, and yields more predictable hierarchical fairness than the older “classic” method.
- You can configure which fair-share algorithm is used; Fair Tree is the recommended/default behavior.

Configured priority weights (how to control influence)
- Weights live in slurm.conf (PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAssoc, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, and TRES_weight_* for resources like cpu/gpu/mem).
- Effect: increasing a weight multiplies the associated factor’s contribution and thus increases that factor’s influence on final priority. Decreasing it reduces influence.
  - Example: raising PriorityWeightFairshare makes the scheduler much more responsive to accounting-based under/over service.
  - Example: TRES_weight_gpu raises or lowers the importance of GPU usage in priority calculations (useful if you want GPU jobs favored/disfavored).
- Tuning considerations:
  - Weights are relative. If two factors both have large weights, both will strongly affect ordering — the absolute integer values matter only for relative scaling.
  - Be mindful of other factors: Age rewards longer-waiting jobs; JobSize can be used to favor smaller jobs to improve throughput; QOS/partition weights can enforce site policy.
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife (and PriorityUsageResetPeriod) control how historic usage affects fairshare; shorter half-life makes the system “forgive” past usage faster.

Tools to inspect and debug
- sprio (sprio -l) — shows each pending job’s factor contributions so you can see which factors dominate.
- sshare — shows fair-share usage and effective shares for accounts/users.
- scontrol show config — shows current priority weights and PriorityType.
- scontrol_show (job) or squeue + scontrol_show for detailed job info if you’re diagnosing a specific job’s priority or why it’s pending.

Practical tuning tips
- Start with modest weights and adjust one factor at a time; use sprio to measure factor contributions.
- If fairness across users/accounts is the main concern, increase PriorityWeightFairshare and configure PriorityDecayHalfLife according to how quickly you want balances to change.
- If you need to prioritize GPU work specifically, use TRES_weight_gpu rather than changing global factors that also affect CPU jobs.
- Remember: fairshare orders jobs, it does not enforce hard limits. Use accounts/associations with limits in the accounting DB if you need hard caps.

If you want, I can:
- show how your cluster is currently configured (PriorityType, PriorityWeights, PriorityDecayHalfLife) — I would run scontrol show config and sshare/sprio to gather live info, then explain which factors are dominating and recommend specific weight changes; or
- interpret sprio output for specific queued jobs you point to.

Which of those would you like me to do?

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain burst buffer directives and stage-in or stage-out behavior
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, doc‑grounded summary of burst buffer job directives and how stage‑in / stage‑out behave in Slurm (based on the Slurm Burst Buffer Guide).

What the directives are and where to put them
- Burst buffer directives are placed as commented lines in batch scripts (they begin with the plugin's directive string, e.g. #DW, #BB_LUA, or another configured Directive). They may appear before, after, or interspersed with #SBATCH lines.
- The same directives can be given on the command line via --bb (inline directives) or --bbf <file> (a file containing directives). Note: --bb cannot create/destroy persistent buffers (that is plugin dependent).
- Plugin must be enabled (BurstBufferType in slurm.conf) for directives to take effect.

Common directive forms / examples
- DataWarp (typical): e.g.
  - In script: #DW jobdw capacity=1GiB access_mode=striped type=scratch
  - srun example: srun --bb="capacity=1G access=striped type=scratch" ./a.out
- Lua plugin: default directive is #BB_LUA (or whatever is configured). If present, the lua hooks run and implement stages.
- Persistent buffers (DataWarp): #BB create_persistent name=<name> capacity=<size> [...] and #BB destroy_persistent name=<name> [hurry]

What stage‑in and stage‑out are (lifecycle)
- Slurm drives burst buffer operations at fixed points in the job lifecycle:
  - staging-in / staged-in: data is copied from the backing storage (or persistent buffer) into the allocated burst buffer before the job's tasks start.
  - pre-run: burst buffer is staged-in and any pre-run hooks complete; job then transitions to running.
  - running: job executes using the burst buffer.
  - post-run / staging-out / staged-out: after the job completes (or on teardown), data is copied from the burst buffer back to the requested destination (stage‑out).
- These burst buffer states are visible in Slurm as BurstBufferState in scontrol show job (examples: staging-in, staged-in, running, staging-out, teardown, complete, teardown-fail).
- There are explicit timeouts and parameters (e.g., StageInTimeout, StageOutTimeout, ValidateTimeout, OtherTimeout) that govern how long stage-in/stage-out may run before being treated as a failure.

Behavioral notes and failure modes
- All configured burst buffer hooks/scripts for the plugin are run at the appropriate stage (data_in/test_data_in before run; data_out/test_data_out after run, etc., for the lua plugin).
- If stage-in fails or times out, Slurm may not start the job (job will be prevented from entering running). If stage-out fails, teardown-fail or other error states may result—check job's BurstBufferState and plugin logs.
- For heterogeneous jobs, burst buffer hooks run once per component that has directives.
- Persistent burst buffers (DataWarp) have their own lifecycle (allocating/allocated/deleting/deleted) separate from job-specific buffers.

Monitoring and status commands
- scontrol show job <jobid> includes BurstBufferState and other burst buffer fields for that job.
- scontrol show burst gives plugin/pool totals, allocated buffers, per‑user usage, and configured timeouts.
- Use sview or the burst buffer plugin logs for more detailed troubleshooting.

Accounting and configuration points
- To have Slurm account for burst buffer usage, add the plugin TRES (e.g., bb/datawarp or bb/lua) to AccountingStorageTres in slurm.conf.
- Pools, granularity, and plugin-specific options are configured in burst_buffer.conf or via the plugin (lua script or DataWarp config).

Quick best practices
- Put directives at script top so they’re obvious and parsed before scheduling.
- Test stage-in/out with small jobs and --bbf files to verify paths and permissions.
- Watch scontrol show job and scontrol show burst to confirm staged-in and staged-out transitions; review plugin timeouts if stage operations take longer than expected.
- For persistent buffers, explicitly create/destroy with #BB create_persistent / destroy_persistent (DataWarp).

contains the following:

If the Directive option is not specified in burst_buffer.conf, then
the default directive for this plugin (`#BB_LUA`) will be used.
Since this plugin was designed to be generic and flexible, this plugin only
requires the directive to be given. If the directive is given, Slurm will run

## Heterogeneous Job Support [#het-job-support](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
Heterogeneous jobs may request burst buffers. Burst buffer hooks will run
once for each component that has burst buffer directives. For example, if a
heterogeneous job has three components and two of them have burst buffer
directives, the burst buffer hooks will run once for each of the two components
with burst buffer directives, but not for the third component without burst
buffer directives. Further information and examples can be found in the
heterogeneous jobs page.

## Command-line Job Options [#command-line](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
In addition to putting burst buffer directives in the batch script, the
command-line options `--bb` and `--bbf` may also include
burst buffer directives. These command-line options are available for salloc,
sbatch, and srun. Note that the `--bb` option cannot create or
destroy persistent burst buffers.
The `--bbf` option takes as an argument a filename and that file
should contain a collection of burst buffer operations identical to those used
for batch jobs.
Alternatively, the `--bb` option may be used to specify burst
buffer directives as the option argument. The behavior of this option depends
on which burst buffer plugin is used. When the `--bb` option is
used, Slurm parses this option and creates a temporary burst buffer script file
that is used internally by the burst buffer plugins.

Burst buffer resources can be placed in an advanced reservation using the
BurstBuffer option.
The argument consists of four elements:
`[plugin:][pool:]#[units]`

- pool specifies a burst buffer resource pool. If "type" is not specified, the number is a measure of storage space.

Jobs using this reservation are not restricted to these burst buffer
resources, but may use these reserved resources plus any which are generally
available. Some examples follow.

slurm.conf:
```text
BurstBufferType=burst_buffer/lua
```
The lua plugin calls a single script which must be named burst_buffer.lua.
This script needs to exist in the same directory as slurm.conf. The following
functions are required to exist, although they may do nothing but return
success:
- slurm_bb_job_process
- slurm_bb_pools
- slurm_bb_job_teardown
- slurm_bb_setup
- slurm_bb_data_in
- slurm_bb_test_data_in
- slurm_bb_real_size
- slurm_bb_paths
- slurm_bb_pre_run
- slurm_bb_post_run
- slurm_bb_data_out
- slurm_bb_test_data_out
- slurm_bb_get_status
A template of burst_buffer.lua is provided with Slurm:
`etc/burst_buffer.lua.example`
This template documents many more details about the functions such as
required parameters, when each function is called, return values for each
function, and some simple examples.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.conf.html)
burst_buffer.conf is an ASCII file which describes the configuration
of burst buffer resource management.
This file is only required on the head node(s), where the slurmctld daemon
executes.
The file will always be located in the same directory as the slurm.conf .
Parameter names are case insensitive.
Any text following a "#" in the configuration file is treated
as a comment through the end of that line.
Changes to the configuration file take effect upon restart of

of the command "scontrol reconfigure".

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain pending reasons Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, and QOS limits
results.agent_response:
Good — I looked up the Slurm documentation on job reason codes, QOS and resource limits and summarized the four pending reasons you asked about (Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOS limits), what they mean, common causes, and quick checks/fixes.

Summary (per Slurm docs)
- Slurm shows one reason code for a pending job even when multiple constraints apply. See "Job Reason Codes" and "Resource Limits" in the Slurm docs.

1) Resources
- What it means: the scheduler could not find sufficient free resources (TRES such as CPUs, memory, GPUs, or other requested resources) to satisfy the job request.
- Common causes: cluster is busy; not enough free CPUs, memory or GPUs; job requests more resources than any single node or partition provides; partition-level limits.
- What Slurm does: the job remains PENDING until matching resources free up.
- How to investigate:
  - Check queue: squeue (including the REASON column).
  - Check node/partition availability: sinfo -Nel or sinfo to see idle/allocated nodes and per-node resources.
  - Inspect job request: scontrol show job <jobid> (look at ReqTRES / GRES / NumNodes / MinNodes / CPUs / Mem).
- How to mitigate:
  - Reduce requested resources or node layout (fewer CPUs, smaller memory, fewer GPUs).
  - Pick a partition with suitable resources.
  - Wait or schedule to run when load decreases; request smaller per-node resource usage that can fit existing free nodes.

2) Priority
- What it means: higher-priority jobs are ahead in the scheduling order for the same partition or resources, so this job is not yet eligible to be scheduled.
- Why it happens: Slurm uses the multifactor priority plugin (factors: age, fairshare, job size, QOS, etc.). Jobs with higher composite priority are selected first.
- What Slurm does: the job remains PENDING until higher-priority jobs are scheduled/started or its computed priority increases.
- How to investigate:
  - Show priorities: sprio (or sprio -l) to list job priority factors/values.
  - Check queue ordering and competing jobs: squeue, sdiag for scheduler diagnostics/backfill info.
- How to mitigate:
  - Request a higher QOS (if allowed) or a different account with better priority.
  - Ask admins about QOS priority weights (PriorityWeightQOS) or fairshare settings.
  - For urgent work, admins can use sacctmgr/QOS changes or set a higher priority QOS (admin action).

3) ReqNodeNotAvail
- What it means: the job requested specific nodes, node features, or constraints and those requested nodes are not currently available; the scheduler could not allocate nodes matching the request.
- Common causes:
  - Job requested specific node names (sbatch --nodelist=...) and those nodes are down/reserved/drained/allocated.
  - Requested node features or constraints (e.g., --constraint=, feature/GRES) do not match currently idle nodes.
  - Reservation or maintenance holds nodes, or nodes are powered down / rebooting.
- What Slurm does: the job waits until requested nodes become available or the constraints match.
- How to investigate:
  - Inspect job details and requested nodes/features: scontrol show job <jobid> (check NodeList, Constraint, ReqNodes, ReqTRES).
  - Check node state and reasons: sinfo -Nel and sinfo_reasons (or scontrol show node <nodename>).
  - Check reservations: scontrol reservation show (or scontrol_reservation_show).
- How to mitigate:
  - Remove explicit node requests or loosen constraints (use generic partitions, remove strict --nodelist or --constraint).
  - Use a different partition or request fewer/smaller nodes.
  - Contact admins to release reservations or address node maintenance.

4) QOS limits (shown as assorted reason codes such as AssocMax, Max*PerAccount, or explicit QOS-related reasons)
- What it means: the job would violate a configured limit (QOS, account, or partition-level resource limit), so it is not eligible to run until the limit permits it.
- Common causes:
  - The request would exceed per-job or per-account TRES limits, GrpTRES, MaxTRESPerNode, MaxTRESPERUser, node or partition QOS caps, or aggregate usage thresholds.
  - Partition QOS limits can override job QOS limits unless OverPartQOS is set.
  - Some QOS flags (DenyOnLimit) cause jobs to be rejected at submission rather than just pending.
- What Slurm does: by default the job will pend until limits allow it; if QOS has DenyOnLimit set the job could have been rejected at submission.
- How to investigate:
  - Look at the job and its QOS/account: scontrol show job <jobid>.
  - Check QOS and limits: sacctmgr show qos, and review resource limits documentation (resource_limits).
  - Check association/fairshare usage: sshare and sacctmgr for account association limits.
- How to mitigate:
  - Request a different QOS or account with higher limits (requires permission).
  - Reduce the job’s resource request to fit within limits.
  - Ask admins to adjust QOS/association limits or to enable OverPartQOS/adjust DenyOnLimit behavior if appropriate.

Practical notes
- Only one reason is displayed even when multiple are true; scontrol show job <jobid> plus sinfo/sinfo_reasons and sprio gives the best diagnosis.
- Useful commands: squeue (REASON), scontrol show job <jobid>, sinfo -Nel, sinfo_reasons, scontrol show node <node>, sprio, sdiag, sshare, sacctmgr show qos.
- Admin-only actions (QOS changes, OverPartQOS, DenyOnLimit, reservations, node state changes) require administrator intervention.

If you want, provide a job ID (or a small squeue output) and I can walk through the exact pending reason fields and recommended next steps for that job.

Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.

## The Slurm Fair-Share Formula [#formula](https://slurm.schedmd.com/classic_fair_share.html)
The Slurm fair-share formula has been designed to provide fair scheduling to users based on the allocation and usage of every account.
The actual formula used is a refinement of the formula presented above:
```text
F = 2**(-U E /S)
```

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain job array IDs and %A/%a output filename placeholders
results.agent_response:
Short answer (from the official Slurm docs):

- %A and %a are filename-pattern replacement symbols processed by sbatch when you set output/error filenames (e.g. --output, --error or #SBATCH --output).
  - %A expands to the job array's master job allocation number (the ArrayJobID — the job ID returned by sbatch when you submit the array).
  - %a expands to the job array index (the array element's index value from --array).

Where this comes from: sbatch's "FILENAME PATTERN" section defines %% (literal %), %A (ArrayJobID), %a (array index), %b (array index modulo 10), %j/%J (jobid/step) and other symbols. The job-array page documents SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID / SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID and the ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID job-id notation.

Details and examples
- Submission:
  sbatch --array=1-3 --output=out_%A_%a.txt myscript.sh
  If sbatch replies "Submitted batch job 36" then the three element output files become:
  - out_36_1.txt
  - out_36_2.txt
  - out_36_3.txt
  (%A = 36 for all elements; %a = 1,2,3 respectively.)

- Environment variables (set inside each array task):
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID = the ArrayJobID (master allocation number)
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID = the element index (same as %a)
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX are also provided
  - Each array element also has its own SLURM_JOB_ID (the element’s actual job id)

- scontrol / CLI addressing:
  - Array elements are identified as ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (for example 36_2).
  - scontrol show job 36 shows ArrayJobID and ArrayTaskID fields; scontrol update job=36_2 operates on the single element.

Notes / gotchas
- %A is the array's master allocation number (the jobid returned when you submitted the array) — not the per-element SLURM_JOB_ID if your cluster gives each element a distinct jobid.
- %a is the literal index value you specified with --array; if you used a complex list (e.g. --array=0,10,20) %a expands to 0 / 10 / 20 respectively.
- Use %% to include a literal percent sign in the filename.
- There is also %b (index modulo 10) and %j/%J (jobid/stepid) if you need different numbering.

References
- sbatch FILENAME PATTERN (replacement symbols: %A, %a, %b, %j, %%): Slurm sbatch docs.
- Job Array Support (SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID): Slurm job array docs.

If you want, I can show the exact filename expansion for a specific sbatch --array expression you plan to use.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain job array IDs and %A/%a output filename placeholders
results.agent_response:
Summary (from the official Slurm docs)

- Job-array identifiers
  - ArrayJobID: the job id assigned to the array allocation (the "master" job allocation). In sbatch output this is the id printed when the array is submitted (e.g., "Submitted batch job 36").
  - ArrayTaskID (array index): the index value for the particular element of the array (the numbers you passed to --array, e.g. 1,2,3 or 0-7).
  - Environment variables set for array jobs:
    - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID = the ArrayJobID (first job id of the array)
    - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID = the ArrayTaskID (the element index)
    - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, _TASK_MAX, _TASK_MIN are also provided.

- Addressing array elements to Slurm tools
  - Use ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (e.g. 12345_7) to refer to a specific element with scontrol or squeue. scontrol show job will report ArrayJobID and ArrayTaskID fields.

- Filename pattern placeholders for --output/--error (percent substitutions)
  - %A — Job array's master job allocation number (ArrayJobID)
  - %a — Job array ID (index) number (ArrayTaskID)
  - %b — Job array ID modulo 10
  - %j — jobid of the running job
  - %J — jobid.stepid of the running job (e.g. 128.0)
  - %% — a literal percent sign
  (These are documented under "FILENAME PATTERN" in the sbatch manual.)

Practical implications / examples
- If you submit:
    sbatch --array=1-3 --output=slurm-%A_%a.out my.job
  and sbatch prints "Submitted batch job 36", Slurm will create per-task files:
    slurm-36_1.out, slurm-36_2.out, slurm-36_3.out
  (%A expands to 36, %a to 1/2/3).

- To avoid output-file collisions you should include either %a (per-element index) or %j/%J (task-specific job id/step) in the filename when writing per-element output.

Caveats
- Array job internals and job-id assignment order can make JobID numbers and array indexes appear non-linear (see job array docs). Use the documented placeholders or the SLURM_ARRAY_* env vars inside the job script for robust per-task naming/logic.

If you want, I can give concrete sbatch examples (including use of padding, modulo %b use-cases, or how to reference elements with scontrol) — which would you prefer?

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain job array IDs and %A/%a output filename placeholders
results.agent_response:
Good question — here’s a concise explanation grounded in the sbatch/job-array docs.

What a job-array is
- A job array is a collection of similar batch jobs submitted with sbatch --array. Each element shares the same job script/options but has a distinct array index (task id).

ID terminology
- ArrayJobID (a.k.a. the job array’s master job allocation number): the job ID returned by sbatch for the array submission (this is the array “master” allocation).
- ArrayTaskID (the array index): the element index within the array (the value(s) you gave to --array, e.g. 0,1,2 or 1-10:2).
- Individual array elements can be referenced as ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (for example 123_4).

Environment variables (inside each array task)
- SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID = ArrayJobID
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID = ArrayTaskID
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX are also set.

Filename replacement symbols (used in --output, --error and sbatch filename patterns)
- %A — Job array’s master job allocation number (ArrayJobID). Use when you want the array’s master ID in filenames.
- %a — Job array ID (index) number (ArrayTaskID). Use when you want the per-element index in filenames.
- %b — Job array index modulo 10 (last digit of the index).
- %j — jobid of the running job.
- %J — jobid.stepid of the running job (stepid only for regular steps).
- %% — literal percent sign.

Examples
- sbatch --array=1-3 --output=job_%A_%a.out myscript.sh
  - If sbatch replies "Submitted batch job 100" (ArrayJobID=100), the files created will be:
    - job_100_1.out, job_100_2.out, job_100_3.out
  - Inside each task, SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID=100 and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID will be 1, 2, or 3.

Notes / gotchas
- %A and %a are replaced by Slurm when creating/launching array tasks; they are not shell variables. If you need the values inside the script use the SLURM_* environment variables.
- For non-array jobs %A/%a aren’t meaningful; use %j (jobid) instead.
- You can combine these placeholders arbitrarily in filenames (e.g., --output=%A.%a.%j.out) and escape a literal % with %%.

If you want, I can show a few more concrete filename patterns or list all supported % placeholders from the sbatch docs.

results.agent_response:
Summary (from the Slurm documentation)
- %A and %a are filename-replacement symbols you can use in sbatch --output/--error (and other filename pattern) strings.
  - %A — Job array's master job allocation number (the ArrayJobID). This is the job id assigned to the array as a whole (the "master" ArrayJobID).
  - %a — Job array index (the array task id / element index). This is the per-task index value from the --array specification (e.g. 0..N or 1..N).
- Environment variables set for array jobs:
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID = first job ID of the array (ArrayJobID)
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID = the array index for the running task (same as %a)
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN are also provided.
- Other useful filename symbols:
  - %j — jobid of the running job (per-task JobID)
  - %J — jobid.stepid (e.g., "128.0")
  - %% — literal percent sign
  - %b — job array index modulo 10 (least significant digit)

Practical notes and examples
- If you submit:
  sbatch --array=1-10 --output=job-%A_%a.out myscript.sh
  and sbatch responds "Submitted batch job 12345", then task 3 will create:
  job-12345_3.out
  - %A is constant for the whole array (12345). %a varies per task (1..10).
- If you use %j instead of %A you get the task's unique job id (which can differ from the array master id). Example:
  --output=slurm-%j.out might produce slurm-12346.out for element 1, slurm-12347.out for element 2, etc.
- Use %A when you want a single identifier shared by all array elements (easy to group files). Use %a (or %j) when you need per-task unique filenames to avoid collisions.
- For dependencies and scontrol addressing, array tasks are referenced as <ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskID> (for example 12345_3).
- Be careful about filename collisions: don’t use a constant filename for an array without %a/%j/%A (or the job will overwrite output from concurrent tasks).
- Remember %% to place a literal % in the filename.

Behavioral caveat from the docs
- The ArrayJobID is the jobid of the first element of the array. Slurm’s internal ordering can make the first task a placeholder item; as a result the task with the lowest SLURM_JOB_ID may have the highest SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID. Use SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (or %A/%a) when you need the array-specific identifiers rather than relying on ordering of SLURM_JOB_ID values.

- Show concrete examples with zero-padding approaches (common workaround patterns),
- Explain the difference between SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in more detail,

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain job array IDs and %A/%a output filename placeholders
results.agent_response:
Short answer from the Slurm docs (sbatch + Job Array pages), with examples and the exact meanings:

1) Job-array identifiers — terminology
- ArrayJobID (aka the "job array's master job allocation number")
  - This is the Slurm job ID assigned to the array as a whole (the controller’s ID for the array). The sbatch response shows this master job ID.
  - scontrol fields: ArrayJobID = JobID of the first element of the job array.
- ArrayTaskID (aka the job array index)
  - This is the index value you specified with --array (e.g. 1,2,3 or 0-9). Each array element has its ArrayTaskID.
- Full element form: <ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskID> (example: 12345_3). Many Slurm tools accept that form to refer to a single array element (scontrol, scancel, etc.).
- Environment variables set inside array tasks:
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the array’s master job id (ArrayJobID).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — this element’s array index (ArrayTaskID).
  - Other related variables: SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MAX, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN.

2) Filename replacement symbols used by --output/--error (from sbatch)
- %A — Job array’s master job allocation number (ArrayJobID). Same value for every element in that array.
- %a — Job array index number (ArrayTaskID). Varies per element.
- %j — jobid of the running job (the per-element jobid).
- %J — jobid.stepid (for steps; not typically needed for simple batch scripts).
- %b — job array index modulo 10 (useful for sharding into 10 buckets).
- %% — literal percent sign (escape).

3) Practical examples
- sbatch --array=1-3 --output=slurm-%A_%a.out myjob.sh
  - If sbatch returns "Submitted batch job 36" (ArrayJobID=36), files created will be:
    - slurm-36_1.out
    - slurm-36_2.out
    - slurm-36_3.out
  - %A is 36 for all files; %a is 1,2,3 respectively.
- If you want filenames keyed by the element’s unique jobid instead:
  - sbatch --array=1-3 --output=slurm-%j.out myjob.sh
  - Each element gets its own Slurm-assigned jobid in %j (not necessarily equal to ArrayJobID).

4) When to use which:
- Use %A_%a when you want a stable, predictable mapping to the array + index that matches ArrayJobID and the requested index values.
- Use %j when you care about the actual Slurm jobid assigned to that particular element.
- Use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID in your script if you need the index value inside the job (rather than just in the filename).

References: sbatch filename-pattern (%A, %a, %j, %% ) and Job Array docs (ArrayJobID, ArrayTaskID, SLURM_ARRAY_* env vars) from the official Slurm docs.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain array throttling syntax such as --array=0-99%10
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- --array takes an index specification of the form start-end[:step][%max].
- The "%N" part is a concurrency throttle (N = maximum number of array tasks allowed to run at the same time). It is NOT a percentage; it is an absolute count.

Formal breakdown (from the Slurm sbatch / job_array docs)
- Index list: single values, comma-separated values, and ranges are all allowed:
  - 5                -> single element with index 5
  - 1,3,5,7          -> explicit indices 1,3,5,7
  - 1-7              -> indices 1,2,3,4,5,6,7
- Step: append :step to a range to select every step’th index:
  - 1-7:2            -> 1,3,5,7
- Throttle: append %max to limit simultaneous running tasks from that array:
  - 0-99%10          -> indices 0..99, but at most 10 tasks from that array may be RUNNING at once
  - 0-15%4           -> at most 4 simultaneous tasks (example from the docs)
  - %1               -> run array tasks serially (one at a time)

- Array tasks are still regular jobs for enforcement of limits like MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, QOS, account limits, etc.
- Environment variables you can use inside the job script: SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN/MAX.
- squeue prints array elements compactly (e.g., JOBID_[1-1024]); scancel can target elements with jobid_1 or jobid_[1-3].

- show verbatim doc snippets or the job_array.html URL, or

Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.

individual ArrayJobID .

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.
Since each array element can have a different exit code, the interpretation of
the afterok and afternotok clauses will be based upon the highest
exit code from any task in the job array.
When a job dependency specifies the job ID of a job array:
The after clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array start.
The afterany clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete.
The aftercorr clause is satisfied after the corresponding task ID in the

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain array throttling syntax such as --array=0-99%10
results.agent_response:
Short answer: the % part caps how many array tasks from that single job may run at once. The full sbatch array syntax is:

- --array=<index-list>[%<max_running>]

Where:
- <index-list> may be
  - a single index (e.g. 5),
  - a comma-separated list (e.g. 1,3,5,7),
  - a range (e.g. 0-99),
  - a range with step (e.g. 1-7:2 produces 1,3,5,7).
- %<max_running> is an integer that limits the maximum number of simultaneously running tasks from that job array (an absolute count, not a percent).

Documentation example (paraphrased): "--array=0-15%4" limits simultaneously running tasks from that array to 4.

Concrete examples:
- --array=0-99%10
  - Creates tasks with indices 0..99 (100 tasks total).
  - At most 10 of those tasks will be RUNNING at the same time; others wait in the array’s internal pending queue.
- --array=1-10:2%3
  - Creates tasks 1,3,5,7,9 (step=2) and allows up to 3 of them to run concurrently.
- --array=1,3,5,7%2
  - Four tasks (1,3,5,7) with at most 2 running simultaneously.

Notes and behavior:
- Array tasks are still regular jobs for limits/accounting—subject to MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, QOS/account/account limits, etc.
- The smallest user-specified index may be 0 (default) and MaxArraySize (cluster config) limits the maximum array size.
- Environment variables set inside tasks include SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID; array elements are referenced externally as <ArrayJobID>_<TaskID> (for example 12345_7).
- squeue shows compressed array ranges by default; use squeue --array (or other options) to list elements individually.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain array throttling syntax such as --array=0-99%10
results.agent_response:
Good question — the % in an sbatch --array specification is the job-array “throttle” (max simultaneously running tasks). Key points and examples:

- Basic index ranges and lists
  - --array=0-99 creates tasks with indices 0..99 (100 tasks).
  - You can also use comma lists and steps: --array=1,3,5,7 or --array=1-7:2 (1,3,5,7).

- Throttle syntax
  - Append %N to the array spec to limit concurrency: --array=0-99%10
    - That submits 100 tasks (indices 0..99) but only allows up to 10 tasks from that array to run at the same time. The remaining tasks stay PENDING and the scheduler starts new ones as running tasks finish.
  - The throttle applies per job-array (not globally across all arrays), and it is enforced in addition to normal cluster/user/account limits.

- What you get inside the job
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the array index for this task (e.g., 0..99).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID and other array-related env vars (SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, _TASK_MIN/_TASK_MAX).

- Useful filename substitution in scripts
  - Use %a (or %A, %j, etc.) in --output/--error patterns to include the array index or job id:
    - sbatch --array=0-9 --output=out_%a.txt myscript.sh

- Examples
  - --array=0-99%10  -> 100 tasks, max 10 running at once.
  - --array=1-20:2%4 -> tasks 1,3,5,...,19 (10 tasks total), max 4 concurrently.
  - --array=0,5,10%2 -> 3 specific tasks, at most 2 running simultaneously.

- Behavior/limits to be aware of
  - If you omit %N, the scheduler may start as many array tasks as resources/limits allow.
  - Array tasks still count toward any per-user/account/job limits (e.g., MaxJobs).
  - You can address/cancel individual array elements with jobid_index (e.g., scancel 12345_7).

Reference: Slurm job-array docs (sbatch/job_array) — the %N form is described as “limit the number of simultaneously running tasks from the job array to N.”

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain array throttling syntax such as --array=0-99%10
results.agent_response:
Summary from the official Slurm docs (job_array and sbatch):

- Basic meaning
  - --array=0-99%10 creates an array of tasks indexed 0 through 99 (100 tasks total).
  - The %10 suffix is the array "throttle" and limits the maximum number of array tasks that may be simultaneously RUNNING to 10. As tasks finish, new tasks from the array are started until all indices are run.

- Short explanation / example
  - --array=0-99%10 -> submit indices 0,1,...,99 but only 10 run at any one time.
  - --array=1-10%3 -> at most 3 array tasks run concurrently (others wait).
  - --array=1,3,5,7%2 -> only two of those listed elements may run at once.
  - You can combine range and step: --array=0-99:2%5 -> indices 0,2,4,...,98 with up to 5 concurrent.

- How tasks behave
  - Each array task acts like a regular job (subject to job/account/QOS limits such as MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs).
  - Slurm sets environment variables in the job script: SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID (the index), SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT, SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_MIN/MAX. Use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID inside your script to dispatch work per index.

- Output filenames and IDs
  - Output file patterns can include %A (array job ID) and %a (task index); default is slurm-%A_%a.out.
  - squeue and scontrol represent arrays compactly (e.g., JOBID_[0-99]); individual task records are created as tasks start or change state.

- Notes and limits
  - The percent syntax is documented as "A maximum number of simultaneously running tasks from the job array may be specified using a '%' separator." (sbatch/job_array docs).
  - Cluster configuration may limit array size (MaxArraySize, default 1001) and other job-count limits, so very large arrays may be constrained.

If you want, I can show a small example sbatch script that uses SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID and the throttling, or explain how throttling interacts with partition/node availability.

results.prompt: Use Slurm docs to explain array throttling syntax such as --array=0-99%10
results.agent_response:
Brief summary — syntax components
- Range/list/step: --array=0-99,5,200 or --array=1-7:2
  - 0-99 → indices 0,1,2,...,99
  - 1-7:2 → indices 1,3,5,7 (the :2 is the step)
  - Commas combine ranges and single indices
- Throttle (concurrency limit): the %N suffix
  - --array=0-99%10 limits the number of simultaneously running tasks from that array to 10.
  - The percent value is an absolute count (maximum concurrent tasks), not a percent fraction.
- Combined example: --array=1-20:2%4 → tasks 1,3,5,...,19 but only up to 4 of those run at the same time.

What this means in practice
- sbatch --array=0-99%10 submits 100 array tasks (indices 0..99) but the scheduler will only start at most 10 array tasks from that job at once. As one finishes, another pending array task will start, maintaining up to 10 running until all complete.
- Array tasks are still ordinary jobs for accounting and limits: they obey user/partition/job QOS limits, MaxJobs/MaxSubmitJobs, MaxArraySize, priorities, dependencies, etc.

How to access the index inside your script
- SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID contains the index for the running task.
- SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID (or %A in filename patterns) is the array master job id; %a expands to the task index in filename templates.

Examples
- sbatch --array=0-99%10 myjob.sh
  - 100 tasks (0..99), 10 concurrently running.
- #SBATCH --array=1-8:2%3
  - indices 1,3,5,7 with at most 3 running simultaneously.
- sbatch --array=0-9,20,30-39%5 myjob.sh
  - indices 0–9,20,30–39; up to 5 concurrent.

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm afterok dependency using official docs
results.agent_response:
Summary (official behavior)
- afterok is a job dependency type you can pass to sbatch (or set with #SBATCH --dependency=...).
- Meaning: the dependent job is eligible to start only after all specified jobs have finished successfully (exit code 0).
- It is checked by slurmctld at job completion; sbatch returns immediately with the dependent job ID, but that job will remain PENDING until the afterok condition is satisfied.

Syntax (from sbatch docs)
- Command-line or script directive:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid>[:<jobid>[:...]] myscript.sh
  - or inside a script: #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:12345:12346
- You may specify multiple job IDs separated by ':' (all listed jobs must meet the afterok condition).

Semantics and important notes
- AND semantics: when you list multiple job IDs, all must complete successfully (exit code 0) before the dependent job can run.
- Exit-code semantics: "successful" means the predecessor job(s) exited with code 0. If a predecessor fails (non‑zero exit code), times out, or is cancelled, an afterok dependency on that job will not be satisfied.
- Alternatives:
  - afterany: run after specified jobs finish regardless of exit code.
  - afternotok: run only if specified jobs finish with non‑zero exit (i.e., fail).
  - after: becomes eligible after the specified jobs have started.
- Job arrays and steps: you can reference specific job/step identifiers; consult sbatch/scontrol docs for array/step ID notation if you need element-level dependencies.
- Combining dependencies: you can express different dependency types (see sbatch docs) to build more complex conditions.

Quick examples
- Single predecessor that must succeed:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 step2.sh
- Multiple predecessors:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345:12346 step3.sh
- Use in script:
  - #!/bin/sh
    #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:12345
    ...script body...

Reference
- Official sbatch documentation (dependency option): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html (see --dependency and examples)

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text

```text

```text

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm afterok dependency using official docs
results.agent_response:
Summary (official Slurm behavior)
- Purpose: the afterok dependency makes a job wait until one or more specified jobs have finished successfully (exit code 0).
- Syntax (common forms):
  - CLI: sbatch --dependency=afterok:<jobid>[:<jobid>...]
  - In a script: #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:<jobid>
  - (The docs also show --depend as a short form: --depend=afterok:<jobid>.)
- Multiple job IDs: list them after the colon (colon-separated in examples in the official docs).
- Effect: the dependent job will remain pending until each referenced job has completed with exit code 0. If any referenced job fails/cancels/returns nonzero, the afterok dependency for that referenced job is not satisfied.

Key official-doc details and edge cases
- Job arrays:
  - If you depend on a job array ID, afterok is satisfied only after all tasks in that array complete successfully. The documentation notes that for arrays the interpretation of afterok is based on the highest exit code from any task in the array (so any nonzero exit causes afterok to be unsatisfied).
  - You can depend on specific array elements (examples in the job-array docs).
- Burst buffers:
  - If both jobs use burst buffers, an afterok dependency will wait for the producing job to finish and its burst-buffer stage-out to complete. If the dependent job does not use a burst buffer, it will not wait for stage-out; use afterburstbuffer if you need that.
- Related dependency types (for different semantics):
  - afterany: wait until referenced job(s) complete (regardless of exit code).
  - afternotok: wait until referenced job(s) complete and at least one task fails (nonzero exit).
  - aftercorr: for array jobs, wait for the corresponding element to complete successfully.
  - afterburstbuffer: wait for burst-buffer stage-out to finish (see burst-buffer docs).

Short examples (from docs-style usage)
- Single job:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 myscript.sh
- Multiple jobs:
  - sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345:12346 myscript.sh
- Job array (wait for all elements to succeed):
  - sbatch --depend=afterok:67890 followup.sh

Official references
- sbatch manual (options and --dependency): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html
- Job array dependency semantics (afterok behavior with arrays): https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html
- Burst buffer note about dependencies: https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html

If you want, I can:
- show the exact man-page section text for --dependency, or
- give examples for array-element dependencies (e.g., 123_4), or
- help convert an existing submission script to use afterok. Which would you like?

begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.

complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm afterok dependency using official docs
results.agent_response:
Summary (official Slurm docs)

- What it does
  - afterok is a job dependency type accepted by sbatch/--dependency. A job submitted with --dependency=afterok:<jobid>[:<jobid2>...] will not begin scheduling until the specified job(s) have completed successfully (i.e., exited with code 0). (sbatch doc)

- Syntax / how to use
  - On the sbatch command line:
    - sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 my.job
  - Inside a batch script:
    - #SBATCH --dependency=afterok:123
  - You may list multiple job ids separated by colons:
    - sbatch --dependency=afterok:123:124 my.job
  - For job arrays you can refer to the whole array (ArrayJobID) or specific elements (see examples below). (sbatch, job_array docs)

- Job-array behaviour (important)
  - If the dependency names a job array, afterok is satisfied only after all tasks in that array complete successfully. Because array elements may have different exit codes, the interpretation of afterok for an array is based on the highest exit code from any task in the array (so any non‑zero exit causes afterok to be unsatisfied). (job_array doc)

- Interaction with burst buffers / stage-out
  - If the first job uses burst buffers and the second job depends on it, afterok waits for the job to complete, but will not wait for the first job’s burst-buffer stage-out to finish unless you use afterburstbuffer. Use afterburstbuffer when you need the stage-out to complete before the dependent job runs. (burst_buffer doc)

- Related dependency types (quick reference)
  - after: wait until the named job(s) start.
  - afterany: wait until the named job(s) complete (any exit code).
  - afternotok: wait until the named job(s) complete with any non‑zero exit.
  - aftercorr: for arrays, wait until the corresponding task ID in the specified job completes successfully.
  - afterburstbuffer: wait until named job completes and its burst-buffer stage-out finishes.
  (See sbatch and job_array docs for full details.)

Examples (from docs)
- sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 my.job
- sbatch --depend=afterok:123_4:123_8 my.job2         (wait for specific array elements)
- sbatch --depend=afterok:123 my.job                 (wait for entire array job 123 to complete successfully)

Sources (official Slurm docs)
- sbatch (options & --dependency): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html
- Job arrays and dependency semantics: https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html
- Burst-buffer interaction with dependencies: https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html

If you want, I can paste the exact sbatch --dependency paragraphs or show examples tailored to using job arrays or chaining multiple jobs.

## Security Considerations [#security](https://slurm.schedmd.com/metrics.html)
The metrics system has several important security implications:
- No authentication : There is no built-in authentication mechanism for metrics endpoints. Anyone with network access to the slurmctld port can query metrics.
- PrivateData dependency : The metrics feature is automatically disabled when any PrivateData parameter is set in slurm.conf to prevent exposure of sensitive information.
- Network access : Metrics are exposed through the slurmctld network interface. Consider firewall rules and network segmentation to control access.
- Information disclosure : Metrics may reveal information about cluster utilization, job patterns, and user activity that could be considered sensitive in some environments.

Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote

a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.

procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm afterok dependency using official docs
results.agent_response:
Summary (official Slurm behavior)
- afterok is a job dependency type you pass to sbatch (or put in a #SBATCH --depend=... line). A job with --depend=afterok:<jobid>[...]
  will be eligible to start only after the specified job(s) complete successfully (exit code 0).
- “Successfully” = Slurm records an exit code of zero (the derived exit code is used when jobs have multiple steps). Any non‑zero exit causes afterok to NOT be satisfied.
- For job arrays, afterok against the array ID means the dependent job waits until all tasks in the array complete successfully; when you reference array elements you can use the job_element syntax (e.g. 123_4).

Syntax and examples (from sbatch / job_array docs)
- Basic: sbatch --depend=afterok:123 my.job
- Multiple job IDs: sbatch --depend=afterok:123:124:125 my.job
- Array element(s): sbatch --depend=afterok:123_4 my.job
- Mixed array-elements example (from docs): sbatch --depend=afterok:123_4:123_8 my.job2
- You may also use other dependency types: after (start after start), afterany (start after completion regardless of exit code), afternotok (start if the specified job(s) fail), aftercorr (for corresponding array elements).

Notes / important details from the official docs
- “Complete successfully” is determined by the job’s exit code (Slurm treats non‑zero as failure). See Slurm’s job exit code/derived exit code behavior for jobs with multiple steps.
- When an afterok references a job array, interpretation uses the highest exit code from array tasks; afterok for an array requires all array tasks to finish with exit code 0.
- The --depend option can be supplied on the sbatch command line or inside the batch script via a #SBATCH --depend=... line.

References
- sbatch (options, --depend): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html
- Job array / job dependencies (afterok behaviour, array examples): https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html
- Job exit codes / derived exit code: https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_exit_code.html

If you want, I can:
- Show concrete examples for your workflow (e.g., chain three jobs so the 2nd runs only if the 1st succeeds), or
- Explain how to inspect why a dependent job is still PENDING (what squeue/scontrol fields to check). Which would you like?

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm afterok dependency using official docs
results.agent_response:
Summary (official Slurm behavior)
- Purpose: afterok makes a job wait until one or more other jobs complete successfully. "Successfully" means the producing job(s) finish with an exit code of zero (Slurm state COMPLETED / derived exit code = 0).
- Basic syntax: sbatch --dependency=afterok:JOBID[:JOBID... ] myscript.sh
  - You may list multiple job IDs separated by colons. Different dependency types can be combined by comma, e.g. --dependency=afterok:123,afterany:200.
- What happens at submit: sbatch returns immediately with a job ID; the dependent job is queued and will remain PENDING until the afterok condition is satisfied. The squeue pending reason will show Dependency while waiting.
- Job arrays: if you depend on an array job ID, afterok is satisfied only after all tasks in that array complete successfully. Internally Slurm uses the array's highest exit code when evaluating afterok/afternotok.
- Burst buffer nuance: if both jobs use burst buffers and the dependent job uses afterok, the dependent job will wait until the producing job completes and its burst-buffer stage-out completes. If the dependent job does not use a burst buffer, afterok does not wait for stage-out; to explicitly wait for stage-out use afterburstbuffer.
- Related dependency types (for comparison):
  - afterany: start after the specified job(s) finish for any exit code.
  - afternotok: start only if the specified job(s) finish with a non‑zero exit code (failure).
  - aftercorr / after: other variants exist (see sbatch docs and job-array doc for array-specific behaviors).

Official references
- sbatch --dependency (main syntax and options): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html
- Job array dependency behavior: https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html
- Burst buffer interaction with dependencies: https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html
- Job reason codes (Dependency pending reason): https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_reason_codes.html

If you want, I can:
- Provide concrete examples for common workflows (single-job chaining, array-to-job chaining, combining types), or
- Show how the dependency appears in squeue/scontrol output for a real job ID. Which would you like?

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html)
If two jobs use burst buffers and one is dependent on the other (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterok:123 ...`) then the second job will not
begin until the first job completes and its burst buffer stage-out completes.
If the second job does not use a burst buffer, but is dependent upon the first
job's completion, then it will not wait for the stage-out operation of the first
job to complete.
The second job can be made to wait for the first job's stage-out operation to
complete using the "afterburstbuffer" dependency option (e.g.
`sbatch --dependency=afterburstbuffer:123 ...`).

Snippet:
## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.

config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV
records defined within the cluster itself.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling
upgrades on the cluster as this could lead to the daemons being upgraded sooner

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

Snippet:
## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a
heterogeneous job.

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld

Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
