sbatch will return 0 on success or error code on failure.
 
   
 SCRIPT PATH RESOLUTION 
 
The batch script is resolved in the following order:
 

 
1. If script starts with ".", then path is constructed as:
current working directory / script
 

2. If script starts with a "/", then path is considered absolute.
 

3. If script is in current working directory.
 

4. If script can be resolved through PATH. See path_resolution (7).
 

 

Current working directory is the calling process working directory unless the

 sbatch 
Section: Slurm Commands (1) Updated: Slurm Commands Index 

 
   
 NAME 
sbatch - Submit a batch script to Slurm.
 
   
 SYNOPSIS 
 sbatch [ OPTIONS(0) ...] [ : [ OPTIONS(N) ...]] script(0) [ args(0) ...]
 
Option(s) define multiple jobs in a co-scheduled heterogeneous job.
For more details about heterogeneous jobs see the document
 

 https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html 
 
   
 DESCRIPTION 
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
 
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.
 
sbatch exits immediately after the script is successfully transferred to the
Slurm controller and assigned a Slurm job ID. The batch script is not
necessarily granted resources immediately, it may sit in the queue of pending
jobs for some time before its required resources become available.
 
By default both standard output and standard error are directed to a file of
the name "slurm-%j.out", where the "%j" is replaced with the job allocation
number. The file will be generated on the first node of the job allocation.
Other than the batch script itself, Slurm does no movement of user files.
 
When the job allocation is finally granted for the batch script, Slurm
runs a single copy of the batch script on the first node in the set of
allocated nodes.
 
The following document describes the influence of various options on the
allocation of cpus to jobs and tasks.
 

 https://slurm.schedmd.com/cpu_management.html 
 
   
 RETURN VALUE 
sbatch will return 0 on success or error code on failure.
 
   
 SCRIPT PATH RESOLUTION 
 
The batch script is resolved in the following order:
 

 
1. If script starts with ".", then path is constructed as:
current working directory / script
 

2. If script starts with a "/", then path is considered absolute.
 

3. If script is in current working directory.
 

4. If script can be resolved through PATH. See path_resolution (7).
 

 

Current working directory is the calling process working directory unless the
 --chdir argument is passed, which will override the current working
directory.
 
   
 OPTIONS 
 

 
 
 -A , --account =< account > Charge resources used by this job to specified account.
The account is an arbitrary string. The account name may
be changed after job submission using the scontrol 
command.
 
 
 --acctg-freq =< datatype >=< interval >[,< datatype >=< interval >...] Define the job accounting and profiling sampling intervals in seconds.
This can be used to override the JobAcctGatherFrequency parameter in
the slurm.conf file. < datatype >=< interval > specifies the task
sampling interval for the jobacct_gather plugin or a
sampling interval for a profiling type by the
acct_gather_profile plugin. Multiple
comma-separated < datatype >=< interval > pairs
may be specified. Supported datatype values are:
 
 
 
 task Sampling interval for the jobacct_gather plugins and for task
profiling by the acct_gather_profile plugin.
 

 NOTE : This frequency is used to monitor memory usage. If memory limits
are enforced, the highest frequency a user can request is what is configured
in the slurm.conf file. It can not be disabled.
 
 
 energy Sampling interval for energy profiling using the
acct_gather_energy plugin.
 
 
 network Sampling interval for infiniband profiling using the
acct_gather_interconnect plugin.
 
 
 filesystem Sampling interval for filesystem profiling using the
acct_gather_filesystem plugin.
 
 
 
 

The default value for the task sampling interval is 30 seconds.
The default value for all other intervals is 0.
An interval of 0 disables sampling of the specified type.
If the task sampling interval is 0, accounting
information is collected only at job termination (reducing Slurm
interference with the job).
 

Smaller (non-zero) values have a greater impact upon job performance,
but a value of 30 seconds is not likely to be noticeable for
applications having less than 10,000 tasks.
 

 
 
 -a , --array =< indexes > Submit a job array, multiple jobs to be executed with identical parameters.
The indexes specification identifies what array index values should
be used. Multiple values may be specified using a comma separated list and/or
a range of values with a "-" separator. For example, "--array=0-15" or
"--array=0,6,16-32".
A step function can also be specified with a suffix containing a colon and
number. For example, "--array=0-15:4" is equivalent to "--array=0,4,8,12".
A maximum number of simultaneously running tasks from the job array may be
specified using a "%" separator.
For example "--array=0-15%4" will limit the number of simultaneously
running tasks from this job array to 4.
The minimum index value is 0.
the maximum value is one less than the configuration parameter MaxArraySize.
 NOTE : Currently, federated job arrays only run on the local cluster.
 
 
 --batch =< list > Nodes can have features assigned to them by the Slurm administrator.
Users can specify which of these features are required by their batch
script using this options.
For example a job's allocation may include both Intel Haswell and KNL nodes
with features "haswell" and "knl" respectively.
On such a configuration the batch script would normally benefit by executing
on a faster Haswell node.
This would be specified using the option "--batch=haswell".
The specification can include AND and OR operators using the ampersand and
vertical bar separators. For example:
"--batch=haswell|broadwell" or "--batch=haswell|big_memory".
The --batch argument must be a subset of the job's
 --constraint =< list > argument (i.e. the job can not request only
KNL nodes, but require the script to execute on a Haswell node).
If the request can not be satisfied from the resources allocated to the job,
the batch script will execute on the first node of the job allocation.
 
 
 --bb =< spec > Burst buffer specification. The form of the specification is system dependent.
Also see --bbf .
When the --bb option is used, Slurm parses this option and creates a
temporary burst buffer script file that is used internally by the burst buffer
plugins. See Slurm's burst buffer guide for more information and examples:
 

 https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html 
 
 
 --bbf =< file_name > Path of file containing burst buffer specification.
The form of the specification is system dependent.
These burst buffer directives will be inserted into the submitted batch script.
See Slurm's burst buffer guide for more information and examples:
 

 https://slurm.schedmd.com/burst_buffer.html 
 
 
 -b , --begin =< time > Submit the batch script to the Slurm controller immediately, like normal, but
tell the controller to defer the allocation of the job until the specified time.
 
Time may be of the form HH:MM:SS to run a job at
a specific time of day (seconds are optional).
(If that time is already past, the next day is assumed.)
You may also specify midnight , noon , elevenses (11 AM),
 fika (3 PM) or teatime (4 PM) and you can have a time-of-day
suffixed with AM or PM for running in the morning or the evening.
You can also say what day the job will be run, by specifying
a date of the form MMDDYY or MM/DD/YY 
 YYYY-MM-DD . Combine date and time using the following
format YYYY-MM-DD[THH:MM[:SS]] . You can also
give times like now + count time-units , where the time-units
can be seconds (default), minutes , hours ,
 days , or weeks and you can tell Slurm to run
the job today with the keyword today and to run the
job tomorrow with the keyword tomorrow .
The value may be changed after job submission using the
 scontrol command.
For example:
 
 
 --begin=16:00
 --begin=now+1hour
 --begin=now+60 (seconds by default)
 --begin=2010-01-20T12:34:00
 

 
 
 

Notes on date/time specifications:
  - Although the 'seconds' field of the HH:MM:SS time specification is
allowed by the code, note that the poll time of the Slurm scheduler
is not precise enough to guarantee dispatch of the job on the exact
second. The job will be eligible to start on the next poll
following the specified time. The exact poll interval depends on the
Slurm scheduler (e.g., 60 seconds with the default sched/builtin).
  - If no time (HH:MM:SS) is specified, the default is (00:00:00).
  - If a date is specified without a year (e.g., MM/DD) then the current
year is assumed, unless the combination of MM/DD and HH:MM:SS has
already passed for that year, in which case the next year is used.
 

 
 
 -D , --chdir =< directory > Set the working directory of the batch script to directory before
it is executed. The path can be specified as full path or relative path
to the directory where the command is executed.
 
 
 --cluster-constraint =[!]< list > Specifies features that a federated cluster must have to have a sibling job
submitted to it. Slurm will attempt to submit a sibling job to a cluster if it
has at least one of the specified features. If the "!" option is included, Slurm
will attempt to submit a sibling job to a cluster that has none of the specified
features.
 
 
 -M , --clusters =< string > Clusters to issue commands to. Multiple cluster names may be comma separated.
The job will be submitted to the one cluster providing the earliest expected
job initiation time. The default value is the current cluster. A value of
' all ' will query to run on all clusters. Note the
 --export option to control environment variables exported
between clusters.
Note that the slurmdbd must be up for this option to work properly, unless
running in a federation with FederationParameters=fed_display configured.
 
 
 --comment =< string > An arbitrary comment enclosed in double quotes if using spaces or some
special characters.
 
 
 --consolidate-segments Ensure that all segments from the allocation will be consolidated
into one higher-level aggregated block.
 
This option applies to job allocations.
 NOTE : This option will only work with the topology/block plugin.
 
 
 -C , --constraint =< list > Nodes can have features assigned to them by the Slurm administrator.
Users can specify which of these features are required by their job
using the constraint option. If you are looking for 'soft' constraints please
see --prefer for more information.
Only nodes having features matching the job constraints will be used to
satisfy the request.
Multiple constraints may be specified with AND, OR, matching OR,
resource counts, etc. (some operators are not supported on all system types).
 
 NOTE : Changeable features are features defined by a NodeFeatures plugin.
 
Supported --constraint options include:
 

 
 
 Single Name Only nodes which have the specified feature will be used.
For example, --constraint="intel" 
 
 
 Node Count A request can specify the number of nodes needed with some feature
by appending an asterisk and count after the feature name.
For example, --nodes=16 --constraint="graphics*4" 
indicates that the job requires 16 nodes and that at least four of those
nodes must have the feature "graphics."
If requesting more than one feature and using node counts, the request
must have square brackets surrounding it.
 
 NOTE : This option is not supported by the helpers NodeFeatures plugin.
Heterogeneous jobs can be used instead.
 
 
 AND Only nodes with all of specified features will be used.
The ampersand is used for an AND operator.
For example, --constraint="intel&gpu" 
 
 
 OR Only nodes with at least one of specified features will be used.
The vertical bar is used for an OR operator. If changeable features are not
requested, nodes in the allocation can have different features. For example,
 salloc -N2 --constraint="intel|amd" can result in a job allocation
where one node has the intel feature and the other node has the amd feature.
However, if the expression contains a changeable feature, then all OR operators
are automatically treated as Matching OR so that all nodes in the job
allocation have the same set of features. For example,
 salloc -N2 --constraint="foo|bar&baz" 
The job is allocated two nodes where both nodes have foo, or bar and baz (one
or both nodes could have foo, bar, and baz). The helpers NodeFeatures plugin
will find the first set of node features that matches all nodes in the job
allocation; these features are set as active features on the node and passed to
RebootProgram (see slurm.conf (5)) and the helper script (see
 helpers.conf (5)). In this case, the helpers plugin uses the first of
"foo" or "bar,baz" that match the two nodes in the job allocation.
 
 
 Matching OR If only one of a set of possible options should be used for all allocated
nodes, then use the OR operator and enclose the options within square brackets.
For example, --constraint="[rack1|rack2|rack3|rack4]" might
be used to specify that all nodes must be allocated on a single rack of
the cluster, but any of those four racks can be used.
 
 
 Multiple Counts Specific counts of multiple resources may be specified by using the AND
operator and enclosing the options within square brackets.
For example, --constraint="[rack1*2&rack2*4]" might
be used to specify that two nodes must be allocated from nodes with the feature
of "rack1" and four nodes must be allocated from nodes with the feature
"rack2".
 
 NOTE : This option is not supported by the helpers NodeFeatures plugin.
 
 NOTE : Multiple Counts can cause jobs to be allocated with a non-optimal
network layout.
 
 
 Brackets Brackets can be used to indicate that you are looking for a set of nodes with
the different requirements contained within the brackets. For example,
 --constraint="[(rack1|rack2)*1&(rack3)*2]" will get you one node with
either the "rack1" or "rack2" features and two nodes with the "rack3" feature.
If requesting more than one feature and using node counts, the request
must have square brackets surrounding it.
 
 NOTE : Brackets are only reserved for Multiple Counts and
 Matching OR syntax.
AND operators require a count for each feature inside square brackets
(i.e. "[quad*2&hemi*1]"). Slurm will only allow a single set of bracketed
constraints per job.
 
 NOTE : Square brackets are not supported by the helpers NodeFeatures
plugin. Matching OR can be requested without square brackets by using the
vertical bar character with at least one changeable feature.
 
 
 Parentheses Parentheses can be used to group like node features together. For example,
 --constraint="[(knl&snc4&flat)*4&haswell*1]" might be used to specify
that four nodes with the features "knl", "snc4" and "flat" plus one node with
the feature "haswell" are required.
Parentheses can also be used to group operations. Without parentheses, node
features are parsed strictly from left to right.
For example,
 --constraint="foo&bar|baz" requests nodes with foo and bar, or baz.
 --constraint="foo|bar&baz" requests nodes with foo and baz, or bar and
baz (note how baz was AND'd with everything).
 --constraint="foo&(bar|baz)" requests nodes with foo and at least
one of bar or baz.
 NOTE : OR within parentheses should not be used with a KNL
NodeFeatures plugin but is supported by the helpers NodeFeatures plugin.
 
 

 
 
 --container =< path_to_container > Absolute path to OCI container bundle.
 
 
 --container-id =< container_id > Unique name for OCI container.
 
 
 --contiguous If set, then the allocated nodes must form a contiguous set.
 
 NOTE : This option will only work with the topology/flat plugin.
Other topology plugins modify the node ordering and prevent this option from
taking effect.
 
 
 -S , --core-spec =< num > Count of Specialized Cores per node reserved by the job for system operations
and not used by the application.
If AllowSpecResourcesUsage is enabled a job can override the CoreSpecCount of
all its allocated nodes with this option.
The overridden Specialized Cores will still be reserved for system processes.
The job will get an implicit --exclusive allocation for the rest of
the Cores on the nodes, resulting in the job's processes being able to use (and
being charged for) all the Cores on the nodes except for the overridden
Specialized Cores.
This option can not be used with the --thread-spec option.
 
 NOTE : Explicitly setting a job's specialized core value implicitly sets
the --exclusive option.
 
 
 --cores-per-socket =< cores > Restrict node selection to nodes with at least the specified number of
cores per socket. See additional information under -B option
above when task/affinity plugin is enabled.
 

 NOTE : This option may implicitly set the number of tasks (if -n 
was not specified) as one task per requested thread.
 
 
 --cpu-freq =< p1 >[- p2 ][: p3 ] 
Request that job steps initiated by srun commands inside this sbatch script
be run at some requested frequency if possible, on the CPUs selected
for the step on the compute node(s).
 
 p1 can be [#### | low | medium | high | highm1] which will set the
frequency scaling_speed to the corresponding value, and set the frequency
scaling_governor to UserSpace. See below for definition of the values.
 
 p1 can be [Conservative | OnDemand | Performance | PowerSave] which
will set the scaling_governor to the corresponding value. The governor has to be
in the list set by the slurm.conf option CpuFreqGovernors.
 
When p2 is present, p1 will be the minimum scaling frequency and
 p2 will be the maximum scaling frequency. In that case the governor
 p3 or CpuFreqDef cannot be UserSpace since it doesn't support a range.
 
 p2 can be [#### | medium | high | highm1]. p2 must be greater than p1 and
is incompatible with UserSpace governor.
 
 p3 can be [Conservative | OnDemand | Performance | PowerSave | SchedUtil |
UserSpace]
which will set the governor to the corresponding value.
 
If p3 is UserSpace, the frequency scaling_speed, scaling_max_freq and
scaling_min_freq will be statically set to the value defined by p1 .
 
Any requested frequency below the minimum available frequency will be rounded
to the minimum available frequency. In the same way, any requested frequency
above the maximum available frequency will be rounded to the maximum available
frequency.
 
The CpuFreqDef parameter in slurm.conf will be used to set the governor
in absence of p3 . If there's no CpuFreqDef , the default governor
will be to use the system current governor set in each cpu. Specifying a
range without CpuFreqDef or a specific governor is therefore not allowed.
 
Acceptable values at present include:
 
 
 
 #### frequency in kilohertz
 
 
 Low the lowest available frequency
 
 
 High the highest available frequency
 
 
 HighM1 (high minus one) will select the next highest available frequency
 
 
 Medium attempts to set a frequency in the middle of the available range

results.prompt: Explain Slurm exit code and derived exit code fields from accounting
results.agent_response:
Summary — what the two fields mean
- ExitCode: the raw exit status Slurm recorded for that job (or job step). Format is "exit:signal" where:
  - the left number is the process exit code (0–255, shown unsigned),
  - the right number is the terminating signal number (0 when none).
  Examples: "0:0" = normal success; "1:0" = process returned exit 1; "0:9" or "?:9" indicates the process was killed by SIGKILL (signal 9) and no normal exit value.
- DerivedExitCode: an aggregate/Slurm-derived value stored in the job record in the database. It is initialized by Slurm to the highest exit code observed across the job’s steps (the srun-invoked tasks) and is intended to reflect the overall job outcome after considering all steps.

How they are produced and used
- For sbatch jobs: ExitCode is the return value of the batch script when it terminates.
- For srun steps: each step’s exit code is saved to the step record; ExitCode on the job-level may reflect the batch script; DerivedExitCode aggregates across steps.
- For salloc: ExitCode is the return value that ends the salloc session.
- Any non-zero ExitCode (that Slurm records as non-zero) is treated as a failure and typically produces job state FAILED with pending/termination reason "NonZeroExitCode".
- Exit codes are 8-bit unsigned values (0–255). Negative returns are displayed as the unsigned equivalent.

Why have both fields
- ExitCode shows what the top-level process returned (or the step’s own return).
- DerivedExitCode captures Slurm’s view of the worst/most relevant step result (useful when the batch script returns 0 but an inner srun step failed), and can be used by admins/users to record a corrective/annotated outcome.

Viewing and adjusting
- sacct and scontrol show ExitCode; sacct can show DerivedExitCode via --format= (DerivedExitCode is available as a field).
- sjobexitmod can list and (if needed) modify the DerivedExitCode and the job comment string (useful to annotate a job after inspecting logs/output).

Practical troubleshooting tips
- If sacct shows ExitCode 0 but DerivedExitCode non-zero (or step records show non-zero), inspect the per-step records (sacct with step entries or scontrol show step) and the job stdout/stderr to find which srun command failed.
- If a job is marked FAILED with reason NonZeroExitCode, use the ExitCode and step records to determine whether the failure was a program exit or a signal (kill/oom).
- Use sjobexitmod only when you need to correct/annotate the derived fields in the DB (requires privileges).

If you want, I can show the exact sacct/scontrol fields and example sacct commands to inspect ExitCode and DerivedExitCode.

Snippet:
## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacct.html)
Executing sacct sends a remote procedure call to slurmdbd . If
enough calls from sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmdbd daemon come in at once, it can result in a
degradation of performance of the slurmdbd daemon, possibly resulting in a
denial of service.
Do not run sacct or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmdbd from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sacct to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm exit code and derived exit code fields from accounting
results.agent_response:
Short summary (what each field is and how to read it)

- ExitCode
  - The ExitCode field is the exit status captured for the job (or job step) and is shown in the form exit:signal (for example the docs show 0:0). The left value is the 8‑bit exit/return code, the right value is a terminating signal number when a signal caused termination.
  - Which value is captured:
    - sbatch: the return code of the batch script.
    - srun: the return code of the command run by srun (each step records its own ExitCode).
    - salloc: the return value that terminates the salloc session.
  - Semantics:
    - Exit codes are treated as unsigned 8‑bit (0–255); negative returns are displayed as their unsigned representation.
    - Any non‑zero exit code is treated as a failure and will produce a job state FAILED with reason NonZeroExitCode (unless another failure condition overrides it).

- DerivedExitCode (and the job comment)
  - The DerivedExitCode is a derived/DB field stored with the job record (and an associated comment string). It is initially set by Slurm to the highest exit code returned by the job’s steps (so it reflects step-level failures even when the top-level script returns 0).
  - The DerivedExitCode is maintained by the controller and written to the accounting DB when AccountingStorage is enabled.
  - Administrators can inspect and change the DerivedExitCode and comment with sjobexitmod (the docs show usage and examples where a job’s DerivedExitCode becomes 49:0 with a comment like "out of memory").
  - sacct can display both ExitCode and DerivedExitCode via --format.

Why both exist (practical note)
- ExitCode shows what a specific job entry or step returned; DerivedExitCode gives a concise, DB-level summary of the worst step failure for the whole job (useful when a batch script exits 0 but one of several srun steps failed). The comment field can carry a human explanation that admins or users add.

References (documented behavior)
- Slurm job exit code docs (job_exit_code) describe the exit:signal format, 8‑bit range, step exit capture, DerivedExitCode initialization, and sjobexitmod for modification.
- sacct supports showing ExitCode and DerivedExitCode in accounting output.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm exit code and derived exit code fields from accounting
results.agent_response:
Summary — what each field means
- ExitCode: the raw exit/status information captured for that job or job step. Format is exit:signal where
  - exit = an 8-bit unsigned exit status (0–255) returned by the process (for sbatch the batch script, for srun the executed command),
  - signal = the signal number that caused termination (0 if none).
  Example displays: 0:0 (clean exit), 42:0 (process returned 42), 0:9 (terminated by SIGKILL).
- DerivedExitCode: a job-level, Slurm-derived exit value stored/sent to the accounting DB. It is Slurm’s interpretation of the job’s overall result (initially computed from the job’s steps) and can be edited by an admin with sjobexitmod. It uses the same exit:signal format.

How DerivedExitCode is computed / why it exists
- For multi-step jobs (many srun calls), each step has its own ExitCode. Slurm initializes the job’s DerivedExitCode to reflect the “worst” observed result among the steps — effectively the highest non-zero exit code seen (and the signal if a step was signaled).
- The DerivedExitCode + the optional comment string let Slurm and admins record a single, corrected or annotated job-level outcome (useful when the batch script returns 0 even though a central task failed, or when you want to mark a job as out-of-memory).

Important behaviors and notes
- Non-zero exit status: any non-zero exit portion will be treated as a failure. Slurm will normally record the job State as FAILED with Reason=NonZeroExitCode when applicable.
- Signals: when termination was due to a signal, the signal number is shown after the colon. Example: 0:9 usually means the task was killed by SIGKILL (OOM-kill or administrator/controller kill).
- 8-bit wrap: exit codes are recorded as unsigned 0–255. Negative returns appear as unsigned values in that range.
- DerivedExitCode can be modified by an administrator with sjobexitmod (and the change is reflected in the DB); this is how operators can add a human-readable comment (e.g., "out of memory") and set a different derived code.

How to inspect and adjust them
- View step/job raw details:
  - scontrol show job <jobid> — shows job/step exit codes (scontrol output uses the same exit:signal format).
  - sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode,Comment — shows accounting ExitCode and DerivedExitCode columns.
  - sacct shows step-level ExitCode entries as well (e.g., 12345.batch, 12345.0).
- Edit/annotate derived values:
  - sjobexitmod -l <jobid> — list current DerivedExitCode/comment.
  - sjobexitmod -e <code> -r "<comment>" <jobid> — set DerivedExitCode and comment (admin only).

Examples
- Clean run: ExitCode=0:0, DerivedExitCode=0:0
- Process returned non‑zero: ExitCode=42:0, DerivedExitCode likely 42:0
- Killed by SIGKILL: ExitCode=0:9, DerivedExitCode may be 0:9 (or admin-updated to a different code/comment)
- Script returned 0 but a step failed: DerivedExitCode may be set to the highest failing step (or later adjusted by sjobexitmod).

Practical tips
- When diagnosing why a job shows COMPLETED but actually failed inner work, check both step-level ExitCode rows in sacct and the DerivedExitCode/comment — admins may have updated DerivedExitCode to reflect a detected failure.
- Use the DerivedExitCode field in reports if you want the administrator-corrected job outcome rather than the raw script exit.
- To include these fields in scripts or reports: sacct --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode,Comment.

If you want, I can show the exact sacct/scontrol/sjobexitmod command examples you should run (or parse a specific job’s ExitCode/DerivedExitCode if you give me a job ID).

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm exit code and derived exit code fields from accounting
results.agent_response:
Summary — what the two fields mean
- ExitCode (accounting field): the exit status recorded for the job (the value Slurm shows for the job or step). It is printed as "exit:signal" (for example 0:0, 1:0, 0:9). The first number is the 8‑bit exit code (0–255); the second number is the signal number if termination was by signal (0 if none).
- DerivedExitCode (accounting field): an additional field Slurm maintains in the job record that reflects Slurm’s computed/aggregated exit status for the job (initially set to the highest non‑zero exit code returned by any of the job’s steps). It has the same "code:signal" format and a free‑text comment string may be attached.

Key details and interpretation
- Format: both fields use "EXIT:SIG". Examples:
  - 0:0 → exited normally with code 0 (success).
  - 1:0 → process exited with status 1.
  - 0:9 → terminated by signal 9 (SIGKILL).
  - 255 → negative return values are shown as unsigned 0–255.
- ExitCode vs DerivedExitCode:
  - ExitCode reflects the recorded exit of the job (for sbatch this is the batch script’s return; for srun it’s the invoked command).
  - DerivedExitCode is computed by Slurm from the job’s steps (highest non‑zero step exit) so it can capture internal step failures even when the top‑level script returned 0.
- Job state implications:
  - Slurm treats a non‑zero exit as a failure (job states and reasons like FAILED / NonZeroExitCode will be set when appropriate).
  - DerivedExitCode is intended to make step failures visible in accounting even if the top‑level exit was zero.
- Admin correction:
  - An administrator can view and edit the derived fields with sjobexitmod (sjobexitmod -l <jobid> to list; -e / -r to set exit/comment). This updates the DB record (used for accounting/visibility).
- Viewing the fields:
  - sacct --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode
  - scontrol show job <jobid> (shows ExitCode in scontrol output)
  - sjobexitmod -l <jobid> (shows/edits derived exit and comment)

Practical notes
- Use DerivedExitCode when you want Slurm’s view of step‑level failures (useful for postmortem/accounting) and compare it with ExitCode to find mismatches (e.g., script returned 0 but steps failed).
- For job arrays / heterogeneous jobs, derived code is computed across the relevant steps/tasks (sacct can show per-task step ExitCode lines).
- If you need to correct accounting for a finished job (for example, mark it with an OOM code or add a comment), ask an admin to run sjobexitmod (this changes the DB record).

References
- Slurm job exit codes doc (ExitCode format, signals, derived exit code and sjobexitmod) — see Slurm documentation (sacct, job_exit_code, sjobexitmod).

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm exit code and derived exit code fields from accounting
results.agent_response:
Short answer first
- ExitCode and DerivedExitCode are accounting fields stored for a job (and job steps). Both use the same two-part format ee:ss where ee is the process exit status (what the process returned) and ss is the terminating signal number (0 if none). Example: 0:0 means exited normally with status 0; 1:0 means exited with status 1; 0:9 means it was killed by signal 9 (SIGKILL).

What ExitCode means
- ExitCode = ee:ss for the job/step that Slurm recorded (typically the batch script or the top-level step).  
  - ee > 0 and ss = 0 → the process exited normally with status ee.  
  - ee = 0 and ss > 0 → the process was terminated by signal ss.  
  - Both zero → normal success (0:0).
- If you inspect a process’ shell-style exit status (the value in $?), remember shells report signal-terminated processes as 128 + signal. Example: Slurm shows 0:9 (killed by SIGKILL); the shell $? would be 137 (128 + 9).

What DerivedExitCode is
- DerivedExitCode is a Slurm-determined field (same ee:ss format) that represents Slurm’s “overall” exit decision for the job. It is initially set from the highest exit code observed among the job’s steps, but slurmctld may modify it to reflect other cluster-detected conditions (prologue/epilogue failures, resource limit enforcement, OOM/job preemption, etc.).
- The job record also has a comment string which Slurm can fill with a short explanation (e.g., “out of memory”, “preempted by ...”). DerivedExitCode + comment together are the canonical way Slurm tells you why a job was considered failed even if the job script returned 0.

Common cases and what you’ll see
- Normal success: ExitCode = 0:0, DerivedExitCode = 0:0, State = COMPLETED.
- Script returned non‑zero: ExitCode = N:0, DerivedExitCode usually N:0, State = FAILED (or COMPLETED depending on script and exit handling).
- Killed by signal (SIGKILL/9): ExitCode = 0:9. Shell-style $? = 137. DerivedExitCode will normally reflect the signal (0:9) or may be adjusted.
- Step-level failure but script returned 0: ExitCode might be 0:0 while DerivedExitCode is nonzero (reflects the failed step). Check the comment to learn why Slurm overrode the plain ExitCode.
- Resource enforcement (time limit, memory): Slurm can set DerivedExitCode and comment to indicate TIME_LIMIT or OOM-related termination.

How to inspect these fields
- sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,DerivedExitCode,Comment
- scontrol show job <jobid>   (shows ExitCode and DerivedExitCode among other fields)
- sjobexitmod -l <jobid>     (view the derived fields) — sjobexitmod can also be used by admins to change the DerivedExitCode/comment.

Notes and tips
- For array/heterogeneous jobs look at step/component records: sacct will show component rows (jobid+offset) so you can find which step returned a nonzero exit. DerivedExitCode is computed across steps/components.
- Don’t assume ExitCode alone tells the whole story — when DerivedExitCode ≠ ExitCode, read the comment and per-step sacct rows to find the real cause.
- If you want a single numeric “shell-style” status for a signal termination, compute 128 + signal (e.g., SIGKILL → 137).

If you’d like, I can show sample sacct/scontrol output examples and walk through interpreting a few real job records.

Slurm accounting is mainly focused on parallel computing. For this reason it
gathers statistics at a "task level". A task is a set of user processes which
run in a step, which is part of a job. A user can submit a step with many
parallel tasks, e.g. by calling `srun -n`.
The [JobAcctGather](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) plugin
gathers metrics for some [Trackable Resources (TRES)](https://slurm.schedmd.com/tres.html),
like cpu, memory, energy, etc., at a given interval in the [JobAcctGatherFrequency](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
defined in slurm.conf, or by using the `--acct-freq` option in the
command line. A poll of data is also triggered at the start or the end of a
step.

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm pending reason Priority
results.agent_response:
"Priority" as a pending reason means the scheduler attempted to place the job but chose other jobs with higher computed priority first. In other words, there are eligible resources, but other jobs have higher priority so your job has not been selected yet.

Key points
- Job priority is a single integer (0 .. 4294967295) computed by the configured priority plugin (by default the multifactor priority plugin).
- With the multifactor plugin the priority is a weighted sum of several normalized factors, for example:
  Job_priority = site_factor + WeightAge * age_factor + WeightAssoc * assoc_factor + WeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + WeightJobSize * job_size_factor + WeightPartition * partition_factor + WeightQOS * qos_factor + SUM(TRES_weights * TRES_factors) - nice_factor
  Each factor is 0.0–1.0 and the weights come from slurm.conf (PriorityWeight* settings).
- Common factors that raise or lower priority: job age, user/account fairshare, association/account priority, job size, partition priority, QOS, requested TRES (CPUs/GPUs), and "nice".
- Only one reason is shown for a pending job: the scheduling attempt that the scheduler used found "Priority" to be the blocking reason. Other constraints (resources, licensing, reservations) might also apply but are not shown if priority was the encountered reason.

How to diagnose
- See why a specific job shows Priority: squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %R" (look at the REASON column).
- Inspect the job’s priority value and metadata: scontrol show job <jobid> (shows Priority, SubmitTime, EligibleTime, etc.).
- View factor breakdown and relative priorities: sprio -l (or sprio -j <jobid>) to see fairshare/age/QOS contributions and the computed priority.
- Check configured weights and behavior: scontrol show config (look for PriorityType and PriorityWeight* settings) or read the multifactor priority docs.

What you can do
- For users: changing job parameters that affect factors (different QOS, smaller job size, lower resource requests, or waiting for age to increase) may improve priority.
- For admins: adjust PriorityType or PriorityWeight* settings, QOS/association priorities, or fairshare settings to change scheduling behavior.

If you want, give me a job ID and I’ll inspect that job (I’ll call squeue/scontrol/sprio to show why it’s pending).

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm pending reason Priority
results.agent_response:
"Priority" as a Slurm pending reason means: the scheduler attempted to place the job but chose other jobs first because they have higher scheduling priority. It does not by itself mean a resource limit, dependency, or begin time — it means the job lost the scheduling comparison to one or more other jobs.

What it implies
- Your job is eligible to run (no unmet dependency, begin time, or explicit account/limit block was detected for the scheduling attempt), but other jobs ranked higher and consumed the available scheduling opportunity.
- The scheduler ranks jobs by a numeric priority; higher numeric priority => scheduled earlier.

How Slurm computes that numeric priority
- By default Slurm uses the Multifactor Priority plugin. Job_priority is a weighted sum of factors such as:
  - age (how long the job has waited)
  - association/account priority
  - fairshare (historical usage)
  - job size
  - partition priority
  - QOS priority
  - TRES factors (CPU/GPU weights)
  - site/nice factors
- Each factor is normalized and multiplied by configured weights (see PriorityWeight* settings). The final priority is an integer (0 .. 4294967295); larger is better.

What to check when you see "Priority"
- Inspect the job's numeric priority and the queue ordering:
  - sprio — shows computed priority factors (per-job priority and contributing factors).
  - squeue (include PRIORITY and REASON columns) — shows which jobs are ahead of yours.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> — shows the job's Priority= value and other properties (QOS, account, nice, TRES).
- Check fairshare and effective shares:
  - sshare — to see account/user fairshare usage that may lower/increase priority.
- Check QOS and partition weights:
  - QOS or partition settings may give other jobs elevated priority (or your job lower priority).
- If preemption or backfill is in use, high-priority jobs may preempt or block lower-priority jobs from starting.

Common causes
- Many recent/high-weight jobs were submitted with higher QOS/account priority.
- Your account has low fairshare (used up entitlement), so fairshare factor reduces your priority.
- Partition or association priorities favor other users or partitions.
- Your job is large (job_size factor) and the scheduler is preferring many smaller/higher-priority jobs first (configurable by weights).

If you want help diagnosing a specific job, tell me the job ID and I can show the priority value and the jobs currently ahead of it (I'll run the appropriate Slurm reads).

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm pending reason Priority
results.agent_response:
"Priority" as a Slurm pending reason means: the scheduler considered the job but did not start it because there are one or more other jobs that currently have higher computed priority for the partition/targets the job requests. In short: your job is eligible to run but is behind higher-priority work.

What affects that decision
- Slurm uses a priority plugin (default: priority/multifactor) to compute a numeric job priority. Higher numeric priority = scheduled earlier.
- The multifactor priority is a weighted sum of factors such as:
  - age (how long the job has been waiting)
  - association/account factors (limits, association weight)
  - fairshare (historical usage)
  - job size (smaller jobs sometimes get preference)
  - partition factor
  - QOS factor
  - TRES/resource factors (CPU/GPU weights)
  - nice factor (user-specified de-prioritization)
  - site factor and configured weights in slurm.conf
- Priority numbers are large unsigned integers (0 .. 2^32−1); the scheduler compares those to order the queue.

How to confirm why a particular job shows "Priority"
- See the queue and reason column: squeue (includes the REASON column).
- Inspect the job’s computed priority and other details:
  - sprio (shows per-job priority components and final numeric priority)
  - scontrol show job <jobid> (shows Priority and other job fields)
- Look at scheduler configuration and weights:
  - scontrol show config (check PriorityType, PriorityWeight* settings, PriorityDecayHalfLife, etc.)
  - sprio --weights (shows configured weights) or check priority_multifactor docs
- Check fairshare / usage that influence priority:
  - sshare (fairshare usage per user/account)

What you can do (non-destructive options)
- Wait—age increases job priority automatically.
- Change job request to a less-contended partition or fewer resources (may increase relative priority).
- Request or change a QOS with higher priority (if allowed by admins).
- Reduce job size so it may be favored by job_size_factor or backfill windows.
- If you are an admin, you can tweak slurm.conf priority weights or directly set job priority (scontrol update JobId=... Priority=...), or change QOS/association limits — these are cluster-changing actions and require admin tools.

Notes/tips
- "Priority" differs from reasons like AssocGrp/AssocMax (account/limit problems), BeginTime, Dependency, or Resources — those indicate different blockers. If squeue shows Priority as the sole reason, the job is waiting behind higher-priority jobs rather than being blocked by limits or missing resources.
- Use sprio to see which jobs currently outrank yours and which factors (fairshare, age, QOS, etc.) dominate.

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can show the specific priority value and the jobs ahead (I’ll run squeue/scontrol/sprio for that job).

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm pending reason Priority
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- The pending reason "Priority" means the scheduler attempted to place the job but did not find a placement because other jobs with higher computed priority took the available resources. In other words: your job is eligible to run but is ranked below others by Slurm’s priority system, so it waits.

What determines that priority
- Slurm’s default multifactor priority plugin computes a single numeric priority from a weighted sum of factors (site, age, association, fairshare, job size, partition, QOS, TRES factors, minus nice). See the formula in the Multifactor Priority docs.
- Priorities are integers (0 .. 4294967295). Larger = higher scheduling precedence.
- Common factors: age (older jobs gain priority), association/account priority, fairshare (historical usage), QOS and partition priority, job size (smaller/larger can be advantaged depending on config), per-account limits, and any per-user/account “priority” settings.

When Priority appears vs other reasons
- Only one reason is shown for a pending job. "Priority" is shown when the scheduler’s placement attempt fails because higher-priority jobs occupy the resources needed.
- If resources are simply not present (no free nodes), other reasons such as Resources, NodeDown, PartitionDown, or Coscheduling may appear instead.
- A job can show Priority even if resources are available overall: higher-priority jobs are first in the scheduling order and claim the available slots.

How to inspect why a job is showing Priority
- squeue (shows REASON column): check the job’s REASON.
- scontrol show job <jobid> (shows numeric Priority= value and other job fields).
- sprio (or sprio -l / sprio --weights) to see each job’s computed priority and factor contributions/weights.
- squeue + sprio will let you see the competing jobs, their priorities, and which factor(s) are giving them advantage.

Commands you can run (examples)
- squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.R"     (show job ID, partition, name, user, state, time, REASON)
- scontrol show job <jobid>
- sprio            (or sprio -l) to list job priorities and contributing factors
- sprio --weights  (show configured factor weights)

Ways to get a job to run sooner (user-level options)
- Increase job priority indirectly: request a higher-QOS (if available) or a QOS with higher priority value.
- Use sbatch --nice to lower the job’s nice value (if your cluster allows it), or ask your admin to adjust association/account priority or QOS.
- Submit smaller jobs or change resource request to better fit available nodes (job size factor can matter).
- Wait: age factor increases over time, raising priority.

Admin-level controls (require admin)
- Adjust priority weights in slurm.conf (PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, etc.) and reconfigure.
- Change association/account priority or QOS settings via sacctmgr.
- Inspect scheduler logs or use sprio_weights / scontrol show config for configured behavior.

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can walk through the exact priority values and competing jobs (I’ll show the squeue/scontrol/sprio outputs and interpret them).

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm pending reason Resources
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- The Slurm pending reason Resources means: the scheduler could not find the required free/eligible resources to place the job right now. That includes CPUs, memory, GPUs (GRES), consumable resources (licenses, devices), or hierarchical resources (HRES) defined in resources.yaml.

What it covers (common causes)
- No idle nodes with enough CPUs/memory to satisfy the job's ReqCPUs/ReqMem/ntasks.
- All matching GPU nodes (GRES) are already allocated or drained.
- The job requests a specific node feature/constraint (–C/--constraint) that no idle node satisfies.
- Consumable resources (licenses, specific hardware devices) are exhausted.
- Hierarchical resources (HRES) layers are insufficient where configured.
- Per-account / QOS / association limits have been reached (so resources are effectively unavailable).
- Nodes are down/drained or a reservation is consuming the needed capacity.

How to diagnose (commands to run)
- squeue -j <jobid> (or squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R") — confirm the job’s pending reason is Resources.
- scontrol show job <jobid> — inspect requested TRES, ReqMem, partition, constraint, and other job fields.
- sinfo -Nel (or sinfo -o ...) — see partition/node counts and which nodes are idle vs allocated/drain/down.
- scontrol show node <nodename> — check AllocTRES, Available features and per-node resource counts.
- scontrol_license — check consumable license resources if licenses are used as GRES.
- sinfo -R — show nodes in drain/down states and reasons (if nodes are offline by reason).
- sshare / sacctmgr list (or ask admins) — verify account/QOS limits or associations if you suspect quotas.

How to fix or mitigate
- Reduce resource requests (fewer tasks, lower CPUs, less memory or fewer GPUs) so the scheduler can match smaller packing.
- Remove/relax node constraints (–C/--constraint) or try a different partition.
- Wait until nodes free up, or schedule during lower load.
- If consumable resources/licenses are exhausted, free up holders or request more from admin.
- Ask admins to investigate down/drained nodes or reservations that are consuming capacity.
- If HRES is in use, check resources.yaml and ensure required HRES layers have capacity or change job’s HRES request.
- Consider smaller job walltime so backfill can start it sooner, or enable preemption/QOS options if available.

Notes and gotchas
- "Resources" is a generic scheduler-level reason — it does not by itself say which resource is missing. Use scontrol show job and scontrol show node to find the specific mismatch.
- If a job requests GRES (GPUs), only nodes reported as idle in sinfo count as available for a conditional GPU submit. Allocated/drained/down/mixed nodes do not count as free.
- If you want, give me a job ID and I can run the minimal checks (squeue and scontrol show job) and summarize exactly what resource is lacking.

# Job Reason Codes
These reason codes can be used to identify why a pending job has not yet been
started by the scheduler. There may be multiple reasons why a job cannot start,
in which case only the reason that was encountered by the attempted scheduling
method will be displayed. Refer to the [Scheduling Configuration Guide](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html) for more details.

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm pending reason Resources
results.agent_response:
"Resources" as a Slurm pending reason means: the scheduler could not find any placement that satisfies the job's requested resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs or other TRES/resources, per-node constraints, node features, or hierarchical resources). In short — there are no nodes currently available that meet the job's resource requirements.

What it covers (common causes)
- Requested TRES unavailable: e.g., requested GPUs or a specific gres, but no nodes have that free.
- Per-node or per-job sizing: the job asks for more CPUs, memory, or whole nodes than any eligible node has free.
- Node properties/features mismatch: the job requested a node feature (-C, --constraint) that no idle node has.
- Hierarchical resources (HRES): resources.yaml/HRES constraints block allocation.
- All eligible nodes are allocated, drained, down, or reserved by higher-priority or reservation jobs.
- Fragmentation: enough total resources exist but not co-located on nodes in the shape your job needs (e.g., many single-GPU nodes but the job needs 4 GPUs on one node).
Note: Slurm shows only the first reason encountered; other limiting factors may also exist.

How to diagnose
- See the REASON column in the queue for the job:
  - squeue -j <jobid> -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.6D %R"
- Inspect the job request details:
  - scontrol show job <jobid>
    (check ReqNodes, TRESPerNode/ReqTRES, Constraint, Gres, etc.)
- Check node/partition availability and states:
  - sinfo -Nel     (one-line-per-node view: states and resources)
  - sinfo -p <partition>   (partition summary)
  - sinfo -R     (nodes in down/drain with reasons)
- For GPU/gres checks, list nodes with GPUs and their free/alloc state (sinfo -Nel or sinfo -o) or ask admin for node/GPU report.
- If HRES is used, review resources.yaml and HRES usage (admin).

Typical remedies
- Reduce the job's resource requests (fewer GPUs/CPUs, lower memory, fewer nodes).
- Remove or relax constraints (-C / --constraint) or change partition.
- Split the job into smaller jobs that fit available nodes.
- If you need GPUs, request GPUs in a way matching the cluster's gres naming (check gres/gpu names).
- Wait for running jobs to finish, or request a reservation from admins.
- If nodes are drained/down for maintenance, contact admins to learn ETA.
- If HRES is unexpectedly blocking, ask admins to verify HRES config/availability.

If you give me a job ID I can run the specific squeue/scontrol/sinfo checks and show which exact resource is missing and which nodes/partitions are eligible.

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm pending reason Resources
results.agent_response:
"Resources" is the generic Slurm pending reason that means the scheduler could not find sufficient free resources to satisfy the job's requested resources during the scheduling attempt.

What "Resources" commonly covers
- Not enough free CPUs/cores, memory, nodes, or GPUs to meet the job's requested cpus/mem/tasks/gres.
- Fragmentation: enough aggregate resources exist but not in a layout that satisfies the job’s placement (eg. job needs 4 whole nodes but free cores are scattered).
- All candidate nodes are allocated, drained, down, or reserved.
- GRES (GPU) mismatch: the job requests a GPU type or count not present on any currently idle nodes.
- Hierarchical resources (HRES) or custom resources configured in resources.yaml are not available for the job.
- Resource/account/QOS limits that effectively prevent allocation (these may appear as other reason codes too, but can surface as Resources for the scheduling method used).
- Higher-priority jobs / reservations have blocked the resources from being used by this job.

Important notes
- Slurm only shows the first reason encountered by the scheduling method — other constraints may also be preventing start.
- "Resources" just says “not found now”; it does not indicate which specific resource is missing. Use the detailed inspection commands below to find the exact cause.

Troubleshooting checklist (commands to run and what to look for)
1. Inspect the pending reason and job details
   - squeue -j <jobid> -o "%.18i %.30j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10L %.10R"
     -> verifies the displayed pending reason and job name/user.
   - scontrol show job <jobid>
     -> shows full job request (NumNodes, CPUs/Task, ReqMem, GRES, Constraints, QOS, Account, etc.).

2. See node/partition availability
   - sinfo -N -l or sinfo -p <partition> -l
     -> shows per-node state (idle/alloc/drain/down) and resources per node.
   - sinfo -R
     -> lists nodes in drain/down with reasons (useful if nodes are offline).

3. Check GRES (GPUs) usage and matching
   - sinfo shows GPUs per node; verify job's --gres matches an idle GPU node type.

4. Check for reservations or higher-priority jobs
   - squeue --reservation or squeue -S+P to view reservation-bound jobs.
   - scontrol show reservation <name> (if you suspect a reservation).

5. Check association / account / QOS limits
   - sacctmgr show assoc where user=<user> or scontrol show config / review QOS limits
     -> verify per-user/account per-job/per-node limits that might deny allocation.

6. Consider fragmentation/placement
   - If your job needs whole nodes or exclusive allocation, reduce tasks-per-node, request fewer nodes, or allow shared nodes (if acceptable).

7. If HRES/custom resources are used
   - Review resources.yaml and the job's resource request; missing HRES entries will block scheduling.

When to change the job
- Reduce requested resources (fewer nodes, GPUs, CPUs or less memory) or relax constraints/feature flags.
- Submit to a different partition that has free nodes.
- Wait for currently running jobs to finish or ask admin about reservations/drains.

If you give me a specific job ID I can show the squeue and scontrol output and point to the exact missing resource and next steps.

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm pending reason Resources
results.agent_response:
"Resources" (the pending reason shown by squeue) means the scheduler could not find sufficient trackable resources to place your job given its request and current cluster state. It is a catch‑all that indicates a resource shortfall encountered during scheduling (CPUs, memory, GPUs/GRES, nodes, licenses, HRES, etc.), not a policy/account or dependency blockage.

What it typically means
- Not enough free CPUs or whole nodes that match the job's cpus/memory/per‑node request.
- No nodes with the requested generic resource (GRES) or GPU type (or all matching GPU nodes are allocated/drained).
- Requested memory per node exceeds what's available on any suitable node.
- Node feature/constraint (--constraint, --gres-flags, --licenses, hierarchical resources) prevents a matching allocation.
- The job requests a combination (e.g., many GPUs + large memory) that no single node or set of nodes can satisfy.
- A reservation or current allocations block placement until a future time.
- HRES (resources.yaml) definitions can also cause "Resources" when their planning rules don’t allow a match.

Important notes
- Slurm reports only the first reason encountered by the scheduler, so "Resources" may mask a more specific underlying cause (e.g., GRES shortage, memory, or a feature mismatch).
- For GPU submissions, only idle GPU nodes count as available — allocated/mixed/drained nodes are not considered free for matching.

How to diagnose (commands to run)
- See the job's reason and queue row:
  squeue -j <JOBID> -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R"
- Show detailed job request and TRES:
  scontrol show job <JOBID>
  (look for ReqCPUS, MinNodes/Nodes, ReqMem, Gres, TRES)
- Inspect partition/node availability:
  sinfo -l                              # partition/node states and resources
  sinfo -N -o "%N %t %C %m %G %f"       # per-node CPUs, memory, GRES, features
- If GPUs involved, check GPU node idle counts (treat idle nodes only as available).
- Check reservations that might block placement:
  scontrol show reservation
- Check scheduler/backfill diagnostics and priorities if timing is unexpected:
  sdiag
  sprio -l
- If you need runtime/resource usage of a running job to guide requests:
  sstat -j <jobid>                       (running jobs only)

Common fixes
- Lower requested resources (fewer cpus, less memory, fewer GPUs) or request nodes differently (per‑node vs per‑task).
- Remove or relax constraints/feature requests (or request a different partition).
- Request a different GPU type or omit a specific gres if not required.
- Split a large job into smaller jobs if no single allocation can satisfy it.
- Submit with a different QOS or account if limits are causing denials (but that often shows different reason codes).
- Wait for resources to free (use sinfo/squeue to estimate when), or ask admins to create a reservation if the job must run at a specific time.
- If you believe a resource is idle but Slurm does not see it, ask admins to check node state (drain, down, maintenance) or HRES configuration.

If you give me a job ID, I can show the exact job request fields and the squeue/scontrol lines you should inspect (I’ll run squeue/scontrol for that job if you want).

results.prompt: Explain the Slurm pending reason Resources
results.agent_response:
"Resources" as a Slurm pending reason means: when the scheduler tried to place the job it could not find nodes that satisfy the job's requested resources and constraints. It is the generic "not enough matching resources right now" reason the scheduler reports for a pending job.

What "Resources" can cover
- Insufficient free CPUs/cores (ReqCPUs, --cpus-per-task, ntasks)
- Insufficient memory (ReqMem, --mem, --mem-per-cpu)
- Requested GPUs or other GRES not available (gres/gpu, gres names)
- Node feature/constraint mismatches ( --constraint, --nodelist, features )
- Exclusive node or per-node packing constraints (--exclusive, sockets/cores required)
- Trackable resources (TRES) limits: cpu, mem, tres/gpu, licenses, burst buffers, etc.
- No nodes matching combined constraints (e.g., GPU + a rare feature)
Note: other specific limit reasons (AssocMax, QOS limits, AccountNotAllowed, Priority, Reservation, BeginTime) will show different reason codes — "Resources" specifically means resource availability/matching failure.

How to investigate (quick commands)
- squeue -j <jobid>   — confirm the job is PENDING and shows "Resources" in the REASON column.
- scontrol show job <jobid>   — look at ReqNodes/NumNodes, NumCPUs/CPUsPerTask, TRES/AllocTRES, Gres, MinMemoryNode, Partition, Constraint, QOS, Account. This shows what the job asked for.
- sinfo -Nel -p <partition>    — see per-node states (allocated/idle/drain/down) and node features/GRES; helps find whether any idle nodes can satisfy the request.
- scontrol show node <node>    — inspect specific node capabilities (memory, CPUs, GPUs, features).
- sprio or sdiag (optional)    — if you suspect priority/packing interactions preventing placement.

Typical diagnostic checklist
- Does the job request GPUs or a specific GPU type? If so, are any idle GPU nodes shown by sinfo? (Only idle nodes count as available.)
- Is the requested memory per node greater than any node provides?
- Are your constraints (--constraint, --nodelist) too restrictive?
- Are nodes in the partition drained/down or reserved by a reservation?
- Are per-account or QOS limits reached? (These usually appear as Assoc*/Max* reasons, but check scontrol show job.)
- Is the job requesting whole-node exclusivity but there are only mixed/shared nodes available?

Remedies
- Reduce resource requests (fewer CPUs, less memory, fewer GPUs).
- Remove or relax constraints or node-list filters.
- Try a different partition or QOS.
- Wait until currently running jobs finish or ask admin about reservations/drains.
- If you expect idle GPUs/nodes but sinfo shows none, contact admins (nodes may be down/drained or reserved).
- For complex resource types (licenses, burst buffers, custom HRES), confirm those resources are defined and free.

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can walk through the exact fields to inspect and suggest specific fixes.

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer first: there is no official job-reason named "QOSMaxJobsPerUser" in the Slurm job-reason list. QOS job-count limits are implemented with QOS attributes (MaxJobs / MaxSubmitJobs / GrpJobs / active_jobs in the REST API, etc.) and when those limits block a job the scheduler reports one of the standard association/limit reason codes (for example AssociationJobLimit, AssocGrp*, AssocMax*, Max*PerAccount). The QOS may also use the DenyOnLimit flag to reject jobs at submission instead of letting them pend.

What the pieces mean and how they map to pending reasons
- QOS limits (where you set them with sacctmgr show/modify qos) can include:
  - MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs (job-count style limits),
  - GrpJobs (group/aggregate job-count),
  - GrpTRES / MaxTRES (aggregate resource caps),
  - other Max* or Grp* limits (per-node, per-account TRES, wall time, nodes, …),
  - Flags such as DenyOnLimit or OverPartQOS.
  (The REST API exposes similar fields such as jobs and active_jobs for a QOS.)
- Enforcement and precedence:
  - Limits are applied in the documented hierarchy (Partition QOS, Job QOS, user association, account association, cluster, partition). A limit defined earlier in the precedence chain wins.
  - If the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, jobs that would exceed a QOS 'Max' limit are denied at submission (rejected) rather than queued.
- How those limits show up as squeue/scontrol reasons:
  - AssociationJobLimit — the job's association has reached its maximum job count (common when a per-user/per-account job-count limit is active).
  - AssocGrp* — an aggregate/group limit (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.) has been reached.
  - AssocMax* / AssocMax…Limit / Max*PerAccount — a requested value exceeds a defined maximum for the association/QOS (the job would violate a Max limit).
  - Max*PerAccount (or Max*PerUser variants shown by some installs) appear when a per-account/per-user maximum (on TRES, jobs, nodes, etc.) is violated.
  - (The job_reason_codes documentation lists all reason-code names and short descriptions — use that to match the reason string you see.)
- Important behavior notes:
  - If a QOS limit only becomes true when considering multiple jobs together (group limits), affected jobs will pend with a group/association reason (not necessarily a QOS-named reason).
  - Only the single reason encountered by the attempted scheduling method is shown; other applicable limits may also exist but are not displayed.

How to diagnose a job pending for a QOS limit
- First look at the queue reason: squeue (the pending Reason column) for the job ID.
- If you need more detail: scontrol show job <JOBID> will show the job's QOS, association, and any limit-related fields the scheduler considered.
- Inspect configured limits:
  - sacctmgr show qos format=... (or sacctmgr show qos) to view the QOS attributes (MaxJobs, GrpJobs, DenyOnLimit, …).
  - sacctmgr show assoc user=<user> (or account=<acct>) to see user/account association limits that may override/augment the QOS.
- If a job was rejected at submission, check sbatch/srun error text and whether the QOS has DenyOnLimit enabled.

If you want, tell me a specific job ID (or show the squeue Reason line) and I can walk through the exact mapping and the sacctmgr/scontrol queries to find which configured limit is blocking it.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

following limits: Max[Time|Wall], [Min|Max]Nodes. For these limits, even
if the job is enforced with...

## Coordinator[#coord](https://slurm.schedmd.com/user_permissions.html)
A special privileged user, usually an account manager, that can add
users or sub-accounts to the account they are coordinator over.
This should be a trusted person since they can change limits on account and
user associations, as well as cancel, requeue or reassign accounts of jobs
inside their realm. Note that a coordinator may not increase job limits above
the parent ones.
Set using a table in Slurm's database defining users and accounts for
which they can serve as coordinators.
For configuration information, see the
[sacctmgr](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) man page.

3. The option specified for the cluster.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## QOS examples[#examples](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available
so it is best to use the format option which filters the display.
By default when a cluster is added to the database a default
qos named normal is created.
```text
$ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0
```

Add a new QOS
```text
$ sacctmgr add qos zebra Adding QOS(s) zebra Settings Description = QOS Name $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 0
```
Set QOS priority
```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos zebra set priority=10 Modified qos... zebra $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 10
```
Set some other limits

$ sacctmgr modify qos z...

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.
