results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- QOS MaxJobsPerUser is a QOS-enforced limit that restricts how many jobs a single user may have under that QOS. When a job would exceed a configured QOS limit the scheduler will either pend the job with a reason that indicates which limit was hit or (if the QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit) reject it at submission.
- The pending reason you see in squeue/sview identifies which specific limit blocked the job (e.g., a per-user job count limit, a per-account TRES limit, submit-count limits, etc.). Use squeue (reason column) and scontrol show job <id> to see the exact reason for a pending job.

What MaxJobsPerUser means (and related QOS limits)
- MaxJobs, MaxJobsPerUser (per-user job counts) — limit the number of jobs allowed. If the QOS sets a MaxJobsPerUser (or the association has an equivalent per-user limit), a new job that would make that user exceed the limit will not be started.
- MaxSubmitJobs — controls how many jobs the association/QOS will allow to be submitted (queued) for a user; exceeding it can block submission or cause pending behavior depending on flags.
- MaxTRES / GrpTRES / MaxTRESPerNode / related TRES limits — resource-count limits (CPUs, GPUs, memory) applied per-QOS or per-association; hitting these yields a TRES-related pending reason.
- MaxWall / MaxTime / Min/MaxNodes — other Max* limits that can cause pending reasons when job requests exceed allowed sizes/time.

How that shows up as pending reasons
- The scheduler maps a violated limit to a reason code shown in squeue (or sview). Examples of the kinds of reason you will see:
  - a per-QOS/per-account/per-user job-count limit (MaxJobs or MaxJobsPerUser) → a MaxJobs-type reason
  - submit-count limits (MaxSubmitJobs) → a MaxSubmitJobs/submit-limit reason
  - TRES (CPU/GPU/mem) limits → MaxTRES* or AssocGrp*/AssocMax* style reasons
  - group/association aggregate limits → AssocGrp* reasons
- Only the single reason encountered by the scheduling method is shown. If multiple limits would block the job, only the first-check reason is displayed.

Important behaviors to know
- Limit precedence: Slurm evaluates limits in a hierarchy (Partition QOS, Job QOS, user association, account associations up the chain, cluster). The first level where a limit is defined is the limit that will apply.
- DenyOnLimit flag: If a QOS has Flags=DenyOnLimit, jobs violating that QOS’s Max limits will be denied at submission rather than queued and pending. If DenyOnLimit is not set, jobs that would exceed the limit will typically pend until resources/quotas free up.
- Group (Grp*) limits: Group or association aggregate limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES) are checked when a job is considered for allocation; if starting a job would exceed a group aggregate, it will be blocked and show the corresponding AssocGrp* reason.
- Relative QOS: In newer Slurm versions a QOS can use Flags=Relative so Max limits are interpreted as percentages of cluster resources — the same reason semantics apply, but the value calculation differs.

How to diagnose a job pending for QOS limits
- squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R" (or use sview) — check the REASON column for the pending job.
- scontrol show job <jobid> — get the job’s QOS, QOS limits in effect, and additional fields.
- sacctmgr show qos format=... or sacctmgr show association / sacctmgr show user — inspect the QOS and association limits (MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, GrpTRES, Flags like DenyOnLimit).
- If you see a MaxJobs/MaxSubmitJobs/TRES-related reason, inspect how many jobs or resources the user/account currently has (squeue, sshare) to determine what’s consuming the quota.

Example troubleshooting steps
1. squeue -j <jobid>  -> note the REASON and the QOS used by the job.
2. scontrol show job <jobid> -> confirm job QOS and requested resources.
3. sacctmgr show qos <qosname> format=name,flags,maxjobs,maxsubmitjobs,max_tres,... -> see configured QOS limits and whether DenyOnLimit is set.
4. squeue -u <user> (and sshare) -> count the user’s running/pending jobs and current usage to compare against limits.

How to change limits (admin)
- Use sacctmgr to modify QOS or association limits (sacctmgr modify qos <name> set MaxJobs=..., set Flags=DenyOnLimit, etc.). Because QOS limits override association limits, be sure you understand the hierarchy before changing values.

References
- Slurm documentation: QOS and Resource Limits pages (explain QOS limits, Flags=DenyOnLimit, and the precedence order) and the Job Reason Codes page (lists the reason strings used by squeue).

If you want, tell me a job ID that is pending for you and I can show the exact squeue reason and the QOS/association limits (I will run squeue and scontrol show job as needed).

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with
job arrays. Once one element of a job array is discovered to not be runnable
or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job
array will be quickly skipped.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been
defined in the slurm.conf file. The QOS will only determine job
preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will
override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

## Coordinator[#coord](https://slurm.schedmd.com/user_permissions.html)
A special privileged user, usually an account manager, that can add
users or sub-accounts to the account they are coordinator over.
This should be a trusted person since they can change limits on account and
user associations, as well as cancel, requeue or reassign accounts of jobs
inside their realm. Note that a coordinator may not increase job limits above
the parent ones.
Set using a table in Slurm's database defining users and accounts for
which they can serve as coordinators.
For configuration information, see the
[sacctmgr](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html) man page.

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Summary
- QOS MaxJobsPerUser is a QOS-level limit that caps how many jobs a single user may have under that QOS. When the limit is hit, additional jobs that would violate it will not be scheduled and will show a pending reason tied to the QOS limit (commonly displayed as QOSMaxJobsPerUser).
- A QOS can either cause jobs to pend when limits are hit, or if the QOS has the DenyOnLimit flag set, new submissions that would violate the limit are rejected at submission time instead of being queued.

What QOSMaxJobsPerUser means (behavior)
- The MaxJobsPerUser value on a QOS restricts the number of jobs a single user can have counted toward that QOS. When a user already has that many jobs, any further job that would exceed the limit becomes ineligible for scheduling.
- The scheduler reports the specific reason (for example, QOSMaxJobsPerUser) so you can identify the limit being enforced.
- QOS limits override the same types of limits set on the user/account association (the QOS limits take precedence).

Related pending/reason codes you will see and how to interpret them
- QOSMaxJobsPerUser — the QOS MaxJobsPerUser limit is preventing the job from being scheduled.
- Max*PerAccount / QOSMax* / AssocMax* / AssocGrp* — groupings of reason codes you may encounter when other association- or account-level limits are hit (these are the family names used in the Slurm job reason list). For example, a “Max…PerAccount” reason means a per-account/QOS maximum was exceeded.
- DenyOnLimit (QOS flag) — not a pending reason itself but changes behavior: when set the job will be rejected at submit time rather than queued and shown with a pending reason.

How to investigate a job stuck for this reason
- See the scheduler’s reported pending reason: squeue (the REASON column will show the code such as QOSMaxJobsPerUser).
- For a single job, get the detailed reason: scontrol show job <jobid>.
- Inspect QOS limits (and DenyOnLimit): sacctmgr show qos (or sacctmgr show qos format=... to list specific fields).
- Inspect association/account limits if the reason indicates an association-level limit: sacctmgr show association or sacctmgr show account.

How to remedy or change behavior
- If the limit is appropriate but you need more capacity for a user, increase MaxJobsPerUser on the QOS: sacctmgr modify qos <qosname> set MaxJobsPerUser=<N>
- If you prefer submissions to be rejected instead of queued when limits are exceeded, enable DenyOnLimit on the QOS: sacctmgr modify qos <qosname> set DenyOnLimit=1
- If the limit should be applied differently, consider changing which QOS the job uses, adjusting association/account limits, or increasing the cluster resources available to that QOS.

Notes and troubleshooting tips
- The REASON reported by squeue is the single reason encountered by the scheduler at the time it tried to schedule the job; multiple limits may apply but only one reason is shown.
- QOS limits take precedence over association limits when both exist for the job.
- Exact command output and field names can vary by Slurm version; use scontrol and sacctmgr on your controller to see the precise configured values.

If you want, I can check the live queue or a specific job’s pending reason (squeue / scontrol show job), or list QOS settings on your cluster (sacctmgr show qos). Which job ID or QOS name should I inspect?

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- A QOS "Max jobs per user" limit (set via the QOS Max* limits in the Slurm DB) constrains how many jobs a single user may have under that QOS/association. When that limit is reached, new jobs that would violate it are either pended by the scheduler or rejected at submission depending on the QOS flags.

What the limit actually does
- MaxJobsPerUser (and related Max* limits) are enforced when the scheduler evaluates whether a job may start or be allowed to exist concurrently. The check is applied against the appropriate scope (QOS first if set there, otherwise the association/partition/cluster limits per the hierarchy).
- If a job would violate the limit:
  - If the QOS has the DenyOnLimit flag set, the job will be denied at submission (sbatch fails).
  - If DenyOnLimit is not set, the job is allowed to be submitted but will pend until the limiting condition clears.

How this appears in squeue (pending reasons)
- The scheduler places a short reason string in the squeue "REASON" (or NODELIST(REASON)) column to indicate why a job is pending. Limit-related reasons follow recognizable patterns:
  - Reasons that mention the association or group (Assoc*, Association*) indicate association-level aggregate limits.
  - Reasons that mention Max*/PerUser or Max*/PerAccount indicate a per-user or per-account maximum was hit.
  - If a QOS limit is the cause you will see a reason that points to a QOS/Max limit (the exact token depends on your Slurm build/version and the specific limit; common patterns are QOSMax* or Max*PerUser/PerAccount or AssocMax*).
- Because squeue shows only the reason the scheduler encountered during its attempt, multiple limits might apply but only the first-matched reason is shown.

How to diagnose which limit was hit
- Look at the job’s REASON in squeue first to see the short code the scheduler returned.
- For a specific job id, run scontrol show job <jobid> to see detailed fields (AllocTRES, associations, QOS used) and sometimes more detail about limits applied.
- Inspect QOS and association limits with sacctmgr:
  - sacctmgr show qos
  - sacctmgr show assoc user=<user> or sacctmgr show assoc account=<account>
These show any MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, MaxTRESPerUser, etc., that might be blocking the job.

Common related limits you may run into
- MaxJobs (per QOS/association/partition) — caps concurrent jobs.
- MaxSubmitJobs — caps how many jobs a user may have submitted (affects new submissions).
- MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPERACCOUNT — caps on TRES (CPUs, GPUs, etc.) per user/account.
- Grp* limits — aggregate limits applied across an association/group that can also cause pending reasons.

Behavioral notes and tips
- Hierarchy: Partition-QOS limits are evaluated before job-QOS/association limits unless you set OverPartQOS. This can lead to a partition-level limit appearing to block jobs even if the job’s QOS appears to allow them.
- If you want jobs to be rejected at submit time rather than queued and pended, enable the QOS DenyOnLimit flag for that QOS.
- To unblock/presume jobs: increase the appropriate Max* limit in the QOS or association, change the job’s QOS (if allowed), or free running jobs that count against the limit.
- Use squeue -o with the REASON field (or scontrol show job) to get the exact text that your cluster will display so you can map it to the specific limit.

Example commands (admin)
- View QOS settings: sacctmgr show qos format=Name,MaxJobs,MaxSubmitJobs,DenyOnLimit
- View associations for a user: sacctmgr show assoc user=<user> with detail
- Change a QOS limit: sacctmgr modify qos <qosname> set MaxJobs=<n>
- Toggle deny: sacctmgr modify qos <qosname> set DenyOnLimit=YES|NO

If you tell me a concrete job ID or paste the REASON text you see in squeue, I can explain exactly which limit type that reason corresponds to and suggest the minimal change to fix it.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit

results.prompt: Explain QOSMaxJobsPerUser and related QOS pending reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- QOSMaxJobsPerUser (commonly configured as the QOS field MaxJobsPerUser) is a per-QOS limit that caps how many jobs a single user may have simultaneously under that QOS. It is enforced by the scheduler when evaluating pending jobs.
- When a job would exceed such a limit the scheduler will either pend the job (and assign a pending reason that identifies the violated limit) or—if the QOS has the DenyOnLimit flag—deny the job at submission.

Details and what to expect
- Purpose: MaxJobsPerUser prevents one user from owning more than N concurrent jobs in that QOS. It is set in the Slurm database (sacctmgr) on the QOS record.
- Enforcement behavior:
  - By default a job that would breach a Max* limit will pend until resources/slots become available.
  - If the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, jobs that would violate the QOS Max limits are rejected at submission instead of pending.
  - Limits are applied using Slurm’s hierarchy (partition QOS limits may be applied before the job’s requested QOS unless OverPartQOS is set). See resource-limits documentation for the full precedence order.
- Pending reasons shown by the scheduler:
  - When the scheduler evaluates a pending job and finds it violates a configured resource/association limit, it assigns a job reason describing the limit that was hit. The job reason page documents families such as AssocMax* (association maximums) and Max*PerAccount (per-account-per-QOS maximums).
  - In practice a job blocked by a per-user-per-QOS limit will show a reason that maps to the exceeded limit (examples in the docs include AssocMax* and Max*PerAccount-style reason codes). If DenyOnLimit is in effect the job is rejected instead of receiving a pending reason.
- How to diagnose a job stuck by a QOS limit:
  - Use squeue (include the Reason/REASON column) to see the scheduler’s short pending reason for active queue entries.
  - If squeue’s output doesn’t give enough detail, run scontrol show job <jobid> to get the detailed evaluation/limit fields.
- How to change the behavior:

results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" is the association/group-level GRES (Generic RESource) limit entry shown in sacctmgr/association listings. It represents limits on GRES usage (for example GPUs) that apply to the association (user/account/cluster/partition association) when Slurm evaluates whether a pending job may be allocated resources.

What association (group) resource limits do
- Association limits are per-association attributes maintained with sacctmgr and tested at job allocation time. Example group limits include GrpJobs, GrpTRES (trackable resources), and GRES-specific limits.
- If starting a job would cause any group limit to be exceeded, that job will not be considered for scheduling (it will remain pending). Group limits are enforced before attempting allocation; a job will not be started simply because it could preempt others to satisfy the limit.
- Limits are hierarchical. When multiple limits exist the precedence is: job QOS/partition QOS ordering rules, then user association, account association(s), cluster/root association, then partition-level limits (the first place a limit is defined is used).

Important GRES-specific behavior and pitfalls
- GRES limits are expressed as TRES entries (e.g. gres/gpu) or in higher-level fields such as GrpTRES. You can set limits addressing a specific GRES type (for example MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1).
- Type-specific limits have a design limitation: if a user requests a generic GRES (for example --gres=gpu:2) a limit set on a specific type (gres/gpu:tesla) will not be enforced. In other words, type-scoped limits do not prevent a user from requesting an untyped generic GRES and receiving two devices of that type unless additional submit-time checking is enforced (for example via a Lua job_submit plugin).
- TRES limit modifications using "+=" or "-=" are supported; attempting to set a negative value will set the TRES to zero. Large numeric bounds are handled up to the internal limit noted in the docs.

Operational effects of changing associations/limits
- Changes made with sacctmgr are uploaded to the controllers and take effect immediately for scheduling decisions.
- Deleting an association will immediately cancel running or pending jobs that belong to that association.
- Lowering a limit does not retroactively kill running jobs to satisfy the new limit; it only affects future allocation decisions.

Where to view and manage them
- Use sacctmgr to list and modify associations and their limits (association records contain fields for GrpTRES/GrpJobs/MaxTRESPerUser and related attributes).
- The Slurm resource_limits documentation describes the precedence, semantics, and example formats; the gres documentation describes GRES configuration and limitations.

If you want, I can:
- show the current association limits on this cluster (sacctmgr list association) or
- show any association fields named AssocGrpGRES if you point me to the exact sacctmgr output you saw.

results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" (or more generally the AssocGrp* family) is a scheduler pending/reason code meaning: the job's association (user/account/partition/cluster association) has hit an aggregate GRES/TRES group limit and so the job cannot be allocated.
- GRES (generic resources, e.g. gres/gpu) are treated as TRES for accounting/limits; association-level group limits on GRES are configured via the GrpTRES (trackable resources) association/account/user/cluster fields (e.g., GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8).

Key points (what this means and how it works)
- What is being limited: association "group" limits are aggregate limits applied to an association (user+account+cluster+optional partition). They cap the total resources in-use by that association (running allocations) — e.g., GrpJobs, GrpTRES (cpu, mem, node, or generic resources like gres/gpu).
- GRES as TRES: GRES types (gpu, mps, etc.) are exposed as TRES names like gres/gpu. To limit GPUs for an association you set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=<count>.
- When the limit is checked: Grp* limits are evaluated when the scheduler considers starting a job. If starting the job would make the association exceed any Grp limit, the job is not considered eligible (it will pend). The pending reason shown by squeue will be an AssocGrp* variant (for GRES-related limits you may see names like AssocGrpGRES or AssocGrp*Limit).
- Precedence/hierarchy: limits are applied in this order (first-match wins): user association → account association(s) (hierarchy upward) → cluster/root association → partition/job/QOS specific limits as documented. If a specific association level has no setting, the next level's setting is used.
- Interaction with QOS and DenyOnLimit: QOS flags like DenyOnLimit can make a job be denied at submission if it alone violates a max. For Grp limits, the Grp limit is treated as a Max when deciding DenyOnLimit behavior (see resource_limits docs).
- Changes effect: lowering Grp limits does not kill running jobs to immediately satisfy the new limit; the new lower limit is enforced for future scheduling decisions. Deleting an association can cancel running/pending jobs that belong to it.
- Numeric and update semantics: GrpTRES entries are comma-separated TRES=value assignments (e.g., GrpTRES=cpu=32,mem=200G,gres/gpu=4). You can use "+=" / "-=" when modifying to increment/decrement. Assigning -1 removes a specific TRES limit. Using "-=" to try to make a negative value will set that TRES to 0.

How to view and set these limits (examples)
- Show current association/account limits:
  - sacctmgr show association (or sacctmgr show user/account with WithAssoc) — this displays GrpTRES, GrpJobs, etc.
- Set a GRES group limit (examples — run as an admin with sacctmgr):
  - For a user association:
    sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=4
  - For an account:
    sacctmgr modify account where name=chemistry set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=10
  - Or editing the association directly:
    sacctmgr modify association where user=alice account=chemistry set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=4
- Increment/decrement:
  - sacctmgr modify account where name=chemistry set GrpTRES+=gres/gpu=2
  - To remove the limit: set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=-1 (removes that TRES limit)

Troubleshooting tips
- If a job is pending with reason AssocGrp* (or AssocGrpGRES), inspect the association limits with sacctmgr show assoc (or sacctmgr show user/account) to find which GrpTRES or GrpJobs limit is blocking it.
- Remember that the scheduler tests the aggregate — even if currently some GPUs look free, the job will still pend if starting it would exceed the configured GrpTRES for that job's association.
- Check QOS/partition MaxTRES/MaxJobs settings too — a job can be blocked by a higher-priority limit at the QOS/partition level.

References / authoritative configuration names
- GrpTRES is the canonical place to set per-association aggregate limits on trackable resources (TRES), including generic resources (gres/<name>).
- The scheduler pending reason family is AssocGrp* (AssocGrpGRES being the GRES-related variant) — meaning some association-group aggregate limit was reached.
(These behaviours are described in Slurm's "Resource Limits" and "GRES" documentation; use sacctmgr show/modify to inspect and change association limits.)

If you want, I can:
- show the current GrpTRES/GrpJobs values for a specific user or account (I would run sacctmgr for that); or
- show why a particular pending job is stuck (I would run squeue for the job ID).

Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order

Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database

in the slurm.conf configuration file.

## TRES information[#SECTION_TRES-information](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .
Each TRES has a different limit, e.g., "GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G" would
establish 2 different limits: one for 16 CPUs and another for 32 GB of memory.
Setting a new value for a TRES type does not affect any other TRES types that
were previously specified. For example, on the same entity as above, a
subsequent assignment of "GrpTRES=gres/gpu=2" will result in
"GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G,gres/gpu=2" applying to that entity.

## AutoDetect [#AutoDetect](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,
configuration details will automatically be filled in for any system-detected
GPU. This removes the need to explicitly configure GPUs in gres.conf, though the
Gres= line in slurm.conf is still required in order to tell slurmctld how
many GRES to expect.
Note that AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
and AutoDetect=oneapi need their corresponding GPU management libraries

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).
The total count of shards available on a node should be configured in
the slurm.conf file (e.g. "NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2,shard:64").

results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- AssocGrpGRES (or the equivalent GrpTRES/GrpGRES association field) is the association‑level cap that limits aggregate consumption of generic resources (GRES — e.g. GPUs, MPS, licenses, burst‑buffer quotas) for an association (user/account/cluster/partition combination).
- Association/group resource limits are the TRES/GRES limits set on associations (and on accounts, users, cluster defaults, QOS, partitions) that Slurm enforces when deciding whether a pending job can be allocated.

Concepts and terms
- TRES = Trackable RESources (cpu, mem, node, energy, and generic resources = GRES).
- GRES = Generic RESources (commonly gpu, mps, license, etc.). They are expressed as TRES entries such as gres/gpu or more specific gres/gpu:tesla.
- Association = the tuple (cluster, account, user, optional partition). Limits may be set at user-association, account, cluster, QOS, or partition level; Slurm uses a precedence order when deciding which limit applies.

What AssocGrpGRES (GrpTRES/GrpGRES) does
- It sets an aggregate cap for the association: e.g., GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8 means the association may not have more than 8 GPUs allocated in total across all running jobs that belong to that association.
- The scheduler checks group limits when considering starting a job. If starting the job would make the group total exceed the limit, that job will not be considered for allocation (even if preemption could free resources).
- Group limits are cumulative (they count currently allocated resources) and are enforced at allocation time.

Common related fields / limits
- GrpTRES (or GrpGRES): group/association totals (aggregate caps).
- MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPerAccount / MaxTRESPerJob: per-user / per-account / per-job caps (e.g., max GPUs a single job or user may request/use).
- GrpJobs: maximum number of running jobs in aggregate for the association.
- You can set multiple TRES in the same spec: e.g., GrpTRES=cpu=128,mem=512G,gres/gpu=8

Syntax / examples (sacctmgr)
- Set a group GPU cap for an account:
  sacctmgr modify account where name=chem set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8
- Set a per-user GPU cap:
  sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu=2
- Remove a TRES limit by assigning -1 (or unset the field).
- Inspect defined TRES types:
  sacctmgr show tres
- Inspect association limits:
  sacctmgr show assoc format=Account,User,GrpTRES,MaxTRESPerUser

Important enforcement caveats and gotchas
- Type‑specific vs generic requests: if you set a limit on a specific GRES type (e.g. MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) and a user submits --gres=gpu:2 (generic gpu request), the type‑specific limit may not be enforced. This is a Slurm design limitation — the scheduler can enforce limits for a named TRES exactly as requested, but a generic request can bypass type‑restricted caps. To enforce model‑specific limits reliably you typically require a job_submit plugin (Lua) that forces users to request a specific model or validates requests at submit time.
- Hierarchy / precedence: limits are checked in this order (roughly): Partition QOS -> Job QOS -> User association -> Account association(s) -> Cluster association -> Partition limit. The first place a given limit is defined is used.
- Changing limits: lowering limits does not kill currently running jobs to satisfy the new limit; it only prevents new allocations that would exceed the new limit. Deleting an association will cancel running/pending jobs in that association.
- TRES arithmetic: Grp/Max TRES fields support +/- modifiers (e.g., +=) and large integer ranges; setting negative values via "-=" ends up as 0 — consult sacctmgr docs for exact behavior.

When to use which limit
- Use GrpTRES/GrpGRES to control total concurrent usage of scarce cluster resources (total GPUs for an account or project).
- Use MaxTRESPerUser/MaxTRESPerJob to prevent single users or single jobs from monopolizing multiple devices.
- Use QOS or partition limits for site-wide or partition-wide hard policies and to combine with fairshare.

How to check current settings and usage
- sacctmgr show assoc [with format options] to list association limits (GrpTRES, MaxTRES*, etc.).
- sacctmgr show tres to list available TRES names (how to reference gres/gpu, license names).
- squeue/sinfo to observe current allocations and node/partition state (to see how many GRES are currently allocated/idle).
- Use sreport for historical usage (GPU/GRES hours) if you need accounting/usage numbers.

References
- Slurm resource limits and sacctmgr documentation (see sections on TRES, GrpTRES, MaxTRESPerUser and GRES-specific limits). The docs also include the specific syntax and examples.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current association limits on your cluster (I can run sacctmgr show assoc and sacctmgr show tres) — tell me which association(s) or account/user to inspect.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association

## Tools[#tools](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.

its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.

[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin

in order to optimize performance.

as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources

sacctmgr is used to view or modify Slurm account information.
The account information is maintained within a database with the interface
being provided by slurmdbd (Slurm Database daemon).
This database can serve as a central storehouse of user and
computer information for multiple computers at a single site.
Slurm account information is recorded based upon four parameters
that form what is referred to as an association .
These parameters are user , cluster , partition , and
account . user is the login name.
cluster is the name of a Slurm managed cluster as specified by
the ClusterName parameter in the slurm.conf configuration file.
partition is the name of a Slurm partition on that cluster.
account is the account for a job.

## FLAT FILE DUMP AND LOAD[#SECTION_FLAT-FILE-DUMP-AND-LOAD](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
sacctmgr has the capability to load and dump Slurm association data to and
from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an
existing cluster's associations into a new cluster with similar
accounts. Each file contains Slurm association data for a single
cluster. Beginning with version 25.05, QOS information is included in the
dump file. Comments can be put into the file with the # character.
Each line of information must begin with one of the five titles; QOS ,
Cluster , Parent , Account or User . Following the title
is a space, dash, space, entity value, then specifications. Specifications are
colon-separated. If any variable, such as an Organization name, has a space in
it, surround the name with single or double quotes.

## TRES information[#SECTION_TRES-information](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .
Each TRES has a different limit, e.g., "GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G" would
establish 2 different limits: one for 16 CPUs and another for 32 GB of memory.
Setting a new value for a TRES type does not affect any other TRES types that
were previously specified. For example, on the same entity as above, a
subsequent assignment of "GrpTRES=gres/gpu=2" will result in
"GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G,gres/gpu=2" applying to that entity.

gres.conf is an ASCII file which describes the configuration
of Generic RESource(s) (GRES) on each compute node.
If the GRES information in the slurm.conf file does not fully describe those
resources, then a gres.conf file should be included on each compute node. For
cloud nodes, a gres.conf file that includes all the cloud nodes must be on
all cloud nodes and the controller. The file will always be located in the same
directory as slurm.conf .
If the GRES information in the slurm.conf file fully describes those resources
(i.e. no "Cores", "File" or "Links" specification is required for that GRES

By default, no GRES are enabled in the cluster's configuration.
You must explicitly specify which GRES are to be managed in the
slurm.conf configuration file. The configuration parameters of
interest are GresTypes and Gres .
For more details, see [GresTypes](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) and [Gres](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html) in the slurm.conf man page.
Note that the GRES specification for each node works in the same fashion
as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources
than configured will be placed in a DRAIN state.
Snippet from an example slurm.conf file:
```text

```
Each compute node with generic resources typically contain a gres.conf
file describing which resources are available on the node, their count,

There are cases where you may want to define a Generic Resource on a node
without specifying a quantity of that GRES. For example, the filesystem type
of a node doesn't decrease in value as jobs run on that node.
You can use the no_consume flag to allow users to request a GRES
without having a defined count that gets used as it is requested.

## Socket Affinity Configuration [#Socket_Affinity](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Slurm's job scheduler handles GRES affinity on a socket basis internally.
However, the gres.conf interface allows administrators to specify `Cores` for GPU affinity configuration. This creates
a common misconception that Slurm will respect core-level affinity during job
scheduling, which it does not and never has. This can lead to issues where job
allocations and job steps don't align correctly, since job steps examine cores
while jobs use sockets.
To prevent administrators from specify a core affinity for the device that
Slurm cannot currently respect, Slurm validates that any specified `Cores` align with socket boundaries and will generate
errors if they do not.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

## Tools[#tools](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.
See man sacctmgr for details on this tools and examples of
its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" (or similarly named association field shown by sacctmgr) refers to the association-level group limits that apply specifically to GRES (Generic RESources — e.g., GPUs, licenses, burst buffers). It is how Slurm records or displays the GRES-related group/TRES limits for a user/account/association.

What association (group) GRES/TRES limits are
- TRES = Trackable RESource. GRES is the TRES type for generic resources (typically gpu, license, etc.).
- Association/group limits control aggregate and per-entity use of resources for an association (user+account+cluster+optional partition).
- Common GRES-related limits:
  - GrpTRES (or Assoc group TRES): aggregate limits for the association, e.g. GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8 (at most 8 GPUs in total across that association).
  - MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPerAcct: per-user or per-account maximums (can be type- and model-qualified, e.g. gres/gpu:tesla=1).
  - MaxTRESPerJob: limit of a TRES per single job (e.g. a job cannot request > 4 GPUs).
  - Other related fields: GrpJobs, MaxJobs, etc., which affect job counts rather than TRES counts.

How the limits are expressed (syntax)
- Limits are given as comma-separated TRES=VALUE pairs. Example forms:
  - GrpTRES=cpu=128,mem=512G,gres/gpu=8
  - MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
  - MaxTRESPerJob=gres/gpu=4
- GRES type qualification: you can qualify a GRES by model/type: gres/gpu:tesla or simply gres/gpu. The qualified form targets a specific GRES subtype.

Enforcement and precedence
- When Slurm considers starting a job, it checks association/group limits. If starting that job would exceed any applicable group limit, the job is not considered for allocation (remains pending).
- Precedence order for limits: job QOS / partition QOS and association levels are checked in a defined hierarchy. In general the first-defined limit in the precedence list is used (user association → account association(s) → cluster defaults), with some exceptions documented for certain limits (see Slurm docs).
- Changing limits:
  - If you lower a limit, running jobs are not killed to satisfy the new limit; the new limit is enforced for new allocations.
  - If you delete an association, jobs belonging to it are cancelled immediately.

Important GRES caveat (common pitfall)
- Type-specific limits vs generic requests: if you set a limit for a specific GRES type (e.g., MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) but a user submits with --gres=gpu (no model specified), Slurm may not enforce the type-specific limit. In short: a type-specific limit will not block a generic request for a different/unspecified type. This is a known design limitation; if you need strict enforcement, require users to request specific types (via job_submit plugin or policies).

How to view and change these limits
- View defined GRES types: sacctmgr show tres
- View association limits: sacctmgr show association (use format options to display TRES/GrpTRES/MaxTRES* fields)
- Set/modify limits via sacctmgr. Example (run as admin):
  - sacctmgr modify account where name=chemistry set GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16
  - sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1
- To remove a TRES limit assign -1 (or use sacctmgr syntax to remove that entry).

Recommendations / best practices
- Decide whether you want generic or model-specific enforcement. If model-specific enforcement is required, either:
  - require users to request a model in --gres (enforce with job_submit plugin), or
  - implement a lua job_submit plugin to rewrite/validate requests.
- Use sacctmgr show tres and show association formats regularly to audit active limits.
- Use GrpTRES for aggregate quotas and MaxTRESPerUser/MaxTRESPerJob for per-user or per-job caps.

References / where to read more
- sacctmgr and resource_limits docs in the Slurm manual (commands: sacctmgr show tres, sacctmgr show association; docs: "Resource Limits" and "sacctmgr" pages).

If you want, I can:
- show the current GRES and association limits on your cluster (sac t mgr / sacctmgr queries), or
- give exact sacctmgr command examples tailored to a user/account name you supply.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None
Note: If limits are defined at multiple points in this hierarchy,
the point in this list where the limit is first defined will be used.
Consider the following example:
- MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs is undefined in the partition QOS
- No limits are set in the job QOS and
- MaxJobs=4 and MaxSubmitJobs=50 in the user association
The limits in effect will be MaxJobs=20 and MaxSubmitJobs=50.

following limits: Max[Time|Wall], [Min|Max]Nodes. For these limits, even

over this specific type (e.g. MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 ) if a
user requests a generic gres, the type's limit will not be enforced. In this
situation an additional lua job submit plugin to check the user request may
become useful. For example, if one requests --gres=gpu:2 having a
limit set of MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 , the limit won't be
enforced so it will still be possible to get two teslas.
This is due to a design limitation. The only way to enforce such a limit
is to combine the specification of the limit with a job submit plugin that

## Tools[#tools](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
The tool used to manage accounting policy is sacctmgr .
It can be used to create and delete cluster, user, account,
and partition records plus their combined association record.
See man sacctmgr for details on this tools and examples of
its use.
Changes made to the scheduling policy are uploaded to
the Slurm control daemons on the various clusters and take effect
immediately. When an association is deleted, all running or pending
jobs which belong to that association are immediately canceled.
When limits are lowered, running jobs will not be canceled to
satisfy the new limits, but the new lower limits will be enforced.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .
Each TRES has a different limit, e.g., "GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G" would
establish 2 different limits: one for 16 CPUs and another for 32 GB of memory.
Setting a new value for a TRES type does not affect any other TRES types that
were previously specified. For example, on the same entity as above, a
subsequent assignment of "GrpTRES=gres/gpu=2" will result in
"GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G,gres/gpu=2" applying to that entity.

By default, no GRES are enabled in the cluster's configuration.
You must explicitly specify which GRES are to be managed in the

as the other resources managed. Nodes which are found to have fewer resources
than configured will be placed in a DRAIN state.

If AutoDetect=nvml , AutoDetect=nvidia , AutoDetect=rsmi ,
AutoDetect=nrt , or AutoDetect=oneapi are set in gres.conf ,
configuration details will automatically be filled in for any system-detected
GPU. This removes the need to explicitly configure GPUs in gres.conf, though the

many GRES to expect.

and AutoDetect=oneapi need their corresponding GPU management libraries
installed on the node and found during Slurm configuration in order to work.
Both AutoDetect=nvml and AutoDetect=nvidia detect NVIDIA GPUs.
AutoDetect=nvidia (added in Slurm 24.11) doesn't require the
nvml library to be installed, but doesn't detect MIGs or NVlinks.

results.prompt: Explain AssocGrpGRES and association group resource limits
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- "AssocGrpGRES" is an accounting/association-level concept for GRES (generic resources, e.g., GPUs) that appears in the association/group resource limits exposed by Slurm accounting (sacctmgr/sacct). It expresses the group-level GRES/TRES limits or usage that apply to an association (the association is the combination of user/account/cluster/partition).
- Association/group GRES limits are enforced at job allocation time: if starting a job would cause any group limit to be exceeded, that job will not be considered for scheduling. Limits are applied according to Slurm’s association/limit hierarchy (QOS/partition → job QOS → user association → account association(s) → cluster, etc.).
- GRES limits can be expressed using TRES syntax (examples: gres/gpu=2 or gres/gpu:tesla=1). A notable caveat: a type-specific limit (for example MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1) does not prevent a user from requesting a generic --gres=gpu:2 and thereby obtaining two of that model; enforcing that requires a job_submit plugin or forcing users to request specific types.

Key behavior and admin notes
- Which fields control these limits: association/group-level fields such as GrpTRES (and other Grp* fields like GrpJobs) are used to limit aggregate resources for an association. These are evaluated when the scheduler considers a job for allocation.
- Enforcement prerequisites and effects:
  - AccountingStorageEnforce must include limits (i.e., AccountingStorageEnforce=limits) in slurm.conf for Slurm to enforce association limits.
  - When limits are lowered, running jobs are not retroactively killed to satisfy the new lower limits; new/queued jobs are blocked if they would exceed the lowered limits.
  - Deleting an association will cancel running or pending jobs that belong to that association immediately.
- Scheduling-time semantics: group limits are tested when a job is being considered. If the job would exceed the group limit, it won’t be scheduled even if preemption of other jobs would have freed enough resources.
- GRES type-vs-generic limit caveat: type-aware limits (gres/gpu:MODEL=...) only apply when jobs request that specific type. If users request generic GRES (gres/gpu without a model), the type-specific limit may not be enforced; use a job_submit plugin to require model-specific requests if you need strict enforcement.

How to view/change these limits
- Use sacctmgr to view and edit association limits (the sacctmgr man page and the Resource Limits documentation show the fields and syntax). Typical fields include GrpTRES, GrpJobs and the Max/Min TRES settings; GRES is expressed in TRES form (gres/...).
- Use sacctmgr show association (or sacctmgr list/show account/user with WithAssoc) to inspect current association limits/GrpTRES values; use sacctmgr modify (or add) to change them. Consult the sacctmgr documentation for exact command-line format.

Where to read the authoritative details
- See Slurm’s Resource Limits documentation (resource_limits) for the limit hierarchy and GRES/TRES examples, and the sacctmgr man page for association fields (GrpTRES, GrpJobs, etc.) and sacctmgr syntax.

## Hierarchy[#hierarchy](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order
with Job QOS and Partition QOS order being reversible by using the QOS
flag 'OverPartQOS':
- Partition QOS limit
- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- ReqNodeNotAvail is a Slurm pending reason meaning “the scheduler could not find nodes that satisfy the job’s node/resource constraints right now.” In other words, nodes that would match the job’s request are not currently available (idle) so the job remains PENDING with reason ReqNodeNotAvail.

What ReqNodeNotAvail actually implies
- The scheduler tried to place the job but no node (or set of nodes) meeting the job’s requirements (partition, CPUs, memory, GPUs/GRES, features/constraints, exclusivity, node counts, topology, reservation, QOS/account limits, etc.) was free at that scheduling attempt. Only the first encountered blocking cause is shown, but multiple availability reasons may apply.

Common node-availability causes (why nodes aren’t available)
- Allocated/Busy: Nodes that match are currently RUNNING other jobs (allocated), possibly long-running or exclusive.
- Drained/Draining: Nodes are in DRAIN or DRAINING state (admin flagged for maintenance or reboot).
- Down/Failing: Nodes are DOWN, FAIL or FAILING due to hardware/network problems.
- Reserved: Nodes are reserved for a reservation; jobs not in that reservation can’t use them.
- Feature/Constraint mismatch: Job requested --constraint, --gres, or node features (eg. specific CPU, GPU type) that no idle node currently provides.
- Insufficient per-node resources: Request (eg. GPUs-per-node, CPUs-per-task, huge memory) exceeds what any single idle node can offer.
- Topology/affinity/step packing: Job requests multiple nodes with packing or contiguous topology that aren’t simultaneously free.
- GRES/GPU state: GPUs exist but are in use, isolated, or marked unusable (driver/health issues).
- Partition mismatch or partition limits: The job targeted a partition with no eligible idle nodes or partition-level limits/QOS prevented allocation.
- Account/QOS/association limits: Aggregate/account quotas or QOS limits can prevent allocation that otherwise looks node-eligible (often visible as another reason, but can manifest as ReqNodeNotAvail depending on scheduler checks).
- Licensing constraints: Software licenses required by the job are exhausted and scheduler blocks allocation where license is missing.
- Node feature mis-configuration or admin downlist: Node attributes don’t match current configuration (e.g., updated hardware/labels not reflected).
- Mixed state nodes: Nodes in MIXED state (partially allocated) may not satisfy a multi-slot request.

Quick investigation checklist (commands to run)
- See why a specific job is pending:
  - squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %P %j %u %T %R"   (shows the pending reason column)
  - scontrol show job <jobid>                 (shows requested nodes/GRES/constraints/ReqNodeList)
- Inspect node/partition state and reasons:
  - sinfo -Nel                                (partition/node overview with states)
  - sinfo -R                                  (list nodes in DRAIN/DOWN with reasons)
  - scontrol show node <nodename>             (detailed node state, Reason, GRES, real resources)
- Check reservations and limits:
  - scontrol show reservation <name>          (if you suspect a reservation)
  - sshare / sacctmgr list                     (check fairshare, account, and association limits)
- Scheduler diagnostics:
  - sprio / sdiag                              (priority/backfill diagnostics if scheduling order is a concern)

What to try / how to resolve
- Relax constraints: drop or broaden --constraint, reduce per-node resource requests, or request fewer GPUs/CPUs.
- Try a different partition or explicitly target nodes known to have the required resources.
- Wait or contact users/admins if nodes are legitimately occupied by long jobs.
- If nodes are DRAIN/DOWN, contact admins (or check sinfo_reasons) to get an ETA or to request resume.
- Check reservations/licenses: if a reservation or license is blocking, either schedule within it or ask admin to adjust.
- If you believe the scheduler is mis-reporting, collect: squeue output, scontrol show job, sinfo, scontrol show node for candidate nodes and open an admin ticket with those outputs.

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can run the specific checks (squeue and, if needed, scontrol show job) to show the actual reason and the relevant node/partition state.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- ReqNodeNotAvail means the scheduler could not find nodes that satisfy the job’s node/feature/GRES/TRES/placement requirements. In other words: “required node(s) not available” — not enough suitable idle nodes right now.

Why that happens (common node-availability causes)
1. Nodes are down/drained/failed/being rebooted
   - Nodes in DOWN, DRAIN, FAIL, or FAILING state are not usable for jobs.
2. Nodes are already allocated to other jobs
   - Idle node count is zero or there’s no set of nodes free that match the request.
3. Resource fragmentation / packing constraints
   - The request needs multiple nodes, contiguous nodes, or specific per-node TRES (e.g., 4 GPUs per node) and the remaining idle nodes can’t satisfy that exact packing.
4. Requested node names or node list (NodeList/ReqNode) don’t exist or are offline
   - A user requested specific hostnames that aren’t present or are not in a usable state.
5. Feature/constraint mismatch
   - The job requested a node feature or constraint (e.g., --constraint=avx512, or a GRES label) and no idle node exposes that feature.
6. GPUs or other GRES aren’t free
   - Nodes may be up but their GPUs/GPUs per node are fully allocated (allocated/mixed), so no node has the required free GPUs.
7. Administrative reservation or maintenance reservation
   - A reservation (or maintenance window) can reserve nodes so they’re not available for normal scheduling.
8. Partition or QOS limits or per-account/per-user limits
   - While those often show other reason codes, they can interact so the scheduler cannot place the job on any available node set.
9. Exclusive or shared mode conflicts
   - An exclusive allocation may prevent scheduling another job onto the same node even if some resources look free.
10. “Future” or scheduled state
   - Nodes marked FUTURE or otherwise scheduled for later use aren’t available now.

How to diagnose (quick commands to run)
- See the scheduler’s pending reason: squeue -j <jobid> -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %R"
  - The reason string visible in squeue often shows “ReqNodeNotAvail”.
- Inspect the job’s requirements: scontrol show job <jobid>
  - Look for ReqNodes/ReqTRES/NodeList/NumNodes/Features/Constraints.
- See node and partition states: sinfo
  - Use sinfo_reasons (sinfo -R) or scontrol show node <nodename> to get down/drain reasons.
- Check reservations: scontrol show reservation or squeue --reservation=<name>
- For GPU details, list node GRES/availability: sinfo -o or scontrol show node <node> (look for Gres, AllocTRES).

How to fix or mitigate
- If nodes are down/draining: ask admins to investigate (sinfo_reasons shows the reason).
- If fragmentation is the issue: relax constraints (fewer GPUs per node, allow different nodes, remove exact NodeList or set --ntasks-per-node differently).
- If a feature/constraint mismatch: remove or change the constraint or request a node with that feature.
- If reservation blocks nodes: either wait for reservation to end or request nodes in a different partition/reservation.
- If GPUs are allocated: either wait, request fewer GPUs, or target different nodes/partition.
- If you requested specific nodes that are offline: remove NodeList or pick other nodes.

Notes
- The squeue reason text is what the scheduler encountered for that scheduling pass; multiple deeper causes can exist (e.g., a reservation + lack of matching features). For a single-job deep inspection use scontrol show job and scontrol show node on candidate nodes.
- The canonical Slurm job reason codes and their explanations are in the Slurm docs (job_reason_codes).

If you want, tell me a job ID and I can show the squeue reason and the job’s requested node/TRES details and suggest specific changes.

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- ReqNodeNotAvail is a Slurm pending reason that means: the scheduler could not find nodes that satisfy the job's node-related requirements (count, names, features/constraints, GRES, topology, exclusivity, etc.). In plain terms: the nodes you asked for (or nodes with the resources you requested) aren’t available right now.

What ReqNodeNotAvail commonly covers
- Nodes already allocated: the matching nodes are currently used by other jobs (allocated), so they’re not free.
- Nodes drained/maintenance: nodes are DRAINED for admin maintenance or set DRAIN with a reason.
- Nodes down / hardware failure: nodes are DOWN (failed boot, NIC, disk, health check).
- Reservations: nodes are reserved for a reservation, so they’re not available to normal jobs.
- GRES (GPU) exhaustion: requested GPUs (count, type) are already in use or not present on idle nodes.
- Feature/constraint mismatch: job constraints (e.g., --constraint=skylake, --nodelist, CPU model, node features) don’t match any idle node.
- Memory/CPU shortage: no node has the per-node memory/CPU available to satisfy the request.
- Exclusive / topology requirements: the job needs exclusive nodes, particular multi-node topology (interconnect), or colocated resources that aren’t simultaneously free.
- Licensing or managed resource limits: required software license or managed resource (BurstBuffer, special device) is exhausted.
- Power/boot state or provisioning delays: nodes are powering up, provisioning, or in a suspended/power-saving state and not yet usable.
- Admin set states or manual hold: nodes explicitly set to DRAIN/DOWN/MAINT by admins (often with a reason string).

How it differs from similar reasons
- ReqNodeNotAvail focuses on "requested nodes or node attributes cannot be satisfied." Other reasons like Priority, Dependency, or QOS/AccountNotAllowed are unrelated to node physical availability.

How to investigate (quick checklist)
- Check the job’s pending reason: squeue -j <jobid> (reason column) or scontrol show job <jobid> for more detail.
- Check partition/node summary: sinfo -Nel (shows per-node state and features) and sinfo (partition view).
- See why nodes are marked down/drain: sinfo -R (reasons) or scontrol show node <nodename>.
- Inspect GRES/licenses: scontrol show node <node> (shows Gres/AllocTRES), and scontrol_license (for license counts).

A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For

script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of

result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of

255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- ReqNodeNotAvail is a Slurm pending reason meaning "the scheduler could not find suitable/eligible nodes to satisfy the job's node/resource constraints at scheduling time." In other words, no nodes that match the job's requested partition, features, GRES/TRES, memory/CPU, exclusivity, or reservation constraints were idle/available when the scheduler tried to place the job.

Common node-availability causes (what they mean, how to check, and common fixes)
1) Nodes are DRAINED / DOWN / FAIL / FAILING
   - Meaning: nodes are administratively drained, marked down, or have failed health checks.
   - Check: sinfo -Nel (or sinfo to see partition/node states), sinfo -R (reasons), scontrol show node <nodename>.
   - Fix: operator must investigate hardware/OS and resume or clear drain (scontrol update/SD tools); contact admins.

2) Nodes are allocated / in use by other jobs
   - Meaning: all suitable nodes are currently running other jobs (allocated, MIXED).
   - Check: sinfo -Nel to see A/I counts; squeue to inspect running allocations.
   - Fix: wait, change job size/constraints, or ask for preemption/priority if available.

3) Reservation holds nodes
   - Meaning: a reservation reserves nodes for a user/group/time window.
   - Check: scontrol show reservation <name> or scontrol show reservation (list), squeue --reservation=<name> for queued entries.
   - Fix: schedule around the reservation or ask the reservation owner/admin to change it.

4) Resource mismatch (memory, CPUs, sockets, TRES limits)
   - Meaning: requested per-node memory, CPUs, or per-node TRES exceed what's free on any idle node.
   - Check: scontrol show node <node> (to inspect real node capacity), sinfo -Nel, and compare to job request (sbatch/srun args).
   - Fix: relax request (less memory/CPUs), request more nodes with smaller per-node counts, use a different partition.

5) GRES/GPU availability or GRES matching (GPU-specific)
   - Meaning: requested GPU type/feature/number not free (GPUs are allocated, or node labels/GRES mismatch).
   - Check: sinfo -Nel (shows GPUs per node), squeue to see GPU jobs, scontrol show node <node> to inspect GRES.
   - Fix: change GRES request, wait for GPUs, or target nodes that have the requested GRES. (If you intended a conditional GPU submit: check sinfo first and only submit if Idle GPU node counts > 0.)

6) Feature/constraint mismatch (node features, partitions, CPU architecture)
   - Meaning: job requested -C, --constraint, or --partition features that no idle node matches.
   - Check: sinfo -Nel (features column), scontrol show node <node>, squeue -j <jobid> (reason).
   - Fix: remove/change constraint, use a different partition, or ask admin to tag nodes appropriately.

7) Exclusive/SMT/NUMA/exact-socket placement constraints
   - Meaning: job requested exclusive node usage (--exclusive), specific sockets, or topology that reduces eligible nodes.
   - Check: job submission options and scontrol show node to see topology.
   - Fix: relax exclusivity/topology constraints or increase requested time/window.

8) Account/QOS/association limits or policy blocks
   - Meaning: account, QOS, or fairshare/accounting policy blocks scheduling on some nodes or partitions.
   - Check: squeue for the job reason, sacctmgr show associations, sacctmgr or sshare to inspect shares/limits.
   - Fix: adjust account/QOS, request admin changes, or use a different account/QOS.

9) Licenses or other external resources
   - Meaning: job requires a license or limited resource tracked by Slurm and none are free.
   - Check: scontrol license (scontrol license show / scontrol_license) or the cluster’s license tracking.
   - Fix: wait, free licenses, or use machines without that license.

10) Node reaches site-specific maintenance/evacuation (power, reboot, updates)
    - Meaning: nodes are in maintenance state (FUTURE, POWER, REBOOT).
    - Check: sinfo -Nel and sinfo -R for reasons; scontrol show node.
    - Fix: coordinate with admins; nodes will return when maintenance finishes.

Notes on interpreting the pending reason
- The scheduler only reports the first reason it encountered when attempting to schedule; there may be multiple contributing causes.
- For a specific pending job: start with squeue -j <jobid> (shows the pending reason). If you need more detail, use scontrol show job <jobid>. For node-level details, use sinfo -Nel and scontrol show node <nodename>.
- If you see ReqNodeNotAvail for a job that should be eligible, gather: the job's requested constraints (sbatch header or scontrol show job), sinfo -Nel output, and scontrol show node for candidate nodes, then contact your cluster admins with that collected info.

Quick troubleshooting checklist (for users)
1. squeue -j <jobid> (confirm reason is ReqNodeNotAvail).
2. Review job constraints: scontrol show job <jobid> or check your sbatch options.
3. sinfo -Nel (look for idle nodes matching partition/features/GRES).
4. scontrol show node <candidate_node> to compare capacities (mem, CPUs, GRES).
5. If nodes are DRAIN/DOWN/RESERVED — open a ticket with admins (include sinfo and scontrol outputs).

If you want, tell me a job ID or show your sbatch options and I can walk through the concrete checks/commands to diagnose that specific pending job.
