results.prompt: Explain ReqNodeNotAvail and common node availability reasons
results.agent_response:
Short definition
- ReqNodeNotAvail is a Slurm pending reason that means “the scheduler could not find one or more nodes that satisfy the job’s node/resource/constraint request.” It is not a single cause — it’s the scheduler reporting that, given the job’s requested nodes/features/resources and current cluster/node state, no suitable nodes are currently available.

Common root causes (with what it looks like and why it happens)
- Nodes are Down/Drained or in maintenance
  - Admin-marked states (DOWN, DRAIN, DRAINED, FAIL) remove nodes from the pool, so requests for those nodes/features fail.
- All matching nodes are already allocated or Mixed
  - Nodes that match your constraints may be RUNNING (allocated) or MIXED (partially used) so there aren’t enough free CPUs/GPUs/memory to satisfy the request.
- Requested resources exceed node capacity
  - Job asks for more CPUs, tasks-per-node, memory, or GPUs than any single node (or the required set of nodes) can provide.
- GRES / GPU contention
  - All GPUs on candidate nodes are in use or a specific GPU type/feature (gres) is exhausted.
- Strict node/feature constraints
  - --nodelist, --exclude, --constraint, partition membership, or custom node features restrict which nodes are eligible; none of those nodes are free.
- Topology / layout / gang scheduling requirements
  - Requests that require multiple nodes simultaneously (e.g., --ntasks-per-node or gang allocations) fail if the scheduler cannot reserve the whole set at once.
- Reservations or holds
  - A reservation is consuming or reserving nodes for another job/reservation window; those nodes are not available for general scheduling.
- Access / account / QOS / partition limits
  - The job is eligible only on certain partitions or accounts and those partitions have no available nodes or are restricted.
- Node health or hardware issues
  - Nodes reporting hardware faults or failing health checks may be temporarily withheld by Slurm or by the admin.
- Exclusions (user or admin)
  - Node exclusion lists or per-user/node limits can remove eligible nodes from consideration.

How to diagnose (quick checks)
- From the pending job:
  - squeue -o "%i %P %j %u %t %M %r" or squeue -j <jobid> — shows the pending reason (ReqNodeNotAvail) and partition.
  - scontrol show job <jobid> — shows the job’s requested nodes, constraints, TRES (gres/cpu/mem), and nodelist/exclude settings.
- Inspect partitions and nodes:
  - sinfo — partition-level availability (allocated/idle/down counts) and basic node counts.
  - sinfo -R — lists nodes in down/drain states and the admin-supplied reasons.
  - sinfo -N -l or sinfo --Node — one-line-per-node with features and resources.
  - scontrol show node <node-name> — detailed node state, reason, AllocTRES, GRES in use, and health info.
- If GPUs involved:
  - check GRES usage (scontrol show node) and ensure idle GPU nodes exist for the requested type.
- Reservations:
  - scontrol show reservation or squeue --reservation=<name> to see reservation occupancy.

Common remediation steps
- Relax constraints: remove a strict --nodelist or --constraint, request fewer resources per node, or reduce GPUs/CPUs requested.
- Change partition or QOS: submit to a partition that has idle nodes or with a QOS that allows preemption if configured.
- Wait or requeue: if nodes are currently allocated, wait until they free or requeue with a different resource request.
- Contact admin: if nodes are drained/down for maintenance or failed health checks, ask the admins to inspect or return nodes to service.
- Use smaller / different resource packing: e.g., request fewer tasks per node so partially-used nodes can be used.

When you see ReqNodeNotAvail for a specific job, use scontrol show job <jobid> and sinfo (and scontrol show node on likely candidate nodes) to find exactly which constraint is preventing placement. If you want, tell me a job ID and I can walk through the exact fields to inspect and the most likely fix.

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol requeue does to a Slurm job
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol requeue <jobid> tells slurmctld to put the specified job back on the queue so it can be scheduled again.

What it does in practice
- If the job is RUNNING: Slurm will terminate the running allocation/steps for that job and change the job into a queued state so the scheduler can try to start it again later. The job is marked with the REQUEUED flag.
- If the job is PENDING: the command requests a requeue (it affects how the job is re-considered by the scheduler; behavior can depend on scheduler config and job type).
- For batch (sbatch) jobs, a requeued run normally restarts the job from the top of the job script (unless the job itself implements checkpoint/restart).
- For job arrays or heterogeneous jobs: requeue on the array leader will be applied to all components (requeue is an operation that can be applied to whole arrays/heterogeneous jobs).

Effects visible in accounting/state
- The job gets REQUEUED status/flag and the BatchFlag may be incremented for sbatch jobs when they are requeued.
- Exit codes and accounting records will reflect the termination and requeue event (details depend on accounting/storage configuration).

Who can run it
- Privileged users (Administrators/Operators) or the job’s effective owner (subject to site policy).

When to use vs alternatives
- Use scontrol requeue to retry a job without having users resubmit it manually.
- Use scancel to remove a job completely; use sbatch to submit a new job.

Caveats
- Requeue does not magically preserve in‑memory work—unless the job implements checkpointing, the job will typically start over.
- Local slurm configuration (MaxRequeue, RequeueExit settings, preemption/requeue policies) can influence whether requeue is allowed and how many times it is permitted.

Example
- scontrol requeue 12345

If you want, I can show the exact fields that indicate a job has been requeued (using squeue or scontrol show job) or explain how requeue interacts with your cluster’s Requeue/MaxRequeue settings.

Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol requeue does to a Slurm job
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol requeue <jobid> tells Slurm to take the specified job out of its current allocation and place it back into the pending queue so the scheduler can try to run it again (same job ID).

What actually happens
- If the job is RUNNING: Slurm terminates the job allocation (resources are released), any configured epilog/epilogSlurmctld will run, the job is marked REQUEUED while being processed, its requeue counter/flags are updated, and the job is returned to PENDING so the scheduler can reschedule it.
- If the job is PENDING: the command marks it for requeue (no allocation to terminate) and it remains eligible to be scheduled again.
- Job arrays / heterogeneous jobs: requeue on an array/heterogeneous job leader applies to all tasks/components (you may specify individual array elements with the array notation).
- Interactive allocations: interactive jobs (salloc/srun) are generally not requeued the same way as batch jobs; batch jobs are the usual target for requeue operations.
- Authorization: the command requires the job owner or a privileged user/operator.
- Side effects and limits: prolog/epilog behavior may run on termination and on the subsequent allocation; requeueing can be constrained by site policy/QOS/MaxRequeue settings, so it can be denied or limited by scheduler configuration.

When to use it
- To restart a job after a transient failure or after moving it off problematic nodes, to attempt scheduling on different nodes, or to re-run a batch job without creating a new job submission.

Example form
- scontrol requeue <jobid>

If you want, I can show the exact scontrol manual text or check whether a particular job is requeueable on your cluster.

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol requeue does to a Slurm job
results.agent_response:
Summary: scontrol requeue <jobid> tells Slurm to stop the job’s current running allocation (if any) and place the job back into the pending queue so the scheduler can try to start it again.

Details:
- Effect on a running job: the job’s current allocation is terminated/cleaned up and the job is marked for requeueing (you may see REQUEUED or a related flag). The job’s resources (nodes/CPUs/GPUs) are released and become available to other jobs.
- Effect on scheduling: the job is put back into the pending queue and will be considered by the scheduler for a new allocation like a fresh submission (subject to priorities, QOS, constraints, reservations, etc.).
- BatchFlag: for sbatch (batch) jobs, Slurm increments BatchFlag when a job is requeued (tracking requeue attempts).
- Ownership/permissions: only the job owner (effective owner) or privileged users/operators/administrators may run scontrol requeue.
- Job arrays / heterogeneous jobs: requeue behavior applies to job arrays and heterogeneous jobs in the documented ways (requeueing a job array ID can affect all elements; heterogeneous-job leader requeue applies to components).
- Checkpointing: requeue by itself does not magically restore in-job state. Unless the job uses an application-level checkpoint/restart mechanism or Slurm checkpoint plugins are configured, the restarted job will begin from the start of the job script.
- Use cases: manually force a restart after transient node problems, move a job off nodes, or recover a job after preemption/failure (administrators often use requeue for recovery).

What to look at after running it:
- squeue and scontrol show job <id> to see the job’s new state/flags and BatchFlag changes.
- sacct for historical records of the stopped attempt and the later restarted attempt.

If you want, I can show the scontrol manpage excerpt or examples of scontrol requeue usage.

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol requeue does to a Slurm job
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol requeue <jobid> tells Slurm to stop the job's current attempt and put the job back into the pending queue so it can be scheduled and run again.

What happens when you run it
- If the job is RUNNING: Slurm terminates the current allocation/steps for that job attempt, releases the resources, and marks the job with the REQUEUED flag. The job is then returned to the scheduler as a PENDING job to be reallocated later.
- If the job is PENDING: the command forces the job to be requeued (it becomes eligible for scheduling again). For job arrays, using the array JobID will act on all elements unless you specify a single task (e.g., 12345_7).
- The job keeps its original submission parameters (time limit, resource requests, QOS, etc.), so the requeued run will use the same request set unless you change them.
- For sbatch (batch) jobs, Slurm increments the BatchFlag when a job is requeued; this can be used to track requeue attempts.
- Authorization: you must be the job owner (or have the appropriate privileged/admin level) to run scontrol requeue.

When to use it
- Manually reschedule a job after a transient failure, preemption, or node maintenance.
- Retry a job without creating a new submission (keeps the same JobID or array structure).

Notes and cautions
- scontrol requeue is not the same as scancel. scancel permanently cancels a job; requeue requests another attempt.
- Some site-specific prolog/epilog or accounting behavior may run again on the requeued attempt (depends on local configuration).
- Preemption policies (e.g., PreemptMode=REQUEUE) can also cause automatic requeues without manual scontrol intervention.

Example
- scontrol requeue 12345
- scontrol requeue 12345_7  (single element of an array)

If you want, I can show the scontrol documentation snippet that describes authorization and BatchFlag behavior.

# Job Exit Codes
A job's exit code (aka exit status, return code and completion
code) is captured by Slurm and saved as part of the job record. For
sbatch jobs, the exit code that is captured is the output of the batch
script. For salloc jobs, the exit code will be the return value of
the exit call that terminates the salloc session. For srun, the exit
code will be the return value of the command that srun executes.
Any non-zero exit code will be assumed to be a job failure and will
result in a Job State of FAILED with a Reason of
"NonZeroExitCode".
The exit code is an 8 bit unsigned number ranging between 0 and
255. While it is possible for a job to return a negative exit code,
Slurm will display it as an unsigned value in the 0 - 255 range.

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol requeue does to a Slurm job
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol requeue <jobid> takes an existing Slurm job and places it back onto the pending queue so it will be scheduled again (instead of terminating permanently).

What it does (concise behavior)
- If the job is RUNNING: Slurm will terminate the current allocation/step(s) for that job (graceful termination where configured), mark the job as REQUEUED, free the resources, and create a pending entry so the job can be scheduled again.
- If the job is already PENDING: it will be left in the queue but treated as requeued (may affect priority/age); in practice you use it to move a running job back to PENDING.
- The job keeps its original JobID and most submission parameters (nodes, cpus, time, constraints, account, QoS, etc.).
- A requeued job may start on different nodes when it is next scheduled.

Effects you should know
- The job’s allocation is ended; unless you have checkpoint/restart configured and your job checks for/resumes from checkpoints, the job will restart from the beginning.
- For sbatch (batch) jobs, Slurm records and some flags (e.g., BatchFlag) may be updated to reflect the requeue; accounting/history will show the requeue-related records.
- For heterogeneous jobs and job arrays there are special rules: requeue operations may apply to the entire heterogeneous job leader or to array elements depending on the ID you supply—check scontrol docs for exact syntax.
- Any prolog/epilog scripts or epilog cleanup will run as configured when the allocation ends.

Permissions
- scontrol requeue requires the job owner (effective owner/coordinator) or a privileged user (operator/administrator).

When to use
- Recover a job after a transient failure (if it can restart or resume).
- Force a running job back to the queue (for debugging, resource reshuffling, testing).
- Respond to preemption policies or operator decisions to give up current allocation and try again later.

Caveats
- Requeueing does not automatically preserve in-memory state unless your job implements checkpoint/restart.
- If you want a fresh submission (new JobID) instead of reusing the same job record, cancel and sbatch again instead.

If you want, I can show the exact scontrol syntax and examples or explain how requeue interacts with checkpointing on your cluster.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
Quick summary — what a hold does
- A hold prevents a job from becoming eligible to be scheduled. Held jobs remain in PENDING (or in the queue) until the hold(s) that block them are removed or their other start conditions are met.
- Holds do not by themselves terminate running jobs. (To stop a running job use suspend/requeue/cancel as appropriate.)

Hold types and who sets/releases them
- UserHold
  - Set by the job owner (e.g., sbatch --hold or scontrol hold <jobid>) or by an operator acting on behalf of the user.
  - Can be released by the job owner or by privileged users (admins/operators).
- AdminHold
  - Set by administrators/operators.
  - Only privileged users (admins/operators) may remove this hold.
- SystemHold (sometimes shown as System)
  - Placed by Slurm for internal/system reasons (maintenance, controller actions, etc.).
  - Normally only the system or administrators clear this; users cannot clear SystemHold.
- Dependency hold (Dependency / DependencyHold)
  - Applied automatically when a job is submitted with a dependency (sbatch --dependency=...).
  - Cleared automatically by Slurm once the dependency condition is satisfied. Manual release is not the normal path.
- Array- and component-specific holds
  - For job arrays and heterogeneous jobs there are per-element and leader semantics; you can set/release holds on the array leader or on specific array elements (e.g., 12345 or 12345_7).

Important behavior / semantics
- Holds are cumulative: multiple hold types may be set on the same job. All holds that apply must be removed (or the condition satisfied) before the job becomes eligible to start. Removing only some of the holds does not make the job runnable if any other hold remains.
- A released job still must satisfy all normal scheduling conditions (resources available, begin time, dependencies, QOS/account limits, priority). Releasing a hold only removes that particular eligibility blocker.
- Pending reason and visibility: squeue will show the job as PENDING and usually show a reason such as JobHeld or Dependency; scontrol show job displays the Hold (Hold=...) field listing which holds are set.
- Permission model: most hold/release operations are restricted. Unprivileged users can operate on their own jobs within policy limits; privileged users (admins/operators) can place/remove holds on any job.

Common commands (conceptual)
- Submit held: sbatch --hold … (job starts in a held state)
- Place a hold: scontrol hold <jobid>  (creates a UserHold or operator-set hold)
- Release a hold: scontrol release <jobid>  (removes the specified hold(s) according to permissions)
- Inspect holds and reasons: squeue (see reason column) and scontrol show job <jobid> (see Hold= and detailed fields)

Notes and gotchas
- Putting a hold on a job does not change its submit time or some accounting fields; requeuing vs holding have different effects.
- If a job is held because of a dependency, manually releasing it (if possible) can bypass the dependency logic and may produce unexpected behavior — dependency holds are typically managed by Slurm.
- For job arrays and heterogeneous jobs use the job-array element syntax when you mean a single task (e.g., 12345_3) or operate on the leader to affect the whole group.

If you want, I can:
- Show the hold state for a particular job (I’ll need the job ID), or
- Describe exact scontrol command forms and examples for your Slurm version.

## Burst Buffers [#burst_buffer](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
A burst buffer can either be persistent or linked to a specific job ID.
Since a heterogeneous job consists of multiple job IDs, a job-specific burst
buffer will be associated with only one heterogeneous job component.
Each component can have its own burst buffer directives, and they are processed
separately. Only a persistent burst buffer can be accessed by all components
of a heterogeneous job. Persistent burst buffers are only available in the
datawarp plugin. A sample batch script demonstrating this for the datawarp
plugin is appended.

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
Summary
- A "hold" prevents a job from being considered for scheduling; held jobs remain in PENDING and will not be allocated resources even if dependencies, reservation, or resources would otherwise allow them to run.
- Releasing a hold makes the job eligible again; once released, normal scheduling rules (priority, backfill, dependencies, reservations) determine when it actually runs.

How to set/remove holds
- Submit-time: sbatch --hold will submit the job on hold (it starts PENDING/held).
- Ad-hoc: scontrol hold <jobid> (or scontrol hold jobid=<id>) sets a hold; scontrol release <jobid> removes it.
- There are multiple hold-types (user/admin/system/etc.) with different authorization levels; the exact command forms and options are scontrol hold/release and sbatch --hold.

Who can set and who can clear
- Job owner (unprivileged user): may place and clear USER-type holds on their own jobs.
- Privileged users / administrators (Operator/Administrator): can place and clear ADMIN/SYSTEM and other privileged hold types on any job.
- If multiple holds (different types) exist on a job, all active holds must be cleared before the job becomes eligible to run. Clearing only one hold type is not sufficient if another hold remains.

Visible effects and diagnostics
- Held jobs show as PENDING (PD) in squeue; the REASON/StateReason or scontrol show job output indicates a hold (e.g., JobHeld / Hold flags).
- scontrol show job <id> provides the detailed hold flags and reasons.
- Holds do not consume compute resources while the job is waiting.

Interactions and important notes
- Holds override satisfied dependencies and reservations: a job will remain held even if its dependencies are met.
- Holds apply to the job-level allocation (and therefore affect job steps). For arrays or heterogeneous jobs you can target whole job or specific array elements when using job identifiers that include indices.
- Holds are distinct from suspend/requeue: use suspend/requeue to stop or move a running job; holds are primarily a PENDING-state control.
- Authorization matters: an owner cannot clear an ADMIN or SYSTEM hold set by administrators; admins can clear owner-type holds as well.

Quick examples
- Submit held: sbatch --hold myscript.sh
- Place a hold: scontrol hold jobid=12345
- Remove a hold: scontrol release jobid=12345
- Inspect hold flags: scontrol show job 12345 (look for Hold= / StateReason / JobState)

If you want, I can show the exact hold flags and the REASON text by running squeue / scontrol show job on a specific job ID — tell me which job ID to inspect.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
Summary — what a hold does
- A hold prevents a job from being initiated by the scheduler. Held jobs remain in PENDING and will not be allocated resources until the hold(s) preventing them are removed.
- Holds affect job eligibility only; they do not terminate or change the runtime of an already RUNNING job (use suspend/requeue/cancel to affect running tasks).

Common hold types (what you’ll see in Slurm)
- UserHold: placed by the submitting user (or by scontrol when invoked by that user). Shows as a user-caused hold reason.
- AdminHold: placed by an administrator. Normal users cannot create AdminHold and generally cannot clear it.
- SystemHold: placed by Slurm/system (for example, due to a system condition). Only privileged/system actions clear it.
- A job’s Hold field may list more than one hold type; the job will not run until every active hold is cleared.

How holds are applied and removed
- Submission-time hold: sbatch --hold submits the job in held state.
- Post-submission: scontrol hold JobId=<id> (or the equivalent UI) places a hold. scontrol release JobId=<id> removes hold(s).
- Permissions: who can set/release which holds depends on privileges — users can generally set/release their own UserHold, admins can set/release AdminHold and clear other holds, SystemHold is managed by Slurm/system.
- Releasing: removing all active holds makes the job eligible for scheduling; if resources/priority permit, the scheduler can start it immediately.

Interactions and special cases
- Multiple holds stack: if any hold remains, the job stays pending.
- Job arrays: operations given the array JobID act on the whole array unless an element is explicitly targeted.
- Dependencies / StartTime: a hold is another gating condition. Even after release, other constraints (dependencies, BeginTime, resource limits, QOS/reservation restrictions) can keep the job pending.
- Visibility: squeue will typically show the pending reason (e.g., "UserHold" or "AdminHold"); scontrol show job shows detailed Hold and other fields.
- Holding a running job: placing a hold does not automatically suspend/stop an already running job. Use scontrol suspend / scontrol requeue / scancel for running-job control.

Practical notes
- If you want to temporarily prevent a job from ever starting, you can either put a hold or set StartTime to a later time (scontrol update JobId=<id> StartTime=now+...). Both prevent initiation; StartTime is often easier for planned deferrals.
- To check why a job is not starting, inspect squeue (Reason column) and scontrol show job <id> for the Hold and dependency fields.

If you want exact command syntax or examples for setting/releasing holds in your environment, tell me whether you want user-level or admin-level commands and I can provide concise command examples.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Executing scontrol sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from scontrol or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run scontrol or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to scontrol to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

These are the different possible burst buffer states:
- pending
- allocating
- allocated
- deleting
- deleted
- staging-in
- staged-in
- pre-run
- alloc-revoke
- running
- suspended
- post-run
- staging-out
- teardown
- teardown-fail
- complete
These states appear in the "BurstBufferState" field in the output of
`scontrol show job`. This field only appears for jobs that requested
a burst buffer. The states `allocating`, `allocated`,
`deleting` and `deleted` are used
for persistent burst buffers only (not for job-specific burst buffers). The
state `alloc-revoke` happens if a failure in Slurm's select plugin
occurs in between Slurm allocating resources for a job and actually starting

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
Summary — what a "hold" is
- A hold prevents a job (or job-array element) from becoming eligible to run. Held jobs stay in the queue (PENDING) until the hold(s) are cleared or some other condition changes.
- Holds are separate from job dependencies and resource reasons; a job with any active hold will not be scheduled even if resources and dependencies are otherwise satisfied.

Where you see holds
- scontrol show job <jobid> (or squeue with reason) shows the Hold field/flags and squeue may show a PD reason like "JobHeld".
- sbatch --hold submits a job initially held.

Types of holds and who sets/releases them
- UserHold (or "user"): applied by the job owner (e.g., sbatch --hold or scontrol hold by owner). Owners (and privileged users) can release these.
- AdminHold (or "admin"): applied by an administrator/operator (scontrol hold by admin). Only admins/operators (or privileged users) can remove these.
- SystemHold (or "system"): set by Slurm itself (or by site scripts/plugins) for system-level reasons (e.g., account/quota enforcement, scontrol actions). Usually only admins can clear SystemHold.
- Dependency (or dependency-like states): job dependencies (--depend) are a separate mechanism that can prevent eligibility; they can appear as dependency-related hold/reasons until the dependency is satisfied.
- Note: the exact hold-label text can vary by Slurm version/site plugins (check scontrol show job for the concrete Hold= string).

Multiple holds and their effect
- Holds are cumulative/bitflags. If a job has more than one hold type set, clearing one will not make the job runnable — all active holds that block eligibility must be cleared.
- Once all holds are cleared the job becomes eligible again subject to normal scheduling (priority, resources, QOS, dependencies).

Job arrays
- You can place holds on the whole array (jobid) or on individual elements (jobid_index). scontrol hold/release accepts either form; behavior follows the same cumulative-hold rules.

Running jobs vs held jobs
- Holds are intended for pending batch jobs. Applying a hold does not generally pause/stop an already RUNNING job. To pause a running job, use suspend/resume (scontrol suspend/resume) or administrator-enforced mechanisms. (Some site-specific behavior could differ; consult your admin.)

Common commands (informational)
- Submit held: sbatch --hold myjob.sh
- Add a hold: scontrol hold <jobid>  (owner can hold own job; admin can hold any job)
- Release a hold: scontrol release <jobid>  (only allowed if you have permission to clear that hold)
- Inspect holds/detail: scontrol show job <jobid>  (look for Hold= and for the pending reason)

Practical

array.

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner

scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays
with millions of tasks can be submitted in milliseconds (subject to configured
size limits) and the scheduler can quickly identify cases when no more array
tasks are eligible to start.
All jobs must have the same initial options (e.g., size, time limit), however,
it is possible to change some of these options after the job has begun
execution using the scontrol command specifying the JobID of the array or
individual ArrayJobID .
```text
$ scontrol update job=101 ... $ scontrol update job=101_1 ...
```

When a job array is submitted to Slurm, only one job record is created.
Additional job records will only be created when the state of a task in the
job array changes, typically when a task is allocated resources or its state

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.
Since each array element can have a different exit code, the interpretation of
the afterok and afternotok clauses will be based upon the highest
exit code from any task in the job array.
When a job dependency specifies the job ID of a job array:
The after clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array start.
The afterany clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete.
The aftercorr clause is satisfied after the corresponding task ID in the
specified job has completed successfully (ran to completion with an exit code of
zero).
The afterok clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with
job arrays. Once one element of a job array is discovered to not be runnable
or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job
array will be quickly skipped.

## Other Command Use [#other_commands](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
The following Slurm commands do not currently recognize job arrays and their
use requires the use of Slurm job IDs, which are unique for each array element:
sbcast, sprio, sreport, sshare and sstat.
The sacct, sattach and strigger commands have been modified to permit
specification of either job IDs or job array elements.
The sview command has been modified to permit display of a job's ArrayJobId
and ArrayTaskId fields. Both fields are displayed with a value of "N/A" if
the job is not part of a job array.

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner

scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator

## Notes[#NOTES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/configless_slurm.html)
Starting from Slurm 25.11, there's a new
SlurmctldParameters=reconfig_on_restart option that will make every
restart of slurmctld (process restart not triggered by "scontrol reconfigure")
to trigger a reconfiguration request to all slurmd and sackd daemons. For
"configless" systems this will ensure all processes are running the current
configuration. Some caution should be taken if you intend to perform rolling

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## NSS Configuration [#NSS_CONFIG](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Enabling nss_slurm is as simple as adding slurm to the passwd and
group database in /etc/nsswitch.conf (only on systems that will run
slurmd ). It is recommended that
slurm is listed first, as the order (from left to right) determines
the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.
To enable cloud node name resolution slurm needs to be added to the
to hosts database in /etc/nsswitch.conf .
It is recommended that slurm is listed last.
Once enabled, test it by launching getent queries such as:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent passwd tim tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent group projecta projecta:x:1001:tim
```

results.prompt: Explain Slurm hold and release semantics for jobs
results.agent_response:
Summary
- A "hold" prevents a job from being allocated/run; the job remains in the queue (typically in PENDING) and will not be scheduled until all active holds on it are removed.
- Holds are additive: a job can have multiple hold types at once. Removing one hold does not schedule the job if any other hold remains (or other scheduling constraints still block it).

Hold types and semantics
- UserHold
  - Intended for the job owner (or a user with appropriate privileges).
  - Commonly placed at submission time with sbatch --hold or later by the job owner (or by an admin acting on behalf).
  - The job owner (and admins) can release a UserHold.
- AdminHold
  - Set by administrators (e.g., site policy or manual admin intervention).
  - Ordinary users cannot remove an AdminHold; only admins can release it.
- SystemHold
  - Placed by Slurm/system components for system-level reasons (maintenance, controller action, etc.).
  - Typically cleared by the system or by administrators when the underlying condition is resolved.

Commands and inspection
- Place a hold:
  - sbatch --hold (submit job in held state)
  - scontrol hold <jobid> (place a hold on an existing job)
- Clear a hold:
  - scontrol release <jobid> (release holds; permission rules apply — admins can clear Admin/System holds; owners can clear UserHold)
- Inspect hold/state:
  - squeue shows job state and often a reason column (held jobs display a hold-related reason).
  - scontrol show job <jobid> gives detailed job fields (including hold info).
- Job arrays and components:
  - scontrol operations on an ArrayJobID apply to all elements by default; you can target individual elements with the element-specific jobid (ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID).

Behavioral notes / interactions
- Holds prevent scheduling even if resources are available and any dependencies are satisfied. Releasing the hold only makes the job eligible again; it may still remain pending for other reasons (resources, dependencies, QOS limits, reservations, etc.).
- Holds do not terminate or cancel a job. A held job stays in the queue until released or explicitly cancelled.
- Holding a running job is not the same as suspending it; to stop a running job you would use job suspension/requeue mechanisms (scontrol suspend/requeue), not a hold.
- Permissions matter: who can set/release which hold type follows the Owner vs Admin vs System separation; admins have broader authority.

Practical tips
- Use sbatch --hold if you want a job submitted but prevent it from starting until you explicitly release it.
- Use scontrol show job and squeue to confirm which hold type(s) are present and why a job is not starting.
- If a job remains pending after release, check resource availability, dependencies, partition/reservation constraints, and QOS/limits.

Commands referenced
- sbatch --hold
- scontrol hold <jobid>
- scontrol release <jobid>
- squeue
- scontrol show job <jobid>

Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Explain how scancel sends signals to jobs and steps
results.agent_response:
Summary — what scancel does when you signal or cancel jobs/steps:

- Targets
  - You can target a whole job (1234), a job step (1234.1), or a job-array element (1237_4). You can also supply filters (--user, --partition, --state, etc.).
  - Cancelling an individual job step does not automatically cancel the parent job or release the allocation.

- Sending a specific signal (--signal)
  - scancel --signal=NAME|NUM <targets> sends the named signal to the matching job steps (or to the single step(s) you name).
  - Example: scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3 sends SIGTERM to steps 1 and 3 of job 1234.
  - If you send a signal to an entire job (e.g., scancel --signal=KILL 1235), that signal is delivered to the active steps. Note: sending KILL to a job’s steps will kill those steps but does not perform a job cancel/release of the allocation.

- Canceling a job (no --signal)
  - Invoking scancel without --signal cancels the job. The cancellation sequence is:
    1. Send SIGCONT to all steps (wake them up if stopped).
    2. Send SIGTERM to steps.
    3. Wait the KillWait period (configured in slurm.conf).
    4. If steps haven’t exited, send SIGKILL.
  - This sequence lets steps attempt graceful shutdown before forcible termination and releases the allocation when the job is cancelled.

- Batch-step behavior (--batch)
  - By default, signals other than SIGKILL are not sent to the batch (shell) step. With --batch, scancel will signal only the batch step (useful when the shell needs to trap the signal and perform cleanup).
  - Note: many shells cannot handle signals while a child command is running; the shell often only handles a trapped signal after the child exits.

- Other notes/limits
  - Cancelling steps does not free resources — releasing resources requires cancelling the parent job (unless Slurm is configured otherwise).
  - For heterogeneous jobs in PENDING state, you may only cancel the entire job rather than individual components.

If you want, I can show exact scancel examples for your use case (kill all steps of job X vs cancel job X vs signal only the batch shell). Which do you want?

results.prompt: Explain how scancel sends signals to jobs and steps
results.agent_response:
Summary — what scancel does when it "sends signals"
- scancel is used to either signal job steps (send an arbitrary POSIX signal) or to cancel jobs (default behavior when no --signal is given).
- You may target entire jobs, individual job steps (jobid.step), job-array elements (jobid_index), or filter sets (user, partition, state, etc.).

Canceling a job (no --signal)
- When you run scancel <jobid> (no --signal), scancel initiates an ordered termination sequence:
  1. Send SIGCONT to all steps (wake them if stopped).
  2. Send SIGTERM to all steps.
  3. Wait the KillWait duration from slurm.conf.
  4. If any steps remain, send SIGKILL.
- That sequence attempts a graceful shutdown before forcibly killing tasks.
- Canceling a job releases the allocation; cancelling a single job step does NOT release the allocation (the job must be cancelled to free resources).

Sending an explicit signal (--signal)
- scancel --signal=<SIGNAL> <targets> sends the named signal to the matching job steps (e.g., TERM, KILL, USR1, numeric signals).
- If you specify step IDs (e.g., 1234.1 1234.3) only those steps are signaled.
- Sending a signal to an entire job will signal all active steps for that job.
- Important special-case: sending "KILL" as the signal to an entire job will cancel the active job steps but does not cancel the job itself (the job record remains until explicitly cancelled).

Batch-step behavior (--batch)
- By default, signals other than SIGKILL are NOT forwarded to the batch step (the batch shell script) when a job has a batch step + child tasks.
- Use --batch to signal only the batch step (useful when the shell should trap the signal and perform cleanup). Example: scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236

Addressing examples
- Signal specific steps: scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3
- Cancel job (graceful sequence): scancel 1234
- Send SIGKILL to all steps (but not cancel job record): scancel --signal=KILL 1235
- Signal the batch shell only: scancel --signal=USR1 --batch 1236

Implementation / performance notes
- scancel issues RPCs to slurmctld to request signaling. By default it may make per-job RPCs; using the --ctld option can reduce RPC count since one RPC can ask slurmctld to signal all matching jobs.

- scancel can send arbitrary POSIX signals (name or number) to jobs or individual job steps with --signal (e.g., --signal=TERM, --signal=KILL, --signal=USR1).

- Sending a specific signal with --signal only delivers that signal; it does not by itself perform the full cancel sequence unless you send the signals that cause termination. results.prompt: Explain how scancel sends signals to jobs and steps
results.agent_response:
Short answer: scancel is a client that asks slurmctld to deliver signals; slurmctld tells the slurmd(s) on the node(s) to signal the tracked processes for the targeted job(s)/step(s). The slurmd uses the configured proctrack (e.g., proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux) mechanism to find the task PIDs (or the job’s cgroup) and then send the requested signals to those PIDs (or the group).

Details and important behaviors
- Targets: you can target whole jobs (1234), individual steps (1234.1), array or array-index forms (1237_4), users, partitions, states, etc. Cancelling a job step (1234.1) does not by itself cancel the whole job/allocation; cancelling the job releases the allocation.
- Default cancel sequence (no --signal): scancel jobID performs a polite cancel:
  - sends SIGCONT to all steps to wake them (if stopped),
  - then sends SIGTERM,
  - waits the KillWait time configured in slurm.conf,
  - and if processes are still running finally sends SIGKILL.
  This gives steps a chance to clean up before forcible termination.
- --signal: you can request an explicit signal (name or number) to send instead of the default cancel sequence. Example: scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 sends SIGTERM to step 1 of job 1234.
  - If you send a SIGNAL=KILL to an entire job, Slurm will kill active steps (SIGKILL) but that signal form by itself does not necessarily show as a normal job-cancel operation (see docs for exact semantics).
- --batch (-b): by default signals other than SIGKILL are NOT sent to the batch step (the job’s shell script). Using --batch causes scancel to signal only the batch shell step (useful when the shell should trap the signal) and not other steps.
- Granularity: scancel can signal individual steps (only those will get the signal) or whole jobs (all active steps). Use the job.step syntax to address steps.
- How delivery is implemented: slurmd invokes the proctrack/cgroup or proctrack/linux plugin to enumerate the PIDs for the job/step. The proctrack plugin then issues the kernel signals (or operates via the cgroup interface) to reach every task in the job/step. On systems with cgroups/systemd, Slurm often confines tasks in a cgroup and signals the set of PIDs in that cgroup; on other systems it will signal the recorded PIDs directly.

Systemd is currently the most widely used init mechanism. For this reason
Slurm needs to find a way to coexist with the rules of systemd. The designers of
systemd have conceived a new rule called the "single-writer" rule, which implies
that every cgroup has one single owner and nobody else should write to it. Read

results.prompt: Explain how scancel sends signals to jobs and steps
results.agent_response:
Summary — how scancel actually delivers signals

High-level flow
- scancel (client) issues a request to slurmctld.
- slurmctld sends "signal job" RPCs to the affected slurmd daemons on the node(s) hosting the job.
- each slurmd / slurmstepd then delivers the requested Unix signal(s) to the job step's processes (the job step is managed by slurmstepd which performs the kill/ signal).

What scancel does depending on arguments
- Default cancel (no --signal): scancel will
  1) send SIGCONT to all steps (to wake any stopped tasks),
  2) send SIGTERM,
  3) wait the KillWait interval (from slurm.conf),
  4) if processes still exist, send SIGKILL.
  This sequence cancels the job and releases the allocation.
- --signal=<SIGNAME|NUM> (or -s): send the single specified signal to the targeted job(s) or step(s). This does not by itself necessarily release the job allocation unless you issue a cancel (no --signal).
- Cancelling a job step (e.g., 1234.1) sends the signal only to that step; cancelling a step does not automatically cancel the parent job (the job allocation remains until the job is cancelled).
- Sending KILL to an entire job: the docs note that sending signal=KILL to an entire job will cancel the active job steps but not cancel the job itself (allocation may remain).
- --batch: by default, non-KILL signals are not sent to the batch (shell) step. With --batch, scancel will signal only the batch shell process (useful if you want the shell to trap the signal). Note: most shells cannot handle signals while a child process is running, so trapping only helps between child invocations.
- You may target specific steps, array elements, users, partitions, states, etc. (e.g., scancel --signal=TERM 1234.1 1234.3).

Performance / RPC behavior
- scancel normally queries slurmctld and then issues signal-job RPCs for each matching job.
- With the --ctld option (and appropriate usage), scancel can ask slurmctld to signal all matching jobs with a single RPC — use this for large/bulk operations to reduce load on slurmctld.

Practical recommendations
- To request graceful shutdown: scancel --signal=TERM <job/step> (or simply scancel <job> to follow Slurm’s TERM→KillWait→KILL sequence).
- Use --batch when you specifically want the job’s batch shell to observe a trap.
- For bulk signaling/cancels, prefer --ctld to reduce RPC pressure on slurmctld.
- Remember that signaling a step is different from cancelling the job/allocation; cancel the job to free resources.

If you want, I can show the exact scancel options and examples from the man page.

results.prompt: Compare srun, sbatch, and salloc from the Slurm docs
results.agent_response:
I looked up the Slurm docs for srun, sbatch, and salloc and summarized the practical differences and typical uses below.

Purpose / primary role
- sbatch — Batch submission: submit a job script to the scheduler for queued/executed batch jobs. sbatch returns a job ID and the script runs later under Slurm (outputs go to slurm-<jobid>.out unless overridden).
- salloc — Interactive allocation: request and hold a job allocation (nodes/CPUs/etc.) and run a user command (or open an interactive shell/xterm). The allocation is held until the command or shell exits.
- srun — Job-step launcher / task launcher: start tasks inside an existing allocation (or, if no allocation exists, srun can obtain an allocation and directly launch tasks). Commonly used inside sbatch scripts or inside an salloc session to launch parallel processes.

Typical workflows / when to use each
- Production/scheduled runs: write a batch script and use sbatch. Inside the script use srun to launch the parallel MPI/OMP tasks or serial commands as job steps.
- Interactive debugging or ad-hoc use: use salloc to get nodes/resource and either run srun inside the allocation or get a shell to work interactively on the allocated nodes.
- Single-command launch or step-level control: use srun when you want to launch a parallel job step directly (either inside an allocation or as a one-off allocation+launch).

Blocking / lifecycle differences
- sbatch: non-blocking submit; sbatch returns immediately with a job ID; the job runs later under normal queue lifecycle.
- salloc: blocks while waiting for allocation, then blocks while the allocation/command runs; relinquishes resources when the command/shell exits.
- srun: blocks while the launched tasks run (unless used with –background); if no existing allocation, srun may allocate resources and run, then release them when finished.

Interaction/roles together
- Typical batch script: sbatch myscript.sh -> inside script: srun -nN ./parallel_program
- Interactive allocation: salloc -N4 bash  (now you have an interactive shell on allocated nodes), then srun -n8 ./prog
- Direct launch: srun -N2 -n4 ./prog can be run without sbatch/salloc (Slurm will obtain needed resources for that step).

Other practical notes
- Output: sbatch jobs produce batch output files (slurm-<jobid>.out) by default. salloc/srun interactive runs send stdout/stderr to your terminal unless redirected.
- Environment: allocations set SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_JOB_NODELIST, etc.; srun job-steps inherit the allocation environment when run inside sbatch/salloc.
- Flexibility: srun can be used for fine-grained step control; sbatch is for queuing scripts; salloc is for interactive control and debugging.

If you want, I can paste short canonical examples from the docs (sbatch script example, salloc interactive example, srun examples) or show the exact manpage snippets used. Which would you prefer?

results.prompt: Compare srun, sbatch, and salloc from the Slurm docs
results.agent_response:
Summary comparison (from the Slurm docs)

Purpose
- sbatch: Submit a batch script to the scheduler (non-interactive). The script runs later as a queued batch job.
- salloc: Request an interactive job allocation (a set of nodes/CPUs). When allocation is granted, run a command (or drop you into a shell) while holding those resources.
- srun: Launch job steps / parallel tasks. Can be used inside an existing allocation (sbatch or salloc) or used standalone to obtain an allocation and run a command.

Key behavioral differences
- Interactivity
  - sbatch: non-interactive (submit-and-return; job runs later).
  - salloc: interactive (waits until resources allocated, then runs command or shell; holds allocation until command exits).
  - srun: can be interactive when run from a shell (it will run the command and return); commonly used interactively inside an salloc shell or in a batch script to create job steps.

- Allocation vs launch
  - sbatch: submits a job request (scheduler handles allocation when resources available).
  - salloc: explicitly requests an allocation now (blocks until granted), then you get to use it interactively.
  - srun: launches tasks / job steps; if not already inside an allocation it can implicitly request an allocation for the command.

- Typical usage patterns
  - sbatch: long-running or repeatable batch workflows; use job scripts with #SBATCH directives. Returns a job ID immediately.

Quick summary
- sbatch: submit a batch script to the scheduler. Non-interactive — you submit and the scheduler runs it later; sbatch exits immediately after submission.
- salloc: request/obtain an interactive job allocation (a set of nodes/CPUs/GPU). When allocation is granted it runs the command you gave (or gives you a shell) and holds the allocation until that command exits.
- srun: launch job steps / parallel tasks. srun is the actual task launcher and can be used inside an allocation (recommended), inside a batch script, or (in many setups) to allocate resources and run a job step itself.

- Purpose
  - sbatch: queue a batch job (script) to run later under Slurm’s scheduler.
  - salloc: get an allocation interactively so you can run commands/interactive debugs on allocated nodes.
  - srun: start tasks/job-steps on nodes in an existing allocation (or implicitly request an allocation to run a command).

  - salloc: interactive (gives you a shell or runs an interactive program while holding the allocation).

  - sbatch: you submit a job; Slurm creates the allocation when the job begins; job ends when script ends.

  - sbatch: production runs, scheduled batch workloads, array jobs.
  - salloc: interactive debugging, exploratory runs, starting an interactive MPI session or opening xterm/shell on allocated nodes.

- srun (direct launch):
  - srun -n8 -l hostname
  - srun --pty /bin/bash   (start an interactive shell as a job step)

- Use sbatch for scheduled, reproducible batch workloads and production runs.
- Use salloc when you need an interactive allocation for testing, debugging, or interactive parallel runs.
- Use srun to launch the actual parallel tasks (inside sbatch scripts or salloc shells). You can also use srun alone for quick one-shot runs, but for longer runs or reproducibility prefer sbatch.

Here’s a concise comparison drawn from the Slurm documentation for srun, sbatch, and salloc.

Purpose
- sbatch — submit a batch script to the scheduler. Used for non‑interactive, queued batch jobs. The sbatch client returns a job ID and exits; the job runs later under Slurm control.
- salloc — request and obtain a job allocation (reserved nodes/resources) and then run a command (or open a shell) inside that allocation. Intended for interactive work and allocation-based launches.
- srun — launch job tasks (job steps). srun is used to start parallel/serial tasks inside an existing allocation (created by sbatch or salloc) or, if no allocation exists, can itself obtain an allocation and run the command.

Allocation semantics
- sbatch: submits a job which will allocate resources when scheduled; allocation lifetime = job. Use #SBATCH options inside the script or cli options to request nodes/CPUs/GPU/time.
- salloc: explicitly creates an allocation immediately (once resources available) that you can use interactively. Allocation persists until the command exits (or you release it).
- srun: normally runs job steps within the current allocation. If run outside an allocation, it may allocate resources for the duration of the srun invocation (one‑shot allocation + run).

Interactivity and workflows
- sbatch: non‑interactive batch workflow. Good for production jobs, pipelines, cron, array jobs.
- salloc: interactive allocation; useful for building, debugging, launching interactive MPI jobs, or running an interactive shell or xterm on compute nodes.
- srun: used both interactively and in batch scripts. Inside sbatch/salloc scripts you use srun to spawn the parallel work (MPI ranks, tasks). You can also run srun from a login node to get a one‑off parallel run.

Output / client behavior
- sbatch: returns “Submitted batch job <id>” and exits; job stdout/stderr typically captured to slurm-<jobid>.out (or as configured).
- salloc: waits until allocation granted then runs the specified command (or a shell). Prints “Granted job allocation <id>” and holds the terminal until the command exits, then relinquishes the allocation.
- srun: runs the command and forwards stdout/stderr to the calling terminal (or to job script output when run inside sbatch). If it creates an allocation, it waits until completion and then exits.

Typical examples
- Batch job: sbatch myscript.sh
- Interactive allocation + shell: salloc -N2 --time=01:00:00 bash
- Launch parallel app in an allocation: salloc -N5 srun -n10 ./my_mpi_program
- Launch directly with srun (one‑shot): srun -n8 ./myprog

When to choose which
- Use sbatch for scheduled, repeatable, long or background jobs.
- Use salloc when you need an interactive allocation (debugging, interactive MPI, exploratory runs).
- Use srun to actually start the parallel tasks (from inside sbatch/salloc) or for quick one‑off task launches that may implicitly allocate.

Other notes
- srun creates job steps; resource/environment variables (SLURM_JOB_ID, SLURM_NTASKS, etc.) are provided for allocations and steps.
- Options for CPUs, memory, GPUs, nodes (-N, -n, -c, --gres, --time, QOS, etc.) apply to all three but where they take effect differs: in sbatch they configure the submitted job, in salloc they configure the allocation, in srun they configure the job step or the implicit allocation when used standalone.

Short comparison (from the Slurm docs) — what each command does, when to use it, and quick examples.

srun
- Purpose: launch a job step (one command) under Slurm and/or obtain an allocation and run immediately. It handles task distribution, MPI/PMI launches, and task affinity.
- Behavior: can be used standalone (it will request/obtain resources and block until the step finishes) or inside an existing allocation (sbatch job or salloc allocation) to start additional job steps. By default attaches to your terminal for interactive I/O.
- Typical use: start MPI/parallel tasks, spawn job steps from inside a batch script, or run a single interactive parallel command.
- Example: srun -n32 ./my_mpi_program

sbatch
- Purpose: submit a batch script that Slurm will schedule and run later as a job allocation. sbatch itself returns immediately with a job ID.
- Behavior: non-interactive; Slurm queues the job and launches the script when resources are available. Standard output/error go to slurm-<jobid>.out (unless overridden).
- Typical use: production or long-running jobs you want Slurm to schedule without tying up your shell.
- Example: sbatch --nodes=4 --time=02:00:00 my_script.sh

salloc
- Purpose: obtain an interactive job allocation (a set of nodes/resources) from Slurm, then run a command (or drop you into a shell) using those resources.
- Behavior: blocks while waiting for allocation; when allocation is granted you get an interactive shell or the specified command is run. The allocation is released when the command/shell exits.

results.prompt: Explain what sattach is used for in Slurm
results.agent_response:
sattach is the Slurm client used to attach to a running job step so you can interact with its I/O streams (stdin, stdout, stderr). Key points:

- Purpose: expose the IO streams of one job step’s tasks (so you can view output, send input, or attach a parallel debugger such as TotalView).
- Target: a running job step (srun-created/interactive steps). You specify jobid and optionally a step id (jobid[.stepid]).
- Not usable for: extern or batch steps (their IO channels are not set/forwarded), or for jobs that aren’t currently running.
- Useful options: 
  - --label: prefix output lines with task numbers
  - --input-filter / --error-filter: restrict stdin/stdout/stderr to a single task
  - --layout: request task layout from slurmctld
- How to find steps: use squeue --steps or scontrol show job <jobid> to list step ids before attaching.
- Caveats: sattach issues RPCs to slurmctld — many concurrent calls can degrade controller performance. Also requires appropriate permissions to attach to the job.

Example:
- sattach 12345         (attach to default step of job 12345)
- sattach 12345.1       (attach to step 1 of job 12345)
- sattach --label 12345

Alternatives: use srun --pty for interactive allocations, sstat/scontrol for non-interactive diagnostics, or a parallel debugger that integrates with sattach.

sattach is a Slurm client utility used to attach to the standard input/output/error streams of a running Slurm job step (a job or job step started with sbatch/srun/salloc). Key points
- What it does: connects to a running job step and streams its stdout/stderr (and can forward stdin) so you can observe or interact with the running tasks.
- Common uses: debug or inspect a running MPI/multi-task job, view output from specific tasks, or send input to a task for interactive troubleshooting.

- Limits/requirements: you can only attach to jobs managed by Slurm that are still running and have I/O connected to Slurm; typically you must be the job owner or an admin/privileged user to attach.
- Caution: sattach makes RPC calls to slurmctld; excessive/looped use can degrade controller performance.

Example (concept): attach to job 12345 to stream its live output and optionally interact with it.

results.agent_response:
sattach lets you attach to the IO streams of a running Slurm job step so you can observe (and in limited ways send) live stdin/stdout/stderr for the tasks in that step.

- Performance note: sattach sends an RPC to slurmctld; don’t call it in tight loops (many calls can impact controller performance).

Example usage:
- sattach <jobid[.step]> (attach to the named running step)
- sattach -l <jobid> (attach with labels)

results.prompt: Explain what sattach is used for in Slurm
results.agent_response:
sattach is a Slurm client that connects to an already-running job (or job step) and attaches your terminal to that job’s stdio streams so you can view and/or send standard input and see standard output and error from the job’s tasks.

Key points
- Purpose: attach to the std(in/out/err) of a running job step so you can monitor live output or interact with a running task without restarting/submitting the job.
- Scope: attaches to an existing job or job.step (you supply the jobid and optional step/task selectors).
- Not for starting jobs: sattach does not allocate resources or create a new job; it only connects to an active allocation.
- Typical uses: debug long-running jobs, inspect live logs, send input to an interactive task, or aggregate output from multiple tasks in a job step.

Basic behavior and useful options
- You can target a specific task(s) within the job step and filter streams:
  - --input-filter / --error-filter to direct stdin or show only one task’s stdout/stderr.
  - -l / --label to prefix lines with the originating task number when attaching to multiple tasks.
  - --layout to request task-to-node layout information from slurmctld.
- It contacts slurmctld (RPC). Running many sattach calls (e.g., in tight loops) can overload slurmctld — avoid automated high-frequency calls.
- Permissions: normal users can typically sattach to their own jobs; attaching to other users’ jobs usually requires admin privileges.

Examples
- Attach to job 12345’s main step:
  sattach 12345
- Attach and label output from multiple tasks:
  sattach -l 12345

When to use vs alternatives
- Use sattach when the job is already running and you want live interaction or to watch its stdout/stderr.
- Use srun --pty / salloc when you want to start an interactive allocation from scratch.
- Use sacct/scontrol/squeue/sstat for job metadata, accounting, and non-interactive diagnostics.

Caveats
- Some applications or job configurations may not expose interactive stdin/stdout in a way sattach can use.
- Because sattach sends RPCs to slurmctld, heavy/automated use can degrade scheduler performance.

If you want, I can show the exact sattach command syntax and common flags from the man page.

results.prompt: Explain sbcast and when it helps stage files to allocated nodes
results.agent_response:
Summary
- sbcast is a Slurm utility that copies (broadcasts) a file from the node where it is run to every node in the current Slurm allocation.
- It must be run inside a Slurm allocation (inside a batch job, an salloc/srun shell, or the shell spawned by an allocation).
- Destination (DEST) should be a path on a node-local filesystem (or else the configured BcastParameters directory). If DEST is not fully qualified, Slurm will place the file in the configured broadcast directory or the current working directory.

When sbcast helps (good use cases)
- No or slow shared filesystem: nodes do not share a fast parallel FS (or NFS is a hotspot). sbcast avoids many clients hitting the shared filesystem for the same file.
- Node-local staging for fast I/O: you want to copy a binary, model or dataset to node-local NVMe /tmp or $SLURM_TMPDIR before launching GPU/CPU work.
- Reducing metadata/IO pressure: many ranks/processes opening the same file from a global filesystem can overload metadata servers; staging to local disk reduces that load.
- Packaging a self-contained executable: use --send-libs to include needed shared libraries when launching on nodes that may not have the same environment.
- When launching many tasks that read the same large file in parallel from local disk (e.g., local dataset shards).

When sbcast is not the best choice
- Small files on a fast parallel filesystem: the global FS may already be faster/more convenient.
- Extremely large files (> parallel FS speed): a high-performance parallel FS may outperform node-by-node copies, or you may prefer a pre-staged dataset on local disks via a cluster data-management workflow.
- Frequent repeated sbcast calls: sbcast sends RPCs to slurmctld — many calls can degrade the controller and even resemble a DoS. Don’t call sbcast in tight loops or per-task.

Practical notes and options
- Typical flow in a job script:
  1) inside the job, copy with sbcast: sbcast ./mybinary /tmp/mybinary
  2) make it executable (chmod) and run it with srun or mpirun from the job
- Useful options:
  - --compress / -C (lz4 by default) — reduces network bytes sent for compressible files.
  - --fanout / -F — tune tree fanout for distribution topology.
  - --send-libs — auto-detect and broadcast dependent shared libraries.
  - --preserve / -p — preserve file attributes.
  - --exclude — exclude directories when autodetecting deps.
- DEST should refer to a node-local path. If you leave DEST unspecified, Slurm will use BcastParameters or the current working directory; check your cluster’s slurm.conf/BcastParameters if unsure.
- Cleanup: remove staged files in job epilog or at end of job to avoid filling local storage.

Performance/operational cautions
- sbcast triggers RPCs to slurmctld. Avoid many simultaneous sbcast calls from user scripts or at cluster scale.
- For very large data and high parallelism, test performance: sometimes a parallel filesystem or a coordinated pre-staging tool is faster.
- Do not rely on sbcast for persistent long-term storage — it is for staging within an allocation.

Example
Inside a job script:
- sbcast --compress ./model.tar /tmp/model.tar
- tar -xvf /tmp/model.tar -C /tmp/model_data
- srun --ntasks=... train --data /tmp/model_data

If you want, I can show a concrete sbcast command example tuned for your cluster (suggested DEST path, --fanout, compression) — tell me where you plan to stage files (e.g., /tmp, $SLURM_TMPDIR) and approximate file sizes.

results.prompt: Explain sbcast and when it helps stage files to allocated nodes
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- sbcast copies a file from the job’s control/node to every node in the current Slurm allocation. It is run from inside a job allocation (batch script, salloc/srun shell) and writes the file to a local path on each allocated node.
- Use it when you need a file available on node-local storage (local SSD, tmpfs, /tmp) on every allocated node and either you don’t have a shared filesystem or you need local-disk performance.

What sbcast does
- Broadcasts one source file to all nodes in the active Slurm allocation (single command, Slurm coordinates delivery).
- Destination must be a path local to each node (if not given, obeys BcastParameters or current working directory).
- Can auto-collect and send dependent shared libraries (--send-libs), preserve modes (-p), compress payload (-C), and tune distribution fanout (-F).
- Implemented via RPCs to slurmctld; many concurrent calls can load slurmctld.

When sbcast helps (good use cases)
- There is no shared parallel filesystem, or it is slow/overloaded.
- You need low-latency or high-throughput access to a file from node-local storage (e.g., small executables, per-node worker config, initialization datasets cached to local SSD/tmpfs).
- The file is small-to-medium sized (single large files are OK but very large datasets may be better on a parallel FS or pre-staged by other means).
- You have many nodes and want a single coordinated broadcast rather than looping scp/rsync from the login host.
- You want to stage a binary plus its libraries to local disk (use --send-libs to include dependencies).

When sbcast is not ideal
- You already have a fast parallel/shared filesystem (Lustre, GPFS, etc.). Those often perform better than copying to each node.
- The data is very large (many GB/TB); copying across network to every node may be slower/inefficient compared to serving from a shared FS or preloading on a subset of nodes.
- You have many small files — better to tar/zip into a single file and sbcast that archive, then unpack on nodes.
- You plan to call sbcast repeatedly in a tight loop — avoid that because it stresses slurmctld.

Practical tips / options
- Run inside an allocation: e.g. salloc -N4 ... ; sbcast myprog /tmp/myprog ; srun -N4 /tmp/myprog
- Combine many small files: tar -czf bundle.tgz dir/ ; sbcast bundle.tgz /tmp/bundle.tgz ; srun tar -xzf /tmp/bundle.tgz
- Use compression: -C or --compress=lz4 to reduce network transfer
- Use --send-libs to include ELF shared-library dependencies (helpful for self-contained binaries)
- Use -p/--preserve to keep permissions and timestamps
- Tune distribution with --fanout/-F to change tree fanout if admin defaults are suboptimal
- Avoid running sbcast repeatedly; prefer one broadcast per allocation for staging
- Clean up after job: remove staged files from /tmp or local SSD if needed

Caveats and admin considerations
- sbcast invokes slurmctld RPCs; many simultaneous sbcast calls or scripted loops can overload slurmctld (risk denial-of-service).
- Destination should be local to the node; specifying a path on a shared FS defeats the local-staging purpose.
- Slurm config (BcastParameters, BcastExclude) can affect behavior; admins may tune defaults.

Alternatives
- Shared parallel filesystem (best for large shared datasets).
- rsync/scp in prolog/epilog or a central orchestration step (works if you can parallelize copies safely).
- Container images (Singularity/Apptainer) or bundling apps into an image or module.
- Use a subset of “loader” nodes that download once and then peer-distribute (custom).

Example usage
- Simple broadcast inside allocation:
  sbcast myprogram /tmp/myprogram
  srun -N4 /tmp/myprogram
- Bundle many files and broadcast:
  tar -czf bundle.tgz mydir/
  sbcast bundle.tgz /tmp/bundle.tgz
  srun -N4 bash -c 'tar -xzf /tmp/bundle.tgz -C /tmp && /tmp/mydir/run.sh'

References
- sbcast man page (Slurm docs): https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbcast.html

If you want, I can suggest exact sbcast command lines and a small sbatch or salloc workflow for your specific files, allocation size, and whether your cluster uses local SSDs or a parallel filesystem.

results.prompt: Explain sbcast and when it helps stage files to allocated nodes
results.agent_response:
What sbcast is (short)
- sbcast is a Slurm utility that transmits a file from the node where you run it to every node in the currently active Slurm allocation. It must be run from inside a job allocation (batch job or the shell from salloc/sbatch). The destination path should be on each node’s local filesystem (for example /tmp or $SLURM_TMPDIR).

When it helps (common, practical cases)
- Reduce shared-FS contention: when many tasks on many nodes would simultaneously read the same file from a shared filesystem (NFS/GPFS), sbcast stages a local copy on each node and avoids I/O hot spots.
- Distribute a single executable or small dataset to all allocated nodes (binaries, single data shard, model weights, small VM/container rootfs).
- Stage runtime dependencies: use --send-libs to also broadcast required shared libraries for a standalone binary.
- Use per-node local scratch: when your job needs good local I/O throughput or low-latency access to a file on each node.
- Faster than many ad-hoc per-node scp calls for small-to-moderate size files because Slurm uses a fanout distribution tree and optional compression.

When sbcast is not a good fit
- Very large files or many many small files: sbcast can be slower than a high-performance parallel filesystem, and many sbcast calls (one per file) can overload slurmctld. Tar/pack files first or use the shared FS if it scales better.
- Files that must be available cluster-wide outside the allocation: sbcast only targets nodes in your current allocation.
- If you already have an efficient distribution mechanism (CVMFS, preloaded images, container registry, cluster-wide shared FS), use that instead.

Key options and tips
- --compress / -C: enable compression (lz4 by default); helpful for compressible content.
- --fanout / -F N: tune parallel tree fanout (how many child transfers each node spawns); useful for very large allocations or networks with specific topology.
- --send-libs: autodetect and transmit required shared libraries for an executable.
- --preserve / -p: preserve mode and timestamps.
- --force / -f: overwrite existing files on nodes.
- Tar multiple files into one archive before broadcasting (reduce slurmctld RPCs and overhead), then extract on nodes.
- Put destination on local tmp ($SLURM_TMPDIR or /tmp); check node-local disk free space before staging.
- Avoid looping sbcast calls from scripts (each sbcast triggers an RPC to slurmctld — can overload the controller).

Minimal usage pattern (conceptual)
- Inside your job script or salloc shell:
  1) sbcast /path/on/submit/node/mybin /tmp/mybin
  2) srun chmod +x /tmp/mybin && srun /tmp/mybin  (or use $SLURM_TMPDIR instead of /tmp)

Performance cautions
- sbcast sends RPCs to slurmctld; lots of simultaneous or repeated sbcast calls can degrade the controller. Limit calls and bundle files where possible.
- For very large payloads, benchmark sbcast vs your parallel FS — performance depends on file size, node count, network topology, and slurm.conf BcastParameters.

In short
- Use sbcast when you need a single, consistent local copy of a file on every node in your allocation to avoid shared-FS hotspots or to satisfy local-disk-only requirements. For many files or very large files, bundle them or prefer an alternative distribution mechanism.
