results.prompt: Explain sbcast and when it helps stage files to allocated nodes
results.agent_response:
What sbcast does (short)
- sbcast copies a file from the job’s current host to every node in the job allocation. It’s run from inside a job allocation (batch script or an allocation shell) and creates the file on each node’s local filesystem (or the path configured via BcastParameters).

When using sbcast helps (when it’s a good choice)
- You need the file available on node-local storage (e.g., /tmp, /scratch local) rather than on a parallel filesystem.
- The file will be read concurrently from all nodes (many processes launching the same binary, model, dataset shard, etc.), and the parallel filesystem can become a metadata or bandwidth bottleneck.
- You want a fast node-local copy for startup (binaries, small-to-medium models, small input datasets, job bootstrap scripts, or shared libraries).
- Nodes do not share a performant parallel FS, or that FS is overloaded for your job’s startup pattern.
- You need to stage dependencies (including shared libraries) to ensure identical runtime environment on each node.

When sbcast is not ideal
- Large files (multi-GB/very large datasets) may be better handled by a parallel filesystem, dedicated distributed data service, or an application-level staging (e.g., chunked downloads, a distributed cache).
- If you have a good parallel filesystem that can stream the data efficiently to many tasks, that may outperform sbcast.
- Do not run many sbcast calls in tight loops — each call makes RPCs to slurmctld and can degrade controller performance.

Key options and behaviors to know
- Must run inside an allocated job (after sbatch/salloc); it broadcasts to nodes allocated to that job only.
- DEST should be a path on the node-local filesystem. If not fully qualified, Slurm will place the file in the BcastParameters location or the current working directory.
- --compress / -C: compress the data stream (lz4 or none) to reduce network transfer size.
- --fanout / -F: tune how the broadcast fans out across nodes (controls parallelism of the distribution).
- --send-libs: autodetect and send shared-object dependencies for executables.
- --preserve / -p: preserve file mode and timestamps.
- sbcast uses the controller (slurmctld) to coordinate transfers; many simultaneous sbcast calls or very frequent calls can overload the controller.

Typical usage patterns (examples)
- Stage an executable or script, then run it on all nodes:
  sbcast my_program /tmp/my_program
  srun --nodes=$SLURM_NNODES /tmp/my_program
- Broadcast a model or small dataset to node-local storage:
  sbcast model.tar.gz /tmp/model.tar.gz
  srun --nodes=$SLURM_NNODES bash -c 'tar -xzf /tmp/model.tar.gz -C /tmp && ./run_training'
- Send an executable plus its shared libraries:
  sbcast --send-libs my_bin /tmp/my_bin && srun /tmp/my_bin

Performance tips
- Compress if network bandwidth is the limiting factor and file compresses well.
- Increase fanout for larger allocations so distribution happens in parallel rather than serially.
- Use --preserve for permissions if your job needs executable bits kept.
- Avoid repeated sbcast calls; stage once per allocation, reuse the staged copy.
- If copying many files, consider packaging (tar) and sbcasting the tarball.

Safety and operational notes
- sbcast creates load on slurmctld — do not call it from massive loops or many concurrent clients.
- It only reaches nodes in your current allocation. You cannot use sbcast to push files to arbitrary cluster nodes outside your allocation.
- For very large data, prefer scalable data distribution strategies (parallel FS, data-aware scheduling, distributed caches).

If you want, I can:
- Suggest a concrete sbcast command and an sbatch snippet for your specific file sizes and node count.
- Help pick fanout/compression settings if you tell me file size, nodes count, and whether network or controller load is a concern.

Short answer
- sbcast copies a local file from the job’s submission/allocated shell to every node in the current allocation, writing it to a node-local path you specify. It’s intended for staging executables, libraries, or data onto the compute nodes of a job so tasks read from local storage instead of a shared filesystem.

What sbcast does (key facts)
- Must be run from inside a Slurm allocation (inside a job script or the job’s interactive shell).
- SOURCE is a file on the node where you run sbcast; DEST should be a fully-qualified path on each compute node (a local filesystem path is recommended).
- It sends the file via slurmctld and distributes it to all allocated nodes (tree/fanout distribution).
- Useful options: compression (-C / --compress), preserve mode/ownership (-p), control fanout (-F/--fanout), and --send-libs to include shared-library dependencies.

When sbcast helps (good use-cases)
- Avoiding an NFS/Lustre hotspot at job startup: when many ranks/tasks read the same executable/large shared file at once, copying that file once to each node’s local disk reduces load and improves startup time.
- Staging small-to-moderate sized binaries, shared libraries, or input archives that each node should use locally (e.g., MPI executables, local caches).
- When you need node-local temporary files (local SSDs) for better I/O performance than the cluster parallel filesystem.
- When you want identical files present on every node without requiring a shared filesystem mount.

When not to use sbcast (or be careful)
- Very large datasets: a parallel filesystem is often more efficient for bulk data movement; sbcast can still work but may be slower or stress slurmctld/network.
- Many small files: prefer packaging them into a single archive (tar) before sbcast to avoid extra RPC/overhead.
- Frequent repeated sbcast calls in short loops — sbcast uses RPCs to slurmctld and can overload slurmctld; don’t call it in tight loops.
- If you need the file available cluster-wide outside the allocation or permanently, use shared storage or an installation workflow instead.

Best-practice recommendations
- Run sbcast once in the job prologue (task 0 or before launching many tasks). Example in a batch script:
  - sbcast myprog /local/tmp/myprog
  - then srun --multi-prog or mpirun to launch tasks that use /local/tmp/myprog
- Combine many small files into a single archive, sbcast the archive, then extract on each node.
- Use compression (-C lz4) to reduce transfer size for compressible files; use --fanout to tune distribution for large allocations.
- Use --send-libs if you need the executable’s shared libraries copied as well; use --preserve to keep permissions.
- Check available local disk space on nodes before staging large files.

Example commands
- Copy an executable to /tmp on every allocated node:
  sbcast myprog /tmp/myprog
- Copy with compression and preserve permissions:
  sbcast -C lz4 -p myprog /local/scratch/myprog
- Send an archive and then extract on nodes (recommended for many small files):
  tar -czf archive.tgz dir/
  sbcast archive.tgz /local/tmp/archive.tgz
  srun --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 bash -c 'tar -xzf /local/tmp/archive.tgz -C /local/tmp'

Troubleshooting & performance notes
- If job startup is still slow, measure whether the shared FS is the bottleneck; sbcast helps most when many nodes simultaneously read the same file from the shared FS.
- Avoid many simultaneous sbcast calls that could cause slurmctld performance degradation.
- If you need to stage very large datasets, consider an alternative distribution mechanism (parallel filesystem, dedicated data distribution service, or preloading into node-local caches outside the job).

If you want, I can:
- Suggest an sbcast pattern for a specific job script (give me job size, file sizes, and local path),
- Or review a short job script and insert an sbcast staging step.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm GRES syntax and gpu resource requests
results.agent_response:
Short version first
- GRES is Slurm’s “generic resources” system. GPU requests use the GRES syntax name[:type[:count]] (most sites use the name gpu). Example forms you’ll see:
  - --gres=gpu:2                (request 2 GPUs per allocated node)
  - --gres=gpu:tesla:2         (request 2 GPUs of Type “tesla” per node if configured)
  - --gres=mps:50              (site-specific MPS resource; configured via gres.conf)

- Slurm also provides convenience GPU options that are equivalent in intent:
  - --gpus=<count>             (GPUs required for the job)
  - --gpus-per-node=<count>    (GPUs required on each allocated node)
  - --gpus-per-task=<count>    (GPUs required for each task; requires setting --ntasks)
  These are generally easier to use than manual --gres strings.

GRES syntax details
- Formal form: name[:type[:count]]
  - name — the GRES name as configured (commonly gpu or mps).
  - type — optional string from your gres.conf (GPU model or custom tag).
  - count — integer number of that GRES (defaults to 1 if omitted).
- Example: --gres=gpu:V100:4 requests 4 GPUs of Type “V100” per node (if your admin configured that Type).
- If you omit type: --gres=gpu:2 requests 2 GPUs (any configured type) per node.

How Slurm maps/exports GPUs to jobs
- Node GRES configuration lives in gres.conf and slurm.conf (NodeName ... Gres=...), and Slurm uses that to map physical device files (e.g., /dev/nvidia0) to allocations.
- When Slurm allocates GPUs it sets environment variables (e.g., CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES) so your job sees only the allocated device IDs. Do not assume contiguous device numbering across nodes.
- You cannot (normally) request a specific device index from sbatch; you request resource counts/types and Slurm assigns specific devices.

Per-job vs per-node vs per-task semantics
- --gpus (job-level): requests the specified number of GPUs for the whole job; if the job runs across multiple nodes Slurm will place GPUs according to the allocation rules (typically all requested GPUs may land on one node unless you request per-node).
- --gpus-per-node / --gres=gpu:count (per-node): guarantees that each node granted to your job has that many GPUs.
- --gpus-per-task (per-task): use when you run many tasks and each task needs its own GPU. Example for 8 MPI ranks each with one GPU:
  --ntasks=8 --gpus-per-task=1
  That will allocate at least 8 GPUs overall (one per task).

MPS, fractional sharing and MIG
- CUDA MPS or other fractional-sharing schemes are administratively configured via gres.conf (e.g., Name=mps Count=200). Jobs request the MPS GRES (e.g., --gres=mps:50) rather than raw gpu devices.
- For NVIDIA MIG (A100 slices) the admin can expose MIG instances as distinct GRES types; you request them by the configured name/type.

Select/cons_tres and feature support
- The GPU-specific options (--gpus, --gpus-per-node, --gpus-per-task) require the select/cons_tres plugin on the cluster. If the cluster uses an older select/linux plugin, GPU options may be rejected and you must use --gres instead (or the admin must enable the TRES plugin).

Practical sbatch examples
- Single-node, 4 GPUs:
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:4
  or
  #SBATCH --gpus=4
- Multi-node, ensure 2 GPUs on each node:
  #SBATCH --nodes=4
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
  or
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-node=2
- Many tasks, one GPU per task:
  #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
  #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4   (usually pair GPUs with cpus-per-task)

Debugging and inspection tips
- Ask your admin or check gres.conf and slurm.conf for GRES names/types available on nodes.
- Use sinfo and scontrol to see node GRES info (sinfo -Nel or scontrol show node=node01) and to confirm what GPU types/counts are configured.
- Inside a running job check CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to see which device IDs were assigned.

Notes / best practices
- Prefer the --gpus family for simple counts (newer, integrates with TRES accounting). Use --gres when you need to request a named GRES type exactly as configured in gres.conf (e.g., a specific GPU type or non-GPU generic resources).
- Always request appropriate CPU and memory alongside GPUs (cpus-per-task, mem) to avoid oversubscription.
- If you rely on MPS or MIG-like fractional sharing, read your cluster’s gres.conf policy because those are site-configured and behave differently from integer GPU allocation.

If you want, I can:
- show the GPU types and counts configured on this cluster (I’ll run sinfo/scontrol_show for you), or
- craft an sbatch header for your exact workload (give me tasks, nodes, GPUs-per-task or total GPUs, cpus-per-task, memory, and partition).

results.prompt: Explain Slurm GRES syntax and gpu resource requests
results.agent_response:
Summary — what GRES is
- GRES = Generic RESources. It’s how Slurm advertises and allocates non-CPU resources such as GPUs, MPS slots, MIG instances, license tokens, shards, etc.
- Node-level configuration lives in slurm.conf (Gres= on NodeName lines) and optionally per-node gres.conf (detailed device mapping / AutoDetect). The scheduler matches job requests against the configured GRES.

Key GRES syntax (node config)
- In slurm.conf you typically set: NodeName=node[01-08] Gres=gpu:4,mps:200
- In gres.conf each device can be described; Slurm supports AutoDetect (nvml/rsmi/oneapi) to discover GPU devices.
- GRES element format (job-side requests): name[:type:count]
  - name: GRES name (commonly "gpu")
  - type: optional string to distinguish device types (e.g., v100, a100, or a MIG profile substring)
  - count: number required (integer)
  - Examples: gpu:2   gpu:tesla:2   mps:50

Requesting GPUs at submit time
- --gres (generic): --gres=gpu[:type:count]
  - Example: sbatch --gres=gpu:2  (requests 2 GPUs per allocated node by the select plugin semantics)
  - Example with type: --gres=gpu:V100:2 (requests GPUs whose type string contains "V100")
- Convenience / GPU-specific options (shortcuts; require select/cons_tres plugin):
  - --gpus=N
    - Requests N GPUs for the job allocation (total GPUs for the job). Often equivalent to requesting --gres=gpu:N but semantics depend on whether you combine with -N/-n.
  - --gpus-per-node=N
    - Equivalent to --gres for GPUs: request N GPUs on each allocated node.
  - --gpus-per-task=N
    - Request N GPUs for each task; requires you also set a task count (e.g., --ntasks or srun task counts).
  - --gpus-per-socket, --gpus-per-core also exist for socket/core-level placement in clusters that support them.

How counts map into allocations (common patterns)
- Single-node 2 GPUs: sbatch --gpus=2 or sbatch --gres=gpu:2
- Two nodes, 1 GPU each: sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=1  (get 2 nodes × 1 GPU)
- MPI with one GPU per rank: sbatch --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks-per-node=4  (4 tasks on node, each gets 1 GPU — requires enough GPUs on node)
- If you use --gpus (total) plus multiple nodes, scheduler may place them across nodes to satisfy the total; use --gpus-per-node to guarantee per-node counts.

MIG, MPS, sharding and partial-GPU resources
- MIG: Slurm supports NVIDIA MIG instances. MIG profiles can be exposed as separate GRES; type in name[:type:count] can match a MIG profile substring.
- MPS/sharding: Slurm can expose sharable resources like mps or shard in slurm.conf/gres.conf. You request them with --gres=mps:50 (counts are configured by admin). MPS/shard allocations have special semantics and require appropriate plugins.
- Note: requesting a fractional GPU (percent) is admin-configured via sharding/MPS; plain "gpu:0.5" is not supported — you request integer counts of the configured GRES units.

Environment variables and device visibility
- Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for job steps to limit each step’s visible GPU devices to the ones allocated on that node. This is how Slurm ensures distinct assignments between jobs.
- The exact env vars available can vary by Slurm version and local configuration; always check your job environment if you rely on a specific variable.

Accounting and monitoring
- If AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu is enabled, Slurm will collect gres/gpumem and gres/gpuutil (NVML/rsmi required) for accounting.
- TRES name for GPUs is typically gres/gpu (and can show up in sacct output if accounting is configured).

Requirements & gotchas
- select/cons_tres plugin: the modern --gpus* options and many GRES features require the select/cons_tres plugin; jobs that request GPU options on systems not configured with that plugin will be rejected.
- Types must match admin configuration: if admins used a custom GRES type string in gres.conf (or used MIG profile substrings), you must match that type string when requesting specific types.
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES maps to device indices visible inside the job, not necessarily the physical device IDs you see with nvidia-smi on the whole node. cgroups may be used to restrict device files too.
- If your job is pending with a GPU request, use sinfo and squeue to inspect partition/node GPU availability (and pending reason). If unsure which type to request, ask your cluster admins or inspect node gres with sinfo or node slurmd logs.

Practical examples
- Simple 2-GPU batch script:
  #SBATCH --gpus=2
  #SBATCH -t 02:00:00
  ...
- Request 1 GPU per task for 8 MPI ranks (8 GPUs total, assigned per rank):
  #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
- Two nodes, 2 GPUs per node:
  sbatch -N2 --gpus-per-node=2 myscript.sh
- Request specific GPU type:
  sbatch --gres=gpu:A100:4 my_a100_job.sh

If you want, I can:
- Show exact local examples based on your cluster’s gres configuration (I’d read sinfo/gres or show gres.conf), or
- Help convert a particular MPI/CUDA job script to the correct --gpus/--gres usage for one-GPU-per-rank or multi-GPU-per-node patterns.

Which would you prefer?

```text
## Socket Affinity Configuration [#Socket_Affinity](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Slurm's job scheduler handles GRES affinity on a socket basis internally.
However, the gres.conf interface allows administrators to specify `Cores` for GPU affinity configuration. This creates
a common misconception that Slurm will respect core-level affinity during job
scheduling, which it does not and never has. This can lead to issues where job
allocations and job steps don't align correctly, since job steps examine cores
while jobs use sockets.
```

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).
The total count of shards available on a node should be configured in
the slurm.conf file (e.g. "NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2,shard:64").

results.prompt: Explain Slurm GRES syntax and gpu resource requests
results.agent_response:
Summary — what GRES is
- GRES = Generic RESources. GPUs are usually exposed to Slurm as a GRES named "gpu" (configured in slurm.conf and/or gres.conf).
- The canonical GRES request form is: name[:type:count]
  - name = resource name from configuration (commonly "gpu")
  - type = optional subtype (GPU model or MIG profile string)
  - count = how many of that resource (see “per node vs. per job” below)

Common request options (equivalent/alternate forms)
- --gres=gpu[:type:count]
  - The --gres argument is interpreted as “generic resources required per node”.
- --gpus
  - Requests GPUs per job (shorthand). Good when you want a total number of GPUs for the job, not a per-node value.
- --gpus-per-node
  - Equivalent to --gres=gpu:count (i.e., GPUs requested on each allocated node).
- --gpus-per-task / --gpus-per-socket
  - More specific granular requests (per task or per socket) and require matching task/socket layout.

Syntax details and examples
- Basic per-node request:
  - sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:2
    - Means 2 nodes, and on each node allocate 2 GPUs ⇒ total GPUs = 2 nodes * 2 GPUs = 4 GPUs.
- Request X GPUs total on one node:
  - sbatch --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:4
  - or sbatch --nodes=1 --gpus=4
- Request a specific GPU type (type must match the GRES type configured in gres.conf):
  - sbatch --gres=gpu:V100:2
    - Requests 2 GPUs of type "V100" per node.
- Per-task GPUs:
  - sbatch --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1
    - This requests 1 GPU for each of 4 tasks ⇒ total 4 GPUs (Slurm will place tasks/nodes to satisfy that).
- Multiple GRES in one job:
  - sbatch --gres=gpu:2,license:matlab:1
    - Request 2 GPUs per node and 1 MATLAB license per node (example).

How counts are applied (important)
- --gres is per node. If you use --gres alone you must combine it with --nodes/--ntasks to get the total.
- --gpus (without the “per-” qualifier) typically means GPUs per job (total requested for the whole job).
- --gpus-per-node is per node (same semantic as --gres for GPUs).
- --gpus-per-task multiplies by the number of tasks to form the total GPU request.

Type field and MIG
- The optional type allows selecting a model or MIG profile: name:type:count.
- For MIG (A100) or other partitioned GPUs, the type string is matched to the configured MIG profile. Use the exact substring that the node advertises.
- If you need specific MIG instances, ensure node gres.conf and slurmd are configured to advertise them.

Sharing, sharding, MPS
- By default Slurm will allocate GPUs to jobs according to the configured counts; GPU sharing behavior depends on how the GRES is configured:
  - Exclusive allocation (one job per GPU) is typical.
  - Sharding or MPS can be configured so multiple jobs share a GPU — this requires cluster-side configuration (slurm.conf/gres.conf and select/cons_tres settings).
- If you plan to oversubscribe GPUs, check with cluster admins and the node’s gres.conf settings.

Practicals / best practices
- Always request matching CPU resources: e.g., --cpus-per-task or --ntasks-per-node so you don’t get CPU-starved while waiting for GPUs.
- If you want X GPUs total but don’t care about node packing, use --gpus=X (shorthand) and let Slurm place them.
- To force all GPUs on one node, use --nodes=1 --gpus=4 (or --gres=gpu:4).
- To see what GPUs and GRES a node advertises, use: sinfo -Nel or scontrol show node <nodename>. (These show the Gres= entries.)
- Slurm sets environment variables (e.g., CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES) inside the job so your CUDA/CuPy/PyTorch code sees only the allocated devices — code usually just works without extra binding.

Quick cheat-sheet lines to put in job headers
- 2 GPUs on any node (job-wide placement):
  - #SBATCH --gpus=2
- 2 GPUs per node across 3 nodes (total 6 GPUs):
  - #SBATCH --nodes=3
  - #SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
- 1 GPU per task, 8 tasks (total 8 GPUs):
  - #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  - #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
- Request specific GPU model (if supported):
  - #SBATCH --gres=gpu:V100:2

Troubleshooting / checks
- If your request is rejected, common causes:
  - Cluster not configured with select/cons_tres plugin.
  - Requested type not present on any node.
  - Not enough GPUs in the partition/node.
- To inspect cluster GRES config and availability: sinfo -Nel, scontrol show node, or ask your admin for the gres.conf entries.

If you want, I can:
- Show examples tailored to your cluster (I can run sinfo/scontrol to show what GPU types and counts are actually advertised) — tell me which partition or node to inspect.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm GRES syntax and gpu resource requests
results.agent_response:
Good question — here’s a compact, practical guide to Slurm GRES and GPU request syntax, what Slurm does with your request, and common examples / pitfalls.

1) Basics — what GRES is
- GRES = Generic RESources. GPUs are usually configured as gres objects (Name=gpu) on each node (in slurm.conf and/or per-node gres.conf).
- The scheduler only grants GRES that are declared on nodes. The gres.conf/slurm.conf setup and the configured select plugin determine available GPU types and counts.

2) Core --gres syntax
- Form: --gres=name[:type[:count]]
  - name: resource name (usually gpu)
  - type: an optional type string (used to distinguish models, MIG sizes, etc.)
  - count: how many of that resource you request (defaults to 1 if omitted)
- Multiple different GRES can be requested by comma: --gres=gpu:tesla:2,shard:10
- Example: --gres=gpu:2  (request two GPUs; equivalent to gpu:count=2)
- Example: --gres=gpu:tesla:1  (request 1 GPU of type containing substring "tesla")

3) Convenience GPU options
- Newer Slurm provides higher-level flags (requires select/cons_tres plugin):
  - --gpus=N  (request N GPUs for the job)
  - --gpus-per-node=N  (force N GPUs on every allocated node)
  - --gpus-per-task=N  (allocate N GPUs for each task)
  - --gpus-per-socket (less common; per-socket request)
- These map to TRES/gpu accounting when the plugin is installed.

4) Request semantics (important)
- --gres=gpu:2 requests 2 GPUs per node unless using a per-job form such as --gpus (behavior depends on plugin and Slurm version). Prefer the explicit option you need:
  - To get exactly N GPUs total across job: use --gpus=N (if supported) or control with --nodes and --gpus-per-node.
  - To get N GPUs on each node: use --gres=gpu:N or --gpus-per-node=N.
  - To give each task a GPU: use --gpus-per-task=1 with --ntasks or task count.
- Slurm enforces exclusivity only if GPUs are configured as exclusive or if cgroup/device constraints are used. Shared modes (MPS, sharding, MIG) permit multiple allocations on same physical GPU depending on admin config.

5) Types, MIG, and advanced selection
- The optional type string can represent GPU model or MIG profile substring (e.g., --gres=gpu:a100-7g.10gb:1). When AutoDetect=nvml and MIG is configured, Slurm can present MIG profiles as types; the type is matched as a substring as reported by slurmd.
- You cannot generally pick a specific GPU device by its UUID via --gres; selection is by configured GRES types and counts. Admins can map device files in gres.conf which influences allocation.

6) What Slurm sets inside your job
- Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for job steps so the job sees only the GPUs allocated to it (per-node, per-step).
- Newer Slurm versions also set variables like SLURM_JOB_GPUS / SLURM_STEP_GPUS (lists of allocated GPU ids/UUIDs) and SLURM_GPUS_ON_NODE, when available — check your Slurm version and configuration.
- If cgroups device/file visibility is enabled, the job cannot access GPU device files not assigned to it.

7) MPS, sharding, and sharing
- MPS: request gres=mps:N (if configured) to use CUDA MPS sharing. Admin must configure counts in slurm.conf/gres.conf.
- Sharding allows multiple jobs to share a GPU by allocating “shard” GRES; it does not fence GPU contexts and is for homogeneous workloads.
- MIG: Slurm supports NVIDIA MIG when configured (AutoDetect=nvml). Treat MIG instances as individual GPUs and use the type string to request particular MIG sizes.

8) Accounting and TRES
- GPU allocations are recorded as a TRES (tres/gpu or gres/gpu) for scheduling and accounting if AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu is enabled.
- gpumem and gpuutil can be reported if configured (nvml/rsmi).

9) Examples
- Batch script header (common):
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:4
  (gives 4 GPUs per node or total depending on plugin/version; prefer --gpus for total)
- Request 2 GPUs total (if supported):
  sbatch --gpus=2 myjob.sh
- Request 1 GPU per MPI task (4 tasks):
  sbatch --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1 my_mpi_job.sh
- Request 2 GPUs on each node allocated (3 nodes => 6 GPUs total):
  sbatch --nodes=3 --gpus-per-node=2 myjob.sh
- Request GPUs of a specific type (admin-defined substring):
  sbatch --gres=gpu:rtx6000:2 myjob.sh

10) Troubleshooting / tips
- If a request is rejected: check sinfo and node gres configuration (ask admin or run sinfo -R / scontrol show node).
- To see how many GPUs you have on a node: sinfo or nvidia-smi on the node (if you can access it).
- If CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES isn't what you expect, the node’s slurmd/gres/cgroup configuration may differ; ask the admin or inspect slurm.conf/gres.conf.
- Use scontrol show node <node> to inspect the node’s Gres and GresTypes if you have permission.

11) Summary recommendations
- Prefer --gpus / --gpus-per-node / --gpus-per-task when select/cons_tres is enabled — they are clearer and map to TRES.
- Use --gres=gpu[:type:count] when you need to request specific GRES types or when the cluster uses legacy GRES config.
- Rely on CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES inside the job to find which devices you can use; do not assume physical device indices match cluster-wide indices.

If you want, I can:
- Show exact syntax fragments from the Slurm docs for any of the options (sbatch/srun/gres) or
- Give ready-to-use sbatch header examples tailored to your workload (MPI / PyTorch / single-node multi-GPU), or
- Check your cluster’s available GPU resources and types (I can run sinfo for you) — tell me which partition or node to inspect.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm GRES syntax and gpu resource requests
results.agent_response:
Summary — two syntaxes
- --gres=name[:type:count]  (generic resource request; treated per node)
- Convenience options equivalent to or layered on top of GRES for GPUs:
  - --gpus=<count>            (GPUs required per job)
  - --gpus-per-node=<count>   (GPUs required per node; equivalent to --gres for gpu)
  - --gpus-per-task=<count>   (GPUs required per task)

Key rules and semantics
- --gres: format is name[:type[:count]]. For GPUs the name is usually "gpu". Example forms:
  - --gres=gpu:2           (2 GPUs per node)
  - --gres=gpu:V100:2      (2 GPUs per node of type V100 — the "type" must match what is configured in gres.conf/slurm.conf)
- --gpus is a job-level request (total GPUs for the job). --gpus-per-node and --gpus-per-task express per-node or per-task counts.
- Behavior is plugin-dependent: the --gpus and --gpus-per-* shortcuts require Slurm's select/cons_tres configuration. If your cluster uses a plain GRES setup, use --gres.
- When you combine node count and per-node requests: total GPUs allocated = nodes * (gpus-per-node) (or nodes * count in --gres).
- When you use --gpus-per-task with --ntasks, Slurm will try to allocate one GPU for each task (useful for one-GPU-per-rank MPI).

Examples
- Request 2 GPUs on one node (per-node and single-node):
  #SBATCH --nodes=1
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:2
  or
  #SBATCH --gpus=2
- Request 1 GPU on each of 4 nodes:
  #SBATCH --nodes=4
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-node=1
  or
  #SBATCH --nodes=4
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
- Request 1 GPU per MPI rank (8 ranks):
  #SBATCH --ntasks=8
  #SBATCH --gpus-per-task=1
- Request specific GPU model if configured:
  #SBATCH --gres=gpu:V100:2
  (Type string must match the Type/name given in gres.conf or slurm.conf.)

Environment variables (what Slurm sets for your job)
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set for each job step so your process sees only the GPUs allocated to it (device IDs are local to the node).
- Slurm may also export variables such as SLURM_CPUS_PER_GPU when cpus-per-gpu is used; exact variables can vary by Slurm version and configuration.

Cluster-side configuration you should know
- The actual GPU names/types and counts are configured in slurm.conf and gres.conf on the nodes. If a type/name is requested that doesn't exist, the job will be rejected or remain pending.
- Features like MPS or GPU sharding require additional config (gres/mps or shard counts) and change how fractions or multiple jobs can share GPUs.
- The scheduler enforces allocations. You cannot rely on libraries enumerating all /dev/nvidia* devices; use the Slurm environment variables and CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES inside the job.

Common pitfalls & tips
- Per-node vs per-job confusion: --gres is per node; --gpus is per job. Pick the right one for multi-node jobs.
- If you ask for --gpus-per-task but don’t set ntasks as you expect, you may not get the intended mapping.
- If you need a specific model, using the type field in --gres is usually better than generic constraints, but both can work depending on how the cluster is configured.
- If you expect GPU sharing (MPS/sharding), confirm the cluster’s gres.conf and that the select/cons_tres plugin supports your intended sharing mode.
- To see what GPUs a node advertises: ask your admin or inspect sinfo / scontrol show node (your cluster may expose Gres info).

If you want, I can:
- Give ready-to-copy sbatch header templates for common workflows (single-GPU training, multi-node MPI with 1 GPU/rank, multi-GPU single-node).
- Check your cluster’s configured GPU types/counts (I can run sinfo/scontrol_show if you want me to inspect the live cluster).

results.prompt: Explain --gres=gpu:N and GPU allocation behavior
results.agent_response:
Summary: --gres=gpu:N (and the newer --gpus family) request N GPU devices from Slurm for your job. Slurm allocates GPUs as generic resources (GRES) and enforces those allocations per node or per task depending on the option you choose. Slurm also sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for each job step so your process sees only the GPUs assigned to it.

Key points

- Basic syntax and equivalents
  - --gres=gpu:N requests N GPUs (GRES) per node for the job allocation.
  - Modern alternatives: --gpus=N, --gpus-per-node=N (equivalent to --gres=gpu:N), --gpus-per-task=M (request per task/rank).
  - You can request a specific GPU type with name[:type:count], e.g. --gres=gpu:tesla:2.
  - These options work with sbatch, srun and salloc (they are supported by the select/cons_tres plugin).

- Per-node vs per-task vs total
  - By default --gres/gpu is "per node". Example: sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:2 → Slurm will try to give 2 GPUs on each of the 2 nodes (total 4 GPUs).
  - --gpus-per-task and --gpus-per-node change semantics:
    - --gpus-per-task=1 with --ntasks=4 on one node → 4 GPUs on that node (1 per task).
    - --gpus-per-node behaves like --gres=gpu:N (N per node).
  - There is no built-in "give me N GPUs across the whole job regardless of nodes" flag in the simple per-node syntax; you request per-node counts or per-task counts that determine the total.

- Exclusivity, sharing, and special cases
  - By default GPUs are allocated exclusively (a GPU assigned to one job will not be given to another concurrently).
  - GPU sharing is possible only if the cluster is configured for it (examples: NVIDIA MPS configured as a separate GRES type, or administrator-configured fractional/shared GRES via gres.conf). This requires admin-side configuration and the select/cons_tres plugin features.
  - MIG devices can be reported and used when AutoDetect and driver support are present; MIG handling and accounting have special considerations (NVML/MIG limits).

- How Slurm exposes allocated GPUs to your job
  - Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for each job step that runs on a compute node so the process sees only the GPUs assigned to that step on that node.
  - CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set when tasks are launched on a compute node (each step); for sbatch it reflects node 0 of the allocation for the batch-script’s top-level environment.
  - The mapping renumbers the assigned physical GPUs to a local 0..(N-1) index in the environment. Your program sees device 0 as the first assigned physical device, etc.
  - Container runtimes that honor CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (or NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES) will inherit the same mapping, so GPU isolation works inside containers.

- enforce-binding and affinity
  - Some Slurm configs support --gres-flags=enforce-binding which tightens assignment and binding behavior (bind GPUs to tasks/cores). Admin configuration and Slurm version determine exact behavior. When enforce-binding is active, Slurm more strictly ensures tasks are pinned to the allocated GPU(s) and sets the environment for that binding.

- Accounting and metrics
  - GPUs are tracked as a TRES (gres/gpu) when configured. If AccountingStorageTRES includes gres/gpu, Slurm can record GPU usage metrics (withnvml/rsmi support).
  - Note: NVML may not provide utilization metrics for MIG slices; accounting behavior differs for MIG.

- What happens if resources aren’t available
  - If the requested GPUs (per node or per-task) cannot be satisfied, the job remains PENDING until an allocation matching the request becomes possible.
  - Slurm’s scheduler enforces those counts when placing jobs; partial allocations that don’t meet the per-node/per-task constraint are not granted.

Examples
  - sbatch --gres=gpu:2 myjob.sh
    -> requests 2 GPUs on every node allocated to the job (common for single-node jobs).
  - sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:2 myjob.sh
    -> requests 2 GPUs on each of 2 nodes (total 4 GPUs).
  - sbatch --ntasks=4 --gpus-per-task=1 my_mpi_job.sh
    -> requests 1 GPU for each of the 4 tasks (if they are placed on one node, that node needs 4 GPUs).
  - srun --gres=gpu:1 --pty bash
    -> starts an interactive step with 1 GPU allocated on the node the step runs on.

Quick tips / troubleshooting
  - If your job still sees all GPUs (not only assigned ones): make sure you launch tasks via srun inside the allocation (srun sets per-step envs), and check cluster version/config and whether Slurm is configured to set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.
  - Use nvidia-smi inside the job to verify which physical device corresponds to your CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES mapping.
  - If you need GPU sharing or fractional GPUs, talk to your cluster admins — it requires special gres.conf and scheduler configuration (MPS, fractional GRES, or explicit MIG configuration).
  - If you need a GPU on only one node in a multi-node job, request per-task GPUs and control task placement, or request one node with --nodes=1 plus other nodes without GPUs.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact behavior on your cluster (how many GPUs per node, how CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is being set) — I would run sinfo and/or show an example srun/sbatch allocation for your cluster, or
- give concrete sbatch/srun examples tailored to your workload (MPI, PyTorch DDP, containers).

# "Configless" Slurm
"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of
configuration files on the Slurm controllers — "configless" in Slurm's
parlance means that the compute nodes, login nodes, and other cluster hosts
do not need to be deployed with local copies of these files.
The slurmd on startup will reach out to a slurmctld that you specify and the
config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV
records defined within the cluster itself.

results.prompt: Explain --gres=gpu:N and GPU allocation behavior
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- --gres=gpu:N requests N generic GPU resources. By default --gres is interpreted as "per node": --gres=gpu:2 asks for 2 GPUs on every allocated node.
- There are more convenient aliases/variants:
  - --gpus=N (request N GPUs for the whole job)
  - --gpus-per-node=N (equivalent to --gres=gpu:N)
  - --gpus-per-task=N (request N GPUs for each task)
  - --gres=gpu:TYPE:COUNT (request GPUs of a specific type/MIG slice)
- Slurm enforces exclusivity and sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES (and similar per-step environment) so each job-step/task only sees its assigned GPUs.

Behavior and examples
1) --gres=gpu is per-node
- sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:2 ... => scheduler will give you 2 GPUs on each of the 2 nodes (total GPUs = 4).
- sbatch --gres=gpu:2 --nodes=1 ... => 2 GPUs on the single allocated node.

2) --gpus vs --gpus-per-node (--gres)
- sbatch --gpus=4 --nodes=2 ... => requests 4 GPUs total. Scheduler will pick nodes and distribute GPUs to satisfy the total (commonly 2+2 if each node has ≥2 GPUs), but exact packing depends on node capacities and availability.
- sbatch --gpus-per-node=2 --nodes=2 ... (same as --gres=gpu:2 --nodes=2) => rigidly 2 GPUs on every node.

3) Per-task GPU requests
- sbatch --ntasks=8 --gpus-per-task=1 ... => 1 GPU allocated to each task (8 GPUs total). Slurm will place tasks across nodes to satisfy that (spreading or packing depending on policy).
- If you instead used --gres=gpu:2 plus --ntasks=8, the scheduler gives 2 GPUs per node; how tasks map to those GPUs depends on how you launch them (srun binding) and on your tasks-per-node.

What Slurm sets for you inside the job
- For each job step launched on a node Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES so that processes only see the GPU device indexes assigned to them on that node. This makes it safe to run multiple jobs/steps on the same physical node without interfering.
- The exact device index values are the local device numbers as reported by the driver/NVML or as configured in gres.conf; Slurm remaps visibility so each job sees only its assigned subset.
- Note: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set per-node/per-step when tasks start; interactive allocation tools (salloc) may not export a global CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES until you srun a step.

Device selection, types, and MIG
- gres supports a type field: --gres=gpu:V100:2 or --gres=gpu:MIG-<slice>:N (if your gres.conf and Slurm are configured for MIG). This lets you request particular device types or MIG slices.
- AutoDetect=nvml (common) populates device info from the driver; gres.conf can override explicit device files/affinity if needed.

Accounting and enforcement
- GPUs are tracked as a TRES (gres/gpu). If configured (AutoDetect=nvml + AccountingStorageTRES=gres/gpu) Slurm can collect gpu memory and utilization metrics (gres/gpumem, gres/gpuutil).
- Enforced access to device files is typically done via cgroups so a task cannot open other /dev/nvidia devices even if the driver enumerates them — Slurm can restrict device-node visibility.

Common gotchas and tips
- If you want a fixed total (not per-node), prefer --gpus=N; if you want per-node parity, use --gres=gpu:N or --gpus-per-node.
- For per-task GPU workloads use --gpus-per-task (or combine --ntasks with explicit resource requests) to avoid accidental oversubscription.
- Check device mapping inside the job: run nvidia-smi (or nvml-based tool) in your job step to confirm which physical GPUs you were given and the mapping to CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.
- If your cluster uses MIG, be explicit about types if you need a particular slice.
- The select/cons_tres plugin must be in use for --gpu* options to be honored; otherwise Slurm will reject GPU requests.

If you want, I can give concrete sbatch/srun examples for your use case (single-node multi-GPU training, multi-node data-parallel, mixed CPU-only + GPU tasks), or explain how to verify allocations with sinfo/squeue and nvidia-smi.

```text
results.prompt: Explain --gres=gpu:N and GPU allocation behavior
results.agent_response:
Summary first
- --gres=gpu:N (the historical generic-resource form) requests N GPUs per node for your job step.
- Slurm also provides user-friendly aliases: --gpus=<count> (GPUs per job/allocation), --gpus-per-node=<count> (GPUs per node), and --gpus-per-task=<count> (GPUs attached to each task).
- Slurm will allocate whole GPU devices unless your cluster is configured for sharing (MPS, sharding, or MIG slices). Slurm then sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES inside the job to make only the allocated device(s) visible.

Details

1) The request forms and what they mean
- --gres=gpu[:<type>:]<count>
  - The gres option is a per-node generic-resource request. By default that means "<count> GPUs per node".
- --gpus=<count>
  - Requests <count> GPUs for the whole job/allocation (total across nodes).
- --gpus-per-node=<count>
  - Equivalent to asking for that many GPUs on every node in the allocation.
- --gpus-per-task=<count>
  - Requests that many GPUs for each task (requires supplying a task count). Slurm tries to place/assign GPUs so each task gets the requested number.

Note: the --gpu* options require the select/cons_tres plugin (and proper gres.conf / slurm.conf) on the cluster; otherwise the request will be rejected.

2) How Slurm chooses devices and what your job sees
- Device mapping: GPUs are configured via gres.conf (or autodetected). Slurm maps the logical "gpu" gres units to physical device files (/dev/nvidia0, /dev/nvidia1, or MIG slice devices) on each node.
- Visibility: for each job step that runs on a node, Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to a comma-separated list of node-local device indices that the step may use. This is done per node and per step:
  - For sbatch the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES you see in the job environment reflects the allocation on node 0 of the allocation (sbatch sets the environment only from node 0).
  - When tasks are launched on other nodes, the step-launch environment for those tasks will also have CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES set on that node to the devices allocated there.
- Device numbering is node-local. "GPU 0" on nodeA is independent of "GPU 0" on nodeB.
- If the cluster is configured to use cgroups to restrict device node access, Slurm may also hide or whitelist /dev/nvidia* devices inside the job's cgroup in addition to setting CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES.

3) Whole-device vs sharing
- By default Slurm allocates whole GPUs (one gres unit = whole device).
- Sharing options:
  - MPS (CUDA Multi-Process Service): when configured, Slurm can allocate fractional MPS resources (configured via gres/mps).
  - Sharding: Slurm's sharding feature lets you configure many shards per GPU and allocate them as GRES; this does not fence the hardware — it's a logical share.
  - MIG (NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU): Slurm can be configured (AutoDetect=nvml, and correct gres.conf) to detect and allocate MIG slices as separate GRES units. Behavior depends on how the system admin set up gres.conf.
- If your site supports any of the above, you must check how the cluster exposes those resources (gres type names, environment vars, or device files).

4) Binding GPUs to tasks (common patterns)
- If you want 1 GPU per MPI rank / per process:
  - Use --gpus-per-task=1 and launch one task per rank (e.g., srun --ntasks=NUM_RANKS ...). Slurm will attempt to assign distinct GPUs to each task.
- If you want N GPUs on each node for a single multi-GPU job:
  - sbatch --gres=gpu:N -N1 or sbatch --gpus-per-node=N -N1
- If you request a total number of GPUs (--gpus=TOTAL) across multiple nodes, Slurm will distribute GPUs across nodes to satisfy the count and your other constraints (node count, partitions, etc.).
- Newer Slurm versions provide --gpu-bind (and related options) to control how GPUs are selected/mapped to tasks (see your cluster docs / man page).

5) How to confirm what you got (debugging tips)
- Inside a job step run:
  - echo $CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
  - nvidia-smi -L
  - nvidia-smi topo - or nvidia-smi (shows devices visible and UUIDs)
- From the controller/admin side use: scontrol show job <jobid> (AllocTRES, GresDetail) or scontrol show node to inspect gres configuration (admins). As a user, check your job environment variables as above.

6) Practical examples
- Request 2 GPUs on a single node:
  - sbatch --gpus-per-node=2 -N1 ...
  - or sbatch --gres=gpu:2 -N1 ...
- Request 8 GPUs total and let scheduler pick nodes:
  - sbatch --gpus=8 ...
  - The scheduler may give 4 nodes × 2 GPUs each, or 2 nodes × 4 GPUs each, depending on availability and constraints.
- Request 1 GPU per task for a 16-rank job:
  - sbatch --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks=16 ...
```

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).

```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```

### Special case - manual startup [#manual_startup](https://slurm.schedmd.com/cgroup_v2.html)
Starting slurmd from systemd creates the slurmd unit with its own cgroup.
Then slurmd starts the slurmstepd.scope which in turn creates a new cgroup
tree. Any new process spawned for a job is migrated into this scope. If,
instead of starting slurmd from systemd, one starts slurmd manually from the
command line, things are different. The slurmd will be spawned into the same
terminal's cgroup and will share the cgroup tree with the terminal process
itself (and possibly with other user processes).

environment variable. This variable is normally set by systemd when it starts
a process and is a way to determine if slurmd has been started in its own

```text
results.prompt: Explain --gres=gpu:N and GPU allocation behavior
results.agent_response:
Summary — what --gres=gpu:N means
- "--gres=gpu:N" requests N generic GPU resources per node for your job. It is equivalent to "--gpus-per-node N" (when Slurm is using the select/cons_tres plugin).
- There are also options with different semantics:
  - --gpus=<M> requests M GPUs per job (total across the allocation).
  - --gpus-per-node=<N> requests N GPUs per node (same as --gres=gpu:N).
  - --gpus-per-task=<k> requests k GPUs for each task (works with a task count).

How Slurm allocates those GPUs
- Allocation is done per-node (for --gres=gpu:N / --gpus-per-node) or per-job (for --gpus). If you ask for N GPUs per node and you get X nodes, total GPUs = N * X.
  - Example: #SBATCH --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:2  → 2 GPUs on each node, total 4 GPUs.
  - Example: #SBATCH --gpus=4 --nodes=2  → 4 GPUs total; Slurm will place those 4 across the allocation (not necessarily 2 per node).
- GPUs are consumable integer resources by default. Slurm reserves whole GPU devices, not fractional GPU time, unless the cluster is explicitly configured for sharing (see MPS, MIG, or custom GRES entries).
- Slurm maps specific device IDs on each node and sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for each job step so the job sees only its assigned GPUs on that node. The variable is set when tasks are launched on compute nodes (sbatch’s top-level env may only reflect node 0).

Per-task behavior and task layouts
- If you run multiple tasks on a node (multiple tasks-per-node), how GPUs are divided depends on:
  - whether you used --gpus-per-task (or --gres per task) and the task count; Slurm will allocate GPUs per task accordingly, or
  - if you only requested GPUs per node, Slurm gives N GPUs to the node and it’s up to your task launcher / MPI / application to place tasks onto those GPUs.
- For deterministic per-task GPU assignment use --gpus-per-task together with --ntasks or use srun with task-affinity options.

Device naming, types, and selection
- The --gres argument accepts the form name[:type:count]. You can request a specific GPU type if configured in gres.conf (e.g., --gres=gpu:V100:2).
- Slurm uses the cluster’s gres.conf mapping (dev nodes like /dev/nvidia0, /dev/nvidia1, or MIG partitions) when assigning device indices.

Sharing (MPS / MIG / custom)
- NVIDIA MPS, MIG, or cluster-specific GRES entries can allow multiple jobs to share a physical GPU. That must be enabled/declared in gres.conf and supported by the select/cons_tres plugin. In those cases the GRES entry may represent slices or MPS capacity rather than whole devices.
- Without such configuration, jobs get exclusive GPUs.

What you will see and how to inspect
- Inside a running job step: echo $CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES shows the devices the step may use on that node.
- From the scheduler / admin view:
  - scontrol show job <jobid> shows AllocTRES / Gres and the node list for that job.
  - scontrol show node <nodename> or sinfo / sinfo -N shows per-node GRES and availability.
- If a job was rejected because the gres/cons_tres plugin isn’t configured, Slurm will reject GPU requests (look for messages from sbatch/salloc).

Common pitfalls
- Confusing “per node” vs “per job”: using --gres=gpu:N with multiple nodes multiplies the GPU count unless you intended a total-GPU request.
- Expecting fractional GPU sharing without cluster configuration (MPS/MIG) — by default Slurm reserves whole GPUs.
- Assuming CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES lists cluster-wide IDs — it’s per-node and remapped so the job only sees its local assigned GPUs.

If you want, I can:
- Show exact fields to check in scontrol show job / scontrol show node (example output fields), or
- Give example sbatch/srun lines for common layouts (4 GPUs total spanning 2 nodes, or 2 GPUs per node with 4 tasks per node).
```

```text
results.prompt: Explain --gres=gpu:N and GPU allocation behavior
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise, practical explanation of what --gres=gpu:N does and how Slurm allocates and exposes GPUs to jobs.

What --gres=gpu:N means
- --gres=gpu:N (or equivalently --gpus-per-node=N) requests N generic GPU resources of type "gpu" on every allocated node for the job step. The form can include an optional type: name[:type:count] (e.g., --gres=gpu:V100:2) to request GPUs of a particular GRES type.
- --gpus (no “-per-node”) requests GPUs for the whole job (GPUs required per job), while --gpus-per-task asks for GPUs assigned to each task. (These GPU-specific options require the select/cons_tres plugin and that GRES be configured.)

How many GPUs you actually get
- Multi-node job: total GPUs = N * nodes_allocated when you use --gres=gpu:N.
  Example: sbatch --nodes=3 --gres=gpu:2 … → 3 nodes × 2 GPUs/node = 6 GPUs total.
- With --gpus (per-job): Slurm will allocate the requested number across the nodes it selects (not necessarily evenly unless constrained).
- With --gpus-per-task: Slurm assigns the given count to each task. You must specify task counts (ntasks) correctly so the scheduler can satisfy the request.

How Slurm exposes GPUs inside the job
- Slurm sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for each job step on each node so the job sees only its allocated GPUs on that node. Slurm typically remaps the physical device IDs so the job sees its GPUs as 0..(N-1) on that node.
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is set only when tasks are launched on a compute node (not globally for salloc before node allocation).
- Some installations also set SLURM_* GPU environment variables (behavior/version-dependent), but CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is the canonical mechanism.

Exclusive vs shared GPU usage
- GPUs are normally exclusive GRES: once allocated to a job, that GPU isn’t given to another job.
- Sharing is possible only if the cluster admin has configured a sharing mechanism (MPS, sharding, or custom gres.conf entries). Example: GRES=mps or shards can allow multiple jobs to share GPU resources subject to admin config.
- If you need fractional usage (percent of a GPU), ask about MPS/sharding on your cluster — you cannot request “0.5 GPU” without cluster-level sharing support.

MIG and heterogeneous GPUs
- Slurm supports NVIDIA MIG: MIG instances can be advertised as separate GRES entries and scheduled like distinct GPUs if configured (AutoDetect=nvml in gres.conf). You can request specific MIG types via the type string.
- For heterogeneous nodes (different GPU models), use type in the GRES request to ensure a node with the correct GPU type is chosen.

Task-to-GPU binding
- --gpus-per-task makes Slurm bind GPUs to individual tasks. When you run srun/sbatch with multiple tasks on the same node, Slurm will set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES for each task so tasks get different GPUs (subject to configuration).
- If task/CPU placement and GPUs-per-task are inconsistent (e.g., too many tasks on a node for available GPUs), the job may remain pending until a node with enough GPUs is found.

Common gotchas and tips
- Remember that --gres=gpu:N is per node. If you expected N total GPUs for a multi-node job, use --gpus (per-job) or calculate N_total / nodes.
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES inside the job typically lists only the local allocation and is remapped to 0..N-1 — don’t assume these indices match the global physical device numbers unless you inspect the node.
- If your job needs specific physical device IDs (rare), use a prolog/epilog or node-local discovery inside the job to map the physical devices from SLURM-provided info.
- If your job needs to run multiple processes on the same GPU (sharing), check whether your cluster supports MPS/sharding and how to request it (gres=mps:count).
- If GPU requests are rejected, verify that GRES is configured on the nodes and that you used the correct syntax/type.

Examples
- sbatch --gres=gpu:2 myscript.sh
  - Allocates 2 GPUs on each allocated node for the job step.
- sbatch --gpus=4 myscript.sh
  - Requests 4 GPUs for the whole job; scheduler will place them across nodes as needed.
- sbatch --gpus-per-task=1 --ntasks=8 myscript.sh
  - Requests 1 GPU for each of 8 tasks (total 8 GPUs required), scheduler will place tasks/nodes accordingly.

If you want, I can:
- Show the exact env vars your cluster sets inside a job (requires running a job or inspecting node config), or
- Explain how to request MIG instances or MPS/shard sharing on your specific cluster (I can check your cluster’s gres configuration if you want).
```

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Node Configuration[#node_config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Node parameters of interest include:
Feature [#Feature](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
A node feature can be associated with resources acquired from the
cloud and user jobs can specify their preference for resource use with
the `--constraint` option.
NodeName [#NodeName](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)

## SIGNALS AND ESCAPE SEQUENCES[#SECTION_SIGNALS-AND-ESCAPE-SEQUENCES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
Signals sent to the srun command are automatically forwarded to
the tasks it is controlling with a few exceptions. The escape sequence
<control-c> will report the state of all tasks associated with
the srun command. If <control-c> is entered twice within
one second, then the associated SIGINT signal will be sent to all tasks
and a termination sequence will be entered sending SIGCONT, SIGTERM,
and SIGKILL to all spawned tasks.
If a third <control-c> is received, the srun program will be
terminated without waiting for remote tasks to exit or their I/O to
complete.
The escape sequence <control-z> is presently ignored.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

### Valid and Invalid Requests [#Valid](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:

```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```

```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```

salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:

The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text

```

must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)

to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill

are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm --constraint syntax for node features
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Use -C or --constraint to select nodes by their configured Feature tokens (the Feature= list on each NodeName in slurm.conf).
- The constraint value is a boolean expression of feature names; use & (AND) or comma (,) for AND, | for OR, and parentheses to group. Quote the expression so the shell doesn’t split it.

Details and examples
- Features: Nodes are tagged in slurm.conf (or helpers.conf) with Feature=token1,token2,...; --constraint matches those tokens.
- Operators:
  - & or , — logical AND (both features must be present)
  - | — logical OR (one or the other)
  - ( ) — grouping/precedence
- Quoting: put the whole expression in quotes, e.g. -C "gpu&v100" or -C "(gpu|fpga),ssd".
- Examples:
  - -C "v100" — any node with feature v100
  - -C "gpu|fpga" — nodes with gpu OR fpga
  - -C "gpu,ssd" (or -C "gpu&ssd") — nodes that have both gpu AND ssd
  - -C "(gpu|fpga),highmem" — nodes that are highmem AND either gpu or fpga

Notes
- --constraint matches the feature tokens assigned to nodes; it filters at job submission time.
- There is a separate "extra constraints" mechanism (SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints) with its own key/value syntax if your site uses node Extra fields rather than Feature tokens.

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.

## Timers
Slurm has a variety of timers to control when to consider a node DOWN,
when to purge job records, how long to give a job to gracefully terminate, etc.
SlurmctldTimeout : How many seconds the backup controller waits before
becoming the active controller
SlurmdTimeout : How many seconds the Slurm controller waits for the slurmd
to respond to a request before considering the node DOWN
InactiveLimit : How many seconds the Slurm controller waits for srun
commands to respond before considering the job or job step inactive and
terminating it. A value of zero indicates unlimited wait
MinJobAge : How many seconds the Slurm controller waits after a
job terminates before purging its record. A record of the job will
persist in job completion and/or accounting records indefinitely,
but will no longer be visible with the squeue command after puring

# Slurm Workload Manager
Slurm is an open-source workload manager designed for Linux clusters of
all sizes.
It provides three key functions.
First it allocates exclusive and/or non-exclusive access to resources
(computer nodes) to users for some duration of time so they can perform work.
Second, it provides a framework for starting, executing, and monitoring work
(typically a parallel job) on a set of allocated nodes.
Finally, it arbitrates contention for resources by managing a queue of
pending work.
Slurm's design is very modular with dozens of optional plugins.
In its simplest configuration, it can be installed and configured in a
couple of minutes (see [Caos NSA and Perceus: All-in-one Cluster Software Stack](http://www.linux-mag.com/id/7239/1/)
by Jeffrey B. Layton).
More complex configurations can satisfy the job scheduling needs of
world-class computer centers and rely upon a

Slurm can be configured to collect accounting information for every
job and job step executed.
Accounting records can be written to a simple text file or a database.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text

```

must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features
become available but not active. Any feature not defined by
NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.
Example:
```text
slurm.conf: NodeFeaturesPlugins=node_features/helpers NodeName=cloud[1-5] ... State=CLOUD Feature=f1,f2,l1 NodeName=cloud[6-10] ... State=...
```

If a feature is defined in the helpers.conf and is not defined on a

slurm.conf, that feature is treated as a changeable/rebootable feature by the
controller. For example, if feature fa is defined on node node1 in
the slurm.conf but is only listed on node2 in the

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.
