### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

scontrol is used to view or modify Slurm configuration including: job,
job step, node, partition, reservation, and overall system configuration. Most
of the commands require elevated permissions to run (also see the

nodes which can be used to simplify the partition configuration section,

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill

nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Summary — what node features are
- A node feature is a short string tag assigned to a compute node (examples: gpu, v100, ssd, nvme, infiniband, ib, highmem). Features describe hardware, software, or site-specific capabilities that the scheduler can match against job requests.
- Features are visible in two forms:
  - AvailableFeatures: features the node is capable of (from slurm.conf or a NodeFeaturesPlugin).
  - ActiveFeatures: features currently active on that node (what the scheduler actually uses for matching).
- Features can be static (defined in slurm.conf) or dynamic via a NodeFeaturesPlugin/helpers (used for power-saving/cloud nodes or other runtime state changes). Features defined by a NodeFeaturesPlugin may be “available but not active” until the node is prepared for the job.

How features are used for placement
- Filtering candidate nodes: When you request a feature the scheduler only considers nodes that match that feature expression (usually ActiveFeatures). In effect a feature request narrows the pool of candidate nodes before the normal resource-selection/allocation logic runs.
- Example effect: --constraint=gpu limits placement to nodes tagged with the gpu feature. Combined constraints (see next section) further narrow choices, which can increase wait time if matching nodes are scarce.
- Dynamic activation: If a feature is defined as available but not active (e.g., powered-down cloud nodes), and a job requests that feature, Slurm can allocate and activate that node (power it on / enable the feature) at allocation time. Features not managed by NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.
- Interaction with other resources: Features are one of several filters the scheduler uses (along with partition, QOS, TRES/GRES, CPU/memory requests, topology, affinity). A node may match a feature but still be unsuitable (insufficient CPUs, memory, or GRES), so jobs can still remain pending even when nodes with the feature exist.
- Fragmentation and scheduling behavior: Rare/unique features reduce packing flexibility. If you request many specific features you may force the scheduler to leave small unusable islands of capacity or increase job wait times. Conversely tagging similar nodes with a common feature can make placement more predictable.

Feature expressions / syntax (common usage)
- Request a single feature:
  - sbatch --constraint=gpu
- Logical combinations (supported operators): & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), ! (NOT), parentheses for grouping.
  - sbatch --constraint="gpu&ssd"   (nodes that have both gpu AND ssd)
  - sbatch --constraint="v100|a100" (nodes with v100 OR a100)
  - sbatch --constraint="gpu&!v100" (gpu nodes that are NOT v100)
  - sbatch --constraint="(a100|v100)&nvme" (A100 or V100 nodes that also have nvme)
- Tip: use explicit operators and parentheses to avoid ambiguity.

Commands to inspect and change features
- See a node’s current features:
  - scontrol show node=<nodename>  → look for ActiveFeatures= and AvailableFeatures=
  - sinfo --Node or sinfo -Nel also shows features in the node list output
- Change a node’s ActiveFeatures (requires admin privileges):
  - scontrol update NodeName=<node> ActiveFeatures=<comma-separated-features>

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Short, focused guide to "node features" and how they affect placement in Slurm.

What a "feature" is
- A feature is a string tag attached to a node (e.g., gpu_v100, infiniband, ssd, cuda11). It is metadata the scheduler uses to decide which nodes satisfy a job's requirements.
- Features are configured in slurm.conf (NodeName ... Feature=...) or provided dynamically by node feature plugins/helpers (NodeFeaturesPlugins / helpers.conf) or via the node "Extra" JSON (see extra_constraints).

Where features appear in Slurm
- scontrol show node <node> shows ActiveFeatures and AvailableFeatures fields.
- slurm.conf can use Feature= in NodeSets/NodeName to group nodes by feature.

Active vs available (and changeable features)
- ActiveFeatures: features currently enabled/active on that node.
- AvailableFeatures: features the node is capable of (may be present but not currently active).
- Features defined/managed by NodeFeaturesPlugins (helpers) can be "available but not active" (common with cloud/power-save nodes). When a job requests such a feature, slurmctld may allocate and activate (power-on or run helper) the node at allocation time.
- Any feature not managed by NodeFeaturesPlugins is normally always active.

How jobs request features (and extra constraints)
- --constraint / -C: request nodes that have a given feature string (common for hardware/software labels). Example usage pattern: sbatch --constraint=<feature>
  - The scheduler filters nodes to only those that match the requested feature(s).
- SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints + --extra: lets jobs request key/value filters against the node Extra JSON (e.g., numeric or boolean attributes). This supports comparison operators and boolean composition (AND/& or OR/| as configured). Use this when you need numeric/structured matching beyond simple tags.

How features affect placement (scheduler behavior)
- Filtering: a feature requirement reduces the set of eligible nodes. If no eligible nodes exist, the job remains pending until a matching node becomes available (or the job is cancelled).
- Activation at allocation: if a requested feature is only available (not active), slurmctld may allocate that node and run the helper/power-up path to make the feature active — this can add allocation latency while the node boots/activates.
- Backfill/planning: features reduce backfill flexibility. Jobs that request changeable features or extra constraints are harder for the scheduler to backfill accurately because the node state can change.
- Heterogeneity: if you request only a feature, Slurm may allocate multiple nodes that all satisfy that feature but are otherwise heterogeneous. If you need fully identical nodes, combine partition, nodeset, and features, or document expected homogeneity.
- Fragmentation: many fine-grained feature labels can fragment resources (fewer nodes match each label), increasing queue times for constrained jobs.
- Node reboots/changes: changing a node's active features (via helpers or scontrol update ActiveFeatures=...) may require a reboot; that affects node availability.

Practical implications & tips
- Prefer partitions or nodesets when you want broad separation (e.g., all GPU nodes in a gpu partition) and use features for finer-grained selection (GPU model, NIC type, installed software).
- For cloud/power-save nodes, expect extra allocation latency when features are activated; document which features are changeable.
- Use descriptive, consistent feature names (hardware_model, driver_version, software_x.y) to avoid accidental mismatches.
- Avoid excessive per-job unique feature labels; they fragment the scheduler and hurt throughput.
- If you need numeric or structured matching (e.g., free disk GB, temperature), use Extra + SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints and request via --extra.
- To inspect a node’s features and their status: scontrol show node <nodename>. To see partition/node counts use sinfo. (Use these commands to check feature activation and which nodes are eligible.)

When a requested feature isn't found
- If you request a feature and no nodes currently match, the job will wait. For changeable features, the scheduler may be able to activate matching nodes (with extra delay); otherwise you’ll need admins to add/label nodes or adjust partitions/features.

If you want, I can:
- Show the feature lists and active/available status for specific nodes (I can run scontrol show node or sinfo for those nodes) — tell me which node(s) to inspect.
- Help craft constraints or extra expressions for a particular selection (give the feature names or desired properties).

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text
a=1.23 a= b a!=1.24 a!=1.23|foo!=blah b=200 b=true foo =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
Here are some examples of invalid requests:
Invalid comparison operator:
```text
a, =0.00000001) ((c =0.1)
```
The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text
a!=1.23 b=0 b=false foo>baz ((c =0.00001)
```
Reminder: in order for two numbers to be considered equal, their difference
must be less than 0.0001. This is why 0.0001 is not considered equal to 0 and
thus the request `c>=0.0001` is not fulfilled,
but 0.00000001 is considered equal to 0 and thus the request

# Slurm Workload Manager
Slurm is an open-source workload manager designed for Linux clusters of
all sizes.
It provides three key functions.
First it allocates exclusive and/or non-exclusive access to resources
(computer nodes) to users for some duration of time so they can perform work.
Second, it provides a framework for starting, executing, and monitoring work
(typically a parallel job) on a set of allocated nodes.
Finally, it arbitrates contention for resources by managing a queue of
pending work.
Slurm's design is very modular with dozens of optional plugins.
In its simplest configuration, it can be installed and configured in a
couple of minutes (see [Caos NSA and Perceus: All-in-one Cluster Software Stack](http://www.linux-mag.com/id/7239/1/)
by Jeffrey B. Layton).
More complex configurations can satisfy the job scheduling needs of
world-class computer centers and rely upon a

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Summary — what node “features” are
- A feature is an arbitrary label (string) assigned to a node (e.g., gpu_v100, skylake, ssd). Features are metadata used by the scheduler to decide which nodes are eligible for a job.
- Features are configured in slurm.conf (Feature= on NodeName= lines) or set/updated at runtime with scontrol (scontrol update NodeName=... Features=...) or by node-helper plugins (helpers.conf / NodeFeaturesPlugins).
- There are two kinds of feature data:
  - built-in/static features (always “active”),
  - plugin/helper-managed features (may be “available” but not active until the node is powered up or rebooted). Requesting an available-but-inactive feature can cause the controller to bring a node up or activate the feature.

How features affect placement (high level)
- Filtering: when a job requests a feature, Slurm will only consider nodes that report that feature. That immediately reduces the set of eligible nodes and therefore can increase queue time.
- Boolean/compound requests: requests can express multiple feature requirements (AND/OR/grouping) so you can request nodes having feature A and B, or A or B. Exact expression syntax available depends on your Slurm version/site config (check man/sbatch or your local docs).
- Node activation: for cloud/helper-managed features, requesting an available-but-inactive feature may cause Slurm to allocate and then activate/power the node. This can increase job start latency while nodes are provisioned.
- Backfill and scheduling accuracy: dynamic features (helpers/extra fields) that change frequently reduce backfill accuracy and can make scheduling slower or less optimal. Slurm warns about frequent changes to node extra data.
- Fragmentation and heterogeneity: requiring narrow features (many specific labels) fragments the resource pool. Jobs needing many nodes with the same feature may wait longer because Slurm must find enough matching nodes. Heterogeneous allocations (different components separated by “:”) are possible but more complex for placement.
- Resource types vs features: features are labels only — they do not automatically reserve GPUs/other devices. Use GRES (Generic RESources) for device accounting (GPUs, licenses). Use features for node attributes that are not separately tracked (architecture, special NICs, site tags).

Common ways to request features
- --constraint or -C (feature name) — ask only nodes that have the named feature (exact syntax and expression capabilities may vary by site).
- Use heterogeneous job syntax (colon-separated components) when you need different node types in a single job.
- For advanced filtering of JSON-style node extra data, clusters may enable SchedulerParameters=extra_constraints and you can use --extra with comparison expressions (e.g., a=1.23, foo!=bar, boolean operators & and |). Note: extra constraints require that feature data is present in the node’s extra field and are disabled by default.

Practical tips / best practices
- Prefer GRES/partitions/QOS/CPUs-per-task when you need concrete resource guarantees (GPUs, cores, memory). Use features for topology or special hardware labels that aren’t tracked as resources.
- Avoid overly specific constraints unless you really need them — they reduce eligible nodes and increase wait time.
- If you must use dynamic features (cloud / helper-managed), expect longer start latency when nodes are powered up or rebooted to activate features.
- Test your constraint expression and see eligible nodes with sinfo or scontrol:
  - sinfo -Nel  (shows nodes and their Feature column)
  - scontrol show node=<nodename>  (shows Features= and other node fields)
- If a job isn’t starting and you used a feature constraint, check sinfo / squeue reasons: there may be zero nodes that match, or matching nodes may be drained/down/in use.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current node feature listing (run sinfo -Nel) for this cluster, or
- Check whether a particular feature (name you give) has any idle nodes available.

Which would you like? (If you want an action that would change state — e.g., submit a job requesting a feature — I’ll hand that off to the operator per policy.)

## NODE CONFIGURATION[#SECTION_NODE-CONFIGURATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The configuration of nodes (or machines) to be managed by Slurm is
also specified in /etc/slurm.conf .
Changes in node configuration (e.g. adding nodes, changing their
processor count, etc.) require restarting or reconfiguring all slurmctld
and slurmd daemons.
All slurmd daemons must know each node in the system to forward
messages in support of hierarchical communications.
Only the NodeName must be supplied in the configuration file.
All other node configuration information is optional.
It is advisable to establish baseline node configurations,
especially if the cluster is heterogeneous.
Nodes which register to the system with less than the configured resources
(e.g. too little memory), will be placed in the "DOWN" state to

# Slurm Workload Manager
Slurm is an open-source workload manager designed for Linux clusters of
all sizes.
It provides three key functions.
First it allocates exclusive and/or non-exclusive access to resources
(computer nodes) to users for some duration of time so they can perform work.
Second, it provides a framework for starting, executing, and monitoring work
(typically a parallel job) on a set of allocated nodes.
Finally, it arbitrates contention for resources by managing a queue of
pending work.
Slurm's design is very modular with dozens of optional plugins.
In its simplest configuration, it can be installed and configured in a
couple of minutes (see [Caos NSA and Perceus: All-in-one Cluster Software Stack](http://www.linux-mag.com/id/7239/1/)
by Jeffrey B. Layton).
More complex configurations can satisfy the job scheduling needs of
world-class computer centers and rely upon a

## Command Options[#command](https://slurm.schedmd.com/core_spec.html)
All job allocation commands ( salloc , sbatch and srun )
accept the -S or --core-spec option with a core count value
argument (e.g. "-S 1" or "--core-spec=2").
The count identifies the number of cores to be reserved for system overhead on
each allocated compute node. Note that the --core-spec option will be
ignored if AllowSpecResourcesUsage is not enabled in your slurm.conf.
Each job's core specialization count can be viewed using the scontrol ,
sview or squeue command.
Specification of a core specialization count for a job step is ignored
(i.e. for the srun command within a job allocation created using the
salloc or sbatch command).
Use the squeue command with the "%X" format option to see the count
(it is not reported in the default output format).

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

"Configless" Slurm is a feature that allows the compute nodes —
specifically the slurmd process — and user commands running on login
nodes to pull configuration information directly from the slurmctld instead of
from a pre-distributed local file. Your cluster does require a central set of

config files will be pulled to the node. This slurmctld can be identified by
either an explicit option, or — preferably — through DNS SRV

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Explain node features and how they affect placement
results.agent_response:
Short version
- A node feature is a boolean tag (an attribute) assigned to a node that describes a capability or property (example: gpu, rtx3090, ib, ssd, highmem).
- When a job requests a feature (typically with --constraint or #SBATCH --constraint), the scheduler filters nodes and will only place the job on nodes whose feature expression evaluates true. If no eligible nodes exist, the job remains pending.
- Features are purely a placement/filter mechanism (unlike GRES/TRES which represent countable resources).

Details and behaviors you should know
1) Where features come from
- Static: Features can be listed in slurm.conf on a NodeName line (Feature=...).
- Dynamic / changeable: NodeFeaturesPlugins (helpers.conf) can report and modify features at runtime. Those plugin-managed features can be “available but not active” (common for cloud/on‑demand nodes) and require activation at allocation or a reboot to change.

2) Active vs available (important for cloud/elastic nodes)
- Features not managed by a NodeFeaturesPlugin are always active.
- For plugin-managed features, a node may advertise a feature as available but it isn’t active while the node is powered down. If a job requests such a feature, the controller can select that node and cause the feature to be activated (power up, run helper, etc.) at allocation time.
- Some feature changes require a reboot; helpers and the configured RebootProgram govern that behavior.

3) How jobs request features (placement syntax and logic)
- Jobs request features with --constraint (sbatch/srun/salloc). The scheduler evaluates the request against node feature sets and only considers nodes that match.
- Boolean expressions are supported so you can combine attributes: AND/OR and parentheses are used to build expressions (e.g., request A AND (B OR C)). Different sites accept the usual symbols (& and |, commas for AND, parentheses) — check your cluster’s exact accepted operators in local docs.
- If no node satisfies the constraint expression, the job stays pending until nodes become eligible.

4) How this affects placement and scheduling
- Feature constraints reduce the pool of eligible nodes; the scheduler’s allocation, backfill and site_factor logic operate only over that reduced pool.
- Requesting narrow or uncommon features can increase queue wait time because fewer nodes match.
- If a requested feature must be activated (cloud/available-but-not-active), allocation may trigger node start/reboot and that latency is part of placement.
- Features do not consume numeric resource counts; they are boolean selectors. For countable resources (GPU count, licenses) use GRES/TRES/License mechanisms.

5) Operational notes for admins/users
- Admins define features on nodes (slurm.conf, helpers.conf/plugins) and should document which features are changeable or cloud-managed.
- Users can combine constraints with other resource requests (CPUs, memory, gres). If you think a job is stuck pending because of a feature, inspect node feature lists (sinfo / scontrol show node) to see which nodes advertise the needed feature and whether it’s active or only available.
- Changing a node’s feature or activating plugin features may require node reboot or helper actions.

Example (conceptual)
- sbatch --constraint="gpu&rtx"  — asks only nodes that advertise both gpu and rtx features.
- If rtx is a plugin-managed feature and nodes with rtx are powered down, the controller may power them up to satisfy the allocation.

If you want, I can show how to list the features currently advertised on your cluster’s nodes (sinfo / scontrol show node) so you can see which features are active vs available.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:

slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'

```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```

salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

## MPI SUPPORT[#SECTION_MPI-SUPPORT](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
MPI use depends upon the type of MPI being used.
There are three fundamentally different modes of operation used
by these various MPI implementations.
1. Slurm directly launches the tasks and performs initialization
of communications through the PMI2 or PMIx APIs.
For example: "srun -n16 a.out".
2. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using Slurm's infrastructure (OpenMPI).
3. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using some mechanism other than Slurm,
such as SSH or RSH.
These tasks are initiated outside of Slurm's monitoring
or control. Slurm's epilog should be configured to purge
these tasks when the job's allocation is relinquished,
or the use of pam_slurm_adopt is highly recommended.

ignored if AllowSpecResourcesUsage is not enabled in your slurm.conf.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

Here are some examples of valid requests:
```text

```

Invalid comparison operator:

The following --extra requests are not fulfilled by this node:
```text

```

## Overview [#Overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Extra data may be added to a node, and jobs may request extra constraints
to filter nodes based on their extra data. This is disabled by
default, but may be enabled in slurm.conf. Warning : Slurm's backfill
scheduler cannot accurately plan nodes for jobs whose request extra constraints
are not immediately satisfied. This means that the more often extra data for
nodes is changed, the less accurate the backfill scheduler will be.

## MPI SUPPORT[#SECTION_MPI-SUPPORT](https://slurm.schedmd.com/srun.html)
MPI use depends upon the type of MPI being used.
There are three fundamentally different modes of operation used
by these various MPI implementations.
1. Slurm directly launches the tasks and performs initialization
of communications through the PMI2 or PMIx APIs.
For example: "srun -n16 a.out".
2. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using Slurm's infrastructure (OpenMPI).
3. Slurm creates a resource allocation for the job and then
mpirun launches tasks using some mechanism other than Slurm,
such as SSH or RSH.
These tasks are initiated outside of Slurm's monitoring
or control. Slurm's epilog should be configured to purge
these tasks when the job's allocation is relinquished,
or the use of pam_slurm_adopt is highly recommended.

## Node Extra Data [#Node_Extra_Data](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
A node's extra data is a json formatted string. It may be initialized on
slurmd startup with the --extra flag for slurmd. For example:
```text
slurmd --extra '{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
Or, it may be updated with scontrol. For example:
```text
scontrol update nodename=node123 extra='{ "a": 1.23, "b": true, "c": 0, "foo": "bar", "zed": 23 }'
```
This defines the features that may be requested by the --extra option in
salloc, sbatch, and srun. Values may be any string, number, or boolean value.

### Warnings [#Warnings](https://slurm.schedmd.com/extra_constraints.html)
Whitespace characters are not treated specially. Any whitespace characters will
be considered part of a key or value. This means that the following is invalid:
```text
--extra " (a=b)"
```
The space at he beginning is parsed as a key of a request. Then the opening
parenthesis character is recognized as an invalid character for either a key
or a comparison operator. This request would result in the job being rejected.
However, this is valid:
```text
--extra "( a=b)"
```
This has a single request. The key is " a", the comparison operator is "=", and
the value is "b".
This same warning applies to single and double quotes. These are not considered
special characters, and thus are part of a string. Thus, bar and "bar" are not
equal.

## Requesting container jobs or steps [#request](https://slurm.schedmd.com/containers.html)
salloc , srun and sbatch (in Slurm 21.08+) have the
'--container' argument, which can be used to request container runtime
execution. The requested job container will not be inherited by the steps
called, excluding the batch and interactive steps.
- Batch step inside of container: ```text sbatch --container $ABS_PATH_TO_BUNDLE --wrap 'bash -c "cat /etc/*rel*"' ```
- Batch job with step 0 inside of container: ```text sbatch --wrap 'srun bash -c "--container $ABS_PATH_TO_BUNDLE cat /etc/*rel*"' ```

results.prompt: Explain --licenses requests and license pools in Slurm
results.agent_response:
Summary
- In Slurm, "licenses" are tracked consumable resources (like CPUs or GPUs) that the scheduler can allocate to jobs to prevent oversubscription of commercial-software licenses.
- Admins define license pools (local or remote) and counts; users request licenses at job submission with -L/--licenses or as a TRES (license/<name>).
- Slurm enforces license counts in scheduling: a job requesting licenses will not start until the requested license count is available.

Key concepts
- License pool: a named resource (e.g., ansys, matlab) with a Total count and runtime counters (Used, Free, Reserved). Pools can be configured in slurm.conf (local licenses) or in the accounting DB via sacctmgr (managed/remote).
- Local vs Remote:
  - Local licenses are declared in slurm.conf with the Licenses option (example: Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100). These are visible to the controller directly.
  - Remote licenses are managed via sacctmgr as resources and can include server/serverType metadata. Slurm itself doesn’t automatically query third‑party license servers; admins can integrate with them (see “dynamic licenses”).
- Dynamic licenses: admins can periodically update LastConsumed using sacctmgr (e.g., from lmstat), and Slurm will use LastConsumed/LastDeficit to account for external checkouts.
- TRES mapping: license resources are tracked as TRES when configured (AccountingStorageTRES can include license/<name>) so you can also request them via --tres-per-task. When used as TRES, they integrate with accounting and TRES-based scheduling.

How users request licenses
- sbatch/salloc/srun: use -L or --licenses
  - Syntax (common forms): -L name[:count] or -L name@server[:count]
  - Examples:
    - sbatch -L ansys:2 job.sh  (request 2 ansys licenses)
    - sbatch -L nastran@flex_host job.sh  (request remote nastran license)
- As TRES:
  - --tres-per-task=license/<name>=N (requires license be configured in AccountingStorageTRES)
  - Useful when you want per-task accounting rather than top-level job request.

Admin commands / inspection
- scontrol show lic  — see license pools and state (fields: LicenseName, Total, Used, Free, Reserved, Remote, LastConsumed, LastDeficit, LastUpdate).
  - Example output fragment: LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98 Remote=no
- sacctmgr add/modify resource — add license resources to the accounting DB, distribute counts across clusters, set server/serverType, allowed percentage, etc.
  - Example: sacctmgr add resource name=nastran cluster=fluid,pdf count=100 allowed=50 server=flex_host type=license
- To implement dynamic updates, admins run a script that polls the external license server and updates sacctmgr (set lastconsumed=...), which the controller uses to compute deficits/reservations.

Scheduler behavior / effects
- Jobs requesting license counts consume those resources when they are allocated (Used increases, Free decreases).
- If insufficient Free licenses exist, the job will remain PENDING until licenses are freed or counts are updated; the pending reason will reflect resource shortages.
- Reserved shows admin-held licenses that are not available to normal scheduling.
- Slurm will not automatically check out licenses from third‑party servers—admins must synchronize counts for remote/dynamic licenses.

Troubleshooting & tips
- If jobs remain pending and you suspect license exhaustion: run scontrol show lic to inspect Free/Used/Reserved and verify the correct license name was requested.
- For external license managers, set up a periodic sync that updates sacctmgr LastConsumed so Slurm’s view matches the license server.
- Use --tres-per-task when you need per-task license accounting or when integrating with TRES-based limits/quotas.
- Be explicit with server-qualified names for remote licenses (name@server) to avoid ambiguity across clusters.

Quick examples
- Submit requesting two ansys licenses:
  - sbatch -L ansys:2 job.sh
- Check license pools:
  - scontrol show lic
- Add a remote license resource:
  - sacctmgr add resource name=nastran cluster=fluid,count=100 server=flex_host type=license

If you want, I can:
- show exact scontrol show lic output from your cluster (I can run that if you ask), or
- help craft a sacctmgr command to add/configure a license resource.

results.prompt: Explain --licenses requests and license pools in Slurm
results.agent_response:
Summary — what a "license" request is
- In Slurm a "license" is a consumable resource (a TRES) that jobs can request. Administrators define license pools (counts) and Slurm will allocate those license units to jobs at submission time and keep them allocated until the job ends.
- Jobs request licenses with sbatch/srun using -L/--licenses (or by requesting a license TRES via --tres-per-task). Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh requests 2 units from the license pool named "ansys".

License pools and where they come from
- Local licenses (slurm.conf): simple static pools can be declared in slurm.conf, e.g.
  Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100
  Slurm reports these pools via scontrol show lic LicenseName=<name>.
- Accounting DB (sacctmgr) resources: administrators can create license-type resources in the SlurmDB (sacctmgr add resource ... type=license) and set counts, cluster allocations, server metadata, and allowed percentages per cluster.
- Remote/dynamic licenses: Slurm can track licenses that are managed by an external license server. A site script can periodically sync the external server’s current usage to Slurm (sacctmgr update resource ... lastconsumed=...). Slurm uses LastConsumed/LastDeficit to account for “missing” licenses and to reserve capacity accordingly.

How to request licenses in submissions
- Short form: sbatch -L license_name:count script.sh
  Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 train.sh
- As a TRES (per-task): sbatch --tres-per-task=license/ansys=1
  If you use the TRES form, the license name must also be present in AccountingStorageTRES or configured as a resource in sacctmgr so accounting/scheduling recognize it.
- The scheduler treats license units like other consumable resources: a job will not start unless the requested license units are free.

What Slurm tracks and how to inspect it
- scontrol show lic LicenseName=<name> — shows Total, Used, Free, Remote, etc. Example output snippet:
  LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98 Remote=no
- sacctmgr show resource (or sacctmgr show resources format=...) — shows resources defined in the accounting DB, cluster allocations, server, type, count, allowed percentage.
- For dynamic/remote sync you’ll see LastConsumed and LastDeficit fields in the sacctmgr resource settings.

Scheduling behavior and implications
- Licenses are global consumable resources; the scheduler decrements the Free count when it dispatches a job and reclaims on job end.
- If insufficient license units are free, jobs will remain PENDING until license capacity is freed or the request is changed.
- Licenses can be scoped/partitioned via the accounting DB (per-cluster allocation or percentage splits) for multi-cluster deployments.
- Slurm does not itself contact external license managers (unless you add your own sync scripts); remote server and server-type fields are informational and used with site integration or scripts.

Administration: adding and managing license pools
- Add a resource in the accounting DB:
  sacctmgr add resource name=nastran cluster=clusterA,count=100 type=license server=flex_host servertype=flexlm
- Update counts or lastconsumed:
  sacctmgr update resource nastran set count=120
  sacctmgr -i update resource nastran set lastconsumed=42
  (An update to sacctmgr will be pushed to controllers so allocations change.)
- For slurm.conf Licenses=... edits you must restart/reload slurmctld appropriately.

Common operational notes and best practices
- Use descriptive license names (e.g., ansys, fluent) when defining pools; users request the same name.
- For external license managers, run a periodic sync script to set lastconsumed so Slurm’s view stays accurate (see Slurm docs’ dynamic license example).
- Monitor with scontrol show lic and sacctmgr show resource; alert if Free becomes low or LastDeficit grows.
- If you want per-task accounting of license use, use --tres-per-task=license/<name>=N and ensure AccountingStorageTRES includes license/<name>.
- Document license request syntax for users to avoid over-requesting (jobs that request more licenses than they actually need can starve others).

Troubleshooting
- Job pending with license shortage: run scontrol show lic and sacctmgr show resource to see Free/Used and whether LastDeficit is non‑zero.
- If users report licenses available on the license server but Slurm shows a deficit, check your sync process (update LastConsumed) and sacctmgr settings for allowed/allocated counts across clusters.

References / commands
- Request: sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh or sbatch --tres-per-task=license/ansys=1
- Inspect: scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys ; sacctmgr show resource
- Admin: sacctmgr add|update resource ... type=license

If you want, I can:
- Show the exact scontrol/sacctmgr commands/examples for your site (tell me if you use slurm.conf Licenses or sacctmgr resources), or
- Draft a small license-sync script that updates sacctmgr based on an external license manager’s lmstat output.

results.prompt: Explain --licenses requests and license pools in Slurm
results.agent_response:
Short overview
- Slurm treats software licenses as cluster-level shared resources (pools) you can request at job submit. This lets the scheduler prevent oversubscription of limited licenses the same way it handles CPUs or GPUs.
- You request licenses with sbatch/srun/salloc using -L/--licenses (or by exposing them as a TRES and requesting via --tres-per-task). Licenses are configured either locally (slurm.conf) or centrally (sacctmgr / slurmdbd) as “remote” license resources.

How licenses are configured
- Local licenses (cluster-local): set in slurm.conf, e.g.
  Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100
  These are visible via scontrol show lic and are fully managed by the controller.
- Remote licenses (database-managed): added with sacctmgr as resources (type=License). These can be assigned to clusters and split by count/percentage. Example:
  sacctmgr add resource name=nastran cluster=fluid,pdf count=100 allowed=50 server=flex_host type=license
- Dynamic updates: starting with recent Slurm versions you can update LastConsumed via sacctmgr so Slurm can track external license-server usage and compute LastDeficit.

How to request licenses in a job
- Short form: sbatch -L <name>[:count] script.sh
  - Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 job.sh  (requests 2 ansys licenses for the job)
- For remote licenses you may need to include server: sbatch -L nastran@flex_host:1 job.sh
- Alternative: expose license as a TRES (AccountingStorageTRES) and use --tres-per-task; useful if you want per-task accounting or to mix with other TRES usage.

Allocation semantics (Used / Free / Reserved)
- scontrol show lic prints fields like: LicenseName=<name> Total=<N> Used=<u> Free=<f> Reserved=<r> Remote=<yes|no> LastConsumed=... LastDeficit=...
- Total = configured pool size.
- Used = number currently allocated to running jobs (licenses currently consumed by scheduled/running jobs).
- Free = Total - Used - Reserved (licenses available to schedule new jobs).
- Reserved = licenses set aside by an explicit Slurm reservation (scontrol create reservation) or other reservation mechanism. Reserved licenses are not available for general scheduling while the reservation is active.
- Pending jobs that cannot be scheduled because there aren’t enough Free licenses remain PENDING; they do not normally increment Used. (The scheduler allocates/marks licenses as Used when it assigns the job — i.e., at scheduling/allocation time.)
- If you use dynamic (remote) license tracking, LastConsumed/LastDeficit help Slurm account for licenses that are checked out outside Slurm; admins update LastConsumed via sacctmgr so Slurm can withhold a matching number of licenses.

Common admin/user operations
- View pools: scontrol show lic
- Add/modify remote license resource: sacctmgr add/modify resource ...
- Reserve licenses for a window or user/group: scontrol create reservation ... (reservation can include license resources)
- Sync external license server counts into Slurm: sacctmgr update resource ... set lastconsumed=<n>

Practical tips and pitfalls
- Slurm does not automatically talk to FlexNet, RLM, etc.; remote license entries are only as accurate as the admin updates them (unless you implement periodic sync scripts to run sacctmgr updates).
- If you request a license name that is not configured (or request more than available), your job will stay pending until enough licenses are free.

Snippet:
## Licenses Overview [#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Slurm can help with software license management by assigning available
licenses to jobs at scheduling time. If the licenses are not available, jobs
are kept pending until licenses become available. Licenses in Slurm are
essentially shared resources, meaning configured resources that are not tied to
a specific host but are associated with the entire cluster.
Licenses in Slurm can be configured in two ways:
- Local Licenses: Local licenses are local to the cluster using the slurm.conf in which they are configured.
- Remote Licenses: Remote licenses are served by the database and are configured using the sacctmgr command. Remote licenses are dynamic in nature as upon running the sacctmgr command, the slurmdbd updates all clusters the licenses are assigned to.

results.prompt: Explain --licenses requests and license pools in Slurm
results.agent_response:
Summary — what a "license" is in Slurm
- Slurm can manage software licenses as schedulable resources (like GPUs or CPUs). Licenses are added as resources (TRES of type license) and the scheduler will account for and enforce their total counts when placing jobs.
- Admins define license pools (counts, local vs remote, cluster allocation) in Slurm’s configuration and accounting DB; users request them on job submission.

Key admin concepts
- Local licenses: configured in slurm.conf with the Licenses= option, e.g. Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100. These are static counts known to the controller.
- AccountingStorageTRES: to record license usage in accounting, map license names to a TRES string (e.g. AccountingStorageTRES=license/fluent). This lets Slurm track license consumption in sacct/sreport.
- License resources in the accounting DB: sacctmgr add resource ... (type=License) is used to create/allocate license pools, including multi-cluster splits (allowed % per cluster) or server/serverType metadata for remote license systems.
- Remote and Dynamic licenses: Slurm can represent remote license servers (metadata only). From Slurm 23.02 onward you can update LastConsumed in the accounting DB so Slurm computes LastDeficit (licenses that must be reserved because they appear checked out to external servers). Admins typically run a periodic script that queries the real license server (lmstat or similar) and updates sacctmgr with the current consumption so Slurm’s view stays in sync.

How users request licenses (job submission)
- The supported submission option is -L or --licenses. Example:
  sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh
  This requests 2 units from the license pool named "ansys".
- You can request multiple licenses separated by commas, and combine with other resource requests.
- Alternative: request licenses as a TRES per task with --tres-per-task=license/<name>:N. If you use this, the license name must also be present in AccountingStorageTRES so accounting and job matching work correctly.
- Requests consume the license count for the job’s lifetime (until job completes or is cancelled).

How Slurm enforces and reports licenses
- Slurm tracks Total, Used, Free for each license pool. You can view them with scontrol show lic or the scontrol_license read. Example from docs:
  scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98 Remote=no
- When a job requests more licenses than are free in the pool, the scheduler will not place the job; the pending reason will reflect the resource shortage (inspect squeue to see the pending reason).
- For remote/dynamic scenarios, if the accounting DB shows fewer free licenses due to LastConsumed/LastDeficit, Slurm will reserve licenses accordingly to avoid oversubscription.

Admin operations and scripts
- Add/update license pools with sacctmgr (add resource name=<name> type=License count=<N> [cluster=... allowed=... server=...]).
- To keep remote license counts accurate, run a periodic script that queries the license server and runs sacctmgr to update lastconsumed; Slurm will incorporate those updates into scheduling decisions.
- Ensure AccountingStorageTRES includes license/<name> if you intend to use --tres-per-task to request licenses.

Practical notes / best practices
- Use -L for straightforward license requests. Use --tres-per-task when you need per-task license accounting, but ensure AccountingStorageTRES is configured.
- Treat Slurm’s license objects as “bookable slots” — they don’t automatically talk to third‑party license managers unless you implement synchronization (the remote/server fields are informational).
- Monitor license usage with scontrol show lic and include license metrics in any usage reports (sreport can summarize resource usage if configured).
- If jobs are stuck pending for licenses, check squeue to see the pending reason and inspect scontrol show lic to confirm current Free/Used counts.

References / commands (docs)
- sbatch/salloc/srun -L/--licenses option
- slurm.conf: Licenses= and AccountingStorageTRES=
- sacctmgr add resource / sacctmgr update resource (for pools and LastConsumed)
- scontrol show lic and scontrol_license to view current pools
- See Slurm “Licenses” guide and “Job Reason Codes” in the official docs for full details.

If you want, I can:
- show the current license pools on your cluster (scontrol show lic / scontrol_license), or
- walk through an example sacctmgr command to add a new license pool — which would be an admin action (I would hand that off to the operator).

results.prompt: Explain --licenses requests and license pools in Slurm
results.agent_response:
Quick overview — what Slurm licenses are
- Slurm treats software licenses as a cluster-wide, trackable resource (a TRES: Trackable RESource). Jobs can request licenses at submission time; the scheduler will only start a job when the requested license units are available.
- Licenses are consumed at job start and released at job end (like CPUs or GPUs).

How to configure licenses
- Local licenses (defined in slurm.conf):
  - Example: Licenses=fluent:30,ansys:100
  - These are static counts local to the cluster and visible via scontrol show lic.
  - If you want accounting/tracking, add the license name to AccountingStorageTRES (e.g. AccountingStorageTRES=license/fluent).
- Remote / pooled licenses (managed across clusters or via sacctmgr):
  - Use sacctmgr to add resources representing license pools: sacctmgr add resource name=<name> cluster=<clusters> count=<total> allowed=<percent|count> server=<host> servertype=<type>
  - This lets you split a central license pool between multiple clusters (allowed can allocate percentages or counts per-cluster).
  - Remote licenses appear as Remote=yes in scontrol show lic and are driven/updated from the SlurmDB.

How jobs request licenses
- sbatch/srun/salloc option: -L, --licenses
  - Syntax: -L <licname>:<count> (for remote you can include server: name@server)
  - Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh
- Alternatively, request a license via TRES: --tres-per-task=license/<name>=<count>
  - If you use TRES-based license requests you must list the license TRES in AccountingStorageTRES so accounting/tracking works.

What the scheduler does with license requests
- Licenses are treated as a shared cluster resource. If enough license units are free, the job will be allocated and the license count is decremented (Used increases, Free decreases). If not enough are free, the job remains PENDING until licenses free up.
- The scheduler enforces license counts like any tracked resource; jobs asking for more licenses than configured will never start.

Viewing and managing license state
- scontrol show lic [LicenseName=<name>] — shows Total, Used, Free, Reserved, Remote, LastConsumed, LastDeficit, LastUpdate.
- sacctmgr show resource / sacctmgr list resource — used to inspect and modify configured (remote/pooled) license resources and per-cluster allocations.
- To change counts or allocations: sacctmgr modify resource ... (or add/remove resources).

Dynamic / external license-server integration
- Slurm does not automatically talk to FlexLM/RLM/etc. by itself. Admins typically run a small script that polls the license server (lmstat, rlm queries) and then updates the Slurm DB with sacctmgr update resource <name> set lastconsumed=<n>.
- Slurm uses LastConsumed/LastDeficit to reflect externally-observed use and to adjust available capacity (e.g., LastDeficit helps the controller account for licenses “missing” from Slurm’s perspective).
- You can also use sacctmgr to set aside (reserve) some licenses for a cluster or purpose.

Common admin examples
- Local (slurm.conf):
  - Licenses=matlab:50
  - View: scontrol show lic
- Remote/pooled across clusters:
  - sacctmgr add resource name=nastran cluster=fluid,pdf count=100 allowed=50 server=flex_host servertype=flexlm
  - Users submit: sbatch -L nastran@flex_host script.sh
- Dynamic update script pattern:
  - poll license server -> sacctmgr -i update resource <name> set lastconsumed=<n>

Best practices / notes
- Choose one mechanism consistently: local Licenses in slurm.conf for simple single-cluster setups; sacctmgr-managed remote resources for multi-cluster pools or when integrating with external license managers.
- If you use --tres-per-task for licenses, ensure AccountingStorageTRES includes the license type so accounting and billing work.
- Use scontrol show lic to debug availability; jobs pending for a license will remain in the queue until Free ≥ requested count.
- Coordinate any external license-server checkouts carefully so Slurm’s view (LastConsumed) stays synchronized with the real license server to avoid overcommit or unnecessary pending jobs.

If you want, I can:
- Show example sacctmgr and scontrol commands (concrete syntax).
- Walk through a short admin script to poll lmstat and update Slurm with sacctmgr.

## Dynamic Licenses [#dynamic_licenses](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Starting with Slurm 23.02, the LastConsumed field for remote licenses
is designed to be periodically updated with the active use count from a license
server. An example script for FlexLM's lmstat command is provided below —
similar scripts can be easily constructed for other license management
stacks.
```text

```

Remote licenses do not offer any kind of integration with third party
license managers by themselves. The use of the "Server" and "ServerType"

## Licenses Overview [#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/licenses.html)
Slurm can help with software license management by assigning available
licenses to jobs at scheduling time. If the licenses are not available, jobs
are kept pending until licenses become available. Licenses in Slurm are
essentially shared resources, meaning configured resources that are not tied to
a specific host but are associated with the entire cluster.
Licenses in Slurm can be configured in two ways:
- Local Licenses: Local licenses are local to the cluster using the slurm.conf in which they are configured.
- Remote Licenses: Remote licenses are served by the database and are configured using the sacctmgr command. Remote licenses are dynamic in nature as upon running the sacctmgr command, the slurmdbd updates all clusters the licenses are assigned to.

Summary — what "--reservation" does
- --reservation=<name> (sbatch/srun/salloc) requests that Slurm place the job into a named reservation. If the reservation is not MAGNETIC, the job must explicitly specify the reservation name to run on those reserved resources.
- A job that uses a reservation must be fully contained within the reservation’s resources and time window (start/end). If the reservation ends, the job will be canceled unless controller option ResvOverRun permits an overrun.

How reservations are created (admin side)
- Reservations are created with scontrol create reservation ... and include fields such as:
  - ReservationName (auto-generated if not given)
  - StartTime / EndTime / Duration
  - Nodes / NodeCnt / CoreCnt (or explicit node list)
  - Partition (a reservation normally is tied to one partition unless explicit nodes are specified)
  - Users / Accounts / QOS (who may use the reservation)
  - Flags (MAGNETIC, OVERLAP, REPLACE, REPLACE_DOWN, etc.)
- Reservations may reserve nodes, cores, licenses, burst buffers.

Access control rules (who may run in a reservation)
- Allow lists and deny lists:
  - You can specify Users=alice,bob or Accounts=proj1,proj2 to allow only those users/accounts.
  - You can also exclude a user or account by prefacing the name with a minus sign, e.g. User=-alice or Account=-proj2. Exclusions override positive membership (i.e., prevent that entity from using the reservation even if their account is listed).
- QOS and partition may also be restricted on the reservation.
- Matching logic:
  - When a job is considered for the reservation, Slurm checks the job’s user, account, QOS and partition against the reservation’s allow/deny lists. The job must satisfy the reservation’s access constraints (and resource/partition constraints) to be eligible.
  - If the reservation is not MAGNETIC, the job must explicitly request --reservation=<name> to run in it (and still must satisfy access rules).
  - If the reservation has the MAGNETIC flag, eligible jobs that do not name the reservation may be “attracted” and started in the reservation automatically (only if they meet the reservation’s access/resource constraints). Note: MAGNETIC does not attract heterogeneous jobs unless they explicitly request the reservation.
- Partition and node constraints:
  - A reservation is normally associated with a single partition and cannot span partitions unless created with explicit node lists.
  - Reservations can be for full nodes or specific cores; some flags/behaviors differ for partial-node reservations.
- Overlap and replacement:
  - By default reservations do not overlap in time on the same nodes; use the OVERLAP flag to allow overlapping reservations.
  - REPLACE or REPLACE_DOWN flags change how reserved nodes are maintained when nodes go down or are allocated elsewhere (e.g., allow swapping in new idle nodes).
- Priority/accounting effects:
  - Using a reservation does not itself change a job’s base priority calculation, but jobs using reservations are considered for scheduling on the reserved resources before non-reserved jobs (effectively a scheduling advantage).
  - Jobs run in a reservation are accounted to the job’s user/account. If reserved resources are unused, accounting may attribute unused resources equally among the users/accounts associated with the reservation (see reservation accounting rules).

Practical examples
- Submit requesting a reservation (user-side):
  - sbatch --reservation=my_res job.sh
- Admin create example:
  - scontrol create reservation ReservationName=my_res StartTime=now Duration=60 NodeCnt=2 Users=alice,brenda Partition=gpu

Caveats & important notes
- Jobs must fit entirely inside the reservation (resource and time). Partial fits are not allowed.
- Magnetic reservations can start eligible jobs that don’t explicitly name the reservation; regular reservations require an explicit --reservation.
- Heterogeneous jobs and MAGNETIC: heterogeneous jobs are not attracted by MAGNETIC unless they explicitly request the reservation.
- If you need a reservation to span multiple partitions use explicit node lists (it’s not the normal case).
- For precise semantics, behaviors and flags see Slurm’s reservation documentation (scontrol create reservation, scontrol show reservation, and the reservations section of Slurm docs).

If you want, I can:
- show reservations currently defined on the cluster (scontrol_reservation_show), or
- explain a particular flag (MAGNETIC / OVERLAP / REPLACE) in more depth, or
- give example scontrol create lines for common policies. Which would you like?

results.prompt: Explain --reservation and reservation access rules
results.agent_response:
Summary — what “--reservation” does
- --reservation=<name> (sbatch/srun/salloc) tells Slurm to place the job into an existing reservation named <name>. The job must fit entirely inside the reserved resources/time window to start there.
- If a job runs in a reservation it will be considered for the reserved resources before ordinary (non‑reserved) jobs; this effectively gives eligible jobs precedence on the reserved resources. It does not magically change the job’s base priority calculation — it is an allocation mechanism that affects scheduling order for those resources.

How reservations are created (admin side, brief)
- Admins create reservations with scontrol create reservation ... or via reservation APIs. Typical fields: StartTime, Duration (or EndTime), Partition, Nodes or NodeCnt/CoreCnt, User(s), Account(s), QOS, and Flags.
- Example (admin): scontrol create reservation StartTime=now Duration=60 NodeCnt=1 User=alice Partition=gpu

Reservation access controls (who may / may not use it)
- Reservations carry explicit access rules; you can allow or deny use by:
  - user= (single user or comma list)
  - account= (account name or list)
  - qos= (QOS list)
  - partition= (partition list)
- Deny syntax: prefix a name with a minus to prevent it. Example: user=-alan prevents user alan from using the reservation even if they are submitting under an allowed account.
- Access rules are combinable. A reservation can be limited to one or more accounts, users, QOS values, and/or partitions; only jobs that meet the reservation’s access criteria (and resource/time fit) may use it.

Magnetic reservations
- Flag: flags=magnetic
- Normal behavior: jobs must explicitly request the reservation (sbatch --reservation=NAME).
- MAGNETIC behavior: eligible jobs that match the access rules are allowed to run in the reservation without specifying the reservation name — the reservation “attracts” those jobs.
- Note: magnetic reservations do NOT attract heterogeneous jobs unless they explicitly request the reservation.

How users request/use reservations
- Request in submission: sbatch --reservation=RESNAME my.job, or srun/salloc --reservation=RESNAME.
- The job’s requested nodes/cores/time must be entirely contained within the reservation’s resources and time window; otherwise the job won’t start in that reservation.
- When the reservation end time is reached the reserved job will be cancelled unless ResvOverRun in slurm.conf allows limited overrun.

Other useful flags and behaviors
- flags=replace / REPLACE_DOWN: control whether Slurm should replace down/drained nodes (or even allocated nodes) to maintain the reservation size (admin-level control).
- Reservations are normally bound to a single partition (they cannot span partitions) unless created with explicit node names across partitions.
- Reservations may be used for nodes, cores, licenses, or burst buffers. Reserved licenses and burst buffers have slightly different semantics than node/core reservations.

Visibility and admin commands
- Inspect reservations: scontrol show reservation or scontrol show res ReservationName=NAME.
- When created, Slurm generates a reservation name if one is not provided (often user suffixing).
- Admins can include or exclude specific users/accounts in the reservation creation command.

Practical tips / gotchas
- If you expect a job to run in a reservation but it doesn’t start: verify the job requested exactly fits reservation resources, the reservation is active during requested time, and the job meets the reservation’s access rules.
- For magnetic reservations, check that the job is homogeneous (heterogeneous jobs will not be auto-attracted).
- Negative access entries (user=-name or account=-account) override permissive entries for that identity.
- Reservation use does not remove the need to request correct resources (CPUs, GPUs, nodes, time) — the job must still request what you actually need and what the reservation covers.

Quick examples
- Submit into an existing reservation:
  - sbatch --reservation=teamX_res myscript.sh
- Admin create allowing one account and denying one user:
  - scontrol create reservation StartTime=2026-05-10T09:00:00 Duration=2:00 Account=teamX User=-bob Partition=gpu NodeCnt=2

If you’d like, I can:
- Show current reservations on your cluster (scontrol show reservation) — tell me whether you want a full listing or a specific reservation name.

Below is a concise summary of the sbatch/srun --reservation option and the common reservation access rules and behaviors in Slurm.

What --reservation does
- --reservation=<name> (sbatch, srun, salloc) tells Slurm to schedule the job inside the named reservation. The job must fit completely inside the reservation’s resources and time window.
- If a job runs inside a reservation it is considered for those reserved resources first (the reservation acts as a scheduling boost), but specifying a reservation does not otherwise change a job’s base priority.
- If the reservation expires while a job is running, the job will be canceled at EndTime unless ResvOverRun (slurm.conf) or other configuration allows overrun.

How reservations are created/managed (admin only)
- Reservations are created/edited/deleted by administrators (scontrol create/delete reservation, scontrol update, etc.). Users cannot create cluster-wide reservations unless given special privileges.
- Use scontrol show reservation (or scontrol show res) to list reservation details; scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name> shows the ACLs and resource scope.

Reservation resource types and scope
- Reservations may reserve whole nodes or specific core counts (NodeCnt/CoreCnt), licenses, or burst buffers.
- A reservation is normally tied to a single partition (unless nodes are explicitly listed when creating it).
- A job requesting a reservation must request resources that lie within the reservation (nodes, cores, mem, time); heterogeneous jobs have special limitations (see MAGNETIC notes below).

Access controls / ACLs
- A reservation can restrict who may use it by specifying one or more of:
  - Users= (allow user list)
  - Accounts= (allow account list)
  - QOS= (allow QOS list)
  - Partition= (restrict to a partition)
- ACLs are inclusive: specifying Users=alice,bob means alice OR bob may use it (job must match one).
- Exclusions are supported by prefixing a name with '-' in the ACL lists: Users=-baduser prevents that user from using the reservation even if they otherwise match an allowed account.
- If an ACL lists accounts, the job must be submitted under one of those accounts (or a user that matches Users=). If multiple ACL fields are present the job must satisfy all stated constraints.

MAGNETIC reservations (automatic attraction)
- By default, a job must explicitly name a reservation to run inside it.
- A reservation with the MAGNETIC flag “attracts” eligible jobs that meet the ACLs even when those jobs do not name the reservation; the reservation will pull matching jobs onto reserved nodes.
- Magnetic reservations do not automatically attract heterogeneous jobs — those must explicitly request the reservation name.

Other useful flags and behaviors
- REPLACE (and REPLACE_DOWN): can be used to keep a reservation’s size constant by replacing downed or allocated nodes (administrator-configurable; read the docs for limitations).
- Reservations that reserve licenses or burst buffers behave slightly differently than core/node reservations — check doc for reservation-specific details for non-core resources.
- Reservation names are typically returned/printed when created; jobs must use that exact reservation name (or rely on MAGNETIC attraction if enabled).
- Jobs that request only part of a reservation’s resources must still be fully contained (they cannot exceed the reservation’s resources or time).

How users typically request a reservation
- Explicit request: sbatch --reservation=<RESNAME> myscript.sh
- Interactive: salloc --reservation=<RESNAME> ... or srun --reservation=<RESNAME> ...
- If you try to use a reservation you are not allowed to access (ACL mismatch), Slurm will reject the job submission or place it pending with an access-related reason.

Where to check details (as a user)
- Ask your admin for the reservation name and ACLs, or run (if permitted): scontrol show reservation <name> (admins can always run this).
- If your job is pending while trying to use a reservation, check squeue for the pending reason; admins can inspect reservation internals.

If you want, I can:
- Show the reservation ACL and resource scope for a specific reservation (provide reservation name) — read-only (I’ll run scontrol/scontrol_reservation_show).
- Explain a specific pending reason you see when trying to use a reservation (provide job ID or squeue output).

Quick reference — what “--reservation” is and how reservation access rules work in Slurm.

What a reservation is
- A reservation reserves specific resources (nodes, cores, or TRES) for a defined time window (StartTime / Duration / EndTime) so only approved jobs may use them.
- Reservations are created/managed by the admin (scontrol create/update/delete reservation) and can be shown with scontrol show reservation or scontrol show res <name>.

How jobs use a reservation
- Submitting a job that should run in a reservation: sbatch/srun/salloc --reservation=ReservationName (or the job will start there automatically only if the reservation has the MAGNETIC flag — see below).
- By default, jobs must explicitly request the reservation name. MAGNETIC reservations “attract” matching jobs even if they don’t specify the reservation name.

Access-control fields (rules for who/what can use a reservation)
- When creating a reservation you must specify at least one access control field. Common fields:
  - Users (User= or Users=): a list of allowed users.
  - Groups (Group= or Groups=): a list of allowed Unix/GID groups.
  - Accounts (Account= or Accounts=): allowed accounting accounts.
  - QOS (QOS=): allowed Quality-of-Service values.
  - AllowedPartitions / Partition: partitions the reservation applies to.
- Important rule: Users and Groups are mutually exclusive — you cannot specify both.
- Logical combination: If you specify multiple access-control fields, a job must satisfy all of them to be allowed into the reservation. Example: Accounts=foo,QOS=high means the job must run under account foo AND request high QOS.
- Exclusions are supported: prefixing a value with '-' denies that entity (for example Users=-alice denies user alice even if their account would otherwise allow it).
- You can restrict by partition(s) and by specific nodes or node counts (Nodes=, NodeCnt=, CoreCnt=, TRES=).

Reservation behavior/flags that affect access
- MAGNETIC: jobs that meet the access controls can be scheduled into the reservation without specifying --reservation explicitly.
- REPLACE / REPLACE_DOWN: control whether nodes which are currently allocated or down are replaced to maintain reservation size.
- IGNORE_JOBS: allow creation even if running jobs overlap (useful for maintenance).
- MAINT (maintenance) flag: used to mark maintenance reservations (affects accounting/semantics).
- Other flags control exclusivity and replacement policy — check scontrol docs for the full list.

Practical examples (conceptual)
- Reserve node05 for user alice for 1 hour:
  scontrol create reservation User=alice Nodes=node05 StartTime=now Duration=60
- Reserve two nodes for account foo but exclude user bob:
  scontrol create reservation Accounts=foo Users=-bob Nodes=node[01-02] StartTime=...

Notes and tips
- A job must match all specified access controls; specifying multiple access fields is an AND, not OR.
- Use scontrol show reservation (or squeue --reservation=<name>) to inspect which jobs are tied to a reservation.
- Use MAGNETIC sparingly — it can make reservations “attract” jobs and reduce manual --reservation usage, but can interact subtly with heterogeneous jobs and backfill.
- Admins should be aware reservations affect scheduling and backfill: the scheduler will avoid starting jobs that cannot finish before a reservation start time unless the reservation allows replacement/ignore options.

- Show current reservations on this cluster (scontrol_reservation_show) and explain their access rules, or
- Help craft an scontrol create reservation command for a specific policy (give me the users/accounts/partitions/nodes/time).
