```text
Summary — what --reservation does
- --reservation=<name> (sbatch/srun/salloc) tells Slurm to place the job into a named reservation so it will start on the reserved resources during the reservation window.
- By default a job will only run in a reservation if it explicitly requests that reservation (unless the reservation has the MAGNETIC flag — see below).

Key reservation properties (how reservations are defined)
- Created/managed with scontrol create/update reservation and inspected with scontrol show reservation (or scontrol show res).
- Reservations are time-bounded: StartTime, Duration or EndTime.
- Resources can be expressed as Nodes, NodeCnt, CoreCnt, TRES, etc.
- Flags control special behaviors (common ones):
  - MAGNETIC — “attracts” eligible jobs that do not explicitly name the reservation (jobs that meet the access controls may be placed into it).
  - REPLACE / REPLACE_DOWN — control whether allocated/down/drained nodes are replaced to maintain reservation size.
  - (Other flags exist; see docs for full list.)

Access control rules (the important part)
- At least one access-control field must be set when creating a reservation: Users, Groups, Accounts, QOS, or AllowedPartitions.
- Multiple access-control fields can be specified; a job must meet all specified fields to use the reservation. In other words, access-control fields are effectively ANDed. Example: Accounts=foo,QOS=high means the job must run under account foo AND use QOS high.
- Users and Groups are mutually exclusive: you may specify Users OR Groups, not both.
- Deny entries are supported by prefixing the name with a minus sign. Example: Users=-alan prevents user alan from using the reservation even if other fields would otherwise allow it (e.g., the job’s account matches).
- AllowedPartitions can restrict which partition(s) the reservation applies to (jobs must run in those partitions).
- If the reservation lists specific nodes, only those nodes are reserved.
- Jobs must request the reservation (sbatch --reservation=<name> / srun --reservation=<name> / salloc --reservation=<name>) unless the reservation is MAGNETIC.

Practical implications
- To run under a reservation, ensure the job’s account/QOS/user/partition match the reservation’s access lists exactly (or the reservation is magnetic and will “attract” the job).
- If you want a reservation that only a particular account may use, set Accounts=<acct>. If you want to allow a few specific users from that account, also set Users=<userlist> (remember Users+Accounts are ANDed).
- To prevent a single user in a permitted account from using the reservation, use Users=-baduser.
- Magnetic reservations are useful for letting eligible jobs start without each job naming the reservation; be cautious with heterogeneous jobs (magnetic reservations cannot attract heterogeneous jobs unless the job explicitly requests the reservation).

Examples
- Create a simple reservation for account teamA on nodes node01–node04 for 2 hours, usable by users alice and bob:
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=teamA_res StartTime=now Duration=2:00 Nodes=node[01-04] Accounts=teamA Users=alice,bob
- Deny user alan even though account matches:
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=teamA_res Accounts=teamA Users=-alan Nodes=node01 StartTime=now Duration=1:00
- Submit a job into a reservation:
  sbatch --reservation=teamA_res job.sh
- Make a reservation magnetic so eligible jobs can be placed there automatically:
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=mag_res StartTime=now Duration=1:00 Nodes=node05 Flags=MAGNETIC Users=user1

Where to look next
- scontrol create reservation and scontrol show reservation pages (Slurm docs) for the full set of create/update fields and flags.
- Use scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name> to inspect access lists for an existing reservation.

If you want, I can:
- show current reservations on your cluster (scontrol show reservation) or
- craft a specific scontrol create reservation command for your desired users/accounts/nodes/time.
```

## Magnetic Reservations [#magnetic](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
The default behavior for reservations is that jobs must request a
reservation in order to run in it. The MAGNETIC flag allows you to
create a reservation that will allow jobs to run in it without requiring that
they specify the name of the reservation. The reservation will only "attract"
jobs that meet the access control requirements.

heterogeneous jobs will only run in magnetic reservations if they explicitly

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"

Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One

## TRES information[#SECTION_TRES-information](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .

establish 2 different limits: one for 16 CPUs and another for 32 GB of memory.

subsequent assignment of "GrpTRES=gres/gpu=2" will result in

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been
defined in the slurm.conf file. The QOS will only determine job
preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will
override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

## FLAT FILE DUMP AND LOAD[#SECTION_FLAT-FILE-DUMP-AND-LOAD](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
sacctmgr has the capability to load and dump Slurm association data to and
from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an
existing cluster's associations into a new cluster with similar
accounts. Each file contains Slurm association data for a single
cluster. Beginning with version 25.05, QOS information is included in the
dump file. Comments can be put into the file with the # character.
Each line of information must begin with one of the five titles; QOS ,
Cluster , Parent , Account or User . Following the title
is a space, dash, space, entity value, then specifications. Specifications are
colon-separated. If any variable, such as an Organization name, has a space in
it, surround the name with single or double quotes.

the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been

preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the

override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

One can specify a Quality of Service (QOS) for each job submitted
to Slurm. The QOSs are defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr
command. Jobs request a QOS using the "--qos=" option to the
sbatch , salloc , and srun commands.

### Resource Limits[#limits](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Each QOS is assigned a set of limits which will be applied to the
job. The limits mirror the limits imposed by the
user/account/cluster/partition association defined in the Slurm
database and described in the [Resource Limits page](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html). When limits for a QOS have been defined, they
will take precedence over the association's limits.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm
scheduler will preempt the running job.

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
To summarize the above, the QOSs and their associated limits are
defined in the Slurm database using the sacctmgr utility. The
QOS will only influence job scheduling priority when the multi-factor
priority plugin is loaded and a non-zero "PriorityWeightQOS" has been
defined in the slurm.conf file. The QOS will only determine job
preemption when the "PreemptType" is defined as "preempt/qos" in the
slurm.conf file. Limits defined for a QOS (and described above) will
override the limits of the user/account/cluster/partition
association.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that
is allowed to preempt a running job of another QOS, the Slurm

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).
NOTE : When Flags=Relative is added to a QOS, slurmctld
must be restarted or reconfigured for the flag to take effect.
Generally, the limits on a relative QOS will be calculated relative to the
resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the

from a file. This method can easily add a new cluster or copy an
existing cluster's associations into a new cluster with similar
accounts. Each file contains Slurm association data for a single

dump file. Comments can be put into the file with the # character.

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.

resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be
interpreted as 50% of all CPUs in the cluster.

Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.

```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with

### Job Preemption [#preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine
whether it can preempt a running job. It is important to note that the QOS
used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).
The QOS can be assigned (using sacctmgr ) a list of other
QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## Relative QOS [#relative](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.
Memory limits should be set with no units. Although the default units (MB) will
be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).

resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be

Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued

details.

configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"
is set to "preempt/qos", a queued job's QOS will be used to determine

used to determine if a job is eligible for preemption is the QOS associated
with the job and not a [Partition QOS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html).

QOSs that it can preempt. When there is a queued job with a QOS that

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

### Job Scheduling Priority [#priority](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
To enable the QOS priority component of the multi-factor priority
calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.
A job's QOS only affects is scheduling priority when the
multi-factor plugin is loaded.

## TRES information[#SECTION_TRES-information](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Trackable RESources (TRES) are used in many QOS or Association limits
(GrpTRES* / MaxTRES*). When setting limits, one or more comma-separated
"TRES=value" assignments can be specified.
Each TRES can be one of the Slurm defaults (e.g., cpu , mem ,
node ), or any defined generic resource. You can see the list of available
resources by running sacctmgr show tres .
Each TRES has a different limit, e.g., "GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G" would
establish 2 different limits: one for 16 CPUs and another for 32 GB of memory.
Setting a new value for a TRES type does not affect any other TRES types that
were previously specified. For example, on the same entity as above, a
subsequent assignment of "GrpTRES=gres/gpu=2" will result in
"GrpTRES=cpu=16,mem=32G,gres/gpu=2" applying to that entity.

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.
Slurm's backfill scheduler takes into consideration every running job.
It then considers pending jobs in priority order, determining when and where
each will start, taking into consideration the possibility of

In Step 3, Slurm distributes tasks to the nodes that were selected for
the job/step in Step 1. Each task is distributed to only one node, but more than one
task may be distributed to each node. Unless overcommitment of CPUs to tasks is
specified for the job, the number of tasks distributed to a node is
constrained by the number of CPUs allocated on the node and the number of CPUs per
task. If consumable resources is configured, or resource sharing is allowed, tasks from
more than one job/step may run on the same node concurrently.

results.prompt: Explain QOS limits such as MaxWall, MaxJobs, and GrpTRES
results.agent_response:
Short explanation of the common QOS limits and how they behave in Slurm:

- MaxWall
  - What it is: the maximum wall‑clock time (runtime) a job may request when using that QOS (format is a time value like 01:00:00).
  - Effect: it constrains the job's requested time. If a job requests more than the QOS MaxWall the cluster’s configured behavior (and QOS flags such as DenyOnLimit) determines whether the job is rejected at submission or the request is otherwise constrained/handled — administrators typically either reject the submission or enforce the smaller limit at allocation.
  - Notes: MaxWall is one of the time/node limits with special precedence rules in Slurm’s hierarchy; check the QOS and partition settings to see which limit wins.

- MaxJobs
  - What it is: the maximum number of concurrently running jobs allowed for the entity the limit is set on (a QOS, user association, account, etc.).
  - Effect: if starting a job would make the number of running jobs exceed MaxJobs for that entity, the job will not be started until resources are available. If the QOS has DenyOnLimit set, a submission that would violate MaxJobs can be rejected at submit time instead of simply pending.
  - Related limits: MaxSubmitJobs (controls number of jobs a user/account may have submitted/pending) and GrpJobs (aggregate running jobs limit for a group/account).

- GrpTRES
  - What it is: group (aggregate) limits expressed as TRES (Trackable RESources) like cpu, mem, node, or generic resources (gres). Example syntax: GrpTRES=gres/gpu=8,cpu=128,mem=512G.
  - Effect: GrpTRES limits the sum of the named resources used by all jobs in the group/association/QOS/partition. Slurm tests GrpTRES when it considers starting a job — if launching the job would push the aggregate usage over the GrpTRES value, the job will not be considered for allocation (it will remain pending). If DenyOnLimit is set the job may be rejected at submission instead.
  - Typical uses: enforce a cap on total GPUs, total CPUs, or total memory used by an account or QOS so one group can’t monopolize a resource pool.

How limits are evaluated (important rules)
- Limits are hierarchical. Slurm checks limits in a defined order (partition QOS, job QOS, user association, account, cluster, partition), and the first applicable limit wins (there are special-case exceptions for some limits like MaxWall/MaxTime).
- Grp* (group) limits are evaluated at job allocation time and are considered like a Max limit when DenyOnLimit is set.
- DenyOnLimit flag: when set for a QOS (or association), jobs that would violate a Max limit are rejected at submission time rather than pend.
- TRES names: use Slurm TRES names (cpu, mem, node, gres/gpu, etc.). You can list available TRES with sacctmgr show tres on a system.

Examples
- QOS A sets MaxJobs=10 → users or that QOS can have at most 10 running jobs at once.
- QOS B sets GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16 → the total GPUs used by all jobs tied to that QOS/account cannot exceed 16.
- QOS C sets MaxWall=12:00:00 → jobs requesting more than 12 hours will be subject to the QOS/deny policy (rejection or limit enforcement).

Commands to inspect/change (admin)
- View QOS limits: sacctmgr show qos format=... (or sacctmgr show qos)
- See available TRES: sacctmgr show tres
- Modify QOS or association limits: sacctmgr (admins only)

If you want, I can:
- Show the QOS limits currently configured on your cluster (sacctmgr/sacctmgr show qos) — I’ll run the docs/lookup first if you want an explanation, or run the Slurm read tools to fetch live values. Which would you like?

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
sacctmgr is used to view or modify Slurm account information.
The account information is maintained within a database with the interface
being provided by slurmdbd (Slurm Database daemon).
This database can serve as a central storehouse of user and
computer information for multiple computers at a single site.
Slurm account information is recorded based upon four parameters
that form what is referred to as an association .
These parameters are user , cluster , partition , and
account . user is the login name.
cluster is the name of a Slurm managed cluster as specified by
the ClusterName parameter in the slurm.conf configuration file.

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.
When this flag is set, all resource limits are treated as percentages of the
total resources available. Values higher than 100 are interpreted as 100%.

be displayed, the limits will be enforced as a percentage (1MB = 1%).

resources in the whole cluster. For example, `cpu=50` would be

results.prompt: Explain Slurm Fair Tree fairshare scheduling
results.agent_response:
Summary
- Fair Tree is Slurm’s modern fair‑share ranking algorithm (default since 19.05). It ranks every user/association so the scheduler can prefer under‑served accounts/users while preserving parent/child ordering guarantees. The algorithm produces a numeric FairShare factor per user (higher → higher priority contribution).

Key concepts
- Level Fairshare (LF): computed per association among its siblings as LF = S / U
  - S = normalized shares for the association = Sraw_self / (Sraw_self + Sraw_siblings)
  - U = normalized effective usage = Uraw_self / (Uraw_self + Uraw_siblings)
  - LF ∈ [0.0 .. ∞). LF > 1 means “under‑served” (should get higher priority); LF in (0,1) means “over‑served”. If an association has no usage, LF can be ∞.
- Tree model: Slurm builds a rooted, ordered (plane) tree of associations (root → accounts → users → projects, etc.). At each node it computes Level Fairshare values for that node’s children.
- Sorting & traversal: children of each node are sorted by their Level Fairshare (highest first). The tree is visited in depth‑first pre‑order; when a user node is visited it is assigned the next rank.
- Final FairShare factor: a user’s final FairShare factor is derived from that pre‑order rank (the highest ranked user receives 1.0; others are rank / total_associations). This yields a single comparable fairshare factor for every user association.

What that means for scheduling
- The algorithm ensures that if account A (a sibling of B) ranks higher than account B, then all children of A rank higher than all children of B — i.e., account-level priority is preserved for its users.
- Under‑served users/accounts get larger Level Fairshare and therefore get ordered earlier (higher FairShare factor) so they receive relatively more scheduling priority.
- Because Fair Tree ranks every association, the administrator must consider how that interacts with other priority factors (multifactor plugin weights).

Practical/admin notes
- Requires the Slurm accounting DB (slurmdbd) for usage and shares data; shares are configured with sacctmgr.
- View computed values with: sshare -l (shows Level FS, FairShare, Level, etc.).
- Fair Tree is used by the priority/multifactor plugin; tune PriorityWeightFairshare and PriorityCalcPeriod to control its impact and recalculation frequency. scontrol reconfigure does not force an immediate recompute — you may need to wait for the next PriorityCalcPeriod.
- Advantages vs. the old Classic algorithm: preserves parent/child ordering, avoids precision loss in ranking, and makes account-level priorities easier to reason about.
- Ties are allowed and handled deterministically by the traversal/sorting rules.

Where to read more
- Official Slurm docs: fair_tree algorithm page (Slurm Workload Manager — fair_tree) and priority/multifactor plugin documentation.

If you want, I can:
- Show the current FairShare/Level FS for users on your cluster (I’d run sshare -l), or
- Walk through a small numeric example with concrete shares/usage to illustrate how LF and final ranks are computed. Which would you prefer?

## Level Fairshare Calculation [#fairshare](https://slurm.schedmd.com/fair_tree.html)
The Level Fairshare equation is described below. Under-served associations
will have a value greater than 1.0. Over-served associations will have a value
between 0.0 and 1.0.

normalized to the shares assigned to itself and its siblings:

U

the account's usage:

results.prompt: Explain Slurm Fair Tree fairshare scheduling
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Fair Tree is Slurm’s current fair-share ranking algorithm (used by priority/multifactor). It ranks every user/association in a tree-shaped account hierarchy so that siblings are compared only to each other, then the tree is traversed (depth‑first, pre‑order) to produce a strict ranking. That ranking becomes the fairshare factor used by the scheduler (higher = higher priority).

Why Fair Tree exists / benefits
- Preserves parent/child ordering: if account A (a parent or sibling) ranks above account B, then every child/user under A ranks above every child/user under B. This prevents coordinators of sub-accounts from accidentally outranking users in other accounts.
- Stable numeric ordering: reduces precision/tie problems present in the older Classic algorithm.
- Ranks all associations (active or inactive), producing a global ordering used by the multifactor plugin.

High-level algorithm (steps)
1. For each node (association/account/user) compute a Level Fairshare value that considers only that node and its siblings (uses configured shares and each sibling’s usage).
2. For each subtree, sort the children by their Level Fairshare (highest first).
3. Build a rooted, ordered tree with children sorted left→right; perform a depth‑first pre‑order traversal:
   - Visit a child subtree fully before moving to the next sibling.
   - When you encounter a user association during traversal assign it the next rank.
4. Convert the user’s rank into the final fairshare factor: rank / total_number_of_user_associations (the top‑ranked user gets 1.0).

Important operational details
- Uses accounting DB usage and configured shares (Assoc/Account shares). Fair Tree requires the Slurm accounting DB to calculate usage-derived values.
- Priority decay: usage values are decayed using PriorityDecayHalfLife and recalculated every PriorityCalcPeriod. Those parameters control how long past usage affects fairshare.
- The multifactor plugin then multiplies the fairshare factor by PriorityWeightFairshare when computing Job_priority (see priority/multifactor).
- sshare -l shows FairShare and “Level FS” columns. Level FS may be shown as “inf” if an association has no usage.
- scontrol reconfigure does not necessarily trigger an immediate Fair Tree recompute — the algorithm runs on its scheduled calculation period; you may need to wait one PriorityCalcPeriod or force a recompute via the scheduler’s normal recalculation mechanisms.

Practical admin notes and recommendations
- Because Fair Tree produces a global strict ordering, you should pick PriorityWeightFairshare carefully (often lower than historical defaults). The docs suggest using a smaller weight (even as low as 1–2 × number_of_associations) depending on other priority factors.
- Configure PriorityDecayHalfLife and PriorityCalcPeriod to match how quickly you want past usage to fade.
- Verify results with sshare -l and sprio (or sprio --weights) to see how fairshare contributes to overall priority.
- Be aware that inactive associations are still ranked; this affects how ties and ordering behave site‑wide.

Short example intuition
- Suppose two sibling accounts A and B. If A’s Level Fairshare > B’s Level Fairshare, then during traversal all users under A will be visited before any users under B — so every child of A will have a higher fairshare rank (and thus higher fairshare factor) than every child of B. Within A, children are ordered by their own Level FS and so on down the tree.

References / commands to inspect (docs/tools)
- Docs: fair_tree algorithm page in the Slurm docs (fair_tree.html) and priority/multifactor page.
- Inspector commands: sshare -l (view fairshare and Level FS), sprio (priority factors), and check Priority* settings in slurm.conf (PriorityType, PriorityCalcPeriod, PriorityDecayHalfLife, PriorityWeightFairshare).

If you want, I can:
- Walk through a concrete example using your real account/usage data (need sshare output), or
- Show which slurm.conf settings to change for a particular site policy. Which would you like?

results.prompt: Explain Slurm Fair Tree fairshare scheduling
results.agent_response:
Summary
- Fair Tree is Slurm’s hierarchical fair‑share algorithm (default since 19.05). It ranks every user association (users/accounts) using a tree-based traversal so that higher‑priority accounts push all their child associations above lower‑priority accounts. The rank becomes the user’s fairshare factor used by the priority/multifactor plugin.

Key concepts and formulas
- Associations and tree: Slurm builds a rooted ordered tree of associations (accounts → subaccounts → users). Sibling associations are compared only with each other when computing their “level” value.
- Level Fairshare (LF): for each association at a level, LF = S / U
  - S (Shares Norm) = assigned shares for that association divided by the sum of raw shares of that association + its siblings (range 0..1).
  - U (Effective Usage) = usage for that association divided by the sum of usage of that association + its siblings (range 0..1).
  - LF > 1: under‑served (should get priority). LF between 0 and 1: over‑served.
  - If usage U = 0 for an association, LF is treated as infinity (so inactive associations get high priority until they consume resources).
- Tree traversal & ranking:
  - For each parent, compute LF for its children, sort children in descending LF, then visit children in that order with a depth‑first pre‑order traversal.
  - While visiting, assign ranks to user associations (one pre‑order pass). The highest ranked user gets the top position.
- Final fairshare factor:
  - The user’s fairshare value = rank / (total number of user associations). The top user gets 1.0; lower ranks get fractional values.

Why it’s different / benefits
- Hierarchical consistency: If account A outranks sibling B, all children of A will outrank all children of B (preserves account ordering across children).
- Deterministic ranking with less precision loss than the Classic algorithm.
- Inactive users/accounts can jump to high priority until they consume their fair share (LF infinite behavior).
- Prevents account coordinators from accidentally harming cross‑account priorities via local share tweaks.

Operational notes and tuning
- Requires the Slurm accounting DB for usage and share values.
- You can view computed fairshare values with: sshare -l (shows FairShare and Level FS).

results.prompt: Explain Slurm Fair Tree fairshare scheduling
results.agent_response:
Summary
- Fair Tree is Slurm's modern fair-share algorithm (default since 19.05) for computing the fairshare factor used by the priority/multifactor plugin.
- It ranks every user-association in the account/user tree so that higher‑level priority propagates deterministically to children: if account A outranks sibling account B, then every user under A outranks every user under B.

Key concepts and steps
1. Associations and tree
   - Slurm builds a rooted (ordered) tree of associations (accounts and users).
   - Each node has: assigned shares (Sraw) and measured usage (Uraw). Usage is measured in TRES-seconds (CPU-seconds or other TRES units) and is decayed over time.

2. Level Fairshare (LF)
   - For each set of siblings, Slurm computes a Level Fairshare for each child:
     LF = S / U
     where
       S = Sraw_self / (sum of Sraw for self + siblings)   (normalized shares among siblings)
       U = Uraw_self / (sum of Uraw for self + siblings)   (normalized usage among siblings; uses decayed Uraw)
   - LF > 1.0 → under-served (should get higher priority). LF < 1.0 → over-served.

3. Tree traversal and ranking
   - Children of each node are sorted by LF (descending).
   - The tree is visited depth‑first in that sorted order.
   - Users are encountered in pre-order and assigned ranks as they are visited.
   - The user’s FairShare factor = rank / total_number_of_user_associations (so the top-ranked user gets 1.0).

4. Ties
   - Siblings with identical LF get the same rank.
   - If a user equals an account-level LF, the user takes the same rank as the highest-ranked user of that account.
   - Sibling accounts that tie have their children merged before descent.

5. Usage decay and timing
   - Usage used in Uraw is decayed with an exponential half-life set by PriorityDecayHalfLife in slurm.conf (default about 7 days). If PriorityDecayHalfLife=0, no decay is applied.
   - PriorityCalcPeriod defines how often fairshare (and decay) is recalculated.
   - Usage is reported by sshare (sshare -l shows FairShare, Level FS, Raw/Nrm Usage).

6. Integration with priority/multifactor
   - The FairShare factor is one multiplier in the priority/multifactor plugin. Its impact is scaled by PriorityWeightFairshare (and any other configured priority weights).
   - Because Fair Tree ranks every association (even inactive ones), administrators may need to tune PriorityWeightFairshare (often much smaller than in older setups) so other priority factors remain useful.

Practical notes / admin tips
- Requires the Slurm accounting DB (SlurmDBD) because usage and shares come from accounting.
- Use sshare -l to inspect shares, raw/normalized usage, Level FS, and final FairShare.
- Changing to Fair Tree with scontrol reconfigure will not necessarily force an immediate recalculation; wait for the next PriorityCalcPeriod iteration.
- If you need deterministic control, tune shares at the account/user level, and adjust PriorityDecayHalfLife and PriorityWeightFairshare to control how historical usage and fairshare affect scheduling.

Short numeric example
- Two sibling accounts A and B: Sraw_A=2, Sraw_B=1 → Snorm_A=2/3, Snorm_B=1/3.
- If decayed usage Uraw_A=0.9, Uraw_B=0.1 → Unorm_A=0.9/(0.9+0.1)=0.9, Unorm_B=0.1/1.0=0.1.
- LF_A = (2/3)/0.9 ≈ 0.74 (over-served), LF_B = (1/3)/0.1 ≈ 3.33 (under-served).
- B’s subtree will be visited before A’s, so users under B receive higher fairshare ranks (and thus higher fairshare factors).

Where to read more
- The definitive reference is Slurm’s Fair Tree documentation (search “Slurm Fair Tree Fairshare algorithm” or see fair_tree.html) and the priority/multifactor docs (priority_multifactor.html). Use sshare -l on your cluster to inspect the live fairshare values.

If you want, I can:
- Show you the current fairshare values for a particular user or account (sshare output) — tell me the username or account.

Summary — what Fair Tree does
- Fair Tree is the default Slurm fair‑share algorithm (since ~19.05). Its goal is to produce stable, hierarchical fairshare priorities so that users in a "higher priority" account always rank above users in a lower priority sibling account, and to avoid precision/tie problems that the older Classic algorithm could produce.

Core idea (high level)
- Slurm builds the account/user hierarchy as a rooted ordered tree (accounts → subaccounts → users).
- At each tree level Fair Tree computes a single numeric Level Fairshare (LF) for each sibling association (account or user) based only on that association’s shares and usage relative to its siblings.
- The tree’s children are sorted by LF (highest first) and then the tree is traversed in depth‑first pre‑order. Users are assigned a global rank during that traversal.
- The user’s final fairshare factor = user_rank / total_number_of_user_associations (so the top ranked user gets 1.0).

Level Fairshare formula (exact)
- LF = S / U
  - S (Shares Norm) = Sraw_self / (Sraw_self + sum Sraw_siblings)
  - U (Effective Usage) = Uraw_self / (Uraw_self + sum Uraw_siblings)
- S and U are in [0.0 .. 1.0]. LF is in [0.0 .. ∞). 
  - LF > 1.0 → under‑served (should get more priority)
  - LF between 0 and 1 → over‑served (should get less)

Ranking / traversal
- For each node: compute LF for its immediate children, sort children by LF descending, then visit children in that order.
- When a child is a user association, assign it the next global rank as it’s visited.
- Because sorting is done per‑level and then visited depth‑first, if account A > account B at one level, all children of A will rank higher than all children of B.

Tie handling (important)
- Sibling associations with identical LF get the same rank.
- If a user has the same LF as a sibling account, the user receives the same rank as that account’s highest ranked child.
- Sibling accounts with identical LF have their children lists merged (preserving order) before descent.

Practical notes / commands
- Use sshare -l to see both the final FairShare and the Level FS (Level Fairshare) values.
- Level FS may be shown as infinity when an association has no usage (no denominator in U).
- Fair Tree replaces the older Classic algorithm but you can still choose Classic via configuration if needed.
- The algorithm prevents local account coordinators from accidentally making their users outrank other accounts’ users in unintended ways because ranking respects the hierarchical ordering.

Interpretation for admins and users
- If you want to raise an account’s long‑term priority relative to its siblings, increase its shares (Sraw).
- If an account appears under‑served (LF≫1), its jobs will get higher fairshare priority until usage catches up.
- Fair Tree is mainly about ordering/ranking. The numeric final fairshare is a normalized rank value used by the priority plugin (multifactor) together with age, QOS, etc.

If you want, I can:
- show a small worked numeric example (accounts, shares, usage → Level FS → traversal → final ranks), or
- point to the specific sections of the Slurm docs (Level Fairshare, Algorithm, Ties) for copyable formulas and examples. Which would you prefer?

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

## FairShare=parent[#parent](https://slurm.schedmd.com/classic_fair_share.html)
It is possible to disable the fairshare at certain levels of the fair share
hierarchy by using the `FairShare=parent` option of sacctmgr.
For users and accounts with `FairShare=parent` the normalized shares
and effective usage values from the parent in the hierarchy will be used when
calculating fairshare priories.
If all users in an account are configured with `FairShare=parent`
the result is that all the jobs drawing from that account will get the same
fairshare priority, based on the accounts total usage. No additional fairness
is added based on a user's individual usage.

## Level Fairshare Calculation [#fairshare](https://slurm.schedmd.com/fair_tree.html)
The Level Fairshare equation is described below. Under-served associations
will have a value greater than 1.0. Over-served associations will have a value
between 0.0 and 1.0.
```text
LF = S / U
```
LF
is the association's Level Fairshare
S
also known as Shares Norm, S is the association's assigned shares
normalized to the shares assigned to itself and its siblings:
`S = Sraw self / Sraw self+siblings`
U
also known as Effective Usage, U is the association's usage normalized to
the account's usage:
`U = Uraw self / Uraw self+siblings`
U and S are in the range `0.0 .. 1.0` . LF is in the
range `0.0 .. infinity`.

results.prompt: Explain sprio priority components and weights
results.agent_response:
Summary
- sprio reports the components (factors) the Multifactor Priority plugin uses to compute each job's scheduling priority and can also show the configured weights.
- The job priority is a weighted sum of enabled factors (plus a site factor and minus a nice factor). sprio helps you see each factor's contribution so you can understand why jobs are ordered.

The factors shown by sprio (what they mean)
- Age: how long the job has been waiting and eligible to run. Grows over time up to PriorityMaxAge (then caps at 1.0). Requires the accounting DB for correct computation.
- Association (assoc): a factor tied to the job’s association (account/user/account hierarchy).
- Fairshare: how under‑ or over‑consuming an account is relative to its entitlement (the fairshare algorithm may be the default or a variant such as depth‑oblivious).
- JobSize: reflects requested resources (CPUs or nodes). Behavior depends on PriorityFavorSmall and PriorityFlags (can favor small jobs or large jobs, or scale by size/time).
- Partition: per‑partition priority factor (administrator can bias partitions).
- QOS: factor from the job’s Quality Of Service.
- TRES factors: per-TRES factors (e.g., cpu, gpu) representing the amount requested of each tracked resource.
- Site factor: admin or site-specific factor (site_factor or a plugin).
- Nice factor: user-set adjustment that is subtracted from the total priority.

Weights and numeric behavior
- Each factor produces a floating value typically in [0.0, 1.0].
- Each factor is multiplied by a configured weight (e.g., PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightAssoc, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS). TRES weights use TRESWeight_<type>.
- Weights are unsigned 32‑bit integers in slurm.conf; they scale the importance of their factor.
- Final formula (from the docs, simplified):
  Job_priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge * age_factor + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor + PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor + SUM(TRESWeight_x * TRES_factor_x) - nice_factor
- The computed job priority is an integer (range 0 .. 4,294,967,295). Larger = higher scheduling priority.

sprio usage notes
- sprio (no flags) lists pending jobs with columns for JOBID, PRIORITY, AGE, FAIRSHARE, JOBSIZE, PARTITION, QOS, etc.
- sprio -w shows the configured weights (PriorityWeight*) so you can see how much each factor is scaled.
- sprio -n shows normalized factor values (useful to inspect relative contributions independent of weight).
- Use sprio --jobs or --users to limit output to particular jobs/users.

Configuration pointers (what to change if you want different behavior)
- Edit slurm.conf weights: PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightAssoc, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, and TRESWeight_<type>.
- Options that affect factor computation: PriorityMaxAge, PriorityFavorSmall, PriorityFlags (e.g., SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME), and the chosen fairshare implementation.
- Changes require updating slurm.conf and reconfiguring the controller (administrative action).

Quick interpretation advice
- If one factor value is near 1.0 and its weight is large, that factor dominates the priority.
- Use sprio -w to see weights and sprio -n to compare normalized factor magnitudes; multiply normalized factors by weights to understand each factor’s contribution to the job’s PRIORITY column.

If you want, I can:
- run sprio on the cluster to show current per‑job factors and weights (read-only). Would you like that?

## Age Factor[#age](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
Note: Computing the age factor requires the installation

will max out to 1.0.

results.prompt: Explain sprio priority components and weights
results.agent_response:
Short answer: sprio shows the Multifactor priority plugin’s component breakdown for each pending job. Job_priority is a weighted sum of several normalized factors; each factor is a float (0.0–1.0) and each weight is an integer configured in slurm.conf. Increasing a weight makes that factor contribute more to the job’s composite priority.

What the factors are (brief)
- Age: how long the job has been eligible to run. Grows with wait time until PriorityMaxAge caps it. (Requires Slurm accounting DB for correct aging.)
- Association: account/association-specific factor (assoc-level priority adjustments).
- Fairshare: how the user/account’s historical usage compares to their entitlement — higher fairshare factor raises priority for underused accounts and lowers it for overused ones. (Requires slurmdbd/accounting.)
- JobSize: reflects requested size (CPUs/nodes); behavior is affected by PriorityFavorSmall (favor small jobs if YES).
- Nice: per-job user-controlled niceness; the nice value is subtracted from the final priority.
- Partition: partition-associated priority factor.
- QOS: quality-of-service priority assigned by QOS; only used if PriorityWeightQOS > 0 and the QOS grants priority.
- Site: an admin/site-defined factor (via custom plugin or site_factor).
- TRES: per-TRES-type factors (e.g., cpu, gpu) so requests for specific resources can carry their own factor.

Formula (conceptual)
Job_priority = site_factor
 + PriorityWeightAge   * age_factor
 + PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor
 + PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
 + PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
 + PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
 + PriorityWeightQOS  * qos_factor
 + SUM( TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X )
 - nice_factor

Notes on ranges and types
- Each factor is 0.0–1.0 (floating point).
- Weights are unsigned 32-bit integers (configured in slurm.conf).
- Final job priority is an integer (0 .. 4294967295); larger → higher scheduling precedence.

Common slurm.conf knobs
- PriorityType=priority/multifactor (enable plugin)
- PriorityWeightAge=1000
- PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
- PriorityWeightJobSize=1000
- PriorityWeightPartition=1000
- PriorityWeightQOS=0
- PriorityMaxAge=14-0 (sets how long until age_factor → 1.0)
- PriorityDecayHalfLife (controls decay of historical usage for fairshare)
- PriorityFavorSmall=YES|NO (affects job size factor)
- PriorityUsageResetPeriod (when to reset usage accounting)

sprio utility notes
- sprio prints the weighted components for pending jobs (columns like JOBID PRIORITY AGE FAIRSHARE JOBSIZE PARTITION QOS).
- sprio -n shows normalized factor values (0–1).
- sprio -w shows the configured PriorityWeight* and TRES weights.
- Use sprio --jobs or --users to inspect specific jobs/users.

Tuning guidance (short)
- To emphasize wait time, raise PriorityWeightAge (or shorten PriorityMaxAge).
- To enforce fairshare more, raise PriorityWeightFairshare and tune PriorityDecayHalfLife/UsageResetPeriod.
- To prefer small or large jobs, toggle PriorityFavorSmall and adjust PriorityWeightJobSize.
- Be careful: weights interact; changes can have non‑linear effects on queue ordering.

If you want, I can:
- show the currently configured PriorityWeight* and related settings from your cluster’s slurm.conf (lookup via scontrol_show_config), or
- run sprio on your cluster to display per-job factor breakdowns (requires slurmdbd for fairshare/age). Which would you like?

results.prompt: Explain sprio priority components and weights
results.agent_response:
Short answer: sprio shows the breakdown of Slurm's multifactor job priority. Each job's priority is a weighted sum of several normalized factors (0.0–1.0) multiplied by administrator-configurable integer weights. sprio can print the per-factor contributions (-n shows normalized factors, -w shows configured weights).

Details

1) The priority components (factors)
- Age — how long the job has been waiting (capped at PriorityMaxAge). Requires accounting (slurmdbd).
- Association — association/account-specific priority (association priorities are normalized).
- Fairshare — restores balance between promised vs consumed resources (depends on PriorityDecayHalfLife, usage reset, and slurmdbd).
- Job size — larger jobs can get more priority (or smaller if PriorityFavorSmall=YES).
- Nice — user-supplied nice that lowers priority (this factor is subtracted).
- Partition — per-partition priority factor.
- QOS — per-QoS priority factor.
- Site — site-defined factor (via site_factor or job_submit/site plugin).
- TRES factors — one factor per TRES type requested (CPUs, GPUs, licenses, burst buffer, etc.); more requested TRES increases that factor.

All factors themselves are floating point values normalized into the 0.0–1.0 range.

2) How weights work
- The final job priority is an integer computed roughly as:
  Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge * age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor) + SUM( TRES_weight_X * TRES_factor_X ) - nice_factor
- Weights are unsigned integers (32-bit). The larger the weight, the more influence that factor has on the final priority.
- Factor values are 0.0–1.0, so the weight effectively scales the contribution into the integer priority space.
- The priority value range is 0 .. 4294967295 (uint32). Higher numbers = higher priority.

3) Practical notes / tuning guidance
- Default weight values in slurm.conf are small (1), but examples commonly set weights large (e.g., PriorityWeightFairshare=10000, PriorityWeightAge=1000) so differences in fractional factors produce meaningful integer differences. If weights are too small, distinct factor values may collapse to the same integer contribution.
- Use PriorityMaxAge to control how long until age_factor reaches 1.0, and PriorityDecayHalfLife / PriorityUsageResetPeriod to control fairshare behavior.
- PriorityFavorSmall controls whether small or large jobs are favored by the JobSize factor.
- TRES weights let you prioritize jobs that request certain resources (e.g., licenses, GPUs).

4) Commands to inspect
- sprio — show per-job weighted contributions (default output).
- sprio -n — show normalized factor values (0.0–1.0).
- sprio -w — show the currently configured PriorityWeight* and TRES weights.
- Check slurm.conf entries: PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, plus TRES weights and Priority* settings.

If you want, I can:
- show the current weights on this cluster (sprio -w / check slurm.conf) — or
- explain how to set example weights for a specific policy (e.g., favor short jobs vs. enforce fairshare). Which would you prefer?

results.prompt: Explain sprio priority components and weights
results.agent_response:
Short answer: sprio shows the breakdown of the Multifactor priority components that Slurm’s priority/multifactor plugin uses. A job’s composite priority is a weighted sum of several normalized factors (each 0.0–1.0) multiplied by administrator-configured integer weights. The weights live in slurm.conf (PriorityWeight*) and you can inspect current per-job components with sprio and the configured weights with sprio -w.

Canonical formula (from the plugin):
Job_priority = site_factor
+ PriorityWeightAge    * age_factor
+ PriorityWeightAssoc  * assoc_factor
+ PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor
+ PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor
+ PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor
+ PriorityWeightQOS     * qos_factor
+ SUM_over_TRES( PriorityWeightTRES_<type> * TRES_factor_<type> )
- nice_factor

Key points about components and weights
- Factors (age_factor, fairshare_factor, etc.)
  - Each is a floating point in [0.0, 1.0], normalized for that factor.
  - Represent the job’s relative value for that dimension (e.g., age_factor grows as the job waits; TRES_factor reflects requested amount of a tracked resource).
- Weights (PriorityWeight*)
  - Unsigned integers (32-bit) configured by the admin in slurm.conf.
  - Scale the importance of each factor in the final integer priority.
  - Larger weight → that factor has more influence on ordering.
  - The final Job_priority is an unsigned 32-bit integer (0 .. 4294967295); bigger = higher priority.
- The “nice” factor is subtractive: a job/user “nice” lowers priority.
- TRES factors
  - There is a factor per tracked TRES (cpu, gpu, license, burstbuffer, …). The admin configures TRES-related priority influence via PriorityWeightTRES (or per-type entries); more requested TRES can increase job priority when TRES weights are positive.
- Association factor
  - Reflects the job’s association/account/group and any association-level priority characteristics.
- Fairshare factor
  - Measures the gap between promised and consumed resources (accounting DB required); favors users/accounts below their fair share.
- Job size factor
  - Reflects job resource size (nodes/CPUs) — can be used to favor large or small jobs depending on configuration.
- Partition and QOS factors
  - Partition: per-partition configured priority adjustments.
  - QOS: each QOS can have a priority value; PriorityWeightQOS enables that contribution.

Useful commands
- sprio — show each pending job’s component contributions.
- sprio -n — show normalized factors.
- sprio -w — show the configured PriorityWeight* values.
- Edit weights in slurm.conf (PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightAssoc, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, PriorityWeightTRES, SiteFactor, etc.) and reconfigure/restart as needed.

How to think about tuning
- Increase PriorityWeightAge to reduce starvation (older jobs rise faster).
- Increase PriorityWeightFairshare to prioritize users/accounts underused relative to their share.
- Increase PriorityWeightJobSize to favor big parallel runs (or keep small to reduce queue fragmentation).
- Use PriorityWeightTRES to give explicit weight to GPUs, licenses, burstbuffers, etc.
- Combine weights carefully — since factors are normalized, relative weights determine trade-offs.

If you want, I can:
- show the current sprio breakdown and weights on this cluster (sprio / sprio -w), or
- suggest a recommended weight configuration for a specific policy goal (e.g., favor GPUs, reduce small-job starvation). Which would you like?

results.prompt: Explain sprio priority components and weights
results.agent_response:
Good question — sprio shows how Slurm’s multifactor priority plugin breaks a job’s scheduling priority into components and how each is weighted. Summary first, then short details for each component and how weights work.

Summary / formula
- Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge * age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc * assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare * fairshare_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize * job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition * partition_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS * qos_factor) + SUM(PriorityWeightTRES_type * TRES_factor_type) - nice_factor
- factors are floating-point values in [0.0, 1.0]; weights are unsigned integers (configured in slurm.conf).
- The final job priority is an integer (0 .. 4294967295). Larger => higher scheduling precedence.
- sprio displays the per-job components. sprio -n shows normalized factors (0..1); sprio -w prints the configured PriorityWeight* values.

Components (what each measures and key knobs)
- Age
  - Represents how long a job has been eligible to run (wait time).
  - Grows with wait time until it caps at PriorityMaxAge (configurable).
  - Controlled by PriorityWeightAge.
- Association
  - Factor associated with the job’s association/account (assoc-level configuration).
  - Controlled by PriorityWeightAssoc.
- Fairshare
  - Reflects how much of the cluster resources the user/account has already consumed vs. their shares.
  - Jobs for under-served accounts get higher fairshare_factor.
  - Requires accounting (slurmdbd) and is affected by share configuration and decay/half-life.
  - Controlled by PriorityWeightFairshare. There is also a depth-oblivious variant (PriorityFlags) with different formulas.
- Job size
  - Based on requested CPUs or nodes; can favor large or small jobs depending on PriorityFavorSmall.
  - PriorityFlags and SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME alter behavior (e.g., size relative to time).
  - Controlled by PriorityWeightJobSize.
- Nice
  - User-controlled “nice” level; treated as a subtractive component (nice_factor is subtracted).
  - Not multiplied by a PriorityWeight; included as the -nice_factor term.
- Partition (partition/job factor)
  - Per-partition priority factor; jobs in higher-priority partitions get higher partition_factor.
  - Controlled by PriorityWeightPartition.
- QOS
  - A QOS can have an associated priority value; if enabled, that contributes to the job priority.
  - Controlled by PriorityWeightQOS (must be set > 0 to take effect).
- Site
  - A site-specific factor provided by a site_factor plugin or job_submit plugin; additive (site_factor).
  - Useful for local custom logic.
- TRES (Trackable RESources)
  - A factor per TRES type (GPUs, licenses, burst buffers, etc.), representing the TRES requested/allocated.
  - Each TRES type may be weighted (PriorityWeightTRES and TRESBillingWeights play roles).
  - Controlled by PriorityWeightTRES (and per-TRES weight settings).

Using sprio
- sprio lists JOBID, overall PRIORITY, and the component columns (AGE, FAIRSHARE, JOBSIZE, PARTITION, QOS, …).
- sprio -n shows normalized 0..1 factor values.
- sprio -w prints the configured PriorityWeight* values (what each factor is multiplied by).

Tuning
- Change weights in slurm.conf (PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, PriorityWeightAssoc, PriorityWeightTRES, etc.).
- After changing weights you must reload/reconfigure the controller (e.g., scontrol reconfigure) to apply them.
- Be cautious: large integer weight differences can dominate priorities; use sprio to inspect effects before wide rollout.

If you want, I can:
- show the currently configured PriorityWeight* values on this cluster (sprio -w / scontrol show config) — I can run the appropriate read tools and report back, or
- walk through an example sprio output line and explain how the numeric final priority was constructed. Which would you prefer?

## Job Priority Factors In General [#general](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)
The job's priority at any given time will be a weighted sum of all the
factors that have been enabled in the slurm.conf file. Job priority can be
expressed as:
```text
Job_priority = site_factor + (PriorityWeightAge) * (age_factor) + (PriorityWeightAssoc) * (assoc_factor) + (PriorityWeightFairshare) * (fair-share_factor) + (PriorityWeightJobSize) * (job_size_factor) + (PriorityWeightPartition) * (priority_job_factor) + (PriorityWeightQOS) * (QOS_factor) + SUM(TRES_weight_cpu * TRES_factor_cpu, TRES_weight_ * TRES_factor_ , ...) - nice_factor
```
All of the factors in this formula are floating point numbers that
range from 0.0 to 1.0. The weights are unsigned, 32 bit integers.

The generalized formula for R is a bit more complex. It involves a
local usage ratio r l :
```text
r l = r / (U all_siblings /S all_siblings )
```

total usage ratio of all the siblings at his level including
itself. For example, assuming that all the children of an account have
used in total two times their combined shares (which equal the shares

one third.

```text
R = R parent * r l ^k
```

The main formula for calculating the fair-share factor of an account is:
```text
F = 2^(-R)
```
where:
F
is the fair-share factor
R
is the effective usage ratio of the account
This formula resembles the original fair-share formula, and
produces the same result for an account at the first level of the tree
(under root). Indeed, for first-level accounts, the effective usage
ratio R is equal to the usage ratio r defined as:
```text
r = U/S
```
where:
S
is the normalized shares
U
is the normalized usage factoring in half-life decay
which is the same as the original formula.
