results.prompt: Explain sinfo node states such as idle, alloc, drain, and down
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise explanation of the common sinfo node states you asked about and what they mean for scheduling and troubleshooting.

- idle
  - Meaning: The node is up and not currently allocated to any job. It is available for new job allocations.
  - Scheduler implication: Jobs can be placed on the node immediately (subject to partition/QOS constraints).
  - How to inspect: sinfo -N (or sinfo -l) shows node-listed as idle.

- alloc (allocated / ALLOCATED)
  - Meaning: The node (or some of its resources) has been allocated to one or more jobs and is serving those jobs.
  - Variants: ALLOCATED+ or mixed states indicate the node is allocated to active jobs and there are jobs starting/finishing or some resources still free.
  - Scheduler implication: The scheduler will not place new allocations that conflict with the current allocation; some backfill/partial allocations may be possible depending on free resources.

- drain (DRAINING / DRAIN / DRAINED)
  - Meaning: The node has been taken out of normal service so it will not accept new allocations. Typical workflow:
    - DRAINING (often shown as drain): node set to be drained; running jobs continue until completion.
    - DRAINED: node is drained and currently has no running jobs.
  - Typical causes: Administrator-requested maintenance, upgrades, hardware repair, or to remove a node from the pool before reboot.
  - Scheduler implication: No new jobs are started on the node; existing jobs are allowed to finish (unless forcibly cancelled).
  - How to inspect reason: scontrol show node <nodename> will include the drain reason.

- down (DOWN)
  - Meaning: Slurm has determined the node is not responding or is otherwise unavailable (powered off, network unreachable, failed health check).
  - Typical causes: Node crashed, unreachable, out-of-band power-off, or repeated heartbeat failures.
  - Scheduler implication: The node will not be allocated to jobs until it is brought back up and set to an available state.
  - How to inspect reason: sinfo -R (shows nodes in DOWN/DRAIN states and reasons) or scontrol show node <nodename>.

Quick notes and useful checks
- Mixed/partial states: A node can be partially used (some CPUs/GPU allocated) and appear as MIXED/MIX in some outputs; sinfo -N or scontrol show node gives per-node resource details.
- Suffix flags: sinfo can show suffix flags like ! (not responding), ~ (powered off), @ (pending reboot), $ (reservation-maintenance) — these give additional context about node condition.
- Commands to inspect details (read-only): sinfo -N -l, sinfo -R, and scontrol show node <nodename> will show state, resource allocation, and the admin reason text.

If you want, tell me a node name (or paste sinfo output) and I can explain that node’s current state and reason.

results.prompt: Explain sinfo node states such as idle, alloc, drain, and down
results.agent_response:
Good question — sinfo reports a compact node-state code that tells you whether a node can accept new work, is servicing jobs, or needs admin attention. Brief definitions and notes:

- idle
  - Meaning: Node is up and available for scheduling; no jobs are currently allocated.
  - Effect: Jobs may be placed on this node.

- alloc (or allocated / ALLOCATED)
  - Meaning: One or more jobs have been allocated the node.
  - Effect: The node will not be used for other jobs until the allocation(s) end. You may also see ALLOCATED+ when the node is allocated and additional jobs are in the process of being started there.

- drain (DRAINING / DRAINED)
  - Meaning: Administrator-requested state to remove the node from normal scheduling.
    - DRAINING: node is marked to drain; running jobs continue to run but no new jobs will be started.
    - DRAINED (or drain): node has finished running jobs and is now not accepting new jobs.
  - Typical use: planned maintenance, retire node, or to prevent new jobs while current jobs finish.
  - Effect: Scheduler will not place new allocations on the node; running jobs are allowed to finish.

- down
  - Meaning: Node is not responding or has been marked unreachable/unusable by Slurm.
  - Effect: Node will not be allocated; requires admin intervention (investigate network/OS/munge/slurmd).
  - Note: If a non-responsive node remains, it is usually shown as DOWN (vs temporary NOT_RESPONDING suffixes).

Common additional states/flags you may encounter:
- mixed — some CPUs/GPUs on the node are allocated while others are free (common with multi-job packing).
- fail / failing — node has reported hardware/software failure or was administratively marked failed.
- reserved — node held for a reservation (you’ll see “reservation” context).
- POWER_ states (~, %, !, etc.) — node powering up/down or powered off.
- Suffix flags: a short character after the state can indicate special conditions (e.g., ~ = not responding / powered off, $ = in maintenance/reservation, @ = pending reboot, ^ = reboot issued, - = planned by backfill).

How to get more detail
- For the per-node reason field: scontrol show node=<nodename> (shows Reason, State, etc.).
- To list nodes in drain/down states or see reason summaries: sinfo -R or sinfo --states=drained (or your cluster’s sinfo_reasons view).

If you tell me a node name or paste a sinfo line you’re seeing, I can explain that specific state and any suffix flags.

results.prompt: Explain sinfo node states such as idle, alloc, drain, and down
results.agent_response:
Brief definitions (how they appear in sinfo and what they mean)

- IDLE
  - Meaning: the node is up and available for scheduling; no jobs are currently allocated.
  - Behavior: new jobs may be placed on the node according to scheduling rules.

- ALLOC (or ALLOCATED)
  - Meaning: the node has one or more running job allocations.
  - Behavior: the node’s resources are reserved for those jobs and are not available for new allocations (unless the node is shared/multi-job capable).

- DRAIN (or DRAINING / DRAINED)
  - Meaning: the node has been marked so that no new jobs will be started there. Existing running jobs are allowed to finish (unless a force option was used).
  - Why admins use it: for maintenance, software updates, graceful retire, or to remove the node from service without killing current jobs.
  - Behavior: sinfo shows the node as unavailable for new allocations; once running jobs complete the node usually becomes DRAINED (or remains in a non-allocable state) until an admin RESUMEs it.

- DOWN
  - Meaning: the node is considered unavailable because it failed (lost contact), powered off, or was administratively marked as down.
  - Behavior: the scheduler will not place jobs on it. Jobs already running may be terminated or requeued with NODE_FAIL depending on configuration. An admin must investigate/fix and then mark the node up/resume it.

Quick notes and tips
- DRAIN vs DOWN: DRAIN is for graceful removal (jobs finish); DOWN indicates a failure/unreachable state and is usually corrective-action driven.
- Mixed/partial states: a node can show as MIXED if some CPUs/GPUs are allocated while others are free. sinfo summarizations sometimes show per-node state flags.
- To see administrative reason text (why a node is DRAIN/DOWN) use sinfo -R or sinfo_reasons / scontrol show node <nodename>.
- State names you’ll commonly see in sinfo: UNKNOWN, IDLE, ALLOCATED (ALLOC), MIXED, DRAIN, DOWN, FAIL, MAINT (maintenance), RESERVED.

If you want, I can show the current node states for a partition (sinfo) or check the reason text for a specific node — tell me which partition or node name to inspect.

results.prompt: Explain important scontrol show job fields
results.agent_response:
Here are the most useful fields you’ll see in scontrol show job <jobid>, grouped and explained so you know what to check when diagnosing/summarizing a job.

Identification
- JobId — the Slurm job numeric id (e.g., 12345). Always include this when talking about a job.
- JobName — user-specified job name (sbatch --job-name).
- UserId / GroupId — owner and UNIX/GID (often shown as name(uid)).
- Account — accounting project the job is charged to.

Scheduling / policy
- Partition — partition the job was submitted to.
- QOS — quality-of-service used (affects priority/limits).
- Priority — scheduler priority value (higher = scheduled earlier).
- Dependency — job dependency string (afterok, afterany, etc.).
- Reservation — reservation name if the job is tied to one.

State & why
- JobState — current state (PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, etc.).
- Reason — short scheduler reason for PENDING (e.g., Resources, Priority, QOSLimit). First place to look when a job is stuck.
- BatchFlag — indicates sbatch/batch behavior (batch jobs set =1).
- Requeue / Restarts — whether job is eligible to be requeued and how many restarts.

Timing
- SubmitTime — when the job was submitted.
- StartTime — when the job started (or estimated start if pending).
- EndTime — end/finish time (if completed).
- RunTime (or RunTimeRaw / Elapsed) — how long the job has run.
- TimeLimit — requested walltime (sbatch --time). If running longer than this the job will be killed.

Resources requested / allocated
- NumNodes / Nodes / NodeList — requested number of nodes and the concrete node list allocated (NodeList shows names like node[01-02]).
- NumCPUs / NumTasks / CPUsPerTask — CPU/core counts and task layout (e.g., NumCPUs=32, NumTasks=8).
- ReqMem / ReqTRES — requested memory/TRES; TRES (trackable resources) string lists e.g. cpu=,mem=,gres/gpu=.
- AllocTRES — actually allocated TRES for the job (shows what the job currently holds).
- Gres / GresUsed — generic resources requested e.g. gres=gpu:1 and how many are in use.
- TresPerNode / TresPerCPU (when present) — per-node/per-CPU allocation breakdown.

Allocation details (where to look for per-node info)
- AllocNode:Sid — the local node and system id making the allocation (useful for debugging node-local issues).
- NodeAddr / NodeList — address/list of nodes allocated.
- Flags / StateFlags — extra flags describing the job/step state (suspend, restarting, etc.).
- Partition/Features — on some configs you’ll see requested node features (e.g., feature=volta) used to match nodes.

I/O & environment
- WorkDir — working directory where the job runs.
- StdOut / StdErr — paths for stdout/stderr (can be %j-expanded).
- Command / BatchScript (when shown) — the sbatch script path or submitted command (privileged users or with details).

Exit / accounting
- ExitCode — exit code and signal for completed jobs (format exit:sig). Crucial when diagnosing failures.
- TresUsage / Usage (not always shown) — actual consumption summary (CPU, memory) when available; for detailed accounting use sacct.

Job arrays & steps
- ArrayJobId / ArrayTaskId — for array elements (e.g., 2000_5).
- Steps — scontrol shows step-level info for multi-step jobs; use scontrol show step <jobid> for step details.

Useful tips
- If a pending job shows Reason=Resources, check NodeList/Partition via sinfo and current queue via squeue for contention.
- For per-node CPU/memory placement use scontrol show job <id> Details (or -d) which prints CPUs/NUMA/memory allocated per node.
- For historical resource usage or final accounting (completed jobs) use sacct — scontrol is a live-view tool.
- For very terse pending reasons use squeue first (scontrol will give more detail for some fields).

If you want, tell me a JobId and I can walk through a real scontrol show job output and point to the exact fields relevant to its state.

results.prompt: Explain important scontrol show job fields
results.agent_response:
Below are the scontrol show job fields that are most useful to read and why they matter. I’ve grouped them by purpose (identity, scheduling, resources, timing, I/O & control, and failure/troubleshooting).

Identity / ownership
- JobId — unique numeric job identifier (what you use with squeue/scontrol/scancel).
- JobName — human name given at submit; helpful when multiple jobs from same user exist.
- UserId / GroupId — owner and group (often shown as name(uid)); needed for access/authorization checks.

Scheduling / policy
- Partition — partition the job was submitted to (affects available resources and limits).
- Account / QOS — accounting and quality-of-service used for scheduling/limits and fairshare.
- Priority — scheduler priority value; higher is scheduled earlier.
- Reservation — name of any reservation the job is tied to (if set).

State & reason
- JobState — RUNNING / PENDING / COMPLETED / FAILED / CANCELLED / SUSPENDED / etc.
- Reason — short pending reason shown for PENDING jobs (eg, Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail). Useful for “why isn’t it starting?” troubleshooting.
- Nodes / NodeList / NumNodes — nodes allocated (for RUNNING) or requested (for pending). NodeList shows concrete node names.
- AllocNode:Sid — the node and system id that granted the allocation (useful for debugging allocation ownership).
- BatchFlag — indicates how the job was submitted (BatchFlag=1 for sbatch); increments on requeue.

Requested vs allocated resources
- TRES and ReqTRES — requested Trackable RESources (e.g., tres=cpu=4,mem=32G,gres/gpu=2). Shows what the job asked for.
- AllocTRES — resources actually allocated to the job (what the system gave). Compare AllocTRES vs ReqTRES to confirm allocations.
- NNodes / NTasks / CPUsPerTask / NumCPUs — counts of nodes, tasks, CPUs per task or total CPUs: how the job is sized across nodes.
- ReqMem / MinMemoryPerNode / MinMemoryCPU — memory request settings (per node or per job); important for OOM problems.
- Gres / ReqGRES — generic resources requested (often GPUs). If you requested GPUs, check that AllocTRES shows gres/gpu entries.

Time & timing
- SubmitTime — when the job was submitted.
- EligibleTime — when the job became eligible to run (after dependency/wait conditions).
- StartTime — actual start time (for RUNNING/COMPLETED jobs).
- EndTime — completion time (for COMPLETED/FAILED).
- TimeLimit / TimeMin — requested runtime limit and minimum time; useful to know if a job may be preempted or killed for exceeding limit.
- RunTime / Elapsed — how long the job has been running (for RUNNING jobs).

I/O, environment, control
- WorkDir — working directory where the job started.
- StdOut / StdErr — paths to stdout/stderr files (where application logs go).
- Command (or BatchScript) — the submitted command or path to batch script (so you can inspect what ran).
- Dependency — any job dependencies (afterok, afterany, etc.).
- Requeue / Reboot / Hold — flags controlling requeueing, reboot on failure, or hold status.

Exit / failure diagnostics
- ExitCode — format "<exit>:<signal>" for finished jobs; primary indicator of why a job failed.
- Reason (for COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELLED) — may include cause text for failure.
- State and related message — together with ExitCode, tells whether the job was preempted, killed by the system, timed out, or finished normally.

Advanced / detailed fields (use scontrol show job <id> with details)
- LaunchParameters / JobStepInfo — per-step allocation details when a job uses multiple steps.
- NumCPUsAlloc / CPUSets / NUMA info — CPU placement and NUMA memory allocation (only shown with details).
- AllocNodes / NodeState info — per-node CPU/memory mapping for the job (useful for NUMA/debug performance problems).

Quick usage tips
- For “why pending” start with squeue (shows Reason column); scontrol show job <id> gives fuller fields including dependencies and requested resources.
- If a job fails, inspect ExitCode, StdErr path, and the JobState/Reason in scontrol output.
- Compare ReqTRES / ReqMem / NTasks with AllocTRES / AllocNodes to spot partial allocations or unmet requests (common with GRES/GPU requests).

If you want, I can:
- show a concrete example scontrol show job output and annotate each field, or
- explain any specific field in more depth (which field?).

results.prompt: Explain important scontrol show job fields
results.agent_response:
Good question — scontrol show job prints many fields. Below are the most important ones to know, what they mean, and how to use them when inspecting or troubleshooting a job.

- JobId
  - Unique numeric job identifier. Use this when querying other Slurm commands (squeue, sacct, scontrol).

- JobName
  - Human name given at submit (sbatch --job-name). Helpful for quick identification.

- UserId / GroupId
  - Owner and group (user(uid)). Useful for filtering and ownership checks.

- Account / QOS
  - Accounting account and quality-of-service. QOS can affect priority, limits, and preemption.

- Partition
  - Partition the job was submitted to. Resource availability and policies are partition-specific.

- JobState
  - Current state (PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, SUSPENDED, etc.). First field to read when diagnosing.

- Reason (or StateReason)
  - If PENDING, shows why (e.g., Resources, Priority, Dependency, QOSMaxCPU). Critical for understanding why a job won’t start.

- Dependency
  - Any job dependencies (afterok:12345, afterany:...) that must be satisfied before this job may start.

- SubmitTime / EligibleTime / StartTime / EndTime / RunTime or Elapsed
  - Timestamps for lifecycle events:
    - SubmitTime: when job was submitted.
    - EligibleTime: when it became eligible to run (after holds/dependencies).
    - StartTime: when allocation began (or N/A if not started).
    - Elapsed / RunTime: how long it has been running.
  - Compare these to TimeLimit for time usage and billing.

- TimeLimit / TimeMin
  - Requested walltime limit and minimum time. Important for expected runtime and scheduler backfill.

- Nodes / NodeList / NumNodes / NNodes
  - How many nodes requested/allocated and which nodes (NodeList). If pending due to node availability, NodeList/NumNodes shows the request shape.

- CPUs / NTasks / CPUSPerTask / TasksPerNode
  - CPU/task layout (how many tasks, cores per task). Check these against partition node capacities.

- ReqMem / ReqCPUS / ReqGRES / TRES / AllocTRES
  - Resource requests and allocations:
    - ReqMem / ReqCPUS: requested memory and CPUs.
    - ReqGRES / GRES: requested generic resources (GPUs).
    - TRES / AllocTRES: trackable resources (cpu, mem, gpu) that were allocated. Useful when investigating GPU or memory shortages.

- GresUsed / Gres
  - Which GPUs (or other GRES) were allocated/used. Useful for GPU accounting and debugging device-level failures.

- AllocNode:Sid
  - The node and system id that performed the allocation (shown for running jobs). Useful for node-level debugging.

- StdOut / StdErr / WorkDir
  - Paths to job stdout/stderr and working directory (where the batch script ran). First place to look for application logs.

- BatchFlag
  - Indicates batch-style submission (sbatch) vs interactive; increments when job is requeued. Helps reason about requeues.

- ExitCode
  - For finished jobs, exit status formatted as "rc:signal". Use to tell whether the job exited cleanly or was killed by a signal.

- Hold/HoldReason
  - Whether job is held (user/administrator hold) and why. Held jobs won't become eligible until released.

- Reservation
  - Reservation the job is tied to (if any). Reserved resources can affect scheduling eligibility.

- ArrayJobId / ArrayTaskId
  - For job arrays: array parent id and the specific task index (e.g., 1000_5).

- Priority / PriorityTier
  - Effective scheduling priority and tier. Explains ordering when resources are contested.

- Flags / Features / Constraint
  - Any special flags, required node features, or CPU architecture constraints. If constraints don’t match available nodes, the job will stay pending.

Quick troubleshooting checklist using these fields
- Job is PENDING: check JobState + Reason, Dependency, Hold, Partition, ReqGRES/TRES, and Constraints.
- Job won't get GPUs: check ReqGRES/GRES, TRES, partition GRES capacity (compare with sinfo).
- Job unexpectedly short or killed: check ExitCode, StdErr, and AllocNode:Sid to find node logs.
- Job started on wrong node-type: check NodeList, Constraint/Features, and the allocated TRES.

If you want, tell me a JobId and I can walk through a real scontrol show job output and highlight the relevant lines.

Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays

results.prompt: Explain important scontrol show job fields
results.agent_response:
Good question — scontrol show job prints many fields. Below are the most important ones you’ll see and what each means, with notes on when they’re useful for debugging.

General identity and accounting
- JobId — numeric job identifier (use this to reference the job in other commands).
- JobName — user-supplied job name (helpful when reading lists).
- UserId / GroupId — submitting user and primary group (shows UID/GID and numeric id).
- Account — accounting/project the job is charged to.
- QOS — job QOS (affects limits, preemption, priority).
- Partition — partition the job was submitted to.

State, timing, and lifecycle
- JobState — current state (PENDING, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, etc.). Primary field for quick status.
- Reason — why a pending job is blocked (resources, priority, reservation, dependency). Crucial for “why not starting”.
- SubmitTime — when the job was submitted.
- EligibleTime — earliest time job is eligible to run (after dependency or reservation).
- StartTime — when job started (or scheduled start).
- EndTime — completion time (for finished jobs).
- RunTime / Elapsed — elapsed runtime for running or finished jobs.
- TimeLimit — requested maximum runtime.
- TimeLeft — remaining runtime (running jobs).

Resource requests vs allocations
- ReqTRES / ReqNodes / NNodes / NTasks / CPUS — what the job requested (TRES = trackable resources; can include cpu,gpu,mem,node).
- Gres (or GRES) — requested generic resources (e.g., gres=gpu:4).
- AllocTRES / AllocNodes / NodeList / NumNodes — what Slurm actually allocated (AllocTRES shows actual allocated cpu/gpu/mem counts).
- Nodes / NodeList — node count and the actual hostnames assigned (NodeList may be a list/range).
- AllocNode:Sid — local node and system id creating the allocation (admin-level; useful for debugging allocation ownership).

I/O, environment, and control
- WorkDir — working directory used by the job.
- StdOut / StdErr — paths where stdout/stderr were written (often in job's submission output).
- Command / BatchScript — command line or script path (what is executed).
- BatchFlag — indicates sbatch/batch submission (BatchFlag=1 for sbatch); increments on requeues.

Exit and error information (after completion)
- ExitCode — exitcode formatted as <exit>:<signal> (e.g., 0:0 means clean exit).
- State after completion — COMPLETED / FAILED / TIMEOUT / CANCELLED appear in JobState.

Dependencies, preemption, and limits
- Depend — job dependencies (afterok, afterany, etc.).
- Priority / PriorityFactor(s) — scheduler priority of job (reason for being scheduled earlier/later).
- QOSLimits / OverTimeLimit / PreemptMode — policy-related fields that affect runtime/behavior.

Other useful fields
- Flags / StateFlags — internal flags (checkpointed, requeued, etc.).
- Reservation — reservation name if job is tied to a reservation (shows “reservation”).
- EligibleNodes / ReasonInfo (detailed pending information) — more granular pending diagnostics (may require more verbose show).

Practical tips
- For “why won’t this start?” look at JobState + Reason + ReqTRES/Gres + Priority + Depend + Reservation.
- For running-job resource issues check AllocTRES, NodeList, RunTime, and StdErr paths.
- ExitCode + JobState tells you whether a job failed or was killed by a signal.
- Use scontrol show job <jobid> to get these fields; add the “details”/verbose option if you need per-node allocation breakdown.

If you want, give me a specific job ID and I can explain that job’s scontrol fields line-by-line.

- EndTime (or End) — scheduled/completed end time if available.  
- Dependency — job dependencies (afterok, afterany, aftercorr, etc.).

Resources requested vs allocated
- Partition — partition the job was submitted to / allocated from.  
- NumNodes / Nodes — number of nodes requested / allocated.  
- NodeList — list or range of nodes allocated (or planned nodes).  
- NumCPUs / CPUS — number of CPUs/cores requested or allocated.  
- ReqMem / MinMemory — memory requested.  
- TRES (or ReqTRES) — requested Trackable RESources (e.g., cpu=...,mem=...,gpu=...).  
- AllocTRES — actually allocated TRES (shows what the job actually received).  
- Gres — generic resources (often gpus) requested (gres/gpu:2 etc.).  
- TresPerNode / CPUTasksPerNodel — per-node allocation details (when present).

Allocation / node details
- AllocNode:Sid — the node and system id performing the allocation (local allocator info).  
- Features / Constraint — node features or constraints used for matching (e.g., specific CPU type).  
- NumCPUsPerTask / TasksPerNode / Sockets/Cores/Threads — task/core topology if set or shown.  
- NodeList/NodeAddr (when present) — concrete node hostnames or addresses.

Job script, I/O, and environment
- Command (or BatchCommand / BatchScript path) — the command or path to the batch script (may be viewable via scontrol write batch_script).  
- StdOut / StdErr — configured stdout/stderr file paths.  
- WorkDir — working directory used for the job.  
- Environment / PassEnv — environment variables or whatever was recorded (may be limited for unprivileged users).

Exit / final state info (for completed jobs)
- ExitCode — formatted as "<exitcode>:<signal>" (e.g., 0:0 means exit 0).  
- ExitCodeDetail / Reason — more info if non-zero or signalled.

Array & batch metadata
- ArrayJobId, ArrayTaskId, ArrayTasks — job array identifiers and index range (if part of an array).  
- BatchFlag — indicates sbatch-submitted batch jobs (BatchFlag=1) and increments if requeued.  
- RequeueCount / Requeued — requeue/restart counts or flags.

Reservations / special scheduler flags
- Reservation — reservation name if the job is running under a reservation.  
- Hold/Dependency flags — HoldReasons or whether the job was submitted with a hold.  
- Flags — internal flags set on the job (internal use).

Administrative / debugging fields
- Comment / Reason (from scontrol show job -d) — extra scheduler/admin comments.  
- SuspendTime / SuspendCount — suspend-related fields if suspended.  
- PriorityFactor / FairShare info — scheduling-fairshare or priority factors (sometimes present in diagnostic output).  
- Account or QOS limits that affected scheduling (may appear in admin views).

Quick usage tips
- Use scontrol show job <jobid> to get the full record; add the "details" option (or scontrol show job -d) on systems that support it to see per-node CPU/memory allocations.  
- For a short view of state and reason use squeue; for historical exit codes and resource usage use sacct.  
- ExitCode format is important: "<code>:<signal>". If non‑zero, check StdErr and sacct for details.

- Walk through a real scontrol show job <jobid> output and explain each field, or  
- Provide a compact cheat-sheet of the top 8–10 fields to check when debugging a stuck or failing job.

results.prompt: Explain safe syntax for scontrol update on jobs
results.agent_response:
Good question — here’s a concise, practical guide to safe scontrol update usage for jobs (syntax, examples, and cautions).

Basic form
- scontrol update <field>=<value> [<field>=<value> ...]
- Identify the job with JobId=, job=, or for arrays/hetjobs use:
  - Array element: <ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskID> (e.g. 101_4)
  - Heterogeneous component: <JobID>+<component> (e.g. 123+2)
- Use scontrol show job <JOBID> to inspect the job before and after changes.

Common fields you may update
- TimeLimit=<time> — set or adjust a job's time limit. Formats accepted:
  - minutes (e.g. 90), mm:ss, hh:mm:ss, days-hours, days-hours:minutes, etc.
  - Special: UNLIMITED
  - You may prefix with + or - to increment/decrement the current limit (e.g. TimeLimit=+30 adds 30 minutes).
- JobName=<name> — rename the job.
- Account=<account> — change the job account (subject to permissions/policies).
- QOS=<qosname> — change the job QOS (subject to limits).
- Priority=<value> — change job priority (privileged users only).
- Partition=<partition> — (usually only pending jobs can be moved; subject to limits).
- Other documented job update fields — consult scontrol(1) for the full list.

Examples
- Increase time by 30 minutes:
  scontrol update JobId=123 TimeLimit=+30
- Set absolute 2-hour limit:
  scontrol update JobId=123 TimeLimit=02:00:00
- Change job name:
  scontrol update JobId=123 JobName="analysis-run"
- Change a heterogeneous component’s account:
  scontrol update JobId=123+2 Account=research

Rules, permissions, and safety notes
- Authorization: an administrator or the job’s effective owner (or account Coordinator with proper permissions) is required to update most fields. Privileged users can bypass some limits.
- Pending vs running: many fields may only be changed while the job is PENDING. Some (e.g., certain TimeLimit updates) can apply to running or suspended steps — check scontrol docs and verify with scontrol show job.
- Be careful changing QOS/Account/Partition/TimeLimit as that can violate configured limits, change billing/accounting, or cause unexpected behavior (admin changes may override job/user limits).
- Use increments (TimeLimit=+N) when you want a minimal-risk extension rather than replacing with an exact value.
- Avoid using scontrol update to perform lifecycle actions that have dedicated commands (e.g., use scontrol hold/release, scontrol requeue, or scancel instead of trying to force state changes with update).
- Quote values containing spaces or special characters: JobName="my job 1"
- Confirm changes: always run scontrol show job <JOBID> after the update to verify the exact fields changed.

Array and heterogeneous specifics
- Job arrays: scontrol update job=101 updates all elements; use 101_5 to target element 5 only.
- Heterogeneous jobs: update the leader (jobid=123) to change fields that apply to all components, or use 123+N to change a single component.

Quick safe workflow
1) scontrol show job 123
2) decide and prepare the exact scontrol update key=value pairs
3) scontrol update JobId=123 TimeLimit=+30 JobName="x"
4) scontrol show job 123 to confirm

Reference
- scontrol(1) update job fields (Slurm docs) — fields, formats, and authorization rules.

If you tell me a concrete change you want to make (job ID and desired fields), I can:
- show the exact scontrol command you should run, and
- list any permission or pending/running caveats relevant to that job.

results.prompt: Explain safe syntax for scontrol update on jobs
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise, safe reference for using scontrol update on jobs.

Basic syntax
- scontrol update job=<JobID> Field=Value [Field2=Value2 ...]
- For array jobs use either the array job id to affect all elements: job=<ArrayJobID>
  or a single element: job=<ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskID> (e.g., job=101_3)

Key points / safety rules
- Always identify the job explicitly with job=<id>. Do not rely on implicit context.
- Most fields can only be changed while the job is PENDING; only a subset may be changed for RUNNING or SUSPENDED jobs. Check scontrol show job=<id> first.
- Unprivileged users may only change their own jobs (and only certain fields). Privileged users (admins/operators) can change any job and may bypass policy limits.
- Some fields are read-only and cannot be updated (e.g., AllocNode:Sid, BatchFlag, ExitCode). If in doubt, use scontrol show job to inspect allowed fields and current values.
- Be conservative: change one field at a time and verify the effect with scontrol show job=<id>.
- Avoid changing state (hold/release/requeue) with generic update — use the specific scontrol_* commands or scancel as appropriate.

Common safe examples
- Rename a job:
  scontrol update job=12345 JobName=new_name
- Extend time limit (use HH:MM:SS or minutes form as your Slurm supports):
  scontrol update job=12345 TimeLimit=02:00:00
- Change QOS or Priority (requires appropriate permissions):
  scontrol update job=12345 QOS=high Priority=3000
- Change account (may be restricted by policy):
  scontrol update job=12345 Account=projectX
- Update an array element:
  scontrol update job=2000_5 TimeLimit=00:30:00

Quoting and formatting
- Values with spaces should be quoted (shell quoting), e.g., JobName="analysis run".
- Numeric fields (Priority, NumNodes) expect integers. TimeLimit accepts common Slurm time formats (consult local scontrol/sbatch docs if unsure).
- Use exact field names and capitalization as shown by scontrol show job.

Recommended safe workflow
1. Inspect the job: scontrol show job=<JobID>
2. Decide the single change you need and confirm you have permission.
3. Run the update: scontrol update job=<JobID> Field=Value
4. Confirm: scontrol show job=<JobID>
5. If multiple changes are needed, repeat steps 2–4 rather than batching many risky edits at once.

If you want, tell me a specific field or job ID you plan to change and I can point out whether it’s typically allowed for PENDING vs RUNNING jobs and any permission concerns.

results.prompt: Explain safe syntax for scontrol update on jobs
results.agent_response:
Good question — here are concise, safe rules and examples for using scontrol update on jobs.

Basic syntax
- scontrol update JobId=<jobid> Field1=Value1 Field2=Value2 ...
- No commas between assignments; use = with no extra spaces around the equals.
- Always target a specific job with JobId=<id> to avoid accidental mass changes. Omitting JobId or using broader selectors (JobName=..., User=...) can modify many jobs.

Authorization & safety
- scontrol update requires you be the job's effective owner (or Coordinator) or a privileged user (Operator/Administrator). Privileged users can bypass many policy limits.
- Most fields may only be changed while a job is PENDING; only a subset can be changed for RUNNING or SUSPENDED jobs. Check your local policy or try scontrol show job <id> to confirm.
- For heterogeneous jobs: update the leader (jobid) to affect all components; you can address components with jobid=123+2 (plus-sign) when applicable.
- For job arrays and array-task addressing, use the array element syntax (ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID) where required (e.g., 345_7).

Common safe field examples
- Change time limit:
  scontrol update JobId=123 TimeLimit=02:00:00
  (TimeLimit accepts formats like MM, HH:MM:SS, or D-HH:MM:SS depending on config.)
- Change job name (usually pending jobs only):
  scontrol update JobId=123 JobName=new_name
- Change account/QOS (usually pending jobs; privileges may apply):
  scontrol update JobId=123 Account=myacct QOS=high
- Change requested priority (often restricted to privileged users):
  scontrol update JobId=123 Priority=100
- Set node list for pending allocations:
  scontrol update JobId=123 NodeList=node[01-02]
- Heterogeneous job component account change:
  scontrol update jobid=123+2 Account=abc

Best practices (to avoid mistakes)
- Always include JobId=<id>. If you mean to act on many jobs, be explicit — don’t omit JobId casually.
- Preview job state before and after:
  squeue -j <jobid>   (or) scontrol show job <jobid>
- After update, confirm with:
  scontrol show job <jobid>
- If unsure about permission or allowed fields, run the doc/help for scontrol or ask an administrator. Privileged updates can violate policy limits (e.g., extend beyond partition max time).
- When scripting: fail-safe by validating the job ID and state via squeue or scontrol show job before running scontrol update.

Notes and gotchas
- Field names are case-insensitive but use canonical names (JobId, TimeLimit, JobName, Account, QOS, NodeList, Priority).
- Quoting: values normally do not need quotes; if you must include special characters or spaces (rare for job fields), quote appropriately for your shell.
- Be careful with selectors like JobName= or User= — these will match multiple jobs if not restricted and can apply the update broadly.

If you want, tell me a concrete change you need to make (the Job ID and the fields/values) and I’ll show the exact scontrol update command you should run and what to check first.

results.prompt: Explain safe syntax for scontrol update on jobs
results.agent_response:
Good question — scontrol update is powerful and can change many jobs if used incorrectly. Below is a compact, safe reference: syntax, common editable fields, examples, and safety checklist.

Basic syntax
- scontrol update job=<jobid> Key=Value Key2="Value with spaces" ...
- Key=Value pairs are separated by spaces. Quote values that contain spaces or shell-sensitive characters.
- For job arrays:
  - job=<ArrayJobID> affects the whole array.
  - job=<ArrayJobID>_<ArrayTaskID> (e.g., 1234_5) targets a single array element.

Important safety rules
- Always include the job=<jobid> argument. Omitting job= (or using a non-specific selector such as JobName alone) can modify many jobs.
- Inspect first: run scontrol show job=<jobid> (or squeue -j <jobid>) to see current state and fields before changing anything.
- Prefer changing one field at a time. Verify the result with scontrol show job=<jobid>.
- Be mindful of privileges: unprivileged users may only modify their own jobs and only certain fields; privileged users (admins/operators) can change more and can violate normal policy limits.
- Many fields are only editable while the job is PENDING. Some fields may be changed on RUNNING or SUSPENDED jobs, but this depends on the field and site policy.
- Don’t assume a change will be accepted: TimeLimit, Partition, QOS, and other changes may be constrained by account/QoS/partition limits and may be rejected unless done by a privileged user.

Commonly edited fields (examples and notes)
- TimeLimit: set runtime limit
  - Format: HH:MM:SS, MM, or D-HH:MM:SS (site may accept other forms). Example:
    - scontrol update job=12345 TimeLimit=02:00:00
  - Note: changing TimeLimit on a pending job is common; raising time over partition/account max may be blocked for non-privileged users.
- JobName:
  - scontrol update job=12345 JobName="new_name"
- QOS:
  - scontrol update job=12345 QOS=high
  - May be restricted by account/QOS associations.
- Account:
  - scontrol update job=12345 Account=myacct
- Priority:
  - scontrol update job=12345 Priority=1000
- TRES/ReqTRES (resource requests like GPUs):
  - scontrol update job=12345 TRES=gres:gpu:2
  - Typically only allowed while PENDING; changing resources for running jobs is often not allowed.
- NodeList/NumNodes:
  - scontrol update job=12345 NodeList=node01 (usually only before allocation; changing nodes for a running job is generally not possible)
- Array elements:
  - scontrol update job=2000_3 TimeLimit=01:00:00 (affects only element 3)

Fields you cannot (or normally should not) change
- AllocNode:Sid, ExitCode, BatchFlag — allocation-specific/read-only fields shown by scontrol show job.
- Many allocation/exit fields are read-only — check scontrol show job output for read-only keys.

Examples (safe, minimal)
- Inspect:
  - scontrol show job=12345
- Change time limit:
  - scontrol update job=12345 TimeLimit=03:00:00
- Rename:
  - scontrol update job=12345 JobName="analysis_v2"
- Change QOS (privileges permitting):
  - scontrol update job=12345 QOS=high

Quick verification workflow (recommended)
1. squeue -j 12345 or scontrol show job=12345 — confirm state (PENDING vs RUNNING) and current values.
2. scontrol update job=12345 <single change>
3. scontrol show job=12345 — confirm the change, and check for any scheduler messages/errors.

Final cautions
- Never run broad updates without confirming target scope. For example, using JobName=foo without job= may affect multiple users’ jobs.
- If you need to change many jobs programmatically, script carefully and test on one job first.
- When in doubt about whether a field can be changed for a given job/state, inspect with scontrol show job and consult your cluster admin or the site Slurm policy.

If you want, tell me a specific field and job state (PENDING or RUNNING) and I’ll show the exact safe command and any likely restrictions.

results.agent_response:
Good question — here’s a concise, safe reference for using scontrol update on jobs (documentation-backed examples and warnings).

Basic form
- scontrol update JobId=<jobid> Field1=Value1 Field2=Value2 ...
- For job arrays: use ArrayJobID to target all elements (e.g., JobId=101) or an element with an underscore (e.g., JobId=101_5).
- Multiple assignments are separated by spaces.

Examples
- Inspect first:
  - scontrol show job 12345
- Change time limit (pending jobs normally; may be restricted by QOS/account limits):
  - scontrol update JobId=12345 TimeLimit=02:00:00
  - Time formats: SS, MM:SS, HH:MM:SS, or D-HH:MM:SS (use the cluster’s accepted formats).
- Rename a job:
  - scontrol update JobId=12345 JobName="analysis-step1"
- Add/change a comment:
  - scontrol update JobId=12345 Comment="Needs longer runtime for debugging"
- Change a single array element:
  - scontrol update JobId=101_3 TimeLimit=01:00:00
- Change QOS or Priority (usually restricted — admin or owner+permissions required):
  - scontrol update JobId=12345 QOS=high
  - scontrol update JobId=12345 Priority=1000

Quoting and spacing
- If a value contains spaces or special chars, quote it: JobName="my job" Comment="needs GPU"
- Use the exact FieldName=Value form (no space around =).

What you can and cannot safely change
- Many fields can only be changed while the job is PENDING; some may be changed on RUNNING or SUSPENDED jobs — check scontrol show job first.
- Unprivileged users can only modify their own jobs and only certain fields; privileged users (admins/operators) can modify any job and may bypass some policy limits.
- Some fields are read-only and cannot be updated (examples): AllocNode:Sid, BatchFlag, ExitCode. Use scontrol show job to see fields and state.
- Changing resource allocations (nodes, CPUs) or partition is generally not supported for an existing allocation — re-submit or requeue if you need a different allocation.

Safety recommendations
- Always inspect the job first: squeue -j <id> or scontrol show job <id> to confirm state/fields.
- Prefer changing pending jobs; avoid changing running allocations unless you understand scheduler/accounting/running-step effects.
- Be cautious with TimeLimit, QOS, and Account changes — they may be constrained by account, QOS, or partition limits and can be denied for unprivileged users.
- When in doubt about a field name or allowed values, consult scontrol documentation or your cluster admin. Example doc page: scontrol(1) / scontrol update job in the Slurm manual.

If you want, tell me a concrete change you’re trying to make (job ID and desired fields) and I’ll show the exact scontrol command and note whether it’s likely to be allowed.

Job arrays offer a mechanism for submitting and managing collections of
similar jobs quickly and easily, useful for repetitive workloads that follow a
common job pattern. This greatly improves overall performance, since job arrays

results.prompt: Explain scontrol update NodeName state drain and resume semantics
results.agent_response:
Short answer first
- scontrol update NodeName=<n> State=DRain marks nodes so the scheduler will not start any new jobs there. Existing jobs are left to finish. If jobs are running the node shows as DRAINING while those jobs complete, and then becomes DRAINED (or stays DRAIN if it was already idle). State=RESUME (sometimes called "undrain") clears the drain and returns the node to normal eligibility (UP/IDLE) so the scheduler can allocate new jobs.

Details / semantics and useful notes
- Purpose
  - Drain = remove the node from scheduling eligibility for new allocations (for maintenance, reboot, debugging, etc.).
  - Resume = return the node to normal scheduling eligibility.

- What happens to running jobs
  - Running jobs are not killed by a plain State=DRain. The node will be shown as DRAINING while those jobs run to completion. After jobs finish the node will show as DRAINED (if it was drained) and remain out of service until you resume it.
  - There are other node-state variants (e.g., DRAIN_FORCE / POWER_DOWN_FORCE / POWER_DOWN_ASAP) or tools to forcibly remove jobs; plain drain does not force-stop jobs.

- Immediate vs. transitional states
  - If a node is idle when you set State=DRain, Slurm will make it unavailable immediately (you’ll see it in a DRAIN/DRAINED state).
  - If the node has allocations, Slurm sets it to DRAINING until allocations complete, then to the drained state (DRAINED/DRAIN).

- How to clear the drain
  - Use scontrol update NodeName=<n> State=Resume (or State=undrain/resume depending on UI/case) to clear the drain reason and let the node return to normal. If the node is still DOWN or failed health checks the controller may not mark it IDLE—slurmd must re-register and the node must be healthy.

- Persistence
  - Drain/DRAINING/DRAINED state and the associated Reason are kept across controller checkpoints/restarts (they are persistent until explicitly cleared).

- Reason field
  - You can supply a textual reason: scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=Drain Reason="hw maintenance".
  - The Reason is recorded and visible via scontrol show node or sinfo -R.

- Permissions
  - Modifying node state requires privileged permissions (Administrator/Operator level).

- Interactions to be aware of
  - scontrol cancel_reboot undrains a node and clears the reason if the drain was created by an ASAP reboot request.
  - Power-management states (POWER_DOWN, POWER_DOWN_ASAP, POWER_DOWN_FORCE) combine draining and power actions and have slightly different semantics (they may call suspend programs or mark nodes for power down after draining).
  - A resume will not magically make a node usable if the node is DOWN, FAILING, or otherwise unhealthy; run scontrol show node to inspect the current NodeState and Reason.

Quick examples
- Drain a node for maintenance:
  - scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=Drain Reason="maintenance"
- Resume (undrain) a node:
  - scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=Resume
- Check state/reason:
  - scontrol show node node01
  - sinfo or sinfo -R (to list nodes and reasons)

If you want, I can show the exact fields you’ll see with scontrol show node (example output) or point you to the scontrol manpage section covering node update semantics.

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"

A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```

Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.

Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs
will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the

## NODE CONFIGURATION[#SECTION_NODE-CONFIGURATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The configuration of nodes (or machines) to be managed by Slurm is
also specified in /etc/slurm.conf .
Changes in node configuration (e.g. adding nodes, changing their
processor count, etc.) require restarting or reconfiguring all slurmctld
and slurmd daemons.
All slurmd daemons must know each node in the system to forward
messages in support of hierarchical communications.
Only the NodeName must be supplied in the configuration file.
All other node configuration information is optional.
It is advisable to establish baseline node configurations,
especially if the cluster is heterogeneous.
Nodes which register to the system with less than the configured resources
(e.g. too little memory), will be placed in the "DOWN" state to

results.prompt: Explain scontrol update NodeName state drain and resume semantics
results.agent_response:
Summary
- scontrol update NodeName=<nodes> State=DRAIN: marks the node(s) as drained so the scheduler will not allocate any new jobs to them.
- scontrol update NodeName=<nodes> State=RESUME: clears the drain state so the node(s) become eligible for scheduling again (they will accept new jobs when idle).

What "State=DRAIN" actually does
- Prevents new allocations: the scheduler will not place new jobs on the drained node(s).
- Does not immediately kill running jobs: currently running jobs remain and are allowed to run to completion (the drain just prevents future allocations). If you want running jobs removed immediately you must cancel or requeue them (scancel / scontrol requeue) — the node drain command itself does not evict jobs.
- Node remains marked with the drain reason (if given) until an explicit resume/undrain is done or a special system action clears it. You can record why you drained the node with Reason="text":
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN Reason="maintenance"
- Some higher-level actions (for example POWER_DOWN_ASAP or an ASAP reboot) will drain the node and may be able to clear the drain state later (e.g., cancel_reboot can undrain a node that was drained for an ASAP reboot).

What "State=RESUME" does
- Clears the DRAIN flag so the node becomes schedulable again. If the node is currently free it will be considered IDLE and will receive new allocations; if it still has running jobs it will remain allocated until those jobs finish, and only accept new jobs once its state permits scheduling.
- Resume does not force jobs to start on the node immediately — it simply returns the node to normal availability for the scheduler.

Related notes and caveats
- Authorization: node state updates are privileged operations (Operator/Administrator).
- Use scontrol show node <node> or sinfo to inspect a node’s current State and Reason.
- There are other node states / update variants (DOWN, POWER_DOWN_ASAP, POWER_DOWN_FORCE, etc.) that have different semantics (e.g., indicate failures or trigger power-management hooks). Don’t confuse DRAIN (prevent scheduling) with DOWN (node considered offline/bad) or power-down states (which may call SuspendProgram).
- If you need an immediate evacuation, you must explicitly cancel/requeue running jobs; draining alone will not do that.
- For documented command syntax and all node-state options see scontrol documentation (scontrol update NodeName=... State=... and the Node specification section).

Examples
- Drain with a reason:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN Reason="kernel upgrade"
- Resume (undrain):
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=RESUME

Use scontrol show node node01 or sinfo to verify the node’s state and the Reason field after performing these actions.

A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the

scontrol update nodename= state=power_

Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner

results.prompt: Explain scontrol update NodeName state drain and resume semantics
results.agent_response:
Summary — what the commands do
- scontrol update NodeName=<node-list> State=DRAIN[,Reason="..."]
  - Marks the specified node(s) as drained so the scheduler will not place any new allocations there.
  - Running jobs are not automatically preempted by the drain operation; they continue to run to completion (or until separately cancelled/requeued).
  - The node(s) remain in the drained state until an explicit resume/clear is performed.
  - You may supply a Reason string which is recorded and visible in node/reason listings.

- scontrol update NodeName=<node-list> State=RESUME
  - Clears the drain marking and returns the node(s) to normal scheduling eligibility (they will appear idle/allocatable and the scheduler may assign new jobs).
  - Use this to return nodes to service after maintenance.

Key notes and semantics
- Authorization: updating node state requires appropriate administrative privileges (see scontrol docs for required AdminLevel).
- Targets: NodeName accepts single names, ranges (e.g., node[01-10]) or special names (e.g., ALL).
- Drain does not implicitly kill or requeue running jobs; if you need running jobs removed you must cancel/requeue them separately.
- Drain is persistent until cleared with RESUME (or other explicit state changes); it is used for planned maintenance or to prevent new allocations.
- There are related node-state actions for power-saving and automated suspend (examples: POWER_DOWN, POWER_DOWN_ASAP, POWER_DOWN_FORCE) that combine draining semantics with node power management; POWER_DOWN_ASAP in particular will drain the node and then attempt to power it down using the configured SuspendProgram.
- Use sinfo / scontrol show node to confirm the node state and view the recorded reason.

Common examples
- Mark a node for maintenance:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN Reason="maintenance"
- Return a node to service:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=RESUME

For exact syntax, authorization requirements, and the full list of node state keywords (POWER_DOWN_*, etc.), see the scontrol documentation.

A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:
POWER_DOWN [#POWER_DOWN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.
POWER_DOWN_ASAP [#POWER_DOWN_ASAP](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs
will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the
node.

results.prompt: Explain scontrol update NodeName state drain and resume semantics
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- State=drain: marks the node so Slurm will not allocate any new jobs to it. If jobs are currently running the node will be left to finish those jobs; while jobs remain it is reported as DRAINING and once idle it is reported as DRAINED. No new allocations are placed on a drained node.
- State=resume (undrain): clears the drain so the node becomes allocatable again (i.e., it is returned to normal/idle/allocatable state).

Details and related semantics (from the Slurm docs)
- Drain semantics: a drain prevents new work from being scheduled on the node. Running jobs are allowed to complete; during that time the node is shown as DRAINING and after they finish it becomes DRAINED. (Power-save variants such as POWER_DOWN_ASAP combine draining with a subsequent power-down action — POWER_DOWN_ASAP “will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the node.”)
- Resume/undrain: an undrain (resume) operation returns a drained node to normal so it can be allocated again. For nodes drained as part of an ASAP reboot/power-down workflow there are helper commands (for example cancel_reboot) that will undrain and clear the reason if appropriate.
- Reason and persistence: Slurm records a Reason for nodes placed into DOWN/DRAINED states (the configuration and node entries include a Reason field). slurmctld preserves DRAINED and DRAINING node states (and associated Reason) across its checkpoints/restarts.
- Reporting: sinfo and scontrol show node state flags such as DRAINING and DRAINED; these are the indicators schedulers and admins should use to understand node availability.
- What this does NOT do: draining does not forcibly kill running jobs (unless you use a force/other action). Draining only prevents new allocations and allows current work to finish (or be handled separately by admin action).

Typical usage examples (conceptual)
- scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN  — request the node be drained (can be combined with a Reason field).
- scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=RESUME — undrain the node so it becomes allocatable.

If you want, I can paste the exact scontrol syntax/fields from the Slurm manpage or show how to include a Reason string.

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner

## Manual Power Saving[#manual](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:
POWER_DOWN [#POWER_DOWN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but
won't have any effect until the configured SuspendTimeout is
reached.
POWER_DOWN_ASAP [#POWER_DOWN_ASAP](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will drain the node and mark it for power down. Currently running jobs
will complete first and no additional jobs will be allocated to the
node.

## OPTIONS[#SECTION_OPTIONS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurmctld.html)
-c [#OPT_-c](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurmctld.html) Clear all previous slurmctld state from its last checkpoint.
With this option, all jobs, including both running and queued, and all
node states, will be deleted. Without this option, previously running
jobs will be preserved along with node State of DOWN, DRAINED
and DRAINING nodes and the associated Reason field for those nodes.
NOTE : It is rare you would ever want to use this in production as all
jobs will be killed.
-D [#OPT_-D](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurmctld.html) Run slurmctld in the foreground with logging copied to stderr.
This limits the resilience of 'scontrol reconfigure' and should be
avoided in production.

A node can be manually powered up and down by setting the state of the
node to the following states using `scontrol`:
```text
scontrol update nodename= state=power_
```
`scontrol update` command actions/states of interest:
POWER_DOWN [#POWER_DOWN](https://slurm.schedmd.com/elastic_computing.html)
Will use the configured SuspendProgram program to explicitly
place a node in power saving mode. If a node is already in the process of
being powered down, the command will only change the state of the node but

results.prompt: Explain scontrol update NodeName state drain and resume semantics
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol update NodeName=<node-list> State=DRAIN marks the node(s) so Slurm will not allocate any new jobs on them. Existing running jobs stay untouched and continue to run until they exit (Slurm does not kill or requeue them just because you issued State=DRAIN).
- scontrol update NodeName=<node-list> State=RESUME (or State=resume) clears the drain state so the node(s) become eligible for new allocations again (subject to normal scheduling, partition, QOS, etc.). If jobs are still running when you RESUME, the node will reflect its current allocation; once those jobs finish it will show idle and can accept new jobs.

What the commands control
- Preventing new allocations: DRAIN stops the scheduler from placing additional jobs on the node(s) immediately.
- Running jobs: DRAIN does not forcibly stop or requeue currently running jobs. They run to completion unless you separately scancel or requeue them.
- Pending jobs: Jobs already allocated to a node (e.g., in CONFIGURING) will still proceed; jobs that would otherwise be scheduled to that node will not be assigned while it is drained.
- RESUME: removes the DRAIN flag/mark and returns the node to normal scheduling eligibility.

Common options and notes
- Reason: you can record a human-readable reason when draining (Reason="maintenance") and that reason is shown by node-status tools.
- Visibility: sinfo / scontrol show will show the node state/flags so admins and users can see the drain reason and that allocations are blocked.
- Difference from DOWN/FAIL: DRAIN is an administrative prevention of new allocations (for maintenance, etc.). DOWN or NODE_FAIL indicate node failure/unavailability — those states are used for nodes that have problems and may have different scheduler/cleanup behavior.
- Forcing behavior: if you want running jobs removed or requeued when taking a node out of service, you must take explicit action (scancel, scontrol requeue/hold, or use other scontrol options); DRAIN alone does not perform that.
- Timing: a node set to DRAIN becomes ineligible for new allocations immediately; its apparent state (allocated vs idle) will continue to reflect current jobs until those jobs end or are removed.

Examples
- Drain with a reason:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=DRAIN Reason="kernel upgrade"
- Make node usable again:
  scontrol update NodeName=node01 State=RESUME

Behavior summary
- DRAIN = block new allocations; let current allocations finish.
- RESUME = clear the drain, restore normal eligibility for scheduling.

That covers the intended semantics and typical admin usage for State=DRAIN and State=RESUME.

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol reconfigure does and when it should be used
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol reconfigure tells the Slurm controller (slurmctld) to re-read its configuration and request that Slurm daemons (slurmd, etc.) adopt updated settings — without restarting daemons.
- Use it when you have changed Slurm configuration files and want most settings applied immediately without a full restart of daemons.

What it does (behavior)
- Causes slurmctld to reload slurm.conf and other config files that Slurm supports being reloaded (examples in the docs: mpi.conf, burst_buffer.conf, power-save related settings, topology files, plugin parameters that are declared reloadable).
- slurmctld updates its in-memory configuration and sends RPCs to slurmd (and other daemons where applicable) so they re-read their local config as supported.
- It does not stop or requeue running jobs; allocations normally remain in place. It is a live reconfiguration mechanism rather than a restart.
- ReconfigFlags in slurm.conf control special reconfigure behaviors (for example, keep or change power-save exclusions when reconfiguring).

When to use it
- After editing slurm.conf or other reloadable Slurm config files and you want to apply the changes immediately without restarting slurmctld/slurmd.
- When you change parameters that are documented as reloadable (check the docs for the specific file/parameter).
- To propagate non-disruptive changes cluster-wide while minimizing service interruption.

When it is NOT enough / caveats
- Some settings cannot be changed via reconfigure and require a daemon restart (or a coordinated restart of slurmctld/slurmd). The docs list which parameters are reloadable; if unsure, a restart may be required.
- Certain subsystem configuration (for example accounting daemon slurmdbd settings, or changes to plugin binaries) may require restarting that daemon or a rolling restart — verify per-component docs.
- Reconfiguring frequently or running many RPCs can stress slurmctld; avoid scripting rapid repeated reconfigures.
- Complex changes to node/partition topology or node name changes may have additional operational steps; validate before applying.

Recommended workflow
1. Edit the config file(s) on the controller(s).
2. Validate syntax and expected values (review file, run any local checks your admins use).
3. Run scontrol reconfigure on the controller:
   - scontrol reconfigure
4. Verify with:
   - scontrol show config (to inspect the active configuration),
   - sinfo / scontrol show node (to confirm node/partition effects),
   - review logs if unexpected behavior appears.
5. If a setting did not take effect, consult the Slurm docs to see whether that setting requires a restart; perform a restart if necessary.

References / pointers
- See the Slurm documentation for scontrol and the specific config files (ReconfigFlags, which files/parameters are reloadable) before relying on reconfigure for critical changes.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Executing scontrol sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from scontrol or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run scontrol or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to scontrol to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol reconfigure does and when it should be used
results.agent_response:
What it does (high level)
- scontrol reconfigure tells the Slurm controller (slurmctld) to reload its configuration from the current slurm.conf (and other config files that Slurm supports) and to push a reconfiguration request to the daemons (slurmd, sacctd, etc.). It applies many configuration changes without stopping or restarting slurmctld/slurmd.

How it works (brief)
- slurmctld rereads its configuration and updates in-memory data (partitions, node lists, topology, some plugin settings, etc.).
- slurmctld notifies downstream daemons to reload their configs where supported. Which exact settings are applied is controlled in part by ReconfigFlags in slurm.conf.

Typical things scontrol reconfigure is used for
- Apply edits to slurm.conf (add/remove nodes, change partition parameters, modify weights/QOS associations) without a full daemon restart.
- Reload supported auxiliary config files (mpi.conf, burst_buffer.conf, etc.) that Slurm docs say are reconfigurable.
- Make rolling, low-disruption changes in production where possible.

What it does not always do / when a restart is required
- Not every config change can be applied by reconfigure. Changes that require loading different plugin binaries, major structural changes, or certain low-level parameters may require restarting slurmctld and/or slurmd on affected hosts.
- Some ReconfigFlags change what reconfigure will or will not touch (for example, power-save related exceptions). Consult ReconfigFlags/KeepPowerSaveSettings if you manage power-save features.
- If slurmctld or slurmd are running different versions or if config syntax is invalid, reconfigure may fail or require a restart to recover.

Practical advice / best practices
- Use scontrol reconfigure to minimize disruption when applying routine configuration edits (node additions, partition tunings, minor plugin config changes).
- For potentially disruptive changes (plugin upgrades, major auth/accounting changes, rolling upgrades), plan for a controlled restart of slurmctld/slurmd instead.
- After reconfigure, verify the new state with scontrol show config, sinfo, and squeue, and check slurmctld/slurmd logs for errors.
- If in doubt, test the change in a staging environment first.

Command form
- Run on the controller as a Slurm admin (usually root): scontrol reconfigure

If you want, I can show the exact ReconfigFlags and which config files on your version of Slurm are reconfigurable (or look up the specific items that require restart) — tell me your Slurm version or ask me to fetch the relevant doc snippets.

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol reconfigure does and when it should be used
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol reconfigure tells the Slurm controller (slurmctld) to reread its configuration and ask the Slurm daemons (slurmd, sackd, etc.) to reload config without doing a full process restart. It is the supported way to apply many configuration changes on a running cluster with minimal disruption.

What it does (technical summary)
- Sends an RPC to slurmctld asking it to reload slurm.conf and other configuration files (cgroup.conf, burst_buffer.conf, mpi.conf, plugin configs, etc.) and to propagate the new configuration to slurmd/sackd where possible.
- Daemons may re-read files or be signalled (equivalent to a SIGHUP in many cases) so settings that are reconfigurable take effect immediately.
- Reconfig behavior is controlled by ReconfigFlags (for example KeepPowerSaveSettings affects how power‑save state is preserved across a reconfigure).
- It is not a code upgrade — it does not replace running binaries or change options that were set on daemon command lines.

When to use scontrol reconfigure
- After editing slurm.conf or one of the Slurm config files when the change is supported by dynamic reconfigure and you want to avoid a full daemon restart.
- To update scheduling, partition, qos, plugin configuration, cgroup settings, burst-buffer settings, or many runtime parameters that Slurm documents as reconfigurable.
- When you want to roll out configuration changes without interrupting running jobs (for supported parameters).

When a full restart is still required (common examples / gotchas)
- Some changes cannot be applied dynamically and require restarting the daemons. Examples include (but are not limited to):
  - Changing daemon command-line options (ports, daemon-level --conf-server/--authinfo, a different Munge socket location).
  - Major node identity changes (renaming nodes / very large topology changes) — check docs; node definition changes sometimes require restarting/reconfiguring all slurmd and slurmctld.
  - Changes to binaries (upgrades) — you must restart to run new executables.
  - Certain plugin/init behaviors or configuration parameters that the docs explicitly mark as “restart required.”
- If you are unsure whether a particular parameter can be reconfigured, check the documentation for that parameter or confirm with a staged test.

Practical guidance / safe workflow
1. Check the docs for the files/parameters you changed (the slurm.conf, cgroup.conf, burst_buffer.conf pages indicate whether scontrol reconfigure applies).
2. Make the change on the controller (and on nodes if needed).
3. Optionally run scontrol show config (and inspect logs) to confirm current settings.
4. Run scontrol reconfigure on the controller to apply the change.
5. Watch slurmctld and slurmd logs for errors and verify cluster state (sinfo, squeue) after the reconfigure.
6. Schedule reconfigures during low load if possible; avoid scripting frequent/infinite scontrol calls (it’s an RPC and can overload slurmctld).

Warnings and tips
- scontrol reconfigure is an RPC to slurmctld — many repeated calls can degrade the controller. Don’t call it in tight loops.
- Some cluster features have ReconfigFlags that change how reconfigure behaves (for example preserving power-save state). Review those flags if you use power-save or other delicate features.
- When in doubt, test on a small subset or in a staging environment; if a setting really requires a restart, plan a maintenance window.

If you want, tell me which file/parameter you changed and I can check the docs for that specific setting and say whether scontrol reconfigure should be sufficient or if a restart is required.

## PARTITION CONFIGURATION[#SECTION_PARTITION-CONFIGURATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The partition configuration permits you to establish different job
limits or access controls for various groups (or partitions) of nodes.
Nodes may be in more than one partition, making partitions serve
as general purpose queues.
For example one may put the same set of nodes into two different
partitions, each with different constraints (time limit, job sizes,
groups allowed to use the partition, etc.).
Jobs are allocated resources within a single partition.
Default values can be specified with a record in which
PartitionName is "DEFAULT".

results.prompt: Explain what scontrol reconfigure does and when it should be used
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol reconfigure tells slurmctld to reread its configuration and push the relevant configuration changes out to the other Slurm daemons (slurmd, slurmdbd/sacctd where applicable) without restarting daemons. It is the normal, low-disruption way to make many configuration changes take effect.

What it actually does
- Causes slurmctld to reread slurm.conf and other Slurm config files (and, where supported, plugin config files like mpi.conf, burst_buffer.conf, power_save.conf, etc.) and to distribute the new settings to the daemons.
- Triggers re-evaluation of scheduler state and some runtime behavior (partitions, node features, accounting/QOS/limits, priority/fairshare recalculation, etc.).
- Does not stop or restart the daemons; it requests in-place reconfiguration. Some changes are applied immediately, others are controlled by ReconfigFlags settings (for example, power-save related flags) or are deliberately preserved.
- Not every configuration item is reconfigurable — some settings are read only at daemon startup or when a plugin is (re)loaded. Those still require a daemon restart.

When to use scontrol reconfigure
- After editing slurm.conf or associated Slurm config files when the change is reconfigurable and you want to apply it without restarting slurmctld/slurmd.
- To push updated partition/node definitions, QOS/accounting parameter changes, scheduler-weight changes, license updates, or many policy changes with minimal interruption.
- When you want to avoid downtime: reconfigure is preferred over a full restart when possible.

When reconfigure is NOT enough / use restart instead
- Changes to core daemon binaries, plugin binaries, or parameters that are documented as being read only at startup (for example certain plugin parameters, some cgroup plugin internals, or kernel-level resource changes) require restarting slurmctld/slurmd (or a rolling restart for slurmds).
- If you need a clean state or suspect daemon memory corruption or hard failures, prefer restart.

Practical notes and recommended workflow
1. Edit the config files on the controller (and any plugin config files as required).
2. Run scontrol reconfigure on the controller.
3. Verify with:
   - scontrol show config (or scontrol show config | less) to see the running config,
   - sinfo / scontrol show node to confirm node/partition updates,
   - controller and slurmd logs for any errors or warnings.
4. If some expected changes did not take effect, consult ReconfigFlags in the docs and, if necessary, plan a maintenance window to restart the appropriate daemons.

Caveats
- Some reconfiguration actions (e.g., power-save behavior, suspend/resume exceptions) are influenced by ReconfigFlags; check those if behavior is unexpected.
- Although low-disruption, reconfigure can change scheduling decisions and node/partition visibility; do this with awareness on production clusters and notify users when you modify major scheduling/policy settings.

If you want, I can:
- show which parameters in your current config are reconfigurable (we can look them up in the docs), or
- after you change a specific file I can walk you through the verification steps to confirm the new values took effect.
