results.prompt: Explain what scontrol reconfigure does and when it should be used
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- scontrol reconfigure tells the Slurm controller to reread its configuration files and push a runtime reconfiguration to other Slurm daemons (slurmd, slurmdbd/sacctd where applicable) without restarting processes. It is the standard way to apply many config changes in-place.

What it actually does
- The controller rereads its configuration files (slurm.conf and other Slurm *.conf files that the controller reads) and applies allowed changes to the running daemons.
- slurmctld sends reconfigure requests to slurmd and other daemons so they can update their in-memory configuration.
- Which settings take effect at runtime depends on the parameter and on plugin support; some settings are dynamically reconfigurable, others require a daemon restart or even a full rolling restart of binaries.

When to use scontrol reconfigure
- After editing configuration files for settings that are documented as reconfigurable (partitions, many scheduler/sched parameters, gres changes, some plugin settings, burst_buffer.conf/mpi.conf, power-save exceptions, etc.).
- To push configuration changes cluster-wide without interrupting daemons.
- During planned maintenance or automated workflows when you want to avoid full daemon restarts.

When NOT to rely on scontrol reconfigure (restart required)
- Changing things that cannot be reloaded at runtime (binary-level plugin changes, changing ProctrackType to a new plugin binary, certain security/authentication backend changes, some low-level slurmctld options). Those require restarting the affected daemons (slurmd/slurmctld/slurmdbd).
- Kernel-level or OS-level changes on nodes; those need node restarts or slurmd restarts.
- If you need to guarantee no transient scheduler behavior changes for running jobs—some reconfigure actions can change scheduling decisions or node states.

Caveats and operational notes
- Some reconfiguration behaviors are controlled by ReconfigFlags (for example, whether power-save exceptions are preserved). Check relevant docs (ReconfigFlags) if that matters.
- Errors in the edited config may cause scontrol reconfigure to fail; check slurmctld logs after running it.
- Many config changes affect new allocations or scheduling decisions; running jobs are generally unaffected except for features that directly affect job cgroups, tracking, or node state.
- Test critical changes on a staging/test controller if possible, and perform reconfigure during low load for safety.

Quick checklist before running
- Validate config syntax/values (review slurm.conf and related .conf files).
- Run scontrol show config to inspect current effective settings.
- Consider checking sinfo/squeue to see cluster state before applying changes.
- After reconfigure, watch slurmctld/slurmd logs and run sinfo/scontrol show config to confirm the new values took effect.

If you want, I can list common parameters that are safe to reconfigure versus those that normally require a restart for your Slurm version. Which Slurm version are you running?

results.prompt: Explain sdiag scheduler diagnostic fields
results.agent_response:
sdiag reports counters and timing metrics from slurmctld that help diagnose scheduler behavior (threads, RPC/agent activity, job lifecycle, scheduling/backfill work, and cycle timing). Below are the common fields you will see and what each means.

Global / slurmctld execution
- Server thread count — number of active slurmctld threads handling RPCs and internal work; high values indicate heavy slurmctld load.
- RPC/agent counts — counts of agent/RPC activity (connections, created agents, RPC requests). spikes show increased client or controller activity.

Job lifecycle counters
- Jobs submitted / launched / completed / failed / cancelled / requeued / resumed — cumulative counters of job state transitions seen by slurmctld since the last reset. Use these to understand submission/completion rates and error volume.
- Steps created / steps completed — counts for job steps (task-level entities) created and finished.

Scheduling cycle timing and counts
- Scheduling cycle count — number of scheduler iterations (how many times the scheduler loop ran).
- Cycle time (min / avg / max) — how long scheduler iterations are taking; long or widely varying cycle times indicate expensive scheduling work or resource contention inside slurmctld.
- Work items per cycle / evaluated jobs per cycle — how much work the scheduler is doing each iteration.

Backfill and scheduling-plugin statistics
- Backfill evaluations / accepted / rejected (or similar) — how often the backfill logic examines pending jobs and whether they were allowed to run; useful to see whether backfill is effective.
- Backfill window / backfill checks — counts/metrics indicating how many potential placements the backfiller inspected; very large counts indicate heavy backfill computation.

Resource / allocation activity
- Node updates / node state changes — how many node status updates or reconfigurations slurmctld processed.
- Allocation/TRES changes — counters of resource allocation events (CPUs, GPUs, memory) handled.

Other diagnostic counters
- Preemptions / evictions / reservations handled — counts of preemption or reservation actions the scheduler took.
- Deferred/gang/heterogeneous job bookkeeping — counters related to special scheduling behaviors (if used).

Operational notes for interpretation
- sdiag shows cumulative counters reset at midnight UTC by default; use sdiag --reset to zero counters when you want to measure a fresh interval.
- High server thread count, large numbers of RPCs, or long scheduler cycle times indicate controller load; investigate submission rates, polling/monitoring clients, or expensive scheduling rules/plugins.
- Large backfill evaluation counts with few accepts can indicate inaccurate time limits on running jobs or an overly expensive backfill policy.
- Use sdiag sparingly: each invocation is an RPC to slurmctld and frequent calls can affect controller performance.

Output formats / options
- sdiag -a (default) prints the full set of counters; --json is available for machine parsing.
- There is a --reset option to clear the counters after you capture a baseline.

If you want, tell me which sdiag section you have output for (paste it) and I can explain the specific counters and what to watch for.

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.

results.prompt: Explain sdiag scheduler diagnostic fields
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise field-by-field explanation of the common sdiag (scheduler diagnostics) output and how to interpret each metric.

General notes
- sdiag --all is the usual mode; sdiag --reset clears the counters (they’re also reset automatically at midnight UTC by default).
- You can emit JSON (--json) for programmatic parsing.
- sdiag reports counters and timing information about slurmctld behavior (threads, RPCs/agents, scheduling cycles, backfill/reservations, job dispatching). High counts or long times generally indicate load or scheduler work that may need tuning.

Primary fields and meaning

- Server thread count
  - Number of active slurmctld threads. A higher number means slurmctld is processing many concurrent tasks (submits, completions, RPCs). Persistently high values can indicate heavy load.

- Agent thread count
  - Number of worker/agent threads used by slurmctld to perform asynchronous work. Similar interpretation to server threads; growth signals concurrent internal work.

- Scheduling cycle count (or Scheduler cycles)
  - How many scheduling iterations the controller has performed. Each cycle examines the queue and attempts to dispatch eligible jobs.

- Avg / Min / Max scheduling cycle time
  - Timing statistics (often in microseconds or milliseconds) for scheduling iterations:
    - Avg cycle time: typical cost of a scheduler iteration.
    - Max cycle time: worst-case iteration — useful to spot occasional expensive computations.
  - Long average or large max times mean the scheduler is spending a lot of CPU/time evaluating the queue (could be many jobs, complex constraints, or expensive backfill evaluation).

- Jobs considered / Jobs examined (per cycle or total)
  - How many pending jobs the scheduler looked at while deciding what to start. High ratio of considered→started indicates wasted work if many are repeatedly re-examined but never run.

- Jobs started / Jobs dispatched
  - Number of jobs the scheduler actually launched. Compare to “jobs considered” to judge efficiency.

- Jobs rejected / Jobs deferred / Jobs failed to start
  - Jobs that could not be scheduled (due to policies, resources, time limits, or heterogeneous constraints) or that failed during allocation. Use these to find scheduling bottlenecks or misconfigurations.

- Backfill statistics (Backfill windows / Backfill attempts / Backfill jobs started / Backfill failures)
  - Counts/timings for the backfill algorithm:
    - How many candidate backfill windows were evaluated.
    - How many backfill-starts succeeded vs. deferred/failed.
  - Large numbers of attempted windows with few starts suggest fragmentation or unsuitable job time limits.

- Reservation checks / Reservation evaluations
  - How often reservations are consulted during scheduling. Useful if you use advance/reservation-based allocations.

- Queue scan totals / Queue scan time
  - Aggregate time spent scanning the job queue (often separate from cycle time). High values point to expensive queue evaluation (many jobs, complex constraints).

- RPC / Event counters
  - Counts of RPCs or events processed by slurmctld (client requests, plugin calls, etc.). High RPC rates may indicate heavy client activity or monitoring tools over-querying slurmctld.

- Priority/fairshare evaluations (if present)
  - Number/timing of priority calculations. Expensive priority computations (many users/accounts) will increase scheduler cycle time.

How to use sdiag data
- Look for correlations: high Avg cycle time + many jobs considered + few jobs started = inefficient scheduling or resource fragmentation.
- Use Max cycle time to find occasional expensive iterations (helps track down specific problematic jobs or constraints).
- If backfill is expensive (many windows tried), encourage users to set realistic time limits or tune backfill parameters.
- If RPC or thread counts are high, investigate frequent client calls (monitoring scripts, polling) or scale scheduler resources.
- Use --json for automation and --reset to get a fresh baseline after making config changes.

If you want, tell me the exact sdiag output you have (paste it) and I’ll point to the specific fields in that output and what to investigate.

## Limitations [#limitations](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and
memory in the future.
This typically requires the backfill scheduler be able to allocate each
component of a heterogeneous job on a different node in order to begin its
resource allocation, even if multiple components of the job do actually get
allocated resources on the same node.

results.prompt: Explain sdiag scheduler diagnostic fields
results.agent_response:
Good question — sdiag is the Slurm scheduling diagnostic tool that prints many counters about slurmctld activity, scheduler work, backfill, and job dispatching. Below are the common sdiag fields you’ll see (field names as printed by sdiag --all), what each means, and short guidance on interpreting them.

Global / daemon
- Server thread count  
  Number of active slurmctld threads. High values mean slurmctld is busy (submissions, dispatches, RPCs); sustained high counts → controller load/throughput issue.

- Agent thread count  
  Number of worker/agent threads (helpers used by the controller). Similar interpretation as server threads.

RPC / client activity
- RPC requests / RPC failures (or RPC messages)  
  Number of RPC calls received by slurmctld (and any failed RPCs). Spikes = many client commands or monitoring tools; failures indicate comms problems.

Job submission / lifecycle
- Jobs submitted / Jobs completed / Jobs failed / Jobs requeued  
  Counters for lifecycle events. Large numbers of failed or requeued jobs point to job-launch failures, node problems, or user-script issues.

Queue / scheduling workload
- Queue depth  
  Number of pending jobs the scheduler is considering (a snapshot of backlog). High queue depth means many jobs waiting; investigate priority/fairshare, resource shortages, or scheduling bottlenecks.

- Jobs considered / Candidates examined  
  How many pending jobs or candidate placements the scheduler evaluated per cycle. Very high values per cycle indicate expensive scheduling decisions (many partitions/nodes to scan).

Scheduling cycle / timing
- Scheduling cycles (count)  
  Number of scheduler cycles performed.

- Scheduling cycle time (min / avg / max)  
  Time spent per scheduler cycle. If avg or max is large, scheduler loop is slow — could be due to many jobs, expensive backfill computations, or a plugin/DB latency.

Dispatch / launch
- Dispatches (or Jobs dispatched)  
  Number of job dispatch attempts (start requests to nodes).

- Failed dispatches (or Launch failures)  
  How many dispatch attempts failed (node launch, proctrack, or communication problems). Non-zero values require checking node health, munge/ssh, and node daemons (slurmd) logs.

Backfill / windowing
- Backfill windows created / windows used  
  Number of backfill windows the scheduler computed and how many were actually used to start lower-priority jobs.

- Backfill attempts / Backfill failures  
  Attempts to start backfill jobs and how many failed. High failures → inaccurate job time limits, resource fragmentation, or node/launch issues.

- Largest / average backfill window (size/time)  
  Size or duration of computed windows; small windows limit ability to backfill.

Allocation scanning / node work
- Nodes scanned per allocation (or Node checks)  
  How many nodes the scheduler scanned while looking for fit. Large values indicate expensive placement decisions or large cluster size being brute-forced.

Preemption / gang/timeslice counters
- Preemptions / Suspends / Resumes (if configured)  
  Counts of preemptive actions or timeslice/gang scheduler operations. High numbers reflect active preemption policies or gang/time-slicing activity.

Priority / fairness diagnostics
- Fairshare adjustments / Priority updates (sometimes shown)  
  Counters related to priority recalculation; frequent/slow updates can affect scheduling responsiveness.

Misc / housekeeping
- Backfill lookups / Reservation checks / DB queries  
  Counts of extra work slurmctld does (checking reservations, consulting slurmdbd). Many DB queries or slow DB responses can slow scheduling.

What to watch for (practical guidance)
- High scheduling cycle times + high “jobs considered” or “nodes scanned” → scheduling is the bottleneck; consider tuning SchedulerType/SchedulerParameters, reducing expensive plugins, or limiting per-cycle work.
- Large queue depth but low dispatch count → resources constrained (no eligible nodes) or priorities/QOS preventing starts.
- Non-zero failed dispatches / launch failures → investigate node slurmd logs, node health, network/Munge, and proctrack plugin.
- Backfill windows = 0 or very small → job time limits may be inaccurate or fragmentation prevents backfill; encourage accurate time estimates or adjust backfill params.

Notes and tips
- Field names and exact output can vary by Slurm version and enabled scheduler plugins. Values are reset at midnight UTC by default; sdiag --reset clears counters immediately.
- Use sdiag --all for the full display or sdiag --json for machine-readable output.
- sdiag is an RPC to slurmctld — don’t run it in tight loops (it can add load).

If you want, paste your sdiag --all output (or run sdiag --json and paste the JSON) and I’ll interpret the specific counters and point to likely tunables or troubleshooting steps.

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

on startup. This thread sleeps for the configured SchedulerTimeSlice
interval. When it wakes up, it checks each partition for suspended jobs. If

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will
allow them to start and finish quick...

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

If ongoing access to Archived/Purged data is required at your site, it is
possible to create an archive instance of slurmdbd. Data previously archived

keeping the production database at a manageable size while making sure old
records are still accessible.

## Sharding [#Sharding](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gres.html)
Sharding provides a generic mechanism where GPUs can be
shared by multiple jobs. While it does permit multiple jobs to run on a given
GPU it does not fence the processes running on the GPU, it only allows the GPU
to be shared. Sharding, therefore, works best with homogeneous workflows. It is
recommended to limit the number of shards on a node to equal the max possible
jobs that can run simultaneously on the node (i.e. cores).
The total count of shards available on a node should be configured in
the slurm.conf file (e.g. "NodeName=tux[1-16] Gres=gpu:2,shard:64").
Several options are available for configuring shards in the gres.conf file
as listed below with examples following that:

results.prompt: Explain sdiag scheduler diagnostic fields
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, field-by-field explanation of the sdiag scheduler diagnostic output and what each value means / when to investigate it.

General notes
- Most timing values are in microseconds (µs) unless otherwise noted.
- Counters are either since the last reset (default: midnight UTC) or since slurmctld start (where documented).
- Use sdiag --reset as an operator to zero the counters; use --json/--yaml for machine-readable output.

1) slurmctld / agent / DBD runtime metrics
- Server thread count
  - Number of active slurmctld threads. If this is often near MAX_SERVER_THREADS in slurm.conf, slurmctld may be CPU/IO bound.
- Agent queue size
  - Number of enqueued outgoing RPCs waiting for delivery to slurmd agents (internal retry list). Growing queue → communication/backpressure.
- Agent count
  - Number of agent threads (each can spawn worker threads).
- Agent thread count
  - Total active threads created by agent threads.
- DBD Agent queue size
  - Messages queued for SlurmDBD. If this grows (especially > ~50% of MaxDBDMsgs) check slurmdbd or DB connectivity/latency.

2) Job counters
- Jobs submitted / started / completed / canceled / failed
  - Simple counters since last reset. “started” includes backfilled starts. A jump in failed or canceled can indicate slurmd/node or user/job issues.
- Job states ts / Jobs pending / Jobs running
  - Timestamp when the snapshot was taken and instantaneous counts of PENDING and RUNNING jobs.

3) Priority-based scheduling cycle (main scheduler)
- Last cycle
  - Time spent in the last scheduling cycle (µs). A single cycle does priority-ordered scheduling attempts.
- Max cycle
  - Maximum cycle time observed since reset.
- Total cycles
  - Sum of all cycle times since reset (µs).
- Mean cycle
  - Average scheduling cycle time (µs).
- Mean depth cycle
  - Average number of jobs processed per cycle (depth = jobs examined).
- Cycles per minute
  - Frequency of scheduling cycles (helpful to see if scheduler is running very frequently or rarely).
- Last queue length
  - Number of pending jobs considered in the last cycle.
Interpretation: long or frequently-spiking cycle times suggest expensive scheduling work (many jobs, heavy backfill, locks held long). Investigate large queue lengths, scheduling locks, or plugins (fairshare, multifactor priority cost).

4) Backfill scheduler block
- Total backfilled jobs (since last slurm start / since last stats reset)
  - How many jobs were started via backfilling.
- Total backfilled heterogeneous job components
  - Count for heterogeneous job components.
- Total cycles / Last cycle when / Last cycle / Max cycle / Mean cycle
  - Same semantics as main scheduler but for the backfill algorithm (µs). Backfill cycles are typically more expensive.
- Last depth cycle / Last depth cycle (try sched)
  - Number of jobs considered in the last backfill cycle; the “try sched” version counts only jobs that had a chance to start (i.e., not ineligible due to limits/dependencies).
- Depth Mean / Depth Mean (try sched)
  - Averages of the above over cycles.
- Last queue length / Queue length Mean
  - Number of jobs pending to be processed by backfill (a job is counted once per partition requested).
- Last table size / Mean table size
  - Number of distinct time slots tested by the backfill scheduler in the last iteration and mean. Larger table sizes increase backfill CPU costs. Table size is influenced by backfill settings (bf_min_age_reserve, bf_min_prio_reserve, bf_resolution, bf_window).
- Latency for 1000 gettimeofday() calls
  - Microsecond measurement of gettimeofday() syscall latency measured at controller startup; can indicate host syscall timing overhead.

When to worry: large/backfill cycle times, large table sizes, or deep backfill depths indicate backfill cost; tune bf_* settings or job time limits to reduce.

5) RPC statistics
- Frequently issued RPCs (by msg type)
  - For each RPC: count, total time consumed, average time (µs). Use these to spot expensive operations or noisy RPC types.
- RPCs by user ID
  - Which users generate many/slow RPCs (e.g., submitting many small jobs or polling).
- Pending RPC statistics
  - Types/counts of RPCs currently queued on the agent queue and up to the first 25 individual pending RPCs (type + destination host list). This is cached and refreshed every ~30s.
Interpretation: many pending RPCs or slow/expensive RPC types can indicate node communication problems, overloaded slurmds, or user-side hot loops.

6) Misc / other blocks
- Pending outgoing RPCs (detailed list)
  - Shows destination nodes and RPC types still pending; helps find problematic nodes or network partitions.
- RPCs total lifetime stats
  - These are accumulated for the slurmctld lifetime unless reset.

Troubleshooting tips (quick)
- If Server thread count ≈ MAX_SERVER_THREADS often → consider increasing MAX_SERVER_THREADS or investigate sources of high load (many submissions, RPCs).
- If DBD Agent queue grows → check slurmdbd and database responsiveness; ensure MaxDBDMsgs is appropriate.
- If backfill table size / backfill cycle time is large → tune bf_min_age_reserve, bf_resolution, bf_window or encourage more accurate per-job time limits.
- If many pending RPCs or slow RPCs → check network, slurmd health on affected nodes (sinfo, sinfo_reasons, scontrol show node), and per-node logs.
- If a particular RPC type or user dominates time → inspect user behavior (high submission rate, frequent squeue polls) or the plugin implementing that RPC.

Where to look next
- Use sinfo/sinfo_reasons and scontrol show node to inspect node health if pending RPCs point to hosts.
- Use sprio/sdiag together to correlate priority factors with scheduling cycle behavior.
- For historical patterns, run sdiag regularly or collect sdiag --json output into a monitoring system.

If you want, I can:
- Show a short example sdiag output and annotate the fields, or
- Run sdiag on your cluster and interpret the current values (I’ll call sdiag if you want a live readout).

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will
allow them to start and finish quick...

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

Section: Slurm Commands (1) Updated: Slurm Commands Index 

 
   
 NAME 
sdiag - Scheduling diagnostic tool for Slurm
 
   
 SYNOPSIS 
sdiag
 
   
 DESCRIPTION 
sdiag shows information related to slurmctld execution about: threads, agents,
jobs, and scheduling algorithms. The goal is to obtain data from slurmctld
behavior helping to adjust configuration parameters or queues policies. The
main reason behind is to know Slurm behavior under systems with a high throughput.
 

It has two execution modes. The default mode --all shows several counters
and statistics explained later, and there is another execution option
 --reset for resetting those values.
 

Values are reset at midnight UTC time by default.
 

The first block of information is related to global slurmctld execution:
 
 
 Server thread count The number of current active slurmctld threads. A high number would mean a high
load processing events like job submissions, jobs dispatching, jobs completing,
etc. If this is often close to MAX_SERVER_THREADS it could point to a potential
bottleneck.
 
 
 Agent queue size Slurm design has scalability in mind and sending messages to thousands of nodes
is not a trivial task. The agent mechanism helps to control communication
between slurmctld and the slurmd daemons for a best effort. This value denotes
the count of enqueued outgoing RPC requests in an internal retry list.
 
 
 Agent count Number of agent threads. Each of these agent threads can create in turn a group
of up to 2 + AGENT_THREAD_COUNT active threads at a time.
 
 
 Agent thread count Total count of active threads created by all the agent threads.
 
 
 DBD Agent queue size Slurm queues up the messages intended for the SlurmDBD and processes them in a
separate thread. If the SlurmDBD, or database, is down then this number will
increase.
 
The max queue size is configured in the slurm.conf with MaxDBDMsgs. If this number begins to grow more than half of the max queue size, the slurmdbd
and the database should be investigated immediately.
 
 
 Jobs submitted Number of jobs submitted since last reset
 
 
 Jobs started Number of jobs started since last reset. This includes backfilled jobs.
 
 
 Jobs completed Number of jobs completed since last reset.
 
 
 Jobs canceled Number of jobs canceled since last reset.
 
 
 Jobs failed Number of jobs failed due to slurmd or other internal issues since last reset.
 
 
 Job states ts: Lists the timestamp of when the following job state counts were gathered.
 
 
 Jobs pending: Number of jobs pending at the given time of the time stamp above.
 
 
 Jobs running: Number of jobs running at the given time of the time stamp above.
 
 
 
 

The next block of information is related to main scheduling algorithm based
on jobs priorities. A scheduling cycle implies to get the job_write_lock lock,
then trying to get resources for jobs pending, starting from the most priority
one and going in descending order. Once a job can not get the resources the
loop keeps going but just for jobs requesting other partitions. Jobs with
dependencies or affected by accounts limits are not processed.
 
 
 Last cycle Time in microseconds for last scheduling cycle.
 
 
 Max cycle Maximum time in microseconds for any scheduling cycle since last reset.
 
 
 Total cycles Total run time in microseconds for all scheduling cycles since last reset.
Scheduling is performed periodically and (depending upon configuration)
when a job is submitted or a job is completed.
 
 
 Mean cycle Mean time in microseconds for all scheduling cycles since last reset.
 
 
 Mean depth cycle Mean of cycle depth. Depth means number of jobs processed in a scheduling cycle.
 
 
 Cycles per minute Counter of scheduling executions per minute.
 
 
 Last queue length Length of jobs pending queue.
 
 
 
 

The next block of information is related to backfilling scheduling algorithm.
A backfilling scheduling cycle implies to get locks for jobs, nodes and
partitions objects then trying to get resources for jobs pending. Jobs are
processed based on priorities. If a job can not get resources the algorithm
calculates when it could get them obtaining a future start time for the job.
Then next job is processed and the algorithm tries to get resources for that
job but avoiding to affect the previous ones , and again it calculates
the future start time if not current resources available. The backfilling
algorithm takes more time for each new job to process since more priority jobs
can not be affected. The algorithm itself takes measures for avoiding a long
execution cycle and for taking all the locks for too long.
 
 
 Total backfilled jobs (since last slurm start) Number of jobs started thanks to backfilling since last slurm start.
 
 
 Total backfilled jobs (since last stats cycle start) Number of jobs started thanks to backfilling since last time stats where reset.
By default these values are reset at midnight UTC time.
 
 
 Total backfilled heterogeneous job components Number of heterogeneous job components started thanks to backfilling since
last Slurm start.
 
 
 Total cycles Number of backfill scheduling cycles since last reset
 
 
 Last cycle when Time when last backfill scheduling cycle happened in the format
"weekday Month MonthDay hour:minute.seconds year"
 
 
 Last cycle Time in microseconds of last backfill scheduling cycle.
It counts only execution time, removing sleep time inside a scheduling cycle
when it executes for an extended period time.
Note that locks are released during the sleep time so that other work can
proceed.
 
 
 Max cycle Time in microseconds of maximum backfill scheduling cycle execution since last reset.
It counts only execution time, removing sleep time inside a scheduling cycle
when it executes for an extended period time.
Note that locks are released during the sleep time so that other work can
proceed.
 
 
 Mean cycle Mean time in microseconds of backfilling scheduling cycles since last reset.
 
 
 Last depth cycle Number of processed jobs during last backfilling scheduling cycle. It counts
every job even if that job can not be started due to dependencies or limits.
 
 
 Last depth cycle (try sched) Number of processed jobs during last backfilling scheduling cycle. It counts
only jobs with a chance to start using available resources. These
jobs consume more scheduling time than jobs which are found can not be started
due to dependencies or limits.
 
 
 Depth Mean Mean count of jobs processed during all backfilling scheduling cycles since last
reset.
Jobs which are found to be ineligible to run when examined by the backfill
scheduler are not counted (e.g. jobs submitted to multiple partitions and
already started, jobs which have reached a QOS or account limit such as
maximum running jobs for an account, etc).
 
 
 Depth Mean (try sched) The subset of Depth Mean that the backfill scheduler attempted to schedule.
 
 
 Last queue length Number of jobs pending to be processed by backfilling algorithm.
A job is counted once for each partition it is queued to use.
A pending job array will normally be counted as one job (tasks of a job array
which have already been started/requeued or individually modified will already
have individual job records and are each counted as a separate job).
 
 
 Queue length Mean Mean count of jobs pending to be processed by backfilling algorithm.
A job is counted once for each partition it requested.
A pending job array will normally be counted as one job (tasks of a job array
which have already been started/requeued or individually modified will already
have individual job records and are each counted as a separate job).
 
 
 Last table size Count of different time slots tested by the backfill scheduler in its last
iteration.
 
 
 Mean table size Mean count of different time slots tested by the backfill scheduler.
Larger counts increase the time required for the backfill operation.
The table size is influenced by many scheduling parameters, including:
bf_min_age_reserve, bf_min_prio_reserve, bf_resolution, and bf_window.
 
 
 Latency for 1000 calls to gettimeofday() Latency of 1000 calls to the gettimeofday() syscall in microseconds,
as measured at controller startup.
 
 
 
 

The next blocks of information report the most frequently issued
remote procedure calls (RPCs), calls made for the Slurmctld daemon to perform
some action.
The fourth block reports the RPCs issued by message type.
You will need to look up those RPC codes in the Slurm source code by looking
them up in the file src/common/slurm_protocol_defs.h.
The report includes the number of times each RPC is invoked, the total time
consumed by all of those RPCs plus the average time consumed by each RPC in
microseconds.
The fifth block reports the RPCs issued by user ID, the total number of RPCs
they have issued, the total time consumed by all of those RPCs plus the average
time consumed by each RPC in microseconds.
RPCs statistics are collected for the life of the slurmctld process unless
explicitly --reset .
 
 

The sixth block of information, labeled Pending RPC Statistics, shows
information about pending outgoing RPCs on the slurmctld agent queue.
The first section of this block shows types of RPCs on the queue and the
count of each. The second section shows up to the first 25 individual RPCs
pending on the agent queue, including the type and the destination host list.
This information is cached and only refreshed on 30 second intervals.
 
   
 OPTIONS 
 
 
 -a , --all Get and report information. This is the default mode of operation.
 
 
 -M , --cluster =< string > The cluster to issue commands to. Only one cluster name may be specified.
Note that the slurmdbd must be up for this option to work properly, unless
running in a federation with FederationParameters=fed_display configured.
 
 
 -h , --help Print description of options and exit.
 
 
 --json , --json = list , --json =< data_parser > Dump information as JSON using the default data_parser plugin or explicit
data_parser with parameters. Sorting and formatting arguments will be ignored.
 
 
 --no-trunc Do not truncate long lines to 80 char.
 
 
 -r , --reset Reset scheduler and RPC counters to 0. Only supported for Slurm operators and
administrators.
 
 
 -i , --sort-by-id Sort Remote Procedure Call (RPC) data by message type ID and user ID.
 
 
 -t , --sort-by-time Sort Remote Procedure Call (RPC) data by total run time.
 
 
 -T , --sort-by-time2 Sort Remote Procedure Call (RPC) data by average run time.
 
 
 --usage Print list of options and exit.
 
 
 -V , --version Print current version number and exit.
 
 
 --yaml , --yaml = list , --yaml =< data_parser > Dump information as YAML using the default data_parser plugin or explicit
data_parser with parameters. Sorting and formatting arguments will be ignored.
 
 
 
   
 PERFORMANCE 
 

Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
 

Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.
 
   
 ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES 
 

Some sdiag options may be set via environment variables. These
environment variables, along with their corresponding options, are listed below.
(Note: Command line options will always override these settings.)
 
 
 SLURM_CLUSTERS Same as --cluster 
 
 
 SLURM_CONF The location of the Slurm configuration file.
 
 SLURM_JSON Control JSON serialization:

 pretty Output JSON in pretty format to make it more readable.

 compact Output YAML as compact as possible.

results.prompt: Explain sdiag scheduler diagnostic fields
results.agent_response:
Good question — sdiag is the Slurm scheduling-diagnostics tool that prints counters and timings from slurmctld to help you tune scheduler settings and understand scheduler behaviour. Below is a concise guide to the common sdiag sections/fields and what they mean and imply.

General notes
- Run with --all to see all counters, or --json for machine-readable output. --reset clears the counters (they also reset automatically at midnight UTC).
- sdiag issues an RPC to slurmctld; don’t poll it in tight loops (it can add load to the controller).

Top-level / control-plane fields
- Server thread count
  - Number of active slurmctld threads. High values indicate slurmctld is busy handling submissions, dispatches, RPCs, etc.
- Agent thread count
  - Threads used by scheduling/agent work (depends on build/plugins). A sustained high value means many concurrent scheduling tasks.

Scheduler loop / cycle timing
- Scheduling cycles (or Scheduling iterations)
  - How many main scheduling iterations have run (since last reset).
- Total/average/max scheduling cycle time
  - Wall-time spent running the scheduler loop (total) and per-cycle avg/max. Long/variable cycle times indicate expensive scheduling work—look at sched_interval, default_queue_depth, or expensive plugins (backfill, constraints).
- Scheduling events / event-triggered attempts
  - Counts of event-triggered scheduling attempts (e.g., job submit, job completion). Large numbers here show many reactive scheduling triggers.

Job counters
- Jobs added
  - Number of jobs the controller has ingested.
- Jobs evaluated / Jobs considered
  - How many pending jobs were evaluated by the scheduler logic.
- Jobs dispatched / Jobs started
  - How many jobs were actually dispatched/started on compute nodes.
- Jobs completed
  - Counts of job completions observed by slurmctld.

Backfill / placement statistics (sched/backfill)
- Backfill attempts / Backfill successes
  - Number of times backfill logic attempted to place lower-priority jobs and how often it succeeded.
- Backfill windows considered / backfill windows scanned
  - How many candidate backfill time windows were evaluated. Many windows scanned with few successes can indicate inaccurate time limits or fragmentation.
- Jobs started by backfill
  - How many jobs were started due to backfilling.
- Average backfill evaluation time
  - Time spent per backfill evaluation; high values suggest expensive backfill computations (consider tuning default_queue_depth, partition_job_depth, or backfill plugin parameters).

Queue-depth / evaluation depth
- default_queue_depth
  - The configured number of jobs the scheduler will consider on many events (default 100). If sdiag shows many evaluations relative to this, you may need to tune it.
- partition_job_depth
  - Per-partition depth limiting how many jobs are considered in a full scheduling pass (reflected in counters).

Preemption / requeue / timeslicing / gang-scheduler metrics
- Preemption/Preempt attempts and successes
  - How often higher-priority jobs preempt lower-priority ones and whether preemption succeeded.
- Timeslice / suspended / resumed counts (if gang/timeslicer enabled)
  - Counts of timeslice suspends/resumes; large numbers indicate frequent timeslicing activity.

Per-partition/per-plugin breakdowns
- sdiag often shows per-partition counters: scheduling attempts, backfill attempts, jobs started, evaluations. Use those to identify which partition has the most scheduling cost or backfill difficulty.
- Heterogeneous job counters if heterogeneous support is used (components deferred, expected start recorded, etc.).

Diagnostics / error counters
- Failed dispatches / failed evaluations
  - Number of times a scheduling decision failed (e.g., due to node issues or selection plugin errors). Investigate scontrol/sinfo and node reasons.

How to interpret and act
- High Server thread count + long scheduling cycle times
  - Controller is overloaded. Consider reducing sdiag frequency, increasing slurmctld resources (CPU), or tuning sched_interval/default_queue_depth/partition_job_depth.
- Many backfill attempts but few backfill starts
  - Check job time-limit accuracy (backfill relies on expected end times). Consider encouraging users to set realistic time limits or tune backfill parameters.
- Large numbers of job evaluations per event
  - Reduce default_queue_depth/partition_job_depth to limit per-event work or tune SchedulerParameters (defer, sched_interval) to prefer periodic comprehensive scheduling.
- Frequent preemption or timeslicing activity
  - Review PreemptionMode, QOS and Gang scheduling parameters; note suspended jobs can hold memory and reduce effective capacity.

When to run other tools
- For per-job pending reasons or “why is this job not starting?”: use squeue (and scontrol show job for detailed pending reason).
- For priority/fairshare: run sprio and sshare.
- For long-term usage/consumption: use sreport or sacct.

If you want, I can:
- Show an annotated example sdiag output and map each line to the explanations above, or
- Run sdiag on the cluster now and summarize the controllers’ current scheduler counters (I’ll call sdiag and report results). Which would you prefer?

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.
Slurm's backfill scheduler takes into consideration every running job.
It then considers pending jobs in priority order, determining when and where
each will start, taking into consideration the possibility of

## System Administrator Information [#sys_admin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a
heterogeneous job.
The spank_init_post_opt() function is invoked once for each component of a
heterogeneous job. This permits site defined options on a per job component
basis.
Scheduling of heterogeneous jobs is performed only by the sched/backfill
plugin and all heterogeneous job components are either all scheduled at the same
time or deferred. The pending reason of heterogeneous jobs isn't set until
backfill evaluation.
In order to ensure the timely initiation of both heterogeneous and

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then
the new job is suspended. All jobs are tracked in a per-partition job queue
within the gang scheduler logic.

## Timeslicer Design and Operation [#time_slice](https://slurm.schedmd.com/gang_scheduling.html)
When enabled, the gang scheduler keeps track of the resources
allocated to all jobs. For each partition an "active bitmap" is maintained that
tracks all concurrently running jobs in the Slurm cluster. Each time a new
job is allocated to resources in a partition, the gang scheduler
compares these newly allocated resources with the resources already maintained
in the "active bitmap".
If these two sets of resources are disjoint then the new job is added to the "active bitmap". If these two sets of resources overlap then

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.

Snippet:
## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

Slurm is designed to perform a quick and simple scheduling attempt at

results.prompt: Explain sreport cluster utilization reports
results.agent_response:
Brief overview — what "sreport cluster utilization" shows
- Purpose: sreport cluster utilization summarizes how cluster resources were used over a time window. It is an accounting-level usage report (reads SlurmDB/sacct data).
- Primary metric: "Allocated" time = node time that was in use by active jobs or active reservations. By default usage values are shown in CPU-minutes (so divide by 60 for CPU-hours).
- Output columns you will commonly see:
  - Cluster — cluster name
  - Allocated — time nodes were used by jobs/reservations (CPU‑minutes)
  - Available — total node time available during the period (CPU‑minutes)
  - Util% (or Usage) — Allocated / Available expressed as a percent
  - Down — time nodes were Down or fully Drained (also counts slurmctld downtime if TrackSlurmctldDown is enabled)
  - Idle — Available − Allocated − Down (time nodes sat idle)
  - Reservation info — when relevant, time consumed by reservations or associations

Important semantics / pitfalls
- Allocated includes active reservations that are being used, but does NOT include reservations created with MAINT or IGNORE_JOBS flags (those are excluded from "Allocated" for cluster-utilization).
- Reservations assigned to whole accounts may cause idle reservation time to be split or counted differently; see Account/Association options when drilling down.
- The report uses the accounting DB (slurmdbd). If jobs or nodes aren’t recorded there, they won’t appear.
- Units: default is CPU‑minutes. If you need GPU‑hours or other TRES metrics, use the appropriate sreport subreport/options (see docs) or convert CPU‑minutes to hours by dividing by 60.
- Down time reported includes nodes marked Down/Drained; investigate sinfo/sinfo -R for per-node reasons if you need remediation details.

Common subreports and options you’ll use
- sreport cluster utilization Start=<time> End=<time>
  - simple cluster-level utilization for the window
- sreport cluster AccountUtilizationByUser Start=<time> End=<time>
  - show usage broken down by account → user
- sreport cluster AccountUtilizationByQOS, UserUtilizationByAccount, WCKeyUtilizationByUser, etc.
- Useful flags: --cluster / -M to choose a cluster (or --all_clusters), Start= and End= to set the window.
- Example:
  - sreport cluster utilization Start=2024-04-01 End=2024-04-07
- Output is best interpreted as "CPU‑minutes used over period"; convert to CPU‑hours or normalize by node-count to reason about percent utilization.

When to use it
- To track historical cluster utilization (overall % busy vs idle)
- To compare account or user consumption over a time window
- To quantify wasted time (idle vs down) for capacity planning or maintenance impact

If you want, I can:
- show the exact sreport command for a particular time range or cluster, or
- run a sample sreport for a window (Start=... End=...) and return the live results (I’ll need to query SlurmDB). Which time range should I use?

results.prompt: Explain sreport cluster utilization reports
results.agent_response:
Summary — what the report is
- sreport cluster utilization produces historical usage summaries from the Slurm accounting DB (slurmdbd). It aggregates node/resource usage over a time window and can break usage down by account, user, QOS, WCKEY or by tracked resources (TRES: CPUs, GPUs, memory, etc.).
- Typical uses: chargeback, capacity planning, finding idle/busy periods, and measuring CPU/GPU-hours consumed by accounts or users.

How to run (typical forms)
- Minimal example (time window required):  
  sreport cluster utilization Start=2024-04-01 End=2024-04-30
- Common variants:  
  sreport cluster AccountUtilizationByUser Start=... End=...  
  sreport cluster UserUtilizationByAccount Start=... End=...  
  You can also specify Cluster=, --local/--all_clusters, TopCount=, and other sreport params.

Key fields and what they mean (cluster utilization report)
- Cluster: cluster name used for the report.
- Allocated: time that nodes were in use with active jobs or an active reservation (this excludes reservations created with MAINT or IGNORE_JOBS).
- Idle: time nodes were available but not running jobs.
- Down: time nodes were marked Down or fully Drained (and may include time slurmctld was unresponsive if configured).
- OverCommitted: time nodes were reported running more work than their nominal capacity (occurs when oversubscribe is enabled or accounting reports overcommit).
- PlannedDown / Reported: other categories used to account for planned maintenance or reported usage—depending on config.
- TresName / TresCount / Used: when the report is TRES-aware (e.g., CPU, gpu), TresName is the resource name, TresCount is count of those resources, and Used is the aggregate usage for that TRES over the window (units depend on the report — commonly CPU minutes/hours or GPU minutes).
- Units: the report header states units (often CPU minutes or minutes). Convert to hours by dividing by 60 when needed.

Formats and breakdowns
- The cluster report supports multiple sub-reports/formats: Utilization, AccountUtilizationByUser, AccountUtilizationByQOS, UserUtilizationByAccount, WCKeyUtilizationByUser, etc. Use the sub-report name to get per-account, per-user, or per-QOS views.
- Use the FORMAT or the sub-report name to select what columns you want. The docs list available format options for each report.

Interpretation tips
- Allocated + Idle + Down (+ OverCommitted + PlannedDown + ...) should sum to the total possible node-time for the window — compare Allocated vs Idle to see utilization ratio.
- If you need GPU-hours, use a TRES-aware report (report will show TresName=gpu and Used in GPU-minutes or GPU-hours depending on header).
- Reservations: time consumed by normal reservations counts toward Allocated; reservations flagged MAINT/IGNORE_JOBS are not counted in Allocated.
- If the cluster uses multiple clusters or federation, supply --cluster or --all_clusters to control scope.

Practical suggestions
- Always set Start= and End= to the exact window you want (e.g., Start=2024-04-01 End=2024-04-30).
- Use TopCount, Cluster=, Account= or Partition= filters to focus reports.
- For machine-readable output consider the command’s parseable options (check sreport --help or docs for --parsable2 / output formatting).
- Remember sreport reads the accounting DB — if slurmdbd/sacct is not configured you’ll get no data.

If you want, I can:
- Show an example report for a specific Start/End (I’ll need the time range and whether you want CPU or GPU usage), or
- Explain a particular field or a sample sreport output you have — paste the output and I’ll interpret it.

results.prompt: Explain sreport cluster utilization reports
results.agent_response:
Overview
- sreport reads Slurm accounting rollups (slurmdbd hourly/daily/monthly) and produces usage/cluster utilization reports from the SlurmDB data.
- The cluster utilization reports summarize how cluster resources (CPU/GPU/other TRES) were used, idle, or unavailable during a time window — useful for billing, capacity planning, or identifying wasted time.

How to run a cluster utilization report (examples)
- Basic (default units are CPU minutes unless you ask for a different TRES):
  - sreport cluster utilization Start=2024-04-01 End=2024-04-30
- Report GPU usage (set TRES):
  - sreport cluster utilization Start=2024-04-01 End=2024-04-30 -t tres=gres/gpu
- Per-account / per-user breakdown:
  - sreport cluster AccountUtilizationByUser Start=2024-04-01 End=2024-04-30
- Parsable output (pipe-delimited):
  - Use the interactive parsable/parsable2 modes or redirect with --format options described in the manpage.

Key behavior & caveats
- Rollup selection: sreport uses the largest rollup table (monthly/daily/hourly) that can cover your Start/End range. Short windows use hourly rollups; long windows may use daily/monthly — this affects resolution.
- Units: by default usage is shown as CPU minutes (or CPU hours). When you specify -t/--tres you get usage in the requested TRES (e.g., GPU minutes for gres/gpu).
- Performance: sreport queries slurmdbd. Repeated/looped calls can overload slurmdbd — batch queries sparingly.

Important fields in the cluster Utilization report
- Allocated — time nodes were in use with active jobs or an active reservation. (Excludes reservations created with MAINT or IGNORE_JOBS flags.)
- Idle — time nodes were up but not running jobs or assigned to active reservations.
- Down — time nodes were marked Down or fully Drained, or slurmctld was not responding (if configured to track that).
- PlannedDown / Planned — time nodes were scheduled/planned for downtime (maintenance windows).
- OverCommitted — time counted when nodes were oversubscribed (more resource usage recorded than capacity, e.g., when oversubscribe is enabled).
- Reported — the total usage reported in the rollups for the TRES (the precise meaning depends on the report format; often the sum of used/allocated reported to accounting).
- TresCount / TresName — which TRES (resource types) and the count the report rows refer to (e.g., cpu, gres/gpu).
- Proper / Used (seen in some format options) — format-specific fields; "Used" typically indicates resource usage attributed to the entity (account/user) and "Proper" is a formatting/attribution field used in hierarchical breakdowns (see manpage format options).

Reservation handling and attribution
- Idle reservation time (time reserved but unused) is split evenly among accounts/users that have access to the reservation in some reports.
- If a reservation is assigned to whole accounts, idle time may be counted at the association/account level rather than the user level; parent account usage can be larger than the sum of children because of that.

Common follow-on reports
- Per-account / per-QoS usage: AccountUtilizationByUser, AccountUtilizationByQOS
- User top consumers: sreport user TopUsage
- Job size distributions: sreport job SizesByAccount

Where to read more
- The sreport manpage has full descriptions (FORMAT options, all report names, and the EXPLANATION OF REPORT FIELDS). See the sreport documentation on the Slurm site (sreport(1)) for exact field definitions and all CLI options.

If you want, I can:
- Show exact sreport command lines for your cluster and timeframe (tell me Start/End and whether you want CPU or GPU usage), or
- Explain how a particular field in your current sreport output maps to accounting rows if you paste the output.

results.prompt: Explain sreport cluster utilization reports
results.agent_response:
Summary — what "sreport cluster utilization" shows
- It’s an sreport report type that summarizes cluster resource usage (usage = accumulated resource time) over a time window.
- Output is reported in resource-time units (CPU minutes/hours, GPU minutes/hours, or other TRES units) and breaks usage into categories such as Allocated, Idle, Down, OverCommitted, PlannedDown, Reported, etc.
- The report can be grouped by account, user, QOS, or WCKey (work category), or shown as overall utilization.

Key fields you will see (common names and meanings)
- Cluster: cluster name.
- Allocated: time nodes were in use with active jobs or active reservations (does not include reservations created with MAINT or IGNORE_JOBS).
- Idle: time nodes were up but not running jobs (available).
- Down: time nodes were marked Down or fully Drained, or time slurmctld was not responding (if TrackSlurmctldDown enabled).
- OverCommitted: time resources were oversubscribed (jobs using more TRES than configured).
- PlannedDown: time set aside for planned outages/maintenance.
- Reported: total time reported by the nodes (useful as a sanity check).
- TresName / TresCount: which TRES (trackable resources) the numbers are for (for example CPU, GPU, node) and the count/unit used in the report.
- Start / End / Usage header: indicates the time window and the units used (e.g., “Usage reported in CPU Minutes”).

Typical command forms
- Basic: sreport cluster utilization Start=YYYY-MM-DD End=YYYY-MM-DD
- Example (one-hour sample): sreport cluster utilization Start=2024-04-01T00:00:00 End=2024-04-01T01:00:00
- Use named cluster: sreport --cluster=<name> cluster utilization Start=...
- Change columns/format: sreport cluster utilization Start=... End=... Format=Utilization
- Other useful cluster reports: AccountUtilizationByUser, AccountUtilizationByQOS, UserUtilizationByAccount (use the REPORT name after “cluster”).

How to interpret results
- Units matter: the header will show whether numbers are CPU minutes, GPU minutes, or node-minutes. Divide/convert as needed for CPU-hours or GPU-hours.
- Allocated vs Reported: Allocated is time in use; Reported is what nodes reported. If they differ, check node reporting or accounting settings.
- Down and PlannedDown remove capacity from the available pool — high Down time explains low utilization.
- OverCommitted > 0 means jobs were allowed to oversubscribe TRES (check oversubscribe settings or job submissions requesting more tasks than available resources).

Common filters/usage patterns
- Narrow time windows with Start= and End= to get hourly/daily reports.
- Combine with --cluster or -M to select a different named cluster in a federation.
- Use Format= to select fields or to produce Account/User breakdowns (e.g., AccountUtilizationByUser).
- For GPU-specific analysis, look at TresName=gres/gpu entries or format outputs that include TresName/TresCount.

Caveats and dependencies
- sreport reads accounting data in the SlurmDB (slurmdbd). If slurmdbd or accounting isn’t configured, reports will be incomplete or fail.
- Reservations created with MAINT or IGNORE_JOBS are not counted in Allocated.
- If node reporting is flaky or slurmctld was down, Down/Reported values may reflect that (TrackSlurmctldDown affects counting).
- Overcommitment reporting depends on how TRES accounting and job submissions are configured.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact Format= fields for a specific report name, or
- construct a concrete sreport command for your cluster/time window and explain the columns you’ll get. Which time window or cluster would you like to inspect?

results.prompt: Explain sreport cluster utilization reports
results.agent_response:
Short answer: sreport's "cluster utilization" reports summarize how cluster resources (CPU/GPU/memory, nodes) were used over a time window using accounting data from SlurmDB. They show usage (CPU/GPU/node minutes or hours), idle/time-down, and how usage is apportioned by account/user/QOS, so you can answer “how busy was the cluster and who used it?”

What the report contains (key fields)
- Allocated — time nodes were in use by active jobs or active reservations (this counts jobs inside reservations).
- Idle — time nodes were up and available but not running jobs.
- Down — time nodes were marked Down or fully Drained (and, optionally, time slurmctld was unresponsive if TrackSlurmctldDown is enabled).
- PlannedDown — time nodes were put into planned maintenance.
- OverCommitted — time nodes/TRES were charged beyond their physical capacity (oversubscription/shared scheduling).
- Reported / Cluster — totals/summary columns for the cluster and the reporting period.
- TresCount / TresName — which TRES (trackable resources: CPU, gres/gpu, memory, etc.) the usage numbers refer to.
- Other derived columns — depending on the sub-report you request you’ll also see Account, User, QOS, Wckey, % of cluster, etc.

Units and scope
- Usage is reported in time × resource units (the header will show the unit, commonly CPU minutes or CPU hours).
- The report is produced from SlurmDB (sreport uses accounting records), so it requires slurmdbd and accounting to be enabled and populated.

How to run common queries
- Cluster-wide utilization for a date range:
  sreport cluster Utilization Start=2024-04-01 End=2024-04-30
- Recent week:
  sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-7days
- See usage broken down by account or user:
  sreport cluster AccountUtilizationByUser Start=2024-04-01 End=2024-04-30
- Request specific output columns (FORMAT):
  sreport cluster Utilization Start=... Format=Cluster,Allocated,Idle,Down,TresCount,TresName

Interpretation tips
- Allocated + Idle + Down + PlannedDown should sum up to the total reportable node time for the period (modulo OverCommitted/reporting rounding).
- “Allocated” counts both jobs and reservations with active jobs. Reservations created with MAINT or IGNORE_JOBS are not counted as Allocated.
- OverCommitted flags indicate charged usage > physical capacity (useful to detect oversubscription or accounting oddities).
- Use TresName/TresCount to focus on GPU (gres/gpu) usage vs CPU-only usage.

Caveats and troubleshooting
- If SlurmDB is not configured or there is no historical data, sreport may return empty results.
- sreport reports what’s in accounting — if jobs were misconfigured/charged incorrectly, investigate with sacct/scontrol_show.
- For detailed per-job accounting or failed/completed histories use sacct; sreport is for aggregated usage/summary reports.

Where to read more
- The sreport reference (sreport(1)) documents all report types and FORMAT options — see the Slurm sreport manual for full field definitions and example invocations.

If you want, I can:
- show one or two example sreport commands tailored to your cluster/time window, or
- explain how to interpret a specific sreport output you have (paste the output).

results.prompt: Explain Slurm federation concepts and federated jobs
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise, practical summary of Slurm federation and how federated jobs behave, with the key concepts, lifecycle, submission options, admin notes, and common pitfalls.

1) What is federation (high level)
- Federation lets multiple independent Slurm clusters cooperate so a single job submission can be attempted on many clusters (peer‑to‑peer scheduling).
- A job submitted into a federation is replicated as “sibling” jobs on eligible clusters; clusters independently try to schedule the job using their local policies.
- The cluster where the user submits the job is the origin cluster. The origin coordinates sibling activity and keeps the canonical view of the federated job.

2) Important terms
- Federated job: the job as known to the federation (unique across the federation).
- Origin job / origin cluster: the job and cluster where the submission occurred.
- Sibling job / sibling cluster: a copy of the federated job submitted to another cluster.
- Siblings viable / siblings active: clusters where siblings could run vs where sibling copies exist now.
- Revoked (RV): state used for sibling copies that must be removed once a sibling elsewhere starts.

3) Federated job IDs
- Federated job IDs are unique across the federation. Internally bits encode origin cluster ID and local job ID (e.g., low bits = local job id, high bits = cluster origin id). You can use the job ID to identify the origin cluster.

4) Job lifecycle / scheduling
- Submission: origin submits the job locally and also arranges sibling submissions to other clusters that are “viable.”
- Scheduling: each cluster independently evaluates the sibling and, when it believes it can allocate resources, coordinates with the origin to reserve/allocate.
- Start: when a cluster successfully starts the job it notifies origin; origin tells sibling clusters to revoke/remove their sibling jobs (those siblings move to a revoked state).
- Requeue: if a federated job is requeued the origin may re‑submit siblings to viable clusters; the job can later run on a different cluster.
- Cancel/Modify: cancel/modify requests are routed via the origin; canceling the federated job will remove sibling copies.
- Interactive jobs and job arrays are supported, but behavior and limitations are documented (interactive sessions still coordinate via origin).

5) How to submit and control which clusters are tried
- sbatch / salloc / srun support federation submission options:
  - -M, --clusters=<cluster_list> — submit to a chosen set of clusters (origin will pick one cluster from the list to be the origin and will only create siblings on the listed clusters).
  - --cluster-constraint=[!]<constraint_list> — constrain which clusters are viable.
- If you do not restrict clusters, the federation configuration determines which clusters are viable targets.

6) Commands and job inspection
- squeue has federation-aware options:
  - --sibling shows sibling jobs instead of merging them.
  - Long-format fields: cluster, siblingsactive, siblingsviable, siblingsactiveraw, siblingsviableraw.
- scontrol show job / scontrol show step can show detailed federated job info.
- Admins use sacctmgr to create/modify federations (sacctmgr add/modify federation; cluster membership is stored in the accounting DB).

7) Configuration and admin notes
- Federations are created with sacctmgr; clusters are added to a named federation. A cluster may be a member of only one federation at a time.
- The origin cluster must be reachable by siblings (network/connectivity).
- If a cluster is removed from a federation without draining it first, running jobs that originated there continue to run as non‑federated; pending origin jobs remain pending on origin as non‑federated while sibling jobs are re evaluated.
- Accounting/user mappings, accounts, and QOS policies should be reconciled across clusters if you expect consistent behavior and accounting. (Exact requirements depend on your site configuration.)

8) Limitations and gotchas
- Not intended for extreme job submission rates; SchedMD documentation warns about scale (e.g., very large numbers of jobs/day).
- Scheduling decisions, policies, and available resources differ per cluster — job runtime/limits or available features (GPUs, specialized hardware) may vary.
- Because coordination goes through the origin cluster, origin availability and network reliability matter.
- Sibling jobs are copies: you should be aware of any site‑specific prolog/epilog, environment, or file‑system differences that could affect execution.
- Monitoring/logging and accounting can be dispersed; use squeue/sacct and the federation fields to trace federated jobs.

9) Typical use cases
- Spread load across several cooperating clusters so users get faster starts when one site is busy.
- Provide transparent access to resources that are managed by different administrative domains but agree to cooperate.
- Allow a job to “race” on multiple clusters so the first that can run wins (useful for many interactive or short‑wait tasks).

10) Troubleshooting hints
- If siblings never start: check network connectivity between controllers and that clusters are listed as viable in squeue output (siblingsviable).
- To see where a federated job is running or which siblings exist: squeue --format=... with cluster/siblingsactive fields or squeue --sibling.
- If scheduling seems inconsistent, verify account/QOS limits and resource/FEDERATED configuration across clusters.

References and where to read more
- Slurm Federated Scheduling Guide (Slurm docs): federation.html — provides configuration examples, detailed state descriptions, submission examples, and limitations.

If you want, I can:
- show specific squeue/scontrol fields to inspect a federated job (if you give a job ID), or
- show example sbatch commands with -M/--cluster-constraint for a realistic submission.

results.prompt: Explain Slurm federation concepts and federated jobs
results.agent_response:
Below is a focused, practical summary of Slurm federation and how federated jobs behave.

Overview
- Federation lets multiple independent Slurm clusters cooperate in a peer‑to‑peer manner so a job submitted to one cluster is replicated (as “sibling jobs”) across other clusters in the federation. Each cluster then independently tries to schedule the job under its own policies.
- A federated job has a single federated job ID that is unique across the federation and encodes the origin cluster and local job id.

Core concepts and terminology
- Origin cluster / origin job: the cluster where the user submitted the federated job and the origin copy of that job.
- Sibling job / sibling cluster: a copy of the origin job submitted to another cluster in the federation.
- Federated job ID: a globally unique job ID across the federation (bits encode cluster origin + local ID).
- Revoked (RV) state: siblings that are removed after another cluster starts the job are often put into a revoked state.
- Federation membership: clusters are added to a federation in the accounting DB (sacctmgr). A cluster may be a member of only one federation.

How submission works (user view)
- Commands: sbatch, salloc, srun support federation options. Common options:
  - -M, --clusters=<cluster_list> — submit to one cluster chosen from the list and limit sibling submissions to the specified clusters.
  - --cluster-constraint=[!]<constraint_list> — constrain which clusters are eligible by attributes/constraints.
- When you submit, the origin cluster creates the federated job and submits sibling jobs to the eligible clusters you permitted. Each cluster receives a local copy and tries to schedule it.

How scheduling / start / cancellation are coordinated
- Scheduling is independent per cluster but coordinated through the origin:
  - When a cluster determines it can allocate resources, it contacts the origin to ensure no other cluster is allocating at the same time. If it succeeds in starting, it notifies the origin.
  - The origin then tells other sibling clusters to remove their pending copies (they become revoked or are removed).
- When a sibling begins running, other sibling copies are removed—only one copy runs across the federation.
- Cancels: scancel on the federated job will cancel the running sibling and/or pending siblings. scancel offers a --sibling=<cluster_name> option to cancel a specific sibling copy.

Administration / configuration notes
- Federation is configured with sacctmgr (create a federation, add/remove clusters, set cluster->federation mappings).
- If you remove a cluster from a federation without draining it first, running jobs that originated on the removed cluster will continue running as non-federated jobs; pending jobs may revert to non-federated behavior—so it’s recommended to drain before removing.
- Each cluster keeps its local scheduling, policies, QOS, and accounting; those policies still apply to sibling jobs on each cluster.
- The origin cluster is the coordination point for communications about start/cancel/revoke.

Limitations and caveats
- Not intended for extremely high job throughput (the docs warn about scaling beyond tens of thousands of jobs/day).
- Networking, authentication, and sacctmgr/accounting must be configured consistently across clusters.
- Data locality and shared filesystem: federated jobs may start on any cluster, so ensure data access / staging and software availability are handled appropriately.
- Fairshare/accounting interactions can be complex — ensure accounts/QOS are configured across clusters if you want consistent limits.
- Software versions and environment should be compatible across clusters to avoid failures when a sibling runs on a different site.

Practical tips / best practices
- If you want to limit where a job may run, use -M with a small list of clusters or use cluster constraints.
- For data‑heavy jobs, prestage input or use a shared filesystem; otherwise test job behavior if it runs on a remote cluster.
- Test federation with small, short jobs to validate account mappings, permissions, and data access before broad use.
- Admins: remove a cluster only after draining active federated traffic to avoid surprising state changes for users.

Useful commands (user/admin examples)
- Submit to a limited set of clusters:
  - sbatch -M clusterA,clusterB myscript.sh
- Specify cluster constraints on submission:
  - sbatch --cluster-constraint="!clusterC" myscript.sh
- Cancel a sibling on a particular cluster (admin/user):
  - scancel --sibling=clusterA <federated-jobid>

References
- See the Slurm Federated Scheduling Guide (federation.html) for configuration details, federated job ID encoding, and full semantics of submission/scheduling/requeue/cancel behavior.

If you want, I can:
- show specific command examples for your environment (if you tell me cluster names you plan to use), or
- summarize admin steps to create a federation in sacctmgr.
