results.prompt: Explain Slurm strigger events and triggers
results.agent_response:
Summary
- strigger is the Slurm tool to set, list (get) and clear event-driven triggers. Triggers watch Slurm events (job or node events, controller/burst-buffer events) and run an arbitrary program when the event occurs.
- Typical uses: notify admins on node failures, run a cleanup/notify script shortly before a job hits its time limit, or take action when a node is drained or goes down.

How it works (behavior)
- Commands: strigger --set, --get, --clear.
- strigger registers a trigger record (resource, event type, optional offset, program to run).
- Slurm checks for trigger events periodically (default ~15 seconds). Any events that occur within that interval are checked against registered triggers and the trigger program is executed once for events in that interval.
- OFFSET is specified in seconds; negative offsets request that the program run before the event (e.g., offset=-300 means 5 minutes before a job time limit).
- RES_ID can be a job id, a hostlist, or "*" for all hosts (depending on RES_TYPE).
- Permissions: users can create triggers relevant to their resources (typical case: their jobs). Some clear/management operations and global actions are restricted to root (see manpage).

Common trigger types (TYPE)
- job-related:
  - time — when a job reaches its time limit (use OFFSET to run before the limit)
  - fini — when a job finishes/terminates
- node-related / general:
  - down — node goes down
  - up — node returns up
  - drained — node is marked drained
  - idle — node becomes idle
  - reconfig — node or partition reconfiguration
- controller / service events:
  - backup_slurmctld_assumed_control, backup_slurmctld_failure, backup_slurmctld_resumed_operation
  - burst_buffer — burst buffer error
(See strigger manpage for the full option list and exact names.)

Output / fields you’ll see with --get
- TRIG_ID — trigger identifier
- RES_TYPE — "job" or "node"
- RES_ID — job id or hostlist (or "*")
- TYPE — trigger type (time, fini, down, up, drained, idle, reconfig, etc.)
- OFFSET — seconds (negative indicates before the event)
- USER — who registered it
- PROGRAM — pathname of program to execute
- (The manpage documents the full output fields.)

Examples
- Run notify.sh 5 minutes before job 1234 hits its time limit:
  strigger --set --type=time --jobid=1234 --offset=-300 --program=/home/alice/notify.sh
- Show triggers for a node or hostlist:
  strigger --get --node=node01
- Remove a trigger by its ID:
  strigger --clear --id=42

Caveats and best practices
- Triggers are not instantaneous — they are evaluated on the periodic check interval and executed once per interval for events that happened during that period.
- Avoid tight loops calling strigger (each call is an RPC to slurmctld); excessive calls can degrade slurmctld performance.
- Test trigger programs carefully (environment, permissions, PATH) because they run under slurmctld context or the requesting user depending on configuration.

Reference
- See the strigger manpage for full syntax, all supported event names and permissions: https://slurm.schedmd.com/strigger.html

If you want, I can:
- show example strigger commands tailored to a use case (jobs vs nodes), or
- walk through a specific trigger you want to create (I’ll explain exact flags and any permission considerations).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/strigger.html)
Executing strigger sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from strigger or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run strigger or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to strigger to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr add, modify, and delete safety implications
results.agent_response:
Short answer: sacctmgr add/modify/delete change the accounting DB (slurmdbd) and therefore can immediately affect scheduling, access, fairshare/priority, and reporting. They are powerful admin operations — do backups, review staged transactions, and prefer interactive (non-immediate) mode for risky changes.

What each verb can do and its safety implications
- add (create)
  - Effects: creates accounts/users/qos/associations/clusters. Controls who can submit and which account jobs will be charged to.
  - Risk: accidentally creating a wrong association or parent-child account can give unintended access or incorrect fairshare buckets.
  - Safety: low-impact by itself, but wrong adds can open access or misattribute usage.

- modify
  - Effects: changes attributes (limits like MaxJobs, MaxWall, TRES limits, Fairshare, DefaultQOS, QOS properties) for users/accounts/associations.
  - Risk: can immediately change scheduling decisions: tighten limits can block or preempt queued jobs; loosen limits can let users consume resources; changing fairshare or QOS can drastically reorder priorities; changing limit units (TRES) can cause jobs to be rejected or pending with AssocMax/AssocGrp reasons.
  - Safety: high risk to cluster behavior — affects both pending and future scheduling. Changes should be planned and communicated.

- delete (remove)
  - Effects: removes users/accounts/qos/cluster records or associations. The delete command modifies associations and the accounting DB state.
  - Risk: deleting an account or user association can cause queued jobs to be disallowed (AccountNotAllowed) or prevent reporting; bulk deletes (or clean=account,qos,user) can remove many entities at once. Some delete operations cascade (or are constrained by a hierarchy) — be careful with cluster/account hierarchy.
  - Safety: destructive. Always export or dump relevant data first.

Important operational & audit notes
- Transactions and commit model: sacctmgr supports an interactive mode where changes are staged and you then commit. The -i / --immediate flag commits without prompting. Use interactive mode for multi-step changes so you can review before commit.
- Audit trail: sacctmgr records transactions in the DB (you can list transactions). Use this for auditing and to track who made what change.
- Historical job records: Job/accounting records are stored in slurmdbd. Deleting accounts/users changes associations going forward; historical job records remain in the DB, but reporting/correlation can be affected if you remove the entities you rely on. Export data if you depend on historical mappings.
- Propagation/time-to-effect: slurmctld/slurmd scheduling decisions consult the accounting DB; changes propagate but there can be a short window depending on configuration. Expect near-immediate effect on scheduling/priorities.
- Permissions: sacctmgr requires database admin privileges. Limit who can run sacctmgr to prevent accidental or malicious changes.
- No dry-run option: there is no generic "dry-run" flag; use interactive mode or practice on a test DB/cluster.

Common risks that lead to outages or user impact
- Setting overly strict limits (maxjobs, maxnodes, billing limits) that immediately change many pending jobs to a blocked state.
- Removing or renaming the account that many users submit under, causing mass submission failures or rejected pending jobs.
- Changing fairshare or defaultQOS without coordination, suddenly moving long-running users to the front or deprioritizing others.
- Running bulk delete/clean operations without scoping (clean=account,qos,user) — can remove large sets of accounts/QoS/users.
- Mistyping where-clauses in modify/delete that match more rows than intended.

Practical safe workflow (recommended)
1. Inventory and review:
   - sacctmgr list associations cluster=... account=... user=... format=... to see current associations.
   - sacctmgr list qos, accounts, users to confirm names and scope.
2. Export/backup:
   - sacctmgr dump cluster=<name> file=backup.cfg (or use your DB backup procedures for slurmdbd).
3. Test in interactive mode:
   - Start sacctmgr interactive session, run add/modify/delete commands, then run sacctmgr list/show to review staged changes.
   - When satisfied, run commit; if not, run rollback (or simply exit without commit in interactive mode).
   - Alternatively, use -i only when you mean to commit immediately.
4. Make minimal incremental changes:
   - Prefer small, well-scoped changes (one association or one limit at a time) and monitor effects.
5. Communicate and monitor:
   - Notify affected users before making broad changes (especially limits or defaultQOS).
   - After commit, monitor squeue/sinfo and transactions (sacctmgr list transactions) and be prepared to revert or adjust.
6. Revert and remediation:
   - If something breaks, restore from dump or recreate associations as needed. Use the transaction log to understand exactly what changed.

Useful commands to help be safe
- sacctmgr list associations ... (review current state)
- sacctmgr show transactions format=... (audit recent changes)
- sacctmgr dump cluster=<name> file=<file> (export current DB data)
- Use interactive sacctmgr (no -i) and explicitly run commit when ready

Summary checklist before making changes
- Have a current slurmdbd/DB dump or export.
- Confirm exact target names with sacctmgr list.
- Use interactive mode to stage changes; avoid --immediate unless confident.
- Make one small change at a time and monitor scheduling effects.
- Limit who can run sacctmgr and record changes (transaction logs).

If you want, I can:
- list the current associations that match a pattern (showing how a planned change would target records), or
- produce a step-by-step command example for a safe modify/delete (e.g., how to safely change MaxJobs for a single account) — tell me which you'd prefer.

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr add, modify, and delete safety implications
results.agent_response:
Summary — what sacctmgr changes affect
- sacctmgr talks to slurmdbd and edits the accounting database (users, accounts, associations, limits, fairshare, QOS links, etc.). These changes affect scheduling decisions (limits, fairshare), user defaults, and accounting reports site-wide.
- Most add/modify/delete operations change association metadata only. Historical job records are stored in the DB independently; they are not normally removed just by deleting an association. Explicit archive/purge operations can remove job/event records and are irreversible if configured to purge.

Safety implications and risks (by operation)

1) sacctmgr add (create user/account/cluster/association)
- Risk: accidental creation of accounts/users with wrong defaults (DefaultAccount, DefaultWCKey, AdminLevel, fairshare) so new jobs may be charged to the wrong account or inherit incorrect limits.
- Scheduling impact: adding an account with a high fairshare or a QOS association can change future scheduling/fairshare calculations.
- Mitigation: review intended defaults before adding; use sacctmgr show/list to confirm existing associations; create in a test/staging DB if available.

2) sacctmgr modify (change limits, fairshare, adminlevel, default account, etc.)
- Risk: changing per-user or per-account limits (MaxJobs, MaxWall, GrpTRES, GrpJobs, TRES limits, DefaultQOS, Fairshare, etc.) can immediately affect scheduling decisions:
  - Lowering limits may prevent queued jobs from starting (or stop future submissions).
  - Raising limits can allow resource bursts or bypass intended quotas.
  - Changing fairshare values reorders priority calculations and can shift job start order.
- Operational risk: changing DefaultAccount or AdminLevel can affect who can manage an account and which account new jobs use.
- Mitigation:
  - Inspect the existing association(s) with sacctmgr show or sacctmgr list associations (use format= to see relevant fields).
  - Apply conservative changes and monitor scheduler behavior.
  - Prefer incremental modifications and communicate with affected users.
  - When scripting changes, avoid --immediate unless you intend to commit without human confirmation.

3) sacctmgr delete (remove user/account/association)
- Risk: deleting an account or user association can:
  - Remove a billing/accounting target for future jobs (users may not be able to submit if account required).
  - Remove coordinator privileges or orphan sub-accounts.
  - Cause confusion in reports and fairshare calculations.
- Historical records: deleting an account or user association does not usually delete historical job records by default; however, archive/purge operations (sacctmgr archive/dump with purge options or slurmdbd purge settings) can remove job/event data permanently and are irreversible.
- Operational hazard: deleting an account that still has active users or policies can leave users unable to run jobs or change default accounts unexpectedly.
- Mitigation:
  - Use sacctmgr list and sacct to confirm whether there are active or recent jobs tied to the account/user.
  - Backup the SlurmDB (dump or slurmdbd DB backup) before destructive deletes.
  - Avoid running archive/purge options without a verified backup. Note from docs: archive dump with purge is irreversible.
  - Communicate deletions to affected groups and coordinate maintenance windows.

Other important safety notes and best practices
- Transaction / confirmation behavior:
  - By default sacctmgr prompts to confirm a transaction. The -i/--immediate flag commits without confirmation — use it only in tested automation.
- Backups and recovery:
  - Always backup slurmdbd data (dump or DB-level backup) before mass deletes or bulk modifications.
  - Test restore procedures in a staging environment periodically.
- Auditing & logging:
  - Changes via sacctmgr are recorded in slurmdbd logs and the DB; review logs after major changes.
- Review before change:
  - Use sacctmgr show/list (with WithAssoc or format=) to inspect the exact associations and limits you will change.
  - Use sacct and sacctmgr list associations to check for historical and active jobs related to the target account/user.
- Staging/testing:
  - Apply changes first in a staging cluster or test project to observe scheduling/fairshare effects if possible.
- Coordination:
  - Inform users when modifying limits or deleting accounts (especially if account is required to submit).
- Concurrency:
  - Concurrent sacctmgr changes can race; coordinate multi-admin operations and check the database after changes.
- Minimizing impact:
  - Prefer modifying limits on specific association rows rather than deleting and recreating entities unless necessary.
  - Use non-destructive operations (modify metadata) to achieve administrative goals when possible.

Quick checklist before running sacctmgr delete/modify/add
1. sacctmgr list/show associations for the target(s) (verify Cluster, Account, User, Partition, limits, DefaultQOS).
2. sacct -S (or sacct -u user / sacct -A account) to check historical and recent jobs tied to the entity.
3. Backup slurmdbd (DB dump).
4. Plan communication to affected users and coordination window if needed.
5. Apply change in staging if feasible; then apply in production. Avoid --immediate in interactive sessions unless confident.
6. Verify results (sacctmgr list, sshare, sprio) and monitor scheduling behavior.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact sacctmgr fields to inspect for a given account/user (examples of sacctmgr list/show commands), or
- produce a small pre-change checklist or script snippet (non-destructive) you can run to collect the necessary pre-change facts. Which would you prefer?

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr add, modify, and delete safety implications
results.agent_response:
Short answer: sacctmgr add/modify/delete change the accounting database (slurmdbd) and can immediately and permanently change who can submit, what limits apply, fairshare, and associations between users/accounts/clusters/partitions. They are powerful admin actions — use them with backups, narrow where clauses, and audit logging.

What they actually change
- sacctmgr modifies the Slurm accounting DB (slurmdbd), not the job state in slurmctld. However accounting changes affect future scheduling/submit decisions (limits, QOS, fairshare) and can therefore change cluster behavior immediately.
- add creates accounts/users/associations.
- modify changes attributes (fairshare, maxjobs, maxwall, QOS, parent, etc.). Those limits are enforced for future submissions and may influence scheduler decisions (and preemption) depending on site config.
- delete removes entities or associations. Deleting an account or user can remove the association used for job submission/limits; this can block new submissions or change accounting attribution.

Key safety implications / risks
- Broad deletes are dangerous: deleting an account will remove associations for all users under it and can break submit-time validation. Deleting users/accounts in use may lead to rejections for future submissions.
- Cascading effects: account hierarchy and associations are interconnected. Deleting a parent or changing parents can affect many child accounts/users.
- Limits and QOS changes can impact scheduling immediately. Modifying limits downwards (e.g., set maxjobs=0 or reduce MaxWall) can cause users to be unable to submit, and may change preemption decisions.
- No automatic job cancellation, but scheduling/priority may change. Running jobs generally continue, but behavior may vary with site policies if QOS/limits are used for preemption or enforcement.
- Human error / incorrect where clauses can match many rows; a simple typo can delete or change many associations.
- Concurrency and availability: changes go through slurmdbd; network or DB issues can leave operations incomplete or require recovery.
- Permissions: sacctmgr requires administrative privileges — misuse by an admin is a single point of failure.

Practical safety checklist (recommended)
1. Preview before you change
   - Use list/show to inspect targets:
     - sacctmgr show associations (or sacctmgr list associations where ...)
     - sacctmgr list account, user, association to confirm exactly what will be affected
2. Avoid wildcard deletes; scope with explicit where clauses
   - Use where name=foo cluster=bar account=baz to limit scope.
3. Use interactive commit and review transactions
   - By default sacctmgr expects you to commit changes instead of immediately applying them; avoid --immediate (-i) during exploratory work.
   - After changes, review: sacctmgr list transactions to audit what changed, who did it, and when.
4. Back up the slurm DB before bulk changes
   - Use sacctmgr archive dump (or a DB backup method) to create a restore point you can load if needed.
5. Prefer deactivation over deletion
   - If you want to stop use of an account/user temporarily, consider modifying limits (e.g., set maxjobs=0 or change state/description) rather than deleting the entity.
6. Test in staging
   - For bulk or scripted changes, test on a non-production SlurmDB instance first.
7. Use explicit modifies not txt edits
   - Use sacctmgr modify ... set <attrs> with precise attribute names. Don’t script blind edits without list/show checks.
8. Be careful when automating
   - If scripting, consider non-interactive use of --immediate but ensure your script validates targets first and logs the change.
9. Keep an audit trail and inform stakeholders
   - Notify affected users before cutting their account or lowering limits. Use the transactions log for postmortem.

Recovery options if something goes wrong
- Restore from archive dump (sacctmgr archive load) or DB-level backup.
- Recreate deleted accounts/users and re-add associations if you have a dump or manual record.
- Use sacctmgr list transactions to determine exactly what changed and when; this helps construct a targeted reversal.
- For accidental limit changes, immediately modify back to prior values (if known) to restore service.

Permissions and governance
- Only users with accounting admin privileges should run sacctmgr operations.
- Implement change-control: require review/approval for mass deletes or limit reductions.

Short examples and hints
- Preview associations: sacctmgr show associations cluster=CLUSTER format=Account,User,Partition
- Temporarily block a user: sacctmgr modify user where name=alice set maxjobs=0 (safer than delete)
- Backup before bulk changes: sacctmgr archive dump file=/tmp/sacctmgr-backup.sql

If you want, I can:
- produce a concrete pre-change checklist you can follow interactively, or
- review a specific sacctmgr command or where clause and point out exactly what it will affect. Which would you like?

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr add, modify, and delete safety implications
results.agent_response:
Summary — what to watch for
- sacctmgr modifies the Slurm accounting DB (slurmdbd) — associations are the Cluster+Account+User(+Partition) records that the scheduler uses for limits, fairshare, default QOS, etc. Changes to accounts/users/QOS/limits affect scheduling and future job submissions, and can change which pending jobs are eligible to start.
- Unsafe edits can: block users from submitting, make pending jobs unschedulable, change priorities/fairshare, remove coordinator/admin privileges, orphan or remove associations, or otherwise change accounting and reporting. Because these are DB changes, mistakes can require restoring a backup.

Concrete safety implications by action
- sacctmgr add (create)
  - Low risk for existing jobs: adding accounts/users/QOS generally enables capabilities (new account, new association, more privileges). It won’t retroactively break running jobs.
  - Use-case risks: accidentally creating duplicate or misconfigured associations (wrong cluster/partition/account) can confuse accounting or allow unintentional access.
  - Safety tips: specify cluster/account/partition explicitly, and verify with sacctmgr list/show after adding.

- sacctmgr modify
  - Scheduling & limits: changes to limits (MaxJobs, MaxTRES, GrpJobs, GrpTRES, MaxWall, DefaultQOS, Fairshare, etc.) influence scheduler decisions. The docs note group limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES…) are tested when a job is considered for allocation — i.e., limits primarily affect scheduling of new/pending jobs.
  - Permissions & roles: changing AdminLevel, coordinator flags, or UsersAreCoords changes who can manage accounts.
  - Potential surprises: lowering group limits or per-user limits can make already-pending jobs unschedulable; raising limits can allow a flood of new jobs to start. Some attributes are inherited by child accounts so modifying a parent can have broad scope.
  - Safety tips: preview existing values with sacctmgr show/list and sshare (fairshare view); prefer targeted modify with a precise where clause; test changes in interactive mode before committing.

- sacctmgr delete
  - Broad impact: deleting an account, user, or association removes that entity from the Slurm accounting DB. That prevents future submissions using that account/association and can remove coordinator privileges.
  - Running jobs: the documentation treats associations and accounts as DB metadata used by the scheduler. It does not describe deletion as automatically killing running jobs; however deleting an account or association can prevent future accounting or make re-association awkward. Deleting entities with children (account hierarchies) may fail or produce unexpected consequences if not done in the proper order.
  - Danger: a too-broad delete (missing or incorrect where clause) can remove many associations at once.
  - Safety tips: always use an explicit where clause (cluster=..., account=..., user=...), list associations first, and prefer deleting only the specific association or leaf account. Don’t delete parent accounts before children.

Operational controls and safety procedures
- Interactive mode vs immediate:
  - Run sacctmgr without --immediate to use interactive mode; you can stage commands and then run commit to apply changes. This is safer for reviewing batched edits.
  - Use --immediate (or -i) only when you are sure — it commits without confirmation.
- Preview and verify:
  - Use sacctmgr list/show (and sacctmgr list associations, sacctmgr show account/user/qos) to inspect current state before changes.
  - Check scheduler effects with squeue/sinfo/sshare after committing if you expect scheduling or fairshare changes.
- Back up the accounting DB:
  - Use sacctmgr archive dump (or the DB backup mechanism for slurmdbd) to export a flat-file snapshot before destructive changes so you can restore with archive load if needed.
- Narrow, auditable changes:
  - Use precise where= filters to scope add/modify/delete.
  - Log/record the exact commands and rationale; prefer small, incremental changes.
- Test-first:
  - If possible, test the change in a staging cluster or with non-production accounts/users.
- Recovery plan:
  - Have a DB dump or snapshot ready. Know how to load it (sacctmgr archive load) and involve DB/Slurm admins if you need to recover.
- Communicate:
  - Inform affected users before making changes that affect submission ability, limits, or fairshare. Coordinate if you will remove or change accounts.

Examples of common mistakes
- Running sacctmgr delete account name=X cluster=Y without verifying children → accidentally remove sub-accounts or associations.
- Lowering GrpJobs/GrpTRES too far → many pending jobs become unschedulable.
- Removing a coordinator flag or AdminLevel without warning → users lose management ability unexpectedly.
- Using --immediate for a multi-change script with a bug → immediate commit of many unwanted changes.

Useful commands to run before/after edits
- Preview: sacctmgr list associations cluster=<cluster> format=Account,User,Partition,Fairshare,...
- Inspect entity: sacctmgr show account name=<acct> ; sacctmgr show user name=<user> cluster=<cluster>
- Backup: sacctmgr archive dump file=<file>
- Interactive: sacctmgr (enter interactive mode), make edits, then commit
- Recover: sacctmgr archive load file=<file> (restore from dump)

Bottom line (short)
- Adds are relatively safe but check names/associations.
- Modifies change scheduler behavior for new/pending jobs — preview and stage changes.
- Deletes are highest risk — back up, scope narrowly, review associations, and use interactive/commit workflow.

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr add, modify, and delete safety implications
results.agent_response:
Short summary
- sacctmgr add/modify/delete change the Slurm accounting database (slurmdbd). These changes affect accounting, fairshare, QOS and association limits and therefore can change scheduling decisions immediately for pending/new jobs. They do not edit slurm.conf or node state, but can indirectly prevent or allow jobs to start.
- Treat sacctmgr writes as high-impact administrative operations: back up the DB (dump), preview changes, use interactive mode, and coordinate with users.

Concrete safety implications (what to watch for)
- Permissions/authority: sacctmgr write operations require Slurm DB (slurmdbd) admin/operator privileges. Misuse can give or remove privileges (Admin/Operator, reservation rights).
- Immediate vs interactive commit:
  - Interactive mode lets you stage several add/modify/delete commands and review before committing.
  - The -i / --immediate option commits without confirmation. Don’t use -i unless sure.
- Backups & rollback:
  - Use sacctmgr dump or archive to export associations/accounts before making changes. You can reload with sacctmgr load if needed.
  - There is no automatic transactional “undo” of arbitrary destructive edits—plan for restore from dump if needed.
- Effects on scheduling and job eligibility:
  - Limits and QOS (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, MaxTRES, DefaultQOS, etc.) are consulted when a job is considered for allocation. Modifying group limits or QOS can immediately make pending jobs ineligible to start (or eligible).
  - Changes to TRES limits using +=/-= take effect and are bounded; accidental large changes can prevent scheduling or allow excessive resource use.
  - Fairshare/fair-share allocations are taken from the DB; changing shares changes job priority ordering and can reorder the queue.
- Deleting accounts/users/associations:
  - Deleting an account or user removes the association records in the DB. This can:
    - Affect how future job submissions are validated (submission without a valid account may be refused or billed to a default account depending on your config).
    - Change how pending jobs are evaluated (they may become ineligible if their account/QOS/association no longer exists or no longer meets limits).
  - Running jobs typically continue to run; however, behavior may depend on your site configuration and federation behavior. (Because site setups vary, assume deletes may affect pending-job eligibility and accounting; test or consult site policy.)
- QOS and preemption:
  - Changing QOS flags, grace times, or group limits can cause preemption decisions or change preemption eligibility. That may terminate or preempt running jobs if policy requires.
- Federation and cluster edits:
  - Removing a cluster from a federation or changing federation associations can change behavior for federated jobs; docs explicitly note running jobs may continue but pending federated jobs’ behavior changes.
- Audit & accounting integrity:
  - AdminComment and other accounting fields can be modified only by admins; modifying these affects reports and auditing.
  - Deleting entities can make historical accounting records harder to interpret; prefer to archive before removing.

Safe workflow / checklist (recommended)
1. Inspect current state
   - list associations and limits: sacctmgr show associations (or sacctmgr list account,user,qos,cluster) and use squeue/sacct to find active or pending jobs tied to the target accounts/users.
2. Backup
   - sacctmgr dump cluster=<name> file=backup.cfg (or use archive/dump) before destructive changes.
3. Stage changes interactively
   - Run sacctmgr in interactive mode, apply add/modify/delete commands without -i, review the planned changes, then commit.
4. Preview impact on queue
   - Use squeue and sprio/sshare/sdiag to see how priority/eligibility might change. Consider running sprio and sshare after edits to validate expected priority/fairshare effects.
5. Communicate
   - Notify affected users if you’ll delete accounts or change quotas/limits. Give a maintenance window if changes may delay jobs.
6. Commit and monitor
   - Commit changes (or use --immediate if already validated) and monitor squeue, slurmctld logs, and sdiag/sprio/sstat to confirm expected results.
7. Rollback if needed
   - If something breaks, restore from the dump file (sacctmgr load file=backup.cfg) or recreate associations. Test restore in staging first where possible.

Examples of safe commands to preview and protect yourself
- Preview association(s): sacctmgr show association withassoc cluster=<cluster> account=<acct> user=<user>
- List accounts/QOS: sacctmgr list account cluster=<cluster>; sacctmgr list qos
- Dump for backup: sacctmgr dump cluster=<cluster> file=/root/backup-<date>.cfg
- Use interactive mode to stage changes: sacctmgr (then run add/modify/delete inside, review, then commit)
- Use --immediate only after review: sacctmgr modify account where name=<acct> set GrpJobs=50 --immediate

Common gotchas to call out
- Using -i/--immediate without a dump can make mistakes hard to undo.
- Deleting an account that is the DefaultAccount for users can break future job submissions for those users.
- Changing group limits/QOS can silently block large numbers of pending jobs from ever starting.
- TRES arithmetic (+=/-=) can produce very large or zero values if misused; verify with sacctmgr show after change.
- Assumptions about running jobs: some changes (especially in federated setups) may behave differently—confirm with your cluster’s policy and test.

If you want, I can:
- give a short sample interactive sacctmgr session that shows safe staging and commit steps, or
- produce a one-line checklist script (commands to run in order) you can copy to run on your cluster (I will not run them).

## SPECIFICATIONS FOR USERS[#SECTION_SPECIFICATIONS-FOR-USERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Users can be created, modified, and deleted with sacctmgr. These
options allow you to set the corresponding attributes or filter on them
when querying for Users.
It is important to recognize the difference between a User and an Association.
There is a User entity that exists for each unique username. However, there
can be multiple User Associations for the same User. The combination of a
Cluster, Account, User, and optionally a Partition constitute a User
Association. When adding an existing User to another Account, you are creating

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr archive, dump, and load workflows
results.agent_response:
Short summary — what each command does
- sacctmgr dump: write a flat-file representation of cluster association data (Cluster, Account, User, Parent, QOS lines). Use when copying/migrating or backing up account/QOS/association configuration.
- sacctmgr load: read a previously-created dump (or archive) file and insert/reconcile its associations into the SlurmDB (slurmdbd). Can be used to restore or import cluster associations.
- sacctmgr archive dump: export historical accounting records (jobs, events, etc.) to an archive file and (optionally) purge those records from the database. This is for long-term archival and database housekeeping.
- sacctmgr archive load: import archived accounting data back into the SlurmDB from an archive file.

Key differences
- dump/load (flat-file) = cluster association metadata (accounts, users, QOS, cluster definitions). Format is human-readable lines starting with QOS/Cluster/Parent/Account/User and colon-separated specs.
- archive dump/load = accounting records (job records, events). These are archival snapshots of historical data and are used to move, back up, or purge older accounting data.

Important behaviors & options
- Permissions: sacctmgr dump/load and archive operations must be run as a Slurm administrator (or root).
- File location: archive load requires the file to exist on the slurmdbd host (not necessarily the admin’s workstation). ArchiveDir in slurmdbd.conf is the default archive directory.
- Non-destructive vs destructive:
  - sacctmgr dump is non-destructive.
  - sacctmgr archive dump can be destructive if you include purge options — once records are purged they cannot be recovered except from the archive file you created. The operation cannot be rolled back.
- Purge control: archive dump honors either explicit command-line purge options or the Purge* settings in slurmdbd.conf (examples: PurgeJobAfter, PurgeEventAfter); if you don’t specify archiving options the configured slurmdbd.conf defaults are used.
- Load idempotency/duplicates: archive load will not insert records that already exist in the DB; attempting to load the same archive twice will fail for duplicate records. For association load (dump/load), there are options such as clean= to remove existing cluster/associations before loading, and insert/SQL options in advanced cases — read the man page for exact flags.
- Version compatibility: archive files from the current or prior Slurm releases can normally be loaded.

Typical workflows (step-by-step)

1) Backup or migrate cluster associations (accounts/QOS/users)
- On source cluster:
  - sacctmgr dump cluster=<clustername> file=<clustername>.cfg
- Transfer file to destination slurmdbd host.
- On destination:
  - (optional) sacctmgr load file=<clustername>.cfg
  - Use clean=account,qos,user if you intend to replace existing data (be careful; this deletes things).
- Verify associations with sacctmgr show and in the web UI (if present).

2) Archive old accounting data and purge DB
- Decide retention policy and test in a staging DB first.
- On slurmdbd host (example):
  - sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/archive Jobs=yes Events=yes PurgeJobAfter=365d PurgeEventAfter=365d
- Confirm archive file(s) were written to Directory (ArchiveDir default if unspecified).
- Verify integrity of archive files and then confirm the DB size/records decreased.

3) Restore archived accounting records
- Ensure the archive file is present on slurmdbd host.
- sacctmgr archive load File=/archive/<archivefile>
- Note: records already in DB will not be reloaded; duplicates will cause load to fail for those records.

Practical advice / safety checklist
- Always back up the SlurmDB (database) before archive/purge or destructive load/clean operations.
- Test load/archive workflows in a staging environment first.
- Keep copies of archive files outside the slurmdbd host (off-host backups) because purge is irreversible without those files.
- Verify file ownership/permissions so slurmdbd can read archive files.
- Use sacct/sacctmgr show queries after operations to confirm expected results.
- Consult the sacctmgr man page (sacctmgr(8) or Slurm docs) for exact option names and more advanced flags (clean=, insert=, Directory=, Jobs, Events, PurgeJobAfter, PurgeEventAfter, File=, Cluster=, etc.).

If you want, I can:
- show exact example commands tailored to your cluster names and retention window, or
- run checks (e.g., list ArchiveDir contents or show current association dump) — tell me which cluster name or archive path to reference.

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr archive, dump, and load workflows
results.agent_response:
Short summary
- "sacctmgr archive dump" — export historical accounting records (jobs, events) to a flat archive file; typically used before purging old rows from the SlurmDB (irreversible if you also purge).  
- "sacctmgr archive load" — import an archive file back into the SlurmDB (file must be readable on the slurmdbd host). Loads fail if the same records already exist.  
- "sacctmgr dump" / "sacctmgr load" (the flat-file dump/load feature) — export and import accounting association data (clusters, accounts, users, QOS) used for copying or restoring association/configuration data, not the per-job accounting rows.

Details and recommended workflows

1) archive dump — export accounting rows
- Purpose: write job and/or event rows from the SlurmDB to an archive file. Commonly used to offload old accounting data before purging it from the database to reclaim space.
- Key options (from docs): Directory (where to write archive files), Jobs (archive Jobs), Events (archive Events). If purge is requested (or configured in slurmdbd.conf via PurgeJobAfter / PurgeEventAfter), the corresponding rows will be removed from the DB when the archive operation runs.
- Important properties:
  - The operation is destructive when combined with purge: once rows are purged from the DB they are removed from live accounting and recovery requires the archive file.
  - If you do not supply purge in the command, slurmdbd.conf purge settings will determine whether rows are removed.
  - Archive files are created under the ArchiveDir used by slurmdbd (check slurmdbd.conf).
- Typical workflow:
  1. Verify current usage and retention settings (inspect slurmdbd.conf ArchiveDir, PurgeJobAfter, PurgeEventAfter).
  2. Run archive dump with appropriate time filters and Directory/job/event flags to create the file.
     Example (template): sacctmgr archive dump directory=/path/to/arch jobs=yes events=yes starttime=YYYY-MM-DD endtime=YYYY-MM-DD purge=yes
     (Use real options and time filters appropriate for your version/config.)
  3. Verify the archive file(s) exist and contain expected data.
  4. If purge=yes was used, verify data was removed from the DB (sacct queries).
  5. Back up the archive file to reliable storage.

2) archive load — restore accounting rows from an archive
- Purpose: load previously-created archive files back into the SlurmDB (repopulate purged rows or migrate accounting data).
- Key points:
  - The archive file must be present on the slurmdbd host (the host running the daemon), not just the client machine.
  - The loader will refuse to insert records that already exist in the database — attempting to load the same archive twice will error.
  - Archive files from current and prior Slurm releases can be loaded (backwards compatibility).
  - There are options (e.g., Insert/SQL control) to affect how data is inserted; consult the sacctmgr archive load section for your version.
- Typical workflow:
  1. Copy the archive file to the slurmdbd host (and into ArchiveDir if that’s required for your setup).
  2. Run sacctmgr archive load file=/path/to/archive-file
  3. Verify inserted rows with sacct (or sacctmgr queries).
  4. If load fails because of duplicate records, inspect whether partial loads happened and resolve (may require DB cleanup or a fresh DB restore).

3) sacctmgr dump / sacctmgr load — associations (clusters/accounts/users/QOS)
- Purpose: export and import accounting association/config data used to configure clusters, accounts, users, parents, and QOS. Useful to copy accounting setup to another cluster or back up associations.
- File format basics:
  - Each non-comment line begins with one of: QOS, Cluster, Parent, Account, User, followed by " - " then the entity name and colon-separated specs. Lines may contain quoted values for strings with spaces. Comments begin with #.
  - Since v25.05 QOS info is included in the dump.
- Important rules:
  - There is an order dependency: define Cluster entries before Accounts, and Accounts before Users. The dump file is organized to preserve that, and load reconciles with existing DB entries.
  - sacctmgr dump/load must be run as a Slurm administrator (root).
  - sacctmgr load supports options such as clean=... (to remove existing data), Cluster= (rename the cluster during load), and others — check the man page for exact options.
- Typical workflow:
  1. Export current associations: sacctmgr dump cluster=<clustername> file=/path/cluster.cfg
  2. Inspect the file, edit if you need to change names or defaults.
  3. On the target DB: sacctmgr load file=/path/cluster.cfg  (or use clean=account,qos,user to replace certain types)
  4. Verify with sacctmgr show cluster/account/qos/user.

Operational checklist & safety practices
- Always back up your SlurmDB (and the slurmdbd configuration) before destructive operations.
- Keep archive files in reliable, tested storage and validate them (sample them with sacct or tools) before purging the DB.
- Test archive load and association load on a non-production/test DB first to validate behavior and options for your Slurm version.
- Confirm the archive file is on the slurmdbd host before running archive load.
- Use sacct and sacctmgr show queries to validate results after dump/load/archive operations.
- Read the sacctmgr man page for your Slurm version — option names and behaviors vary across releases.

Where to look in the docs
- sacctmgr(1) archive dump / archive load (section: archive dump / archive load) — options like Directory, Events, Jobs, PurgeEventAfter, PurgeJobAfter, File, Insert.
- sacctmgr(1) dump / load (flat-file dump/load) — format details for QOS, Cluster, Parent, Account, User and examples.

- show the exact sacctmgr command-syntax snippets from the manual for your installed Slurm version, or
- draft a safe example runbook for archiving jobs older than X days (including the exact arguments you should run) — tell me your Slurm version and desired retention window.

The HDF5 Profile Plugin requires a common shared file system on all
the compute nodes. While a job is running, the plugin writes a
file into this file system for each step of the job on each node. When
the job ends, the merge process is launched and the node-step files
are combined into one HDF5 file for the job.

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr archive, dump, and load workflows
results.agent_response:
Summary first
- sacctmgr supports two related but different workflows:
  1) Accounting-data archive (sacctmgr archive dump / sacctmgr archive load) — export and (optionally) purge historical Jobs/Events/etc. from the slurmdbd accounting DB into archive files, and later restore them.
  2) Flat-file association dump/load (sacctmgr dump / sacctmgr load) — export and import association metadata (Clusters, Accounts, Users, QOS, Parent relationships) to/from a human-editable cfg-style file for copying or restoring configuration.

I’ll explain each workflow, important options, examples, and best-practices.

A — Accounting archive workflow (sacctmgr archive dump)
Purpose
- Export job/event/accounting records to a flat archive file so old accounting data can be kept offline and optionally removed from the live slurmdbd DB to reduce DB size.

Key behaviors and constraints
- Archive files are written on the slurmdbd host (the machine running slurmdbd).
- You can choose which record types to archive (Jobs, Events, etc.). If you request purge, the matching records are removed from the DB permanently — this cannot be rolled back.
- If you don’t specify specific options, slurmdbd.conf defaults (ArchiveDir, Purge settings) are used.
- Archive files are not overwritten: repeated archives create new files (older files are preserved).

Important options (common)
- Directory=path  — destination directory for the archive file (must be accessible on slurmdbd host).
- Jobs=yes|no, Events=yes|no  — decide which record types to archive.
- StartTime= / EndTime=  — time window for the archive.
- Purge= yes|no (or governed by PurgeJobAfter/PurgeEventAfter in slurmdbd.conf) — remove archived records from DB.

Example (conceptual)
- sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/var/lib/slurmdbd/archives Jobs=Yes Events=No StartTime=2023-01-01 EndTime=2023-12-31 Purge=Yes

What to check before running
- Confirm ArchiveDir and slurmdbd permissions.
- Verify you really want Purge=Yes; perform a non-purging dump first to inspect the file.
- Ensure you have a good DB backup (mysqldump/pg_dump) if you may need to recover.

B — Accounting restore workflow (sacctmgr archive load)
Purpose
- Load previously archived accounting files back into the slurmdbd DB.

Key behaviors and constraints
- The archive file must exist on the slurmdbd host.
- The load will not insert records that already exist in the DB; attempting to load the same archive twice will fail or report duplicate records.
- You can control SQL insertion behavior (Insert option) and other load options.
- Archive files from prior Slurm releases can be loaded, but validate compatibility for major version changes.

Important options (common)
- File=path  — archive file to load (on slurmdbd host).
- Insert=Yes|No  — control SQL INSERT vs other behavior (check man page for details).
- Other flags to control behavior (refer to your slurm version docs).

Example (conceptual)
- sacctmgr archive load File=/var/lib/slurmdbd/archives/cluster-archive-20231231.tar

Tips for loading
- Inspect the archive file before load to confirm contents.
- If restoring after a purge, ensure no conflicting records exist; the load will skip/complain on duplicates.
- Check slurmdbd logs for errors if load fails.

C — Association dump/load workflow (flat-file) — sacctmgr dump / sacctmgr load
Purpose
- Export cluster association metadata (Cluster, Parent, Account, User, QOS) into a readable cfg-style file and import it to create or reproduce associations in another DB/cluster.

Key behaviors and constraints
- Each dump file contains association data for a single cluster.
- Since v25.05 QOS data is included in the dump.
- The file format uses lines prefixed with the entity name (QOS, Cluster, Parent, Account, User) and colon-separated specs. Comments allowed with #.
- You must be a Slurm administrator or root to run dump/load.
- sacctmgr load will reconcile imported associations with existing DB entries. Use clean=... to remove/replace existing data if you want a fresh import.

Important options (common)
- sacctmgr dump cluster=<name> file=<file.cfg>
- sacctmgr load file=<file.cfg> [clean=account,qos,user] cluster=<new_name>
  - clean controls whether to delete existing cluster/accounts/qos/users before loading.

Examples
- Dump:
  - sacctmgr dump cluster=mycluster file=mycluster.cfg
- Load:
  - sacctmgr load file=mycluster.cfg
  - sacctmgr load file=mycluster.cfg clean=account,qos,user cluster=newclustername

Use cases
- Copying account/QOS setup from one cluster to another.
- Backing up accounting associations before DB maintenance.
- Re-creating cluster associations after a DB restore.

D — Recommended workflow and best-practices
- Always take a DB backup (mysqldump/pg_dump) before any destructive operation (purge/archive with Purge=Yes).
- For archiving: run a non-purging archive first (omit Purge or set Purge=No) to examine the produced archive file.
- Confirm archive files are stored in the configured ArchiveDir and have correct ownership/permissions for slurmdbd to read/write.
- Use time windows (StartTime/EndTime) to limit the archive scope and keep archive file sizes manageable.
- When loading archives, check for duplicates and version compatibility. Don’t load the same archive twice.
- For association loads, use clean= cautiously — it can remove existing accounts/QOS/users if requested.
- Monitor slurmdbd logs for errors during archive/load and check sacct/sacctmgr queries afterward to confirm expected records are present.

E — Troubleshooting pointers
- Missing file errors: ensure File/Directory path is on the slurmdbd host and readable by slurmdbd user.
- Duplicate-record errors on load: those records already exist in DB; use a DB backup/restore workflow if you need replacement.
- If archive/load fails with DB errors, check slurmdbd logs and DB server health.
- For format/questions, consult the sacctmgr man page (sacctmgr(8)) — the archive/dump/load sections describe all supported options and exact file formats.

If you want, I can:
- Show the exact man-page option snippets for your installed Slurm version (lookup_slurm_docs for specific flags), or
- Provide example sacctmgr commands tailored to your cluster names/paths (tell me cluster name and archive directory) — note: those would be suggestions only (no state change).

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr archive, dump, and load workflows
results.agent_response:
Summary — what each command does
- sacctmgr archive dump / sacctmgr archive load
  - Purpose: archive (export) historical accounting data (jobs, step events, cluster events) to files and later restore them into the SlurmDB (slurmdbd).
  - Typical use: move old job/event records out of the live DB to shrink/trim the DB, and later restore if needed.
- sacctmgr dump / sacctmgr load
  - Purpose: export and import association/metadata (Cluster, Account, Parent, User, QOS) as a flat text file for copying or restoring the accounting configuration.
  - Typical use: clone associations to a new cluster, backup/restore cluster-account-user-QOS configuration, or move config between clusters.

Key differences
- archive (dump/load) handles accounting history (job/event records). It is about data retention and purging.
- dump/load (flat-file) handles association metadata (clusters, accounts, users, QOS). It is about configuration transfer/backup.

Important behavior & options (practical notes)
- Permissions and host:
  - Both sacctmgr dump/load and archive operations must be run as a Slurm administrator (root or slurm admin).
  - Files referenced must be accessible from the slurmdbd host (not necessarily the machine where you run the command).
- archive dump
  - Writes accounting data to archive files. Use options to control what’s archived (Jobs, Events, Directory).
  - Archiving alone does not necessarily purge records — purge occurs only if you include purge options on the command or have PurgeJobAfter / PurgeEventAfter settings in slurmdbd.conf. The command text warns this operation cannot be rolled back once purge runs.
  - Directory= lets you choose where archive files are stored (otherwise slurmdbd.conf ArchiveDir applies).
  - Be careful: archive+purge permanently removes records from the live DB unless you later restore from the archive files.
- archive load
  - Loads previously archived accounting files back into the DB.
  - The loader will not re-import records that already exist; trying to load the same archive twice will result in an error/duplicate-record refusal.
  - Archive files from current or earlier Slurm releases can be loaded (normal version compatibility caveats apply).
  - File paths must resolve on the slurmdbd host.
- dump (flat-file)
  - Exports association data to a human-readable flat file. If file not specified, a default filename using the cluster name is created.
  - File format: lines starting with one of the titles QOS, Cluster, Parent, Account, or User followed by " - <entity> <specs>" with colon-separated specs; comments allowed with #. QOS info is included (newer Slurm versions).
  - Useful to move associations between clusters or to create a source-of-truth backup.
- load (flat-file)
  - Loads association flat files into the DB. By default the data is reconciled with existing DB entries (it will merge/reconcile).
  - Options:
    - file=<filename> — which file to load (must be on slurmdbd host).
    - clean=... — remove the existing cluster (and optionally account,qos,user) before loading if you want a fresh import. Use with caution.
    - Cluster=... — override the cluster name in the file if needed.
  - Must be run as an administrator.

Typical workflows (step-by-step patterns)
1) Backing up association config (flat-file)
   - sacctmgr dump <cluster-name> file=<cluster>.cfg
   - Store cluster.cfg off-host or in version control.
   - To restore or copy to another cluster: transfer the file to the target slurmdbd host and run sacctmgr load file=<cluster>.cfg (use clean=... only if you want to remove existing associations first).

2) Archiving old accounting data (safe trim of DB)
   - Verify slurmdbd.conf settings (ArchiveDir, PurgeJobAfter, PurgeEventAfter).
   - Run: sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/path/to/dir Jobs=Yes Events=Yes Purge=Yes (options depend on your desired time filters).
   - Confirm archive files were created under ArchiveDir (or Directory you set).
   - If Purge is used, the old records will be removed from the DB — keep the archive files in a safe place to enable later restore.

3) Restoring archived history
   - Ensure the archive file(s) are present on the slurmdbd host.
   - Run: sacctmgr archive load File=/path/to/archive-file
   - If some records already exist in DB, archive load will not insert duplicates and may error if you attempt to load the same archive twice—load only once per archive file unless you clean the DB of those records first.

Best practices and cautions
- Always back up your accounting DB and archive/flat files before destructive operations.
- Understand the difference: use dump/load for association metadata, archive dump/load for historical job/event data.
- Archive+purge is irreversible for the live DB unless you have the archive files; keep those files and verify successful creation.
- Run archive/dump during low-load windows if possible and ensure sufficient disk space in ArchiveDir.
- When moving associations between clusters, check the file format and the ordering (clusters should exist or be created; sacctmgr load reconciles but read docs about clean= behavior).
- Test load on a staging DB if possible, especially when using clean= or when importing large archive files.

Useful quick examples
- Export associations: sacctmgr dump mycluster file=mycluster.cfg
- Import associations: sacctmgr load file=mycluster.cfg
- Archive accounting (example skeleton): sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/archive/path Jobs=Yes Events=Yes Purge=Yes
- Restore archived accounting: sacctmgr archive load File=/archive/path/archive-file

References
- See sacctmgr(1) archive, dump, and load documentation in the Slurm manual for full option lists and exact syntax.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact sacctmgr command examples with commonly-used option names and sample flags, or
- walk through a safe test plan (backup → dump → archive+purge → verify → restore) tailored to your slurmdbd.conf and retention policy. Which would you like?

results.prompt: Explain sacctmgr archive, dump, and load workflows
results.agent_response:
Short overview — two related but different sacctmgr file workflows

- sacctmgr dump / load (flat-file dump/load)
  - Purpose: export and import accounting associations (Cluster, Account, User, Parent, QOS) — essentially the accounting configuration.
  - Typical use cases: copy association setup from one cluster to another, back up account/QOS/user associations, rebuild associations after DB restore.
  - Command family: sacctmgr dump ... and sacctmgr load file=<file>
  - File format: human-readable flat file where each line begins with one of the titles (Cluster, Account, User, Parent, QOS) followed by entity and colon-separated specs. Comments allowed with #. (QOS included beginning v25.05.)
  - Important notes:
    - Must be run as Slurm administrator/root.
    - When loading, records are reconciled with existing ones (load will not blindly duplicate). There is a clean option (clean=...) to remove existing cluster/associations/account/qos/user entries before import if you want to start fresh.
    - Order matters conceptually: clusters should exist before accounts, and accounts before users; sacctmgr load reconciles but you should still prepare files or use clean appropriately.
    - If no file argument to dump, a filename defaulting to <clustername>.cfg is generated.

- sacctmgr archive dump / archive load (accounting archive)
  - Purpose: export historical accounting data (jobs, events) to archive files and optionally remove (purge) those records from the slurmdbd DB; and later re-import archived accounting data.
  - Typical use cases: offload old job/event rows to archive files to shrink the active DB, transfer archived history to another slurmdbd, or temporarily purge old records.
  - Command family: sacctmgr archive dump <options> and sacctmgr archive load file=<file>
  - Key options (common/important):
    - Directory= — where to write/read archive files (must be accessible on the slurmdbd host).
    - Jobs=, Events= — which data types to include in the archive.
    - Purge-related options: archive dump will only remove rows if a corresponding purge option is specified (or configured via slurmdbd.conf PurgeJobAfter/PurgeEventAfter). Be careful: the dump+purge operation cannot be rolled back.
    - File parameter to point to a specific archive file for load.
    - Archive files from current or prior Slurm releases may be loaded.
  - Important notes:
    - The archive file must be present on the slurmdbd host (not necessarily your local shell).
    - archive load will refuse to load records that already exist in the DB (it does not silently duplicate). If you try to load the same archive twice you’ll get errors for duplicate records.
    - slurmdbd can be configured to create archive files automatically; manual sacctmgr archive dump should be used only when you understand the purge consequences.
    - archive dump is irreversible once purged — keep backups of archive files.

Suggested workflows and examples

1) Back up / move associations (dump → transfer → load)
- On source cluster (admin/root):
  - sacctmgr dump cluster=<clustername> file=/tmp/cluster-assoc.cfg
- Transfer the file to the destination slurmdbd host.
- On destination cluster (admin/root):
  - Option A — merge into existing DB:
    - sacctmgr load file=/path/cluster-assoc.cfg
  - Option B — replace cluster associations for a named cluster:
    - sacctmgr load file=/path/cluster-assoc.cfg clean=cluster
    - Or to remove accounts/qos/users as well: clean=cluster,account,qos,user
- Verify with sacctmgr list or sacctmgr show commands.

2) Archive old accounting data (archive dump), with optional purge
- Decide retention and archive directory configured or passed.
- Manual archive-only (no purge):
  - sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/archive/path Jobs=Yes Events=No
  - This writes archive files but does not remove DB rows unless purge options or slurmdbd.conf purge settings are used.
- Archive + purge (destructive):
  - sacctmgr archive dump Directory=/archive/path Jobs=Yes PurgeJobAfter=now-365days
  - Or rely on slurmdbd.conf PurgeJobAfter/PurgeEventAfter settings (check them first).
  - IMPORTANT: this can’t be rolled back after purging; ensure archive files are safely copied off the slurmdbd host before or immediately after.
- Confirm produced files in the Directory and check their timestamps/content.

3) Restore archived accounting (archive load)
- Make sure the archive file is on the slurmdbd host and accessible.
- sacctmgr archive load File=/archive/path/archivefile
- If records already exist the load will not insert duplicates and will report errors for duplicates — load is intended to restore data not to re-ingest the same history repeatedly.

Practical tips, checks, and safety
- Always run these commands as a Slurm admin/root.
- Check slurmdbd.conf for ArchiveDir, PurgeJobAfter, PurgeEventAfter before running archive dump; automated purging may already be configured.
- For any destructive purge, copy/archive the generated archive files to a safe backup location first.
- Test loads on a staging DB if you must validate import behavior (especially when migrating clusters).
- Use sacctmgr dump/load for configuration (associations) and sacctmgr archive dump/load for historical accounting records — don’t confuse the two.
- Read the sacctmgr man page or the sacctmgr archive and dump/load sections before running in production; there are additional options (Insert, clean, etc.) that affect behavior and recovery.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact sacctmgr subcommand syntax for your current Slurm docs (I can fetch the relevant man snippets), or
- prepare a safe step-by-step runbook for an archive+purge operation tailored to your slurmdbd.conf settings (I’d first read your slurmdbd.conf ArchiveDir/Purge settings).

## ARCHIVE FUNCTIONALITY[#SECTION_ARCHIVE-FUNCTIONALITY](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sacctmgr.html)
Sacctmgr has the capability to archive to a flatfile and or load that
data if needed later. The archiving is usually done by the slurmdbd
and it is highly recommended you only do it through sacctmgr if you
completely understand what you are doing. For slurmdbd options see
"man slurmdbd" for more information.
Loading data into the database can be done from these files to either
view old data or regenerate rolled up data.
For information about configuring an archive server see
<[https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html#archive](https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html)>.

results.prompt: Explain sbatch mail notification options
results.agent_response:
Summary — what controls job email
- Two sbatch options: --mail-user=<addr> (who gets the mail) and --mail-type=<types> (which events trigger mail).
- You can set them on the sbatch command line or inside a batch script with #SBATCH lines. Command-line options override environment variables, which override #SBATCH lines in a script.
- Mail delivery uses the Slurm MailProg / configuration on the cluster; if no MailProg is configured mail may not be sent.

Flags and usage
- --mail-user=address
  - Example: --mail-user=alice@example.edu
  - Sets the email recipient. If not given, mail normally goes to the submitting user’s account (unless the site admin has changed defaults).
- --mail-type=type[,type...]
  - Provide one or more comma-separated event types. Example: --mail-type=END,FAIL

Common mail-type values and what they mean
- BEGIN — send mail when the job allocation begins (job starts running).
- END — send mail when the job terminates normally (job finished).
- FAIL — send mail when the job fails (non-zero exit, killed, etc.).
- REQUEUE — send mail when the job is requeued.
- ALL — shorthand to request mail for all supported events.
- ARRAY_TASKS — for job arrays: send mail for each individual task (rather than only the array master).
- STAGE_OUT — send mail when staged output is completed (used with burst buffers/stage-out features).
- TIME_LIMIT — notifications related to job time limits (warnings/notifications).
- TIME_LIMIT_90 (and other TIME_LIMIT_<N>) — a warning when the job reaches a percentage of its time limit (90% is common).
- STOP — send mail when the job is stopped (scontrol stop or similar).

Notes and tips
- Pick only the events you need to avoid email spam (e.g., --mail-type=END,FAIL is common).
- For job arrays, ARRAY_TASKS is useful to get per-task notifications. Without it, you may only get mail for the array master.
- Use full email addresses with --mail-user to ensure external delivery.
- If you see no mail even though options are set, check with your admin whether MailProg and MailType are configured in slurm.conf and whether outbound mail from compute nodes is allowed.

Examples
- In a script:
  #SBATCH --mail-user=alice@example.edu
  #SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
- On the command line:
  sbatch --mail-user=alice@example.edu --mail-type=BEGIN,END myscript.sh

If you want, I can paste the exact manpage text or show full example scripts.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text

```

```text

```

Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.

procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Explain sbatch mail notification options
results.agent_response:
Summary
- sbatch supports two related options to send email about job events:
  - --mail-user=<user@host> (or #SBATCH --mail-user=...) — destination address(es).
  - --mail-type=<TYPE[,TYPE...]> (or #SBATCH --mail-type=...) — which events trigger mail.

Common usage
- In a batch script:
  #SBATCH --mail-user=alice@example.com
  #SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
- On the command line:
  sbatch --mail-user=alice@example.com --mail-type=END,FAIL myjob.sh

mail-type basics
- Accepts a comma-separated list of event names.
- Typical event names: BEGIN (job started), END (job finished), FAIL (job failed), REQUEUE (job requeued).
- ALL requests all supported notifications; NONE disables notifications.
- Many Slurm releases also provide additional types (for example, time-limit warnings such as TIME_LIMIT or percent warnings like TIME_LIMIT_90, and other events). Check your sbatch man page for the complete set available on your system.

mail-user and defaults
- If you set mail-type but do not set mail-user, mail is sent to the submitting user’s default address.
- You may list multiple addresses (comma-separated) depending on site config.

Precedence / where to set
- You can specify options in the script with #SBATCH directives, via environment variables (SBATCH_*), or on the sbatch command line.
- Command-line options override environment variables; environment variables override #SBATCH lines in a script.

Notes
- The controller sends the messages when the corresponding event occurs; content and formatting are controlled by Slurm and site mail configuration.
- If you need exact mail-type names supported on your cluster, check the sbatch man page (man sbatch) because available types can vary by Slurm version and site configuration.

results.prompt: Explain sbatch mail notification options
results.agent_response:
sbatch provides two options to control e‑mail notifications for a job:

- --mail-user=ADDRESS
  - Set the destination e‑mail address for notifications (example: --mail-user=you@example.com).
  - Can be given on the sbatch command line or as a #SBATCH directive in the job script.

- --mail-type=TYPE[,TYPE...]
  - Select which job events trigger an e‑mail. Multiple events are provided as a comma‑separated list.
  - Common event types you will see documented and can use include: BEGIN, END, FAIL, REQUEUE, ALL, NONE, ARRAY_TASKS, TIME_LIMIT, STAGE_OUT, NODE_FAIL.
    - BEGIN: send when the job allocation starts.
    - END: send when the job finishes normally.
    - FAIL: send when the job fails (non‑zero exit or other failure conditions).
    - REQUEUE: send when the job is requeued.
    - TIME_LIMIT: send when the job reaches (or is about to reach, depending on configuration) its time limit.
    - ARRAY_TASKS: send notifications for individual array tasks rather than only the master array job.
    - ALL: shorthand for getting notifications for all (or most) events.
    - NONE: disable notifications (or omit --mail-type to get no mail).
    - STAGE_OUT / NODE_FAIL: other system/cluster-specific events may be available on some installs.
  - Use e.g. --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL to get mail at start, successful end, and failure.

Examples:
- sbatch --mail-user=you@example.com --mail-type=END myscript.sh
- In a script:
  #SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
  #SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL

Notes and caveats:
- The cluster’s mail/send subsystem (sendmail/postfix or similar) must be configured; if the admin has disabled mail or the MTA is misconfigured you may not receive mail.
- Exact mail‑type token availability and any additional types (or short‑hands) are determined by your Slurm version/configuration; check your system’s sbatch manpage or the sbatch documentation for the full, authoritative list for your cluster.

results.prompt: Explain sbatch mail notification options
results.agent_response:
sbatch supports a small set of mail-related options you use to tell Slurm when to send job-status email and where to send it.

How to set them
- On the sbatch command line:
  - --mail-user=<address>
  - --mail-type=<type>[,<type>...]
- In a batch script use #SBATCH directives:
  - #SBATCH --mail-user=you@example.com
  - #SBATCH --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL
- Environment variables are also supported (e.g., SBATCH_MAIL_USER, SBATCH_MAIL_TYPE). Note the precedence: command-line options override environment variables, and environment variables override #SBATCH directives in the script.

Common mail-type values and meaning
- NONE — do not send any mail.
- BEGIN — send mail when the job begins (allocation granted / job started).
- END — send mail when the job finishes (regardless of success/failure).
- FAIL — send mail when the job fails (abnormal exit/failed).
- REQUEUE — send mail if the job is requeued.
- ALL — shorthand to request all the common notifications (convenience alias).
- TIME_LIMIT / TIME_LIMIT_xx (percent thresholds) — send warning when job is approaching its time limit (clusters may provide variants like TIME_LIMIT_90 etc.; exact names available in your Slurm docs/config).
- ARRAY_TASKS — affects array-element notifications (send per-array-element notices).

Usage notes and tips
- You can supply multiple types as a comma-separated list (e.g., --mail-type=BEGIN,END,FAIL).
- Use --mail-user to give one or more recipient addresses (site policy may affect allowed formats).
- Email notifications depend on MTA/configuration on your cluster; administrators can disable or alter mail delivery.
- For job arrays, use the array-specific mail-type (or ARRAY_TASKS) to control element-level messages.
- If you need fine-grained control beyond these built-in events, consider writing a small wrapper in your batch script to send mail (mailx, sendmail, curl to an alert webhook) at any programmatic point.

If you want, I can show exact --mail-type tokens supported on your cluster (and any cluster-specific behavior) — ask and I’ll look them up in your Slurm docs/config.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote

in a denial of service.

procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## System Administration [#administration](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A new configuration parameter has been added to control the maximum
job array size: MaxArraySize . The smallest index that can be specified
by a user is zero and the maximum index is MaxArraySize minus one.
The default value of MaxArraySize is 1001.
The maximum MaxArraySize supported in Slurm is 4000001.
Be mindful about the value of MaxArraySize as job arrays offer an easy way
for users to submit large numbers of jobs very quickly.
The sched/backfill plugin has been modified to improve performance with
job arrays. Once one element of a job array is discovered to not be runnable
or impact the scheduling of pending jobs, the remaining elements of that job
array will be quickly skipped.

## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been
reached in the script, no more #SBATCH directives will be processed. See example
below.

## NODE CONFIGURATION[#SECTION_NODE-CONFIGURATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The configuration of nodes (or machines) to be managed by Slurm is
also specified in /etc/slurm.conf .
Changes in node configuration (e.g. adding nodes, changing their
processor count, etc.) require restarting or reconfiguring all slurmctld
and slurmd daemons.
All slurmd daemons must know each node in the system to forward
messages in support of hierarchical communications.
Only the NodeName must be supplied in the configuration file.
All other node configuration information is optional.
It is advisable to establish baseline node configurations,
especially if the cluster is heterogeneous.
Nodes which register to the system with less than the configured resources
(e.g. too little memory), will be placed in the "DOWN" state to
avoid scheduling jobs on them.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.
