## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## Preemption Design and Operation [#operation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html)
The SelectType plugin will identify resources where a pending job can
begin execution. When PreemptMode is configured to CANCEL ,
SUSPEND or REQUEUE , the select plugin will also preempt running
jobs as needed to initiate the pending job. When
PreemptMode=SUSPEND,GANG the select plugin will initiate the pending
job and rely upon the gang scheduling logic to perform job suspend and resume,
as described below.
The select plugin is passed an ordered list of preemptable jobs to consider for
each pending job which is a candidate to start.
This list is sorted by either:
- QOS priority,
- Partition priority and job size (to favor preempting smaller jobs), or
- Job start time (with PreemptParameters=youngest_first ).

```text
function slurm_job_submit(req, partitions, uid)

return check_qos(req, desc)

function check_qos(req, desc)
local qos = read_str_field(req, desc, "qos")
if qos == "premium" then
slurm.log_user('premium job disabled at present, please use regular')
return slurm.ERROR
end
local user_balance, acct_balance, cost_est
user_balance = get_user_balance(job, desc)
cost_est = get_cost_estimate(job, desc)
if user_balance < cost_est then
req['qos'] = 'scavenger'
end
return slurm.SUCCESS
end
function read_str_field(req, desc, field)
local value = ""
if desc ~= nil and desc[field] ~= nil then
value = desc[field]
end
if req ~= nil and req[field] ~= nil then
value = req[field]
end
return value
end
```

- Added new “Expedited Requeue” mode for batch jobs. Batch jobs with –requeue=expedite will automatically requeue on node failure, or if the batch script returns a non-zero exit code and one or more Epilog scripts fail. Expedited requeue jobs are eligible to restart immediately, are treated as the highest priority job in the system, and their previously allocated set of nodes will be prevented from launching other work.

### Task Data[#task](https://slurm.schedmd.com/hdf5_profile_user_guide.html)
JobAcctGatherType =jobacct_gather/linux
is required in slurm.conf to collect task data.
Appropriately set task=freq in either JobAcctGatherFrequency in slurm.conf
or in --acctg-freq on the command line.
Each data sample in the Task Time Series contains the following data
items.
Date Time
Time of day at which the data sample was taken. This can be used to
correlate activity with other sources such as logs.
Time
Elapsed time since the beginning of the step.
CPU Frequency
CPU Frequency at time of sample.
CPU Time
Seconds of CPU time used during the sample.
CPU Utilization
CPU Utilization during the interval.
RSS
Value of RSS at time of sample.
VM Size
Value of VM Size at time of sample.
Pages
Pages used in sample.
Read Megabytes
Number of megabytes read from local disk.
Write Megabytes
Number of megabytes written to local disk.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## NODE CONFIGURATION[#SECTION_NODE-CONFIGURATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The configuration of nodes (or machines) to be managed by Slurm is
also specified in /etc/slurm.conf .
Changes in node configuration (e.g. adding nodes, changing their
processor count, etc.) require restarting or reconfiguring all slurmctld
and slurmd daemons.
All slurmd daemons must know each node in the system to forward
messages in support of hierarchical communications.
Only the NodeName must be supplied in the configuration file.
All other node configuration information is optional.
It is advisable to establish baseline node configurations,
especially if the cluster is heterogeneous.
Nodes which register to the system with less than the configured resources
(e.g. too little memory), will be placed in the "DOWN" state to
avoid scheduling jobs on them.

The partition configuration permits you to establish different job
limits or access controls for various groups (or partitions) of nodes.
Nodes may be in more than one partition, making partitions serve
as general purpose queues.
For example one may put the same set of nodes into two different
partitions, each with different constraints (time limit, job sizes,
groups allowed to use the partition, etc.).
Jobs are allocated resources within a single partition.
Default values can be specified with a record in which
PartitionName is "DEFAULT".

When a GRES has a type associated with it and a limit is applied
over this specific type (e.g. MaxTRESPerUser=gres/gpu:tesla=1 ) if a
user requests a generic gres, the type's limit will not be enforced. In this

become useful. For example, if one requests --gres=gpu:2 having a

slurm.conf is an ASCII file which describes general Slurm
configuration information, the nodes to be managed, information about
how those nodes are grouped into partitions, and various scheduling
parameters associated with those partitions. This file should be
consistent across all nodes in the cluster.

and partitions. Any text following a "#" in the configuration file is treated
as a comment through the end of that line.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

Summary (live data)
- sshare (fairshare): account=research, user=alice, RawShares=0.600, NormShares=0.420, EffectvUsage=1.800.
- sprio (per-job priority rows): "No pending jobs match the filter." — there are currently no pending jobs for alice to show a per-job priority breakdown.
- Configured multifactor weights: PriorityWeightAge=1000, PriorityWeightFairshare=10000, PriorityWeightJobSize=100, PriorityWeightPartition=500, PriorityWeightQOS=1000.

What those sshare fields mean (brief)
- RawShares: the configured share weight assigned to alice (0.600).
- NormShares: that raw share normalized against other accounts/users (0.420) — this is her entitlement fraction used in fairshare calculations.
- EffectvUsage: the recent scaled usage (1.800) that Slurm uses to compare against NormShares when computing the fairshare factor.

Interpretation for alice
- Alice’s EffectvUsage (1.800) is substantially higher than her NormShares (0.420). Ratio ≈ 1.800 / 0.420 ≈ 4.3 — she has used about 4.3× her normalized share in the usage window.
- The fairshare factor (a value between 0.0 and 1.0 used by the Multifactor plugin) is derived from this comparison: users who have used significantly more than their entitlement get a much smaller fairshare factor, which reduces job priority; users who have used less get a factor closer to 1.0, increasing priority.
- Because PriorityWeightFairshare=10000 (the largest weight), the fairshare factor is the dominant term in the job-priority sum. In the priority formula:

results.prompt: Explain scheduler health using diagnostics, controller ping, and queue pressure
results.agent_response:
Good question — "scheduler health" is best judged by three complementary views: slurmctld responsiveness (scontrol ping), internal scheduler diagnostics (sdiag), and live queue pressure (squeue/sinfo + priority). Below is a compact checklist of what each tool shows, what to look for, and what to do when you see problems.

1) Controller responsiveness — scontrol ping
- What it does: simple RPC test to slurmctld. Returns a quick success/pong or times out/fails.
- How to run: scontrol ping
- What to watch for:
  - Success with low latency: controller reachable and accepting RPCs.
  - Timeouts/connection errors or very high latency: slurmctld overloaded, hung, or there are network/RPC problems.
- Immediate actions on failure: check slurmctld process, examine slurmctld logs (/var/log/slurmctld.log), check controllers’ CPU/memory, check network connectivity between clients and controller, verify slurmctld not blocked on I/O or DB calls.

2) Scheduler diagnostics — sdiag
- What it does: internal counters and timing for slurmctld — thread counts, scheduling cycles, backfill stats, jobs considered vs scheduled, cycle times, etc.
- How to run: sdiag --all
- Key fields to inspect and how to interpret them:
  - Server thread count: high number suggests heavy load (many concurrent RPCs/events).
  - Scheduling cycle counts and cycle times (min/avg/max): long or growing cycle times indicate the scheduler is taking longer each pass — symptomatic of overload, very large queue, or inefficient scheduling parameters.
  - Jobs evaluated / Jobs scheduled per cycle: low schedule rate with many jobs evaluated = difficulty matching resources (fragmentation, tight constraints).
  - Backfill statistics: many backfill blocks or failed backfills → backfill not effective (fragmentation, reservations, or mis-sized job windows).
  - Counters for rejected/failed scheduling attempts (if present): points to a recurring problem in placement logic or resource accounting.
- Notes: sdiag counters reset daily by default — compare to baseline. Use sdiag output to quantify whether the issue is chronic or sudden.

3) Queue pressure and per-job reasons — squeue, sinfo, sprio
- What to use:
  - squeue -o "%i %P %u %j %T %M %R" (or similar) to see job IDs, partition, user, name, state, elapsed/wait time, and REASON.
  - squeue --states=PD to list pending jobs and their REASON codes.
  - sinfo -Nel (or sinfo --Node) to check node counts and per-node resource availability.
  - sprio to show why jobs have a given priority (fairshare, age, QOS, partition).
  - sinfo_reasons to list nodes that are down/drained and their reasons.
- Key indicators of queue pressure:
  - High pending-to-running ratio or a growing backlog over time (queue depth).
  - Long job ages (many hours/days waiting).
  - REASON column values:
    - Resources (or ReqNodeNotAvail): insufficient matching resources → consider more capacity, adjusting job sizes, or enabling preemption/backfill.
    - Priority: low priority/fairshare/QOS → investigate sprio and association/QOS limits.
    - AssociationJobLimit / AssocGrp*Limit: account/association limits blocking jobs.
    - Dependency/StateDependent: user-submitted dependencies or holds.
  - Partition node counts: sinfo shows NODES(A/I/D). If I (idle) = 0 and many pending → capacity shortage. For GPU submissions treat only idle GPU nodes as eligible (allocated/mixed/down/drained do not count).
- Useful checks:
  - Longest-waiting jobs: identify heavy or stuck users/groups.
  - Growing backlog rate: compare squeue outputs over time or use monitoring graphs.
  - sprio output to see if fairshare or QOS is pushing jobs to the back.

4) Putting the three together — common problem signatures
- slurmctld unresponsive + sdiag shows rising cycle times/threads:
  - Likely controller overload. Check logs, CPU, memory, RPC counts, slurmdbd latency (if used).
- scontrol ping OK, sdiag healthy, but many Pending with REASON=Resources:
  - Cluster capacity problem or fragmentation. Actions: add nodes, reconfigure partition sizing, enable/improve backfill, encourage flexible requests (fewer strict node/GPU constraints).
- scontrol ping OK, sdiag shows fast cycles but many Pending with REASON=Priority or AssocLimit:
  - Policy/accounting configuration issue. Use sprio and sacctmgr to inspect limits/QOS/fairshare.
- sdiag shows many evaluated jobs but few scheduled per cycle:
  - Fragmentation or restrictive constraints. Consider packing policy changes, node feature labels, or job packing adjustments.
- Backfill is ineffective (backfill blocks/collisions):
  - Check job time estimates, backfill window configuration, reservations, or node fragmentation.

5) Practical commands to run when investigating
- scontrol ping
- sdiag --all
- squeue -o "%i %P %u %j %T %M %R" --states=PD,R
- sinfo -Nel
- sinfo_reasons
- sprio
- scontrol show config
- Check logs: tail -n 200 /var/log/slurmctld.log (on controller) and slurmdbd log if using accounting.

6) Recommended monitoring / alerts
- Alert if scontrol ping fails or latency jumps.
- Alert if scheduling cycle average time increases beyond normal baseline (e.g., sustained growth vs last week).
- Alert on sustained backlog growth (pending count rising for X minutes/hours).
- Alert on unusual REASON spikes (e.g., sudden jump in AssociationJobLimit or NodeDown reasons).

If you want, I can:
- Walk through interpreting a recent sdiag + squeue snapshot (paste outputs), or
- Run the key read-only checks (scontrol ping, sdiag, squeue, sinfo) against the live cluster and summarize findings.

Which would you like me to do?

results.prompt: Explain scheduler health using diagnostics, controller ping, and queue pressure
results.agent_response:
Short answer: use sdiag to measure scheduler behavior (cycle times, backfill efficiency, queue depth), scontrol ping to verify the controller is responsive and has low RPC latency, and squeue/sinfo/sprio to measure queue pressure and the reasons jobs are stuck. Combine those signals to decide whether the scheduler is healthy, overloaded, misconfigured, or blocked by resources/policy.

What each tool tells you
- sdiag
  - Purpose: scheduler diagnostics / health summary.
  - Key signals to read: scheduling cycle time (min/avg/max), backfill efficiency (percent), queue depth/backlog statistics, number of scheduling decisions, and any reported scheduling failures or long-running cycles.
  - Interpretation:
    - Low/short cycle times (milliseconds → single-digit seconds) and high backfill efficiency (close to 100%) usually mean the scheduler is keeping up and using idle resources well.
    - Rising average or max cycle times, wide variance, or many long cycles indicate slurmctld CPU/lock contention, heavy scheduling load, or pathological job patterns (very large numbers of small jobs, many small reservations).
    - Low backfill efficiency indicates idle capacity that the scheduler cannot use (often due to inaccurate time limits on running jobs, strict constraints, or complex placement policies).

- scontrol ping
  - Purpose: verify the controller (slurmctld) process is responsive to RPCs.
  - What to expect: a quick success response (typically sub-millisecond to low milliseconds on a healthy controller on the same LAN) or a failure/time-out if the controller is unreachable or overloaded.
  - Interpretation:
    - Successful, low-latency pings => controller responsive.
    - Increased latency (tens to hundreds of ms) or failed pings => network problems, slurmctld overloaded, or RPC backlog. Investigate slurmctld CPU, process state, system load, and network latency.
    - If ping fails, check slurmctld logs, system load, and whether slurmctld or munge crashed.

- squeue (and sinfo, sprio)
  - Purpose: measure queue pressure and why jobs are pending.
  - Useful queries:
    - squeue --states=PD,R to get counts and ages of pending/running jobs.
    - squeue -o "%i %u %t %M %S %R" to show jobID, user, state, time, submit/start time, and Reason.
    - squeue --states=PD -o "%i %u %M %R" | head to surface the oldest pending jobs and their Reason codes.
    - sinfo -Nel to see node states (idle/alloc/drain/down) and whether nodes are available to satisfy pending requests.
    - sprio to see whether backlog is due to priority/fairshare.
  - Key things to inspect:
    - Pending job counts and longest pending age: a small queue with short pending times is healthy; large backlogs and very old jobs indicate resource shortage or policy limits.
    - Pending reason codes: Resources (not enough nodes/gpus/cpus), QOS/Assoc limits (policy), License (no free license), PartitionDown/NodeDown, ReqNodeNotAvail, or Priority-related reasons all point to different fixes.
    - Whether many jobs are waiting for the same small set of resources (e.g., all want 8 GPUs on a specific partition) — that’s a resource mismatch, not necessarily scheduler fault.
    - sprio/sdiag/sshow to understand priority/fairshare impacts.

How to combine signals (triage logic)
- Controller responsiveness (scontrol ping)
  - If ping fails or is very slow → stop here: controller or network issue. Fix slurmctld, restore munge, or resolve network problems before other fixes.
- Scheduler internals (sdiag)
  - If sdiag shows long scheduling cycles and low backfill efficiency while controller ping is fine → slurmctld is overwhelmed (CPU, lock contention, pathological job patterns). Actions: raise slurmctld resources (CPU/cores), tune scheduling parameters (reduce expensive plugins or adjust scheduling interval), or investigate job submission patterns (coalesce very many tiny jobs).
  - If sdiag is healthy but queue is large → likely resource shortage or policy limits (not scheduler responsiveness). Check squeue reasons and sinfo.
- Queue pressure (squeue + sinfo + sprio)
  - If most pending jobs show Reason=Resources and sinfo reports few idle nodes → capacity problem. Consider adding nodes, changing partition sizing, or encouraging smaller jobs/more flexible requests.
  - If many jobs blocked by Assoc/Acct/QOS limits → adjust accounting or QOS policies.
  - If Reason=ReqNodeNotAvail or PartitionDown → resolve node health/reservations/drain states.
  - If Reason=License or GRES-related → check scontrol_license and apportioned licenses/gres availability.

Concrete checklist and commands to run (quick triage)
1. Verify controller reachable:
   - scontrol ping
   - If this fails/timeouts, check slurmctld, munge, system logs.
2. Get scheduler diagnostics:
   - sdiag
   - Look at scheduling cycle times, backfill efficiency, queue depth.
3. Inspect queue pressure:
   - squeue --states=PD -o "%i %u %t %M %S %R" | head
   - squeue --states=PD -O "jobid,name,user,prio,timeused,reason"
   - sinfo -Nel
   - sprio
4. Look for policy/resource blocks:
   - If squeue Reason shows AssociationJobLimit/AssocMax*Limit -> run sacctmgr show associations or sacctmgr list to inspect limits.
   - If licenses are implicated -> scontrol_license
5. If sdiag shows long cycles and scontrol ping is slow but squeue doesn’t indicate resource shortage:
   - Check slurmctld host CPU/memory, disk I/O, and slurmctld logs (/var/log/slurmctld.log).
   - Consider increasing slurmctld CPUs or tuning scheduler plugins and scheduling interval.

Common warning signs of unhealthy scheduler
- scontrol ping fails or has high latency.
- sdiag: average/max scheduling cycle time much larger than normal; rapidly growing queue depth; backfill efficiency dropping.
- squeue: sustained large pending backlog, many old pending jobs, pending reasons pointing to resources/policies rather than transient placement.
- sprio: priority starvation where fairshare/QOS causes large waits.
- Many node drains or frequent node state flaps visible in sinfo or sinfo_reasons.

Metrics to collect for longer investigation
- Regular sdiag snapshots (cycle times, backfill efficiency) over time.
- scontrol ping response times / failures.
- squeue pending counts and oldest pending age by partition/user.
- slurmctld host metrics: CPU, RSS, context switches, run queue, disk I/O, and network latency.
- slurmctld logs around times of long cycles or failures.

When to escalate to operator/admin
- scontrol ping fails or is inconsistent → immediate operator action.
- sdiag shows severe scheduler thrashing (very long cycles, scheduler loops) or persistent low backfill despite idle nodes → needs config or capacity change.
- Queue pressure caused by account/QOS/limits or license exhaustion → admin/policy change.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact commands to collect these fields in your environment, or
- run the read-only Slurm queries (scontrol ping, sdiag, squeue, sinfo, sprio) now and summarize live results.

Which would you like me to do next?

## Backfill Scheduling [#backfill](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sched_config.html)
The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and
responsiveness than otherwise possible.
Backfill scheduling will start lower priority jobs if doing so does not delay
the expected start time of any higher priority jobs.
Since the expected start time of pending jobs depends upon the expected
completion time of running jobs, reasonably accurate time limits are important
for backfill scheduling to work well.
Slurm's backfill scheduler takes into consideration every running job.
It then considers pending jobs in priority order, determining when and where

results.prompt: Explain scheduler health using diagnostics, controller ping, and queue pressure
results.agent_response:
High level: use three quick checks together to tell whether the scheduler is healthy, why jobs are stuck, and whether the scheduler itself is the bottleneck.

1) What each tool shows and why it matters
- scontrol ping
  - Purpose: basic liveness/latency check for the controller (slurmctld).
  - What to expect: a short affirmative reply (commonly "slurmctld: OK") with low RTT.
  - Interpretation: a successful, low-latency ping means the controller process is reachable. a failed/timeout or high latency suggests slurmctld is unhealthy, overloaded, or network/IPC problems; fix the controller before blaming scheduling policy.

- sdiag
  - Purpose: scheduler diagnostics — scheduling cycle stats, backfill behavior, and queue/scheduling throughput.
  - Key metrics to read:
    - scheduling cycle time (median/mean or recent cycle latency): how long each scheduling pass takes.
    - queue/depth or jobs considered per cycle: how many jobs the scheduler must examine.
    - backfill statistics (efficiency, time saved): how effectively the scheduler fills gaps.
    - counts of fast vs slow scheduling decisions (if present).
  - Interpretation:
    - Normal: short cycle times (milliseconds–low hundreds ms depending on cluster size), steady queue depth, decent backfill utilization.
    - Warning: sustained long cycle times (seconds or repeatedly high) or growing queue depth → scheduler is CPU-bound or overwhelmed with decisions.
    - Low backfill efficiency + many idle nodes → fragmentation or policy mismatch (jobs can’t be placed although capacity exists).

- queue pressure (squeue + sinfo)
  - Purpose: operational view of demand and blocking reasons.
  - Important checks:
    - pending job count and age distribution (how many are pending, how long they’ve waited).
    - per-job Pending Reason field (Resources, QOSLimit, Priority, Dependency, PartitionDown, NodeNotAvail, etc.).
    - partition/node availability and states (sinfo) — drained/down nodes reduce effective capacity.
    - ratio of RUNNING : IDLE nodes, and whether many nodes are in state MIXED/ALLOCATED.
  - Interpretation:
    - Many short-lived pending jobs or very large bursts can cause scheduler thrash.
    - If many jobs pending with reason=Resources and sinfo shows idle nodes, that suggests placement fragmentation or mismatched resource requests (e.g., exclusive node requests, GRES mismatch).
    - If reason=QOSLimit/AssocMax*Limit, it’s an accounting/quota issue, not scheduler cycles.
    - If reason=PartitionDown/NodeDown, capacity is reduced and you need node repair/resume.

2) How to combine the three to diagnose common problems
- Controller-down symptoms
  - scontrol ping fails → do not trust sdiag/squeue. Remedy: check slurmctld service, controller logs, node connectivity.
- Scheduler overloaded (backlog)
  - scontrol ping OK, sdiag shows long scheduling cycle times and increasing queue depth, and squeue shows growing pending job counts (especially many short jobs or many submissions).
  - Interpretation: scheduler can’t keep up with decision volume. Actions: throttle submissions (QOS/submit limits), increase scheduling resources (CPU/threads for slurmctld if supported), tune sched_config, or reduce job churn.
- Capacity mismatch / fragmentation
  - scontrol ping OK, sdiag cycle times normal, but squeue shows many pending jobs with reason=Resources while sinfo shows some idle nodes.
  - Interpretation: placement fragmentation, GRES/feature mismatch, or jobs request exclusive nodes/too-large resources. Actions: review requested resources, relax exclusivity, enable node sharing, or change partition config.
- Policy/accounting limits
  - Many jobs pending with reason=QOSLimit/Assoc*Limit and sprio/sshare show users/accounts exhausted.
  - Interpretation: enforce/adjust QOS or account limits, or grant temporary exceptions.
- Backfill problems
  - sdiag shows very low backfill efficiency and squeue shows small holes in node allocations.
  - Interpretation: either backfill window too small or job sizes/constraints produce fragmented free space. Actions: tune backfill parameters, allow smaller backfill windows, enable more flexible placement.

3) Practical checklist & commands to collect evidence
- Quick liveness
  - scontrol ping
    - Expect OK; capture any latency or error.
- Scheduler diagnostic snapshot
  - sdiag
    - Save the scheduling cycle times, queue depth, and backfill stats.
- Queue pressure snapshot
  - squeue --states=PENDING,RUNNING -o "%.18i %.30j %.8u %.10T %.10M %.10R"
    - Look at counts, Pending Reason, job age.
  - sinfo -R or sinfo -Nel
    - See nodes in down/drain and node reasons (sinfo_reasons if available).
- Priority/fairshare
  - sprio (and sshare) to see whether priority/fairshare is holding jobs.
- If scontrol ping fails
  - Check slurmctld logs (usually /var/log/slurmctld.log) and system service status on controller host.

4) Quick triage playbook (what to do first)
- If scontrol ping fails: isolate controller, check slurmctld, network, restart controller only after review of logs.
- If sdiag shows high cycle time: collect sdiag repeatedly (to see trends), capture slurmctld CPU/memory usage, and consider submission throttles or slurmctld resource increase.
- If squeue shows many pending + sinfo shows idle nodes: inspect Pending Reasons, job resource requests, and node feature/GRES labels.
- If many jobs blocked by limits: inspect QOS/account associations (sacctmgr/sreport) and adjust limits or grant exceptions.

5) What “healthy” looks like (concise)
- scontrol ping: responsive, low latency.
- sdiag: short scheduling cycle times for cluster size, stable queue depth, reasonable backfill efficiency.
- squeue/sinfo: pending counts small or short-lived, pending reasons meaningful (not dominated by Resources with idle nodes), few nodes down/drained.

If you want, I can:
- run the three checks now (scontrol ping, sdiag, squeue + sinfo) and summarize live health and concrete fields to act on, or
- give a short template of exact commands and parsing snippets to automate ongoing health monitoring.

Which would you prefer?

results.prompt: Explain relevant Slurm configuration for scheduling and accounting
results.agent_response:
Good question — scheduling and accounting are tightly linked in Slurm. Below is a concise, actionable overview of the most relevant slurm.conf / slurmdbd / sacctmgr settings and where they interact, plus checks and common pitfalls.

High-level components
- slurmctld (scheduler): governed by slurm.conf and priority plugin settings.
- slurmd (node agents): report usage and enforce cgroups.
- slurmdbd (accounting DB daemon): stores historical usage and is required for fairshare, age, and many accounting-based features.
- sacctmgr / sreport / sshare / sprio: admin tools to inspect and manage accounting, shares, and priorities.

Scheduling configuration (slurm.conf and plugins)
1. Priority plugin
- PriorityType
  - Common value: priority/multifactor — the Multifactor plugin composes priority from age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, site factors, and requested TRES.
- Priority weights (how factors combine)
  - PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
  - The composite job priority = site_factor + PriorityWeightAge*age_factor + PriorityWeightFairshare*fairshare_factor + ... (weights are numeric).
- PriorityFlags
  - Toggles behavior (examples: NO_FAIR_TREE to use classic fairshare, SMALL_RELATIVE_TO_TIME, etc.).
- PriorityDecayHalfLife
  - Controls decay of historical usage for fairshare. Example: 7-0 means a 7‑day half-life. 0 disables decay (requires other usage reset policy).
- PriorityCalcPeriod / PriorityUsageResetPeriod / PriorityMaxAge
  - Control recalculation cadence, when usage is reset, and the max age factor value.

2. Fairshare and accounting dependency
- Fairshare requires slurmdbd (AccountingStorage) and properly configured association shares.
- sacctmgr is used to set "Fairshare" (Share) values on accounts/users/associations.
- If you want fairshare-based scheduling, ensure AccountingStorageType points to slurmdbd and slurmdbd is running.

3. QOS and partition factors
- QOS definitions (sacctmgr) can set priorities, limits, preemption behavior, and priority caps.
- Partition factors and per-partition PriorityWeightPartition influence job order by partition.

4. Job size / age / nice / site factors
- PriorityFavorSmall (YES/NO) controls whether small jobs get more priority.
- Age factor grows while a job is eligible to run; PriorityMaxAge caps it.
- Site / job_submit plugins allow custom site_factor or submission-time modifications.

5. Preemption and backfill
- PreemptType / PreemptMode / PreemptExemptTime set how preemption works (requeue, suspend, preempt).
- Backfill: the scheduler supports backfilling; relevant settings live in scheduler plugin parameters (multifactor scheduling uses scheduler logic and backfill capability).

6. TRES-based weighting
- You can weight specific TRES (e.g., GPUs, CPUs) via TRES weights so jobs requesting expensive TRES are evaluated differently.

Accounting configuration (slurmdbd, slurm.conf, job accounting)
1. AccountingStorage
- slurm.conf keys:
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost / Port /User /Loc depending on DB backend
  - AccountingStorageEnforce: controls enforcement level on job submit (values like associations, all, nojobs, nosteps). Use to block submissions that violate associations/limits.
- slurmdbd.conf: DB connection settings, auth, and retention configuration.

2. Job usage collection and completion logging
- JobAcctGatherType (e.g., jobacct_gather/linux) and JobAcctGatherFrequency: configure how resource usage (RSS, maxrss, CPU) is gathered.
- JobCompType / JobCompLoc (job completion logging plugin) — where completion records are sent if not using slurmdbd.

3. sacctmgr associations, accounts, QOS
- Use sacctmgr to create accounts, users, set DefaultQOS, set Share/Fairshare, set limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.).
- Grp* limits are checked when considering starting jobs — these can block allocation if limits would be exceeded.
- DefaultQOS, QOSMaxJobs, QOSMaxSubmitJobs etc. control per-user/ per-account behavior.

4. Reporting and tools
- sshare shows fairshare and effective shares.
- sprio shows priority breakdown per job and the active weights.
- sreport generates accounting usage (CPU/GPU-hours) reports.
- sacct for historical job records; sacct requires accounting data (slurmdbd or jobcomp to storage).

Practical examples (typical lines)
- slurm.conf (examples)
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife=7-0
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityFavorSmall=YES
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost=slurmdbd.example.edu
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobAcctGatherFrequency=30
- sacctmgr (examples)
  - sacctmgr add account mygroup Cluster=clustername Description="Research group"
  - sacctmgr modify account mygroup set Fairshare=100
  - sacctmgr modify user alice set DefaultAccount=mygroup

Checks and diagnostics (read-only commands)
- scontrol show config — view current slurm.conf settings (PriorityType, AccountingStorageType, JobAcctGatherType).
- sprio -w — view current priority weights and plugin behavior.
- sshare -l — check fairshare allocation and recent usage.
- sdiag — scheduler diagnostics and backfill statistics.
- scontrol ping — check controller responsiveness.
- sacctmgr list associations — inspect accounts, shares, and limits.

Common pitfalls and recommendations
- Fairshare/age requires slurmdbd; without it fairshare/age factors are not computed.
- If PriorityDecayHalfLife is 0 you must manage usage resets (PriorityUsageResetPeriod).
- Changing slurm.conf requires restart or SIGHUP of slurmctld to take effect; slurmdbd config changes require restart of slurmdbd.
- AccountingStorageEnforce can block users unintentionally — test changes in a staging environment first.
- Ensure JobAcctGatherType is enabled and frequent enough to capture required metrics (increase frequency for finer accounting).
- When tuning weights, use sprio and sshare to observe results and iterate: small changes to PriorityWeightFairshare can have large effects.

If you want, I can:
- Show the cluster’s current config snippets (scontrol show config) and priority/fairshare state (sprio, sshare) to make concrete recommendations.  
- Or provide a sample minimal slurm.conf + slurmdbd.conf snippet for a typical research cluster tuned for fairshare.

Which would you like next?

pathname. These modifiers would be replaced with cluster name or other
information depending on which modifier is specified. If the included file
is not an absolute path name (i.e. it does not start with a slash), it will
searched for in the same directory as the slurm.conf file.

EXAMPLE

```text
ClusterName=linux include /home/slurm/etc/%c_config # Above line interpreted as # "include /home/slurm/etc/linux_config"
```

The following slurm.conf parameters are used to configure the Multifactor Job
Priority Plugin. See slurm.conf(5) man page for more details.
PriorityType
Set this value to "priority/multifactor" to enable the Multifactor Job
Priority Plugin.
PriorityDecayHalfLife
This determines the contribution of historical usage on the
composite usage value. The larger the number, the longer past usage
affects fair-share. If set to 0 no decay will be applied. This is helpful if
you want to enforce hard time limits per association. If set to 0
PriorityUsageResetPeriod must be set to some interval.
The unit is a time string (i.e. min, hr:min:00, days-hr:min:00, or
days-hr). The default value is 7-0 (7 days).

results.prompt: Explain relevant Slurm configuration for scheduling and accounting
results.agent_response:
Below is a focused, practical summary of the Slurm configuration knobs you should know when designing scheduling and accounting behavior. I organize it by purpose (scheduler, resource selection, enforcement & limits, accounting) and call out the related config names and where they live (slurm.conf vs slurmdbd.conf vs sacctmgr).

1) Where settings live
- slurm.conf — primary cluster config (scheduler type/parameters, partitions, select/plugin options, priority weights, AccountingStorage* entries that point at the accounting backend).
- slurmdbd.conf — Slurm Database Daemon configuration (only used if AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd).
- sacctmgr — CLI for creating accounts, users, QOS, associations and limits stored in the DB (used when slurmdbd is active).
- Job completion/gather plugins — configured in slurm.conf (JobAcctGatherType, JobCompType) and may also involve files/DB.

2) Scheduling: core slurm.conf options
- SchedulerType
  - e.g., SchedulerType=sched/backfill or sched/builtin. Controls which scheduling algorithm/backfill engine is used.
- SchedulerParameters
  - Plugin-specific flags that tune backfill, job sorting, or other scheduler internals (depends on SchedulerType).
- PreemptType and PreemptMode
  - Controls whether and how queued jobs may preempt running jobs (e.g., preempt/qos).
- FastSchedule
  - FastSchedule=1 reduces evaluation overhead for large clusters (tradeoff: slightly different scheduling semantics).
- DefMemPerCPU / DefMemPerNode
  - Defaults used by scheduler for memory accounting & resource fit decisions when jobs don’t specify memory.
- Partition-specific settings
  - Partition definitions in slurm.conf can include priority, max time, nodes, and attached Partition QOS. Partition-level limits can override association/QOS limits.

3) Priority (multifactor) and job ordering
- PriorityWeight* parameters (set in slurm.conf) when using priority/multifactor:
  - PriorityWeightAge — weight for job age
  - PriorityWeightFairshare — weight for historical fairshare
  - PriorityWeightJobSize — larger jobs can be favored or penalized
  - PriorityWeightQOS, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightTRES, etc.
  - These numeric weights are combined by the multifactor priority plugin to compute job priority.
- Fairshare
  - Fairshare data is maintained (via the DB) and influences scheduling when PriorityWeightFairshare > 0.
- QOS interaction
  - QOS attributes (priority, preemptible targets, limits) are defined with sacctmgr and are only applied for scheduling when multifactor priority and the relevant weights are enabled.

4) Resource selection and accounting granularity
- SelectType and SelectTypeParameters
  - e.g., SelectType=select/cons_res and SelectTypeParameters=CR_CPU_Memory (or CR_Core_Memory). Controls resource model (TRES-based vs older core-based).
- TRES (Trackable RESources)
  - TRES are used for CPU, GPU, memory, licenses, etc. Many QOS/accounting limits are expressed as TRES.
- Enforceable defaults
  - Accurate TRES and DefMemPerCPU help ensure the scheduler fits jobs correctly and accounting records useful data.

5) Backfill and scheduling policies
- Backfill is typically enabled with sched/backfill; SchedulerParameters tune backfill window and behavior.
- Backfill policy interacts with preemption and reservations. Use PreemptType and QOS to control preemption when needed.

6) Job completion / accounting gathering (plugins in slurm.conf)
- JobAcctGatherType
  - Commonly set to jobacct_gather/linux (gathers task-level memory/CPU info) or jobacct_gather/cgroup on systems using cgroups. This plugin produces per-job resource-usage info.
- JobAcctGatherFrequency
  - How often resource usage is polled by the gatherer (controls precision vs overhead).
- JobCompType
  - Controls where Job Completion records go: jobcomp/none, jobcomp/filetxt, jobcomp/slurmdbd, etc. If using slurmdbd, use jobcomp/slurmdbd or let the slurmdbd collect records.
- JobCompLoc / JobAcctGather parameters
  - File locations for jobcomp filetxt, or plugin-specific parameters.

7) Accounting backend and enforcement (AccountingStorage* in slurm.conf and slurmdbd.conf)
- AccountingStorageType
  - e.g., accounting_storage/slurmdbd (recommended for robust DB-backed accounting). Alternatives: accounting_storage/none, accounting_storage/filetxt, etc.
- AccountingStorageHost / AccountingStorageUser / AccountingStoragePort / AccountingStorageLoc / AccountingStoragePass
  - slurm.conf entries that point the controller to the database/slurmdbd.
- AccountingStorageEnforce
  - Controls enforcement at submission/allocation time. Options include associations, limits, qos, all, etc. If you need to block a job at submit-time for exceeding limits, enable the appropriate enforcement options.
- slurmdbd.conf
  - configures DB connection parameters (MySQL/MariaDB), archive/purge and credentials. SlurmDBD must be running on the host where slurmdbd.conf is present.

8) Associations, QOS and limits (sacctmgr-managed)
- sacctmgr entities: Account, User, QOS, Association
  - Use sacctmgr to create accounts and set association limits (MaxJobs, MaxSubmitJobs, GrpTRES, MaxTRESPerUser, MaxTRESPERUSER, etc.).
- QOS
  - Define per-QOS limits and priorities; QOS can also be attached to partitions (Partition QOS). QOS controls preemption sets when PreemptType=preempt/qos.
- Common limit fields
  - GrpTRES — group TRES limits (tested at allocation time),
  - MaxTRESPerUser / MaxTRESPERUSER — caps per-user TRES consumption,
  - MaxJobs / MaxSubmitJobs — limit concurrent or queued jobs.
- Enforcement semantics
  - Many limits are checked during job start; AccountingStorageEnforce can move some checks to submission time. Group/association limits are enforced at scheduling/allocation time so they can block job start when limits are reached.

9) Reporting and tools
- sacct — historical accounting (requires job completion info in DB or filetxt)
- sreport — usage reports (CPU/GPU hours by user/account/partition)
- sstat — live resource usage for running jobs
- sacctmgr — manage accounts, QOS, associations and view limits
- scontrol show config / scontrol ping — controller diagnostics

10) Operational notes & best practices
- Consistent user names/UIDs across clusters if sharing a SlurmDBD.
- Decide retention: configure slurmdbd archive/purge before DB grows too large.
- Tune JobAcctGatherFrequency and the gather plugin to balance overhead vs accuracy.
- Use AccountingStorageEnforce to decide whether limits should block submission or only allocation.
- Restart/HUP: many slurm.conf changes take effect only after restart or SIGHUP of slurmctld (slurmdbd likewise needs restart for slurmdbd.conf changes).
- Test QOS/association limits in a staging setup — enforcement behavior (submit-time vs start-time) can be subtle.
- Use select/cons_res + TRES for modern heterogeneous clusters (GPUs, licenses, burst buffers).

11) Example (representative slurm.conf lines)
- Scheduler setup
  - SchedulerType=sched/backfill
  - SchedulerParameters=bf_continue,interactivity
- Priority weights
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityWeightJobSize=100
- Accounting backend
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost=slurmdbd.example.org
  - AccountingStorageUser=slurm
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations,limits,qos
- Job accounting plugins
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobAcctGatherFrequency=30
  - JobCompType=jobcomp/slurmdbd

If you want, I can:
- show which of these settings are active on your cluster (I would call scontrol_show_config and scontrol_show_config or scontrol_ping / scontrol show config and slurmdbd info), or
- give a concrete example sacctmgr sequence to create accounts, QOS and limits for a sample project, or
- recommend a minimal working configuration for a GPU-enabled research cluster (tuning knobs and suggested values).

Which of those would you like me to do next?

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with
`GrpTRES` set to the desired resource limits.

Slurm offers two ways for a queued job to preempt a running job,
free-up the running job's resources and allocate them to the queued
job. See the [Preemption description](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) for
details.
The preemption method is determined by the "PreemptType"
configuration parameter defined in slurm.conf. When the "PreemptType"

results.prompt: Explain relevant Slurm configuration for scheduling and accounting
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact reference of the Slurm configuration knobs that are most relevant when you design scheduling policy and accounting. I include what each setting does, typical values or choices, and practical notes (what you must enable to get full accounting/fairshare behavior).

High-level picture
- Scheduling (slurmctld / slurm.conf): controls how jobs are prioritized/selected and when/backfill decisions are made (PriorityType, SchedulerType, SchedInterval, select/cons_res).
- Accounting (slurmdbd + slurm.conf + sacctmgr): records job completions and usage to a database, enforces association/QoS/limit policies, and enables reporting/fairshare state.
- Interaction: PriorityType can include fairshare; fairshare state is stored/updated in the accounting DB (SlurmDBD) so accurate fairshare requires accounting enabled.

Key scheduling-related slurm.conf parameters
- PriorityType
  - Defines which priority plugins are used (common plugins: priority/multifactor, priority/basic). Use multifactor to combine age, fairshare, job size, QOS, partition, etc.
  - Example: PriorityType=priority/multifactor
- Priority weights and tuning (when using multifactor)
  - PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife (controls how historical usage decays for fairshare), and PriorityFlags to tweak behavior (e.g., ignore certain classes).
  - Tuning notes: raise WeightFairshare to favor users with low historical usage; adjust decay half-life to control how quickly past usage becomes irrelevant.
- SchedulerType
  - Controls which scheduler implementation runs (e.g., sched/builtin or sched/backfill). Use sched/backfill to enable backfill behavior.
  - Example: SchedulerType=sched/backfill
- SchedInterval
  - How often the scheduler rebuilds the feasible set and reorders pending jobs (seconds). Shorter interval = more responsive but more CPU used by slurmctld.
- SelectType / SelectTypeParameters
  - Resource selection plugin (select/cons_res is common). SelectTypeParameters sets how allocation is done (e.g., CR_Core, CR_Socket, CR_CPU_Memory); important for correct packing and for TRES accounting.
- Preemption / Backfill / Topology
  - You can enable preemption plugins and backfill tuning via SchedulerType and SchedulerParameters. Preemption behavior is controlled by PreemptType/PreemptMode / associated QOS settings.
- Resource definitions that affect scheduling
  - NodeName / PartitionName: node sizes, CPUs, memory, GRES (GPUs) and partitions determine which jobs are eligible.
  - DefMemPerCPU, OverSubscribe and MaxCPUsPerNode influence packing and per-job resource limits.
- TRES (Trackable RESources)
  - Slurm uses TRES names (cpu, mem, gres/gpu, license, etc.) for limits, accounting and QOS. Define GRES on nodes (e.g., Gres=gpu:4) so GPUs are visible and charged.

Key accounting-related parameters (slurm.conf + slurmdbd.conf)
- AccountingStorageType
  - Tells slurmctld how to store accounting. Typical production configuration: AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd and run slurmdbd as middle tier into MySQL/MariaDB.
- AccountingStorageEnforce
  - Comma-separated enforcement options to require valid associations/limits at submission time (examples: associations and limits). Controls whether submissions are rejected or allowed to pend when they violate association/QoS/limit rules.
  - Use carefully: enabling strict enforcement can cause job submissions to be rejected if sacctmgr associations/limits are not configured.
- JobAcctGatherType (and gather plugin)
  - Controls how resource usage for running jobs is gathered (commonly jobacct_gather/linux). The gather plugin supplies per-job CPU, memory, I/O and GPU accounting used for billing/fairshare.
  - JobAcctGatherParams (plugin-specific) tune sampling frequency or enabled metrics.
- JobCompType
  - Where job completion records are sent. Use jobcomp/slurmdbd to write completion records into the accounting DB via slurmdbd.
- slurmdbd.conf (SlurmDBD)
  - DbdHost, StorageType (mysql/mariadb), StorageUser/StoragePass, LogFile, PurgeJobAfter, Archive options.
  - slurmdbd sits between slurmctld and the SQL DB; it is strongly recommended for security and scalability.
- sacctmgr (account/association/QoS setup)
  - To enable limits and enforcement you must create accounts, users, and associations with sacctmgr, and add QOS objects and limits (MaxWall, MaxTRESPerUser, GrpTRES, etc.).
- QOS and limits
  - QOS objects give per-QOS priorities and limits. QOS flags include DenyOnLimit (reject on submit if limits violated), EnforceUsageThreshold, and UsageThreshold.
  - Limits often use TRES names: MaxTRESPerUser, MaxTRESPerAccount, GrpTRES, etc.
- Fairshare / sshare
  - Fairshare state is stored in the accounting DB. Use sshare to view fairshare effective shares and historical usage. PriorityType must include fairshare and slurmdbd/accounting must be enabled for it to work correctly.
- Reporting and tools
  - sacct (historical job accounting), sreport (aggregated usage reports), sshare (fairshare view), sacctmgr (manage accounts/QoS/associations).

Minimal example (typical lines in slurm.conf)
- Scheduler/priority/accounting essentials:
  - SchedulerType=sched/backfill
  - SchedInterval=30
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
  - PriorityWeightAge=1000
  - SelectType=select/cons_res
  - SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core_Memory
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=associations,limits
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobCompType=jobcomp/slurmdbd

What you must do to enable functional accounting + fairshare
1. Install and configure slurmdbd and a SQL database (MySQL/MariaDB). Configure slurmdbd.conf with StorageType, StorageUser, StoragePass, and DbdHost.
2. Point slurmctld at slurmdbd: set AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd in slurm.conf.
3. Enable job accounting & job completion plugins: JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux and JobCompType=jobcomp/slurmdbd.
4. Use sacctmgr to create accounts, users, and associations and to define QOS objects and limits. If you want enforcement, set AccountingStorageEnforce appropriately.
5. Tune PriorityType weights and PriorityDecayHalfLife to shape fairshare behavior; use sshare to inspect fairshare allocations.

Practical tuning tips
- Start with moderate SchedInterval (20–60s) and increase scheduler interval only if slurmctld CPU usage is a problem.
- If backfill is valuable for utilization, enable SchedulerType=sched/backfill and test with realistic job mixes.
- Test AccountingStorageEnforce in “audit” mode first (don’t immediately reject jobs) so you can verify sacctmgr associations and limits are correct.
- Use QOS DenyOnLimit for strict control of runaway submissions; use EnforceUsageThreshold for automatic throttling before hard deny.
- For GPU clusters, ensure nodes declare GRES=gpu:N and that TRES accounting is configured so fairshare and limits count GPU hours.

Where to read more (official docs)
- slurm.conf reference and parameters (PriorityType, AccountingStorageEnforce, JobAcctGatherType, JobCompType, etc.): https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html
- slurmdbd.conf (database/back-end) reference: https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurmdbd.conf.html
- QOS and resource limits: https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html
- Accounting and reporting: https://slurm.schedmd.com/accounting.html

If you want, I can:
- Inspect your current cluster’s slurm.conf and slurmdbd.conf (read-only) and highlight the exact parameters you have set and what they mean; or
- Show the current accounting/fairshare state (ssh-less read) by calling scontrol_show_config, scontrol_ping, sshare, or sdiag and summarize recommended tuning changes.

Which of those would you like me to do next?

## RELOCATING CONTROLLERS[#SECTION_RELOCATING-CONTROLLERS](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
If the cluster's computers used for the primary or backup controller
will be out of service for an extended period of time, it may be
desirable to relocate them.
In order to do so, follow this procedure:
1. Stop the Slurm daemons on the old controller and nodes.
2. Modify the slurm.conf file appropriately.
3. Copy the files from the StateSaveLocation to the new controller or ensure
that they are accessible to the new controller via a shared drive.
4. Distribute the updated slurm.conf file to all nodes.
5. Restart the Slurm daemons on the new controller and nodes.
There should be no loss of any pending jobs. Any running jobs will get the
updated host info and finish normally.
Ensure that any nodes added to the cluster have the current
slurm.conf file installed.

primary controller...

## Configuration[#config](https://slurm.schedmd.com/resource_limits.html)
Scheduling policy information must be stored in a database
as specified by the AccountingStorageType configuration parameter
in the slurm.conf configuration file.
Information can be recorded in a [MySQL](http://www.mysql.com/) or
[MariaDB](https://mariadb.org/) database.
For security and performance reasons, the use of
SlurmDBD (Slurm Database Daemon) as a front-end to the
database is strongly recommended.
SlurmDBD uses a Slurm authentication plugin (e.g. MUNGE).
SlurmDBD also uses an existing Slurm accounting storage plugin
to maximize code reuse.
SlurmDBD uses data caching and prioritization of pending requests
in order to optimize performance.
While SlurmDBD relies upon existing Slurm plugins for authentication
and database use, the other Slurm commands and daemons are not required
on the host where SlurmDBD is installed.

results.prompt: Explain relevant Slurm configuration for scheduling and accounting
results.agent_response:
Below is a focused, practical summary of the Slurm configuration items that actually affect scheduling decisions and accounting. I describe what each option does, where it’s configured (slurm.conf vs slurmdbd.conf / sacctmgr), typical values/choices, and short guidance on how to use them together.

1) Where things live — the big picture
- slurm.conf (on controller and nodes): the central place for scheduler plugins and cluster/partition/node parameters that control how jobs are matched to resources and how priority is calculated.
- slurmdbd.conf + slurmdbd daemon + sacctmgr: the Slurm Database Daemon and DB configuration — stores historical accounting, QOS, accounts, associations, and limits. sacct, sreport, sshare, and sacctmgr talk to the DB.
- sacct / sreport / sshare / scontrol / sdiag: tools that read schedule/accounting state (used for monitoring and troubleshooting).

2) Scheduling: key slurm.conf settings and concepts
- Priority plugin
  - PriorityType
    - Usually set to priority/multifactor (default). Enables weighted multi-factor priority computation.
    - Example: PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - Priority factors and weights
    - PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightJobSize, PriorityWeightPartition, PriorityWeightQOS, etc.
    - Job_priority = weighted sum of enabled factors; larger weight => more influence.
    - Example: PriorityWeightFairshare increases fair-share effect on job order.
  - Fairshare / decay
    - PriorityDecayHalfLife controls how historical usage decays (time string, e.g. 7-0 for 7 days).
    - PriorityUsageResetPeriod resets accumulated usage (useful if you want periodic resets).
    - PriorityMaxAge sets how long the age factor ramps up.
    - Use these to tune how “past usage” penalizes heavy consumers vs new users.
- Backfill and scheduler plugin
  - SchedulerType (and plugin choice): default uses sched/backfill. Backfill allows running smaller queued jobs when they won’t delay higher priority jobs.
  - SchedulerParameters: plugin-specific tuning (depends on your Slurm version).
- Preemption
  - PreemptType and PreemptMode determine whether queued higher-priority jobs can preempt running jobs and how (suspend, requeue, kill).
  - Common pattern: PreemptType=preempt/qos to use QOS relationships; configure QOS preemption lists via sacctmgr.
- Resources and resource selection
  - SelectType / SelectTypeParameters
    - Modern clusters use select/cons_tres (or select/cons_res) to schedule on TRES (trackable resources like cpu,mem,gpu).
    - SelectTypeParameters=CR_Core_Memory or similar for older select/cons_res behavior.
  - TRES and GRES
    - TRES (trackable RESources) are slurm’s unified resource model (cpu,mem,gres/gpu,licenses).
    - GRES.conf + GresTypes controls GPU allocation details.
    - Configure TRES billing/weights if you want CPU vs GPU to affect priority or accounting.
  - DefMem, DefMemPerCPU, DefCPUPerGPU: defaults used when jobs do not request explicit mem/CPU.
- Job launch / tracking (affects accounting accuracy)
  - ProctrackType (e.g., proctrack/cgroup) and TaskPlugin (e.g., task/cgroup) with cgroup jobacct gathering
  - JobAcctGatherType and JobAcctGatherFrequency: controls how job resource usage is collected (required for accurate sacct data).
  - If you want per-process CPU/memory accounting, enable jobacct_gather/cgroup or jobacct_gather/linux.
- Partition configuration (partition-level policies)
  - PartitionName entries in slurm.conf control node groupings and default constraints (DefaultTime, MaxTime, AllowAccounts, AllowQOS).
  - Partition-level limits can be enforced or overridden by QOS/association limits.
- Misc scheduler tuning
  - SchedulerTimeSlice, FastSchedule, MaxJobCount, and other plugin parameters — tune for scheduler responsiveness and scale.

3) Quality of Service (QOS) and limits — configured in the DB (sacctmgr)
- QOS basics
  - QOS entries live in the Slurm DB and are created/modified with sacctmgr.
  - QOS attributes include: Priority (affects multi-factor priority), MaxJobs, MaxWall, MaxNodes, GrpTRES (group TRES limits), DenyOnLimit, PreemptMode, Flags (e.g., OverPartQOS).
  - Use QOS to implement buckets (premium/normal/low) with different priority, limits, and preemption rules.
- How QOS interacts with priority and scheduler
  - PriorityWeightQOS (in slurm.conf) must be non-zero to include QOS priority in the multifactor calculation.
  - If PreemptType=preempt/qos, QOS preemption settings in the DB control which QOS can preempt which.
- Association limits (users/accounts)
  - sacctmgr associations attach users to accounts and define per-association limits: MaxJobs, MaxCPUs, GrpCPUs, GrpTRES, MaxWall, etc.
  - GrpTRES can cap aggregate GPUs/CPUs for an account or user across the cluster or per partition.
- Typical workflow
  - Create accounts and users in DB (sacctmgr add account / user)
  - Create QOS entries (sacctmgr add/modify qos) and associate to accounts/users
  - Set association limits (sacctmgr modify user where=... set MaxJobs=..., GrpTRES=...).

4) Accounting architecture and slurmdbd
- slurmdbd and DB backend
  - slurmdbd (configured by slurmdbd.conf) writes accounting data to an SQL backend (MySQL/MariaDB/Postgres). slurmdbd.conf contains DB connection (StorageType, StorageHost, StorageLoc, StorageUser).
  - slurm.conf must be pointed to AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd and AccountingStorageHost set appropriately (or local DB in small setups).
- What is stored / how to use it
  - sacct shows job start/stop/exitcode and resource usage (if jobacct is enabled).
  - sreport generates aggregated usage reports (CPU-hours, GPU-hours) by user/account/partition over time windows.
  - sshare displays effective fairshare values and historical usage for associations.
- Ensuring accurate accounting
  - Enable JobAcctGatherType and Proctrack/TaskPlugin appropriately (cgroup is recommended).
  - Ensure slurmd and slurmctld can communicate reliably with slurmdbd and DB (scontrol ping + slurmdbd logs help debug connectivity).
  - Configure JobAcctGatherFrequency sensibly to balance load vs timeliness.

5) Resource billing and weights
- TRES billing weights and TRESType
  - You can set billing weights so CPU-hours and GPU-hours (TRES types) count differently toward fairshare and usage (BillingWeights, TRESBillingWeights).
  - Example: set a higher weight for gres/gpu to make GPUs “more expensive” in fairshare calculations.
- sreport / sshare usage
  - Use sreport to create chargeback/usage reports by account / user / partition and to drive quota decisions.
  - Use sshare (or scontrol show assoc) to inspect the fairshare/usage numbers that influence PriorityWeightFairshare.

6) Practical tuning tips and examples
- To enable multifactor fairshare with 7-day decay:
  - slurm.conf:
    - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
    - PriorityDecayHalfLife=7-0
    - PriorityWeightFairshare=10000
    - PriorityWeightAge=1000
    - PriorityMaxAge=14-0
- To use QOS priority and preemption:
  - slurm.conf: PriorityWeightQOS=1000, PreemptType=preempt/qos
  - DB: sacctmgr add qos premium; sacctmgr modify qos premium set priority=2000, preempt_mode=REQUEUE (or specify preempt list)
- To enable accounting DB:
  - slurm.conf: AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd, AccountingStorageHost=<slurmdbd host>
  - slurmdbd.conf: StorageType=accounting_storage/mysql (or account_storage/postgres), StorageUser/StoragePass/StorageLoc etc., DBDHost/DBDPort as needed.
- To account for GPUs properly:
  - Configure GRES on nodes, GresTypes=gpu in slurm.conf, GRES.conf describing GPU devices, and use TRES/GRES limits in QOS/association.

7) Common pitfalls
- Not enabling jobacct_gather + cgroup/proctrack => sacct shows little or no accurate usage.
- Forgetting to set PriorityWeightQOS to include QOS in priority calculation.
- Setting PriorityDecayHalfLife too long/short: too-long makes heavy users permanently penalized; too-short erodes fairshare effect.
- Not attaching QOS or associations correctly in DB => limits and preemption not applied.
- Mismatched slurm.conf across nodes (node resource mismatches lead to DOWN states).
- Overly aggressive JobAcctGatherFrequency or too-frequent DB writes can overload slurmdbd/DB on very large clusters.

8) Useful commands (read-only) for verification and operations
- Inspect scheduler and priorities: sdiag, sprio, scontrol show config
- Inspect fairshare and usage: sshare, sreport
- Manage QOS/accounts: sacctmgr
- Inspect accounting DB entries: sacct starttime=... format=...
- Show reservations: scontrol show reservation
(These are read-only; change operations use sacctmgr/scontrol and must be done by operators.)

9) Short checklist when deploying or changing scheduling/accounting
- Ensure slurm.conf sets the desired PriorityType and weights.
- Choose and configure SelectType (cons_tres) and GRES if you have GPUs.
- Configure cgroup/task plugins and jobacct_gather for accurate usage.
- Install slurmdbd, configure slurmdbd.conf DB connection, and point slurm.conf AccountingStorageType to slurmdbd.
- Create accounts/users and QOS/associations in DB (sacctmgr), set sensible GrpTRES/GrpCPUs limits and QOS priority.
- Test with a small set of jobs and validate sacct/sreport/sshare outputs before rolling wide.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact slurm.conf keys and a minimal working example file tailored to your cluster (small/medium/large), or
- list the sacctmgr commands to create a sample account/QOS/association for a “premium” and “normal” class,
- or explain any particular parameter in more detail (PriorityDecayHalfLife, PreemptType, select/cons_tres, cgroups, or slurmdbd DB settings). Which would you like next?

## QOS examples[#examples](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
QOS manipulation examples. All QOS operations are done using
the sacctmgr command. The default output of 'sacctmgr show qos' is
very long given the large number of limits and options available
so it is best to use the format option which filters the display.
By default when a cluster is added to the database a default
qos named normal is created.
```text
$ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0
```
Add a new QOS
```text
$ sacctmgr add qos zebra Adding QOS(s) zebra Settings Description = QOS Name $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 0
```
Set QOS priority
```text
$ sacctmgr modify qos zebra set priority=10 Modified qos... zebra $ sacctmgr show qos format=name,priority Name Priority ---------- ---------- normal 0 zebra 10
```

results.prompt: Explain relevant Slurm configuration for scheduling and accounting
results.agent_response:
Below is a focused, practical explanation of the Slurm configuration items that matter most for scheduling behavior and for accounting/enforcement. I cover where each setting lives (slurm.conf vs SlurmDBD/sacctmgr), what it does, typical knobs to tune, and quick commands you can run to inspect them.

High-level split
- Scheduling configuration: mainly in slurm.conf (SchedulerType, select/consumable-resource plugins, priority/ backfill / preemption parameters, partitions, GRES, TRES). These determine how jobs are ordered, what resources are considered, and how the scheduler backfills or preempts.
- Accounting/enforcement: SlurmDBD + sacctmgr and slurm.conf accounting plugins (AccountingStorage*, JobAcctGather*, JobCompType, AccountingStorageEnforce). These collect usage, configure accounts/QOS/limits, and enforce caps.

Key scheduling items (slurm.conf and related)
- Partitions
  - PartitionName entries in slurm.conf define which nodes/jobs belong to logical queues, default time limits, QOS visibility, and accessibility. Partitions are a fundamental scheduling scope (scheduling decisions, limits, preemption often partition-aware).
  - Inspect: scontrol show partition or sinfo.

- Node selection and resource model
  - SelectType / SelectTypeParameters (e.g., select/cons_res) — choose the resource selection plugin that models CPUs, memory, and consumable resources (TRES).
  - GRES (Generic RESources) for GPUs: configured per node and referenced in partitions; GRES entries ensure GPUs are scheduled correctly.
  - TRES (Trackable RESources): CPU, mem, gres/gpu, energy — used for accounting and limits.

- SchedulerType and backfill
  - SchedulerType (e.g., sched/backfill) selects the scheduler implementation. Backfill behavior and reservation enforcement are controlled by SchedulerParameters and scheduler plugin configuration.
  - SchedulerParameters: tune backfill, preemption, job packing and other behavior. Example knobs influence backfill aggressiveness, job packing and job re-queue handling.
  - Also relevant: MaxJobCount/MaxJobComp/DefTimeSlice for scheduler fairness and cycle behavior.

- Priorities and fairshare
  - PriorityType: which factors are used (priority/multifactor, priority/multifactor/size/fairshare, etc.).
  - PriorityWeightFairshare, PriorityWeightAge, PriorityWeightJobSize (and other PriorityWeight*): set the relative importance of fairshare, age, and job size in the final priority calculation.
  - PriorityDecayHalfLife: how quickly historical usage decays for fairshare.
  - Fairshare works against associations in the accounting DB (shares assigned to accounts/users); the scheduler multiplies that with priority weights.

- Preemption
  - PreemptType, PreemptMode, PreemptExemptTime and QOS preemption settings: control whether higher-priority jobs can preempt lower-priority ones and how that happens (suspend, requeue, checkpoint).
  - QOS entries can be marked preemptive or preemptible.

- Consumable resource enforcement
  - Ensure SelectTypeParameters are set to enable consumable resources (so memory/gpu are not double-allocated).
  - DefMemPerCPU, DefCpuPerTask, and TaskPlugin settings influence default resource accounting.

Key accounting items (SlurmDBD, sacctmgr, slurm.conf)
- Accounting storage & job accounting gathering (slurm.conf + slurmdbd)
  - AccountingStorageType / AccountingStorageHost / AccountingStorageUser etc. in slurm.conf tell slurmctld where to send accounting records (commonly slurmdbd).
  - SlurmDBD has its own slurmdbd.conf for DB connection (MySQL/MariaDB). Use SlurmDBD to centralize accounting across clusters.
  - JobAcctGatherType (e.g., jobacct_gather/linux) and JobAcctGatherFrequency control how resource usage (TRES) is sampled for jobs.
  - JobCompType: how job completion records are written (to file or to DB).

- Accounting enforcement
  - AccountingStorageEnforce: a comma-separated list of items to enforce from the DB (examples: limits, associations, qos — exact syntax depends on your Slurm version). When set, slurmctld prevents users from exceeding configured limits.
  - When enforcing, sacctmgr configured limits and QOS rules are actively applied at job submit time and/or at scheduling.

- sacctmgr associations, accounts, users and limits
  - Associations: the DB object that ties user -> account -> cluster -> optional partition.
  - sacctmgr is used to create accounts, assign users to accounts, set DefaultQOS, and set limits/weights.
  - QOS: configured via sacctmgr (or scontrol), QOS entries control Priority, MaxJobs, MaxWall, Preempt, and group resource limits.
  - Limits: per-user or per-account limits such as MaxSubmitJobs, MaxJobs, MaxJobsPerUser, MaxTRESPERUser, MaxTRESPERAccount (names vary by version). These prevent runaway usage and are enforced (if AccountingStorageEnforce includes limits).

- TRES accounting and capping
  - TRES is the canonical resource accounting unit. You can set group TRES limits (GrpTRES) or per-account/user limits to cap CPU-hours, GPU-hours, etc.
  - QOS and association settings can be used to constrain time- or resource-based usage (for example, group CPU-minutes or GPU-minutes).

Common administrative commands to inspect/configure
- View current slurm controller configuration: scontrol show config
- View partitions: scontrol show partition or sinfo
- View nodes and GRES: sinfo --Nodes or scontrol show node <node>
- Check priority/fairshare state: sprio and sshare
- View accounting DB objects: sacctmgr show associations, sacctmgr show accounts, sacctmgr show users, sacctmgr show qos
- View configured licenses: scontrol_license
- Generate usage reports: sreport (CPU-/GPU-hours, by user/account/partition)

Practical recommended settings & best practices
- Use SlurmDBD for production accounting — it centralizes usage, enables sacct/sreport, and allows enforcement.
- Enable JobAcctGatherType and an appropriate JobAcctGatherFrequency (e.g., 30–60s) so accounting reflects actual resource use (helpful for fairshare and billing).
- Model GPUs and other special hardware with GRES and ensure select/cons_res or equivalent consumable selection so resources are not double-allocated.
- Use PriorityType with PriorityWeightFairshare tuned to your sharing policy; set PriorityDecayHalfLife to match how quickly you want historical usage to wash out.
- Define QOS entries for key user groups with MaxJobs/MaxWall/GrpTRES caps rather than global hard caps; use sacctmgr to maintain accounts and associations.
- Enable AccountingStorageEnforce for the enforcement you intend (e.g., enforce=limits,qos) once your DB data and associations are correct — otherwise enforcement can reject valid submissions.
- Test preemption behavior carefully on a smaller partition before enabling cluster-wide.

Example snippets (conceptual)
- slurm.conf (examples of keys to check)
  - PriorityType=priority/multifactor
  - PriorityWeightFairshare=1000
  - PriorityWeightAge=100
  - SchedulerType=sched/backfill
  - SelectType=select/cons_res
  - JobAcctGatherType=jobacct_gather/linux
  - JobAcctGatherFrequency=30
  - AccountingStorageType=accounting_storage/slurmdbd
  - AccountingStorageHost=slurmdbd.example.com
  - AccountingStorageEnforce=limits,qos,associations

- sacctmgr examples
  - sacctmgr add account mygroup Cluster=cluster1 Description="Research"
  - sacctmgr add user alice Account=mygroup
  - sacctmgr create qos high Priority=1000 MaxJobs=50 GrpTRES=gres/gpu=100
  - sacctmgr modify account mygroup set Fairshare=100

When to check live config (I can run these reads for you)
- If you want me to inspect your cluster’s actual configuration values I can run:
  - scontrol show config (controller config)
  - sinfo (partition/node overview)
  - sacctmgr show associations/accounts/qos (accounting state)
  - sshare (current fairshare usage)
Tell me which of the above you want me to fetch and I’ll run the reads and summarize what your current settings imply for scheduling and accounting.

results.prompt: Explain the current job array situation and task-level identifiers
results.agent_response:
Summary — how Slurm represents job arrays and the per-task identifiers

- Array vs element
  - A job array is a single submission that creates many jobs (elements). Example: sbatch --array=1-4 job.sh creates four elements.
  - The array as a whole is identified by the ArrayJobID (the JobID of the first element). Individual elements are addressed as ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (for example 12345_2).

- Key environment variables (set inside each array task)
  - SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID — the JobID of the first element (the array identifier).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID — the array index for this task (the value from --array, e.g. 2).
  - SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT / _MAX / _MIN — count and bounds of the array indices.
  - SLURM_JOB_ID — the unique Slurm job id for this particular element (you can also see the combined form 12345_2 externally).
  - SLURM_PROCID — NOT the array index; this is the MPI/parallel rank (process index) within a job step.

- How Slurm displays and references elements
  - squeue/sacct/scontrol can show array elements; they appear as ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID (or with separate ArrayJobID/ArrayTaskID fields in scontrol show).
  - To operate on a whole array or a range:
    - scancel 12345 cancels the entire array.
    - scancel 12345_1-3 cancels tasks 1..3.
    - scontrol show job 12345_2 shows the specific element.

- sbatch substitutions and filenames
  - In sbatch scripts you can use %A -> array job id, %a -> array task id (e.g., --output=out_%A_%a.txt).

- Ordering / placeholder behavior (important caveat)
  - By default Slurm may create a “placeholder” element; the first task submitted is often a placeholder and can be scheduled last. Because of that, the numeric relationship between SLURM_JOB_ID and SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID can be non-intuitive: the element with the lowest SLURM_JOB_ID may have the highest SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID. Don’t rely on SLURM_JOB_ID ordering to infer SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID order.

- Practical tips
  - Inside a task use SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID to index per-task input files or parameters.
  - If you need to target or report on one element from outside Slurm, use the ArrayJobID_ArrayTaskID syntax (12345_7).
  - Use scontrol show job <array>_<task> for element-level details (resources, reason, exit codes).

If you want, I can:
- show current job arrays from the live queue (squeue) and list their element counts and pending/running states, or
- show details for a specific array (scontrol show job 12345) — tell me which array ID or which job ID to inspect.

Quick primer on Slurm job dependency semantics
- Syntax (sbatch): --dependency=<type>:<jobid>[:<jobid>...]
  - Example: sbatch --dependency=afterok:12345 myscript.sh
- Common dependency types:
  - after:<jobid> — start after the specified job(s) start.
  - afterany:<jobid> — start after the specified job(s) complete (any exit code).
  - afterok:<jobid> — start after the specified job(s) complete successfully (exit code 0).
  - afternotok:<jobid> — start after the specified job(s) complete with a non‑zero exit code.
  - aftercorr:<array_jobid> — for job arrays: satisfied after the corresponding array element completes successfully.
  - singleton — ensure only one job with the same name/user is running at a time (starts when none conflicting are running).
- Multiple job IDs in one dependency are combined logically (all listed jobs must meet the condition).
- Job arrays:
  - after: array ID — satisfied after all tasks in array start.
  - afterany: array ID — satisfied after all tasks in array complete.
  - afterok/afternotok behave relative to all tasks in the array (see array docs).
- Behavior:
  - When the dependency condition is satisfied, the job becomes eligible and the scheduler will consider it for allocation.
  - Dependencies are encoded on the job record (Dependency=...), visible via scontrol show job.
  - You can set dependencies at submission time (sbatch) or modify pending jobs as allowed (scontrol update job=... Dependency=...), but modifying is a mutating action.
