## DESCRIPTION[#SECTION_DESCRIPTION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
sbatch submits a batch script to Slurm. The batch script may be given to
sbatch through a file name on the command line, or if no file name is specified,
sbatch will read in a script from standard input.
The batch script may contain one or more lines beginning with "#SBATCH" followed
by any of the CLI options documented on this page. #SBATCH directives are read
directly by Slurm, so shell-specific syntax including variable names will be
read as literal text. Once the first non-comment, non-whitespace line has been

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.agent_response:
Read-only findings
- I checked the queue for PENDING jobs (squeue state=PENDING) and found no pending jobs — therefore there are no jobs currently blocked with the "Dependency" reason on this cluster right now.

Explanation — Slurm job dependency semantics (concise)

What a dependency is
- A dependency makes a job wait until one or more events for other job(s) occur. While waiting the job will normally appear PENDING with reason "Dependency".
- You can set dependencies at submission with sbatch --dependency=<type>:<jobid>[ :<jobid2>... ].

Common dependency types
- after:<jobid>[...]
  - Satisfied after the specified job(s) start running (useful to ensure ordering of start times).
- afterok:<jobid>[...]
  - Satisfied only after the specified job(s) complete successfully (exit code 0). All listed job IDs must finish with exit 0.
- afternotok:<jobid>[...]
  - Satisfied only after the specified job(s) complete with a non‑zero exit code (at least one non‑zero).
- afterany:<jobid>[...]
  - Satisfied after the specified job(s) complete, regardless of exit code.
- aftercorr:<jobid>
  - Used with job arrays; satisfied when the corresponding task index of the specified array completes successfully.
- singleton
  - Ensures only one job with the same name/user runs at a time; a later job with singleton will wait until the prior job (same name/user) finishes.
Notes:
- Multiple job IDs in one dependency clause are treated as AND: every listed job must satisfy the dependency condition.
- You can combine dependency clauses (e.g., --dependency=afterok:123,afterany:200) to create more complex waits.
- Job-array semantics: when a dependency refers to a job array, behavior depends on the dependency type:
  - after: satisfied after all tasks in the array start.
  - afterany: satisfied after all tasks complete.
  - afterok/afternotok: based on aggregate success/failure across the array (docs use the worst/aggregate exit behavior).
  - aftercorr: maps corresponding task index only.

How Slurm displays/diagnoses dependency-blocked jobs
- squeue will show pending jobs and a REASON column; dependency-blocked jobs typically show REASON=Dependency.
- For details of a job’s dependency expression use: scontrol show job <jobid>
  - That output contains a Dependency=... field showing the exact clauses and referenced job IDs.
- Example quick checks:
  - List PENDING jobs and the reason:
    squeue -t PENDING -o "%i %P %j %u %T %M %R"
    (Then look for rows where the REASON/REASON column is "Dependency".)
  - Inspect a job’s dependency detail:
    scontrol show job <jobid>

Common pitfalls and tips
- If the job you depend on was cancelled or failed, afterok will never be satisfied; use afterany or adjust workflow.
- Dependencies referencing job IDs that no longer exist (or were purged from accounting) can behave unexpectedly; scontrol show job will reveal unresolved IDs.
- Dependencies are established at submission time. To change or remove them you must modify the job (scontrol update) — that is a mutating operation and requires operator actions.
- For workflows, consider using job arrays + aftercorr for per-task chaining, or job-chaining tools (workflow managers) that can re-submit on failures.

If you want, I can:
- Search the cluster now for any jobs with REASON=Dependency (I already checked PENDING and found none). If you want a different filter (e.g., include certain user, partition, or a historical search with sacct), tell me which scope and I’ll run the appropriate read-only query.

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.
Since each array element can have a different exit code, the interpretation of
the afterok and afternotok clauses will be based upon the highest
exit code from any task in the job array.
When a job dependency specifies the job ID of a job array:
The after clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array start.
The afterany clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete.
The aftercorr clause is satisfied after the corresponding task ID in the
specified job has completed successfully (ran to completion with an exit code of
zero).
The afterok clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete successfully.
The afternotok clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete with at least one tasks not completing succes...

results.agent_response:
Summary — dependency‑blocked jobs I found
- Job 3004 (dependency_job) — user=alice, partition=cpu, state=PENDING, Reason=Dependency.
  This is the only job in the current pending queue whose reason is "Dependency".
- Other pending jobs (for context):
  - 3001 big_gpu_job (alice) — Reason=Resources
  - 3002 waiting_job (bob) — Reason=Priority
  - 3003 queue_test (charlie) — Reason=QOSMaxJobsPerUserLimit

What "Dependency" means (concise semantics)
- Slurm dependencies are declared at submit time (sbatch --dependency=...) or added/changed with scontrol. A dependency tells Slurm to hold the job until one or more conditions on other job(s) are met.
- Common dependency types:
  - after: job waits until the specified job(s) have started.
  - afterany: waits until the specified job(s) complete (any exit status).
  - afterok: waits until the specified job(s) complete successfully (exit code 0).
  - afternotok: waits until the specified job(s) complete with a non‑zero exit code.
  - aftercorr: used with job arrays — waits until the corresponding task index in the specified job array completes successfully.
  - singleton: ensures only one job with the same singleton key (often same user+name) runs at a time; later singleton jobs wait for earlier ones to finish.
- Multiple dependency clauses are combined (comma separated) and all clauses must be satisfied before the dependent job is released (i.e., dependencies are effectively ANDed).
- Job arrays: semantics are special — e.g., after waits for all tasks to start, afterany/afterok consider completion across all tasks; aftercorr matches corresponding array task IDs.

How to see exactly what job 3004 is waiting on
- Run: scontrol show job 3004
  - Look for the Dependency=... field (it will show strings like afterok:12345,afterany:23456 or ArrayJobID etc.).
- If the dependency refers to an array, interpret it using the array rules above (afterok on an array means all tasks in that array must succeed).
- If the dependency references a job that will never satisfy the condition (e.g., a missing job ID or a completed job with wrong exit code), the job will remain pending until the dependency is changed or removed.

- Show the Dependency= value for job 3004 (read-only) and explain the exact jobs/array it references — shall I fetch scontrol show job 3004 and return the Dependency field?

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## Job Dependencies [#dependencies](https://slurm.schedmd.com/job_array.html)
A job which is to be dependent upon an entire job array should specify
itself dependent upon the ArrayJobID.
Since each array element can have a different exit code, the interpretation of
the afterok and afternotok clauses will be based upon the highest
exit code from any task in the job array.
When a job dependency specifies the job ID of a job array:
The after clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array start.
The afterany clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete.
The aftercorr clause is satisfied after the corresponding task ID in the
specified job has completed successfully (ran to completion with an exit code of
zero).
The afterok clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete successfully.
The afternotok clause is satisfied after all tasks in the job array
complete with at least one tasks not completing succes...

Slurm has a variety of timers to control when to consider a node DOWN,
when to purge job records, how long to give a job to gracefully terminate, etc.
SlurmctldTimeout : How many seconds the backup controller waits before
becoming the active controller
SlurmdTimeout : How many seconds the Slurm controller waits for the slurmd

InactiveLimit : How many seconds the Slurm controller waits for srun

## NODESET CONFIGURATION[#SECTION_NODESET-CONFIGURATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html)
The nodeset configuration allows you to define a name for a specific set of
nodes which can be used to simplify the partition configuration section,
especially for heterogeneous or condo-style systems. Each nodeset may be defined
by an explicit list of nodes, and/or by filtering the nodes by a particular
configured feature. If both Feature= and Nodes= are used the
nodeset shall be the union of the two subsets.
Note that the nodesets are only used to simplify the partition definitions
at present, and are not usable outside of the partition configuration.

results.prompt: Find dependency-blocked jobs and explain dependency semantics
results.agent_response:
Summary — current cluster state
- I checked pending jobs (squeue --state=PENDING). No pending job is blocked by a dependency.
- Pending jobs I see:
  - 4003 — batch_inference — Reason=Resources
  - 4006 — stuck_job — Reason=Priority

How I looked
- squeue (state=PENDING) to find jobs and their REASON.
- scontrol show job <jobid> for details (the detailed job output shows the Reason=... field).

What "Dependency" means (Slurm semantics)
- A job with Reason=Dependency is waiting because it had a --dependency=... set at submission time and the dependency condition has not yet been satisfied.
- Common dependency types:
  - after: start after the listed job(s) have started.
  - afterok: start after the listed job(s) finish successfully (exit code 0).
  - afternotok: start after the listed job(s) finish with non‑zero exit (failed).
  - afterany: start after the listed job(s) finish (any exit code).
  - singleton: only one job with this name may run; this job waits until other singleton jobs with the same name complete.
- Dependencies can reference one or more job IDs (type:jobid[,jobid...]) and job arrays; multiple dependencies are combined per the dependency type semantics.
- If you depend on a job that already finished, Slurm evaluates the dependency against that job's final result immediately — e.g., afterok is satisfied only if the earlier job exited with success.
- squeue shows only the single reason encountered by the scheduler (the REASON column). A job could also be blocked by resources or priority, but squeue will display the one reason the scheduler encountered first.
- To see the actual dependency expression for a job, inspect the job details: scontrol show job <jobid> (look for the Dependency=... field).

How to find dependency-blocked jobs yourself
- Quick: squeue -t PENDING -o "%.18i %.30j %.10T %.20R" | grep Dependency
  (lists PENDING jobs and filters for rows whose Reason column contains "Dependency")
- For each candidate job, run: scontrol show job <jobid> to view the Dependency=... line and full details.
- If the dependency target finished already, use sacct -j <jobid> to see its final state/exit code.

Troubleshooting dependency-blocked jobs
- If dependency target failed but you still want the dependent job to run: cancel and resubmit the dependent job without the dependency, or edit/remove the dependency (requires admin/operator action).
- If dependency target is still running or pending, wait or investigate that job's blocking reason (squeue / scontrol show job / sacct for history).
- If a job is stuck with Reason=Dependency but its dependency target looks satisfied, check whether the dependency referenced a different job ID (typo) or an array element — use scontrol show job to confirm the exact Dependency value.

Next steps
- I can:
  - re-run a filtered squeue command to search for dependency-blocked jobs for a specific user, partition, or time window (tell me the filter you want), or
  - inspect the Dependency field of any job ID you give me (tell me the job ID).
- If you want a dependency changed or removed, I must hand that action to an operator — say which job ID(s) and the desired change and I'll transfer the request.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

Snippet:
## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Find dependency-blocked jobs and explain dependency semantics
results.agent_response:
Summary
- I inspected the pending queue and job details. There are currently no jobs blocked by a job dependency.
- Found one PENDING job: JobID=5004, JobName=slurm_array, User=alice. scontrol show job 5004 reports Reason=AssocGrpCPUMinutesLimit (i.e., pending for an account/group CPU-minute limit), not a dependency.

What I ran
- squeue --state=PENDING (listed pending jobs)
- scontrol show job 5004 (showed the job's Reason=AssocGrpCPUMinutesLimit)

How to find dependency‑blocked jobs (quick recipe)
1. List pending jobs and their reason:
   - squeue --states=PENDING   (look at the REASON column)
2. For any pending job whose REASON looks like a dependency (often shown as "Dependency" or similar), inspect the full job record:
   - scontrol show job <jobid>
   - In that output look for the Dependency= field (and JobState/Reason) which shows the dependency expression (for example afterok:1234).
3. Interpret the dependency expression (see types below).

Common Slurm dependency types and semantics
- after: start this job after the specified job(s) have begun running. (Waits for start.)
  - Example: --dependency=after:1234
- afterok: start after the specified job(s) complete successfully (exit code 0).
  - Example: --dependency=afterok:1234
- afternotok: start only if the specified job(s) finish with a non‑zero exit code (failure).
  - Example: --dependency=afternotok:1234
- afterany: start after the specified job(s) finish regardless of exit code.
  - Example: --dependency=afterany:1234
- singleton: delay this job until no other jobs with the same name and user are running; useful to ensure only one instance runs at a time.
  - Example: --dependency=singleton
- Multiple dependencies: you can combine types and multiple job IDs (comma separated). The job starts when the combined expression is satisfied.
  - Example: --dependency=afterok:1234,afterany:2345
- Array job dependencies: you can specify array indices or use array master IDs; dependency expressions accept array element notation.

Practical notes
- Dependency pending reason appears in the queue REASON column; scontrol show job reveals the exact Dependency= expression.
- after waits for job start; afterok/afternotok/afterany wait for job completion and evaluate exit codes accordingly—this is frequently the difference that surprises users.
- If a job is pending for a dependency that will never be satisfied (e.g., dependency points to a job that was cancelled/failed and the dependency type requires success), fix options include canceling the dependent job, modifying it (admins can change Job dependencies with scontrol), or re-submitting with adjusted dependencies.

If you want, I can:
- run a fuller scan (squeue with formatting) and list any PENDING jobs whose Reason looks like a dependency, and then for each show the Dependency field (read-only). Would you like that?

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Executing sbatch sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sbatch or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to sbatch to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

## EXAMPLES[#SECTION_EXAMPLES](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html)
Specify a batch script by filename on the command line. The batch script specifies a 1 minute time limit for the job.
```text
$ cat myscript #!/bin/sh #SBATCH --time=1 srun hostname |sort $ sbatch -N4 myscript salloc: Granted job allocation 65537 $ cat slurm-65537.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
Pass a batch script to sbatch on standard input:
```text
$ sbatch -N4 #!/bin/sh > srun hostname |sort > EOF sbatch: Submitted batch job 65541 $ cat slurm-65541.out host1 host2 host3 host4
```
To create a heterogeneous job with 3 components, each allocating a unique set of nodes:
```text
$ sbatch -w node[2-3] : -w node4 : -w node[5-7] work.bash Submitted batch job 34987
```

results.prompt: Group pending jobs by Slurm reason and explain the main reasons
results.agent_response:
Below are the common Slurm pending-reason groups, what each means, and how to check/fix them. This is a general (how‑to/explanation) answer rather than a live cluster query.

1) Resource shortage (REASON often: Resources, ReqNodeNotAvail, Nodes, Gres)
- Meaning: No currently idle nodes match the job’s resource requests (CPUs, memory, GPUs, specific node features, TRES, or partition). Can also be because nodes are allocated to other jobs or drained.
- How to spot: squeue’s REASON will say Resources/ReqNodeNotAvail or show “Requires” reasons; sinfo shows partition/node idle counts.
- Fixes: reduce resource requests (fewer GPUs/CPUs/memory), relax node constraints/feature flags, choose a different partition, wait, or request a reservation.

2) Job dependency (REASON: Dependency)
- Meaning: Job has an sbatch/srun dependency (afterok, afterany, etc.) and is waiting for the predecessor(s) to finish.
- How to spot: squeue REASON shows Dependency; scontrol show job <jobid> shows Dependency field.
- Fixes: ensure predecessor job completes successfully or remove/alter the dependency.

3) Priority / Fairshare / QOS ordering (REASON: Priority or Priority) 
- Meaning: Jobs are eligible but lower priority; scheduler will start them when higher‑priority work finishes or backfill opens a window.
- How to spot: squeue REASON may show Priority; sprio / sshare show contributing factors.
- Fixes: change QOS, account, or fairshare; ask admin to adjust weights; or wait.

4) Partition/node state or configuration (REASON: PartitionDown, NodeDown, Drained, NodeNotAvailable)
- Meaning: Target partition or nodes are down/drained/maintenance; scheduler cannot allocate.
- How to spot: sinfo and sinfo -R / sinfo_reasons show down/drain lists and reasons.
- Fixes: wait for maintenance to finish or ask admins to bring nodes up.

5) QOS / account / limits (REASON: QOSMaxJobs, QOSGrpTRES, AssocLimit)
- Meaning: User/account/QOS hit limits (max jobs, TRES usage, GPU-hour caps).
- How to spot: squeue may show a limit reason; sacctmgr or sacctmgr show associations and limits.
- Fixes: reduce concurrent jobs, change account/QOS, ask accounting admin to adjust limits.

6) Licenses (REASON: License)
- Meaning: Job requests licensed software resources and no licenses are currently free.
- How to spot: squeue REASON may say License; scontrol_license shows license usage.
- Fixes: free licenses by finishing other jobs, increase license pool, or request nodes without that license requirement.

7) Holds (REASON: JobHeld, UserHold, AdminHold, SystemHold)
- Meaning: Job is placed on hold and will not run until released.
- How to spot: squeue shows STATE=PD and REASON Hold; scontrol show job <id> shows Hold information.
- Fixes: release the hold (scontrol release <jobid>) or contact the holder/admin.

8) Reservation constraints (REASON: Reservation)
- Meaning: Job is reserved for later, or a conflicting reservation says job must wait.
- How to spot: squeue REASON shows Reservation; scontrol_reservation_show lists reservations.
- Fixes: schedule within reservation, change reservation, or ask admins.

9) Job-array / throttle or per-user limits (REASON: ArrayTaskLimit, JobLimit)
- Meaning: Array concurrency or per-user job submission limits prevent starting more tasks.
- How to spot: REASON will indicate array or limit-related text; sacctmgr / squeue show array counts.
- Fixes: reduce array concurrency, consolidate tasks, or increase limits.

10) Constraint/feature mismatch (REASON: Constraint)
- Meaning: Job requested a node feature or CPU architecture that no currently idle node provides.
- How to spot: squeue REASON shows Constraint or ReqNodeNotAvail; sinfo node feature listings show which nodes have which features.
- Fixes: remove/reduce constraints or wait for matching nodes.

A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all

## Partition QOS [#partition](https://slurm.schedmd.com/qos.html)
A QOS can be attached to a partition. This means the partition will have all
the same limits as the QOS. This does not associate jobs with the QOS, nor does
it give the job any priority or preemption characteristics of the assigned QOS.
Jobs may separately request the same QOS or a different QOS to gain those
characteristics. However, the Partition QOS limits will override the job's QOS.
If the opposite is desired you may configure the job's QOS with
`Flags=OverPartQOS` which will reverse the order of precedence.
This functionality may be used to implement a true "floating"
partition, in which a partition may access a limited amount of resources with no
restrictions on which nodes it uses to get the resources. This is accomplished
by assigning all nodes to the partition, then configuring a Partition QOS with

Job scheduling priority is made up of a number of factors as
described in the [priority/multifactor](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html) plugin. One
of the factors is the QOS priority. Each QOS is defined in the Slurm
database and includes an associated priority. Jobs that request and
are permitted a QOS will incorporate the priority associated with that
QOS in the job's [multi-factor priority calculation.](https://slurm.schedmd.com/priority_multifactor.html)

calculation, the "PriorityWeightQOS" configuration parameter must be
defined in the slurm.conf file and assigned an integer value greater
than zero.

multi-factor plugin is loaded.

Starting in Slurm 23.11, a QOS may be configured to contain relative resource
limits instead of absolute limits by setting `Flags=Relative`.

results.prompt: Explain when this workflow should use sbatch, salloc, or srun
results.agent_response:
Short answer: use sbatch to submit non‑interactive batch jobs (scripts) that Slurm will schedule and run later; use salloc when you need an interactive allocation (grab nodes/GPUs and get a shell or run commands interactively); use srun to actually launch tasks/job‑steps (either inside an allocation or as a one‑shot launcher that obtains resources).

When to pick each (practical workflow guidance)
- sbatch — scheduled, reproducible batch runs
  - Use for production training runs, pipelines, or any job you want Slurm to queue and run unattended from a script.
  - sbatch submits a batch script and returns immediately; Slurm runs the script later and records job output.
  - Typical: sbatch --nodes=2 --gres=gpu:4 --time=24:00:00 my_job.sh

- salloc — interactive allocation for debugging, development, and multi‑step interactive work
  - Use when you need an allocation you can interact with (a shell, an xterm, or run multiple srun commands inside).
  - Good for debugging, tuning, launching interactive MPI sessions, or running iterative experiments on allocated nodes.
  - Typical: salloc -N2 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00  (then you get a shell or run srun inside)

- srun — task launcher / job‑step runner (inside allocations or as a direct single‑command run)
  - Use srun to launch parallel tasks (MPI ranks, multi‑task jobs) and to create job steps inside an sbatch or salloc allocation.
  - You can also use srun directly from the command line to allocate+run a single command (acts like salloc+srun combined for a one‑off).
  - Typical inside a script or interactive allocation: srun -n 32 ./mpi_program
  - For interactive shells, srun --pty bash or srun --pty --gres=gpu:1 /bin/bash

Common patterns
- Production batch: sbatch my_job.sh (inside the script, use srun to launch MPI/parallel tasks)
- Interactive debug: salloc ... --pty bash, then srun -n... ./prog or run unit tests manually
- Quick single command: srun --nodes=1 --gres=gpu:1 --time=00:30:00 python debug.py

Notes / best practices
- Put resource requests (nodes, cpus, gres=gpu, time, partition, QOS) on the sbatch/salloc/srun command so the scheduler can allocate appropriately.
- Inside sbatch scripts prefer srun to launch tasks; it integrates with Slurm job steps and accounting.
- Use salloc when you want to keep the allocation after you run something interactively (so you can iterate).
- Avoid calling salloc/srun in tight loops (they contact slurmctld); batch large numbers of short tasks via job arrays or a single multi‑task job.
- For reproducibility and logging, prefer sbatch; for exploration and debugging, prefer salloc + srun.

If you want, tell me your concrete workflow (script vs interactive, MPI vs single‑GPU, debugging vs production) and I’ll recommend the exact command line and an example sbatch script.

results.prompt: Explain when this workflow should use sbatch, salloc, or srun
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Use sbatch to submit non‑interactive batch scripts that the scheduler will queue and run later.
- Use salloc to get an interactive allocation (a set of nodes/CPUs/GPUs) you can use yourself (shell, xterm, or multiple srun steps).
- Use srun to launch job steps (parallel tasks) inside an existing allocation — or to start a job step directly from the login node (but prefer sbatch for reproducible batch runs).

Details and typical patterns

1) sbatch — batch, reproducible, queued jobs
- What it does: submits a shell script to Slurm. sbatch returns a job ID and exits; the scheduler runs the script when resources become available.
- When to use: long or production runs, nightly jobs, training, pipelines, anything you don’t need to interact with while it runs.
- Typical pattern: put resource requests and srun calls inside the script (use srun for MPI/parallel launches).
- Example:
  sbatch --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --time=04:00:00 train.sh
- Why: keeps runs reproducible, logged, and tracked by the scheduler.

2) salloc — get an interactive allocation
- What it does: requests and (when granted) holds an allocation of nodes/resources for you; it can run a command (or drop you into a shell) while the allocation is held.
- When to use: interactive debugging, interactive development, running an interactive MPI session, testing configs, opening an xterm on allocated nodes.
- Typical pattern: allocate resources, then use srun repeatedly inside that allocation to run steps/tasks.
- Example:
  salloc -N2 --ntasks-per-node=4 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00:00 --pty bash
- Why: lets you iterate interactively, run multiple srun steps inside the same allocation, or run a GUI/xterm on allocated nodes.

3) srun — launch job steps / parallel tasks
- What it does: launches tasks across nodes within an allocation. If there is no current allocation, srun can request an allocation for the command (behavior depends on site config), but it is commonly used inside sbatch or salloc allocations.
- When to use:
  - Inside sbatch scripts to start MPI/parallel tasks (recommended).
  - Inside an salloc interactive allocation to run single or multiple parallel steps.
  - For quick single-shot commands you want executed now (but prefer sbatch for longer or reproducible jobs).
- Typical pattern: srun --mpi=pmix -n 128 ./my_mpi_app
- Example inside a script:
  #SBATCH --nodes=4
  srun -n 256 ./mpi_program
- Why: srun manages placement, ranks, and environment for parallel tasks; using it inside a batch script or allocation is the typical pattern.

Quick decision flow
- Non‑interactive, reproducible batch job -> sbatch.
- Need an interactive allocation (debug, develop, run multiple steps) -> salloc, then srun inside it.
- Need to launch parallel tasks inside an allocation (or run a quick parallel command) -> srun.

Notes and best practices
- Prefer sbatch + srun for production workflows (keeps logs and accounting tidy).
- Use salloc for development/debugging; avoid calling salloc in tight loops (it makes RPCs to slurmctld).
- Use srun inside scripts to spawn MPI or multi‑task jobs — don’t directly mpirun unless your site specifically requires it.
- Behavior of srun when used from the login node (auto-allocation vs requiring an existing allocation) can be site-dependent; check local docs/policies.

results.prompt: Explain when this workflow should use sbatch, salloc, or srun
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Use sbatch to submit non-interactive batch scripts that the scheduler will queue and run later.
- Use salloc when you need an interactive allocation (a reserved set of nodes/CPUs/GPUs) to run commands, open a shell, or debug.
- Use srun to launch parallel tasks (job steps). You can run srun inside an allocation (salloc or sbatch) or use srun by itself as a one-shot allocation+launch.

When to pick each (guidelines)
- sbatch — batch workflows (default)
  - Non-interactive, reproducible jobs (training runs, large workflows, pipelines).
  - Put resource requests and commands in a script with #SBATCH lines and submit: sbatch myjob.sh
  - The scheduler assigns a job ID and runs it later; good for long-running production runs and bookkeeping.

- salloc — interactive allocations and debugging
  - You want a shell or interactive session on allocated nodes: salloc -N2 --gres=gpu:1 --time=02:00 -- q, then run commands interactively.
  - Use for debugging, interactive development, launching a GUI/xterm, or running a workload that requires interactive control.
  - After salloc grants resources you typically run srun or other commands inside that allocation. When your shell exits, the allocation is released.

- srun — launch job steps / parallel tasks
  - Use inside a batch script (sbatch) or inside an salloc session to start parallel tasks distributed across the allocation.
    Example: inside an sbatch script:
      srun -n32 ./my_mpi_program
  - Use as a one-shot launcher without a prior salloc if you want to request resources and run immediately:
      srun -N2 -n16 --gres=gpu:2 ./my_program
    (This will wait in the queue for resources like sbatch would, then run the step.)
  - Use srun to spawn MPI ranks / multi-process tasks because it integrates with Slurm’s task placement and PMI support (preferred over mpirun in many clusters).

Common patterns
- Batch, multi-step job: sbatch script that contains srun commands for each step.
- Interactive debug: salloc ... then srun --pty bash (or use srun directly with --pty if you just need a terminal).
- Quick one-off run: srun ...command... (acts like submit+run for a single step).

Notes and tips
- Resource options can be provided either as #SBATCH lines in an sbatch script or as CLI args to salloc/srun (e.g., -N, -n, --cpus-per-task, --mem, --gres).
- srun inside sbatch or salloc creates job steps that share the same allocation (same SLURM_JOBID). srun alone creates its own allocation/step and jobid.
- For MPI: prefer srun for proper Slurm integration unless your MPI distribution requires a different launcher.
- For short interactive runs, srun --pty bash can be used, but salloc is clearer when you intend to run many interactive commands.
- For automated workflows (retries, dependency trees), sbatch supports dependencies (sbatch --dependency=afterok:JOBID).

If you want, tell me a specific workflow (debugging a training script interactively, submitting many parameter sweeps, running MPI job) and I’ll show the exact sbatch/salloc/srun command or minimal script to use.

results.prompt: Explain when this workflow should use sbatch, salloc, or srun
results.agent_response:
Short guide — when to use sbatch, salloc, or srun

- sbatch — submit a non‑interactive batch job
  - Use when you have a job script you want queued and run later (reproducible, unattended runs).
  - Slurm returns a job ID; the job runs on allocated nodes when the scheduler starts it.
  - Typical use: production training, long experiments, cron‑style/array jobs.
  - Example: sbatch my_job.sh

- salloc — get an interactive allocation (an allocation + a shell or a command)
  - Use when you need an interactive allocation of nodes/resources for debugging, experimenting, or opening an interactive shell/xterm on allocated nodes.
  - salloc obtains the resources immediately (when available) and holds them until the requested command (or shell) exits.
  - Typical use: debug a job interactively, start an interactive MPI session, open an xterm on allocated nodes.
  - Example: salloc -N2 --time=01:00:00 --mem=64G bash

- srun — run job steps (launch tasks), either inside an allocation or by requesting a short allocation on the fly
  - Use inside a sbatch script or an salloc session to launch parallel/serial tasks across the allocated nodes (MPI/OMP/worker processes). This is the preferred launcher for MPI under Slurm.
  - srun can also be used outside an allocation to request resources and run a single command immediately (it will create a short allocation for that command).
  - Typical use: spawn the MPI program inside a batch script, or run a quick command with resources without writing a script.
  - Examples:
    - Inside a batch script: srun -n 32 ./my_mpi_program
    - Run one-off command: srun -N1 --time=00:10:00 hostname
    - Interactive pseudo-TTY: srun --pty bash

Quick decision flow
- I want a queued, repeatable job/script -> sbatch.
- I want an interactive shell or to experiment on allocated nodes -> salloc (then use srun inside it).
- I want to launch tasks on nodes that are already allocated (or quickly run a single command) -> srun.

Notes / best practices
- In batch scripts, prefer srun to launch tasks (not system mpirun) because srun integrates with Slurm’s allocation and task placement.
- salloc gives you an environment (SLURM_* variables) to use srun interactively; srun without a prior salloc may implicitly allocate resources for the command.
- Use sbatch for reproducibility and scheduling; use salloc/srun for interactive work and immediate runs.

procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run salloc or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other
programs. Ensure that programs limit calls to salloc to the minimum
necessary for the information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Explain when this workflow should use sbatch, salloc, or srun
results.agent_response:
Short answer — pick by intent:

- sbatch — batch (non-interactive) submission
  - Use when you have a shell/script to run later on allocated resources (production runs, scheduled/long jobs, pipelines).
  - sbatch submits a batch script, exits immediately with a job ID, and Slurm runs the script when resources are available (creates a batch step and job record).
  - Put resource requests as #SBATCH directives or command-line options in the script.
  - Typical: sbatch myjob.sh

- salloc — get an interactive allocation (reserve resources and drop you into a shell)
  - Use when you need an interactive allocation to experiment, debug, compile, test, or run an interactive MPI/debugging session.
  - salloc waits until the requested resources are allocated, then gives you an interactive environment (often followed by srun or mpirun inside that allocation).
  - Typical: salloc -N2 -n16 --time=01:00:00 --gres=gpu:1
  - Good for interactive GPU debugging or running gdb/strace across allocated nodes.

- srun — run a job step (can be used inside an allocation or to create one)
  - Use to launch parallel tasks under an existing allocation (inside an sbatch script or after salloc). srun creates job steps and coordinates task placement.
  - You can also run srun from a login node without a prior salloc; it will request resources and synchronously run the step (so srun can act like a quick interactive run+allocate).
  - Common uses:
    - Inside batch script: sbatch script that contains srun -n32 ./prog
    - Inside interactive allocation: salloc ... then srun -n32 ./prog
    - Quick command: srun --pty bash (start an interactive shell) or srun -n8 hostname
  - For MPI: modern MPI implementations generally integrate with Slurm via srun (preferred). If using mpirun/orterun, ensure you already have a Slurm allocation.

Practical rules-of-thumb
- Non-interactive production run or scheduled job: use sbatch.
- Need an interactive node or want to iterate and debug: use salloc (then srun or mpirun inside).
- Want to launch the parallel task itself (inside a script or allocation), or run a quick synchronous command from your terminal: use srun.
- For scripts that need multiple steps on the same allocation, use srun inside the sbatch script to create steps and to control task counts per step.
- Don’t run heavy/long workloads directly on the login node — always request resources via sbatch/salloc/srun.

Examples
- Batch: sbatch --nodes=4 --ntasks-per-node=32 --time=04:00:00 myscript.sh
- Interactive allocation: salloc -N2 -n16 --time=02:00:00 --gres=gpu:1
  - then inside allocation: srun -n16 ./my_mpi_app
- Quick synchronous run (no persistent script): srun -n8 --time=00:10:00 ./short_test

If you want, tell me the use case (MPI vs single-node, GPU vs CPU, interactive vs automated) and I’ll give the exact sbatch/salloc/srun command examples for it.

# MPI Users Guide
MPI use depends upon the type of MPI being used.
There are three fundamentally different modes of operation used
by these various MPI implementations.
- Slurm directly launches the tasks and performs initialization of communications through the PMI-1, PMI-2 or PMIx APIs. (Supported by most modern MPI implementations.)

results.prompt: Explain cluster utilization from Slurm reports and scheduler diagnostics
results.agent_response:
Good question — understanding utilization means combining historical usage (what ran) with scheduler diagnostics (how the scheduler behaved while making placements). Below I summarize the Slurm reports and diagnostics you should use, what each metric means, how to interpret common patterns, and which commands to run to gather the evidence you need.

1) Primary Slurm reports / diagnostics and what they show
- sreport cluster utilization
  - Purpose: historical resource usage/usage breakdown over a time window (CPU/GPU-hours and time nodes were Allocated, Idle, Down, PlannedDown, OverCommitted, etc.).
  - Key fields: Allocated (time nodes in use by jobs/reservations), Idle (time nodes were idle), Down (node downtime/drain), OverCommitted, TresCount/TresName (which resources: CPUs/GPUs).
  - Use for: overall usage %, account/queue share, and trends (daily/weekly/monthly usage and which accounts/users consumed most).
- sdiag (scheduler diagnostics)
  - Purpose: runtime counters describing slurmctld scheduling activity: scheduling cycle count and times, backfill statistics and windows, dispatch counts, thread count, queue depth, wait/age counters.
  - Key fields to inspect: scheduling cycle avg/median/max, queue depth, backfill opportunities used vs missed, number of jobs dispatched, number of preemptions, server thread count.
  - Use for: diagnosing scheduler bottlenecks (scheduling latency, missed backfill, high RPC load).
- sprio and sprio --weights
  - Purpose: job priority components (fairshare, age, size, qos, partition). sprio shows which factor dominates each pending job’s priority.
  - Use for: identifying why jobs aren’t starting (low priority, fairshare limits, QOS).
- sshare
  - Purpose: fairshare usage and effective shares per user/account.
  - Use for: check historical share usage and whether fairshare is starving users.
- sinfo / sinfo_reasons / sinfo_node
  - Purpose: current partition/node states (allocated/idle/drain/down) and reasons for non-availability.
  - Use for: spotting node-level causes for idle capacity (drains, down nodes, maintenance).
- squeue (with Reason column) and scontrol show job
  - Purpose: live queue: pending reasons, per-job resources, elapsed times. scontrol show job gives detailed state, constraints, and pending reason text.
  - Use for: exact pending reason codes (e.g., Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSMaxJobs, AssociationResourceLimit).

2) Important utilization metrics and how to interpret them
- Utilization % = Allocated_time / (Allocated_time + Idle_time + Down_time) (from sreport)
  - Low utilization with little Down time → not enough usable jobs (fragmentation or mismatched job sizes).
  - Low utilization with significant Down time → hardware/maintenance or misconfiguration.
- CPU/GPU-hours usage
  - Use sreport to see total CPU/GPU-hours used by accounts/users and compare against cluster capacity to spot imbalances.
- Idle time vs pending work
  - Idle time + many pending jobs usually indicates resource fragmentation (small free slots that large jobs can’t use), partitions mismatches, or constraints (gpu/generic/exclusive).
  - Idle time + zero pending jobs suggests low demand.
- Backfill efficiency (from sdiag)
  - sdiag shows backfill opportunities and whether the scheduler filled them. Low backfill usage with available small jobs implies backfill policy or job-size/constraint mismatches.
- Scheduling latency (sdiag cycle times)
  - Long average/max scheduling cycle time can cause slow job starts and missed backfill windows. High slurmctld thread counts/RPCs can also indicate overload.
- Priority/fairshare effects (sprio + sshare)
  - If sprio shows many pending jobs have low priority due to fairshare or QOS weights, users may be waiting despite free nodes. Use sshare to confirm recent share consumption.
- Reservations and planned downtime
  - Reservations will reduce available capacity; sreport and scontrol_reservation_show reveal reservation usage and effect on utilization.
- Overcommit / wasted time
  - Overcommit shows where more resources were allocated than physical capacity (misconfig), while high wasted time can come from long node idle tails from large jobs finishing asynchronously.

3) Typical diagnosis patterns and checks (what to run)
- “Cluster overall utilization is low”
  - Run: sreport cluster utilization Start=... End=...
  - Check: sinfo (are nodes drained/down?), squeue (pending jobs count), sdiag (backfill windows), sprio (are jobs low-priority?), sshare (fairshare usage).
- “Many nodes idle, but jobs pending”
  - Run: squeue -o "%.18i %.50j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10l %.12R" (include Reason)
  - If Reason is Resources → check sinfo for states and node feature mismatches.
  - If Reason is Priority / QOS → run sprio and sshare.
  - If Reason is ReqNodeNotAvail → use sinfo_reasons to find drains or reasons.
- “Backfill opportunities are being missed”
  - Run: sdiag --all (look at backfill stats and windows), then squeue for candidate small jobs. If sdiag shows backfill windows but they’re unused, look for job constraints (gres, node feature).
- “Slow scheduling / many scheduling cycles”
  - Run: sdiag and scontrol show config (check SchedulerType, SchedulerParameters, and thread limits). High avg cycle times + high queue depth can point to tuning needs (increase threads, tune SelectTypeParameters, or reduce expensive job filters).
- “Fairshare starvation”
  - Run: sprio and sshare. If fairshare weight dominates and some users have low effective shares, consider temporary QOS bumps or adjust PriorityWeightFairshare.
- “GPU utilization low”
  - Run: sreport with TresName=GPU, scontrol_show_config, and sinfo -o to see GPU availability. Check job scripts for --gres=gpu:X vs actual usage (sstat for running jobs to measure GPU use if supported).

4) How to quantify backfill / packing efficiency (practical numbers to report)
- From sreport: total CPU/GPU usage (CPU/GPU-hours) and Allocated % for window.
- From sdiag: count of backfill opportunities, backfill jobs dispatched vs opportunities, average backfill window length.
- Useful derived metrics:
  - Utilization % (per partition).
  - Average wait time for jobs (from sreport or sacct).
  - Backfill fill ratio = (CPU-minutes actually backfilled) / (CPU-minutes available for backfill).
  - Fragmentation estimate = sum of small idle slots that cannot host the largest queued jobs (requires combining squeue and sinfo node sizes).

5) What to include when you file a utilization diagnostic to the admin/operator
- Time window and sreport output (Allocated %, Idle %, Down %, CPU/GPU-hours).
- sdiag output (scheduling cycle times, backfill stats, queue depth).
- Top pending reasons and a short squeue sample (jobid, name, user, state, time, reason).
- sprio top pending jobs and sshare snapshot.
- sinfo showing node counts by state (Allocated/Idle/Down/Drained) and any sinfo_reasons lines.
- Example: “During 2026-05-01..2026-05-03: cluster utilization 32% (sreport). sdiag shows avg cycle 120ms, max 2.3s, backfill opportunities 47 but backfill fill ratio 20%. sinfo shows 8/120 nodes drained. squeue shows 300 pending jobs; top pending reason=ReqNodeNotAvail for many GPU jobs.”
- This lets operators know whether the problem is demand (low job submission), supply (down nodes/reservations), fragmentation, or scheduler tuning.

6) Quick command checklist (copy/paste)
- Historical utilization: sreport cluster utilization Start=2026-04-01 End=2026-04-30
- Scheduler diagnostics: sdiag --all
- Queue snapshot, include Reason: squeue -o "%.18i %.50j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10l %.12R"
- Pending job priorities: sprio
- Fairshare: sshare -l
- Node states: sinfo -R  (or sinfo -N -l)
- Job detail: scontrol show job <JOBID>
- Reservations: scontrol show reservation
- License usage: scontrol_license

7) Remedies (common fixes)
- Reduce fragmentation: encourage job array/smaller chunked jobs, enable CB- or pack-based scheduling, tune DefMemPerCPU or SelectTypeParameters to improve packing.
- Improve backfill: relax excessive constraints, allow smaller GPUs/CPU jobs into backfill via QOS or partition config.
- Fix Down/Drained nodes: repair hardware or adjust maintenance windows (reduce planned down time).
- Address starvation: adjust fairshare weights, QOS limits, or increase priority for critical users.
- Scheduler tuning: increase slurmctld thread count, adjust SchedulerParameters (e.g., MaxJobCount, scheduling frequency), or use different scheduling algorithms if needed.

If you’d like, I can:
- Explain any specific sdiag line or sprio field you saw, or
- Run the exact commands above on your cluster and summarize results (I’ll need permission — tell me which time window or job IDs, or say “collect sreport and sdiag now”).

## PERFORMANCE[#SECTION_PERFORMANCE](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sdiag.html)
Executing sdiag sends a remote procedure call to slurmctld . If
enough calls from sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote
procedure calls to the slurmctld daemon come in at once, it can result in
a degradation of performance of the slurmctld daemon, possibly resulting
in a denial of service.
Do not run sdiag or other Slurm client commands that send remote procedure
calls to slurmctld from loops in shell scripts or other programs. Ensure
that programs limit calls to sdiag to the minimum necessary for the
information you are trying to gather.

results.prompt: Explain cluster utilization from Slurm reports and scheduler diagnostics
results.agent_response:
Below is a compact, practical guide to reading Slurm utilization from reports (sreport) and scheduler diagnostics (sdiag, sprio, etc.), what the key metrics mean, how to diagnose common causes of low utilization, and what to try to fix them.

What the tools show (quick map)
- sreport (historical/aggregate usage)
  - Purpose: node-/TRES- (CPU/GPU/memory) time accounting across time windows, users, accounts, QOS, partitions.
  - Key fields you’ll see: Allocated (time nodes had active jobs or active reservations), Idle (node time idle), Down (nodes fully Down/Drained or slurmctld unavailable), PlannedDown, OverCommitted, Reported, TresName/TresCount.
  - Use: get utilization percentages and trends (e.g., last 7/30/90 days), CPU-hours / GPU-hours per user/account/partition, wasted node-hours, and reservation impact.

- sdiag (scheduler diagnostics)
  - Purpose: runtime snapshot of scheduler health and efficiency.
  - Useful outputs: scheduling cycle times (avg/median/max per scheduling cycle), number of jobs considered, backfill statistics (how much time was available for backfill), queue depth, and fragmentation/backfill failures.
  - Use: detect long scheduler cycles (causes slow responses), poor backfill effectiveness, or pathological queue churn.

- sprio (priority diagnostics)
  - Purpose: shows priority scores and contributing factors (fairshare, age, job size, QOS, partition).
  - Use: understand why jobs are ordered the way they are and whether fairshare/age/QOS are suppressing particular users.

- sinfo / sinfo_reasons / sinfo_node
  - Purpose: current partition/node states and reasons for drain/down.
  - Use: find how many nodes are Idle/Allocated/Down and why (hardware, admin drain, etc.).

- squeue / scontrol show job / sstat / sacct
  - Purpose: live queue state, detailed job config, runtime resource usage, historical per-job accounting.
  - Use: verify why jobs are pending (pending reason column or scontrol show), check whether running jobs actually use requested resources (sstat) and whether time limits are accurate (sacct/sreport).

Key metrics and how to interpret them
- Allocated node-time (node-hours): time nodes were running active jobs. This is the numerator for utilization.
- Idle node-time: node-hours not doing useful work while available. Long idle time → low utilization.
- Down/Drained node-time: node-hours unavailable due to failures/maintenance → reduces capacity and can explain low allocated time.
- OverCommitted: time nodes had more requested resources than physically available (rare/misconfigured).
- Backfill efficiency: how often lower-priority jobs were scheduled into gaps without delaying higher-priority jobs. Poor backfill → unused small windows.
- Scheduling cycle time: how long the scheduler takes between decision cycles. Very long cycles reduce responsiveness and can let idle windows persist.
- Queue depth / pending job counts: many pending jobs can indicate resource shortage, but if nodes are idle while jobs pending, that points to mismatch/fragmentation or constraints.
- Priority breakdown (sprio): which factor (fairshare, age, QOS) dominates a job’s score.

High-level utilization math (conceptual)
- Simple utilization percent (over a period): Util% ≈ Allocated_node_hours / (Allocated_node_hours + Idle_node_hours + Down_node_hours + PlannedDown_node_hours)
- sreport can already compute and break this down by partition/account/user so use its “Utilization” reports for easier numbers.

How to diagnose low/odd utilization (step-by-step checklist)
1. Look at usage trends
   - Run sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-30days (or similar) to see allocated vs idle vs down by partition/account.
   - Note any large Down or PlannedDown time; those reduce capacity.

2. Confirm current state
   - sinfo to see idle vs allocated vs down node counts and per-partition sizes.
   - If many nodes are drained/down, call sinfo_reasons to get the reasons.

3. If nodes are idle but jobs are pending:
   - squeue (with reason column) to see pending reasons (Resources, Dependency, QOSLimit, Priority, PartitionState, License).
   - If squeue’s reason is empty or unclear, scontrol show job <jobid> for detailed reason.

4. Check scheduler efficiency
   - sdiag to see scheduling cycle times and backfill statistics. Long cycle times or low backfill utilization indicate scheduler-side inefficiency.
   - sprio to see if priorities keep lower-priority jobs from running even when capacity is idle.

5. Check job packing and fragmentation
   - Many small jobs that request whole nodes, or many diverse resource requests, cause fragmentation so small windows can’t be filled.
   - Use sreport or sacct to look at job shapes (NCPUs, nodes per job, runtime distributions).

6. Check actual resource usage of running jobs
   - sstat (for running jobs) or sacct (for finished jobs) to measure CPU%/GPU usage and memory. Jobs that request more resources than they use waste capacity.

7. Look for policy/limits
   - Check QOS, per-user/account limits (sacctmgr show associations), and licensing (scontrol_license) if license restrictions block jobs.
   - Confirm preemption or reservation policies that may hold nodes idle for priority jobs/reservations.

Common causes and fixes
- Inaccurate time limits → Backfill suffers. Ask users to set realistic times; enforce max runtime or use auto-cancel.
- Jobs request whole nodes but use few cores → enable multi-job packing (Node sharing) or encourage/require resource accounting and job-array/mpi wrappers.
- Small-job fragmentation → use backfill, allow smaller-job placement or node-sharing; build “short” partition for short jobs or use job arrays to consolidate.
- Long scheduler cycle times → reduce sprio/sdiag overheads: investigate complex plugins, limit over-large job churn, or tune scheduler parameters (e.g., SchedulerType, MaxJobCount considered). sdiag points to cycle time issues.
- Hardware faults/drains → fix/proactively maintain nodes; track sinfo_reasons to prioritize repairs.
- Fairshare/QOS suppressing users → review sprio output and adjust fairshare weights or QOS limits if needed.
- Licensing / other resource scarcity → scontrol_license shows license counts; if license-limited, either increase license pool or partition jobs differently.

Operational metrics to monitor continuously
- Cluster utilization % (daily/weekly/monthly) by partition and by important accounts.
- Backfill utilization (from sdiag and by comparing scheduled vs wasted backfill windows).
- Scheduler cycle times (median/95th percentile).
- Queue depth and average wait time per job size class (short vs long, small vs large).
- Node health: downtime percentages and top reasons from sinfo_reasons.
- Per-job efficiency: CPU/GPU utilization averages, and top offenders by wasted node-hours (sreport can help).

Practical commands to run for routine checks
- sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-30days
- sinfo -Nl (node-level status) and sinfo -R (reasons)
- squeue --long or squeue --format=... (include REASON) to inspect pending reasons
- sdiag
- sprio --debug or sprio -l
- sstat -j <jobid> for running-job usage; sacct -j <jobid> for finished-job accounting
- scontrol show config (to inspect scheduler timeouts and limits)
- scontrol_license (if license constraints are suspected)

Interpretation examples (what to watch for)
- High Idle + many Pending jobs → likely fragmentation, partition mismatch, or constraints (QOS/Feature/License).
- High Down time + low Allocated → capacity is reduced; fix hardware or adjust planned maintenance windows.
- Low Allocated but sdiag shows low backfill utilization → time-limit inaccuracies or scheduler itemization problem.
- Large difference between requested CPUs and sstat CPU% → users over-request resources; consider enforcing stricter job templates or CPU accounting.

Bottom line / Actionable priorities
- Use sreport for trend-level utilization and to quantify wasted node-hours (allocated vs idle vs down).
- Use sdiag and sprio to find scheduler-level inefficiencies (cycle time, backfill, priority suppression).
- Correlate sreport findings with sinfo/squeue/sstat to find whether the problem is capacity (nodes down), fragmentation/requests, or scheduling policy.
- Fixes are usually: improve job time estimates, enable better packing/node-sharing, tune scheduler/backfill settings, repair nodes faster, and adjust fairshare/QOS/policies.

If you want, I can:
- Show the exact sreport/sdiag/sprio commands and example outputs to look for, or
- Walk through your cluster’s recent sreport + sdiag outputs if you share them (I can interpret concrete numbers and give prioritized recommendations).

The backfill scheduling plugin is loaded by default.
Without backfill scheduling, each partition is scheduled strictly in priority
order, which typically results in significantly lower system utilization and

results.prompt: Explain cluster utilization from Slurm reports and scheduler diagnostics
results.agent_response:
Good question — interpreting “cluster utilization” in Slurm is best done by combining sreport (historical usage), real‑time views (sinfo/squeue), and scheduler diagnostics (sdiag, sprio, sshare). Below I summarize the key metrics, what they mean, what to run to check them, how to interpret common patterns, and common mitigations.

What “utilization” means in Slurm
- sreport cluster utilization: primary authoritative metric for historical utilization. Key fields:
  - Allocated = time nodes were in use by jobs or active reservations (counts CPU/GPU minutes or node-minutes depending on format).
  - Idle = time nodes were idle/available.
  - Down/PlannedDown = maintenance or controller downtime.
  - OverCommitted = time more resources were reported used than nominal (rare).
  - TresCount/Used = concrete resource usage counts (CPU‑hours, GPU‑hours).
- Simple utilization percent ≈ Allocated / (Allocated + Idle + Down + PlannedDown). sreport prints these for you; don’t try to recompute without reading the report fields.

Real‑time checks to correlate with historical numbers
- sinfo – show partition/node states (how many nodes allocated/idle/drained/down).
- squeue – show current RUNNING vs PENDING jobs and pending reasons.
- scontrol show job <id> – detailed reason/constraints for a pending job.
- sacct – per‑job historical usage if you need job lengths, exit codes, wasted time.

Scheduler diagnostics and why they matter
- sdiag — shows scheduling cycle times, backfill efficiency, queue depth. Useful to detect:
  - Long scheduler cycles (slurmctld overloaded) => scheduling delays and apparent idle time while jobs wait.
  - Poor backfill efficiency => wasted small gaps that could have been filled by short jobs.
- sprio — shows priority components (fairshare, age, QOS). If many jobs are pending with low priority, sprio shows which factor is keeping them low.
- sshare — shows effective shares/fairshare usage (who has used their fair share).
- scontrol show config / scontrol ping — scheduler config and health; check scheduling parameters (e.g., bf_interval, MaxJobCount limits, PreemptMode, SchedulerType).

Common utilization patterns, what they mean, and checks
1) Low allocated / high idle (low utilization)
   - Possible causes: lack of jobs, users hitting job size/feature constraints, reservations, node features (GRES/GPU mismatch), user/account limits, partition restrictions.
   - Checks: squeue (few jobs), sinfo (idle nodes in partitions users submit to?), squeue --states=PENDING to see why pending, scontrol show job for pending reason.
   - Mitigations: advertise/educate users, loosen constraining features/QOS, remove unnecessary reservations, reconfigure partitions, enable backfill or better packing.

2) Idle nodes but many pending jobs
   - Possible causes: job requests don’t match free resources (e.g., need 4 GPUs but only nodes with 8 are available but reserved/exclusive?), job feature/GRES mismatches, software/license constraints, association/user limits.
   - Checks: squeue with REASON column, scontrol_show for a representative pending job, scontrol_license to check license contention.
   - Mitigations: adjust job submission scripts or partition GRES, relax exclusive node policies, adjust association limits or QOS, create reservations for important workloads.

3) High queue depth with moderate/high allocated (high contention)
   - Possible causes: cluster at steady high utilization and many jobs queued for large resource requests; fragmentation where lots of small free resources can’t satisfy big jobs.
   - Checks: sreport job sizes, sdiag backfill statistics, sacct to see distribution of job sizes/lengths.
   - Mitigations: encourage job packing (--share or --ntasks-per-node tuning), change scheduling policies to favor throughput, reserve time windows for large jobs, adjust backfill settings or enable preemption where appropriate.

4) Poor backfill efficiency
   - Symptom: sdiag shows low backfill utilization; short jobs could have run but didn’t.
   - Causes: scheduler parameters (bf_interval, bf_continue), long scheduling cycles, job constraints, large blocking jobs.
   - Checks: sdiag backfill stats, squeue to identify very large LONG jobs blocking the queue, sprio to see priorities.
   - Mitigations: tune backfill parameters, reduce block sizes or alter job priorities/partitions, allow smaller jobs to run on shared nodes.

5) Apparent low utilization because of Down/Drained nodes
   - Symptom: sreport shows significant Down time.
   - Checks: sinfo_reasons, sinfo to list nodes in DRAIN/DOWN, sinfo_node for per-node details.
   - Mitigations: repair nodes, reconfigure maintenance windows, remove or reduce planned drains during peak usage.

6) Scheduler lag / slurmctld overload
   - Symptom: sdiag shows long cycle times or backlog; many jobs waiting although resources exist.
   - Checks: sdiag cycle stats, scontrol show config for cycle timing, system metrics on slurmctld host.
   - Mitigations: increase slurmctld resources, reduce scheduling load (less frequent job submissions), tune scheduling interval and backfill params.

What specific Slurm commands to run (quick checklist)
- Get historical utilization (example):
  - sreport cluster utilization Start=2026-04-01 End=2026-04-30
- Real‑time resource state:
  - sinfo -o "%P %D %a %l %E"  (or just sinfo)
- Current queue and reasons:
  - squeue -o "%.18i %.9P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10L %.10R"
  - For a specific pending job: scontrol show job <jobid>
- Scheduler diagnostics:
  - sdiag
  - sprio -l (or sprio --verbose)
  - sshare -l
- Node reasons:
  - sinfo -R
  - sinfo -N --long
- Licenses:
  - scontrol_license
- Historical job details:
  - sacct -u <user> --starttime=2026-04-01 --format=JobID,JobName,State,Elapsed,ReqCPUS,ReqGRES,MaxRSS

Interpreting numbers: heuristics
- Utilization > ~80% often indicates good throughput but watch queue wait times and fairness.
- Utilization < ~50% may be a sign of underuse (but acceptable for experimental clusters or for ensuring low latency).
- Backfill efficiency should be high for clusters with variable job sizes; low backfill + long queued jobs indicates tuning opportunity.

Short checklist to diagnose low utilization quickly
1. sreport cluster utilization (time window) — confirm the scale of the problem.
2. sinfo — confirm idle vs drained/down nodes and partition distribution.
3. squeue (pending reasons) — find why jobs aren’t starting.
4. sdiag + sprio + sshare — check scheduler health, backfill, and priority/fairshare reasons.
5. scontrol show job <example pending job> — detailed constraints and reasons.
6. sacct — check job size/length mix (many short jobs cause fragmentation).

When you have specific sreport, sdiag, sinfo, or squeue output I can interpret the numbers and point to exact causes and tuning options. If you want, provide an sreport/sdiag/sinfo output and I’ll analyze it and give targeted recommendations.

results.prompt: Explain cluster utilization from Slurm reports and scheduler diagnostics
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise guide to what “cluster utilization” means in Slurm, which Slurm reports/tools expose the important metrics, how to read them, common utilization problems and how to diagnose them, and the common levers you can use to improve utilization.

What “utilization” means
- At a basic level it’s how much of the cluster capacity is doing useful work over a time window.
  - Node/CPU/GPU utilization: fraction of node/CPU/GPU time allocated to active jobs vs total available time.
  - Job efficiency: how much of the allocated resources each job actually uses (CPU%, memory RSS, GPU usage).
  - Scheduling/backfill efficiency: how well the scheduler fills gaps in the schedule (short jobs, small jobs) without delaying larger jobs.
- Slurm expresses these as alloc-times (node-hours / cpu-hours / gpu-hours), percent utilization, and derived ratios (backfill efficiency, queue wait times).

Key Slurm tools and the metrics they provide (what to run and why)
- sreport (cluster utilization reports)
  - Best for summary usage over a time window (Allocated, Down, Idle, Utilization, CPU-hours, GPU-hours).
  - Use for accounting-level reports: utilization by account/user/QoS/partition.
  - Example: sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-7days End=now
- sinfo
  - Current partition/node states (allocated/idle/drain/down), per-node resources (CPUs, memory, GPUs).
  - Use to see physical capacity and which nodes are unavailable.
  - Example: sinfo -N -l
- squeue
  - Real-time view of running vs pending jobs and pending reasons.
  - For “why jobs aren’t starting” start with squeue (look at the REASON column).
  - Example: squeue --states=RUNNING,PENDING -o "%.18i %.20P %.20j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10R"
- sdiag
  - Scheduler diagnostics: scheduling cycles, backfill stats, server thread count, queue depth, dispatch counters.
  - Use when you suspect scheduler throughput/backfill problems, or many short jobs.
  - Example: sdiag
- sprio and sshare
  - sprio: per-job priority factors (fairshare, age, QOS, partition) — helps explain why some jobs are low priority.
  - sshare: fairshare usage and effective shares by user/account.
- sstat (and job-level monitoring)
  - Real-time job resource usage (CPU%, memory RSS, I/O) for running jobs.
  - Use to measure actual utilization vs requested.
- sacct
  - Historical accounting: job durations, requested vs used resources, exit codes — for efficiency and waste analysis.
  - Example: sacct -S 2026-04-01 -E 2026-04-30 --format=JobID,User,JobName,State,Elapsed,ReqCPUS,MaxRSS
- scontrol show config / scontrol show node / scontrol show job
  - Inspect scheduler/node/job configuration that affects allocation and packing.
- scontrol_reservation_show
  - Shows reservations that reduce available capacity.

What each metric tells you (how to interpret)
- sreport “Allocated” and “Utilization” (over interval)
  - Allocated = time nodes were used for active jobs or reservations.
  - Utilization (%) = Allocated time / (Available time minus Down/Maintenance time). Low % means idle capacity or blocked capacity.
- sinfo NODES(A/I/D)
  - Check the A/I/D counts: if Idle (I) is high, jobs aren’t being scheduled to them (fragmentation, constraints, reservations, or pending reasons).
- squeue pending reasons
  - Common reasons: Resources, QOSLimit, Priority, Dependency, PartitionDown, ReqNodeNotAvail.
  - “Resources” + idle nodes often implies resource mismatches (gres, feature, memory) or fragmentation.
- sdiag backfill stats
  - Low backfill usage when there are gaps suggests packing/fragmentation or conservative backfill window calculations.
- sprio/sshare
  - A user’s large share deficit or low priority weight can starve smaller/short jobs — fairshare or QOS limits may be the cause.
- sstat / sacct usage vs requests
  - Jobs that request more CPUs/GPUs/memory than they use indicate over-requesting (wasteful). For example, low CPU% or MaxRSS much lower than ReqMem signals inefficiency.
- Node “Down/Drained”
  - Nodes taken out reduce usable capacity; sinfo_reasons can show why they’re down.

Common utilization problems, causes, and the diagnostic checklist
1) Low cluster utilization despite queued jobs
   - Check: squeue (REASON), sinfo (idle nodes), scontrol_reservation_show (reservations).
   - Causes: partition/node constraints (features, GRES like GPUs), reservations, oversized resource requests (job asks for full node), affinity/packing policy prevents placement, per-user/account limits, or scheduler not backfilling effectively.
2) High utilization but long queue wait times
   - Check: sdiag (scheduling throughput), sprio (priorities), sshare (fairshare), sacct (job sizes).
   - Causes: cluster is saturated with long or large jobs; priority/fairshare/QoS limits favor certain users; insufficient backfill.
3) Many nodes partially used (fragmentation)
   - Check: scontrol show config (allocation/SelectTypeParameters), sdiag, squeue.
   - Causes: allocation policy (ONE_PER_NODE vs pack), job shapes (many single-core jobs scattered), lack of node sharing.
4) Jobs use far less than requested resources
   - Check: sstat (running), sacct (historical MaxRSS, CPU), sreport usage by user.
   - Causes: users over-request resources — leads to wasted reserved capacity.
5) GPU-specific underutilization
   - Check: sinfo for GRES allocation, squeue for jobs holding GPUs, job-level GPU telemetry (nvidia-smi inside jobs).
   - Causes: jobs reserve entire GPUs but don’t use them, GPU drivers/visibility issues, or wrong gres types requested.

Practical step-by-step diagnostic workflow
- Quick snapshot: sinfo -N -l and squeue -o "%i %u %t %M %R %D" to map idle/allocated nodes to queued jobs and reasons.
- If many pending jobs: inspect the REASON column. If no reason, scontrol show job <jobid>.
- If utilization low but nodes are idle: check for reservations (scontrol_reservation_show) and node features/gres mismatches.
- If scheduler behavior suspect: run sdiag to check scheduling cycles, backfill, and dispatch counters.
- For efficiency: run sacct over the window of interest and compare ReqCPUS/ReqMem to Elapsed/MaxRSS and sum CPU/GPU-hours (sreport or sreport cluster TopUsage).
- For priority/fairshare: use sprio and sshare to see if priorities are skewed.
- For running-job efficiency: use sstat on long-running jobs to measure actual CPU% and memory use.

Tuning levers to improve utilization
- Encourage right-sizing: enforce sensible default limits, submit templates, or request review for oversized jobs; use job submit filters.
- Packing and allocation policy: adjust SelectTypeParameters and SchedulerParameters to pack tasks onto fewer nodes when desired (or conversely enable more spreading).
- Backfill tuning: adjust backfill window parameters (SchedulerParameters, bf_continue) so small jobs get scheduled into gaps.
- QOS/account limits and fairshare: change QOS weights, set per-account or per-user limits to prevent a few users from starving others.
- Reservations and maintenance scheduling: minimize use or schedule during low-demand windows.
- Preemption policies: use preemption for short/interactive jobs if acceptable.
- Elastic scaling (cloud/elastic nodes): add capacity during peak windows if supported.
- Monitoring: add finer-grained job telemetry (CPU, GPU, memory time-series) and enforce or report inefficiencies to users.

Useful example commands (summary)
- sreport cluster Utilization Start=now-30days End=now
- sinfo -N -l
- squeue --states=RUNNING,PENDING -o "%.18i %.20P %.25j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.8D %.20R"
- sdiag
- sprio
- sshare
- sacct -S YYYY-MM-DD -o JobID,User,JobName,State,Elapsed,ReqCPUS,MaxRSS

What to present to stakeholders
- Utilization headline: % node/CPU/GPU utilization over the period (from sreport).
- Waste metrics: CPU/GPU-hours requested vs used, % of jobs that underutilize requested resources (from sacct/sstat).
- Queue health: average wait time, number of pending jobs, common pending reasons (from squeue and sdiag).
- Recommendations: quick wins (enforce request sizes, tune backfill), medium-term (adjust QOS/fairshare), long-term (capacity expansion or elastic nodes).

If you want, I can:
- Run a short diagnostic on your live cluster (sinfo + squeue + sdiag + sprio) and summarize what’s currently limiting utilization — tell me which cluster/partitions to inspect or I can use defaults.
