results.prompt: Explain partition constraints and availability for debug
results.agent_response:
Good — here’s a concise explanation of what “partition constraints” and “availability” mean for the debug partition, how they affect job scheduling, and the quick checks you can run.

What a partition (e.g., "debug") can constrain
- Timelimit (TIMELIMIT): max walltime a job may request in that partition (debug often very short, e.g., 30m). Jobs requesting longer than this will be refused or placed in a different partition.
- Job size limits: max/min nodes, tasks, CPUs or memory per job that the partition allows.
- Access controls: which accounts, users, groups, or QOS can submit to the partition (AllowAccounts/AllowGroups/Default/RootOnly).
- Node membership: which nodes are in the partition (Nodes or NodeSet). Nodes may be shared across partitions but with different limits.
- Features/GRES expectations: the partition may be intended for nodes with specific features (e.g., gpu, fastnet). Jobs that use --constraint or --gres must match available node attributes.
- QOS/priority limits: a partition may be associated with particular QOS that impose MaxJobs, MaxWall, or other limits taking effect before user/account limits.
- Reservation and maintenance flags: reservations may reserve debug nodes for a time window; nodes can be drained/down for maintenance and removed from availability.

What “availability” (as shown by sinfo) means and how to read it
- Use sinfo to inspect partition state:
  - sinfo -s or sinfo --partition=debug --long
- Key columns you’ll see:
  - AVAIL / State: whether the partition is administratively up/down and usable.
  - TIMELIMIT: the partition walltime limit.
  - NODES(A/I/O/T) or NODES column: summary of nodes and states. NODES(A/I/O/T) typically shown as Allocated/Idle/Other/Total.
    - Allocated (A): nodes currently running jobs for that partition.
    - Idle (I): nodes free for immediate allocation — these are the nodes eligible for new jobs.
    - Other (O): nodes in other states (drain, down, reserved, etc.).
    - Total (T): total nodes assigned to the partition.
- Example sinfo summary and interpretation:
  - debug up 30:00 0/8/0/8 dev[0-7]
    - TIMELIMIT 30:00, 8 total nodes, 0 allocated, 8 idle → 8 nodes available for new jobs.
  - debug up 30:00 0/0/8/8 dev[0-7]
    - 0 idle, 8 in "other" (likely drained/down/reserved) → no nodes currently available to schedule jobs.

Common reasons debug jobs don’t start (check in this order)
1. Walltime or size exceeds partition limits (request shorter time or smaller node count).
2. Job’s constraints/features do not match any idle node (job used --constraint, --gres, or requested a feature not present).
3. No idle nodes (allocated or reserved) — check NODES(A/I/O/T) in sinfo.
4. Reservation holds the nodes (check scontrol show reservation / squeue --reservation=<name>).
5. User/account/QoS limits or association caps prevent scheduling (check sacctmgr or QOS).
6. Nodes are in DRAIN/DOWN for maintenance (sinfo --states=drain,down or sinfo -N).
7. Pending reasons from the queue (use squeue -p debug to see pending reason strings; for a single job use scontrol show job <jobid> to get the detailed reason).

Quick commands to inspect the debug partition and a job
- Partition/node status:
  - sinfo -s                  # short summary for all partitions
  - sinfo --partition=debug --long
  - sinfo -N --partition=debug   # one line per node
  - sinfo --states=drained,down --partition=debug
- Queue and pending reasons:
  - squeue -p debug
  - squeue -p debug -o "%.18i %.9P %.8j %.8u %.2t %.10M %.10l %.6D %R"  # custom format including REASON
  - scontrol show job <jobid>   # detailed job info & pending reason
- Reservations and access:
  - scontrol show reservation
  - scontrol show partition debug   # if available on your system for partition details
  - sacctmgr list associations or sacctmgr show user <user>  # for account / association limits

Practical tips
- Debug partitions are typically configured to favor very short, small runs: ask for the lowest necessary walltime and node count.
- If you need longer or larger runs, submit to a non-debug partition.
- If your job requests GPUs or specific features, run sinfo -N -o "%N %f %G" (or equivalent) to confirm nodes in debug actually have that feature/GRES.
- When in doubt, check squeue for the job’s pending reason; it’s usually explicit (Resources, Priority, ReqNodeNotAvail, QOSMaxJobs, etc.).

If you want, I can:
- Check the current cluster’s debug partition status now (sinfo) and show how many idle nodes are available; or
- Inspect a specific job in the debug partition (provide job ID) and report why it’s pending.

Slurm's hierarchical limits are enforced in the following order

flag 'OverPartQOS':

- Job QOS limit
- User association
- Account association(s), ascending the hierarchy
- Root/Cluster association
- Partition limit
- None

results.prompt: Explain how license availability affects a future sbatch submission
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- When you request a software license in sbatch, Slurm treats that license like a shared cluster resource. If the requested license count isn't available at scheduling time, your job will remain PENDING until enough licenses are free — it will not start even if compute nodes are idle.
- Licenses are allocated at job start and released when the job (or job step) ends.

How you request a license
- Command-line: sbatch -L license_name:count script.sh
  - Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 myjob.sh
- Or request via TRES: --tres-per-task=license/<name>=N (requires that the license tres is listed in AccountingStorageTRES in slurm.conf).

Where licenses are configured
- Local licenses: configured in slurm.conf (Licenses=...). View with scontrol show lic.
- Remote/dynamic licenses: configured in the accounting DB via sacctmgr and can be periodically updated (LastConsumed/LastDeficit) so Slurm knows how many are effectively available.

How availability affects scheduling (key points)
- Scheduling requirement: Both compute resources (nodes/CPUs/GPUs) AND the requested license(s) must be available for a job to be started. If either is missing, the job stays PENDING.
- Pending reasons: A job waiting for licenses will remain PD and the squeue pending-reason will reflect resource/license constraints (check squeue for the specific reason).
- If you ask for more licenses than exist (or more than the cluster can ever provide), the job will never be satisfied and will remain pending indefinitely unless changed.
- Remote license deficits and reservations: sacctmgr/remote updates can set aside licenses (Reserved/LastDeficit/LastConsumed). Even if Total looks large, Reserved/LastDeficit can reduce Free, causing jobs to wait.

How to inspect and troubleshoot
- Check available counts: scontrol show lic (or scontrol show lic LicenseName=<name>)
  - Output has Total, Used, Free, Reserved, Remote, LastConsumed/LastDeficit for remote licenses.
- See why a specific job is pending: squeue (shows PD and a reason). For more detail, scontrol show job <jobid>.
- If jobs are stuck waiting for licenses while nodes are free, check the license counts (scontrol show lic) and talk to admins to sync with the license server (dynamic license updates via sacctmgr may be needed).

Best practices
- Request only the number of licenses actually needed.
- Prefer TRES-based license accounting if you want per-task granularity — ensure AccountingStorageTRES is configured.
- If using remote license servers, run a periodic sync/update so LastConsumed/LastDeficit reflect reality.
- If a workflow needs guaranteed access, coordinate via reservations or talk to admins to carve out license capacity.

If you want, I can show the current license counts on your cluster (scontrol show lic) or explain the exact pending reason for a specific pending job — which would require running scontrol/squeue.

results.prompt: Explain how license availability affects a future sbatch submission
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- Slurm treats software licenses as cluster-wide consumable resources (TRES). If a job requests a license (sbatch -L name:N or via --tres-per-task), the scheduler will not start the job until that many licenses are available. If they are not available, the job stays PENDING.

What happens when you sbatch with a license request
- Request syntax:
  - sbatch -L <license_name>:<count> script.sh
  - or request it via a TRES (e.g., --tres-per-task=license/<name>=<count>) if your cluster uses AccountingStorageTRES.
- Scheduling effect:
  - The requested license is treated like any other scarce resource (CPUs, GPUs). The job will remain pending until Free >= requested count.
  - Slurm shows license totals as Total, Used, Free (scontrol show lic).
  - While pending, the job blocks other jobs that also request the same license if not enough free licenses remain.
- Visibility:
  - Pending reason columns in squeue may indicate license/resource shortage (you may see a resources/license-related pending reason).
  - Use scontrol show lic or sacctmgr show resource to inspect counts for a specific license (example license name: ansys).
- Reservation/consumption timing:
  - Slurm reserves/allocates license counts as part of scheduling. The cluster reports Used/Free so administrators and the scheduler know how many are reserved/consumed. (Administrators can configure dynamic/remote license updates; see next point.)
- Dynamic/remote licenses:
  - If your cluster integrates with an external license server, Slurm can be updated with the external usage (LastConsumed/LastDeficit), and Slurm will account for those values when deciding availability. Administrators update these with sacctmgr scripts or tools.

Operational notes / pitfalls
- If you request more licenses than exist (or than are currently free), the job will remain pending until licenses are freed or admin updates counts.
- If your site uses --tres-per-task for licenses, the license must be present in AccountingStorageTRES and sacctmgr-managed resources.
- Administrators can check and debug license contention with scontrol show lic, sacctmgr show resource, and by reading squeue pending reasons.

Example
- Submit: sbatch -L ansys:2 job.sh
- Inspect: scontrol show lic  (shows LicenseName=ansys Total=100 Used=2 Free=98)
- If Free < 2, the job will stay PENDING until at least 2 become free.

If you want, I can show the current license counts on your cluster (scontrol show lic / functions.scontrol_license). Would you like me to check?

results.prompt: Explain how license availability affects a future sbatch submission
results.agent_response:
Short answer: Slurm treats software licenses as cluster-wide allocatable resources. If your sbatch requests a license that isn’t free at schedule time, the job will stay PENDING until enough of that license becomes available.

Details — what happens and what to check
- How to request: use sbatch -L name:count (also written --licenses=name:count), or request a license via TRES (e.g., --tres-per-task=license/foo) if the license is configured in AccountingStorageTRES.
- Where licenses are defined: local licenses are configured in slurm.conf (Licenses=...), remote/dynamic licenses are configured/managed with sacctmgr.
- Scheduling behavior: the scheduler treats licenses like a shared TRES. A job that requests N of license X will only be eligible to start when at least N licenses X are free. If not enough are free, the job remains PENDING (reason will indicate resource/license unavailability).
- Allocation lifecycle: when the job starts Slurm increments Used and decrements Free for that license; when the job finishes those license units are released back to Free.
- Remote/dynamic licenses: if admins sync LastConsumed (from an external license server) into the DB, Slurm may account for deficits (LastDeficit) and withhold allocations until the deficit is resolved — this can make jobs stay pending even when the configured Total looks sufficient.
- Failure modes to watch for: requesting more licenses than Total (job will not start until changed); requesting via --tres-per-task without the AccountingStorageTRES mapping (the request may be ignored or misrouted).
- Useful commands (ask your admin or run if you have permissions): scontrol show lic (shows Total/Used/Free), sacctmgr show resource (for remote license config), and squeue / scontrol show job to see pending reason and job license request details.

Recommendation: before submitting, check the license Free count (scontrol show lic LicenseName=<name>) and request only the number you actually need (sbatch -L name:count). If jobs still stay pending and license counts look OK, contact your admins to verify remote-license sync / LastConsumed / LastDeficit settings.

Slurm can help with software license management by assigning available
licenses to jobs at scheduling time. If the licenses are not available, jobs
are kept pending until licenses become available. Licenses in Slurm are
essentially shared resources, meaning configured resources that are not tied to

results.prompt: Explain how license availability affects a future sbatch submission
results.agent_response:
Short answer
- If a job requests a software license when you run sbatch (for example sbatch -L ansys:2), the scheduler treats that license as a cluster resource (a TRES). The job may be accepted but will remain PENDING until the requested license count is available. Slurm will not start the job unless it can allocate the requested licenses.

What happens end-to-end
1. Admin config
   - Licenses are configured either in slurm.conf (local licenses) or in the accounting DB via sacctmgr (remote/dynamic licenses). Each license has a Total count; Slurm tracks Used and Free counts.
   - If you use license requests via TRES (--tres-per-task or --tres), the license name must also appear in AccountingStorageTRES so usage is recorded.

2. How users request licenses
   - Short form: sbatch -L license_name:count script.sh
   - TRES form: sbatch --tres-per-task=license/license_name=count (or --tres=...) depending on your site
   - Either method declares the job’s license needs to the scheduler.

3. Scheduling and start-time behavior
   - The scheduler checks license availability when considering a job for allocation. If the Free count for that license is less than the job’s request, the job stays PENDING.
   - Jobs do not consume license counts until they are allocated/started; Used counts update when the allocation is made (you can see this with scontrol show lic).
   - Backfill/priority still respects license counts: a lower-priority job can only start if enough licenses are free at the time it would start.

4. Local vs remote/dynamic licenses
   - Local licenses (configured in slurm.conf) are static counts maintained by slurmctld.
   - Remote/dynamic licenses can be updated from an external license server (via sacctmgr updates). Slurm uses LastConsumed/LastDeficit info to avoid oversubscription; administrators can push dynamic counts into Slurm so scheduling reflects real license availability.

5. Effects on users and common outcomes
   - Submission is usually accepted; the job becomes PENDING with a reason related to resources/licenses until licenses free up.
   - Jobs do not fail just because licenses are unavailable at submit time; they wait.
   - If you over-request licenses (request more than Total), the job will never start until the request or the license counts are changed.

How to check and troubleshoot
- Check configured and current counts: scontrol show lic  (or scontrol show lic LicenseName=ansys)
- See why a job is pending: squeue -j <jobid> (look at the REASON column) and for more detail scontrol show job <jobid>
- Admins can inspect/adjust license resources with sacctmgr (add/update resource) and push dynamic counts if integrated with a license server.

Example
- Cluster has Licenses=ansys:10, 8 are used → Free=2.
- sbatch -L ansys:3 script.sh → job accepted but stays PENDING until at least 3 licenses are free (e.g., when other jobs release them).

If you want, I can show current license counts on this cluster (scontrol show lic) or explain how to convert an sbatch -L request into a --tres request for your site.

results.prompt: Explain how license availability affects a future sbatch submission
results.agent_response:
Summary — how licenses affect an sbatch submission

- What a "license" is in Slurm
  - A license in Slurm is a cluster-wide shared resource (not tied to a specific node). Examples: license=ansys, fluent, etc.
  - Licenses are configured either in slurm.conf (local licenses) or in the SlurmDB (remote/dynamic licenses).

- How you request licenses when submitting
  - sbatch -L <name>:<count> (short) or sbatch --licenses=<name>:<count>.
    Example: sbatch -L ansys:2 script.sh
  - Alternatively you can request a license as a TRES: --tres-per-task=license/ansys=1 (requires the license be listed in AccountingStorageTRES).

- Scheduling behavior
  - The scheduler treats licenses like any other scarce shared resource. A job that requests N of a license will not be eligible to start until at least N free licenses exist.
  - If the requested license count is not available at submit/schedule time, the job remains PENDING and will be released when enough licenses become free.
  - When a job is allocated, Slurm decrements the license “Free” count and increments “Used”; when the job completes the count is returned.

- Dynamic and remote license effects
  - For remote/dynamic licenses, administrators can update the LastConsumed value (e.g., via sacctmgr) from an external license server. Slurm uses LastConsumed and computes LastDeficit to avoid overcommitting licenses that appear missing.
  - If LastDeficit indicates licenses are missing, the scheduler will reserve (set aside) those licenses and may keep jobs pending even if the total configured count looks sufficient.

- Practical consequences you should expect
  - If you submit with -L and licenses are currently in use, your job will queue and wait for licenses rather than fail.
  - If you forget to request a license that your job’s software actually needs, the job may start but later fail when the software cannot check out a license (that check is external to Slurm). Requesting the license via Slurm is the way to make scheduling respect that dependency.
  - Use --tres-per-task when you want per-task accounting of licenses; ensure the license TRES is configured in AccountingStorageTRES.

- How to check license status (admin/user commands)
  - scontrol show lic (or the scontrol_license view) shows LicenseName, Total, Used, Free.
  - Administrators use sacctmgr to add/update resources and to adjust LastConsumed for dynamic setups.

If you want, I can show the current license list/free counts on your cluster (scontrol show lic). Would you like me to check that?

results.prompt: Explain safe steps for maintenance reservations without changing state
results.agent_response:
Below are concise, safe, read-only steps and best practices for planning and using Slurm maintenance reservations while avoiding node state changes (drain/down) until you are explicitly ready to modify nodes.

1) Plan the window and scope
- Choose nodes (or partitions) and a maintenance window (start time + duration). Prefer low-usage windows.
- Decide whether you need to take nodes completely offline at the maintenance start (this would be a state change later) or just prevent new long-running jobs from starting.

2) Verify current and near-future usage (read-only checks you should run)
- Check current queue and running jobs: squeue (filter by nodes/partition or user).
- Check node/partition availability and counts: sinfo.
- For long-running jobs that could overlap your window, inspect historical runtimes with sacct (user or job filters).
- Check existing reservations: scontrol show reservation (or scontrol show res) and squeue --reservation=<name> to see jobs tied to a reservation.

3) Create the reservation (conceptual / best-practice options)
- Use an advanced reservation with the MAINT (maintenance) flag to mark it as maintenance. MAINT reservations are useful because:
  - They are shown as maintenance in reservation listings.
  - They may overlap other reservations but will prevent jobs that cannot finish before the MAINT start from being started.
  - They appear in usage/reporting as planned downtime.
- If you want the reservation to be a floating window relative to now, use TIME_FLOAT (start=now + offset) so it “floats.”
- Do NOT use flags=IGNORE_JOBS unless you intend to force-cancel or override running jobs — that would evict jobs and is not “safe” if you want to avoid involuntary changes.

Example (conceptual) form:
scontrol create reservation ReservationName=maint-YYYYMMDD StartTime=YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm Duration=minutes Nodes=node[01-04] Flags=MAINT Users=admin

(Do not run that command unless you intend to create the reservation — it changes cluster state.)

4) Minimize user impact without changing node state
- Set the reservation start time a little in the future so you (and users) can see it and react.
- Restrict who can use the reservation (Users= or Account=) so only maintenance jobs or admins can submit into it.
- Use small, rolling reservations (a subset of nodes) to allow staggered maintenance and reduce impact.
- Communicate the window to users and request they avoid launching jobs that exceed the window.

5) Verify effects (read-only checks after creation)
- Confirm the reservation exists and which nodes it covers: scontrol show reservation ReservationName=<name>.
- See which queued/running jobs are tied to or will be affected: squeue --reservation=<name> and squeue filtered to the nodes/partition.
- Use sinfo to see partition/node summaries; some displays will show reserved/maint counts.

6) If you ultimately need nodes idle at start (operations that require state changes)
- Two safe options:
  - Encourage users to finish jobs before the reservation and rely on the MAINT reservation to prevent new long jobs from starting.
  - At a predetermined time, explicitly change node state (e.g., drain) — note: that is a cluster-state change and must be performed deliberately with appropriate operator approval and user notice.

7) Rollback / cleanup (post-maintenance)
- After maintenance, remove or end the reservation (scontrol delete reservation=<name>) and confirm nodes return to normal scheduling. (Deleting the reservation is a mutating action.)

8) Short checklist before executing any mutating step
- Confirm active/running jobs that would be affected (squeue).
- Confirm no critical jobs are running on the targets (sacct / job owners).
- Notify affected users and operations staff.
- Use staged/reservations for rolling maintenance where possible.

Key cautions & behavior notes
- MAINT reservations will prevent starting jobs that cannot complete before the reservation start, but they do not automatically evict running jobs unless ignore_jobs or manual eviction/drain is used.
- Creating a reservation is a state change — plan and communicate before issuing it.
- If you want to avoid any immediate node state change, rely on MAINT reservations + user coordination rather than draining nodes.

References / commands you will normally use for the read-only parts
- squeue (jobs), sinfo (partitions/nodes), sacct (historical runtimes), scontrol show reservation (reservation details), squeue --reservation=<name> (jobs tied to reservation).

If you want, I can:
- Draft a concrete reservation command and a pre-check list for your specific nodes and window (this would be a mutating intent: I must hand off to an operator to create the reservation), or
- Run the read-only checks for your targeted nodes/partition/time (sinfo, squeue, sacct) before you create anything — tell me which nodes/partition and time window to inspect.

## Reservations Floating Through Time [#float](https://slurm.schedmd.com/reservations.html)
Slurm can be used to create an advanced reservation with a start time that
remains a fixed period of time in the future.
These reservation are not intended to run jobs, but to prevent long running
jobs from being initiated on specific nodes.
That node might be placed in a DRAINING state to prevent any new jobs
from being started there.
Alternately, an advanced reservation might be placed on the node to prevent
jobs exceeding some specific time limit from being started.
Attempts by users to make use of a reservation with a floating start time will

1) Define the maintenance window and scope
- Choose concrete StartTime (ISO or relative like "now+2hours") and Duration.
- Decide nodes vs. partition vs. node count. Prefer a specific node list when taking nodes fully offline for maintenance.
- Decide access controls (Users, Accounts, QOS) and whether the reservation should be visible/attractive to jobs (magnetic) or marked for accounting as maintenance (flags=maint).

2) Inspect cluster state (read-only checks to run)
- Inventory partitions/nodes and per-node availability:
  - sinfo (optionally sinfo -N -l) — find idle vs allocated nodes, per-partition context.
  - sinfo_reasons — list nodes already DRAIN/ DOWN and reasons.

- Check current and pending jobs that could overlap your window:
  - squeue (filter by partition or node) — show running and pending jobs and TIME limits.

Below are concise, safe steps and best practices for creating and using maintenance reservations while avoiding unintended state changes (cancels, drains, or job replacement). This is a prescriptive checklist you can follow — none of these steps change cluster state by themselves.

1) Plan the window and scope
- Decide exact nodes (or partitions), start time, and duration. Prefer reserving whole nodes for maintenance (simpler) rather than per-core reservations.
- Choose a reservation name that encodes purpose/date (e.g., maint-kernel-2026-05-10).

2) Inventory current state (read-only checks)
- Check node/partition availability: sinfo (or sinfo --Node) to list nodes and partitions.
- Check running and queued jobs on target nodes: squeue -w nodeX,nodeY (or squeue --nodes=...).
- Check existing reservations: scontrol show reservation (or scontrol_reservation_show).
- Use sacct if you need historical job/run patterns to pick low-impact times.

3) Create a reservation that does NOT force immediate disruption
- Create an advanced reservation scheduled in the future (StartTime=...) and set Duration=... so it only becomes active when you plan to maintain.
- Use Flags=MAINT to mark it as a maintenance reservation (good for accounting and planning).
- Critically: do NOT set Flags=REPLACE or Flags=IGNORE_JOBS unless you explicitly want running jobs to be replaced or ignored. Leaving those out ensures Slurm will not forcibly evict running allocations.
- Example form (adapt to your cluster’s time format and node list):
  scontrol create reservation ReservationName=maint-2026-05-10 StartTime=2026-05-10T01:00:00 Duration=120 Nodes=node[01-04] Flags=MAINT Description="kernel update"
  (This is an example—adjust fields to your environment.)

4) Use floating reservations if you want a sliding maintenance window without immediate node state changes
- TIME_FLOAT reservations can be used to create a floating maintenance window relative to now (they are treated differently in scheduling and prevent new long-running jobs).
- This is useful when you want the reservation to “float” but still block starts that would overlap the intended maintenance.

5) How reservations affect job starts (important safety behavior)
- When a reservation exists for a future period, Slurm will generally prevent new jobs from starting if they cannot complete before the reservation’s start time. This reduces the chance you’ll need to cancel running jobs.
- Creating a MAINT reservation does not, by itself, cancel or requeue currently running jobs unless you used IGNORE_JOBS or REPLACE.

6) Notify users and monitor as the window approaches
- Announce the planned maintenance window and affected nodes/users well in advance.
- Monitor squeue for jobs that will still be running as the start time approaches; follow local policy (wait, ask users to checkpoint, or cancel individual jobs).
- If you must remove running jobs, do so explicitly and with communication (scancel), do not rely on reservation flags that implicitly evict jobs unless you intended that behavior.

7) When ready to start maintenance (this is when you change state)
- If you need nodes pulled out of service immediately, change node state (for example, put nodes into DRAIN with a reason) and then stop or requeue running jobs as required. Note: these are explicit state changes and should be done only when ready.
- After maintenance, clear DRAIN and/or delete the reservation:

8) Clean up and accounting
- Remove the reservation when maintenance is complete (scontrol delete reservation=...).
- Confirm nodes returned to normal with sinfo and check for any blocked jobs.
- Document the maintenance (start/end times) — MAINT reservations are recorded in reports as PlannedDown.

- Delete reservation and clear drains after work is done.

References / notes
- MAINT reservations are intended for system maintenance and are reported as maintenance/planned down in accounting.
- Flags that will forcibly affect running jobs: IGNORE_JOBS (creates reservation even if jobs running), REPLACE (replace allocated nodes). Use these only with explicit intent.

results.prompt: Explain safe steps for maintenance reservations without changing state
results.agent_response:
Below are safe, non‑mutating steps (planning, validation, and examples) you can follow when preparing maintenance reservations. All examples are read‑only checks or command templates — do not run any scontrol create/drain commands unless you intend to change cluster state.

1) Inventory current cluster state and reservations
- Check node/partition availability and states (allocated/idle/drain/down):
  - sinfo  (or sinfo -Nel for per‑node rows)
  - sinfo_node --partition=<partition> --state=ALL
  What to look for: idle node counts in the partition you plan to use, nodes already DRAIN/MAINT/DOWN.
- List existing reservations (to avoid collisions):
  - scontrol_reservation_show
  What to look for: overlapping reservation names/times, partitions/nodes already reserved.

2) Identify jobs that would be affected
- See running and pending jobs (global or by partition/node/user):
  - squeue --states=RUNNING,PENDING --format="%.18i %.20P %.20j %.8u %.8T %.10M %.20R %.20N"
  - squeue --partition=<partition> or squeue --nodelist=<node>
  What to look for: running jobs on target nodes, pending jobs bound to a reservation or partition, pending reasons.
- For any specific running job you might impact, get details:
  - sstat --jobid=<jobid> (running job resource usage)
  - scontrol_show entity=job id=<jobid> (detailed job limits, start time, steps)
- Check historical job durations to pick a safe StartTime/Duration:
  - sacct --user=<user> --starttime=now-30days --format=JobID,JobName,Elapsed,MaxRSS
  What to look for: common job durations so you choose a StartTime that lets most running jobs finish.

3) Choose reservation parameters and flags (planning only)
- Required fields: ReservationName, StartTime (or StartTime=now / TIME_FLOAT), Duration or EndTime, Nodes/NodeCnt, and at least one access control (Users/Accounts/QOS/AllowedPartitions).
- Typical flags and their meaning (use in planning and in your command template):
  - Flags=MAINT  — marks the reservation as maintenance: nodes show in maint state during reservation; usage reporting shows PlannedDown.
  - Flags=IGNORE_JOBS — allows creating a reservation even if jobs are running (you will need to cancel them at start time if you want them gone).
  - Flags=REPLACE or REPLACE_DOWN — controls replacement behavior for down/drained/allocated nodes (careful: REPLACE can move reservations).
  - Flags=TIME_FLOAT — floating reservation that keeps a fixed period in the future (useful for a recurring window without occupying nodes now).
  - Flags=MAGNETIC — attracts matching jobs without them specifying the reservation.
- Access control: restrict who can use the reservation (Users=, Accounts=, QOS=) so production jobs are not unintentionally scheduled.

4) Validate conflict and impact (read-only checks)
- Verify if new reservation would overlap active reservations or nodes:
  - scontrol_reservation_show  (scan times and node lists)
- Find running jobs that will not complete before your planned StartTime:
  - Use squeue elapsed and the typical job walltime (from sacct) to estimate whether they will finish before StartTime.
  - If uncertain, inspect individual jobs with scontrol_show job id=<jobid>.
- If planning a full‑node maintenance, prefer a StartTime far enough in the future to allow currently running jobs to complete; otherwise plan to coordinate cancellation.

5) Communication & policies (non‑Slurm steps)
- Announce maintenance window and reservation name, start/end time, and affected partitions/nodes to all users well ahead of time.
- Provide instructions for users to checkpoint or stop jobs, and give a deadline.
- Offer a fallback contact and expected impact (job cancellations, delayed start).

6) Test on a small scope (recommended)
- Create a short test reservation on one or two nodes (off‑peak) to verify the behavior you expect (reservation visibility, how jobs are prevented from starting there).
  - Use the same Flags you plan to use for the real maintenance to validate effects.
- Review squeue and scontrol_reservation_show after the test to confirm semantics are as you expect.

7) Example command templates (do not run unless ready)
- Template for a planned maintenance reservation (creates the reservation):
  - scontrol create reservation ReservationName=<name> StartTime="YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS" Duration=<minutes> Nodes=<node-list> Users=<admin-user> Flags=MAINT
- If you want to allow the reservation to be created even if jobs are present (you will handle cancellations separately):
  - scontrol create reservation ReservationName=<name> StartTime=<time> Duration=<min> Nodes=<nodes> Users=<user> Flags=MAINT,IGNORE_JOBS
- Floating reservation template:
  - scontrol create reservation ReservationName=<name> StartTime=now+<offset> Duration=<min> NodeCnt=<n> Flags=TIME_FLOAT,MAINT

8) When you are ready to perform the maintenance (procedural sequence; changes cluster state)
- Recommended execution sequence (for the operator to run when ready):
  1. Create reservation with Flags=MAINT and the chosen StartTime/Duration.
  2. Monitor running jobs; at StartTime, either allow running jobs that can finish by EndTime to complete, or cancel them if you used IGNORE_JOBS.
  3. Optionally set nodes to DRAIN (scontrol update NodeName=<node> State=DRAIN Reason="maintenance") to prevent new starts while you work.
  4. Perform maintenance.
  5. Resume nodes (scontrol update NodeName=<node> State=RESUME) and remove/delete the reservation (scontrol delete reservation ReservationName=<name>).
- Note: creating a MAINT reservation itself will mark nodes in maintenance during the reservation window in reporting; draining is optional depending on your workflow.

9) Caveats and gotchas
- By default Slurm will not create a reservation that would evict running jobs unless you use IGNORE_JOBS or later force cancels — plan communications accordingly.
- Flags that replace allocated resources (REPLACE) can change which nodes are in the reservation; only use if you understand the replacement semantics.
- Magnetic reservations can attract jobs unexpectedly; prefer explicit access control for maintenance.
- TIME_FLOAT is useful for “floating” windows but does not itself put nodes in DRAIN — it prevents long jobs from being started.

If you want, I can:
- Run the read‑only checks for your planned node set/partition and a proposed StartTime (sinfo, squeue, scontrol_reservation_show, sacct) and report which running jobs would be impacted and whether idle nodes are available — or
- Produce the exact scontrol create reservation command line filled in from your inputs (ReservationName, Nodes or NodeCnt, StartTime/Duration, Users/Account, Flags) so an operator can run it when ready.

Which would you like me to do next?

results.prompt: Show existing Slurm triggers and explain their event types
results.agent_response:
I checked the cluster for active triggers: No active triggers.

Summary of trigger fields and event (TYPE) meanings (from the strigger documentation)

- Key trigger fields you’ll see
  - TRIG_ID — trigger identifier.
  - RES_TYPE — resource type: job or node.
  - RES_ID — resource identifier: job ID, hostnames, or "*" (any).
  - TYPE — event type that causes the trigger.
  - OFFSET — time offset in seconds (negative = run before the event).
  - USER — owner who created the trigger.
  - PROGRAM — script/program run when the trigger fires.

- Event TYPE values and what they mean
  - time (job only) — job has reached its time limit. Often used with a negative OFFSET to run a warning or graceful shutdown before the limit.
  - fini (job only) — job finished/terminated (completion event).
  - down (job or node) — resource moved into a DOWN state (node failure or resource down event).
  - up (job or node) — resource moved back UP (node recovered).
  - drained (node only) — node was placed into DRAIN state.
  - idle (node only) — node became idle (no jobs running).
  - reconfig (node only) — node underwent a reconfiguration (e.g., after scontrol reconfigure).

- Other notable strigger capabilities
  - There are extra event flags for controller/burst-buffer events (e.g., backup slurmctld assume/failure/resume, burst_buffer errors) that let you trigger on controller or burst-buffer conditions.
  - Triggers are checked periodically (about every 15 seconds); any events occurring within that interval are evaluated and the trigger program is executed once for events in that interval.
  - OFFSET lets you schedule before/after an event (negative OFFSET runs before the event when possible).

If you want, I can:
- Show the raw trigger list again or include the full strigger output (no change to cluster state).
- Create/update/clear triggers for you — if you request that, tell me the resource (job ID or node name(s)), event TYPE, OFFSET, and the program to execute. (Note: creating/updating/clearing triggers modifies cluster state; I will hand that request to the operator.)

results.prompt: Show existing Slurm triggers and explain their event types
results.agent_response:
I checked the cluster and there are no active Slurm triggers right now ("No active triggers.").

Summary of trigger event types and related fields (from the strigger docs)
- Where to list triggers: strigger --get (shows TRIG_ID, RES_TYPE, RES_ID, TYPE, OFFSET, USER, PROGRAM).
- When triggers are evaluated: Slurm checks trigger events on a periodic basis (≈ every 15 seconds). Any events in that interval are compared to configured triggers and the trigger PROGRAM is executed once for matching events.

Key fields you’ll see in strigger output
- TRIG_ID — trigger identifier.
- RES_TYPE — resource type: job or node.
- RES_ID — resource id: job ID, hostlist, or "*" (any).
- TYPE — trigger event type (see below).
- OFFSET — time offset in seconds (negative = before the event).
- USER — who set the trigger.
- PROGRAM — script/command Slurm runs when trigger fires.

Common TYPE values and what they mean
- time (job only)
  - Fires when a job reaches its time limit. OFFSET can schedule the PROGRAM to run before (negative) or after the event.
- fini (job only)
  - Fires when a job finishes/terminates (successful or otherwise).
- down (jobs or nodes)
  - Fires when the resource enters the DOWN state (node failure/unavailable or similar).
- up (jobs or nodes)
  - Fires when the resource leaves the DOWN state or becomes available again.
- drained (node only)
  - Fires when a node is put into DRAIN state.
- idle (node only)
  - Fires when a node becomes idle (no active allocations).
- reconfig (node only)
  - Fires when a node is reconfigured (e.g., after a reconfigure operation).

Other event options documented
- Controller-related events: e.g., backup_slurmctld_assumed_control, backup_slurmctld_failure, backup_slurmctld_resumed_operation, primary_slurmctld_failure — used to trigger on slurmctld failover/failure events.
- Burst buffer and other subsystem error events: there are options to trigger on burst-buffer errors and other subsystem conditions.

Examples (conceptual)
- Run /usr/local/bin/warn_job 5 minutes before job 12345 reaches its time limit:
  - set a job/time trigger with RES_ID=12345, TYPE=time, OFFSET=-300, PROGRAM=/usr/local/bin/warn_job
- Notify admins when any node goes down:
  - set a node/down trigger with RES_ID="*", TYPE=down, PROGRAM=/usr/sbin/slurm_admin_notify

If you want, I can:
- show the (currently empty) strigger --get output again, or
- help you create a trigger (tell me the target job/node, event type, offset, and program); note: creating a trigger changes cluster state so I will transfer this request to the operator for execution. Which would you like?

Results
- Live cluster triggers: No active triggers.

What strigger shows (fields)
- TRIG_ID: trigger identifier
- RES_TYPE: resource type (job or node)
- RES_ID: resource identifier (job ID, host name(s), or '*' for any)
- TYPE: event type (see below)
- OFFSET: time offset in seconds (negative = before the event)
- USER: who created the trigger
- PROGRAM: program/script run when the event fires

Common trigger event types and meanings
- time (job-only): a time-based event for a job (e.g., when a job reaches its time limit or an offset before the time limit).
- fini (job-only): job termination/finish event.
- down (job or node): a node or job has entered the DOWN state (node names or job id are passed to the program).
- up (job or node): a node or job has transitioned to UP.
- drained (node-only): node has been drained (administratively taken out of service).
- idle (node-only): node has become idle.
- reconfig (node-only): a node or controller reconfiguration event occurred.
- primary_slurmctld_failure / backup_slurmctld_failure / backup_slurmctld_assumed_control / backup_slurmctld_resumed_operation: controller failover/health events (trigger when primary/backup slurmctld fails, assumes control, or resumes).
- burst_buffer: burst-buffer related error events.

Behavior notes
- When a trigger event occurs, Slurm runs the configured PROGRAM and passes the relevant resource id(s) (hostlist or job id) as arguments.
- Triggers are checked periodically (defaults to roughly every 15 seconds). Events found during an interval are compared against configured triggers and the program is executed once for that interval.
- OFFSET lets you run the program before/after the event (negative values run before the event when possible).

If you want
- List triggers yourself: strigger --get
- Create or remove triggers: strigger --set / strigger --clear
- I can list triggers again, create a trigger, or remove one — which would you like to do?

results.agent_response:
Live cluster check: No active triggers.

Below is a concise explanation of strigger fields and the supported event (TYPE) values from the Slurm docs (strigger):

- What a trigger record contains (important fields)
  - TRIG_ID — trigger identifier.
  - RES_TYPE — resource type: job or node.
  - RES_ID — resource id: job ID, hostnames, or "*" for any host.
  - TYPE — trigger event type (see list below).
  - OFFSET — seconds offset; negative = run before the event (if applicable).
  - USER — user who set the trigger.
  - PROGRAM — program/script to execute when the trigger fires.

- How triggers are processed
  - Slurm checks trigger events periodically (≈ every 15 seconds). Any events in that interval are matched against configured triggers; each matching PROGRAM is executed once for the interval.

- Common TYPE values and what they mean (resource applicability in parentheses)
  - time (job) — a time event for a job (e.g., elapsed time reached). Often used to notify or act relative to job runtime.
  - fini (job) — job finished/terminated (job only).
  - down (node OR job) — node(s) have entered the DOWN state (or a job’s node went down); can notify admins or take recovery actions.
  - up (node OR job) — node(s) moved to UP (available) state.
  - drained (node) — node(s) were put into DRAIN state.
  - idle (node) — node(s) became IDLE (no allocations).
  - reconfig (node) — node(s) have been reconfigured (for example after a resume/maintenance).
  - controller events (cluster-wide) — e.g., primary_slurmctld_failure, backup_slurmctld_assumed_control, backup_slurmctld_failure, backup_slurmctld_resumed_operation; trigger on controller role/failure changes.
  - burst_buffer (cluster/resource) — burst buffer error events.
  - (Docs list additional specific options; use strigger --help or the strigger manpage for the full option list.)

- Set a trigger (e.g., run /path/to/script 300s before a job’s time limit) — if you want to create/change triggers I will hand this off to the operator. Which action would you like?

results.prompt: Show existing Slurm triggers and explain their event types
results.agent_response:
Result: No active triggers found.

Explanation — trigger fields you’ll see when triggers exist
- TRIG_ID: trigger identifier.
- RES_TYPE: resource type the trigger watches — "job" or "node".
- RES_ID: resource identifier (job ID, hostlist, or "*" for any).
- TYPE: event type that fires the trigger (see list below).
- OFFSET: time offset in seconds (negative = before the event).
- USER: user who created the trigger.
- PROGRAM: program/script Slurm runs when the trigger fires.

Common TYPE values and meaning
- time (job only)
  - Fires relative to a job's time limit. Use OFFSET to run a program before/after the limit (e.g., notify or checkpoint).
- fini (job only)
  - Fires when a job finishes/terminates.
- up (job or node)
  - Fires when a node or job becomes UP/available (node returns to service, or job state moves to RUNNING as applicable).
- down (job or node)
  - Fires when a node or job goes DOWN/unavailable (node failure or job abort).
- drained (node only)
  - Fires when a node enters the DRAIN or DRAINING state.
- idle (node only)
  - Fires when a node becomes IDLE (no allocations).
- reconfig (node only)
  - Fires when a node is reconfigured (scontrol reconfigure or similar).

Behavior notes
- Triggers execute the specified PROGRAM; Slurm passes a resource identifier (e.g., node list or job ID) as an argument to the program.
- Triggers are checked periodically (≈ every 15 seconds), so events are batched within that interval.
- OFFSET may be negative to run actions before the event when possible.

How to inspect and manage triggers
- List current triggers: strigger --get
- Add a trigger: strigger --set ... --program=/path/to/script

results.prompt: Explain node power state and power-save actions available in Slurm
results.agent_response:
Here's a concise summary of Slurm's node power states and the power‑save actions you can use.

What power saving is
- Slurm can suspend (power‑save) and resume nodes automatically or on demand. Suspend/Resume are implemented by user‑supplied programs configured in slurm.conf (SuspendProgram and ResumeProgram) that actually perform the host power actions (cloud API calls, IPMI, etc.). Those programs run as SlurmUser on the controller and should be fault tolerant and able to verify the node came back up.

Node power-related states (common names and sinfo symbols)
- POWER_DOWN (!) — node marked to be powered down (request issued). When it becomes free of running jobs, SuspendProgram is run.
- POWERING_DOWN (%) — node is in the process of powering down (not available for scheduling for SuspendTimeout).
- POWERED_DOWN (~) — node is powered down / in power‑save mode.
- POWER_UP — node marked to be powered up (request issued); ResumeProgram will be run when possible.
- POWERING_UP — node is in the process of powering up.

Manual power actions (scontrol update nodename= state=power_*)
- POWER_DOWN
  - Request the node be placed into power‑save mode via the configured SuspendProgram. If jobs are running, the node will wait until they finish (it only sets the power request).
- POWER_DOWN_ASAP
  - Drain the node and mark it for power down: running jobs are allowed to finish; no further allocations will be made to it.
- POWER_DOWN_FORCE
  - Force the node into power down (intended for more aggressive shutdown). (Admin/operator privilege required; use with care because it will override normal allocation behavior.)
- POWER_UP
  - Request the node be powered up (ResumeProgram will be run). Slurm will attempt to bring the node online so it becomes available for scheduling.

(Documentation shows the POWER_DOWN_* family and POWER_UP lifecycle states; exact availability of additional variants can depend on Slurm version and build.)

Automatic power‑save controls (slurm.conf / partition settings)
- SuspendTime (partition) — how long an idle node must remain idle before Slurm attempts to suspend it.
- SuspendTimeout — how long a node is unavailable while a suspend is in progress.
- ResumeTimeout — how long the controller waits for a node to re‑register after resume before marking it DOWN and requeueing allocated jobs.
- SuspendRate / ResumeRate — throttle how many nodes may be suspended/resumed per interval.
- PowerDownOnIdle (partition) — if YES, nodes in that partition may be requested to power down after being allocated at least one job (behavior described in docs).
- SuspendExcNodes / SuspendExcParts / SuspendExcStates — exceptions to automated suspend behavior (nodes, partitions, or states excluded).

Behavioral notes and gotchas
- Suspend/Resume are handled by external programs (SuspendProgram and ResumeProgram). Those programs must be able to power hosts and, for cloud nodes, boot instances and start slurmd so the node re‑registers.
- While powering down or up, nodes are not available for allocation for the configured SuspendTimeout/ResumeTimeout windows. If a node fails to re-register within ResumeTimeout it can be marked DOWN and any jobs requeued.
- Features and node "active" features: when a node is powered down nodes may have features available but not active; when allocated Slurm will ensure features are activated (useful for cloud images / on‑demand nodes).
- Authorization: changing node state is an administrative action; scontrol node updates require appropriate privileges (operator/administrator).
- Use sinfo and scontrol show node to inspect current node power state and detailed node fields.

Quick example syntax (from the docs)
- scontrol update NodeName=node001 state=POWER_DOWN
- scontrol update NodeName=node001 state=POWER_DOWN_ASAP
- scontrol update NodeName=node001 state=POWER_UP

(These are the documented scontrol update forms for requesting power actions. Actual behavior depends on your slurm.conf power plugin and the configured SuspendProgram/ResumeProgram.)

Slurm provides an integrated mechanism for nodes being suspended (powered
down, placed into power saving mode) and resumed (powered up, restored from

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.

## AUTHORIZATION[#SECTION_AUTHORIZATION](https://slurm.schedmd.com/scontrol.html)
Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.
Note that configuring AdminLevels or Coordinators requires the use of SlurmDBD.
The authorization levels required to execute various commands are defined in the
following table.
scontrol update job: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol requeue: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol update step: Privileged or Effective Owner
scontrol suspend: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol resume: Privileged or Coordinator
scontrol notify: Root, SlurmUser, or direct owner
scontrol write batch_script: Privileged or direct...

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
Slurm provides an integrated mechanism for nodes being suspended (powered
down, placed into power saving mode) and resumed (powered up, restored from
power saving mode) on demand or by request. Nodes that remain IDLE for
SuspendTime will be suspended by SuspendProgram and will be
unavailable for scheduling for SuspendTimeout . Nodes will
automatically be resumed by ResumeProgram to complete work allocated
to them. Nodes that fail to register within ResumeTimeout will become
DOWN and their allocated jobs are requeued. Node power saving can be
manually requested by `scontrol update nodename= state=power_ `. The rate of nodes being resumed or
suspended can be controlled by ResumeRate and SuspendRate .

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"

Coordinators of the corresponding account.

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the

## Resume and Suspend Programs[#resume_suspend](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
The ResumeProgram and SuspendProgram execute as
SlurmUser on the node where the slurmctld daemon runs (primary
and backup server nodes). Use of sudo may be required for
SlurmUser to power down and restart nodes. If you need to convert
Slurm's hostlist expression into individual node names, the `scontrol show hostnames` command may prove useful. The commands used to boot or
shut down nodes will depend upon your cluster management tools.
The ResumeProgram and SuspendProgram are not subject to any
time limits but must have [Fault Tolerance](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html). They
should perform the required action, ideally verify the action (e.g. node boot
and start the slurmd daemon, thus the node is no longer non-responsive
to slurmctld ) and terminate. Long running programs will be logged by

If you want ResumeProgram to boot various images according to job
specifications, it will need to be a fairly sophisticated program and perform
the following actions:

- Determine which image is required for each job. Images can be mapped with [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html).
- Boot the appropriate image for each node.

results.prompt: Explain node power state and power-save actions available in Slurm
results.agent_response:
Below is a concise summary of the node power states Slurm supports and the power‑save actions you can request (manual + automated), with the important semantics and administration notes.

1) How to request a manual power action
- Use scontrol to set a "power_" state on one or more nodes:
  scontrol update NodeName=<nodelist> state=POWER_<ACTION>
  (e.g. state=POWER_DOWN or state=POWER_UP)

2) Manual power actions (common POWER_ actions)
- POWER_DOWN
  - Request that the node enter power‑saving mode by running the configured SuspendProgram.
  - If the node is already in the process of powering down, the state change will be recorded but will not take further effect until SuspendTimeout or the current shutdown completes.
  - Intended for a graceful suspend via the suspend script.

- POWER_DOWN_ASAP
  - Drain the node and mark it for power down once current running jobs complete; no new jobs will be allocated to it.
  - Use when you want graceful completion of current work before suspending.

- POWER_DOWN_FORCE
  - Request an immediate power‑down transition. This is the “force” path — it marks the node for power down without waiting for normal idle/drain behavior.
  - Because this can interrupt normal node lifecycle, running jobs may be affected according to your Suspend/Resume configuration (they can end up requeued or fail if the node does not come back as expected). Use only for urgent cases.

- POWER_UP
  - Request the node be brought out of power saving (ResumeProgram will be executed when feasible).

(Implementations may expose additional site-specific variants; the above are the standard documented actions.)

3) Node lifecycle states you’ll see in sinfo / node listings
- POWER_DOWN — a power‑down request is recorded (symbolized in sinfo).
- POWERING_DOWN — the node is in the process of powering down and will be unavailable for scheduling for SuspendTimeout.
- POWERED_DOWN — node is powered down / in power‑saving mode.
- POWERING_UP — node is being resumed.
- POWER_UP — a power‑up request is recorded.

Symbols and exact text appear in sinfo output when PowerSave is enabled.

4) Automated power‑save components and important config knobs
- SuspendProgram: script/program slurmctld runs to suspend (power down) nodes.
- ResumeProgram: script/program slurmctld runs to boot / resume nodes.
  - These execute as SlurmUser on the controller host; sudo/root access may be required to actually power/boot nodes.
- SuspendTime: how long a node must be idle before Slurm automatically triggers SuspendProgram.
- SuspendTimeout: how long a node is considered unavailable while suspend/boot is happening (nodes are not schedulable for this time).
- ResumeTimeout: how long slurmctld waits for a node to re-register after a resume; if it fails to register the node may be set DOWN and jobs requeued.
- ResumeRate / SuspendRate: control how quickly nodes are resumed or suspended (throttling).
- PowerDownOnIdle (partition-level): when YES, nodes allocated from that partition may be requested to power down after they finish jobs (common for cloud/elastic partitions).
- SuspendExcNodes / SuspendExcParts / SuspendExcStates: configuration lists used to exclude specific nodes/partitions/states from automatic suspends.
- ResumeFailProgram / SuspendFailProgram: optional scripts to run on failure cases.

5) Scheduling & job effects
- POWER_DOWN_ASAP drains (no new allocations); running jobs finish normally.
- POWER_DOWN_FORCE / abrupt powering down can cause allocations to be interrupted; behavior for the affected jobs depends on your cluster configuration (jobs may be requeued, fail, or be treated per preemption/requeue policies). Nodes that fail to re-register within ResumeTimeout are set DOWN and allocations are requeued.
- Cloud / on‑demand nodes often use PowerSave automation to add/remove instances; features tied to nodes may be inactive while the node is powered down and re-activated on resume.

6) Operational recommendations
- Prefer POWER_DOWN_ASAP for graceful maintenance/suspend; use FORCE only for urgent/exception cases.
- Test SuspendProgram/ResumeProgram thoroughly (they run without Slurm job time limits and must be fault tolerant).
- Tune SuspendTime, SuspendTimeout, ResumeTimeout, and ResumeRate/SuspendRate to match your environment and boot/shutdown behaviour.
- Use DebugFlags=Power or logging to track power operations while testing.
- Use SuspendExc* to protect important nodes/partitions from automatic suspends.

If you want, I can:
- show the exact scontrol examples you’d run for a node name you give, or
- show where each of the configuration parameters above lives in slurm.conf (references from the Slurm Power Saving guide).

Slurm provides an integrated mechanism for nodes being suspended (powered
down, placed into power saving mode) and resumed (powered up, restored from
power saving mode) on demand or by request. Nodes that remain IDLE for
SuspendTime will be suspended by SuspendProgram and will be
unavailable for scheduling for SuspendTimeout . Nodes will
automatically be resumed by ResumeProgram to complete work allocated

manually requested by `scontrol update nodename= state=power_ `. The rate of nodes being resumed or

Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and

active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the

## Initial Testing [#initial_testing](https://slurm.schedmd.com/namespace.html)
An easy way to verify that the container is working is to run a job and
ensure that the /tmp directory is empty (since it normally has some other
files) and that "." is owned by the user that submitted the job.
```text
tim@slurm-ctld:~$ srun ls -al /tmp total 8 drwx------ 2 tim root 4096 Feb 10 17:14 . drwxr-xr-x 21 root root 4096 Nov 15 08:46 ..
```
While a job is running, root should be able to confirm that
`/$BasePath/$JobID/_tmp` exists and is empty. This directory is bind
mounted into the job. `/$BasePath/$JobID` should be owned by root,
and is not intended to be accessible to the user.
Additionally, when the Linux plugin is in use, you can confirm that a
PID namespace is in effect by running a job and running "ps". The only visible
PIDs should be related to the job and PID 1 will be named slurmstepd:
[${job_id}.namespace] .

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"
- Privileged Users include all Administrators and any users with
"AdminLevel=Operator"
- Effective Owners of a job or step include the direct owner and all
Coordinators of the corresponding account.

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
Slurm provides an integrated mechanism for nodes being suspended (powered
down, placed into power saving mode) and resumed (powered up, restored from
power saving mode) on demand or by request. Nodes that remain IDLE for
SuspendTime will be suspended by SuspendProgram and will be
unavailable for scheduling for SuspendTimeout . Nodes will
automatically be resumed by ResumeProgram to complete work allocated
to them. Nodes that fail to register within ResumeTimeout will become
DOWN and their allocated jobs are requeued. Node power saving can be
manually requested by `scontrol update nodename= state=power_ `. The rate of nodes being resumed or
suspended can be controlled by ResumeRate and SuspendRate .

Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the

The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a

The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and
memory in the future.
This typically requires the backfill scheduler be able to allocate each
component of a heterogeneous job on a different node in order to begin its

allocated resources on the same node.
In a federation of clusters, a heterogeneous job will execute entirely on
the cluster from which the job is submitted. The heterogeneous job will not
be eligible to migrate between clusters or to have different components of

## Preemption Design and Operation [#operation](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html)
The SelectType plugin will identify resources where a pending job can
begin execution. When PreemptMode is configured to CANCEL ,
SUSPEND or REQUEUE , the select plugin will also preempt running
jobs as needed to initiate the pending job. When
PreemptMode=SUSPEND,GANG the select plugin will initiate the pending
job and rely upon the gang scheduling logic to perform job suspend and resume,
as described below.
The select plugin is passed an ordered list of preemptable jobs to consider for
each pending job which is a candidate to start.
This list is sorted by either:
- QOS priority,
- Partition priority and job size (to favor preempting smaller jobs), or
- Job start time (with PreemptParameters=youngest_first ).

options allow you to set the corresponding attributes or filter on them
when querying for a QOS.
NOTE : The group limits (GrpJobs, GrpTRES, etc.) are tested when a job is

The SelectType plugin will identify resources where a pending job can
begin execution. When PreemptMode is configured to CANCEL ,
SUSPEND or REQUEUE , the select plugin will also preempt running

The backfill scheduler has limitations in how it tracks usage of CPUs and

# Gang Scheduling
Slurm supports timesliced gang scheduling in which two or more jobs are
allocated to the same resources in the same partition and these jobs are
alternately suspended to let one job at a time have dedicated access to the
resources for a configured period of time.
Slurm also supports preemptive job scheduling that allows a job in a
higher PriorityTier partition, or in a preempting QOS, to preempt other
jobs. [Preemption](https://slurm.schedmd.com/preempt.html) is related to Gang scheduling
because SUSPEND is one of the PreemptionMode s, and it uses the Gang
scheduler to resume suspended jobs.
A workload manager that supports timeslicing can improve responsiveness
and utilization by allowing more jobs to begin running sooner.
Shorter-running jobs no longer have to wait in a queue behind longer-running
jobs.
Instead they can be run "in parallel" with the longer-running jobs, which will
allow them to start and finish quick...

## Cloud Accounting[#accounting](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
Information about cloud instances can be stored in the database. This can
be done by configuring instance id/type upon slurmd startup or with
scontrol update . The node's "extra" field will also be stored in the
database.
Configuring cloud information on slurmd startup:
```text
$ slurmd --instance-id=12345 --instance-type=m7g.medium --extra="arbitrary string" . . .
```
Configuring cloud information with scontrol update:
```text
$ scontrol update nodename=n1 instanceid=12345 instancetype=m7g.medium extra="arbitrary string"
```
This data can then be seen on the controller with scontrol show
node . Past and current data can be seen in the database with sacctmgr
show instance , as well as through slurmrestd with the /instance

results.prompt: Explain node power state and power-save actions available in Slurm
results.agent_response:
Here’s a concise summary of Slurm’s node power states and the power‑save actions you can request or configure. This is drawn from the Slurm Power Saving guide (ResumeProgram/SuspendProgram, SuspendTime, ResumeTimeout, etc.).

Overview
- Slurm can suspend (power‑save) and resume nodes automatically or by admin request. Suspend/Resume actions are performed by the cluster’s configured SuspendProgram and ResumeProgram (run as SlurmUser on the controller).
- Nodes in power save are unavailable for scheduling until resumed. Slurm tracks additional power states and provides commands to request power actions.

Node power states (what you will see and what they mean)
- POWER_DOWN: a power‑down request. When the node no longer runs jobs, Slurm will run SuspendProgram to place the node into power saving mode.
- POWER_DOWN_ASAP (also shown as down_asap): drain + mark for power down — running jobs are allowed to finish, no new allocations are made to the node; when idle it will be suspended.
- POWER_DOWN_FORCE (down_force): force power down immediately — Slurm will cancel all jobs on that node, power it down, and reset its state to IDLE (after the action).
- POWERING_DOWN: node is in the process of being suspended/powered down; it will not accept jobs for the configured SuspendTimeout.
- POWERED_DOWN: node is suspended or powered off (in power‑save mode) and is not available until resumed.
- POWER_UP: a request to explicitly bring a node out of power‑save mode; causes ResumeProgram to run when possible.
- POWERING_UP: node is being restored; not yet fully available until ResumeTimeout and slurmd registration succeed.

Manual power actions (scontrol)
- You can request power actions with scontrol update. Example forms:
  - scontrol update nodename=<node> state=power_down
  - scontrol update nodename=<node> state=power_down_asap
  - scontrol update nodename=<node> state=power_down_force
  - scontrol update nodename=<node> state=power_up
- The literal state token used is state=power_<down|down_asap|down_force|up>.

Automatic power‑save configuration (key parameters)
- SuspendProgram / ResumeProgram — scripts or programs that actually perform the shutdown/boot actions (run as SlurmUser on the controller).
- SuspendTime — idle time before a node becomes eligible for automatic suspend.
- SuspendTimeout / ResumeTimeout — maximum time allowed for suspend or resume to complete before Slurm treats the attempt as failed (nodes that fail to resume become DOWN and any jobs are requeued).
- SuspendRate / ResumeRate — limits on how many nodes Slurm will suspend or resume per minute.
- PowerDownOnIdle (partition option) — if YES, nodes allocated once from that partition can be requested to power down after they become IDLE (useful for partitions that should power down after use).
- SuspendExcNodes, SuspendExcParts, SuspendExcStates — exclusions for which nodes/partitions/states are not subject to automatic suspend.

Effects on jobs and failure handling
- POWER_DOWN_ASAP: running jobs finish; node is drained for future allocations.
- POWER_DOWN_FORCE: cancels running jobs on the node (jobs are terminated or requeued depending on configuration).
- If ResumeProgram is invoked and a node does not register within ResumeTimeout, Slurm marks the node DOWN and requeues jobs that required it.
- ResumeFailProgram can be configured to run when resumes fail.
- SLURM_RESUME_FILE (JSON) is provided to ResumeProgram so it can see which jobs/nodes/allocations triggered the resume and take appropriate actions (boot images, etc.).

Sinfo/scontrol visibility and symbols
- sinfo will show power‑state symbols for nodes (POWER_DOWN: !, POWERING_DOWN: %, POWERED_DOWN: ~, POWERING_UP: #).
- scontrol show node and scontrol show config include fields related to last boot time, SuspendTime, etc.

Practical notes / best practices
- SuspendProgram/ResumeProgram must be reliable and fault‑tolerant; they run without Slurm time limits and should verify node availability (slurmd registration).
- Use SuspendRate/ResumeRate to avoid sudden large power changes.
- Use SuspendExcNodes/Parts to protect critical nodes from being suspended.
- Test Resume/Suspend scripts carefully (and test behavior of ResumeTimeout and failure handling) before enabling automatic power saving widely.
- When you need to force immediate administrative change, use power_down_force with care: it will terminate jobs.

If you want, I can:
- show the cluster’s current power‑relevant configuration (SuspendTime, SuspendTimeout, SuspendRate, ResumeProgram, etc.) by reading the controller config (scontrol show config) and partition settings, or
- show the current nodes in power states via sinfo.  

Which would you like me to fetch? (This is read‑only; I will run the appropriate Slurm read tool.)

Slurm provides an integrated mechanism for nodes being suspended (powered
down, placed into power saving mode) and resumed (powered up, restored from
power saving mode) on demand or by request. Nodes that remain IDLE for
SuspendTime will be suspended by SuspendProgram and will be
unavailable for scheduling for SuspendTimeout . Nodes will
automatically be resumed by ResumeProgram to complete work allocated
to them. Nodes that fail to register within ResumeTimeout will become

manually requested by `scontrol update nodename= state=power_ `. The rate of nodes being resumed or

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features
become available but not active. Any feature not defined by
NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.

## Initial Testing [#INITIAL_TESTING](https://slurm.schedmd.com/nss_slurm.html)
Before enabling NSS Slurm directly on the node, you should use the
-s slurm option to getent within a newly launched job step
to verify that the rest of the setup has been completed successfully. The
-s option to getent allows it to query a specific database —
even if it has not been enabled by default through the system's
nsswitch.conf . Note that nss_slurm only responds to requests from
processes within the job step itself — you must launch the getent
command within a job step to see any data returned.
As an example of a successful query:
```text
tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm passwd tim:x:1000:1000:Tim Wickberg:/home/tim:/bin/bash tim@blackhole:~$ srun getent -s slurm group tim:x:1000:tim projecta:x:1001:tim
```

the sequence in which the NSS databases will be queried, and this ensures Slurm
handles the request if able before submitting the query to other sources.

## Resume and Suspend Programs[#resume_suspend](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
The ResumeProgram and SuspendProgram execute as
SlurmUser on the node where the slurmctld daemon runs (primary
and backup server nodes). Use of sudo may be required for
SlurmUser to power down and restart nodes. If you need to convert
Slurm's hostlist expression into individual node names, the `scontrol show hostnames` command may prove useful. The commands used to boot or
shut down nodes will depend upon your cluster management tools.
The ResumeProgram and SuspendProgram are not subject to any
time limits but must have [Fault Tolerance](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html). They
should perform the required action, ideally verify the action (e.g. node boot
and start the slurmd daemon, thus the node is no longer non-responsive
to slurmctld ) and terminate. Long running programs will be logged by

## Overview[#overview](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
Slurm provides an integrated mechanism for nodes being suspended (powered
down, placed into power saving mode) and resumed (powered up, restored from
power saving mode) on demand or by request. Nodes that remain IDLE for
SuspendTime will be suspended by SuspendProgram and will be
unavailable for scheduling for SuspendTimeout . Nodes will
automatically be resumed by ResumeProgram to complete work allocated
to them. Nodes that fail to register within ResumeTimeout will become
DOWN and their allocated jobs are requeued. Node power saving can be
manually requested by `scontrol update nodename= state=power_ `. The rate of nodes being resumed or
suspended can be controlled by ResumeRate and SuspendRate .

## Booting Different Images[#images](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
If you want ResumeProgram to boot various images according to job
specifications, it will need to be a fairly sophisticated program and perform
the following actions:
- Determine which jobs are associated with the nodes to be booted. SLURM_RESUME_FILE will help with this step.
- Determine which image is required for each job. Images can be mapped with [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html).
- Boot the appropriate image for each node.

## System Administrator Information [#sys_admin](https://slurm.schedmd.com/heterogeneous_jobs.html)
The job submit plugin is invoked independently for each component of a
heterogeneous job.
The spank_init_post_opt() function is invoked once for each component of a
heterogeneous job. This permits site defined options on a per job component
basis.
Scheduling of heterogeneous jobs is performed only by the sched/backfill
plugin and all heterogeneous job components are either all scheduled at the same
time or deferred. The pending reason of heterogeneous jobs isn't set until
backfill evaluation.
In order to ensure the timely initiation of both heterogeneous and
non-heterogeneous jobs, the backfill scheduler alternates between two different

Slurm generally classifies users into three authorization levels:
- Administrators include root, SlurmUser, and any users with
"AdminLevel=Administrator"

## Node Features[#nodefeatures](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
Features defined by [NodeFeaturesPlugins](https://slurm.schedmd.com/slurm.conf.html), and
associated to cloud nodes in the slurm.conf , will be available but not
active when the node is powered down. If a job requests available but not
active features, the controller will allocate nodes that are powered down and
have the features as available. At allocation, the features will be made
active. A cloud node will remain with the active features until the node is
powered down (i.e. the node can't be rebooted to get other features until the
node is powered down). When the node is powered down, the those features

NodeFeaturesPlugins are always active.

## Fault Tolerance[#tolerance](https://slurm.schedmd.com/power_save.html)
If the slurmctld daemon is terminated gracefully, it will wait up
to ten seconds (or the maximum of SuspendTimeout or
ResumeTimeout if less than ten seconds) for any spawned
SuspendProgram or ResumeProgram to terminate before the daemon
terminates. If the spawned program does not terminate within that time
period, the event will be logged and slurmctld will exit in order to
permit another slurmctld daemon to be initiated. Any spawned
SuspendProgram or ResumeProgram will continue to run.
When the slurmctld daemon shuts down, any SLURM_RESUME_FILE
temporary files are no longer available, even once slurmctld restarts.
Therefore, ResumeProgram should use SLURM_RESUME_FILE within
ten seconds of starting to guarantee that it still exists.
